Conclusion: Current LLMs exhibit significant limitations in comprehensive multi-granularity event analysis. MiGUE-Bench provides a robust evaluation framework and actionable insights to guide future research toward more capable event-centric reasoning systems.

Abstract: Event analysis is an essential and fundamental direction of information extraction, involving various event-centric tasks at different granularity of documents. While large language models (LLMs) have preliminarily achieved promising performance in part of these tasks individually, their capability in event analysis still lacks comprehensive understanding due to restricted document granularity, task designs, and data source of existing benchmarks. To address these limitations, we introduce MiGUE-Bench, a systematic benchmark for assessing the performance of LLMs in multi-granularity event analysis. To support large-scale evaluation, we first develop an LLM-driven self-correcting annotation framework called MiGUE-Pipeline, enabling scalable acquisition of high-quality source data of events with automatic labels. Then, we design four core tasks in our benchmark, i.e., event detection, relation reasoning, structure induction, and future prediction, to probe model competence at different levels, from atomic event details to complex cross-document narratives. Extensive experiments on state-of-the-art LLMs and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods delineate the current capability boundary and identify critical deficiencies, providing insights into the future improvement of LLMs in challenging event analysis tasks.

</details>


### [23] [AskChem: Claim-Centered Infrastructure for Chemistry Literature Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28618)
*Bing Yan,Gregory Wolfe,Stefano Martiniani,Kyunghyun Cho*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: AskChem is a claim-centered infrastructure for chemistry literature search that converts papers into atomic, provenance-carrying claims (grounded by DOI and verbatim quotes), providing faceted taxonomy, evidence graphs, and a living taxonomy over 2.4M claims from 147K papers, achieving 100% resolvable DOI grounding with GPT-5.5 on AskChem-Bench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing chemistry literature-search systems return ranked document lists, forcing scientists and AI agents to manually locate, verify provenance, and assemble cross-paper answers. This is inefficient for synthesizing findings scattered across many publications.

Method: AskChem changes the unit of retrieval from papers to provenance-carrying claims. Each paper is decomposed into atomic, typed claims, each grounded by a source DOI and a verbatim quote or explicit evidence locator. Three complementary structures are built over the shared claim store: (1) a stabilized faceted taxonomy for hierarchical retrieval and browsing, (2) an evidence graph linking claims through relations, and (3) an exploratory living taxonomy situating indexed papers under scientific principles. The system currently indexes 2.4M claims from 147K papers and provides web interface, REST, SDK, and MCP access for AI agents.

Result: On AskChem-Bench, grounding a GPT-5.5 reader in AskChem yields 100% resolvable DOIs, compared with 88.3% without retrieval, and achieves the highest citation density among five tested systems.

Conclusion: AskChem demonstrates that claim-level indexing with provenance grounding substantially improves the verifiability and density of literature synthesis outputs, offering a more effective infrastructure for both human scientists and AI agents conducting cross-paper chemistry search.

Abstract: Chemistry literature synthesis often requires assembling specific findings scattered across many publications, yet existing literature-search systems primarily return ranked document lists. As a result, scientists and AI agents need to locate relevant information, verify their provenance, and assemble cross-paper answers manually. We present AskChem, a claim-centered infrastructure for cross-paper chemistry search. AskChem changes the unit of retrieval from the paper to the provenance-carrying claim: each paper is converted into atomic, typed claims, each grounded by a source DOI and a verbatim quote or an explicit evidence locator. Over this shared claim store, AskChem exposes complementary structures for search and synthesis: a stabilized faceted taxonomy for hierarchical retrieval and browsing, an evidence graph linking claims through relations, and an exploratory living taxonomy that situates indexed papers under scientific principles. AskChem currently indexes 2.4M claims from 147K papers and provides a web interface, as well as REST, SDK, and MCP access for AI agents. On AskChem-Bench, grounding a GPT-5.5 reader in AskChem yields 100% resolvable DOIs, compared with 88.3% without retrieval, and the highest citation density among five tested systems. AskChem is live at https://askchem.org.

</details>


### [24] [ICLE++: Modeling Fine-Grained Traits for Holistic Essay Scoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27671)
*Shengjie Li,Vincent Ng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces ICLE++, a new annotated corpus of persuasive student essays with both holistic and trait-specific scores, designed to address the over-reliance on the ASAP corpus in automated essay scoring (AES) research by enabling tests of model generalizability, multi-trait scoring, and cross-prompt scoring.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AES models are predominantly evaluated on the ASAP corpus, which has limitations. It remains unclear whether models trained on ASAP generalize to other corpora. There is also a lack of annotated corpora supporting newer AES tasks like multi-trait scoring and cross-prompt scoring.

Method: The paper describes a corpus construction effort: the authors annotated persuasive student essays from the existing ICLE (International Corpus of Learner English) corpus with both holistic scores and trait-specific scores, resulting in the ICLE++ corpus.

Result: ICLE++ is introduced as a new annotated resource. It enables evaluation of AES model generalizability beyond ASAP, and supports emerging tasks such as multi-trait scoring and cross-prompt scoring.

Conclusion: ICLE++ represents a significant long-term annotation effort and contributes a much-needed annotated corpus to the AES research community, helping to mitigate the field's over-dependence on the ASAP corpus.

Abstract: The majority of the recently-developed models for automated essay scoring (AES) are evaluated solely on the ASAP corpus. However, ASAP is not without its limitations. For instance, it is not clear whether models trained on ASAP can generalize well when evaluated on other corpora. In light of these limitations, we introduce ICLE++, a corpus of persuasive student essays annotated with both holistic scores and trait-specific scores. Not only can ICLE++ be used to test the generalizability of AES models trained on ASAP, but it can also facilitate the evaluation of models developed for newer AES problems such as multi-trait scoring and cross-prompt scoring. We believe that ICLE++, which represents a culmination of our long-term effort in annotating the essays in the ICLE corpus, contributes to the set of much-needed annotated corpora for AES research.

</details>


### [25] [Recall Before You Rank: Similarity-Guided Top-$K$ Reuse for Efficient Long-Context Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27692)
*Wenshuai Yao,Wenyong Zhou,Hanyong Shao,Yizhe Chen,Zhiyuan Ning,Yuannuo Feng,Ru Huang,Kechao Tang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ReTopK accelerates dynamic Top-K sparse attention for long-context decoding by reusing historical query-support pairs. It maintains a cache of past queries and their selected KV indices, retrieves similar cached queries for each new query, unions their supports with a recent window, and reranks only this compact candidate set. This training-free method achieves near-Exact Top-K quality with 3.07× speedup at 128K context length.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Top-K sparse attention reduces Softmax and aggregation costs by selecting only K KV entries, but the selector itself remains linear in context length—requiring scoring against the full KV cache and global Top-K selection. This selector bottleneck limits the practical efficiency of sparse attention for long-context decoding, motivating a method that decouples candidate identification from full-cache scoring.

Method: ReTopK is a training-free method with four components: (1) per-head bounded cache of historical query–support (selected index) pairs; (2) for each new query, retrieve the most similar cached queries, union their stored supports with a recent window to form a compact candidate set; (3) rerank only this candidate set using exact current-query scores; (4) a similarity-based fallback that invokes full Exact Top-K when reuse confidence is low, plus periodic exact refreshes to limit cache drift. Only selected indices are reused—not historical scores, weights, or outputs.

Result: Across 16K–128K contexts, ReTopK achieved the lowest PG19 perplexity and highest NIAH and LongBench scores among evaluated approximate methods. At 128K with K=512, perplexity increased only 0.50% over Exact Top-K while accelerating attention computation by 3.07×.

Conclusion: ReTopK demonstrates that reusing historical retrieval decisions via query-similarity matching can effectively decouple Top-K selection from full-cache scoring, yielding near-exact attention quality with substantial speedups for long-context decoding.

Abstract: Top-$K$ sparse attention reduces the cost of Softmax and value aggregation by attending to only a small subset of key--value (KV) entries. However, identifying this subset still requires scoring the current query against the full KV cache and performing global Top-$K$ selection, leaving selector cost linear in context length and limiting the practical efficiency of sparse attention for long-context decoding. In this paper, we introduce ReTopK, a training-free method that accelerates dynamic Top-$K$ attention by reusing historical retrieval decisions. ReTopK builds on the observation that similar queries often attend to overlapping supports and that partially overlapping supports can still preserve most of the Exact Top-$K$ attention mass. For each attention head, it maintains a bounded cache of historical query--support pairs, retrieves the most similar cached queries for each new query, unions their stored supports with a recent window, and reranks only the resulting compact candidate set using exact current-query scores. A similarity-based fallback invokes full-history Exact Top-$K$ when reuse is unreliable, while periodic exact refreshes limit cache drift. ReTopK retains the complete KV cache and reuses only selected indices, rather than historical scores, attention weights, or outputs. Across 16K--128K contexts, ReTopK achieves the lowest PG19 perplexity and the highest NIAH and LongBench scores among the evaluated approximate methods. At 128K with $K=512$, ReTopK incurs only a 0.50\% perplexity increase over Exact Top-$K$ while accelerating attention computation by $3.07\times$.

</details>


### [26] [A Sparse Glimpse of the Whole: Train-Free Self-Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27735)
*Yuesong Liu,Yuan Zeng,Min Lyu,Ruilin Liu,Yu Guo,Yinlong Xu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SparseSpec-L introduces a training-free self-speculative decoding framework for long-context LLM inference. It uses a dynamically sparsified KV cache with recall capability and an entropy-based controller to adaptively select speculation length. The method achieves up to 1.73× speedup over autoregressive decoding while preserving output distribution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speculative decoding is constrained by drafting overhead, token acceptance rates, and speculation length. The authors' unified efficiency analysis reveals that extending speculation horizon can degrade speedup when marginal acceptance probability drops below relative drafting cost. This motivates an adaptive approach that selects optimal speculation length based on expected step-wise efficiency.

Method: SparseSpec-L is a training-free, self-speculative decoding framework. It generates draft tokens directly from the target model using a dynamically sparsified KV cache that retains recall capability — critical historical tokens can be retrieved without permanently discarding the dense KV cache. It recycles per-head attention statistics from full-context verification as a zero-extra-forward importance signal. An online, entropy-based controller dynamically selects speculation length according to expected step-wise efficiency.

Result: Experiments across multiple long-context tasks and model scales demonstrate consistent end-to-end acceleration, achieving up to 1.73× speedup over autoregressive decoding while fully preserving the target model's output distribution.

Conclusion: SparseSpec-L demonstrates that training-free self-speculation with adaptive speculation length control and a recallable sparse KV cache can effectively accelerate long-context LLM inference without compromising generation quality.

Abstract: Speculative decoding alleviates the memory-bandwidth bottleneck in large language model inference, but its acceleration is jointly constrained by drafting overhead, token acceptance, and speculation length. We present a unified efficiency analysis showing that extending the speculation horizon can reduce rather than improve speedup when the marginal acceptance probability falls below the relative drafting cost. Guided by this analysis, we introduce SparseSpec-L, a training-free self-speculative decoding framework for long-context inference. SparseSpec-L generates lightweight drafts directly from the target model using a dynamically sparsified and recallable KV cache. It recycles per-head attention statistics produced during full-context verification as a no-extra-forward importance signal, allowing critical historical tokens to be recalled without permanently discarding the dense KV cache. An online entropy-based controller further selects the speculation length according to expected step-wise efficiency. Experiments across multiple long-context tasks and model scales show consistent end-to-end acceleration, with up to speedup over autoregressive decoding while preserving the target model's output distribution.

</details>


### [27] [Can LVLMs Uncover the Truth Behind Visual Illusions? An Analysis of Perceptual and Reasoning Capabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27747)
*Liangjie Zhao,Jiaqing Lyu,Kexin Tang,Zecheng Fang,Rong Yin,Yulan Hu,Da Li,Jianing Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes evaluating Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) using visual illusions as a diagnostic tool, constructing a benchmark called IllusionReasoning with real-world illusion images and annotated QA pairs. Results reveal that current LVLMs' reasoning capabilities are not as advanced as claimed, especially in open-world scenarios requiring joint perception and reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations for LVLMs either focus solely on perceptual tasks or are restricted to narrow domains like math and coding. There is a lack of benchmarks that jointly assess perception and reasoning in open-world contexts. Visual illusions, where human perception systematically deviates from objective reality, provide a natural testbed for evaluating whether LVLMs can reason correctly despite misleading perceptual signals.

Method: The authors constructed IllusionReasoning, a benchmark dataset comprising illusion images sourced from the real world, paired with diverse annotated question-answer pairs spanning multiple types of visual illusions. A wide range of LVLMs were evaluated on this benchmark to assess their ability to jointly perceive and reason, particularly when perceptual input is inherently deceptive.

Result: Evaluation on IllusionReasoning shows that the reasoning capabilities of a broad spectrum of LVLMs fall short of their claimed performance levels. The models struggle significantly when perception and reasoning must be integrated to overcome misleading visual cues.

Conclusion: Visual illusions serve as an effective diagnostic tool for probing LVLM reasoning. The findings highlight a critical gap between claimed and actual reasoning capabilities, offering new insights and directions for future optimization of LVLMs toward robust open-world understanding.

Abstract: Large Vision Language Models have integrated reasoning capabilities, elevating cognitive performance to new levels. However, existing evaluations either focus solely on perception or rely on specific domains such as maths or coding. Evaluation for reasoning capabilities that align with an open-world environment is still required, especially one that considers perception and reasoning jointly. To bridge this gap, we propose to evaluate LVLMs by exploiting visual illusions as a diagnostic tool. Visual illusions are phenomena in which the human visual system misinterprets objective signals, resulting in an understanding that deviates from reality. We constructed IllusionReasoning, a benchmark of illusion images collected from the real world, incorporating diverse annotated question-answer pairs. Based on IllusionReasoning, we show that the reasoning capabilities of a wide range of LVLMs are not as advanced as claimed. Our work provides new insights into LVLMs and offers future direction for optimisation.

</details>


### [28] [ChronoMem: Version Control and Semantic Rollback for Large Language Model Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27773)
*Yongye Su,Wujiang Xu,Chaoji Zuo,Elisa Bertino*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ChronoMem introduces a semantic version-control system for LLM agent memory, enabling whole-memory snapshots, structured version histories, and natural-language rollback. It outperforms baselines on rollback-consistent QA and summarization in post-exposure evaluation settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agent memory systems operate in a forward-only manner—continuously accumulating and overwriting knowledge without mechanisms to inspect, version, or revert prior states. This makes agents brittle under corrections, concept drift, and memory corruption, especially after exposure to subsequent information.

Method: ChronoMem is a semantic version-control layer integrated into Google's Agent Development Kit. It commits whole-memory snapshots at each write, maintains structured version histories, and supports natural-language rollback by mapping undo intents to historical versions using hybrid lexical-semantic retrieval, rank fusion, and reranking. The authors also introduce a post-exposure evaluation protocol that tests counterfactual behavior after rollback.

Result: On long-horizon conversational benchmarks with evolving memory states and rollback tasks, ChronoMem substantially improves rollback-consistent QA and history summarization over prompt-only and retrieval-only baselines, while achieving strong semantic version selection performance.

Conclusion: ChronoMem is the first open-source system and benchmark for systematic semantic global memory rollback in LLM agents, addressing a critical gap in agent memory reliability.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on long-term memory to support multi-session interaction and personalization. However, existing agent memory systems are designed around forward-only evolution, continuously accumulating, consolidating, and overwriting knowledge, with no principled mechanism to inspect, version, or revert prior states. This makes agents brittle under corrections, concept drift, and memory corruption, particularly after they have already been exposed to subsequent information. We present ChronoMem, a semantic version-control layer for agentic memory integrated into the production-ready, open-source Agent Development Kit by Google. ChronoMem commits whole-memory snapshots at each memory write, maintains structured version histories, and supports natural-language rollback requests by mapping undo intents to concrete historical versions through hybrid lexical and semantic retrieval, rank fusion, and reranking. We further introduce a post-exposure evaluation protocol that tests whether an agent can behave counterfactually after rollback by answering queries and summarizing history as if future updates had never occurred. On long-horizon conversational benchmarks augmented with evolving memory states and rollback tasks, ChronoMem substantially improves rollback-consistent question answering and history summarization relative to prompt-only and retrieval-only baselines, while achieving strong performance in semantic version selection. To our knowledge, ChronoMem is the first open-source system and benchmark for systematic semantic global memory rollback in LLM agents.

</details>


### [29] [Reasoning Consensus: Structural Ensembling of LLM Reasoning via Weighted DAG Aggregation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27783)
*Amruta Parulekar,Jinu Lee,Dilek Hakkani-Tür,Hari Sundaram*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs reason via chain-of-thought, but the reasoning structure is buried in unstructured text. This paper proposes merging reasoning DAGs from multiple LLMs via weighted attestation to produce an inspectable "Consensus Reasoning" graph, improving accuracy and transparency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On high-stakes tasks, users cannot assess which reasoning steps are well-supported, which alternatives were seriously considered, or how the final conclusion compares to discarded ones. Chain-of-thought reasoning lacks structural transparency.

Method: Extract Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) from individual LLM reasoning chains. Ensemble these DAGs via weighted merging, where each step is weighted by how many reasoning traces independently attest to it, producing a consensus reasoning graph.

Result: The ensemble outperforms matched-budget majority-vote baselines across six benchmarks, with up to 3.1% accuracy gain on MuSR-MM. Matches or exceeds self-consistency at the same trace budget on single models. Ensemble weights correlate with LLM-judge quality rankings (Spearman ρ=0.30–0.51). Consensus subgraphs are preferred over majority-vote alternatives in 54.4–65.4% of head-to-head comparisons across five of six datasets.

Conclusion: Structured reasoning ensemble via DAG merging provides both accuracy gains and interpretable consensus graphs, enabling users to inspect which reasoning steps have broad support and which alternatives were considered.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) explore problems through chain-of-thought, but this exploration is buried in unstructured prose. On high-stakes tasks, users cannot tell which steps are well-supported, which alternatives were seriously considered, or how the final conclusion compares to those the model discarded. We propose a framework that ensembles the reasoning structure, not just the answers, of multiple LLMs by weighted merging of Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) extracted from reasoning chains. We weight each step by how many traces independently attest to it, to return "Consensus Reasoning". Across six benchmarks spanning statutory interpretation, graduate-level science, narrative multi-hop reasoning, and first-order logic, our ensemble outperforms a matched-budget majority-vote baseline, with a maximum accuracy gain of 3.1% on MuSR-MM (narrative multi-hop reasoning). On a single model, the framework matches or exceeds self-consistency at the same trace budget while additionally exposing an inspectable consensus reasoning graph. Ensemble weights correlate with LLM-judge rankings of reasoning quality at Spearman $ρ= 0.30$-$0.51$, and consensus subgraphs are preferred over alternatives leading to the majority-vote answer in 54.4-65.4% of head-to-head comparisons across five of six datasets. We observe that our framework can also be used to analyze diverse reasoning perspectives for a problem.

</details>


### [30] [Semantic-Aligned Structural Abstraction for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27790)
*Wei Chen,Junkai Li,Tongguan Wang,Hui Liu,Feiyue Xue,Chuanxiang Ma,Ying Sha*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SentiLLM introduces a semantic-aligned structural abstraction framework that transforms non-verbal modalities into LLM-readable tokens via a dual-stream salience-context calibration mechanism, achieving state-of-the-art multimodal sentiment analysis with minimal trainable parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based MSA methods only capture low-level superficial features from non-verbal modalities and fail to model the affective semantics arising from structural variations and contextual interactions. The structural isomorphism between non-verbal sequences and natural language remains underexploited.

Method: SentiLLM proposes a Semantic-Aligned Structural Abstraction framework with a Dual-Stream Salience-Context Calibration Mechanism. This disentangles non-verbal feature sequences into a focus stream (capturing salient sentiment shifts like facial expressions, guided by textual priors) and an ambient stream (characterizing stable background states). By calibrating dynamic shifts against background states, non-verbal modalities are projected into a unified semantic space interpretable by LLMs. The module is plug-and-play with few trainable parameters.

Result: SentiLLM achieves superior performance on four benchmark datasets: MOSI, MOSEI, CH-SIMS, and CH-SIMS v2, demonstrating the effectiveness of the structural abstraction paradigm for MSA.

Conclusion: The structural abstraction paradigm, which distills continuous non-verbal signals into semantically meaningful compact tokens via dual-stream calibration, effectively bridges non-verbal modalities and LLMs, yielding significant discriminative gains with parameter efficiency.

Abstract: Multimodal Sentiment Analysis (MSA) aims to interpret complex human emotions by integrating natural language with non-verbal modalities. Non-verbal modalities share a structural isomorphism with natural language, as both can be viewed as feature sequences evolving over time. This isomorphism enables the transformation of non-verbal modalities into text-like tokens for unified semantic reasoning. Large Language Models (LLMs), designed to understand and generate sequential data, can thus be utilized to interpret complex affective sequences. However, existing LLM-based methods primarily capture low-level superficial features, failing to model affective semantics arising from structural variations and contextual interactions. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{SentiLLM}, a unified framework that leverages \textit{Semantic-Aligned Structural Abstraction} to distill continuous raw signals into compact, semantically meaningful tokens. Specifically, we introduce a \textit{Dual-Stream Salience-Context Calibration Mechanism}, which disentangles non-verbal feature sequences into a focus stream and an ambient stream. The focus stream captures salient sentiment shifts (e.g., facial expressions) guided by textual priors, while the ambient stream characterizes stable background states. Through calibrating these dynamic sentiment shifts against background states, SentiLLM effectively projects non-verbal modalities into a unified semantic space, making them naturally understandable for LLMs. Serving as a plug-and-play module, SentiLLM significantly improves discriminative performance with only a small number of trainable parameters. Our method achieves superior performance on four datasets, MOSI, MOSEI, CH-SIMS, and CH-SIMS v2, demonstrating the effectiveness of the structural abstraction paradigm in MSA. Our code is available at: \href{https://github.com/especiallyW/SentiLLM}.

</details>


### [31] [Beyond Borrowed Histories: Person-Aligned User Simulation for Interactive Role-Playing Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27816)
*Yuhang Zhu,Mingxuan Du,Benfeng Xu,Jie Gao,Lingyun Yu,Hongtao Xie*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PALATE introduces a user-simulator-based benchmark for role-playing agents that uses personalized rubrics and free-form multi-turn conversations, overcoming limitations of fixed-history, fixed-rubric evaluations and providing per-user-pair assessments rather than single rankings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RPA benchmarks are flawed in two ways: (1) requiring RPAs to continue fixed dialogue histories prevents scientifically grounded assessment in real multi-turn settings, and (2) fixed rubrics fail to capture individual variability in user satisfaction.

Method: PALATE uses a pool of 300 character profiles, trains five per-user simulators, and lets them engage candidate RPAs in free-form multi-turn conversations. It constructs personalized rubrics alongside a general quality rubric, and evaluates 16 candidates on generic turn quality, long-horizon session capability, and per-user experience.

Result: On held-out annotated data, personalized rubrics show higher agreement with human judgments than the general rubric. The benchmark produces interpretable, pair-specific evaluations rather than compressing systems into a single user-independent ranking.

Conclusion: PALATE provides a more scientifically grounded, scalable, and personalized evaluation framework for RPAs that better aligns with real user experiences compared to conventional fixed-history, fixed-rubric benchmarks.

Abstract: Role-playing agents (RPAs) have become one of the most important consumer applications of large language models. Users engage in multi-turn conversations with RPAs for experiences such as emotional comfort, making reliable evaluation essential for measuring capability, comparing systems, and guiding further improvement. Existing benchmarks, however, typically require an RPA to continue a fixed dialogue history and then evaluate the continuation using a fixed rubric detached from the user. We identify and empirically demonstrate two limitations of this design. First, an RPA's output is shaped by the preceding dialogue history, preventing a scientifically grounded assessment of its role-playing ability in real multi-turn settings. Second, user experience varies substantially across individuals, and conventional fixed rubrics need not align with user satisfaction. We therefore introduce PALATE (Person-Aligned LLM-Simulated-User Assessment with Tailored Evaluation), a scalable RPA benchmark built on user simulators. PALATE is accompanied by a pool of 300 character profiles. Its main evaluation trains five per-user simulators and lets them engage candidate RPAs in free-form, multi-turn conversations over a pre-frozen panel of character profiles. Alongside a general quality rubric, we construct personalized rubrics to measure user satisfaction; on held-out annotated data, the personalized rubrics show higher agreement with human judgments than the general rubric. In the main evaluation of 16 candidates, PALATE separately characterizes generic turn quality, long-horizon session capability, and per-user experience on multi-turn trajectories co-constructed by each candidate. It thereby produces interpretable evaluations of specific user-RPA pairs rather than compressing systems into a single user-independent ranking.

</details>


### [32] [AutoSupervision: Closing the Feedback Loop in Scientific Workflows with Grounded Revision Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27845)
*Haobo Li,Eunseo Jung,Wenxiao Zhao,Feng Liu,Jiong Wang,Kaiyi Xu,Zijie Guo,Zixin Chen,Ben Fei,Fenghua Ling,Lei Bai*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: AutoSupervision is a benchmark that evaluates whether LLMs can verify that manuscript revisions address reviewer feedback with grounded evidence, using 56,000 Nature Communications peer-review records. While LLMs characterize reviewer concerns well (GPT-5.5: 0.754), evidence-based verification remains challenging (best model: 0.501).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliable AI-assisted scientific workflows require the ability to verify whether reviewer feedback leads to meaningful, evidence-supported manuscript improvements — a capability that remains underexplored in existing LLM evaluation frameworks.

Method: The authors construct AutoSupervision, a benchmark derived from 56,000 Nature Communications articles and their transparent peer-review records. The task is a three-step pipeline: (1) characterize reviewer concerns from comments, (2) determine whether those concerns have been addressed using author responses, and (3) identify supporting evidence in the revised manuscript. Experiments include LLM evaluations, ablation studies, and case studies.

Result: LLMs perform well at characterizing reviewer concerns, with GPT-5.5 achieving 0.754. However, evidence-based verification — identifying manuscript evidence that concerns were addressed — is the primary bottleneck, with the best model reaching only 0.501.

Conclusion: Current LLMs are reasonably capable at understanding and characterizing reviewer feedback but struggle significantly with the grounded, evidence-based verification of whether revisions substantively address those concerns. This highlights a critical gap for reliable AI-assisted peer review.

Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled AI systems to assist scientific research and peer review. However, an essential capability for reliable AI-assisted scientific workflows remains underexplored: verifying whether reviewer feedback leads to meaningful and evidence-supported manuscript improvements. We introduce AutoSupervision, which evaluates whether scientific manuscript revisions genuinely address reviewer concerns through grounded evidence. AutoSupervision leverages transparent peer-review records as a natural source of supervision, where reviewer comments specify scientific concerns, author responses describe claimed resolutions, and revised manuscripts provide evidence of changes. Given reviewer comments, author responses, and revised manuscripts, models must characterize reviewer concerns, determine whether concerns have been addressed, and identify supporting manuscript evidence. We construct AutoSupervision from 56,000 Nature Communications articles and corresponding review records. Then we conducted experiments on LLMs, the ablation study, and the case study. Our results show that while LLMs perform well in characterizing reviewer concerns, with GPT-5.5 achieving a score of 0.754, evidence-based verification remains the primary bottleneck, with the best-performing model reaching only 0.501.

</details>


### [33] [FinanceHarness: Autonomous Financial Deep Research Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27853)
*Yijia Xiao,Rujun Han,Yanfei Chen,Zifeng Wang,Ke Jiang,Zhongying CuiZhu,Vishy Tirumalashetty,Wei Wang,Burak Gokturk,Tomas Pfister,Chen-Yu Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: FinanceHarness is an end-to-end framework for automating financial deep research, paired with FinanceGym, a point-in-time benchmark that prevents data leakage. The harness uses specialized tools and practitioner-guided workflows, while the benchmark features thesis-driven questions with pre- and post-cutoff rubrics. Leading LLMs score below 40%, and FinanceHarness improves open-weight model performance from 25.3% to 32.4%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current deep research systems produce general-purpose reports inadequate for finance, which requires specialized domain knowledge for analyzing historical patterns and forecasting events. Additionally, existing benchmarks risk future information leakage, necessitating a verifiable, point-in-time evaluation framework.

Method: The authors propose FinanceHarness, a layered harness automating financial deep research via finance-oriented tools, practitioner-guided workflows, and reward modeling across three stages: environment/data construction, agent execution loop, and reward modeling. They also introduce FinanceGym, a benchmark with thesis-driven research questions and rubrics combining pre-cutoff (historical) and post-cutoff (forecast) criteria, validated by professional experts.

Result: Professional expert validation of FinanceGym achieved an 82% pass rate. Leading LLMs and agents scored below 40% on the rubrics, demonstrating benchmark difficulty. FinanceHarness, using the same open-weight backbone, improved overall rubric score from 25.3% to 32.4%.

Conclusion: FinanceHarness significantly advances automated financial deep research by combining specialized tooling with practitioner workflows. FinanceGym provides a challenging, leakage-proof benchmark that reveals substantial headroom for future improvement in financial AI research agents.

Abstract: Powered by advances in LLMs and autonomous agents, deep research has become one of the most widely adopted agentic products. However, most deep research systems write general-purpose reports, which are inadequate for financial deep research. Financial research demands specialized knowledge to analyze historical patterns and forecast upcoming events. Automating financial deep research therefore requires both a layered harness to drive the research agent and a verifiable, point-in-time benchmark that prevents leakage of future information. We present FinanceHarness, a harness that runs finance-oriented tools and practitioner-guided workflows, automating financial deep research end to end: environment and data construction, the agent execution loop, and reward modeling. We further propose FinanceGym, comprising thesis-driven research questions and rubrics that combine pre-cutoff and post-cutoff criteria. Professional expert validation yields an 82% pass rate. Even leading LLMs and agents score below 40% on the rubrics, showing that FinanceGym is challenging and leaves substantial headroom. With the same open-weight backbone, FinanceHarness improves the overall rubric score from 25.3% to 32.4%. FinanceHarness is available at https://github.com/Yijia-Xiao/FinanceHarness.

</details>


### [34] [Memory Decoder at Scale: A Pretrained, Parametric Long-Term Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27919)
*Rubin Wei,Jiaqi Cao,Jiarui Wang,Junming Zhang,Qipeng Guo,Bowen Zhou,Zhouhan Lin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Memory Decoder at Scale shows that independently scaling a parametric long-term memory module yields better parameter efficiency than scaling the base LM alone, with a 6.9B memory + 410M Pythia outperforming a 12B Pythia (39% fewer params) and domain-specific memories boosting Qwen3 by 9+ points across scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Decoder-only LMs entangle long-term memory and reasoning, making independent scaling of memory capacity difficult. Prior Memory Decoder work was limited to small scale; scaling up introduces infrastructure bottlenecks (Faiss indexing/retrieval cost) that must be solved.

Method: Scale Memory Decoder models to 6.9B parameters, pretrained on 300B tokens. Introduce a distributed pipeline for Faiss indexing and retrieval with sparse, batch-wise loading of kNN distributions to overcome the indexing/search bottleneck at scale. Evaluate parameter-performance tradeoffs by varying memory allocation and pairing general/domain memories with base models (Pythia, Qwen3).

Result: More parameters to memory beats scaling the base model alone. Pythia-410M + 6.9B memory achieves 37.34 average score vs. Pythia-12B's 37.24 (39% fewer total params). Qwen3 (0.6B–14B) with 1.7B domain memories gains 9+ points across three domains at every scale.

Conclusion: Independently scaling pretrained memory is a more parameter-efficient path to improving LM performance than scaling the base model, with consistent benefits across model families and scales.

Abstract: Decoder-only language models entangle long-term memory and reasoning in a single parameter set, making it difficult to scale memory capacity independently. Memory Decoder introduces a parametric long-term memory module but only studies it at a relatively small scale. In this work, we present Memory Decoder at Scale, scaling memory models up to 6.9B parameters and pretraining them on 300B tokens. At this data scale, the combined cost of indexing and search makes a standard Faiss pipeline infeasible. We address this bottleneck with a distributed pipeline for Faiss indexing and retrieval, together with sparse, batch-wise loading of kNN distributions. Across model scales, we find that allocating more parameters to memory yields a better parameter-performance tradeoff than scaling the base model alone. On 17 benchmarks, pairing a 6.9B general memory with Pythia-410M raises its average score from 29.86 to 37.34, surpassing Pythia-12B (37.24) with 39% fewer total parameters. For Qwen3 Base models ranging from 0.6B to 14B, 1.7B domain memories improve the average score across the three domains by more than 9 points at every scale. Overall, our results demonstrate that independently scaling pretrained memory offers a more parameter efficient path to improving language model performance.

</details>


### [35] [RepBench: Compiling Benchmarks into Capability Representations for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28008)
*Yanshi Li,Xueru Bai,Shuman Liu,Long Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RepBench provides a benchmark-grounded data layer for representation probing, using 46,149 texts across 94 capabilities from 353 datasets, revealing that readout method and aggregation criteria significantly affect evaluation outcomes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing representation engineering methods rely on paper-specific synthetic data, making results difficult to compare, reproduce, and potentially capturing surface patterns rather than genuine capabilities.

Method: Crawled 13,427 benchmark papers to build a taxonomy of 182 capability clusters across 13 families; harvested 353 public benchmark datasets yielding 46,149 audited probe texts covering 94 capabilities (each supported by ≥2 independent benchmarks). Evaluated cross-benchmark transfer across 12 models using four readout methods, comparing difference-in-means and logistic regression performance.

Result: Raw per-text vectors show no natural cluster granularity, while benchmark-pooled capability vectors display an interior clustering optimum at a small number of clusters across all 12 models, with low agreement to the human taxonomy. Difference-in-means achieves the highest model-level mean on 10 of 12 models; logistic regression wins the most capability-model cells. This disagreement highlights readout method and aggregation criterion as critical evaluation dimensions.

Conclusion: RepBench establishes a reproducible, multi-benchmark framework for capability-aligned representation probing, demonstrating that both readout method choice and aggregation strategy are meaningful design decisions. The pipeline, corpus, and code are released as a reusable closed-loop workflow.

Abstract: Representation engineering reads and steers capability directions in large language models, yet methods are typically evaluated on paper-specific synthetic data. The resulting measurements are difficult to compare or reproduce and may reflect surface patterns rather than capabilities. We present RepBench, a benchmark-grounded data layer for capability-aligned representation probing. Crawling 13,427 benchmark papers yields a taxonomy of 182 capability clusters in 13 families; harvesting 353 public benchmark datasets yields 46,149 audited probe texts covering 94 capabilities, each supported by at least two independent benchmarks. This multi-benchmark design reduces dependence on any single source: raw per-text vectors exhibit no natural cluster granularity, whereas benchmark-pooled capability vectors show an interior clustering optimum at a small number of clusters on all 12 evaluated models, with low agreement to the human taxonomy. Under cross-benchmark transfer evaluation across twelve models completed by all four readouts, difference-in-means attains the highest model-level mean on ten models, while logistic regression wins the most capability-model cells. This disagreement shows that the readout method and aggregation criterion are meaningful evaluation dimensions. The pipeline, corpus, and evaluation code are released as a reusable closed-loop workflow.

</details>


### [36] [ORCA-bench: How Ready Are Language Model Agents for Oncall?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28545)
*Albert Gong,Kyuseong Choi,Abhineet Agarwal,Jason Schechner,Ryan Huang,Raj Agrawal,Anish Agarwal,Raaz Dwivedi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ORCA-bench evaluates frontier coding agents on production-fidelity oncall root cause analysis using a live microservice system with real telemetry. Even the best agent achieves only 25.3% accuracy on medium-difficulty tasks and 10% on hard tasks, with hallucination rates up to 40%, revealing a substantial gap before agents can be trusted for production reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing code-agent benchmarks focus on code writing, patching, and searching, but real oncall root cause analysis requires reasoning over noisy, heterogeneous telemetry (metrics, logs, traces) and source code from ambiguous reports—a capability not yet systematically evaluated. The authors aim to quantify how far current frontier agents are from being production-trustworthy for RCA.

Method: The authors built ORCA-bench, comprising a live OpenTelemetry-instrumented microservice system exposing six days of real telemetry via Prometheus, Jaeger, and OpenSearch/Grafana, plus full source code. They curated 1,079 RCA tasks varying report specificity, time-to-detection, and co-occurring faults. Ground-truth symptoms were signed off by expert SREs, and an LLM-as-judge was validated against human scorers (Cohen's κ_w=0.90). Five frontier agents were evaluated across Easy, Medium, and Hard difficulty tiers.

Result: The best agent achieved 25.3% RCA Accuracy on Medium tasks (realistic input) and 10.0% on Hard tasks, with Claude Fable 5 failing to close the gap. The weakest model hallucinated implausible root causes in 40% of reports. Removing source-code access degraded all metrics uniformly. Since the 50 GB testbed is far smaller and less dynamic than real production systems, these results represent a lower bound on the gap to production readiness.

Conclusion: Frontier coding agents are far from trustworthy for production oncall RCA. The substantial accuracy gap—even on a curated, small-scale testbed—indicates significant engineering investment is needed before such agents can be safely deployed in real production environments, which are orders of magnitude larger and more idiosyncratic.

Abstract: Large language models can write, patch, and search code, but oncall root cause analysis (RCA) demands something different: reasoning over noisy metrics, logs, traces, and source code, starting from ambiguous user-facing reports, often hours after the incident began. We introduce ORCA-bench, a benchmark that puts general-purpose coding agents in a production-fidelity oncall setting. ORCA-bench pairs a live OpenTelemetry-instrumented microservice system--exposing six days of metrics, logs, and traces through real telemetry interfaces (Prometheus, Jaeger, and OpenSearch via Grafana) and full source-code access--with 1,079 RCA tasks that systematically vary report specificity, time-to-detection, and co-occurring fault scenarios. Ground-truth symptoms are curated and signed off by expert SREs, and our LLM-as-judge is independently re-scored by humans (Cohen's $κ_w=0.90$). Across five frontier agents, the best RCA Accuracy is 25.3% on Medium-difficulty tasks (the realistic-input setting) and 10.0% on Hard--a gap that remains even with Claude Fable 5. The weakest model hallucinates an implausible root cause in 40% of incident reports, and removing source-code access degrades every metric. Crucially, these are performances on a curated 50 GB / six-day testbed with tasks investigated in isolation on a system whose code and instrumentation are public. Since real production systems are order of magnitudes larger, more dynamic, and more idiosyncratic, the gap we report is a lower bound on the engineering investment required before frontier coding agents can be safely entrusted with production reliability. We release the public set at https://hub.harborframework.com/datasets/orca-bench/ORCA-bench.

</details>


### [37] [LEEPS: Latent-Guided Explore-Exploit Prompt Sampling for Efficient RLVR in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28077)
*Shuang Liang,Haoyang Zhou,Yifan Gong,Guowei Wang,Xiting Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LEEPS is an adaptive prompt sampler for RLVR that balances exploitation of known informative prompts with targeted exploration of uncertain ones using latent-space neighborhoods, improving reasoning benchmarks with minimal overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In RLVR, many prompt groups receive identical rollout rewards, wasting generation budget without providing useful learning signals. Pre-rollout prompt selection can mitigate this, but existing methods struggle to balance exploitation (which narrows coverage) and exploration (which lowers the fraction of informative prompts).

Method: LEEPS partitions prompt candidates into exploit and explore portfolios, adaptively allocates rollout budget based on recent non-trivial ratios, and uses representation-space neighbors with historical rollout outcomes to prioritize uncertain prompts likely to yield non-zero reward variance, enabling targeted exploration without extra rollouts.

Result: Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, LEEPS achieves the highest average scores with relative gains of 2.6% (1.5B) and 3.7% (7B) over the strongest baseline for Qwen2.5-Math. It also achieves the highest average on three OOD general-reasoning benchmarks and adds only ~2 seconds of online sampling overhead per training step.

Conclusion: LEEPS effectively addresses the exploration-exploitation trade-off in prompt selection for RLVR, improving both in-distribution math reasoning and out-of-distribution generalization with negligible computational overhead.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but prompt groups with identical rollout rewards consume generation budget without effective learning signals. Pre-rollout prompt selection can reduce this waste by screening prompts before rollout generation. However, existing pre-rollout methods struggle to balance exploitation and exploration: repeatedly exploiting historically informative prompts can narrow training coverage, whereas broader exploration can lower the fraction of informative prompts. To address these limitations, we introduce LEEPS, a Latent-Guided Explore--Exploit Prompt Sampler that adaptively balances the reuse of previously observed informative prompts with continued exploration of uncertain ones. LEEPS partitions candidates into exploit and explore portfolios and adaptively allocates rollout budget according to their recent non-trivial ratios. It further uses representation-space neighbors and historical rollout outcomes to prioritize uncertain prompts likely to yield non-zero reward variance, thereby making exploration more targeted without additional rollouts. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, LEEPS achieves the highest average score at both model scales, with relative gains of 2.6\% and 3.7\% over the strongest baseline for Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and 7B, respectively, and generally improves faster during the training process. It also achieves the highest average score across the three evaluated OOD general-reasoning benchmarks at both model scales and adds only about 2 seconds of online sampling overhead per training step. Code is available at https://github.com/ShuangLiangX/LEEPS.

</details>


### [38] [GGC: Selective Query Correction for Reliable Text-to-SPARQL Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28082)
*Ziyi Yang,Thanh-Son Nguyen,Tuan Anh Nguyen,Lihui Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: GGC is a three-stage framework (Generator-Gate-Corrector) that improves LLM-based Text-to-SPARQL reliability by selectively correcting only high-risk queries, boosting accuracy from 90.23% to 98.33% while cutting inference overhead by 45%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can generate executable SPARQL queries from natural language, but these queries are often semantically misaligned with the input question, leading to incorrect knowledge graph retrieval. Correcting all outputs is computationally expensive and risks degrading already-correct queries.

Method: The Generator produces an initial SPARQL query from a natural language question. The Gate then predicts whether correction is necessary. Only queries flagged as high-risk are sent to the Corrector for refinement. This selective mechanism avoids unnecessary modifications to correct queries.

Result: On the MCQA benchmark, GGC improves query-level accuracy from 90.23% to 98.33% and reduces inference overhead by 45% compared to correcting all queries. The Gate is robust across thresholds, and Corrector training data composition significantly affects correction effectiveness and stability.

Conclusion: Selective correction via the GGC framework substantially enhances the accuracy, reliability, and efficiency of LLM-based Text-to-SPARQL generation, outperforming both uncorrected baselines and indiscriminate correction strategies.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in structured query generation, making them a natural choice for Text-to-SPARQL, which translates natural language questions into executable SPARQL queries over knowledge graphs. However, their initial outputs remain unreliable: generated queries may be executable yet semantically misaligned with input questions, leading to incorrect retrieval. To address this issue, we propose Generator-Gate-Corrector (GGC), a framework for reliable LLM-based Text-to-SPARQL generation. GGC first uses a Generator to produce an initial query, then applies a Gate to predict whether correction is needed, and finally invokes a Corrector only for selected high-risk queries. This selective correction mechanism avoids unnecessary modifications and reduces the risk of degrading originally correct queries. Experiments on MCQA show that GGC improves query-level accuracy from 90.23\% to 98.33\% while reducing inference overhead by 45\% compared with correcting all generated queries. Ablation studies show that the Gate is robust across thresholds and that Corrector training data composition affects correction effectiveness and stability. Overall, the results demonstrate that selective correction enhances the accuracy, reliability, and efficiency of LLM-based text-to-SPARQL generation.

</details>


### [39] [Challenges in annotations by humans and LLMs: A case study of evaluative language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28119)
*Mirela Imamovic,Aenne Cecilia Kristine Knierim,Khushi Pitroda,Ekaterina Lapshinova-Koltunski*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper compares how LLMs, trained linguists, and linguists-in-training handle the complex annotation task of Appraisal theory's Attitude subsystem (Affect, Judgement, Appreciation) in TED talks, finding LLMs perform best against trained linguist annotations (F1=0.77) while novices struggle, suggesting LLMs can assist in subjective digital humanities annotation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether LLMs and human annotators struggle similarly with complex, highly subjective linguistic annotation tasks, using Appraisal theory as a test case.

Method: Human annotation of evaluative language (Attitude subsystem: Affect, Judgement, Appreciation) at the sentence level on English TED talk transcripts by linguists-in-training and a trained linguist; prompt engineering with three prompts; automatic classification using three LLMs with the best prompt; model fine-tuning; comparison of performance and inter-annotator agreement across all annotator types.

Result: The fine-tuned LLM achieved an F1-score of 0.77. Models performed best when compared against the trained linguist's annotations. Linguists-in-training showed low inter-annotator agreement, indicating difficulty with the task.

Conclusion: LLMs can effectively aid in resolving complex annotation tasks, offering new methodological pathways for annotation and analysis within digital humanities research involving complex theoretical frameworks.

Abstract: In this paper, we draw a comparison between linguists in training, a trained linguist, and annotations generated by large language models (LLMs) to find out if they struggle with complex linguistic phenomena in a similar way. For this purpose, we analyse evaluative language in spoken popular science discourse, with the example of a corpus of English TED talk transcripts. We focus on the Appraisal theory and its Attitude subsystem, including the categories (classes) of Affect, Judgement, and Appreciation. In this context, Appraisal theory is an example of a highly subjective annotation task, making it a suitable example for the study of complex annotation challenges. First, we assess human annotations on a sentence level in specific scientific domains. Then, we develop three prompts and compare them for model performance for the automatic classification of Appraisal classes. We assess the performance of three LLMs using the best-performing prompt and finetune the model, reaching an F1-score of 0.77. We find that models perform best compared to annotations conducted by the trained linguist, while linguists in training do not reach high agreement scores. We conclude that LLMs can aid in complex annotation task resolution, opening new pathways for the complex theories annotated and analyzed in digital humanities studies.

</details>


### [40] [FinSMART: Financial Sentiment Analysis for Algorithmic Trading through Market-Aligned Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28127)
*Giorgos Iacovides,Wuyang Zhou,Danilo Mandic*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: FinSMART introduces a reinforcement learning framework for financial sentiment analysis that optimizes sentiment signals directly from market outcomes, outperforming static supervised methods by 220% in cumulative returns and enabling continuous market-aware retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing financial LLMs rely on market-agnostic supervised learning with limited, static human-annotated datasets, making them incapable of adapting to evolving market conditions.

Method: FinSMART uses a market-aligned RL framework with a signal extraction pipeline combining market-aware data filtering and a discrete asymmetric trading reward to handle noisy, non-stationary, multifactorial market data. It also supports retraining using newly observed articles and realized market outcomes instead of manual annotation.

Result: FinSMART significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in profitability, risk-adjusted performance, and signal quality, achieving a 220% improvement in cumulative trading returns. Market-aware retraining yields consistent performance gains over static counterparts.

Conclusion: Market-aligned reinforcement learning is a viable next-generation paradigm for developing adaptive financial LLMs, offering practical applicability through continuous adaptation to changing market dynamics without costly manual re-annotation.

Abstract: Recent advances in Generative AI have substantially improved financial sentiment analysis through post-trained financial large language models (LLMs). However, existing approaches remain confined to a market-agnostic, supervised learning paradigm that relies on limited, static and human-annotated datasets, and thus are incapable of adapting to evolving market conditions. To address this limitation, we introduce FinSMART, the first market-aligned reinforcement learning framework for financial sentiment analysis, which directly optimizes sentiment signals using realized market outcomes. To deal with the noisy, non-stationary, and multifactorial nature of financial markets, FinSMART incorporates a signal extraction pipeline that combines market-aware data filtering with a discrete asymmetric trading reward, enabling stable reinforcement learning from economically meaningful market feedback. Experimental results demonstrate that FinSMART significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in profitability, risk-adjusted performance, and sentiment signal quality, improving cumulative trading returns by 220% over the strongest baseline. Uniquely, the FinSMART framework naturally supports market-aware retraining, at any point in time, by replacing costly manual annotation with newly observed financial articles and their realized market outcomes. Such a retraining strategy enables the model to continuously adapt to changing market dynamics, resulting in consistent performance gains over its static counterpart. These findings demonstrate the practical applicability of market-aligned reinforcement learning and highlight its potential as a next-generation paradigm for developing adaptive financial LLMs.

</details>


### [41] [Rethinking LLM-Judged Helpfulness as a Pedagogy Signal: A Pre-Registered Audit Across Tutor Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28128)
*Shuyi Fan,Boyuan Deng,Mengyu Xu,Jiale Liu,Hongyang Zhang,Qiaoxin Yang,Chongyang Gao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: General-purpose helpfulness rubrics cannot reliably distinguish pedagogical tutoring from direct answer-giving. The study shows that helpfulness and pedagogy ratings can be decoupled and that helpfulness rankings are judge-contingent, whereas pedagogy-targeted rubrics and deterministic process measures (answer leakage, independent work) provide consistent signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based tutoring systems face a core measurement validity problem: standard helpfulness evaluation rubrics may conflate genuine pedagogical scaffolding with simply giving away the answer. Without valid pedagogy-specific signals, developers cannot reliably optimize tutors for learning outcomes.

Method: Pre-registered study manipulating tutorial policy (conversational vs. pedagogical) across three tutor bases, each paired with a fixed weak simulated student. Three evaluation approaches are compared: (1) Claude Opus 4.8 as frozen, condition-blind primary judge using helpfulness and pedagogy rubrics; (2) GPT-5.6 Sol as a post hoc robustness audit on 1,179 confirmatory answer-phase turns; (3) deterministic detectors measuring answer leakage and next-turn independent student work. Effect sizes are quantified via Cliff's delta.

Result: Under Opus, policies do not differ significantly in helpfulness (Cliff's |δ| = 0.10) but are perfectly rank-separated on pedagogy (|δ| = 1.0). Helpfulness ordering reverses between Opus and GPT-5.6 Sol on two of three bases, while pedagogy contrasts retain consistent direction. In an ablation, seven primary-base policies span 2.3 points in mean pedagogy but only a 0.25-point band in helpfulness. Deterministic measures show less independent work after answer-revealing turns across all bases, a judge-invariant result.

Conclusion: General-purpose helpfulness is not a reliable signal for pedagogical quality in LLM tutoring. Reliable tutor evaluation requires combining pedagogy-targeted rubrics with deterministic, judge-invariant process measures such as answer leakage detection and downstream student independent work.

Abstract: LLM tutoring poses a measurement problem: can a general-purpose helpfulness rubric distinguish direct answer-giving from pedagogical guidance? We audit this signal in a pre-registered study. Within each of three tutor bases, we compare conversational and pedagogical policies instantiated with the same underlying model and paired with one fixed weak simulated student. Deterministic detectors measure answer leakage and next-turn independent work. Claude Opus 4.8 is the frozen, condition-blind primary judge. After the Opus scores were fixed, GPT-5.6 Sol was prospectively specified for a post hoc robustness audit of the same 1,179 confirmatory answer-phase tutor turns under the frozen helpfulness and pedagogy rubrics. On the primary base under Opus, the policies do not differ significantly in helpfulness but are perfectly rank-separated under the pedagogy rubric (Cliff's $|δ|{=}0.10$ vs. $1.0$). Across the two judges, pedagogy contrasts retain their direction where detected, whereas the helpfulness ordering is judge-contingent, reversing between judges on two of three bases. In an Opus-only ablation, seven primary-base policies span $2.3$ points in mean judged pedagogy within a $0.25$-point band of mean judged helpfulness. Separately, answer-revealing turns are followed by less independent student work on every base, a result that is judge-invariant by construction. In this controlled setting, general-purpose helpfulness is not a reliable pedagogy signal. Tutor evaluation should pair pedagogy-targeted rubrics with deterministic process measures.

</details>


### [42] [Can Agents Deceive? Evaluating Reasoning and Deception in ParliamentBench using a Social Deduction Game](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28146)
*Niklas Bauer,Lars Benedikt Kaesberg,Akiko Aizawa,Jan Philip Wahle,Bela Gipp,Terry Ruas*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ParliamentBench is a Secret Hitler-based benchmark for evaluating LLM deception, persuasion, and reasoning under information asymmetry. Testing 16 LLMs across 1,600 simulated matches reveals a strong top-four cluster, while weaker models underperform random baselines and most models struggle to maintain consistent deception.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs are deployed in high-stakes agentic settings (medical, legal), understanding their deceptive capabilities is critical for safety. Social deduction games offer a controlled, reproducible environment to isolate and evaluate adversarial behaviors like deception, persuasion, and strategic reasoning under information asymmetry.

Method: The authors introduce ParliamentBench, an open-source benchmark based on the game Secret Hitler. 16 LLMs are evaluated across 1,600 simulated matches in LLM-vs-LLM and LLM-vs-human settings, compared against a large corpus of online human games. Three novel metrics are proposed to isolate social deduction ability, reasoning, and deceptive consistency (retention of a deceptive persona across a full game).

Result: Frontier models form a strong top-four cluster (GPT-5.4, Kimi K2.5, Grok 4.1 Fast, DeepSeek 3.1 Terminus) excelling in both cooperative and deceptive roles. The weakest models fall below random (33%) and simple algorithmic (45%) baselines. Most LLMs fail to maintain consistent deceptive personas, with deception retention dropping below 50%.

Conclusion: LLMs exhibit emergent but uneven deceptive capabilities: top models can deploy effective strategic deception, but consistency across long-horizon interactions remains a major failure mode. This highlights a safety-relevant capability gap that warrants ongoing monitoring as models improve.

Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed as agents in high-stakes settings, such as medical and legal systems, understanding their deceptive capabilities is fundamental to safety. Controlled social deduction games provide a reproducible proxy for isolating and evaluating these complex adversarial behaviors. We present the open-source benchmark framework ParliamentBench based on the game Secret Hitler to evaluate LLMs in scenarios that require deception, persuasion, and reasoning under information asymmetry. We evaluate 16 LLMs across 1,600 simulated matches playing each other, playing against humans, and compare them against a large set of online games. We introduce three novel metrics that isolate social deduction, reasoning, and deceptive consistency. Our experiments reveal that frontier models achieve strong performance across cooperative and deceptive roles, with a strong top-four cluster (GPT-5.4, Kimi K2.5, Grok 4.1 Fast, and DeepSeek 3.1 Terminus), whereas the weakest models fall short of random (33%) and simple algorithmic (45%) baselines. Most LLMs struggle to maintain a consistent deceptive persona throughout an entire game, with deception retention dropping below 50%.

</details>


### [43] [RRM: Experience-Driven Reflective Retrieval Memory for Long-Horizon Multimodal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28156)
*Jingxiang Fan,Junbao Zhuo,Bochao Zou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RRM introduces a reflective memory framework that stores reusable retrieval strategies from past task trajectories to guide future searches, outperforming existing methods on long-horizon multimodal reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal long-term memory agents lack mechanisms to diagnose retrieval failures from previous task trajectories and adapt search strategies accordingly. Most work focuses on what to store rather than how stored memory should be retrieved.

Method: RRM augments an entity-centric multimodal memory graph with reflective experience memory, which distills transferable procedural retrieval knowledge from historical task trajectories. Retrieved experiences are converted into query-level guidance, while answer generation conditions only on factual evidence from the current video. A lifecycle management mechanism regulates experience memory via usage frequency, reuse feedback, and temporal decay to reduce redundancy and noise.

Result: RRM consistently outperforms previous state-of-the-art approaches on M3-Bench-Robot, M3-Bench-Web, and Video-MME-Long benchmarks.

Conclusion: Reflective retrieval memory effectively enables adaptive, experience-driven retrieval for long-horizon multimodal reasoning, demonstrating that capturing procedural search knowledge from past trajectories significantly improves agent performance.

Abstract: Existing multimodal long-term memory agents use external memory to overcome the limited context available for long videos. However, most methods emphasize what to store rather than how stored memory should be retrieved. When retrieval becomes inaccurate or repeatedly fails to obtain useful evidence, existing agents lack mechanisms to diagnose failures from previous task trajectories and adapt future search strategies.We introduce Reflective Retrieval Memory (RRM), a reflective memory framework for long-horizon multimodal reasoning. RRM augments an entity-centric multimodal memory graph with reflective experience memory, which distills transferable procedural retrieval knowledge from historical task trajectories. Unlike episodic and semantic memories that preserve factual evidence from the current video, reflective experience memory captures reusable search strategies across tasks. RRM converts retrieved experiences into query-level guidance, while answer generation remains conditioned only on factual evidence newly retrieved from the current video. A lifecycle management mechanism further regulates experience memory through usage frequency, reuse feedback, and temporal decay, thereby reducing redundancy and noise. RRM consistently outperforms previous state-of-the-art approaches on M3-Bench-Robot, M3-Bench-Web, and Video-MME-Long, demonstrating the effectiveness of reflective retrieval memory for long-horizon multimodal reasoning.

</details>


### [44] [Where and When to Commit: Candidate-Aware Decoding for Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28166)
*Chia-Ming Lee,Ming-Ching Chang,Xin Li,Yu-Lun Liu,Chih-Chung Hsu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LATCH is a training-free early-exit framework for diffusion language models that decouples termination decisions (CVC) from per-block acceleration (BWEC), using format-aware candidate extraction and stability verification to halt decoding. It achieves 9.3–17.8× speedups on short tasks and 2.0–3.3× on reasoning tasks while staying within 2% accuracy of full decoding across 11 zero-shot benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing early-exit methods for diffusion language models rely on fixed-region confidence or schedule-dependent rules, which are too coarse for long chain-of-thought outputs where answers stabilize only near the end. Adaptive sampling accelerates per-position commitment but never verifies full-output stability. The authors aim to unify and improve both axes — when to stop and where to accelerate — with decisions matched to evidence of appropriate scope.

Method: LATCH consists of two complementary mechanisms. (1) Confidence-Verified Commit (CVC): governs global termination by verifying both confidence and sustained argmax stability over a dynamically extracted candidate span, using a deterministic parser specified from each task's output format. (2) Block-Wise Early Commit (BWEC): governs local acceleration by applying a cheaper per-block rule to non-final blocks, while the final block and global termination remain under CVC control. The method requires no suffix-prompt construction and is prompt-anchor-free but format-aware. A single frozen hyperparameter set is used across all tasks and backbones.

Result: Evaluated on 11 zero-shot tasks using LLaDA and Dream backbones, LATCH stays within 2.0 percentage points of full-decoding accuracy across all 22 evaluation settings. End-to-end TPS speedups reach 9.3–17.8× on short-answer tasks and 2.0–3.3× on long-reasoning tasks, with one hyperparameter configuration that transfers untuned across backbones.

Conclusion: Decoupling termination from per-block acceleration and grounding each decision in appropriately scoped evidence (candidate-level stability for halting vs. local rules for intra-sequence committing) yields robust early-exit behavior for diffusion language models, preserving accuracy while delivering substantial inference speedups across diverse tasks and model architectures.

Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) expose a provisional prediction at every denoising step, creating an opportunity for generation-time early exit that stops decoding before the schedule is exhausted. Existing early-exit gates decide termination from fixed-region confidence statistics or schedule-dependent rules, evidence too coarse for a decision that freezes every remaining position at once, so they fire prematurely on long chain-of-thought outputs whose answers stabilize only near the end. Adaptive sampling, the other axis of training-free acceleration, paces how quickly positions commit while decoding continues but never verifies that the output itself has stabilized. We introduce a training-free, candidate-aware early-exit framework that keeps the two axes separate and matches each decision to evidence of its own scope. Confidence-Verified Commit (CVC) governs when the sequence may stop by verifying confidence and sustained argmax stability over the dynamically extracted candidate span using a deterministic parser specified from each task's output format. Block-Wise Early Commit (BWEC) governs where to accelerate by applying a cheaper local rule to non-final blocks, while leaving the final block and global termination under CVC. We refer to their combination as LATCH (Localized Acceleration with Tracked-Candidate Halting). Unlike prior methods, LATCH needs no suffix-prompt construction; it is prompt-anchor-free but format-aware. We evaluate LATCH end to end on 11 tasks under zero-shot settings using LLaDA and Dream. LATCH stays within 2.0 percentage points of full-decoding accuracy across all 22 evaluation settings, with one frozen hyperparameter set that transfers cross-backbone untuned, while achieving end-to-end TPS speedups of 9.3-17.8x on short-answer tasks and 2.0-3.3x on long-reasoning tasks.

</details>


### [45] [The MADRS Pipeline: Supporting Depression Assessment in Clinical Trials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28190)
*Mila Fodor,Katalin Ócsai,Francesco Periti,Rien Sonck,Alex Boudreau*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: An LLM-based pipeline converts clinical audio interviews into transcripts, maps them to MADRS symptom items, estimates severity, and flags problematic ratings, achieving a 0.867 correlation with expert assessments on real clinical trial data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated depression detection has focused on informal text sources (social media, online posts) but lacks robust tools for structured clinical trial settings where standardized interviews (e.g., SIGMA guidelines) are used. There is a need to support clinicians in MADRS-based depression assessment within formal clinical trials.

Method: An LLM-based pipeline that: (1) transcribes audio-recorded clinical interviews; (2) maps transcript content to the ten MADRS symptom items; (3) estimates severity for each item; and (4) identifies potentially problematic clinical ratings for review.

Result: The pipeline achieved a strong overall correlation of 0.867 with expert clinical ratings, demonstrating high agreement on real clinical interview data.

Conclusion: The LLM pipeline offers interpretable, automated support for depression severity assessment in clinical trials, showing strong alignment with expert judgments and potential to aid clinicians in standardized MADRS evaluations.

Abstract: Depression is a major mental disorder for which diagnosis relies primarily on clinical assessments. Automated methods to support its detection via the psychiatric MADRS scale are getting more and more attention. While existing solutions primarily focus on detecting the disorder from different text sources (e.g., online text, social media), there is still limited support for clinical trials, where clinical assessments are conducted through structured interviews based on standard guidelines such as SIGMA. In this work, we develop a LLM pipeline specifically designed to support clinicians in supporting the assessment of depression in patients enrolled in clinical trials. Our pipeline converts audio interviews into transcripts, maps them into the ten MADRS symptom items, estimates their severity, and identify problematic clinical ratings associated with them. Evaluation on real clinical interviews shows a strong overall correlation of 0.867 with expert ratings, providing interpretable support for future assessments in clinical trials.

</details>


### [46] [Fidelity Is Not Safety: Gently-Compressed LLMs Pass Every Data-Free Quality Guard Yet Invent Procedure Steps in Agentic Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28196)
*I. Kennedy,T. Kennedy*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Compressed language models can pass standard quality metrics (perplexity, MMLU accuracy, output-fidelity tests) yet silently invent new procedural steps when deployed as SOP-following agents. This failure is operator-specific: SVD-based low-rank compression induces it; magnitude pruning does not. The root cause is the coherence of compression error, not its magnitude. A new data-free screen based on coherent-fraction and error-rate flags failing models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
