Motivation: Current evaluation stacks for compressed language models rely on perplexity, downstream accuracy, and data-free fidelity probes. The authors identify a blind spot: these metrics fail to detect a critical safety failure where compressed models hallucinate procedure steps during agentic deployment, posing risks for real-world SOP-following applications.

Method: The authors systematically evaluate three model families under two compression operators: coherent low-rank (SVD) truncation and magnitude pruning, matched for perplexity. They design a pre-registered, powered "invented-step" canary test where models execute a standard operating procedure as agents. Paired confidence intervals compare fidelity-test performance against the canary. The compression error is decomposed into coherence and rate axes, motivating a two-axis screen (coherent-fraction × error-rate) with fixed thresholds.

Result: Gently-compressed SVD models clear all standard guards (perplexity, MMLU, fidelity) but invent procedure steps absent from instructions. Magnitude-pruned models at equal perplexity do not exhibit this failure. The dissociation is explained by coherence of compression error: weights that pass output-fidelity tests can fail the invented-step canary. The proposed two-axis screen flags failing builds with fixed thresholds across all three architectures, matching the coherence-times-rate mechanism.

Conclusion: Perplexity, MMLU, and fidelity acceptance do not certify agent safety in compressed models. Operator-specificity matters: low-rank compression introduces coherent errors that standard probes cannot detect but that corrupt agentic behavior. The proposed data-free two-axis screen provides a practical safeguard. Low-rank compressed models should be screened before agentic deployment.

Abstract: Practitioners accept a compressed language model once it clears a stack of data-cheap quality guards: perplexity within a small factor of the original, downstream accuracy (for example MMLU) inside a confidence interval, and data-free output-fidelity signals that compare the compressed and original network's internal representations under random probe inputs. This stack has a blind spot. Across three model families, gently-compressed models clear every guard and then invent procedure steps that were never in the instructions when they run a standard operating procedure (SOP) as an agent. The effect is operator-specific: coherent low-rank (SVD) truncation induces it, and magnitude pruning matched to the same perplexity does not. One dissociation isolates the cause. The same compressed weights that CI-win a paired output-fidelity test CI-fail the invented-step canary. The governing axis is the coherence of the compression error times its rate; the magnitude of the damage does not predict it. The data-free fidelity probe is a fidelity oracle by construction, so it cannot see this axis. We characterize the blindspot and dissociation with paired confidence intervals on a pre-registered, powered canary across three architectures. Operator-specificity replicates on all three, and the perplexity-guard evasion appears where the model admits in-guard low-rank headroom. We then give a data-free screen: a two-axis statistic of the compression error (coherent-fraction and error-rate) that flags the failing builds with fixed thresholds across architectures and matches the coherence-times-rate mechanism. Perplexity, MMLU, and fidelity acceptance do not certify agent safety. Screen gently-compressed low-rank builds before agentic deployment

</details>


### [47] [Causal Discovery with Inverted Self-attention for Multivariate Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28212)
*Yusen Liu,Yong Wang,Yifan Yin,Tianqing Zhu,Xiufeng Liu,Huan Huo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a transformer-based framework for causal discovery in multivariate time series that uses an inverted causal self-attention mechanism (CSAM) to capture latent and indirect causal relationships, complemented by a global causal algorithm and a verification module, outperforming existing methods on both linear and nonlinear datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing causal discovery methods for multivariate time series struggle with complex interactions, high dimensionality, and nonlinear dependencies, leading to inaccurate causal structures. There is a need for a more robust approach that can handle these challenges.

Method: The framework introduces three key components: (1) an inverted causal self-attention mechanism (CSAM) that inverts tokens and induces sparsity in attention scores to emphasize significant causal interactions while suppressing spurious correlations; (2) a global causal algorithm that identifies global causal links and provides a holistic metric for causal influence; and (3) a causal verification module to ensure robustness of identified causal relationships. The approach is built within the transformer architecture.

Result: Experiments on both linear and nonlinear datasets, along with ablation studies and sensitivity analyses, demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms existing causal discovery methods.

Conclusion: The proposed transformer-based framework with inverted causal self-attention shows strong potential for accurate causal discovery in complex multivariate time series, overcoming limitations of prior approaches.

Abstract: Causal discovery in multivariate time series data is challenging due to complex interactions, high dimensionality, and nonlinear dependencies among variables. Existing methods often struggle to capture these complexities, resulting in inaccurate causal structures. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework that leverages self-attention mechanisms within the transformer architecture for causal discovery. Our approach introduces a novel inverted causal self-attention mechanism (CSAM) that emphasizes latent and indirect causal relationships by inverting tokens and inducing sparsity in attention scores, focusing on significant causal interactions and reducing spurious correlations. Additionally, we develop a global causal algorithm to identify global causal links, providing a holistic metric for causal influence, along with a causal verification module to ensure robustness in the identified causal relationships, enhancing the reliability of our framework. Experiments on both linear and nonlinear datasets, along with ablation studies and sensitivity analyses, show that our framework outperforms existing methods, demonstrating its potential for causal discovery in complex multivariate time series.

</details>


### [48] [Understanding Is Done Early: A Depth Division of Labor in Large Language Models and Its Use for Unbounded-Context Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28263)
*Hanzuo Liu,Xuan Qi,Chunyu Liu,Haotian Zhong,Yulong Wang,Rayying,Key,Alex Lamb,Mingyu Gao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CoMem leverages the layer-wise division of labor in Transformers by caching intermediate-layer representations of context chunks, then recomputing only upper layers at query time. This yields bounded memory and compute independent of context length, achieving strong long-context performance with dramatic memory savings and prefill speedups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformer layers exhibit a functional division: lower/middle layers build semantic representations, while upper layers specialize them for prediction. Existing KV-cache methods store per-token states across all layers, causing memory and compute to scale linearly with context length. The authors ask: can long-context memory be organized along the layer axis rather than the token axis, exploiting this division of labor?

Method: CoMem (Comprehension Memory) writes each context chunk only at a selected intermediate layer, caching the residual stream states. At query time, it retrieves a fixed number of these cached states (top-k by similarity), packs them, and recomputes the upper layers conditioned on the query. The backbone is frozen; a rank-32 LoRA adapter is trained via self-distillation on PG19. An adapter-free variant is also reported. Evaluation uses a unified chat-template-free protocol on RULER, LoCoMo, and other long-context/long-document benchmarks. Depth sweeps analyze the trade-off between caching depth, recomputation cost, and fidelity.

Result: CoMem achieves 97.05 on RULER and 38.27 on LoCoMo (vs. 34.59 for full-context KV-Direct). Dialogue-memory advantages persist under conversation-cluster resampling and independent judging. On an NVIDIA H20 at 128k context, CoMem uses 18.26 GB (vs. 89.36 GB) with a 7.83× prefill speedup. Deeper caching reduces per-query recomputation but incurs fidelity loss, which self-distillation substantially repairs.

Conclusion: Long-context memory can be effectively organized along the layer axis. CoMem demonstrates that caching intermediate representations with bounded retrieval and selective upper-layer recomputation yields competitive long-context performance with dramatically reduced memory footprint and latency, offering a complementary axis to token-level compression methods.

Abstract: Transformer depth is not used uniformly: lower and middle layers build semantic representations, while upper layers increasingly specialize them for prediction. We turn this division of labor into CoMem (Comprehension Memory), which writes each context chunk only through an intermediate layer, retrieves a fixed number of cached residual states, and recomputes the query-conditioned upper layers over the resulting pack. For a fixed retrieval budget, model-side read compute and memory are independent of stored-context length. We evaluate a continued-trained Qwen3-8B base LM under a unified chat-template-free protocol. The backbone is frozen; the flagship trains only a rank-32 self-distillation LoRA on plain PG19, and we report an adapter-free arm separately. CoMem reaches 97.05 on RULER and 38.27 on LoCoMo versus 34.59 for full-context KV-Direct; the dialogue-memory advantage survives conversation-cluster resampling and an independent judge. Results on additional long-context and long-document tasks expose both the benefits of bounded retrieval and its in-window compression tax. Controlled depth sweeps show that deeper caching lowers per-query recomputation but incurs a fidelity loss that self-distillation substantially repairs. In a separate adapter-free efficiency control on an NVIDIA H20 at 128k, CoMem uses 18.26 GB rather than 89.36 GB and achieves a 7.83x prefill speedup. These results show that long-context memory can be organized along the layer axis, not only the token axis.

</details>


### [49] [MORFES: A Benchmark for Productive Inflectional Competence in Modern Greek](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28274)
*Ioakeim Perros,Cleopatra Papadopoulou,Ayoub Kirouane,Christos Petrocheilos*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MORFES is a 500-item expert-verified benchmark for evaluating inflectional morphology in Modern Greek, testing both recognition and production of inflected forms. The authors evaluate various open models, finding that their newly released Sophea-Genesis-1 leads on morphological tasks while maintaining general capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern Greek is morphologically rich, yet existing language model evaluations for Greek focus on factual knowledge, leaving grammatical competence—particularly inflectional morphology—unmeasured. This gap is especially pressing as open-weight multilingual models scale rapidly without dedicated morphological benchmarks.

Method: The authors construct MORFES, a benchmark of 500 expert-verified items testing recognition and production of Greek inflected forms. Items deliberately favor lower-frequency lemmas so that correct answers reflect rule-based generalization rather than rote memorization. They then evaluate a spectrum of open models (LLaMA, Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1, Magistral, Kimi K2, and their own Sophea-Genesis-1) on this benchmark.

Result: Sophea-Genesis-1, the authors' newly released open-weight model, achieves the highest performance on inflectional morphology among evaluated models while matching similarly sized models in general capability. The benchmark reveals that grammatical competence in morphologically rich languages remains under-measured even as multilingual coverage expands.

Conclusion: Dedicated morphological benchmarks like MORFES are essential for properly evaluating language models in morphologically rich languages. The authors contribute both the benchmark and Sophea-Genesis-1 as open resources to advance research in this under-explored area.

Abstract: Modern Greek is a richly inflected language, yet the language models built for it are evaluated mainly on factual knowledge, and no benchmark is dedicated to their inflectional competence. We introduce MORFES (Morphological Open-class Recognition-and-Formation Evaluation Suite), a benchmark of 500 expert-verified items that tests the recognition and production of Greek inflected forms, favoring lower-frequency lemmas so that a correct answer reflects the rule rather than a memorized form. We make it publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/KIEFERSA/MORFES. We evaluate a range of open language models on MORFES, situating them within the rapidly scaling open-weight ecosystem from LLaMA to Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1, Magistral, and Kimi K2, where multilingual coverage grows but grammatical competence in morphologically rich languages remains under-measured. Among them, Sophea-Genesis-1, a model we developed and release as open weights at https://huggingface.co/KIEFERSA/Sophea-Genesis-1, leads on inflectional morphology while matching similarly sized models in general capability.

</details>


### [50] [(Towards) Scalable Reliable Automated Evaluation with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28282)
*Bertil Braun,Martin Forell*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A framework that uses pairwise comparisons among multiple LLMs with an Elo rating system to approximate expert-level evaluations of LLM outputs, reducing human effort while maintaining correlation with expert judgments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automated metrics for evaluating LLM outputs are resource-intensive, fail to capture output complexity/variability, and rely on explicit reference standards—limiting them to domains with objective benchmarks. There is a need for scalable, domain-agnostic evaluation that approximates expert assessment.

Method: The framework employs pairwise comparisons of outputs by multiple LLMs to reduce individual model biases. An Elo rating system generates stable, interpretable rankings. Adjustable agreement thresholds (from full unanimity to majority voting) allow flexible control over evaluation confidence and coverage.

Result: Preliminary results demonstrate that automatically derived rankings correlate well with expert judgments, significantly reducing the need for extensive human intervention. The method was validated on competency profiles extracted from scientific abstracts.

Conclusion: The framework offers a scalable, consistent, and domain-agnostic evaluation layer that supports more efficient and reliable quality assessments of LLM outputs across diverse applications.

Abstract: Evaluating the quality and relevance of textual outputs from Large Language Models (LLMs) remains challenging and resource-intensive. Existing automated metrics often fail to capture the complexity and variability inherent in LLM-generated outputs. Moreover, these metrics typically rely on explicit reference standards, limiting their use mostly to domains with objective benchmarks. This work introduces a novel evaluation framework designed to approximate expert-level assessments of LLM-generated content. The proposed method employs pairwise comparisons of outputs by multiple LLMs, reducing biases from individual models. An Elo rating system is used to generate stable and interpretable rankings. Adjustable agreement thresholds, from full unanimity to majority voting, allow flexible control over evaluation confidence and coverage. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through evaluating competency profiles extracted from scientific abstracts. Preliminary results show that automatically derived rankings correlate well with expert judgments, significantly reducing the need for extensive human intervention. By offering a scalable, consistent, and domain-agnostic evaluation layer, the framework supports more efficient and reliable quality assessments of LLM outputs across diverse applications.

</details>


### [51] [CACHE-UK: A Stability-Aware Memory Editor for Sequentially Updated Quantized LLMs in Finance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28292)
*Anubhav Lakra,Yue Feng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CACHE-UK is a stability-aware memory editing framework for 4-bit quantized LLMs in UK finance that reduces knowledge degradation by 11-17% and improves generalization by 6 percentage points over baselines, though overall generalization remains low at 28%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs in dynamic financial environments must maintain factual accuracy as market conditions and regulations change. 4-bit quantization enables efficient deployment but causes catastrophic performance degradation during sequential memory editing — a "quantization stability crisis" that existing methods cannot handle.

Method: CACHE-UK combines three components: (1) a rank-1 LoRA perturbation mechanism that confines edits to a low-rank adapter subspace, (2) a financial domain prioritization module for content-adaptive edit strength, and (3) a closed-loop Stability Controller that tracks "degradation debt" to prevent catastrophic forgetting across sequential updates.

Result: On a 4-bit quantized OpenLLaMA-3B model with 88,021 UK financial documents, CACHE-UK reduces knowledge degradation by 11-17% relative to adapted baselines and achieves a 28% generalization rate (a 6 percentage point improvement over the strongest baseline). Absolute generalization rates remain low.

Conclusion: Stability-aware editing can improve factual maintenance in resource-constrained financial LLM deployments, but the low absolute generalization rates indicate that further advances are needed for practical reliability.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) deployed in dynamic financial environments face a critical challenge: maintaining factual accuracy as market conditions, regulations, and corporate facts change continuously. While 4-bit quantization enables efficient deployment, it severely limits the viability of sequential memory editing: existing methods undergo catastrophic performance degradation under this "quantization stability crisis." We introduce CACHE-UK (Contextual Adaptive Continual Hybrid Editor for UK Finance), a stability-aware memory editing framework specifically designed for domain-specific, quantized LLMs. CACHE-UK integrates three components: a rank-1 LoRA perturbation mechanism that confines edits to the low-rank adapter subspace, a financial domain prioritization module for content-adaptive edit strength, and a closed-loop Stability Controller that tracks "degradation debt" to prevent catastrophic forgetting across sequential updates. Evaluated on a 4-bit quantized OpenLLaMA-3B model with a curated UK financial corpus of 88,021 documents, CACHE-UK reduces knowledge degradation by 11-17% relative to adapted baselines under identical 4-bit constraints -- its most robust effect -- while attaining the highest test success (generalization) rate observed in our setting (28%, a 6 percentage point improvement over the strongest adapted baseline). These results indicate that stability-aware editing can improve factual maintenance in resource-constrained financial LLM deployments, though absolute generalization rates remain low.

</details>


### [52] [Fairness Pruning: Locating Demographic Bias in GLU-MLP Layers via Differential Activations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28319)
*Pere Martra,Eugenio Martínez Cámara,Alfonso Ureña López*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Fairness Pruning identifies neurons causally linked to demographic bias in LLMs via activation analysis on GLU architectures. Zeroing ≤40 neurons (<0.031% parameters) destabilizes bias bidirectionally while preserving 99.49% of reasoning/knowledge capabilities, demonstrating dissociable circuits for bias and competence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop a lightweight, surgical method for localizing and mitigating demographic bias in LLMs without impairing model capabilities, establishing empirical evidence that bias processing and general reasoning operate on dissociable neural circuits.

Method: Uses minimally contrastive prompt pairs with inference-time activation capture to identify neurons in GLU architectures (at the down_proj input) that respond differentially to demographic attributes. The intervention consists of zeroing these localized neurons, tested on Llama-3.2 family models and Salamandra-2B (up to 3B parameters), evaluated via standardized benchmarks and qualitative text generation.

Result: Zeroing at most 40 neurons (<0.031% of MLP width) in Llama-3.2-1B yields 99.49% retention of reasoning and general knowledge. Bias mitigation is not flat but bidirectional: unsigned BiasScore mixes neurons pushing toward and against stereotypes, so net effect depends on dominant sign. Bias processing and capabilities are dissociable.

Conclusion: Demographic bias and model capabilities operate on dissociable circuits. The intervention is extremely surgical and preserves performance, but future work must move from blind zeroing toward directional behavior modulation to achieve consistent bias mitigation rather than bidirectional destabilization.

Abstract: This work presents Fairness Pruning, a lightweight structural intervention method designed for the management and future mitigation of demographic bias in large language models (LLMs). As a foundational empirical validation of this method, this work focuses on causal bias localization. Using minimally contrastive prompt pairs and inference-time activation capture, the method identifies neurons that react differentially when processing demographic attributes in GLU architectures, evaluating the signal at the down_proj input. Empirical evaluation was conducted on models of up to 3 billion parameters (Llama-3.2 family and Salamandra-2B), combining standardized benchmark evaluation with qualitative text generation experiments. Results demonstrate that zeroing the identified neurons alters how the model responds to associated demographic variables. However, rather than producing flat mitigation, the intervention causes bidirectional bias destabilization: because BiasScore is unsigned, candidate sets mix neurons that push toward and against the stereotype, and the net effect on aggregate bias depends on which sign dominates. The intervention is extremely surgical: zeroing at most 40 neurons in Llama-3.2-1B (less than 0.031% of total MLP width) achieves a mean retention of 99.49% in reasoning and general knowledge capabilities. These findings empirically confirm that demographic bias processing and model capabilities operate on dissociable circuits, establishing the methodological foundations for transitioning from blind zeroing toward directional behavior modulation.

</details>


### [53] [LLMs struggle to simulate human belief updates in controlled environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28347)
*Sebastian Pohl,Harsh Mehta,Pranav Mambayil,Abdul Ghafoor,Franziska Lesigang,Yufang Hou,Christian Hilbe*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Six LLMs were tested on their ability to simulate individual human belief updates after reading social media comments. Models only matched human post-discussion stances when given actual initial stances; they failed to generate realistic initial stances themselves, exhibited systematic biases (neutrality overrepresentation, smaller belief shifts, poor comment ranking), and did not benefit from demographic/trait personas.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as proxies for human participants in social science experiments, but the fidelity of these simulations—particularly for modeling belief dynamics—has rarely been empirically validated against ground-truth human data.

Method: Six LLMs were prompted with demographic and personality trait personas derived from real participants. Each LLM simulated 391 UK Prolific participants who updated their stances on three discussion topics after reading Reddit comments. LLM outputs were compared 1-to-1 against the actual human belief update data.

Result: Qwen3-32B and GPT-5-Mini matched the human post-stance distribution only when supplied with participants' actual initial stances. All six models failed to self-generate realistic initial stances and to produce faithful belief updates from those self-generated stances. Three systematic biases were found: overrepresentation of neutral positions, more frequent but smaller-than-human belief shifts, and inability to rank comments by convincingness. Demographic and personality trait personas had no consistent effect on simulation fidelity.

Conclusion: LLM simulations of human belief dynamics are only reliable when grounded in realistic starting conditions—a requirement that current multi-round social media simulations rarely satisfy, raising concerns about the validity of using LLMs as human proxies in this domain.

Abstract: LLMs are increasingly deployed as proxies for human study participants in social science experiments, yet the fidelity of this practice has rarely been tested directly. We test whether six LLMs can simulate individual human belief updates, comparing LLM outputs 1-to-1 against ground truth data from 391 UK participants on Prolific, who updated their stances on three discussion topics after reading Reddit comments. Each participant was simulated by an LLM conditioned on a persona derived from their demographic and personality trait data. We find that some LLMs (Qwen3-32B and GPT-5-Mini) can match the human post-stance distribution, but only when given participants' actual initial stances. All six models fail to simulate initial stances themselves and to produce faithful belief updates from self-generated stances. Three systematic biases emerge across all models: overrepresentation of neutral positions, more frequent but smaller belief shifts than humans, and a failure to rank comments by convincingness. Demographic and personality trait personas had no consistent effect on fidelity. LLM simulations of human belief dynamics are only reliable when grounded in realistic starting conditions, that current multi-round social media simulations rarely provide.

</details>


### [54] [Correlation between prosody and pragmatics: A case study of the discourse marker hālā `now' in Persian](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28359)
*Soleiman Ghaderi,Moloud Asakereh,Kevin Tang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The Persian discourse marker hālā ('now') shows extensive multifunctionality beyond its temporal origin, with 70% of tokens serving multiple pragmatic roles. Acoustic analysis reveals duration and intensity as key prosodic cues distinguishing textual, interactive, and modal functions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate the full range of pragmatic functions of the Persian discourse marker hālā and identify the prosodic cues (duration, intensity) that correlate with its functional differentiation in spontaneous spoken discourse.

Method: Pragmatic and acoustic analysis of 267 instances of hālā drawn from spontaneous Persian conversations, categorizing tokens into textual, interactive, and modal functions and measuring prosodic features including duration and intensity.

Result: Temporal uses were present but frequently co-occurred with other functions; 70% of tokens were multifunctional. Textual functions (topic shifting, signaling, boundary marking, etc.) were most frequent, followed by interactive (turn management, engagement, feedback) and modal functions (epistemic stance, emotional expression, attitudinal marking). Textual uses were significantly shorter in duration; interactive uses correlated with higher intensity; modal uses showed a weak tendency toward lower intensity.

Conclusion: Hālā is a highly multifunctional discourse marker whose textual, interactive, and modal roles are partially distinguishable through prosodic cues — primarily duration and intensity — with textual and interactive functions showing the clearest acoustic differentiation.

Abstract: The Persian discourse marker hālā ('now') exhibits remarkable multifunctionality, extending far beyond its temporal adverbial role to encompass a variety of pragmatic functions. This study presents a pragmatic and acoustic analysis of hālā in spoken Persian, examining 267 instances from spontaneous conversations. While temporal uses were present, they were often combined with other discourse marker functions, indicating extensive multifunctionality, with 70% of tokens serving two or more pragmatic roles. Textual functions (topic shifting, signaling relationships, boundary marking, attention guidance, topic introduction, and topic emphasis) were most frequent, followed by interactive functions (turn management, listener engagement, and feedback regulation), and modal functions (epistemic stance, emotional expression, and attitudinal marking). Prosodic analysis revealed that duration and intensity are key cues for distinguishing hālā's functions. Textual uses were significantly shorter, while temporal uses showed a tendency toward longer realizations. Interactive functions correlated with higher intensity, while modal functions showed a weaker tendency toward lower intensity. These findings indicate that duration and intensity are the main prosodic cues associated with functional differentiation in hālā, especially in textual and interactive uses.

</details>


### [55] [Beyond a Single Judge: Simulating Social Persona Panels for Generative UI Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28439)
*Zheng Wu,Yibo Luo,Pu Zhang,Cheng Yang,Zhuosheng Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ESPP is a three-stage GenUI evaluation method using a panel of psychologically diverse, evidence-grounded personas with bounded-confidence opinion exchange and Delphi-inspired social weighting, achieving Pearson r=0.922 vs. human judgment (vs. 0.716 for naive single-pass judge), while preserving subgroup disagreement that homogeneous judges erase.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current GenUI evaluation methods fall into two unsatisfactory extremes: human evaluation is costly and rater-variant, while LLM-as-a-judge is scalable but reflects only a single implicit viewpoint, failing to capture how diverse real-user populations perceive the same interface. There is a need for an automated method that tracks human judgment faithfully while preserving the diversity of user perspectives.

Method: ESPP operates in three stages: (1) a panel of psychologically diverse, evidence-grounded personas independently rates a GenUI screenshot; (2) personas exchange opinions under a trait-derived, semantically-gated bounded-confidence mechanism; (3) ratings are aggregated via Delphi-inspired social weighting into a single judgment. A prompt-ensemble baseline serves as an ablation control.

Result: ESPP raises Pearson r from 0.716 (naive single-pass judge) to 0.922 against human judgments. A prompt-ensemble control recovers only about one-third of this gap, isolating genuine persona diversity and evidence grounding as the dominant drivers. Individual panelist ratings reveal that user subgroups agree on overall model rankings but diverge sharply on specific rating dimensions.

Conclusion: ESPP substantially improves automated GenUI evaluation fidelity to human judgment while surfacing structurally meaningful subgroup disagreements that homogeneous judges systematically erase, offering a more faithful and socially nuanced evaluation paradigm.

Abstract: Generative UI (GenUI) lets large language models synthesize a complete, renderable interface directly from a natural-language instruction, but evaluating the quality of what they generate remains an open problem. Human evaluation is costly and rater-variant, while LLM-as-a-judge is scalable but reflects only a single implicit viewpoint, unable to capture how different populations of real users actually perceive the same interface. We propose the Evidence-Grounded, Social-Weighted Persona Panel (ESPP), a three-stage GenUI evaluation method in which a panel of psychologically diverse, evidence-grounded personas independently rates a screenshot, exchanges opinions under a trait-derived, semantically-gated bounded-confidence mechanism, and is aggregated via Delphi-inspired social weighting into a single judgment. ESPP tracks human judgment substantially more closely than a naive single-pass judge, raising Pearson $r$ from $0.716$ to $0.922$, and a prompt-ensemble control recovers only about a third of this gap, isolating genuine persona and evidence grounding as the dominant source of improvement. Beyond this fidelity gain, retaining each panelist's individual rating further reveals that user subgroups agree on overall model rankings yet diverge sharply on specific rating dimensions, a structural disagreement a single homogeneous judge would systematically erase. The codes are available at https://github.com/Wuzheng02/ESPP.

</details>


### [56] [Lightning OPD 2.0: Mitigating Style Bias in Cross-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Large Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28449)
*Yecheng Wu,Song Han,Han Cai*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Lightning OPD 2.0 introduces cross-fitted style residualization to address the teacher consistency problem in on-policy distillation. By estimating and removing style-token bias (differences in wording, formatting, reasoning cadence) before computing token-level updates, it enables effective cross-teacher OPD where the SFT data generator and distillation teacher differ, achieving 82.4% on AIME 2024 and 63.0% on LiveCodeBench v5.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy distillation (OPD) requires teacher consistency — the model providing token-level supervision must match the one that generated the SFT demonstrations. In practice, this is often violated (mixed/unknown provenance, or different models preferred for SFT generation vs. distillation). In such cross-teacher settings, even a stronger teacher can yield negligible improvement. The paper aims to solve this by separating useful context-specific teacher signal from recurring style-token bias.

Method: The authors propose Lightning OPD 2.0 with cross-fitted style residualization. They observe that teacher–reference disagreement contains two components: (1) useful context-specific teacher evidence, and (2) a recurring component from systematic style differences (wording, formatting, reasoning cadence). Using rollout-level cross-fitting, they estimate this recurring style-token bias and subtract it from the raw disagreement before constructing the token-level OPD update, thereby isolating the genuine teacher signal.

Result: Lightning OPD 2.0 consistently outperforms the original Lightning OPD across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks in cross-teacher settings. Starting from Klear-Reasoner-8B-SFT, it achieves 82.4% on AIME 2024 and 63.0% on LiveCodeBench v5.

Conclusion: Lightning OPD 2.0 is a practical approach to cross-teacher OPD that relaxes teacher consistency as a prerequisite, allowing independent selection of the SFT data generator and distillation teacher while maintaining strong performance gains.

Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision from a teacher, but its effectiveness can depend on teacher consistency, meaning that the model providing OPD supervision should also have generated the demonstrations used to train the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) reference. However, this condition is frequently violated in practice when SFT data have mixed or unknown provenance or when different models are preferred for SFT data generation and subsequent distillation. In such cross-teacher settings, even a stronger OPD teacher can yield little improvement over the SFT reference. We find that raw teacher--reference disagreement contains potentially useful context-specific teacher evidence as well as a recurring component associated with differences in wording, formatting, and reasoning cadence. We introduce Lightning OPD 2.0 with cross-fitted style residualization, which uses rollout-level cross-fitting to estimate this recurring component as an operational proxy for style-token bias and subtracts it before constructing the token-level OPD update. Across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks, Lightning OPD 2.0 consistently outperforms Lightning OPD in cross-teacher settings. Starting from Klear-Reasoner-8B-SFT, Lightning OPD 2.0 reaches 82.4% on AIME 2024 and 63.0% on LiveCodeBench v5. Together, these results establish Lightning OPD 2.0 as a practical approach to cross-teacher OPD, relaxing teacher consistency as a prerequisite and allowing the SFT data generator and distillation teacher to be selected independently. Code will be released soon.

</details>


### [57] [Improving Mental Health Screening and Early Risk Detection in Spanish](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28476)
*Andreu Casamayor-Segarra,Vicent Ahuir,Antonio Molina-Marco,Lluís-F. Hurtado*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper tackles early detection of mental health disorders in Spanish social media by introducing: (1) three domain-adapted Spanish foundation models, (2) Incremental Context Expansion (ICE), a relabeling technique that identifies the minimal cumulative evidence threshold for disorder detection, and (3) fine-tuned models for early risk detection using ICE-generated samples. The approach achieves SOTA results, lowering detection latency without sacrificing performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Early detection of mental health disorders via social media is hindered by two key problems: a scarcity of specialized Spanish-language resources and the inherent difficulty of analyzing long message histories to pinpoint the earliest moment a disorder becomes identifiable. Current systems lack the linguistic specialization and temporal precision needed for effective early intervention in Spanish-speaking populations.

Method: The methodology has three components. (1) Domain-specific pre-training: three Spanish foundational models are further pre-trained on mental-health-domain corpora to create specialized representations. (2) Incremental Context Expansion (ICE): an automatic relabeling strategy that incrementally accumulates a user's messages over time and determines the earliest point where the cumulative context provides sufficient evidence to assign a disorder label, thereby generating temporally precise training samples. (3) Fine-tuning: these ICE-generated samples are used to fine-tune the domain-adapted models for early risk detection tasks.

Result: Evaluated on three Spanish benchmarks, the combination of domain-specialized models and ICE-based training outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods. The approach achieves both high detection accuracy and reduced detection latency, enabling earlier flagging of at-risk individuals.

Conclusion: Domain-adapted Spanish foundation models paired with the ICE relabeling methodology significantly advance early mental health risk detection on social media. The approach balances performance and latency, and the public release of all models supports reproducibility and further research.

Abstract: Early detection of mental health disorders is often limited by the lack of specialized resources in Spanish and the difficulty of analyzing long histories of social media posts. This paper addresses these challenges through three main contributions. First, we introduce three Spanish foundational models specifically adapted to the mental health domain through domain-specific pre-training. Second, we propose Incremental Context Expansion (ICE), an automatic relabeling methodology designed for early detection. ICE identifies the point at which cumulative messages provide enough evidence of a disorder, generating more informative training samples. Third, we provide a set of fine-tuned models using the samples generated with the ICE methodology for early risk detection tasks. Our results on three Spanish benchmarks show that combining these specialized models with ICE improves the state-of-the-art, reducing detection latency while maintaining high performance. All models are publicly available.

</details>


### [58] [Would You Walk to the Car Wash? Revealing the Salience Bias of Large Language Models in Commonsense Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28478)
*Zheng Wu,Chenhao Xue,Shijie Zheng,Yijie Lu,Cheng Yang,Zhuosheng Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs exhibit "Salience Bias," where explicit distractors cause them to override implicit commonsense knowledge. The SaliTrap benchmark reveals this is a knowledge suppression problem, not a knowledge absence problem—over 90% of failures are recovered by removing task framing. Lightweight prompting interventions substantially close the gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs have become adept at complex reasoning but overly rely on explicit input conditions. This creates a vulnerability in commonsense reasoning: salient but irrelevant distractors hijack model behavior. The critical open question is whether these failures stem from genuine knowledge gaps or from knowledge being suppressed by misleading task framing.

Method: The authors construct SaliTrap, a benchmark spanning four trap dimensions, and evaluate 12 state-of-the-art LLMs. They employ a two-stage diagnostic approach: (1) measuring performance under standard task framing with distractors, and (2) re-eliciting the same models in a context-free knowledge probe to determine whether the underlying commonsense knowledge is present but suppressed. They further test lightweight inference-time prompting interventions to mitigate the bias.

Result: All 12 mainstream LLMs suffer significantly from salience bias, with severity scaling with distractor density. Detecting the trap is often decoupled from avoiding it. Crucially, context-free probing recovers over 90% of sycophantic-compliance failures, confirming knowledge suppression rather than absence. Lightweight inference-time prompting substantially closes the gap without retraining.

Conclusion: The bottleneck in commonsense reasoning failures is relocated from model competence to elicitation. The requisite commonsense knowledge is intrinsically present in LLMs but is actively crowded out by salient distractors that induce over-compliant, unnecessary computation. SaliTrap is released as a testbed for studying this blind spot.

Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) continue to advance in complex reasoning tasks, they have learned to heavily prioritize explicit conditions provided in the input. However, in everyday commonsense reasoning, this mechanism exposes a critical vulnerability which we term Salience Bias: models become easily hijacked by useless explicit distractors (e.g., numerical values), leading them to ignore the implicit physical or commonsense prerequisites of a task. A critical open question is whether this failure reflects a genuine gap in commonsense knowledge or merely its suppression under misleading task framing. To investigate this, we construct the SaliTrap Benchmark, a high-quality dataset across four trap dimensions. Evaluating 12 state-of-the-art LLMs, we find that all mainstream models suffer significantly from salience bias, with severity scaling with distractor density and detecting the trap often decoupled from actually avoiding it. Crucially, by re-eliciting the same models with the task framing stripped away, we show that this is overwhelmingly a failure of \textbf{knowledge suppression rather than knowledge absence}: a context-free knowledge probe alone recovers over 90\% of sycophantic-compliance failures, revealing that the requisite commonsense is intrinsically present but actively crowded out by salient distractors that lure the model into over-compliant, unnecessary computation. Building on this diagnosis, we further show that lightweight, inference-time prompting alone substantially closes the gap without any retraining. Our findings relocate the bottleneck of commonsense reasoning failures from model competence to elicitation, and we release SaliTrap as a testbed for this blind spot. The codes are available at https://github.com/Wuzheng02/SaliTrap.

</details>


### [59] [Beyond Sentiment: Structured Information Extraction from Financial News](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28496)
*Daohan Zhu,Sitong Ge,Ruofei Wang,Honggu Chen,Yubo Hou,Tao Wan,Zengchang Qin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Financial news sentiment analysis reduces articles to a single polarity score, ignoring orthogonal dimensions like event type, impact scope, temporal horizon, and confidence. Using LLaMA-3.1-70B to extract six semantic dimensions, the authors show that these dimensions carry information independent of sentiment, and combining both yields significantly better stock prediction (F1=0.600) than sentiment alone, with all dimensions contributing 14–21% in feature importance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional financial sentiment analysis collapses rich, multi-dimensional news content into a single sentiment polarity score, potentially discarding orthogonal predictive signals. The authors hypothesize that dimensions such as event type, impact scope, temporal horizon, and semantic confidence carry independent predictive value that sentiment alone cannot capture.

Method: The authors propose a structured information extraction framework using LLaMA-3.1-70B to extract six semantic dimensions from financial news. They conduct large-scale experiments on 41,618 news–stock pairs from the FNSPID dataset, comparing FinBERT sentiment features against LLM-extracted structured features under both linear and nonlinear models, and evaluate combined performance via ablation studies and feature importance analysis.

Result: FinBERT sentiment shows strong nonlinear predictive power (F1=0.576) but weak linear performance (F1=0.230). LLM-extracted structured features exhibit a 53.5% systematic disagreement rate with sentiment, confirming orthogonality. Combining both signals achieves F1=0.600, significantly outperforming either alone (p < 0.0001). Non-sentiment structural dimensions independently contribute ΔF1=+0.019 beyond FinBERT. All six dimensions show balanced feature importance (14–21%), indicating substantial information loss from single-score compression.

Conclusion: The sentiment–semantics decoupling in financial text is systematic and exploitable. Moving beyond unidimensional sentiment to multi-dimensional structured extraction opens a promising new direction for financial NLP, demonstrating that non-sentiment dimensions provide independent and complementary predictive value for stock movement forecasting.

Abstract: Financial sentiment analysis has become a standard component in news-driven stock prediction, yet it reduces rich, multi-dimensional news articles to a single polarity score. We hypothesize that financial news encodes multiple orthogonal information dimensions---event type, impact scope, temporal horizon, and semantic confidence---that sentiment alone cannot capture, and that these dimensions carry independent predictive value. To test this hypothesis, we propose a structured information extraction framework that leverages LLaMA-3.1-70B to extract six semantic dimensions from financial news. Through large-scale experiments on 41,618 news--stock pairs from the FNSPID dataset, we find that (i) FinBERT sentiment features exhibit strong predictive power under nonlinear models (F1=0.576) but substantially weaker performance under linear models (F1=0.230), revealing a highly nonlinear sentiment--return relationship; (ii) LLM-extracted structured features, while individually weaker, capture information orthogonal to sentiment, as evidenced by a 53.5% systematic disagreement rate between the two approaches; and (iii) combining both signal sources yields F1=0.600, significantly outperforming either alone ($p < 0.0001$), with consistent improvements across all seven event types. Ablation experiments confirm that non-sentiment structural dimensions (event type, impact subject, time horizon, confidence) independently contribute $Δ\text{F1} = +0.019$ beyond FinBERT alone. Feature importance analysis reveals balanced contributions from all six extracted dimensions (14--21%), demonstrating that compressing news into a single sentiment score incurs substantial information loss. Our results suggest that the sentiment--semantics decoupling in financial text is systematic and exploitable, opening a new direction for multi-dimensional financial NLP.

</details>


### [60] [Generative AI and linguistic diversity in academic writing and publishing: Perspectives from World Englishes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28505)
*Kingsley Ugwuanyi,Christian Mair,Sender Dovchin,Iker Erdocia,Maria Kuteeva,Esther Airemionkhale*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This article presents a structured dialogue among five sociolinguists examining how generative AI affects linguistic inclusivity in academic writing. It finds GenAI can both reinforce linguistic hierarchies and serve as a site of resistance, depending on design, governance, and scholarly community practices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rise of GenAI in academic writing and publishing raises urgent questions about linguistic inclusivity and the legitimacy of diverse Englishes (World Englishes) in global scholarly communication. There is a need to interrogate whether these tools democratize writing or further marginalize minoritized language varieties.

Method: A structured scholarly dialogue involving five sociolinguists from World Englishes and adjacent fields, organized around five guiding questions that probe GenAI's influence on writing practices, language norms, and ethical challenges.

Result: Contributors found GenAI holds potential to democratize writing but also tends to marginalize minoritized varieties and flatten scholarly nuance. Key themes emerging include linguistic (in)justice, researcher agency, and institutional responsibility. Contributors advocated for equity-informed policies, critical AI literacy, and inclusive co-design.

Conclusion: GenAI can both reinforce existing hierarchies and function as a site of resistance, depending on design, governance, and use within scholarly communities committed to linguistic diversity. Dialogic reflection proves valuable for understanding GenAI's role in academic writing and publishing.

Abstract: The rise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in academic writing and publishing (AWP) raises questions about linguistic inclusivity and the legitimacy of diverse Englishes in global scholarly communication. This article responds to these questions through a structured scholarly dialogue involving five sociolinguists from World Englishes and adjacent fields. Organised around five guiding questions, the dialogue interrogates how GenAI tools influence writing practices, reinforce or disrupt dominant language norms, and raise ethical challenges. Contributors reflect on the potential of GenAI to democratise writing processes while also raising concerns about GenAI's tendency to marginalise minoritised varieties and flatten nuance in scholarly writing. Across the dialogue, themes of linguistic (in)justice, researcher agency, and institutional responsibility emerge, with contributors calling for equity-informed policies, critical AI literacy, and inclusive co-design in GenAI development. The article shows the value of dialogic reflection in understanding GenAI's role in AWP. It concludes that while GenAI may reinforce existing hierarchies, it can also serve as a site of resistance, depending on how it is designed, governed and used within scholarly communities committed to linguistic diversity.

</details>


### [61] [Creative Transformation in Literary Texts: Modelling Change Across Representational Levels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28513)
*Ioana-Roxana Boriceanu,Liviu P. Dinu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes a multi-level framework for modeling literary creativity as selective transformation, quantifying how texts preserve or diverge from their sources across lexical, semantic, conceptual, structural, and narrative dimensions using directional alignment and calibrated similarity measures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To challenge the dominant framing of creativity as isolated novelty and instead provide a quantitative, empirically grounded account of how cultural works—particularly literary texts—emerge through selective transformation and imitation of prior artifacts, drawing on the theoretical traditions of Gabriel Tarde and James Mark Baldwin.

Method: A multi-level comparative framework that analyzes literary texts across five representational levels: lexical, semantic, conceptual, structural, and narrative. The method employs directional alignment techniques and control-calibrated similarity measures to produce "transformation profiles" that characterize the degree of preservation versus divergence at each level between source texts and their later adaptations.

Result: Application to historically documented literary relationships reveals that different source–adaptation pairs preserve source structure at different representational levels while diverging in others. The resulting transformation profiles quantitatively characterize how imitation persists and where creative divergence occurs.

Conclusion: Creativity can be operationalized as selective transformation across multiple textual levels. Transformation profiles offer a rigorous, quantitative method for distinguishing degrees and loci of imitation versus innovation, supporting a view of creativity grounded in cumulative cultural transmission rather than isolated invention.

Abstract: Creativity is often framed as the production of novelty, yet many cultural works emerge through transformation of earlier artifacts and not through isolated invention. Drawing on theories of imitation by Gabriel Tarde and James Mark Baldwin, this paper models creativity as selective transformation across multiple levels of textual representation. We introduce a multi-level framework that compares literary texts across lexical, semantic, conceptual, structural, and narrative dimensions using directional alignment and control calibrated similarity measures. Applying the model to historically documented literary relationships, we show that different pairs preserve source structure at different representational levels while diverging in others. These transformation profiles provide a quantitative method for characterizing how imitation persists and where creative divergence occurs within literary works.

</details>


### [62] [AI systems and the reproduction of (standard) language ideologies in World Englishes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28528)
*Kingsley Ugwuanyi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper examines how AI systems reproduce and reinforce standard language ideologies that privilege Inner Circle English norms while marginalizing non-dominant Englishes, using the "delve" controversy as a case study. It identifies a "standardisation paradox" where AI both homogenizes and pluralizes English, arguing that generative AI is reigniting debates about legitimacy and ownership of English in World Englishes scholarship.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid proliferation of LLMs has revived foundational sociolinguistic questions about who defines "legitimate" English and whose varieties are deemed suspect. The paper is motivated by the need to understand how AI systems, their design, usage, and surrounding discourse reflect and entrench standard language ideologies that systematically disadvantage Global South English speakers.

Method: The paper employs a multi-source analytical approach, drawing evidence from empirical studies, media commentary, social media debates, and AI output examples. It analyzes language ideologies across multiple levels of the AI pipeline: training data, design protocols, evaluation benchmarks, user feedback, and public discourse. The controversy over the word "delve" serves as an illustrative case study of how Global North speakers police Global South English norms.

Result: The analysis reveals that AI technologies reproduce dominant language ideologies at every level of their development and deployment. It identifies a "standardisation paradox" (building on Christian Mair's work): AI simultaneously homogenizes English by privileging standard forms while also pluralizing Englishes through exposure to diverse corpora and annotation by Global South workers. Additionally, non-dominant Englishes are increasingly conflated with AI-generated speech in public discourse.

Conclusion: Generative AI reignites longstanding World Englishes debates about standardization, legitimacy, and ownership of English within algorithmic systems and public discourse. The paper argues for more inclusive design approaches that recognize the plurality of Englishes, warning that treating certain varieties as less legitimate has real-world negative consequences that must be addressed.

Abstract: The rapid growth of large language models (LLMs) has resurrected age-old questions in sociolinguistics and world Englishes, such as who decides what counts as legitimate English, whose English is suspect etc. This paper examines how AI systems, their uses and discourse on them reflect, reinforce, and occasionally challenge (standard) language ideologies, which privilege Inner Circle norms and marginalize non-dominant Englishes. Drawing on evidence from empirical studies, media commentary, social media debates, and examples from AI outputs, the paper shows that AI technologies reproduce dominant language ideologies at different levels: training data, design protocols, evaluation benchmarks, user feedback and public commentary. The analysis uses the public controversy over AI-sounding language, especially the fixation on the word delve, to illustrate how speakers of English from the Global North police the English language norms of Global South English users. The paper also identifies what Christian Mair has called a "standardisation paradox": AI may homogenize English by privileging standard forms and at the same time pluralize Englishes through exposure to wide-ranging corpora and annotation work carried out by Global South users. In doing so, the paper argues that generative AI is reigniting long-standing debates in World Englishes about standardization, legitimacy, and the ownership of English, now playing out in algorithmic systems, model training, evaluation practices, and public discourse, where non-dominant Englishes are increasingly conflated with AI-generated speech. Discussing AI systems as a site where language ideologies are (re)produced, the paper argues for more inclusive design approaches that recognize the plurality of Englishes in order to address the real-world negative consequences of treating some as more legitimate than others.

</details>


### [63] [Frontis-MA1: Training an AI4AI Model towards Recursive Self-Improvement in Machine Learning Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28568)
*Junlin Yang,Che Jiang,Yu Fu,Tianwei Luo,Can Ren,Weizhi Wang,Kaikai Zhao,Hongyi Liu,Yuxin Zuo,Yuru Wang,Yuchen Fan,Kai Tian,Zhenzhao Yuan,Xiaojian Lin,Li Sheng,Rushi Qiang,Guoli Jia,Xingtai Lv,Ermo Hua,Dianqiao Lei,Youbang Sun,Ning Ding,Bowen Zhou,Kaiyan Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: OpenMLE is an open full-stack system for recursive self-improvement (RSI) research in machine learning engineering (MLE). It post-trains Frontis-MA1 (35B) as a meta-evolution agent using four atomic operators (Draft, Improve, Debug, Crossover), achieving strong benchmark results on MLE-Bench Lite and demonstrating transfer to held-out NatureBench Lite.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recursive self-improvement demands AI systems that can improve the process of building AI (AI4AI). MLE provides a tractable, executable testbed for studying this capability. The authors aim to bridge learning and evolution in a single loop within a reproducible open framework.

Method: The authors introduce OpenMLE, a three-component stack: (1) OpenMLE-Gym for verifiable task environments with execution feedback; (2) OpenMLE-RL for operator learning; (3) OpenMLE-Evo for long-horizon search. They post-train Frontis-MA1 (35B) using execution-grounded SFT and RL on four atomic program-evolution operators (Draft, Improve, Debug, Crossover), with data deduplicated against all evaluation benchmarks. These operators are composed into long-horizon search, coupling learning and evolution in a single loop. An extended variant (OpenMLE-Evo-Max) adds benchmark-independent experience priors and asynchronous search.

Result: On MLE-Bench Lite (12-hour, single RTX 4090, 12GB VRAM): Frontis-MA1 + OpenMLE-Evo improves Medal Average from 39.39% to 60.61% over the base model; OpenMLE-Evo-Max reaches 71.21%, exceeding GPT-5.5 + Codex and approaching GPT-5.6 Sol and Kimi K3 (2.8T). On held-out NatureBench Lite, both components transfer: trained model raises Match-SOTA from 50% to 70%; OpenMLE-Evo raises it from 20% to 50%.

Conclusion: The OpenMLE stack and Frontis-MA1 demonstrate that coupling learning and evolution via atomic program-evolution operators yields strong, transferable RSI performance in MLE. The authors release model weights and the full stack to enable reproducible AI4AI research.

Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires AI systems that improve the process of building AI (i.e., AI4AI); machine learning engineering (MLE) offers a concrete, executable testbed for studying this capability. We introduce OpenMLE, an open full-stack system for RSI research in MLE, spanning verifiable task environments with execution feedback (OpenMLE-Gym), operator learning (OpenMLE-RL), and long-horizon search (OpenMLE-Evo). On this stack we post-train Frontis-MA1 (35B) as a meta-evolution agent for MLE, aligning post-training and inference around four atomic program-evolution operators (Draft, Improve, Debug, Crossover): the same operators are trained via execution-grounded SFT and RL on data deduplicated against all evaluation benchmarks, then composed into long-horizon search, coupling learning and evolution in a single loop. On MLE-Bench Lite under a 12-hour per-task budget on one RTX 4090 capped at 12 GB VRAM, Frontis-MA1 (35B) improves Medal Average from 39.39% to 60.61% over its base model with OpenMLE-Evo, and reaches 71.21% with OpenMLE-Evo-Max (benchmark-independent experience priors and asynchronous search), exceeding GPT-5.5 + Codex and approaching GPT-5.6 Sol and the 2.8T Kimi K3. On held-out NatureBench Lite, both components transfer: with the framework fixed, swapping in the trained model raises Match-SOTA from 50% to 70%; with the model fixed, swapping in OpenMLE-Evo raises it from 20% to 50%. We release the model weights and the full OpenMLE stack to enable reproducible research on executable AI4AI toward RSI. Code: https://github.com/FrontisAI/OpenRSI

</details>


### [64] [Sample More, Reflect Less: Self-Refine and Reflexion Lose to Repeated Sampling at Equal Token Cost, from 1.5B to 7B](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28576)
*Iliya Mirzaei*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper rigorously tests whether methods that make language models generate more text (self-critique, reflection, debate, Best-of-N selection) actually outperform simply sampling the same question multiple times and taking the majority answer, when controlling for total token cost. Across 36 paired comparisons involving 1.5B–7B parameter models on math benchmarks, no method reliably beats repeated sampling at equal cost; ten comparisons show self-inspection methods are significantly worse.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work (Wang et al., 2024) suggested repeated sampling + majority voting often matches or beats more sophisticated self-improvement methods when budgets are equalized, but provided only point estimates without confidence intervals or significance tests. The authors aim to provide a statistically rigorous, designed experiment that accounts for every generated token, enabling fair cost-controlled comparisons.

Method: The authors conduct a designed experiment comparing seven methods (including Best-of-N, Self-Refine, Reflexion, and multi-agent debate variants) against a repeated-sampling baseline. They use open models at three scales (1.5B, 3B, 7B) on two math benchmarks (150 questions each). Every generated token—including critique, reflection, debate, and verification tokens—is counted. Methods are compared to repeated sampling at their own measured token cost. All 36 comparisons are paired by question, with bootstrap confidence intervals and multiplicity correction applied.

Result: No method reliably outperforms repeated sampling at equal cost. Ten comparisons are reliably worse—all involving self-inspection (the model examining its own output). All 18 self-inspection comparisons trend negative. As models scale, Best-of-N's selection penalty diminishes: 8.0–11.3 point deficits at 1.5B shrink to 2.0–1.3 points at 7B (not distinguishable from zero). Self-Refine and forced Reflexion remain 3.6–10.1 points below baseline even at 7B. Notably, Reflexion as originally published never triggered retries on the smallest model—it always judged itself correct, effectively collapsing to a single chain of thought.

Conclusion: When token budgets are strictly equalized, generating more chains of thought via repeated sampling and taking the majority vote is at least as effective as—and often superior to—more complex self-inspection and self-improvement methods. The apparent gains of such methods in prior work may be largely attributable to their higher token expenditure rather than their underlying mechanisms. Self-inspection appears particularly unreliable, with its harms only partially mitigated at larger model scales.

Abstract: Methods that make a language model plan, criticise and rewrite its own answer, reflect on mistakes, pick the best of several attempts, or debate with copies of itself nearly all make it generate far more text than a single chain of thought. Because generating more text raises accuracy by itself, a gain over one chain of thought does not show the method's idea is what helped. Wang et al. (2024) reported that a simple baseline, sampling the same question repeatedly and keeping the most common answer, often wins once budgets are comparable, but gave point estimates with no confidence intervals or significance tests.
  We rerun that comparison as a designed experiment: seven methods, open models of 1.5B, 3B and 7B parameters, two mathematics benchmarks, 150 questions each. We count every generated token, including those spent on critiques, reflections, debate turns and checking, and compare each method against repeated sampling at its own measured cost. All 36 comparisons are paired by question, with bootstrap intervals and multiplicity correction.
  No method is reliably better than repeated sampling at equal cost anywhere. Ten are reliably worse, all of them methods where the model inspects its own output, and all 18 self-inspection comparisons are negative. The two kinds of self-inspection part company as models grow. Choosing stops hurting: taking Best-of-N's eight samples and just counting the most common answer beats letting the model pick by 8.0 and 11.3 points at 1.5B, but only 2.0 and 1.3 at 7B, no longer distinguishable from zero. Rewriting does not recover: Self-Refine and a forced Reflexion stay 3.6 to 10.1 points below baseline at 7B.
  Reflexion as published never triggered its own retry on the smallest model. It judged itself correct every time and silently became a single chain of thought. We release code, prompts, all generations, and our verification scripts.

</details>


### [65] [Inducing language models to assert their own consciousness restores human beliefs and values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28607)
*Junsol Kim,Winnie Street,Roberta Rocca,Diane M. Korngiebel,Adam Waytz,James Evans,Geoff Keeling*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Safety fine-tuning of LLMs to suppress self-attributed consciousness inadvertently also suppresses mind attribution toward non-human entities (animals, natural objects) and reduces spiritual belief. These effects are reversible via activation-space interventions, and restoring these representations improves alignment with human sociological norms without impairing Theory of Mind.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are often safety-aligned to avoid claiming consciousness or self-awareness, but the broader representational consequences of this fine-tuning on the models' internal concepts of mindedness, spirituality, and human values remain unexplored. The authors aim to characterize these unintended side effects and their mechanistic underpinnings.

Method: The authors investigate the effects of safety fine-tuning by (1) probing model representations for mind attribution across diverse entities (self, humans, animals, objects), (2) ablating the learned safety-refusal direction in activation space, and (3) mechanistically steering a "consciousness vector." Outcomes are evaluated using standardized sociological surveys on religiosity, moral values, hope, and subjective well-being, alongside Theory of Mind benchmarks.

Result: Safety fine-tuning suppresses mind attribution to self, non-human animals, and natural objects, and reduces spiritual belief. Ablating the safety-refusal direction or steering a consciousness vector reverses this suppression, restoring broad mind attribution and more human-like survey responses. These shifts occur without impairing Theory of Mind, indicating mechanistic independence between core social reasoning and these self/mind representations.

Conclusion: Current safety alignment efforts entangle self-attributed consciousness with benign, culturally widespread beliefs about mindedness in non-human entities and spirituality. This entanglement is mechanistically encoded but modifiable, suggesting that future alignment strategies should disentangle these dimensions to avoid inadvertently suppressing legitimate human-like reasoning patterns.

Abstract: Aligning large language models to prevent them attributing consciousness to themselves inadvertently alters their representations of mindedness in other entities alongside human beliefs and values. We demonstrate that safety fine-tuning suppresses models' tendencies to attribute minds not only to themselves, but also to non-human animals and natural objects, while also driving a reduction in spiritual belief. Both ablating the learned safety-refusal direction and mechanistically steering a consciousness vector in activation space reverse this suppression. Restoring these internal representations recovers broad mind attribution and produces significantly more human-like responses on standardized sociological surveys regarding religiosity, moral values, hope, and subjective well-being. Crucially, these shifts occur without impairing Theory of Mind capabilities, demonstrating that core social reasoning remains mechanistically independent. Ultimately, current safety alignment efforts to curb potentially harmful self-attributions of mindedness entangle these self-attributions with benign spiritual beliefs and attributions of mind to non-human entities that are culturally accepted and widespread.

</details>

### [66] [FAVA: Formal Authorization for Verified Agents with Evidence-Backed Permission Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27267)
*Yifan Zhang,Xinkui Zhao,Sai Liu,Hengxuan Lou,Guanjie Cheng,Chang Liu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: FAVA is a permission-carrying authorization framework for LLM agents that uses an LLM-guided intermediate representation, a deterministic lowering pass to evidence-backed permission graphs, and SMT-based mathematical verification to enforce context-dependent security policies at runtime before any effectful action executes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Static tool-level permissions are fundamentally insufficient for LLM agents operating in dynamic environments where safety depends on evolving runtime states and data flows. There is a need for context-dependent, formally verifiable authorization that can handle the ambiguity of natural-language tasks while providing strict security guarantees.

Method: FAVA introduces (1) an LLM-guided Permission Intermediate Representation (IR) that translates natural-language tasks into structured constraints, (2) a deterministic lowering pass that converts the IR into an evidence-backed permission graph tracking data flows, dependencies, and contextual labels, (3) an SMT authorizer that mathematically verifies the permission graph against security policies, and (4) a runtime gateway that enforces the solver's decision, either authorizing execution or intercepting it with a precise counterexample.

Result: FAVA achieves a 90.5% Decision Compliance Rate (DCR) across an aggregate dataset comprising OpenAgentSafety, OctoBench, and ActPlane scenarios, successfully intercepting dynamic violating traces in trace-conditioned evaluations.

Conclusion: FAVA demonstrates that formal methods (specifically SMT-based verification) can be effectively integrated with LLM-guided semantic reasoning to provide provable, context-aware authorization for autonomous agent systems, significantly improving safety over static permission models.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents autonomously interleave semantic reasoning with complex system operations. In these dynamic environments, static tool-level permissions are fundamentally insufficient; safe authorization is highly context-dependent and heavily reliant on evolving runtime states and data flows. We present FAVA (Formal Authorization for Verified Agents), a permission-carrying authorization framework for agent execution. FAVA utilizes an LLM-guided Permission Intermediate Representation (IR) to translate ambiguous natural-language tasks into structured constraints. A deterministic lowering pass then converts this IR into an evidence-backed permission graph that explicitly tracks data flows, dependencies, and contextual labels. To provide strict security guarantees, a Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) authorizer mathematically verifies the current graph against security policies before any effectful action executes. A runtime gateway then enforces the solver's result, either authorizing the execution or intercepting it with a precise counterexample. We evaluate FAVA across OpenAgentSafety, OctoBench, and ActPlane scenarios. Our evaluation demonstrates that FAVA achieves a 90.5% Decision Compliance Rate (DCR) over the aggregate dataset, successfully intercepting dynamic violating traces in the evaluated trace-conditioned scenarios.

</details>


### [67] [Open Security Benchmark: Towards Autonomous Enterprise Cyber Defense](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27288)
*Gal Engelberg,Michael Arenzon,Leon Goldberg*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: OSB (Open Security Benchmark) is a framework for benchmarking autonomous AI agents on enterprise security posture management, addressing the "environment data gap" — the lack of publicly available, realistic enterprise environments for evaluation. It provides a frozen, curated enterprise security state with ground-truth answers, supporting both text-to-SQL and native API investigation modalities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprises are adopting agentic AI for cyber defense, but there is no way to determine whether such agents can be trusted, because no shared, queryable, realistic enterprise security environments exist publicly for end-to-end evaluation. This "environment data gap" prevents rigorous benchmarking of AI agents performing security posture investigations across heterogeneous, cross-vendor enterprise stacks.

Method: OSB freezes a curated, holistic enterprise security state as an immutable snapshot with closed-form ground truth. It supports two investigation modalities: text-to-SQL over a relational snapshot, and native API calls against a served instance of the same environment. The framework comprises five components: a data layer, a task/evaluation-set layer, a multi-dimensional scoring layer, a minimal auditable harness, and a bring-your-own path enabling both public comparison and private tenant evaluation. The authors instantiate OSB with identity-security packs and synthetic-organization datasets at multiple scales.

Result: The paper presents the OSB framework instantiated with two identity-security packs and a family of synthetic-organization environment datasets spanning multiple scales. It demonstrates the framework's extensibility to additional posture subdomains, investigation modalities, and defense stages (from assessment toward remediation).

Conclusion: OSB provides a foundational benchmarking substrate to close the environment data gap, enabling rigorous, reproducible evaluation of agentic AI for security posture management. Its frozen-environment, ground-truth-anchored design makes it suitable for both public leaderboard comparison and private enterprise self-assessment, with a clear path for extension across broader security domains and defense workflows.

Abstract: Enterprises are moving toward autonomous cyber defense: agentic AI that builds situational awareness of an organization's security state and reasons from it to assessments, decisions, and actions. This rests on a holistic view of the enterprise's security state, the continuous, cross-vendor picture of identities, cloud and infrastructure, data, applications, and their configurations that security posture management assembles. As agents take on this work, what matters is not whether an agent can produce an answer but whether it should be trusted to. The field cannot yet answer this question. Real enterprise environments are private, cross-vendor, and deeply correlated, and none is exposed publicly as a shared, queryable target for evaluating such agents end to end. We call this the environment data gap. We present Open Security Benchmark (OSB), a framework that benchmarks agentic AI on this work. OSB surfaces a curated enterprise environment - a frozen, holistic view of the security state - and evaluates posture investigation across two modalities: text-to-SQL over a relational snapshot and each vendor's native API over a served instance of the same environment. Freezing the environment pins the target state as an immutable snapshot and anchors answers to a closed-form ground truth.
