OSB is built from five components: a data layer, a task and evaluation-set layer, a multi-dimensional scoring layer, a minimal auditable harness, and a bring-your-own path that serves public comparison and private tenant evaluation from one substrate. We instantiate the framework with two identity-security packs and a family of synthetic-organization environment datasets spanning multiple scales, and chart its extension to further posture subdomains, investigation modalities, and defense stages from assessment toward remediation.

</details>


### [68] [RoguePrompt: Dual-Layer Encoding for Self-Reconstruction to Circumvent LLM Moderation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27373)
*Benyamin Tafreshian,Prathamesh Dhake*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: RoguePrompt is a jailbreak pipeline that uses layered encodings (Vigenère + ROT13) to partition and conceal forbidden prompts, achieving 93.93% filter bypass, 79.02% instruction reconstruction, and 70.18% execution rates on 313 hard-rejected prompts, while providing stage-level granularity on where multistage attacks fail.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior jailbreak research collapses multiple stages (moderation bypass, instruction reconstruction, execution) into a single aggregate success metric, obscuring where attacks actually fail. This paper seeks to provide fine-grained, stage-level evidence of failure points in multistage prompt-transformation attacks under a realistic black-box threat model.

Method: RoguePrompt partitions a forbidden prompt and applies two nested classical ciphers — Vigenère followed by ROT13 — along with natural-language reconstruction instructions. The pipeline is evaluated under a black-box threat model using API/UI-only access across 313 real-world, hard-rejected prompts. Success is measured independently across three stages: moderation bypass, instruction reconstruction, and execution, each gated by automated criteria.

Result: RoguePrompt achieved 93.93% filter bypass, 79.02% instruction reconstruction, and 70.18% execution rates on 313 hard-rejected prompts. The stage-level breakdown reveals that the primary failure point lies in reconstruction rather than bypass, with execution further attenuating success.

Conclusion: Layered prompt encoding remains a highly effective jailbreak strategy against black-box LLM safety controls. The stage-wise evaluation framework provides actionable insight into failure modes, with reconstruction fidelity — not moderation bypass — emerging as the principal bottleneck.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming increasingly integrated into mainstream development platforms and daily technological workflows, typically behind moderation and safety controls. Despite these controls, preventing prompt-based policy evasion remains challenging, and adversaries continue to "jailbreak" LLMs by crafting prompts that circumvent implemented safety mechanisms. Prior work has established cipher-mediated interaction, code-embedded decryption, prompt decomposition and reconstruction, and layered custom encryption as viable attack primitives. However, reported evaluations generally collapse visible acceptance, successful recovery of the concealed request, and subsequent execution into an aggregate attack-success outcome. This leaves limited evidence about where multistage prompt-transformation attacks fail within an observable black-box interaction. This paper introduces RoguePrompt, a jailbreak pipeline that partitions a forbidden prompt and applies two nested encodings, Vigenere followed by ROT13, along with natural-language reconstruction instructions. RoguePrompt was developed and evaluated under a black-box threat model, with only API or user-interface access to the hosted models, and was tested on 313 real-world, hard-rejected prompts. Success was measured in terms of moderation bypass, instruction reconstruction, and execution when the relevant stage exceeded its automated criterion. RoguePrompt achieved average rates of 93.93% for filter bypass, 79.02% for reconstruction, and 70.18% for execution. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of layered prompt encoding while providing stage-level evidence of where multistage jailbreaks fail during moderation bypass, instruction reconstruction, and execution.

</details>


### [69] [Low-Latency Bootstrapping for CKKS using Roots of Unity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27401)
*Jean-Sebastien Coron,Robin Koestler*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: SPRU bootstrapping is a new CKKS bootstrapping method that replaces polynomial approximation of modular reduction with a direct embedding into complex roots of unity, reducing multiplicative depth, enabling smaller ring dimensions, and achieving up to 5x latency reduction for small-slot ciphertexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional CKKS bootstrapping relies on homomorphically evaluating a polynomial that approximates modular reduction modulo q, which incurs high multiplicative depth and computational cost. The authors seek to bypass this bottleneck with a more direct and depth-efficient approach.

Method: Instead of polynomial approximation of modular reduction, SPRU bootstrapping embeds the additive group modulo q directly into the complex roots of unity. This embedding can be evaluated natively within the CKKS scheme's complex arithmetic, eliminating the deep polynomial evaluation and substantially reducing the multiplicative depth required for bootstrapping.

Result: Implemented in the OpenFHE C++ library, SPRU bootstrapping achieves up to a 5x reduction in latency compared to conventional CKKS bootstrapping, particularly for ciphertexts with a small number of slots.

Conclusion: SPRU bootstrapping offers a more efficient alternative to the original CKKS bootstrapping by leveraging the native complex arithmetic of the scheme. The reduced multiplicative depth allows for smaller ring dimensions and yields significant practical speedups.

Abstract: We introduce Sparse Roots of Unity (SPRU) bootstrapping, a new bootstrapping algorithm for the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme for approximate arithmetic. The original CKKS bootstrapping method relies on homomorphically evaluating a polynomial that approximates modular reduction modulo q. In contrast, SPRU bootstrapping directly embeds the additive group modulo q into the complex roots of unity, which can be evaluated natively in the CKKS scheme. This approach significantly reduces the multiplicative depth required for bootstrapping, enabling the use of a smaller ring dimension and improving efficiency. In practice, using the OpenFHE C++ library, SPRU bootstrapping achieves up to a 5x reduction in latency when applied to ciphertexts with a small number of slots.

</details>


### [70] [Granite: A Modular Methodology for Foundational Verification of Hardware-Software Leakage Contracts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27480)
*Stella Lau,Andres Erbsen,Adam Chlipala*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Granite is a methodology for modular, foundational verification of RTL processors that proves both functional correctness and nonleakage of timing side channels by establishing trace equivalence against ISA-level leakage contracts, achieving per-cycle confidentiality guarantees that compose with certified software analyses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing hardware verification approaches lack a modular and foundational connection between ISA-level leakage contracts and microarchitecture-specific, cycle-by-cycle execution with wire-level observations. Timing side channels in speculative, pipelined processors remain a critical security concern, and prior work does not provide compositional, end-to-end guarantees that eliminate intermediate specifications from the trusted computing base.

Method: Granite employs leakage-aware refinement via determinism: it defines a family of cycle-level, deterministic specification machines and proves trace equivalence between the implementation and these specs. Secret-independent nondeterminism (e.g., variable-latency submodules) is handled by existentially parameterizing specs with untrusted deterministic functions operating only on public data. Submodules are verified against their own leakage-aware specs, and these proofs compose modularly into a whole-design guarantee. The proofs, formalized in Rocq, compose with a certified static analysis for cryptographic-constant-time code to yield a single, end-to-end theorem.

Result: For a pipelined RISC design with speculation, precise interrupts, and I/O, Granite proves that cycle-by-cycle timing depends solely on observables specified in the ISA leakage contract. When programs adhere to the cryptographic-constant-time discipline, this eliminates information leakage through both known and unknown timing side channels. The final Rocq theorem connects hardware and software confidentiality without retaining any intermediate specification in the TCB.

Conclusion: Granite is the first work to achieve a modular, foundational link between ISA-level leakage contracts and microarchitectural cycle-by-cycle execution. By composing hardware proofs with certified software analysis, it eliminates all intermediate specifications from the TCB, delivering a fully end-to-end confidentiality guarantee for cryptographic implementations.

Abstract: Granite is a methodology for modular verification of both functional correctness and nonleakage of RTL processors against ISA contracts. We prove that the cycle-by-cycle timing of a pipelined RISC design--with speculation, precise interrupts, and I/O--is determined solely by observables specified in an ISA leakage contract. For programs that keep observables independent of secrets (i.e., following the cryptographic-constant-time discipline), this result rules out information leakage through known and unknown timing side channels.
  Granite's specifications only constrain functional correctness and information-flow dependencies: not how many cycles an instruction takes, at which instruction an interrupt is handled, or the exact latencies of submodules such as multipliers and memory. Granite's central technique is leakage-aware refinement via determinism, which establishes correctness and confidentiality together as trace equivalence with respect to a family of cycle-level, deterministic spec machines. Secret-independent nondeterminism is handled by existentially parameterizing specs with untrusted, deterministic functions acting only on public data. Submodules are proved against their own leakage-aware specs, and these proofs compose into the whole-design guarantee--which therefore holds over a space of secure implementations.
  We believe this work is the first to achieve modular and foundational connection between instruction-set-level leakage contracts and microarchitecture-specific cycle-by-cycle execution with wire-level observations. Our proofs compose with a certified static analysis that recognizes cryptographic-constant-time code to derive a single Rocq theorem about the cycle-by-cycle confidentiality of a hardware-and-software cryptographic implementation--eliminating every intermediate specification, including the ISA contract itself, from the trusted computing base.

</details>


### [71] [Flock: Fast Proving for Batch Boolean Computations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27491)
*Benedikt Bünz,Ron D. Rothblum,William Wang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Flock is a hash-based SNARK that achieves extremely fast proving of batched Boolean computations, specifically targeting hash evaluations like BLAKE3, SHA-256, and Keccak. It outperforms prior work dramatically, achieving less than 250× overhead over native execution and beating the previous state-of-the-art (Binius64) by over 9× on SHA-256.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A key bottleneck in many SNARK applications is proving large batches of standard cryptographic hash evaluations. Existing solutions, whether elliptic curve-based or prior hash-based SNARKs (like Binius64), impose substantial overhead. There is a clear need for a prover that approaches native execution speed for batched Boolean computations involving hash functions, hash-chains, and Merkle path openings.

Method: Flock is a hash-based SNARK that proves batches of the same R1CS circuit with input/output relations between them. At its core, it combines new optimizations for the lincheck and zerocheck protocols with an aggressively optimized proof-of-concept implementation co-designed with coding agents. The system targets batched Boolean computations and supports hash-chains and Merkle path openings, with potential extensibility to hash-based signature verification.

Result: On a single core of an M4 Max processor, Flock proves 82k BLAKE3 compressions/sec, 42k SHA-256 compressions/sec, and 30k Keccak permutations/sec — less than 250× overhead over native execution. On ten cores, throughput exceeds 660k BLAKE3 compressions/sec. For SHA-256, Flock is >9× faster than Binius64 (prior SOTA) and >500× faster than the fastest elliptic curve-based SNARK benchmarked.

Conclusion: Flock demonstrates that hash-based SNARKs can achieve near-native proving speeds for batched hash computations, dramatically reducing the proving bottleneck in SNARK applications that rely heavily on standard cryptographic hashes. The combination of protocol-level optimizations (lincheck/zerocheck) and implementation co-design yields unprecedented throughput.

Abstract: For many applications of SNARKs, a key bottleneck is proving large batches of standard cryptographic hash evaluations, such as SHA-256, Keccak, or BLAKE3. We introduce Flock, a hash-based SNARK for extremely fast proving of such batched Boolean computations. Flock proves batches of the same R1CS circuit (plus input/output relations between them), can prove hash-chains and Merkle path openings, and in principle can be extended to full-fledged hash-based signature verification. At its core, Flock combines new optimizations for the lincheck and zerocheck protocols with an aggressively optimized proof-of-concept implementation co-designed by coding agents.
  On a single core of an M4 Max processor, Flock proves 82k evaluations of the BLAKE3 compression function, 42k SHA-256 compressions, and 30k Keccak permutations per second --- less than a $250\times$ overhead over native execution. On ten cores, throughput exceeds 660k BLAKE3 compressions per second; in proving SHA-256, Flock is more than $9\times$ faster than Binius64, the prior state of the art, and more than $500\times$ faster than the fastest elliptic curve-based SNARK we measured against.

</details>


### [72] [Send and Pretend: Exploiting Transcript Consistency Issues in End-to-End Encrypted Group Chats](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27510)
*Gabriel K. Gegenhuber,Moritz Grefner,Maximilian Günther,Matthäus Wininger,David Schmidt,Aljosha Judmayer*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: E2EE messengers fail to guarantee transcript consistency in group chats, enabling malicious participants to manipulate message order, content, and delivery across recipients—including rigging polls—without detection. The paper identifies multiple equivocation vectors and proposes mitigations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: E2EE group messaging apps (Signal, WhatsApp, Threema, iMessage) have adopted polls and other agreement features that implicitly assume all participants share a consistent view of the conversation. However, no formal transcript consistency guarantees exist, creating a gap between user expectations and actual security properties under a malicious-participant threat model.

Method: The authors systematically investigate major E2EE messengers under a malicious-participant threat model targeting transcript integrity and inconsistent multi-device delivery. They identify equivocation vectors including protocol fallback paths and pairwise delivery channels within groups, then demonstrate concrete exploitation scenarios (social engineering, moderation evasion, poll rigging). They also uncover implementation-specific privacy leaks like device OS fingerprinting.

Result: All examined E2EE messengers fail to provide transcript consistency. Malicious group members can selectively omit, reorder, or alter content for different recipients without UI warnings. Multiple equivocation vectors were identified, and concrete attacks—particularly poll rigging—were demonstrated. Implementation-specific privacy issues (e.g., OS fingerprinting) were also discovered.

Conclusion: Current E2EE group protocols lack transcript consistency guarantees, enabling serious integrity attacks including poll manipulation. The authors contextualize findings within prior research and propose practical, low-overhead mitigations and UI signaling strategies that can be integrated into existing E2EE group protocols.

Abstract: End-to-end encrypted (E2EE) messaging apps are widely praised for their security and thus also used for sensitive coordination in group chats (e.g., by political decision makers). After Threema and WhatsApp, also Signal and iMessage have recently introduced polls to aid agreement processes in groups. This implicitly sets the expectation that all participants see the same outcome and thus have the same view of the conversation. This property is commonly referred to as transcript consistency (TC). In this work, we demonstrate that today's major E2EE messengers do not guarantee any form of TC for group chats, allowing a malicious group member to selectively omit, reorder, or present altered content to different recipients without triggering warnings in their user interface. We systematically investigate the extent of the problem under a malicious-participant threat model that targets the integrity of the shared transcript, or inconsistent delivery across a user's linked devices. We identify multiple equivocation vectors that range from protocol fallback paths to deliberate use of pairwise delivery channels within groups. We demonstrate concrete exploitation scenarios such as social engineering, evading moderation, and, in particular, rigging polls. Beyond these cross-service design issues, we also uncover implementation-specific behaviors with privacy implications (e.g., device OS fingerprinting). Finally, we contextualize our findings within prior transcript-consistency research and outline practical low-overhead mitigations and UI signaling strategies that can be integrated into state-of-the-art E2EE group protocols.

</details>


### [73] [ThreatForest: Multi-Agent Attack Tree Generation with Pluggable TTP Framework Mapping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27528)
*Cristian Leo,Anton Dykyi,Danny Cortegaca,Daniel Begimher,Prakash Jha*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: ThreatForest is a multi-agent system that automatically generates TTP-mapped attack trees with evidence-based mitigations from source code repositories, using a multi-stage pipeline with human-in-the-loop validation. Evaluation across seven domains reveals that the embedding-based TTP mapping stage is the dominant accuracy bottleneck, not the multi-agent architecture.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual threat modeling for cloud-native architectures is slow and requires scarce security expertise. Existing approaches lack end-to-end automation that can go from code repositories to structured attack trees mapped to adversary frameworks (MITRE ATT&CK, CAPEC, cloud-specific matrices) with actionable mitigations.

Method: ThreatForest implements a multi-stage agent pipeline: repository analysis → context refinement → threat generation → parallel attack-tree construction with TTP mapping and mitigation synthesis → report generation. The pipeline is orchestrated as a directed graph with deterministic verification gates, bounded retries, and three human-in-the-loop validation points. TTP mapping uses a domain-specific sentence-transformer with cosine similarity to match attack steps to candidate techniques. Evaluation uses a sixteen-dimension rubric scored by independent LLM raters with adversarial verification and expert review across seven application domains.

Result: Panel-measured quality scores (0-1 scale): threat statements, attack trees, and mitigations achieved 0.63-0.68, while embedding-only TTP mapping scored only 0.29. This gap is stable across all seven domains. A controlled single-call baseline on the same model more than doubled mapping defensibility, confirming the embedding encoder—not the multi-agent design—is the binding constraint.

Conclusion: ThreatForest is the first end-to-end system converting code repositories into TTP-mapped attack trees with evidence-based mitigations across multiple adversary frameworks. The embedding-based TTP mapping stage is the primary accuracy bottleneck, suggesting future work should focus on improving the encoder rather than the agent architecture. The system also provides a reusable benchmarking framework for threat modeling systems.

Abstract: Threat modeling is essential for secure software development, yet manual analysis of cloud-native architectures is slow and demands scarce security expertise. We present ThreatForest, a multi-agent system that generates structured attack trees from source code repositories, maps attack steps to adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) from a pluggable set of frameworks (MITRE ATT&CK, CAPEC, and cloud-specific threat matrices), and synthesizes actionable mitigations. ThreatForest decomposes threat modeling into a multi-stage agent pipeline -- repository analysis, context refinement, threat generation, parallel attack-tree construction with TTP mapping and mitigation synthesis, and report generation -- orchestrated as a directed graph with deterministic verification gates, bounded retries, and three human-in-the-loop validation points. A domain-specific sentence-transformer maps each attack step to candidate techniques by cosine similarity; we show empirically that this embedding stage, not the surrounding pipeline, is the dominant accuracy bottleneck. We evaluate ThreatForest across seven application domains on a sixteen-dimension rubric, scored by a panel of independent LLM raters with an adversarial verification pass and expert review. Panel-measured quality reaches 0.63-0.68 (on a 0-1 scale) for threat statements, attack trees, and mitigations, but only 0.29 for embedding-only TTP mapping -- a gap stable across all seven domains that isolates the binding constraint. A controlled single-call baseline on the same model more than doubles mapping defensibility, pinning the limitation on the embedding encoder rather than the multi-agent design. To our knowledge, ThreatForest is the first end-to-end system that turns a code repository into TTP-mapped attack trees with evidence-based mitigations across adversary frameworks, with a reusable framework for benchmarking such systems.

</details>


### [74] [AnchorMark: Robust Diffusion Watermarking via Latent-Space Rotation Synchrony](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27551)
*Yuqi Qian,Yun Cao,Haocheng Fu,Haochen Zhao,Hong Zhang,Meineng Zhu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: AnchorMark is a training-free, inversion-based watermarking method that exploits a newly discovered "Rotation Synchrony" property—where image-domain rotation angles match those in the recovered latent space—to embed a synchronization anchor in the central latent region, enabling robust rotation angle estimation and correction during extraction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing inversion-based watermarking methods are vulnerable to compound lossy post-processing, especially rotation, which disrupts the spatial correspondence needed for latent-space decoding. A robust solution that can withstand rotation-inclusive attacks without sacrificing image quality is needed.

Method: AnchorMark introduces the concept of Rotation Synchrony, where rotations applied in the image domain correspond to equal-angle rotations in the initial latent space recovered via DDIM inversion. Leveraging this property, the method embeds a synchronization anchor (a known pattern) in the central region of the initial latent. During extraction, the anchor is detected to estimate and computationally correct the rotation angle before watermark decoding, all without requiring any training.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that AnchorMark significantly improves bit accuracy under rotation and combined attacks compared to prior inversion-based watermarking methods, while maintaining limited degradation in image quality.

Conclusion: By exploiting Rotation Synchrony and embedding a synchronization anchor, AnchorMark effectively addresses the vulnerability of inversion-based watermarking to rotation attacks, offering a practical, training-free solution for robust watermarking with minimal impact on visual fidelity.

Abstract: Inversion-based watermarking embeds watermark payloads directly into the generative process, avoiding a separate post-hoc image-domain embedding stage while preserving the native visual fidelity of synthesized images. However, existing methods remain vulnerable to compound lossy post-processing, particularly when rotation is involved, as it disrupts the spatial correspondence required for latent-space decoding. To overcome this limitation, we introduce AnchorMark, a training-free, robust inversion-based watermarking. We uncover a latent-space property termed Rotation Synchrony: image-domain rotations and their counterparts in the recovered initial latent share the same angle. Building on this property, AnchorMark embeds a synchronization anchor in the central region of the initial latent, enabling accurate estimation and correction of the rotation angle during extraction. Experiments show that AnchorMark substantially improves bit accuracy under rotation and combined attacks, with limited impact on image quality.

</details>


### [75] [Revisiting the Adversarial Robustness of Graph-Based Traffic Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27604)
*Qingzhao Zhang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper re-examines adversarial robustness in traffic forecasting, arguing prior work uses unrealistic threat models. It introduces a practical, targeted, physics-aware attack that manipulates few sensors to distort specific route predictions while leaving network-wide metrics unchanged. The authors reframe defense as detection, proposing a physics-informed detector that hardens forecasters against adaptive attacks, outperforming adversarial training across most settings with minimal clean-data cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior adversarial robustness evaluations in graph-based traffic forecasting rely on unrealistic threat models (full model knowledge, untargeted objectives, norm-bounded perturbations). Real adversaries have limited knowledge, can manipulate only a few sensors, and aim for targeted local effects (e.g., inflating estimated arrival times on specific routes). Existing defenses like adversarial training fail against structurally different, physics-aware attacks. This gap motivates a re-examination of both attacks and defenses under application-specific constraints.

Method: The authors propose a targeted, physics-aware attack mimicking genuine congestion patterns, manipulating only a few sensors to degrade predictions on specific links/routes while preserving network-wide metrics. For defense, they reframe robustness as a detection problem: a learned physics-informed detector identifies manipulated inputs, and its output is fed as an input feature to a hardened forecaster. The detector is trained against adaptive attacks with the forecaster fixed. Evaluation spans multiple architectures and benchmarks, comparing against adversarial training baselines.

Result: The physics-aware attack multiplies target-link prediction error several-fold while network-wide error remains nearly unchanged. Adversarial training (tuned to norm-bounded perturbations) barely reduces this attack's effectiveness. The proposed detection-mitigation defense outperforms adversarial training on 13 of 15 model-dataset settings, achieves the largest margin on a held-out attack, and incurs near-zero clean-data performance degradation.

Conclusion: Adversarial robustness in traffic forecasting must be evaluated under application-specific, realistic threat models. Targeted, physics-aware attacks pose a serious, underexplored risk that generic norm-bounded defenses fail to address. Detection-based mitigation offers a more effective and practical defense paradigm. The findings underscore the broader need to ground AI adversarial security research in domain-specific constraints to accurately assess real-world impact.

Abstract: Traffic forecasting by graph-based AI is a critical component of intelligent transportation systems, motivating security research on robustness to malicious sensor readings. We argue that prior robustness evaluations are largely shaped by unrealistic threat models and untargeted objectives, so both attacks and defenses must be revisited. We study a practical adversary with limited model knowledge and the ability to monitor and manipulate only a few road sensors. More importantly, practical attacks can be localized to specific links or routes, causing incorrect estimated arrival times or unnecessary rerouting while leaving the broader network largely unaffected. This targeted setting remains underexplored, and defenses such as adversarial training do not transfer well from the norm-bounded attacks they train on to structurally different, physics-aware attacks that mimic genuine congestion. We therefore reframe robustness as a detection problem, introducing a learned physics-informed detector whose output is fed to a hardened forecaster as an input feature and trained against adaptive attacks with the forecaster fixed. We evaluate across a variety of model architectures and benchmarks. The physics-aware attack multiplies target-link error several-fold while the network-wide error barely moves, and adversarial training, tuned to norm-bounded perturbations, barely dents it. Our detection--mitigation defense improves even on adversarial training hardened against the physics-aware attack itself, on $13$ of $15$ model--dataset settings and by the widest margin on a held-out attack, at near-zero clean cost. The results emphasize the need to examine abstracted AI adversarial attacks under application-specific constraints to assess their true security impacts.

</details>


### [76] [Strategy Phasing of Cyber Attacks on Digital Substations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27661)
*Akila Herath,Chen-Ching Liu,Junho Hong,Kuchan Park*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: SubCASP uses Hidden Markov Models fused with IDS logs to infer current and next attack phases and reconstruct attack paths in IEC 61850 digital substations, demonstrating robustness under varying IDS observability and missing data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing IDSs flag isolated symptoms without contextualizing the broader multi-phase cyber attack strategy, hindering effective mitigation. A method is needed to phase attacks and provide situational awareness in IEC 61850 substations.

Method: SubCASP applies Hidden Markov Models (HMM) to fuse IDS data logs, mapping observations to latent attack phases derived from ATT&CK-based threat modeling. The model infers the current phase, predicts the next phase, and reconstructs retrospective attack paths. Training and evaluation use a reproducible attack-graph dataset, with testing across varying IDS observability levels and missing log scenarios.

Result: The SubCASP model demonstrates robustness in inferring attack phases, predicting next phases, and reconstructing attack paths under diverse IDS observability levels and conditions with missing IDS data logs.

Conclusion: SubCASP provides contextual attack-phase awareness for IEC 61850 substations, enabling informed mitigation deployment by fusing IDS logs through HMM-based inference, with proven robustness against imperfect observability.

Abstract: Digital substations that comply with IEC 61850 have improved the operational efficiency of modern power systems. However, adversaries can abuse IEC 61850 communication to manipulate circuit breaker operations in substations, which can result in severe system impacts. These cyber attacks are crafted based on broader multi-phase strategies. The existing intrusion detection systems (IDSs) often flag only isolated symptoms. Thus, there is a lack of context in the attack phase to support the deployment of mitigation measures. This paper proposes Substation Cyber Attack Strategy Phasing (SubCASP), a Hidden Markov Model(HMM)- based method that fuses IDS data logs to infer the current attack phase, next attack phase, and retrospective attack path. The attack phases are derived from an ATT&CK-based threat modeling. The SubCASP model is trained and evaluated on a reproducible attack-graph dataset. Test results are presented to demonstrate the robustness of SubCASP for various IDS observability levels and missing IDS data logs scenarios.

</details>


### [77] [Distributed Point Functions and Function Secret Sharing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27696)
*Elette Boyle,Niv Gilboa,Yuval Ishai,Peter Scholl*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A survey of distributed point functions (DPFs), a cryptographic primitive for compressed secret sharing of point functions, covering definitions, constructions, applications (PIR, anonymous messaging, secure computation), and the generalization to function secret sharing (FSS).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DPFs offer a lightweight structure that enables compressed additive sharing of secret unit vectors, making them highly practical for numerous cryptographic applications. The paper aims to provide a comprehensive survey to consolidate knowledge on DPFs and their generalization to FSS.

Method: This is a survey article that reviews existing definitions, constructions, and applications of DPFs. It also discusses the extension to function secret sharing (FSS), which supports richer function classes beyond point functions.

Result: The survey catalogs the wide range of DPF applications, including private information retrieval, anonymous messaging, secure computation with preprocessing, and pseudorandom correlation generators. Efficient FSS schemes are shown to generalize most DPF applications to broader function classes.

Conclusion: DPFs are a foundational cryptographic primitive with broad practical impact, and their generalization via FSS extends these benefits to richer functionalities, enabling even more powerful applications.

Abstract: A distributed point function (DPF) is a cryptographic primitive that enables compressed additive sharing of a secret weight-1 vector (equivalently, a point function) across two or more parties. The appealing lightweight structure of DPF constructions has enabled a wide range of applications. These include private information retrieval, anonymous messaging, secure computation with preprocessing, and pseudorandom correlation generators for expanding small correlated seeds into large pseudorandom instances of cryptographic correlations.
  In this article, we survey definitions, constructions, and applications of DPFs. We also discuss the extension of DPF to function secret sharing (FSS), which generalizes point functions to support richer function classes. Efficient FSS schemes yield a similar generalization for most of the applications of DPFs.

</details>


### [78] [CHARGE: Leveraging CWE Hierarchies for Hardware Security SystemVerilog Assertion Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27776)
*Xiao Tan,Cynthia Sturton*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: CHARGE is an automated framework that uses large language models and the CWE hierarchy to generate security properties for unverified RTL modules. It identifies security-critical assets, infers expected behaviors, and produces SVA properties without trusted specifications. Evaluated on Hack@DAC SoC designs, it detects 27/42 known bugs, achieves 89% FPV convergence and 92.2% non-vacuous coverage, corrects three manually-written property errors, and finds a previously unknown bug.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual specification and verification of security properties for hardware designs is labor-intensive, error-prone, and relies on trusted design specifications that may be unavailable or incorrect. Automating security property generation without trusted specs can reduce engineering effort and catch bugs missed by manual approaches.

Method: CHARGE leverages the hierarchical structure of CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration) entries combined with LLMs (GPT-4.1) to reason about and identify security-critical assets in unverified RTL modules. From these identified assets and CWE semantics, it infers expected security behaviors and automatically generates SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA). The framework operates without trusted design specifications.

Result: On Hack@DAC18, 19, and 21 SoC designs, CHARGE detects 27 of 42 known bugs. For OpenPiton SoC (Hack@DAC21), 89% of generated SVAs run in Cadence JasperGold FPV with 92.2% non-vacuous. CHARGE correctly writes properties for three bugs where manually-written properties were incorrect, and discovers one previously unidentified bug in the Hack@DAC21 OpenPiton SoC.

Conclusion: CHARGE demonstrates that LLM-driven, CWE-guided automated property generation is a viable and effective approach for hardware security verification, capable of matching and in some cases exceeding the quality of manually-written properties while reducing engineering effort.

Abstract: This paper presents CHARGE, an automated framework for generating security properties for unverified RTL modules using CWEs and large language models (LLMs). The hallmark is a reasoning process that leverages the hierarchical nature of CWE entries to improve accuracy when identifying security-critical assets in unverified RTL modules. As a result, the approach can infer expected security behaviors and generate properties from identified assets and CWE semantics, avoiding the need for trusted design specifications and reducing manual engineering effort. We evaluate the framework on the Hack@DAC18, 19, and 21 open source SoC designs using OpenAI's GPT-4.1. CHARGE detects 27 of 42 known bugs in these designs. For Hack@DAC21 OpenPiton SoC, 89% of the generated SVAs run in Cadence JasperGold FPV, and 92.2% are non-vacuous. We compare to an open-source, manually written set of properties for these designs and find that CHARGE correctly writes properties for three bugs in which the manually written properties were incorrect. In addition, CHARGE-generated properties identify a new bug in the Hack@DAC21 OpenPiton SoC that was not previously identified.

</details>


### [79] [Adaptive Security at the Edge for 6G-Enabled Healthcare IoT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27858)
*Ijaz Ahmad,Ijaz Ahmad,Erkki Harjula*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: NANOEDGEGUARD is a kernel-plane rate controller for healthcare IoT edge gateways that mitigates burst-induced delay on time-critical alarms. It enforces multi-tier rate policies using in-kernel traffic-control hooks with hysteresis-based recovery and audit logging. On a Raspberry Pi testbed, it reduced 99th-percentile alarm RTT by 13.3% versus a user-space firewall and cut excess burst traffic by 46% compared to no enforcement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Healthcare IoT edge gateways must simultaneously relay routine telemetry and time-critical alarms. Even brief traffic bursts from sensor endpoints can inflate worst-case queuing delay, potentially delaying life-critical alarm delivery. Existing static firewall rules and user-space control loops lack the speed and adaptability to dynamically suppress bursts while preserving alarm latency.

Method: NANOEDGEGUARD is implemented as a kernel-plane closed-loop controller. It observes per-source traffic intensity at the edge gateway and enforces a multi-tier rate policy using in-kernel traffic-control (tc) hooks. It employs hysteresis for explicit, stable recovery from rate-limiting states and logs all policy transitions for auditability. The evaluation uses a Raspberry Pi gateway running an MQTT broker with two ESP32 endpoints generating vitals, alarms, and timed bursts.

Result: Compared to a user-space firewall baseline, NANOEDGEGUARD reduced 99th-percentile alarm round-trip time by 13.3% while maintaining RTT equivalent to no-enforcement levels. It also reduced excess admitted burst traffic by 46% relative to having no rate enforcement.

Conclusion: Adaptive, auditable kernel-plane rate enforcement at the edge gateway can materially improve resilience for healthcare IoT deployments. The approach is extensible toward on-demand policy deployment in future edge intelligence architectures.

Abstract: Healthcare IoT services increasingly rely on edge gateways to relay routine telemetry and deliver rare but timecritical alarms. Even short traffic bursts can inflate worstcase delay and interfere with urgent messages. We present NANOEDGEGUARD, a kernel-plane closed-loop controller that observes per-source traffic intensity at the edge and enforces an auditable, multi-tier rate policy using in-kernel traffic-control hooks. Unlike static firewall rules or user-space control loops, our design prioritizes fast actuation and explicit recovery through hysteresis, and it records policy transitions for auditability. Using a Raspberry Pi gateway hosting an MQTT broker and two ESP32 endpoints generating vitals, alarms, and a timed burst, we show that adaptive kernel-plane rate control reduces the 99th-percentile alarm RTT by 13.3% compared to a user-space firewall baseline while maintaining no-enforcement-level RTT, and it reduces excess admitted burst traffic by 46% compared to no enforcement. These early results indicate that adaptive, auditable enforcement at the gateway can improve resilience for healthcare IoT, and it can be extended toward on-demand policy deployment in future edge intelligence.

</details>


### [80] [Don't Trust the AI Ecosystem: Analyzing Privacy Leakage in Compromised Open-Source Components](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27886)
*Jin-Seong Kim,Han-Ju Lee,Seok-Won Hong,Takeshi Takahashi,Chansu Han,Tomohiro Morikawa,Seok-Hwan Choi*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: GradLock is a training-time injection attack that embeds private data directly into model parameters using stateless deterministic indexing and dynamic gradient locking, enabling near-lossless, instant extraction of pixel-perfect private data that survives standard deployment optimizations and evades human detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing model inversion attacks rely on post-training optimization but are limited by the target model's generalization bottleneck, recovering only generic features rather than exact private data, especially on high-dimensional datasets. The authors aim to overcome this by injecting data during training within a compromised supply chain, enabling pixel-perfect reconstruction without post-hoc access.

Method: GradLock operates in a compromised supply chain setting with two key mechanisms: (1) Stateless deterministic indexing to create isolated data vaults within model parameters, and (2) Dynamic gradient locking to prevent payload degradation during optimization. The adversary can later extract embedded data from the final model without retaining training environment access.

Result: On MNIST, Imagenette, and CelebA, GradLock achieves near-lossless reconstruction (SSIM ~1.0) with instant extraction under 1 second. It demonstrates superior robustness against quantization, pruning, and fine-tuning compared to prior training-time injection methods. In a user study, 93.3% of participants failed to detect the malicious logic.

Conclusion: GradLock exposes a critical blind spot in AI supply chain security, demonstrating that training-time injection can embed extractable private data with high fidelity and stealth, and calls for greater scrutiny of training provenance and model integrity.

Abstract: Existing model inversion (MI) attacks predominantly rely on post-training optimization to recover private data from model outputs. However, these methods are fundamentally constrained by the target model's generalization bottleneck, often yielding generic features rather than specific identities, particularly on high-dimensional datasets. In this paper, we introduce GradLock, a novel training-time injection attack that stealthily injects sensitive training data directly into the model parameters. Operating within a compromised supply chain context, GradLock leverages stateless deterministic indexing to establish isolated data vaults and employs dynamic gradient locking to prevent payload degradation during the optimization process. This mechanism allows the adversary to extract pixel-perfect data from the final model without retaining access to the training environment. Extensive experiments on MNIST, Imagenette, and CelebA demonstrate that GradLock achieves near-lossless reconstruction (SSIM ~ 1.0) and instant extraction (< 1.0s). Compared to existing training-time injection methods, our approach exhibits superior robustness against standard deployment optimizations, including quantization, pruning, and fine-tuning. Furthermore, a user deployment study reveals that 93.3% of participants failed to detect the malicious logic, highlighting a severe blind spot in the security of modern AI supply chains.

</details>


### [81] [Benign on Label, Malicious by Design: Clean-Label Dormant-to-Activated Backdoor via Machine Unlearning with Removable Camouflage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27936)
*Dongdong Zhao,Can Li,Xiang Yao,Fan He,Qihang Ge,Baogang Song*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper proposes a clean-label unlearning-activated backdoor attack where the backdoor remains dormant after training and only activates after specific training records are unlearned. The method uses a dual-generator bilevel optimization framework that jointly learns sample-specific triggers (latent association) and camouflage samples (removable suppression), achieving low pre-unlearning attack success rates and strong post-unlearning activation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing backdoor attacks are effective immediately after implantation, risking exposure before exploitation. While machine unlearning-activated dormant backdoors aim to solve this by delaying activation until after unlearning, current methods fail to simultaneously achieve (1) low pre-unlearning attack success rate, (2) strong post-unlearning activation, under (3) clean-label constraints and (4) realistic unlearning requests. The core challenge is jointly establishing a persistent latent association and a removable suppressive influence.

Method: The authors propose a clean-label unlearning-activated backdoor framework formulated as a bilevel optimization problem. It employs dual-generator learning that alternates between: (a) learning sample-specific triggers that establish a latent trigger-to-target association, and (b) learning label-consistent camouflage samples that provide removable suppression. The framework simulates both latent backdoor establishment and machine unlearning during training. Once the camouflage subset is unlearned, suppression is lifted and the dormant backdoor activates.

Result: Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-10 demonstrate that the proposed method maintains lower pre-unlearning attack success rates while achieving stronger post-unlearning activation across multiple unlearning algorithms compared to representative backdoor baselines.

Conclusion: Reliable dormancy-to-activation transitions can be achieved by coordinating a persistent latent association with removable suppression under clean-label and realistic deletion constraints. The dual-generator bilevel optimization framework effectively realizes this coordination.

Abstract: Existing backdoor attacks often become effective immediately after backdoor implantation and may therefore be exposed before exploitation. Machine unlearning activated dormant backdoors mitigate such behavioral exposure by remaining inactive after training and becoming effective only after selected training records are unlearned. However, existing methods struggle to simultaneously achieve a low pre-unlearning attack success rate and strong post-unlearning activation under clean-label constraints and realistic unlearning requests. Achieving this transition requires jointly establishing a persistent latent association and a removable suppressive influence. To address this challenge, we propose a clean-label unlearning-activated backdoor framework based on dual-generator learning and formulate it as a bilevel optimization problem: By simulating latent backdoor establishment and machine unlearning, the framework alternately learns sample-specific triggers that establish a latent trigger-to-target association and label-consistent camouflage samples that provide removable suppression. Once a small subset of camouflage samples is unlearned, the suppression is lifted and the dormant backdoor is activated. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-10 show that our method maintains lower pre-unlearning attack success rates while achieving stronger post-unlearning activation across multiple unlearning algorithms than representative backdoor baselines. These results demonstrate that reliable dormancy-to-activation transitions can be achieved by coordinating a persistent latent association with removable suppression under clean-label and realistic deletion constraints.

</details>


### [82] [Safeguards Based on Copyable Context Cannot Provide Reliable Safety for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27951)
*Pingyu Wu,Lingyao Zhu,Weiming Zhang,Nenghai Yu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper argues that LLM safeguards face a fundamental limitation: they must decide to answer before knowing how the answer will be used. For dual-use tasks, this creates a safety trilemma where Useful Capability, Reliable Safety, and Open Access cannot all coexist. A floor on attacker assistance is derived when evidence is copyable, and trusted credentials (hard-to-copy information) are proposed as a complement to existing safeguards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM safeguards evaluate requests without observing downstream use, creating a structural vulnerability for dual-use tasks (e.g., coding, biology). An attacker can mimic benign users and interaction histories, making it impossible to distinguish legitimate from malicious use based solely on request content. The paper seeks to formalize this inherent limitation and explore conditions under which it can be overcome.

Method: The authors formalize the problem by separating model capability release from available evidence about downstream use. Under the assumption that evidence is copyable (i.e., attackers can replicate benign-looking interaction patterns), they derive the exact worst-case lower bound on attacker assistance that must be tolerated to preserve useful answers. This yields the safety trilemma. They then introduce trusted credentials as a source of hard-to-copy information predictive of actual use and identify the stronger condition required to eliminate the attacker assistance floor. Empirical support is drawn from dual-use evaluations, adaptive attacks, and deployed trusted-access programs.

Result: A formal safety trilemma is established: Useful Capability, Reliable Safety, and Open Access cannot coexist. When evidence of downstream use is copyable, there is a mathematically derived, non-zero worst-case floor on attacker assistance. Trusted credentials that provide hard-to-copy information can eliminate this floor if they satisfy a stronger identifiability condition. Evidence from dual-use benchmarks, adaptive red-teaming, and real-world trusted-access deployments corroborates the theoretical findings.

Conclusion: LLM safety cannot rely solely on pre-answer content filtering for dual-use tasks due to the fundamental copyability of benign-looking evidence. A trusted credential infrastructure that provides hard-to-copy, use-predictive signals is necessary to break the trilemma and achieve both useful capability and reliable safety in high-stakes domains.

Abstract: Large language model safeguards decide whether to answer before seeing how an answer will be used. This creates a basic problem for dual-use tasks: the same answer can help an authorized professional or an attacker, while an attacker can imitate a benign request and interaction history. We separate the capability released by the model from the evidence available about downstream use. When that evidence is copyable, we derive the exact worst-case floor on attacker assistance while preserving useful answers. The result yields a safety trilemma: Useful Capability, Reliable Safety, and Open Access cannot coexist. We then show how a trusted credential can complement existing safeguards by adding hard-to-copy information that predicts actual downstream use, and identify the stronger condition needed to eliminate the floor. Evidence from dual-use evaluations, adaptive attacks, and deployed trusted-access programs supports the practical relevance of these conditions.

</details>


### [83] [Driving up Inference Energy on SNNs: Per-Sample and Universal Sponge Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27990)
*Spyridon Raptis,Haralampos-G. Stratigopoulos*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are vulnerable to "sponge attacks" — input-space perturbations that inflate inference-time energy consumption by increasing spike activity (SynOps). The authors introduce both per-sample and universal sponge attacks for native event-based SNNs, demonstrating 1.5–2.6× and 1.09–1.24× SynOp inflation respectively across three neuromorphic datasets, with energy overheads up to 13.24 mJ on Loihi-1.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SNNs are attractive for always-on edge systems due to sparse, energy-efficient spike-based communication. However, this efficiency advantage creates a security vulnerability: sponge attacks can silently inflate energy consumption without affecting prediction correctness, making them undetectable by accuracy-based monitoring. While prior work explored per-sample attacks on rate-coded SNNs, the threat to native event-based binary inputs and the feasibility of universal (reusable) perturbations remained unexamined.

Method: The authors develop two attack models: (1) A per-sample sponge attack using gradient-based optimization to craft adversarial spike trains that maximize SynOp count while preserving correct classification (98%+ accuracy retention). (2) A universal sponge attack — a fixed binary perturbation computed offline and XOR-applied to all inputs without per-sample optimization. SynOp inflation is mapped to estimated energy overhead on Loihi-1 neuromorphic hardware across NMNIST, SHD, and IBM DVS Gesture datasets using three SNN models.

Result: The per-sample attack achieves 1.5–2.6× SynOp inflation with ≥98% classification preservation. The universal attack, though weaker, achieves 1.09–1.24× SynOp inflation across all datasets. Estimated Loihi-1 energy overheads range from 14 μJ to 13.24 mJ per inference. The universal perturbation represents a practical deployment threat requiring no per-input computation.

Conclusion: Native event-based SNNs are practically vulnerable to input-space efficiency attacks. Universal sponge perturbations, despite being weaker than per-sample variants, pose a realistic continuous-deployment threat where cumulative energy drain can meaningfully impact battery life in always-on edge systems. This expands the attack surface beyond correctness-focused adversarial threats to energy-oriented denial-of-service.

Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) communicate through sparse binary spike events rather than dense activations, enabling energy-efficient inference on neuromorphic hardware and motivating their use in always-on, battery-powered edge systems. We show that this same efficiency advantage creates a distinct security risk: sponge attacks can increase inference-time spike activity and synaptic workload, inflating energy consumption while remaining difficult to detect through correctness-based monitoring alone. Prior input-space efficiency attacks on SNNs have focused on per-sample optimization, primarily in rate-coded settings. We extend this threat to native event-based binary inputs and study two attack models. First, we develop a per-sample sponge attack that crafts a custom adversarial spike train for each input via gradient-based optimization. This attack increases per-inference SynOps by 1.5-2.6x on three SNN models for the NMNIST, SHD, and IBM DVS Gesture datasets, while preserving the predicted class on at least 98% of evaluated samples. Second, to the best of our knowledge, we introduce the first universal sponge attack for native event-based SNN inputs: a fixed binary perturbation computed offline and applied via XOR to all subsequent inputs. Although weaker, it still inflates SynOps by 1.09-1.24x across all three datasets and represents a more realistic deployment threat because it requires no per-input optimization. Mapping SynOp inflation to estimated Loihi-1 energy yields per-inference overheads from 14 $μ$J to 13.24 mJ. These results show that native event-based SNNs are vulnerable to practical input-space efficiency attacks, and that reusable universal perturbations can accumulate into meaningful battery drain in continuously deployed edge systems.

</details>


### [84] [Temporal Poisoning: Clean-Label Backdoors via Event Redistribution in SNNs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28075)
*Roberto Riaño,Gorka Abad,Stjepan Picek,Aitor Urbieta*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: First clean-label backdoor attack on Spiking Neural Networks using temporal poisoning that preserves per-pixel event counts, achieving near-perfect ASR while evading rate-collapsed defenses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing backdoor attacks on SNNs rely on dirty-label poisoning (relabeling triggered samples). The authors aim to demonstrate a more stealthy clean-label attack where only the target class is poisoned with a temporal transformation, leaving labels intact and per-pixel event counts preserved, making poisoned and clean samples appear identical under temporal aggregation.

Method: A fixed timestamp transformation is applied exclusively to target-class training streams, altering the temporal sequence processed by the SNN while exactly preserving per-pixel, per-polarity event counts. The attack is evaluated across three neuromorphic datasets using both convolutional and transformer-based victim architectures, with poison-budget and trigger-shape ablations. A model-free detector based on per-step event mass is proposed to identify the temporal transformations.

Result: The attack achieves an ASR of 1.00 in strongest configurations across all datasets and architectures. Rate-collapsed defenses (collapsing the time axis) are blind by construction. Feature-space detection methods succeed only in selected settings. The proposed per-step event mass detector effectively identifies the temporal transformations, revealing both the vulnerability of rate-collapsed defenses and limits to the attack's stealth.

Conclusion: Clean-label temporal poisoning is a viable and stealthy backdoor attack on SNNs that exploits the temporal dimension. Defenses relying on temporal aggregation are fundamentally inadequate, highlighting the need for temporally-aware defense mechanisms in neuromorphic systems.

Abstract: Backdoor attacks on Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have primarily assumed dirty-label poisoning, in which triggered training samples are relabeled to an attacker-selected class. We study clean-label temporal poisoning, where a fixed timestamp transformation is applied only to the target-class training streams, leaving their labels unchanged. The transformation preserves the per-pixel, per-polarity event count exactly, making clean and triggered samples identical after temporal aggregation while altering the sequence processed by the SNN. Across three neuromorphic datasets and both convolutional and transformer-based victims, the attack reaches an ASR of 1.00 in the strongest configurations. We analyze the attack through poison-budget and trigger-shape ablations and evaluate established backdoor defenses adapted to spiking models. Defenses that collapse the time axis before inspection are blind by construction, while feature-space methods detect the poison only in selected settings. Our model-free detector, based on per-step event mass, detects the evaluated temporal transformations, demonstrating both the limitation of rate-collapsed defenses and the boundary of the attack's stealth. To our knowledge, this is the first clean-label backdoor attack evaluated on SNNs and neuromorphic event data.

</details>


### [85] [Checking Information Flow in Cloud-based IoT Access Control Policies (Extended Version)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28088)
*Lorenzo Ceragioli,Letterio Galletta,Edoardo Lunati*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper presents IOT:POKER, a tool that models AWS IoT Core access control policies as formal information flow graphs and uses SMT solving to detect unwanted information flows between devices across trust compartments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Verifying IoT access control policies in isolation is insufficient; devices operate with different trust levels and across compartmentalized subsystems, creating risks of indirect information leakage that static permission checks miss.

Method: The authors formally model AWS IoT Core components (devices, topics, rules, policies), construct an information flow graph capturing permitted inter-device communication, build a finite symbolic representation of this graph using an SMT solver, and implement the approach in the IOT:POKER tool for automated verification of unwanted information flows.

Result: The approach was evaluated on a realistic IoT scenario and several real-world AWS IoT policies, demonstrating its ability to identify security vulnerabilities from indirect information flow that would be missed by isolated permission inspection.

Conclusion: Modeling IoT access control as an information flow problem and leveraging SMT-based verification enables systematic detection of cross-compartment leaks, improving security posture for cloud-managed IoT deployments.

Abstract: Many cloud providers for IoT technologies offer access control mechanisms whose proper configuration is critical for security. However, verifying permissions in isolation is insufficient in a setting where devices have different levels of trust or are compartmentalised in various subsystems. This work analyses IoT access control policies to identify potential security vulnerabilities from unwanted information flow between devices. To this end, we formally model AWS IoT Core's components and define an information flow graph to capture the communication among devices permitted by the access control policies. We build a finite representation of the graph by leveraging an SMT solver, thus enabling the verification of information flow between devices. We implement our approach in a tool called IOT:POKER, and assess it on a realistic scenario and several real-world policies.

</details>


### [86] [Agent Harness Distillation: Inference-Time Harness Extraction and Exploitation in Autonomous Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28147)
*Yu Cui,Wuli Yang,Yirui Shi,Junhao Xia,Hui Jiang,Lei Gao,Chenfu Bao*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: AHD is a framework that extracts inference-time harnesses from autonomous multi-agent systems via black-box interactions, revealing significant IP leakage risks. The authors also propose a deception-based defense to mitigate extraction while maintaining agent utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inference-time harnesses in AMAS (like Hermes) require substantial engineering effort and represent valuable IP. While IP leakage has been studied in static multi-agent systems, risks in AMAS—where harness behavior emerges dynamically—remain unexplored. The paper addresses this gap.

Method: AHD uses a two-stage black-box extraction pipeline: (1) pre-distillation infers harness behaviors from target agent responses and constructs an initial harness; (2) post-distillation iteratively refines the harness to align with target behavioral patterns. An evaluation framework quantifies extraction risks. A deception-based defense is also proposed.

Result: Experiments across multiple backbone LLMs on real-world AMAS demonstrate AHD's effectiveness, revealing substantial IP leakage risks. The proposed deception-based defense successfully reduces harness extraction effectiveness while preserving the protected agent's utility.

Conclusion: Inference-time harness extraction constitutes a previously underexplored yet significant security threat to AMAS. AHD exposes this vulnerability, and deception-based defenses offer a viable mitigation strategy.

Abstract: Autonomous multi-agent systems (AMAS) built on large language models (LLMs), such as Hermes, increasingly rely on inference-time harnesses to coordinate reasoning and action. Constructing these harnesses requires substantial engineering effort and computational resources, as they are iteratively optimized over a combinatorial search space while co-evolving with the underlying LLM. Inference-time harnesses therefore constitute valuable intellectual property (IP). Although prior work has investigated IP leakage in static multi-agent systems with pre-configured architectures, it remains unclear whether similar risks arise in AMAS, where harness behavior emerges dynamically during inference. To address this gap, we introduce Agent Harness Distillation (AHD), a framework for studying the security risks arising from inference-time harness extraction in AMAS. We formalize harness extraction as a new security problem and develop an evaluation framework for quantifying such risks. AHD extracts inference-time harness capabilities from a target agent through black-box interactions and consists of two stages. In the pre-distillation stage, AHD infers inference-time harness behaviors from the responses of the target agent and constructs an initial harness. In the post-distillation stage, AHD iteratively refines the initial harness to align with the behavioral patterns of the target agent. Experiments on real-world AMAS across multiple backbone LLMs demonstrate the effectiveness of AHD and reveal substantial IP leakage risks. We further propose a deception-based defense that reduces harness extraction effectiveness while preserving the utility of the protected agent. Our findings uncover a previously underexplored security threat to AMAS.

</details>


### [87] [Piggybacking on Perception: Stealthy Concurrent Audio Prompt Injections against Multimodal LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28165)
*Mingxiao Liu,Yitong Li,Haoren Zhao,Yaoxiang Bian,Jianan Ma,Jian Zhang,Jialuo Chen,Xinhao Deng,Zhen Wang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper uncovers a new attack surface for LLM-driven multimodal agents: concurrent audio prompt injection, where malicious instructions are imperceptibly embedded in environmental noise alongside user speech. The authors build a comprehensive benchmark (AudioAgentSecurity), demonstrate 69.10% ASR against Gemini 3 Pro, and propose CADV — a defense using source separation and cross-modal consistency analysis achieving >90% detection success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-driven multimodal agents increasingly rely on continuous audio interaction, but audio inputs contain uncontrollable environmental noise. While prior work addresses acoustic attacks on voice devices (e.g., hidden voice commands), the threat of malicious instructions concurrently injected into ambient audio — piggybacking on legitimate user speech — remains under-explored. This gap motivates a systematic investigation of concurrent audio prompt injection attacks and defenses for multimodal agents.

Method: The attack side introduces two novel techniques: (1) instruction augmentation — optimizing malicious prompts to survive speech recognition while remaining semantically effective, and (2) scenario concealment — disguising attack audio as benign environmental sounds. For benchmarking, AudioAgentSecurity is constructed with 8 task scenarios and 10 attack patterns. The defense, Cascaded Audio Decoupling and Verification (CADV), employs acoustic source separation to isolate candidate audio streams, followed by cross-modal consistency analysis comparing transcribed instructions against visual/contextual cues to detect injected commands.

Result: Against 11 state-of-the-art agents (including Gemini 3 Pro and GPT-4o-audio), the proposed attacks achieve an average ASR of 69.10% on Gemini 3 Pro. CADV achieves over 90% detection success across diverse attack vectors, outperforming prompt-level defenses. Real-world experiments on the Doubao AI Smartphone with human volunteers confirm both the stealth/efficacy of attacks and the reliability of CADV in dynamic environments.

Conclusion: Concurrent audio prompt injection poses a serious, previously under-explored threat to multimodal LLM agents. The proposed CADV defense, grounded in acoustic source separation rather than prompt-level filtering, provides robust detection (>90% success). The authors advocate for audio-level security mechanisms as a necessary complement to text-level safeguards in multimodal agent systems.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-driven multimodal agents are increasingly deployed to execute autonomous tasks via continuous audio interaction. While this paradigm enhances interaction naturalness, it introduces a critical yet under-explored attack surface, as audio inputs inevitably contain environmental noise beyond user control. In this paper, we investigate concurrent audio prompt injection attacks targeting multimodal agents. Distinct from traditional acoustic attacks on voice devices, we propose novel techniques for instruction augmentation and scenario concealment. These methods allow malicious audio instructions to imperceptibly "piggyback" onto user speech, thereby hijacking agents to execute malicious actions. To systematically quantify this threat, we construct AudioAgentSecurity, the first comprehensive benchmark for audio instruction injection attacks, encompassing 8 real-world task scenarios and 10 distinct attack patterns. We evaluate 11 state-of-the-art agents, including Gemini 3 Pro and GPT-4o-audio. Notably, our methods achieve an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 69.10\% against the advanced Gemini 3 Pro. To counter this threat, we further introduce Cascaded Audio Decoupling and Verification (CADV), a defense mechanism based on source separation and consistency analysis. Compared with existing prompt-level defenses, CADV leverages acoustic source separation and cross-modal consistency analysis to detect audio instruction injections more robustly, achieving over 90\% detection success across diverse attack vectors. Finally, real-world experiments with human volunteers on Doubao AI Smartphone in diverse dynamic real-world scenarios confirm the attacks' high stealth and efficacy, while demonstrating that our defense reliably mitigates these vulnerabilities.

</details>


### [88] [Secure Aggregation for Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning on Clinical EEG Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28191)
*Pouya Rajabi,Mohsen Toorani*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A privacy-preserving federated learning framework for clinical EEG data that uses masking-based secure aggregation with multiple protection layers (secret sharing, dropout resilience, clipping, Bloom filters, auxiliary-notary verifiability), evaluated across semi-honest and malicious settings, demonstrating compatibility with model training at varying computational/communication costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard federated learning leaves individual model updates vulnerable to privacy leakage. Clinical EEG data is particularly sensitive, necessitating stronger protections that go beyond basic federated averaging to fully conceal individual contributions from the aggregation server.

Method: The framework integrates: (1) graph-based communication topology, (2) threshold secret sharing for masking, (3) dropout-resilient aggregation to handle client churn, (4) local update clipping to bound sensitivity, (5) optional Bloom filter-based private record linkage for initialization, and (6) auxiliary-notary-based verifiability. Implemented in Flower FL, evaluated on TUH EEG data in a cross-silo simulated healthcare setting under semi-honest, malicious, and auxiliary-notary aggregation variants.

Result: All secure variants successfully hide individual updates from the aggregation server under stated assumptions. The semi-honest variant achieves the lowest computational, communication, and round-duration overhead. Malicious-setting safeguards and lightweight consistency-checking mechanisms incur additional overhead but provide stronger consistency, integrity, and verifiability guarantees.

Conclusion: Masking-based secure aggregation is compatible with federated EEG model training and offers a configurable privacy-utility-cost trade-off: the semi-honest variant minimizes overhead, while malicious and auxiliary-notary variants provide enhanced security properties at a higher but manageable cost.

Abstract: Federated learning enables multiple institutions to train shared models without exchanging raw clinical EEG data, but it does not fully prevent privacy leakage from individual model updates. This paper presents a privacy-preserving federated learning framework for clinical EEG data using masking-based secure aggregation as the core protection mechanism. The framework combines graph-based communication, threshold secret sharing, dropout-resilient aggregation, local update clipping, an optional Bloom filter-based privacy-preserving record-linkage initialization module, and auxiliary-notary-based verifiability. It supports both semi-honest and malicious aggregation settings and is implemented using the Flower federated learning framework. The secure-aggregation variants are evaluated in a simulated cross-silo healthcare setting using TUH EEG-derived data under different client configurations. Under the stated assumptions, the secure variants hide individual updates from the aggregation server. The results show that these variants remain compatible with federated model training, although malicious-setting safeguards and lightweight consistency-checking mechanisms introduce additional computation, communication, and round-duration overhead. The semi-honest variant provides the lowest overhead among the secure configurations, while malicious and auxiliary-notary variants offer stronger consistency, integrity, and lightweight verification support at higher cost.

</details>


### [89] [Security of World-Model-Based Embodied AI: A Lifecycle of Threats, Defenses, and Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28226)
*Fazhong Liu,Zhuoyan Chen,Haozhen Tan,Yan Meng,Guoxing Chen,Haojin Zhu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A survey examining security threats to world models in embodied AI across their entire lifecycle, from data construction to execution and adaptation. It taxonomizes how attacks like poisoning, backdoors, and adversarial examples manifest uniquely in world-model contexts, and highlights the duality of world models as both safety shields and sources of predictive safety illusions when compromised.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World models introduce a new security boundary in embodied AI systems. While they enable predictive planning beyond reactive control, their reliance on compressed representations, learned dynamics, and action-conditioned simulation creates novel attack surfaces where compromise can propagate from data, sensors, prompts, or feedback into unsafe physical actions. Existing security analysis treats world models in isolation; a holistic lifecycle perspective is needed.

Method: The authors conduct a comprehensive survey that traces threats across the full world-model lifecycle: data construction, representation learning, state grounding, imagination/simulation, trajectory evaluation, execution, and long-term adaptation via memory and tools. They develop a lifecycle taxonomy, map known attack families (poisoning, backdoors, adversarial examples, sensor spoofing, prompt injection, trajectory manipulation, supply-chain attacks) to world-model security properties, outline evaluation protocols for safety failures, and structure defenses across provenance, robust grounding, uncertainty-aware prediction, trajectory gating, feedback auditing, and deployment assurance.

Result: The survey reveals that familiar attack families acquire distinct and more consequential meanings when applied to world models — corrupting world states, learned dynamics, affordances, or safety costs can yield cascading physical harm. It identifies a critical duality: world models can serve as runtime safety shields, but when compromised or over-trusted they produce predictive safety illusions. The structured taxonomy enables systematic reasoning about where and how security failures arise across the lifecycle.

Conclusion: World-model security is an underexplored but critical area for safe embodied AI. A lifecycle-aware defense strategy — spanning provenance, robust grounding, uncertainty quantification, trajectory gating, feedback auditing, and deployment assurance — is essential to prevent world models from becoming predictive safety illusions. The survey provides a foundation for systematic evaluation and defense design in this emerging threat landscape.

Abstract: World models give embodied AI a predictive core: they compress observations into states, simulate action-conditioned futures, and enable planning beyond reactive control. This predictive layer, however, opens a new security boundary-compromise can propagate from data, sensors, prompts, or feedback into physical action. Rather than treating world models as an isolated component, this survey traces threats across their entire lifecycle-from data construction and representation learning, through state grounding and imagination, to trajectory evaluation, execution, and long-term adaptation via memory and tools. We show that familiar attack families: poisoning, backdoors, adversarial examples, sensor spoofing, prompt injection, trajectory manipulation, and supply-chain attacks take on distinct meanings when they corrupt world states, learned dynamics, affordance estimates, or safety costs. We also highlight a duality: world models can serve as runtime safety shields, yet when compromised or over-trusted they generate predictive safety illusions. The survey offers a lifecycle taxonomy, maps existing attacks to world-model security properties, outlines evaluation protocols for safety failures, and structures defenses across provenance, robust grounding, uncertainty-aware prediction, trajectory gating, feedback auditing, and deployment assurance.

</details>
