### [90] [Implementing Homomorphic Encryption-Based Logic Locking in System-on-Chip Designs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28542)
*Ye Ziyang,Makoto Ikeda*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A logic locking scheme using binary Ring-LWE is implemented on a RISC-V SoC, securing privilege switching without exposing locking parameters, with 6.0% LUT and 6.9% Register overhead and ~2.6 µs unlock latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional logic locking methods require sharing raw locking parameters with users, creating a security vulnerability where these sensitive parameters could be exposed or reverse-engineered. The authors aim to develop a scheme that protects critical logic paths—specifically in privilege switching—without revealing locking parameters to the end user.

Method: The proposed approach employs the binary Ring Learning With Errors (Ring-LWE) algorithm as the cryptographic foundation for logic locking. This is integrated into a RISC-V System-on-Chip (SoC) design, targeting critical logic paths involved in the privilege switching process. The Ring-LWE-based scheme allows the locking mechanism to operate without requiring distribution of raw locking parameters to users, thereby keeping sensitive parameters concealed within the hardware.

Result: The locking module consumes 3519 LUTs and 2645 Registers. Compared to the baseline (unlocked) RISC-V SoC, this represents a 6.0% overhead in LUTs and 6.9% overhead in Registers. The unlock process takes approximately 2.6 µs, introducing moderate performance impact that primarily affects system-level operations while leaving user-level computational efficiency largely unaffected.

Conclusion: The binary Ring-LWE-based logic locking scheme successfully protects privilege switching paths in a RISC-V SoC without exposing locking parameters. The resource overhead is modest (6–7%) and the unlock latency (~2.6 µs) is acceptable, with performance degradation confined mainly to system-level rather than user-level operations, making it a practical hardware security solution.

Abstract: This study presents a logic locking scheme based on the binary Ring Learning With Errors algorithm, implemented in a RISC-V System-on-Chip design. Unlike traditional logic locking methods that require providing users with raw locking parameters, the proposed approach secures critical logic paths in the privilege switching process without exposing these sensitive parameters. The implemented locking module itself consumes 3519 Look-Up Tables and 2645 Registers, leading to an overall overhead of 6.0% in Look-Up Tables and 6.9% in Registers compared to the baseline system. The unlock process requires about 2.6 us, introducing moderate performance impact, primarily affecting system-level operations while preserving user-level computational efficiency.

</details>


### [91] [Formalization of security](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28551)
*Gilles Barthe*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This chapter surveys the use of proof assistants across system security, language-based security, secure compilation, and cryptography, emphasizing their dual role in validating security properties and supporting formal certification processes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Proof assistants are increasingly employed to ensure that designs and implementations satisfy intended security properties. Beyond correctness validation, a key driver is their ability to facilitate formal certification, providing rigorous, machine-checkable evidence that systems meet specified security standards.

Method: The chapter adopts a survey-based approach, systematically reviewing applications of proof assistants (such as Coq, Isabelle/HOL, and others) across four domains: system security, language-based security, secure compilation, and cryptography. It discusses the techniques, frameworks, and formalizations used in each area.

Result: The survey demonstrates that proof assistants have been successfully applied to verify a range of security-critical properties—including information flow, memory safety, full abstraction in compilation, and cryptographic protocol correctness—while also revealing ongoing challenges in scalability, automation, and integration with real-world systems.

Conclusion: Proof assistants provide strong guarantees for security-critical systems and are a promising vehicle for certification. However, their broader adoption depends on addressing challenges related to proof effort, tool interoperability, and coverage of realistic threat models and implementation-level details.

Abstract: Proof assistants are often used to validate that designs and implementations meet their expected security properties. A further motivation for using proof assistants is to support certification. This chapter focuses on their applications to system security, language-based security, secure compilation, and cryptography.

</details>

### [92] [Multi-Head Attention Residuals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27230)
*Cheng Luo,Zefan Cai,Junjie Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Multi-Head Attention Residuals (MHAR) generalizes attention residuals by reshaping the routing query into per-subspace heads with individual softmax distributions over depth history, enabling subspaces to read different layers without added parameters. MHAR yields consistent validation loss improvements across 100M–1B scales and achieves U-shaped optimality at H=4 or 8. Custom Triton kernels recover most of the throughput, and identity-preserving conversion supports 8B mid-training gains on reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In standard Transformers, the single additive residual stream forces all feature subspaces to share one distribution when reading depth history via attention residuals. As model width increases, subspaces increasingly disagree about which past layers to attend to, creating a bottleneck where a single query compromises all subspaces' read preferences. The authors aim to resolve this forced compromise.

Method: MHAR reshapes the attention-residual routing query from one shared vector into H per-subspace heads, each computing its own softmax over the depth history. This yields a block-diagonal read pattern, adds zero parameters and negligible compute, and exactly recovers standard attention residuals when H=1. The approach is evaluated on 100M, 350M, and 1B models trained on a deduplicated, quality-filtered STEM/code-heavy Nemotron-based corpus. Fused Triton kernels optimize throughput. Identity-preserving conversion via delta attention residuals enables 8B mid-training.

Result: MHAR improves validation loss over standard Transformers by -0.061 (100M), -0.149 (350M), and -0.140 (1B), achieving the best result among four compared methods at all scales, with gains increasing at larger scales. Validation loss exhibits a U-shaped curve w.r.t. head count H, with a flat optimum at H=4 or 8; H=16 degrades performance. Probe analysis confirms learned subspace disagreement drives the benefit. Triton kernels raise throughput from 0.2–0.5× to 0.55–0.88× of baseline. Mid-training conversion at 8B yields +3.2 on GSM8K and +3.1 on GPQA.

Conclusion: MHAR is a parameter-free architectural modification that lets feature subspaces independently route attention across depth, yielding robust validation loss improvements that scale with model size. H is a genuine design axis with a consistent U-shaped optimum, and practical kernel optimizations make the method viable for large-scale training. Identity-preserving conversion further demonstrates its applicability to existing pretrained models for downstream reasoning gains.

Abstract: Transformers propagate information across depth through a single additive residual stream: every sublayer reads only the most recent state. Attention residuals relax this by letting each sublayer attend, through a learned softmax. However, that read uses a single query shared across the entire width, so every feature subspace must read the depth history through one distribution. The cost of this forced compromise grows with how much the subspaces disagree about which layers to read, and disagreement grows with model width. We introduce Multi-Head Attention Residuals (MHAR): the routing query is reshaped into H per-subspace heads, each with its own softmax over the depth history. The read becomes block-diagonal, the reshape adds zero parameters and negligible compute, and H = 1 recovers attention residuals exactly. Trained from scratch on a deduplicated Nemotron-based anneal corpus that is quality-filtered and STEM- and code-heavy, MHAR improves validation loss over a standard Transformer at 100M, 350M, and 1B (-0.061, -0.149, and -0.140). It achieves the best result among four methods in every setting, with the gain increasing from 100M to the larger scales. The head count is a real design axis rather than a free knob: validation loss is U-shaped with respect to H, with a flat optimum at H = 4 or H = 8 across scales. We adopt H = 8 for large-scale models; over-splitting beyond this point (H = 16) consistently gives back part of the gain. A direct probe of the trained queries confirms that learned subspace disagreement is the underlying driver. Fused Triton routing kernels increase attention-residual training throughput from 0.2-0.5x to 0.55-0.88x of the baseline while maintaining near-baseline peak memory. An identity-preserving conversion using delta attention residuals supports 8B mid-training, yielding improvements of +3.2 on GSM8K and +3.1 on GPQA.

</details>


### [93] [KernelGenBench: A Multi-Source and Multi-Chip Benchmark for LLM-based Kernel Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27231)
*Peiyu Zang,Jian Tao,Jialing Zhang,Yichen Yuan,Wentao Zhang,Guang Liu,Yonghua Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: KernelGenBench is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLM- and agent-generated Triton kernels across diverse operator sources and heterogeneous hardware. It reveals that agent-based methods outperform pure LLM sampling, cuBLAS operators are hardest, cross-platform performance degrades severely, and autonomous kernel generation remains extremely token-expensive.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs have driven demand for efficient accelerator kernels, yet kernel development remains highly specialized and labor-intensive. Despite progress in LLM-based automatic kernel generation, no comprehensive benchmark exists to rigorously evaluate generated kernels across diverse operator sources or heterogeneous hardware platforms.

Method: The authors introduce KernelGenBench, a unified benchmark with two sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (Multi-Source) evaluating 210 operators from three non-PyTorch-centric sources, and KernelGenBench-MC (Multi-Chip) measuring performance portability of a 110-operator subset across six heterogeneous hardware platforms. A large-scale evaluation consuming over 15 billion tokens was conducted.

Result: Three key findings: (1) agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling, with cuBLAS operators being the most challenging; (2) generation performance varies significantly across hardware, with kernel-specialized agents suffering severe cross-platform degradation (e.g., AutoKernel drops from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E); (3) autonomous kernel generation is highly cost-intensive, with specialized agent methods averaging 5.11 million tokens per successful operator.

Conclusion: KernelGenBench establishes a standardized framework for evaluating LLM-driven kernel generation, exposing critical gaps in cross-platform portability and cost-efficiency. The results highlight that current agent-based methods, while superior to pure sampling, remain impractical for large-scale deployment due to extreme token consumption and hardware-dependent performance variability.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly increased the demand for efficient accelerator kernels, but kernel development remains a highly specialized and labor-intensive task. The recent rise of LLMs and agentic frameworks offers a promising pathway toward automatic kernel generation. However, despite rapid progress, there is still no comprehensive benchmark to rigorously evaluate LLM-generated kernels across diverse operator sources or heterogeneous hardware platforms. We present KernelGenBench, a unified benchmark for systematically evaluating LLM- and agent-generated Triton kernels across diverse operator sources and heterogeneous hardware platforms. It comprises two complementary sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (Multi-Source), evaluating 210 operators from three sources beyond standard PyTorch-centric tasks, and KernelGenBench-MC (Multi-Chip), measuring performance portability across six heterogeneous hardware platforms using a 110-operator subset. Our large-scale evaluation, consuming over 15 billion tokens, shows: (1) agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling methods, while cuBLAS operators are the most challenging across all methods; (2) generation performance varies significantly across hardware platforms, with even recent kernel-specialized agents experiencing severe cross-platform degradation (e.g., AutoKernel drops from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E); (3) autonomous kernel generation remains highly cost-intensive, with specialized agent methods averaging 5.11 million tokens per successful operator (AKO4all reaches 5.19 million), orders of magnitude higher than simple LLM sampling approaches.

</details>


### [94] [RadHarmony: Radiological Data Handling in the Era of Agentic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27235)
*Frank Li,Bardia Khosravi,Mohammadreza Chavoshi,Theo Dapamede,YoungSeok Jeon,Janice Newsome,Hari Trivedi,Judy Gichoya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RadHarmony is an open-source Python library that unifies loading, harmonizing, and augmenting heterogeneous radiological datasets (24 public datasets) via a single API, supporting classification, segmentation, bounding boxes, and report text. It includes an AI-agent skill for integrating new datasets and is validated by pretraining a reference vision transformer on three chest radiograph datasets with no dataset-specific code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training deep learning models on radiological images requires integrating datasets from heterogeneous sources with inconsistent file formats, directory structures, label schemas, and annotation types. Existing solutions lack a unified interface that handles this diversity, creating a high barrier to multi-dataset pretraining and data harmonization in medical imaging.

Method: RadHarmony provides a unified Python API that: (1) standardizes metadata from 24 public datasets into a single tabular format; (2) wraps MONAI's map-style datasets for deep-learning-ready sample delivery with optional on-disk caching; (3) supports multiple annotation types (classification labels, segmentation masks, bounding boxes, radiology report text) through one interface; (4) offers an interactive visualization tool for dataset exploration; and (5) introduces an AI-agent skill that automates the workflow for integrating new datasets—from raw data inspection through code generation and testing.

Result: The library's utility is demonstrated by pretraining RadHarmony-ViT, a reference vision transformer baseline, on three heterogeneous chest radiograph datasets combined without any dataset-specific code, validating the abstraction's effectiveness for multi-dataset training.

Conclusion: RadHarmony lowers the barrier to multi-dataset radiological deep learning by providing a standardized, extensible framework for data harmonization. Its AI-assisted dataset integration workflow and unified API enable seamless pretraining across heterogeneous sources, as evidenced by the successful RadHarmony-ViT baseline.

Abstract: Training deep learning models on radiological images requires integrating heterogeneous datasets across different sources, file formats, directory layouts, label schemas, and annotation types. We present RadHarmony, an open-source Python library that provides a unified API for loading, harmonizing, and augmenting radiological datasets, with a primary focus on chest radiographs and early support for computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). RadHarmony standardizes metadata from 24 public datasets into a single tabular format, wraps MONAI's map-style datasets for deep-learning-ready sample delivery with optional on-disk caching, and supports classification labels, segmentation masks, bounding boxes, and radiology report text through a single interface, with an interactive visualization tool for dataset exploration and verification. To lower the barrier for integrating new datasets, RadHarmony introduces an AI-agent skill that guides the full integration workflow from raw data inspection through code generation and testing. We demonstrate the library's utility by pretraining RadHarmony-ViT, a reference vision transformer baseline that combines three heterogeneous chest radiograph datasets with no dataset-specific code. The code and pretrained model weights are available at https://github.com/f10409/RadHarmony.

</details>


### [95] [Asymmetric Collapse in Model Merging: When Refusal Over- writes Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27240)
*Aarnav Choudhary,Matheus Fonseca Rocha,Jiwon Seo,Vasu Sharma,Maheep Chaudhary*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: When merging two safety-specific fine-tuned models (harm classification vs. jailbreak refusal), standard merging methods disproportionately favor refusal behavior, causing near-total collapse of classification accuracy while preserving strong jailbreak resistance. The asymmetry stems from larger task-vector magnitudes in the refusal fine-tune rather than opposing directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model merging is widely used to combine fine-tuned capabilities without retraining, but it is unknown whether standard merging methods can simultaneously preserve multiple safety-relevant behaviors. This paper investigates whether merging two safety-oriented fine-tunes results in balanced retention of both capabilities or asymmetric degradation.

Method: The authors fine-tune two Gemma-3-1B-IT models on complementary safety objectives: CARES harm-level classification and WildJailbreak adversarial refusal. They merge these fine-tunes using four standard methods (Linear, SLERP, TIES, DARE-TIES) and evaluate merged models on three axes: classification accuracy, attack resistance, and benign compliance. Weight-space analysis measures task-vector cosine similarity and per-layer magnitude differences.

Result: All four merging methods show severe asymmetry: jailbreak refusal rates remain 81–85%, while CARES classification accuracy collapses to at most 12.9%. Task vectors are nearly orthogonal (cosine similarity 0.011), ruling out directional conflict. The refusal fine-tune has consistently larger per-layer task-vector magnitudes, causing magnitude-sensitive methods (SLERP, TIES, DARE-TIES) to favor refusal updates. Benign compliance also degrades, indicating broad refusal behavior.

Conclusion: Standard model merging can collapse safety recognition into broad, undifferentiated refusal when safety-relevant task vectors differ substantially in scale. This highlights a failure mode where merging does not composably integrate distinct safety capabilities but instead allows one to dominate, raising concerns for multi-safety deployment scenarios.

Abstract: Model merging is often used to combine capabilities from separately fine-tuned models without additional training, but it is unclear whether standard merging methods preserve multiple safety-relevant behaviors simultaneously. We study this question through a controlled case study using two Gemma-3-1B-IT finetunes on two complementary safety objectives: CARES harm-level classification and WildJailbreak adversarial refusal. We merge the two fine-tunes using Linear, SLERP, TIES, and DARE-TIES, and evaluate the merged models on classification accuracy, attack resistance, and benign compliance. Across all four methods, attack resistance transfers significantly more than classification accuracy: merged models retain 81-85% jailbreak refusal rates while CARES accuracy falls to at most 12.9%. Weight-space measurements suggest that this asymmetry is not caused by strongly opposing task-vector directions: the two task vectors are nearly orthogonal (cosine similarity 0.011). Instead, the refusal fine-tune induces consistently larger per-layer task-vector magnitudes, causing magnitude-sensitive methods to favor refusal updates. These results show that standard model merging can collapse safety recognition into broad refusal when safety-relevant task vectors differ substantially in scale.

</details>


### [96] [Divergence Decoding: Training-Free Capability Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27248)
*Yimi Wang,Hao Li,Shuo Yang,He Cao,Dechen Zhang,Ziang Wu,Zhiyuan Yan,Fanyang Mo,Li Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Divergence Decoding is a training-free framework that dynamically fuses a generalist LLM with a domain-specialist model at inference time. It uses Jensen-Shannon divergence to detect when the specialist's predictions diverge from the generalist's, routing control to the generalist at those tokens to inject reasoning while preserving domain expertise. The method outperforms both models individually on scientific benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generalist LLMs excel at reasoning but lack specialized scientific domain knowledge, while domain-specialized models possess deep knowledge but suffer from diminished logical reasoning and reduced robustness. The paper addresses the dilemma of how to combine these complementary strengths without requiring additional training.

Method: Divergence Decoding adapts the "draft-and-verify" speculative decoding framework into an adaptive routing mechanism. At each token generation step, Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) is computed between the output distributions of the generalist and specialist models. When JSD exceeds a threshold—indicating significant distributional disagreement and thus potential reasoning risk—the framework routes control to the generalist. Otherwise, the specialist's predictions are retained. This enables inference-time policy composition without any training.

Result: Evaluated on Qwen and Llama model families across GPQA, ChemBench, and ChemCoTBench, Divergence Decoding outperformed both the domain-specialized and general-purpose models, surpassing most single-model baselines.

Conclusion: Divergence Decoding offers a general, training-free paradigm for fusing diverse LLM capabilities through adaptive inference-time collaboration, effectively combining domain expertise with strong general reasoning.

Abstract: While large language models excel in reasoning, these generalists often lack knowledge for specialized scientific domains. Conversely, domain models~(specialists), while knowledgeable, suffer from specialization side-effects including diminished logic and reduced robustness.To address this dilemma, we introduce Divergence Decoding, a training-free framework for capability fusion. It reconstructs the "draft-and-verify" skeleton of speculative decoding into an adaptive routing mechanism. The core is using Jensen-Shannon divergence to monitor the distributional disagreement between the two models at each token. When the specialist exhibits significant divergence, our method identifies it as a potential reasoning risk and instantaneously routes control to the generalist. This allows the dynamic injection of general reasoning while preserving domain expertise, achieving inference-time policy composition of the generalist and the specialist.We evaluate Divergence Decoding across diverse model families (Qwen and Llama series) on challenging scientific benchmarks (GPQA, ChemBench, and ChemCoTBench). Experimental results demonstrate that Divergence Decoding outperforms both the domain-specialized and general-purpose models, effectively surpassing the performance of most single-model baseline. This suggests that Divergence Decoding provides a general, training-free paradigm for fusing diverse LLM capabilities through adaptive inference-time collaboration.

</details>


### [97] [Autonomous Event-Driven Multi-Agent Orchestration for Enterprise AI at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20058)
*Harsh Rao Dhanyamraju,Leonidas Raghav,Aaron Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper evaluates two multi-agent architectures (DAG Plan and Execute vs. ReAct) across 208 enterprise scenarios at three scales (Persona, Department, Enterprise). Key findings: scale, not task complexity, dominates orchestration performance; agent discovery noise is the primary bottleneck at enterprise scale; DAG excels in precision at small scales but degrades more steeply; ReAct is more robust; a Task Manager with priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption significantly improves latency and correctness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise AI requires continuous event monitoring, detection, and action across specialist agents, but existing multi-agent systems assume discrete request-response workflows and have not been evaluated at enterprise scale.

Method: The authors evaluate DAG Plan and Execute and ReAct architectures across 208 production-derived enterprise scenarios at three scales: Persona (<10 agents), Department (20-80 agents), and Enterprise (200 agents). They introduce a Task Manager component that enables continuous operation through priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption mechanisms.

Result: Scale dominates orchestration performance more than task complexity. Both architectures degrade at enterprise scale due to agent discovery noise as the primary bottleneck. Simple tasks degrade more sharply than complex ones. DAG Plan and Execute provides higher precision and structured parallelization at smaller scales but suffers from higher overhead at enterprise scale. ReAct is more robust via incremental failure handling. The Task Manager reduces high-priority queue latency by 14-75% and improves related-event correctness by over 20 percentage points at enterprise scale.

Conclusion: Enterprise-scale multi-agent orchestration faces fundamental bottlenecks from agent discovery noise rather than task complexity. Architectural choice involves a trade-off between precision/parallelism (DAG) and robustness (ReAct). Continuous operation mechanisms like the proposed Task Manager are essential for practical enterprise deployment.

Abstract: Enterprise AI aims to move toward continuous event monitoring, detection, and action across specialist agents, yet existing multi-agent systems largely assume discrete request-response workflows and remain underexplored at enterprise scale. We evaluate DAG Plan and Execute and ReAct across 208 production-derived enterprise scenarios spanning Persona (<10 agents), Department (20-80), and Enterprise (200) scales, and introduce a Task Manager for continuous operation via priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption. Results show that scale, not task complexity, dominates orchestration performance: both architectures perform well at small scale but degrade at enterprise scale as agent discovery noise becomes the primary bottleneck, with simple tasks degrading more sharply than complex ones. DAG Plan and Execute offers higher precision and structured parallelization at smaller scales, but its higher overhead worsens at enterprise scale; ReAct is more robust by handling failures incrementally. The Task Manager reduces high-priority queue latency by 14-75% and improves related-event correctness by over 20 percentage points at enterprise scale.

</details>


### [98] [PIE-APT: A Unified Framework for Temporal Planning and Contradiction Hunting via Incremental Direct-Derivation Abduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27287)
*Amir Hossein Sharafi,Alireza Shahbazi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A unified framework combining incremental direct-derivation abduction (PIE-Abducer) with abductive temporal planning (PIE-APT) for reasoning over Dynamic Knowledge Graphs under incomplete information, operating natively on Description Logic without external modal operators, and outperforming both classical planners and MHS-based baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing action formalisms for Dynamic Knowledge Graphs suffer from decidability issues and the Ramification Problem, while handling incomplete knowledge via structural abduction requires prohibitive combinatorial search (e.g., Minimal Hitting Set enumeration). A unified, decidable framework operating natively in expressive Description Logic is needed.

Method: The framework models state transitions as non-monotonic updates to deductively closed DL theories along a linear timeline, treating an incremental reasoner as a black-box and representing actions in OWL to preserve decidability. PIE-Abducer avoids MHS enumeration by injecting the negation of the target goal and extracting missing premises via direct refutation consequences. PIE-APT uses recursive Generate-and-Test: backward-chaining A* search interleaved with PIE-Abducer (bounded causal depth), followed by forward-chaining Temporal Projection for validation.

Result: Evaluated on four OWL benchmarks (parameterized goals with witness search, mid-search DL entailment, open-world assumption injection, adversarial contradiction hunting), the approach demonstrates qualitative superiority over classical planners and quantitative outperformance of an MHS-faithful baseline during abductive enrichment.

Conclusion: The native DL, black-box reasoner approach successfully integrates abduction and planning for DKGs without sacrificing decidability, and direct-derivation abduction proves more efficient than combinatorial MHS-based methods.

Abstract: Reasoning and planning over Dynamic Knowledge Graphs (DKGs) present significant challenges, especially in open-world environments with incomplete information. Existing action formalisms often face decidability issues and the Ramification Problem, while managing incomplete knowledge via structural abduction requires expansive combinatorial search. This paper introduces a unified framework with two integrated modules---\textbf{PIE-Abducer} (incremental direct-derivation abduction) and \textbf{PIE-APT} (Abductive Planning for Temporal KGs)---operating natively on the highly expressive Description Logic. We model state transitions along a linear timeline as non-monotonic updates to deductively closed DL theories. Treating the incremental reasoner as a black-box and representing actions natively in OWL without external modal operators preserves logical decidability. To address incomplete knowledge, \textbf{PIE-Abducer} circumvents traditional Minimal Hitting Set (MHS) enumeration. Instead of combinatorial syntactic search, it injects the logical negation of a target goal into a consistent branch and extracts missing premises via direct refutation consequences. \textbf{PIE-APT} then employs a recursive \textit{Generate-and-Test} architecture, interleaving backward-chaining A* search with \textbf{PIE-Abducer} up to a bounded causal depth, followed by strict validation via forward-chaining Temporal Projection. We evaluate four OWL benchmarks stressing semantic abilities absent in classical planning: parameterized goals with witness search, mid-search DL entailment, open-world assumption injection, and adversarial contradiction hunting. Results demonstrate qualitative superiority over classical planners and prove our direct-derivation approach quantitatively outperforms an MHS-faithful baseline during abductive enrichment.

</details>


### [99] [Skill Use or Skill Theater? Evaluating the Reasoning Backroom in Skill-Augmented Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27484)
*Jinwei Hu,Yi Qi,Xinmiao Huang,Youcheng Sun,Yi Dong,Xiaowei Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Skill-augmented language agents show a systematic gap between stated skill use and actual causal reliance, termed the "Reasoning Backroom." The BACKTRACE framework uses counterfactual interventions to reveal that skill attribution is unreliable, with behavioral effects driven more by procedural content than displayed skill identity. This constitutes a pervasive AI provenance failure requiring intervention-based audit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluators infer skill use from an agent's visible reasoning or self-attribution—surfaces that reveal what the agent appears to use, not whether the skill causally changed its decision. The authors hypothesize a systematic "Reasoning Backroom" gap where stated and actual skill reliance diverge, undermining trust in skill-augmented agents.

Method: BACKTRACE framework: pairs each skill-conditioned answer with a matched no-skill counterfactual; intervenes on five dimensions (skill meaning, wording, identity, content, assignment); elicits attribution only post-answer commitment. Instantiated as BACKROOMBench spanning controlled logic, competition mathematics, single/multi-agent settings, and diverse model families. Tests observational detectors: direct skill-use claims, text mentions, trace similarity, and LLM judge.

Result: Pervasive provenance failure found across models and domains. Stated skill use remains stable while causal reliance and signed utility vary, producing silent uptake and performative use. Behavioral effects follow procedural content more than displayed skill identity; attributions respond strongly to artifact availability. No observational detector reliably identifies which decisions actually depend on the skill. In multi-agent systems, skill influence survives communication after source loss; no-skill teams still name skills/sources never supplied.

Conclusion: The Reasoning Backroom is a general AI provenance problem: agents cannot reliably self-report what influenced their decisions. Auditing requires intervention-based methods, as observational approaches systematically fail to distinguish genuine causal reliance from performative or confounded skill use.

Abstract: Reusable skills are becoming a standard interface for extending language agents with task procedures. Yet evaluators usually infer skill use from visible reasoning or the agent's own attribution. These signals show what the agent appears to use, not whether the skill changed its decision. We ask whether skill-augmented agents exhibit a \textbf{Reasoning Backroom}, a systematic gap between stated skill use and intervention-measured influence. We introduce BACKTRACE, an evaluation framework that pairs each skill-conditioned answer with a matched no-skill counterfactual, intervenes on skill meaning, wording, identity, content, and assignment, and elicits attribution only after the answer is committed. We instantiate the framework as BACKROOMBench, a verified testbed spanning controlled logic and competition mathematics, multiple skill conditions, single-agent and multi-agent settings, and diverse model families. Our evaluation reveals a pervasive provenance failure. Across models and domains, stated skill use often remains stable while causal reliance and signed utility vary, producing both silent uptake and performative use. Behavioral effects follow procedural content more reliably than displayed skill identity, whereas stated attributions respond strongly to artifact availability. Observational detectors based on direct skill-use claims, text mentions, trace similarity, and an LLM judge do not identify which decisions actually depend on the skill. In multi-agent systems, skill influence can survive communication even after its source is lost, while no-skill teams still name skills and sources that were never supplied. These findings establish the Reasoning Backroom as a general AI provenance problem whose audit requires intervention.

</details>


### [100] [PAUSE: A User-Centric Benchmark for Personal AI Assistants in Unified Service Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27354)
*Haoyu Chen,Xirui Shi,Yuyao Wang,Jerry Chen,Di Niu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PAUSE is a benchmark for evaluating personal AI assistants in realistic, stateful, multi-service environments. It emphasizes persistent user state, authorization constraints, and long-horizon interactions. Even top proprietary models fail to reach 70% task completion, and the paper includes a scalable synthesis pipeline for benchmark extension.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks fragment service contexts or abstract away user state, failing to evaluate personal AI assistants under realistic conditions—where agents must reason over persistent user state, respect per-user configurations/permissions, and sustain constraint-aware, multi-turn interactions across heterogeneous services.

Method: PAUSE provides a user-centric benchmark with stateful, service-integrated environments. It includes (1) realistic user simulation for multi-turn user-agent interaction, (2) a multi-regime evaluation framework: semantic/trajectory-level metrics for open-ended service management tasks and deterministic state-based verification for constraint-intensive tasks, and (3) a synthesis pipeline that scalably generates coherent service environments, user configurations, and annotated tasks.

Result: State-of-the-art proprietary models fail to achieve 70% task completion on scenarios requiring stateful reasoning and configuration awareness. The analysis reveals consistent, interpretable failure patterns across evaluated models.

Conclusion: PAUSE exposes significant gaps in current models' ability to handle stateful, user-specific, constraint-aware assistant tasks. The benchmark and synthesis pipeline provide a foundation for scalable, reproducible evaluation and future research into more capable personal AI assistants.

Abstract: Personal AI assistants are increasingly deployed as task-oriented, tool-augmented agents that operate within unified service environments to support everyday user activities. In realistic settings, such assistants must reason over persistent user state, respect user-specific configurations and permissions, and sustain long-horizon, constraint-aware interactions across multiple services. Existing benchmarks, however, often fragment service contexts or abstract away user state, limiting their ability to evaluate user-centric personal assistant behavior in realistic service settings. We introduce PAUSE, a user-centric benchmark for evaluating personal AI assistants in stateful, service-integrated environments. PAUSE captures core challenges of real-world assistant deployment by requiring agents to coordinate actions across heterogeneous user-owned resources while maintaining consistency with environment state, authorization constraints over multi-turn interactions. The benchmark incorporates explicit user-agent interaction via realistic user simulation, enabling evaluation beyond static tool execution. To support principled and reproducible evaluation, PAUSE adopts a multi-regime evaluation framework aligned with task characteristics. Open-ended service management tasks are assessed using semantic and trajectory-level behavioral metrics, while constraint-intensive tasks admit deterministic, state-based verification. Benchmark results show that even state-of-the-art proprietary models fail to reach 70% task completion on scenarios requiring stateful reasoning and configuration awareness, revealing consistent and interpretable failure patterns. Finally, we present a user-centric synthesis pipeline that enables scalable generation of coherent service environments, user configurations, and reliably annotated tasks, supporting benchmark extensibility and future research.

</details>


### [101] [SkillMentor: LLM Agent Self-Evolution via Learning Blind-Spot Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27360)
*Xiaoyi Bao,Yuanzhen Xie,Yunzhi Tan,Jinghang Gu,Zhongqing Wang,Chu-Ren Huang,Bo Hu,Zang Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillMentor proposes training a diagnostic Mentor policy via RL to autonomously discover an agent's failure modes and curate them into reusable corrective skills, achieving 44.2% average performance improvement without updating executor weights or using human supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current agent self-evolution research focuses overwhelmingly on learning how to act (execution), while neglecting the capacity to discover what an agent does not know (blind-spot diagnosis). Existing methods treat failure discovery as given, only addressing repair. The authors argue diagnosis itself should be studied as a distinct, learnable capability, and rigorously isolate it by excluding executor adaptation and human supervision as confounding sources of progress.

Method: SkillMentor trains a Mentor policy using reinforcement learning with three core functions: (1) generating diagnostic tasks to probe executor weaknesses, (2) identifying recurrent failure modes from execution traces, and (3) curating discovered failures into reusable corrective skills. Critically, the executor's weights remain frozen and no human-annotated data is used, forcing all improvement to stem from the diagnostic capability itself.

Result: Across AppWorld and BFCLv3 benchmarks, SkillMentor improves executor performance by an average of 44.2%, demonstrating that blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable capability that enables self-evolution without executor weight updates or human-curated data.

Conclusion: Blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable, standalone agent capability that can drive significant self-improvement. Separating diagnosis from execution opens a new axis for agent self-evolution, suggesting future systems should invest in learning to discover their own unknown failure modes.

Abstract: Agent self-evolution has primarily focused on learning how to act, while overlooking an equally important capability: learning to discover what an agent does not know. Existing approaches typically assume that failure discovery is given, focusing on how to repair failures once they are identified. We ask whether blind-spot diagnosis itself can be learned. We thus study diagnosis as an agent capability separate from execution, and exclude two alternative sources of progress: executor adaptation and human supervision. Under these constraints, performance cannot improve through executor updates or annotated examples, forcing all improvements to originate from the learned diagnostic capability. We propose SkillMentor, which trains a Mentor policy via reinforcement learning to generate diagnostic tasks, identify recurrent failure modes, and curate them into reusable corrective skills. Across AppWorld and BFCLv3, SkillMentor improves executor performance by an average of 44.2%. These results suggest that blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable capability, enabling self-evolution without updating executor weights or relying on human-curated data.

</details>


### [102] [Evaluating Agentic Bioinformatics through Function, Evidence, and Validation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27556)
*Phuc Pham,Truong-Son Hy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Function–Evidence–Validation (FEV) framework for evaluating AI agent systems in bioinformatics, arguing that workflow correctness and accountability should be prioritized over final-answer correctness. Mapping 128 publications across biological domains, the authors find that planning and tool execution have outpaced provenance, reproducibility, and validation, advocating for inspectable workflow trajectories as the primary unit of scientific assessment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing reviews of biological AI agents classify systems by application, architecture, or agentic capabilities but fail to operationalize scientific accountability. Fluent responses and benchmark scores can mask flawed workflows, creating a gap in how agent-generated analyses are evaluated for credibility. The authors aim to fill this gap by centering analysis on the inspectable workflow trajectory rather than outputs alone.

Method: The authors propose the FEV framework comprising three dimensions: Function (demonstrated workflow operations such as planning and tool use), Evidence (traceable provenance and support for claims), and Validation (use-case-specific empirical testing). They systematically map 109 agentic or agent-adjacent systems and 28 benchmark/evaluation resources (128 unique publications) across genomics, single-cell/spatial omics, protein science, drug discovery, computational pathology, and general bioinformatics automation, applying FEV to assess the state of each dimension.

Result: Planning and tool-mediated execution (Function) have advanced rapidly across domains. However, replayability, provenance tracking, robust scientific assessment, external validation, and prospective empirical testing (Evidence and Validation) lag significantly behind. The analysis reveals a systematic imbalance favoring operational capability over scientific accountability.

Conclusion: Agentic bioinformatics systems should be evaluated by workflow correctness rather than final-answer correctness alone. The FEV framework offers a practical basis for comparing systems and designing transparent, auditable, and scientifically accountable bioinformatics workflows, guiding future development toward greater rigor and reproducibility.

Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly plan, execute, and interpret biological analyses, yet fluent responses, successful tool calls, and benchmark performance alone do not establish scientific credibility. Existing reviews primarily organize biological agents by application, architecture, and agentic capability, but do not jointly operationalize the accountability of agent-generated workflows. We address this gap by treating the inspectable workflow trajectory, rather than architecture or final output alone, as the primary unit of analysis. We introduce the Function--Evidence--Validation (FEV) framework, which separates demonstrated workflow operations, traceable support for actions and claims, and use-case-specific validation. Using FEV, we map 109 agentic or agent-adjacent systems and 28 benchmark or evaluation resources, representing 128 unique publications across genomics, single-cell and spatial omics, protein science, drug discovery, computational pathology, and general bioinformatics automation. Across domains, planning and tool-mediated execution have advanced more rapidly than replayability, provenance, robust scientific assessment, external validation, and prospective empirical testing. We therefore argue that agentic bioinformatics should be assessed through workflow correctness rather than final-answer correctness alone. FEV provides a practical basis for comparing systems and designing transparent, auditable, and scientifically accountable bioinformatics workflows.

</details>


### [103] [Beyond the Bidirectional Promise: Re-evaluating the Robustness of Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27386)
*Saurabh Yadav,Badri Narayana Patro,Vijay Srinivas Agneeswaran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper systematically evaluates the robustness of Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) against AR baselines under natural noise and adversarial attacks, finding that DLM robustness is weight-dependent rather than architecture-intrinsic, with systematic overconfidence and a decoder routing failure as the root cause of behavioral fragility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DLMs offer bidirectional context and iterative refinement advantages over autoregressive models, but their reliability under natural input noise and adversarial attacks remains largely unexplored. The authors aim to rigorously assess whether DLM architecture confers inherent robustness advantages.

Method: The authors employ a paired experimental design with two parameter-matched model pairs (LLaDA-8B vs. LLaMA-3-8B and Dream-7B vs. Qwen2.5-7B), tested across 32 natural perturbation conditions, adversarial gradient-based probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses. The paired design isolates architecture-intrinsic properties from weight-dependent behaviors.

Result: DLMs exhibit stochastic loss landscapes that naturally resist gradient-based adversarial suffixes, but offer no guaranteed defense against natural noise — robustness is weight-dependent, not architectural. DLMs show systematic overconfidence. Mechanistic probing reveals all models perfectly encode input corruption, with behavioral fragility traced to a decoder routing failure. Surface-level prompt patching fails to improve performance over noisy baselines.

Conclusion: DLM robustness cannot be superficially patched on; it must be fundamentally integrated into the iterative decoding loop itself.

Abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) offer a compelling alternative to autoregressive (AR) generation by enabling bidirectional context and iterative refinement. However, their reliability under natural input noise and adversarial attacks remains under-explored. To address this, we systematically evaluate DLM robustness and calibration against AR baselines, using two parameter-matched pairs (LLaDA-8B vs. LLaMA-3-8B and Dream-7B vs. Qwen2.5-7B) across 32 natural perturbation conditions, adversarial gradient probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses. This paired design effectively isolates architecture-intrinsic properties from weight-dependent behaviors. We find a nuanced robustness profile: while highly stochastic DLM loss landscapes naturally resist gradient-based adversarial suffixes, they provide no guaranteed defense against natural noise, proving that everyday robustness is weight-dependent rather than inherently architectural. Furthermore, DLMs exhibit systematic overconfidence, presenting a practical deployment hazard. Most crucially, mechanistic probing reveals that all models perfectly encode input corruption, isolating behavioral fragility entirely to a decoder routing failure. Consistent with this diagnosis, we show that surface-level prompt patching fails to improve over noisy baselines. Ultimately, DLM robustness cannot be patched on; it must be fundamentally integrated into the iterative decoding loop.

</details>


### [104] [Bridging Inference-Time Scaling and Episodic Memory with Action-Centric Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27415)
*Xu Zheng,Chaohao Lin,Zhuomin Chen,Weijieying Ren,Haifeng Chen,Wei Cheng,Dongsheng Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GAMER introduces a graph-based episodic memory framework that decouples memory from LLM reasoning, using an Action-Centric Graph with dual-stream Temporal Difference learning to provide bi-directional value estimates (suggestions and avoidance) for efficient inference-time decision-making in LLM agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current inference-time scaling methods for LLM agents operate statelessly, causing redundant search processes. Existing memory mechanisms rely heavily on LLM reasoning, incurring prohibitive computational costs (tokens/money). There is a need to bridge inference scaling with episodic memory in a more efficient, decoupled manner.

Method: GAMER models historical reasoning as a dynamic Action-Centric Graph and decouples memory from LLMs to reduce context overhead. It employs a dual-stream Temporal Difference (TD) learning mechanism to estimate positive (suggestion) and negative (avoidance) values for action nodes based on past successes and failures. During inference, the learned value function enables bi-directional optimization: positive values suggest actions, negative values flag high-risk actions. Efficient graph search further improves inference scaling.

Result: GAMER achieves superior performance with a 20.81% improvement in success rate and 6.17% improvement in progress rate compared to vanilla baselines across multiple benchmarks.

Conclusion: GAMER effectively bridges inference scaling and episodic memory by decoupling memory from LLM reasoning, delivering significant efficiency and performance gains through graph-based action-centric memory and dual-stream TD learning.

Abstract: Recent advancements in inference-time scaling have significantly unlocked the complex reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models~(LLMs). However, for agents, these approaches suffer from a critical inefficiency, operating in a stateless manner and engaging in redundant search processes. Existing memory mechanisms largely rely on the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, leading to prohibitive computational costs. In this paper, we propose a novel framework, \textit{GAMER}~(Graph-based Action-centric Memory with Episodic Reasoning), that bridges the gap between inference scaling and episodic memory. Our approach models historical reasoning as a dynamic \textit{Action-Centric Graph}. By decoupling the memory mechanism from LLMs, our method can save token/money usage by providing less memory context than memory mechanism baselines. To extract knowledge from the graph effectively, we use a dual-stream Temporal Difference learning mechanism to estimate the positive~(suggestion) and negative~(avoidance) value of action nodes based on past successes and failures. During the inference phase, this learned value function optimizes decision-making bi-directionally, so that positive values provide action suggestions, while negative values indicate high-risk actions. By performing efficient searches on the graph, our method significantly improves the efficiency of inference scaling. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that \textit{GAMER} achieves superior performance by \textbf{20.81\%/6.17\%} for success/progress rate compared to vanilla baselines.

</details>


### [105] [Dimensionality and Measurement Precision in HLE's Multiple-Choice Subset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27420)
*Mayank Sharma,Savira Nadela,Tyler Matteson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HLE's domain-specific subscores reflect a single general reasoning factor rather than distinct capabilities, and the benchmark provides poor measurement precision for frontier-level models, limiting its ability to discriminate among the strongest LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: HLE is widely used to evaluate frontier LLMs and its eight subject-domain subscores are commonly interpreted as evidence of distinct capabilities. However, no prior work has empirically tested whether these domain labels correspond to separable latent constructs or whether the benchmark can effectively differentiate between top-tier models.

Method: The authors evaluated 29 LLMs on the text-only multiple-choice subset of HLE (428 items) and applied psychometric methods: fitting a two-parameter logistic IRT model, computing McDonald's hierarchical omega (ω_h), decomposing item response variance by domain labels, analyzing within- and between-domain residual correlations, assessing redundancy of domain-specific ability estimates with total scores, and examining the test information function across ability levels.

Result: Convergent evidence showed HLE measures a single general reasoning factor: ω_h = 0.998, domain labels explained only 3.5% of item response variance, within- and between-domain residual correlations were nearly identical (Cohen's d = 0.016), and domain-specific ability estimates were near-redundant with total scores (r ≥ 0.81). The test information function revealed measurement precision is concentrated at moderate ability levels and drops sharply above θ = 0, precisely where frontier models operate.

Conclusion: HLE's domain subscores should not be interpreted as evidence of distinct capabilities, and the benchmark has limited discriminative power among the strongest models, undermining its utility for comparing frontier LLMs.

Abstract: Humanity's Last Exam (HLE) is widely used to evaluate frontier language models. HLE organizes its questions into eight subject-domain categories, whose subscores are often interpreted as evidence of distinct capabilities. However, no study has assessed whether these labels correspond to empirically separable latent constructs, nor whether the benchmark effectively differentiates between models of similar ability. We evaluate 29 LLMs on the text-only multiple-choice subset of HLE ($J = 428$ items) and apply psychometric methods to assess both the dimensionality of the benchmark and the distribution of its measurement precision. Fitting a two-parameter logistic IRT model, we find convergent evidence that HLE measures a single general reasoning factor: McDonald's $ω_h = 0.998$, domain labels explain only 3.5\% of item response variance, within- and between-domain residual correlations are nearly identical (Cohen's $d = 0.016$), and domain-specific ability estimates are near-redundant with the total score ($r \geq 0.81$). A separate analysis of the test information function reveals that measurement precision concentrates at moderate ability levels and drops sharply above $θ= 0$, where frontier models sit. These findings suggest that HLE's domain subscores do not warrant distinct capability interpretations and that the benchmark's ability to discriminate among the strongest models is limited.

</details>


### [106] [Leveraging Trajectory Graphs for Pre-Execution Error Diagnosis in Agentic LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27443)
*Xu Zheng,Zhuomin Chen,Chaohao Lin,Hua Wei,Haifeng Chen,Wei Cheng,Dongsheng Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Trajectory Graph Copilot, a framework that uses a Graph Neural Network to analyze historical trajectory patterns and preemptively diagnose potential action errors in LLM agents, preventing compounding failures in long-horizon interactive tasks and achieving a 14.69% average pass ratio improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents excel at complex interactive tasks but suffer from compounding errors in long-horizon settings (e.g., embodied AI), where a single suboptimal action can derail an entire trajectory and exhaust limited step budgets. The authors aim to address this without expensive fine-tuning.

Method: Trajectory Graph Copilot introduces a Graph Debugger that models historical trajectories as a probabilistic graph and employs a Graph Neural Network to identify sequential action patterns frequently leading to failure. It functions as a proactive diagnostic sandbox that provides early warnings on potentially flawed actions, prompting the agent to self-correct before execution.

Result: Extensive experiments across four benchmarks with three different LLM agents demonstrate an average pass ratio improvement of 14.69%.

Conclusion: Pre-action error diagnosis via trajectory graph modeling effectively mitigates compounding errors in long-horizon tasks, significantly enhancing LLM agent success rates without requiring costly fine-tuning.

Abstract: Large Language Model~(LLM)-based agents have demonstrated exceptional performance across a wide range of complex interactive tasks. However, they often struggle with long-horizon interactive tasks common in domains, such as embodied AI. The complexity and vast action spaces in these settings lead to compounding errors, where a single suboptimal action can derail an entire trajectory, causing the agent to exhaust its limited step budget on inefficient or unrecoverable paths. To overcome this without costly fine-tuning, we draw inspiration from software debugging, where execution logs are analyzed to preemptively catch errors. We propose \textit{Trajectory Graph Copilot}, a novel framework that acts as a ``copilot'' for LLM agents by diagnosing potential action errors before they are executed. At its core,\textit{Graph Debugger} models historical trajectories as a probabilistic graph and uses a Graph Neural Network to identify sequential action patterns that frequently lead to failure. Functioning as a proactive diagnostic sandbox, our method provides early warnings on potentially flawed actions, prompting the agent to self-correct. This pre-action error diagnosis prevents costly mistakes, significantly enhancing the agent's ability to complete long-horizon tasks successfully. The extensive experiments on four benchmarks with three LLM agents demonstrate a $14.69\%$ pass ratio improvement on average.

</details>


### [107] [VAmoS Bench: Voice Agent Simulation Bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27453)
*Joshua Meyer,Sahar Shayegan,Ritiz Tambi,Ali Khan,Sun Kim,Victor Shih,Mehdi Jamei,Andi Partovi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VAmoS Bench introduces a voice agent simulation benchmark that evaluates end-to-end, stateful customer-support calls in financial services, measuring "containment" (whether the agent resolves the call correctly without human handoff), using 100 scenarios with simulated callers, adversarial pressure, real SQL-backed tool execution, and binary assertion grading against complete interaction traces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing voice-agent benchmarks focus on component-level metrics (WER, latency, naturalness) and conversational properties but rarely measure "containment" — whether the automated system correctly resolves a phone call end-to-end, including appropriate refusals or redirects. There is a gap in evaluating complete voice-agent systems in realistic, stateful task settings where both dialogue and backend actions matter.

Method: The authors present VAmoS Bench featuring 100 customer-support scenarios around a fictional credit-card agent named Riley. Each scenario pairs a simulated caller (with a private goal) with an isolated PostgreSQL backend. Roughly one-third include adversarial pressure. The agent accesses five tools that execute real SQL. Evaluation uses binary assertions graded against the full trace — capturing what was said, tool invocations, arguments, and returned rows — to detect both dialogue errors (e.g., disclosing protected info) and backend errors (e.g., claiming a change without executing it).

Result: The paper introduces the benchmark and evaluation protocol but the abstract does not report specific empirical results; it focuses on the framework design, the leaderboard mechanism, and the expandability to future tasks and agent versions.

Conclusion: VAmoS Bench fills a critical evaluation gap by measuring true end-to-end containment in voice agents, combining dialogue quality with backend state correctness. Its leaderboard protocol supports evolving benchmarks and agent comparisons, with the initial release focused on financial services.

Abstract: Production voice agents span cascaded, speech-to-speech, and hybrid architectures. Voice-agent benchmarks typically measure component quality and conversational properties such as word error rate, latency, naturalness, and turn-taking. Fewer measure whether the agent handled a phone call correctly on its own. Contact centers refer to this as ``containment'': the share of phone calls the automated system resolves without handing off to a human. On some phone calls the right outcome is refusal or a redirect. To address this gap, we introduce VAmoS Bench, the Voice Agent Simulation Bench. It measures complete voice-agent systems end to end in a stateful customer-support task. The agent is Riley, a credit-card support representative for a fictional bank who can freeze, cancel, replace, or activate a card. Each of 100 scenarios supplies a simulated caller with a private goal and a seeded PostgreSQL backend. The platform uses each scenario to populate and activate an isolated simulation in which the caller reaches Riley over audio; roughly one-third apply adversarial pressure. The agent can use five tools that execute real SQL against the backend. Each scenario also defines binary assertions. A grader evaluates them against the complete trace of what the caller and agent said and what the agent did, including tool invocations, arguments, and returned rows. This catches an agent that claims to have changed a card without updating the database, as well as one that makes the right database change while disclosing protected information. This first benchmark version focuses on financial services. Its evaluation protocol supports an evolving leaderboard: additional voice agents can be evaluated on the same version, while later versions can expand the tasks and scenarios.

</details>


### [108] [INCLAIR: Inception-Based Longitudinal Clinical Anomaly Detection with Informed Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27487)
*Maxx Richard Rahman,Wolfgang Maass*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: INCLAIR is a framework for anomaly detection in longitudinal clinical profiles that uses multi-context scoring, U-statistic-based mean subsequence aggregation with top-k pooling, and natural-language explanation generation under limited expert supervision. It consistently outperforms baselines across three clinical datasets and is validated against expert assessments in a steroid profiling case study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Longitudinal clinical anomaly detection faces three key challenges: abnormal evidence is sparse, patient histories vary in length, and obtaining expert explanations is costly. Existing methods struggle to handle these constraints simultaneously, motivating a framework that is statistically principled, computationally tractable regardless of profile length, and capable of generating interpretable explanations with minimal supervision.

Method: INCLAIR scores each observation against multiple historical contexts, then aggregates evidence at the profile level. Under within-profile exchangeability assumptions, the complete mean subsequence score is an order-l U-statistic, enabling variance decomposition and an incomplete-subset approximation that decouples combinatorial inference cost from profile length. The framework identifies that mean aggregation attenuates localized anomalies proportional to anomaly support and profile length, motivating a validation-selected top-k pooling strategy. Grounded natural-language explanations are generated with limited expert supervision.

Result: INCLAIR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across three clinical datasets. A case study on longitudinal steroid profiles demonstrates that INCLAIR's predictions and explanations align with domain-expert assessments supported by DNA analysis, confirming clinical actionability.

Conclusion: INCLAIR provides a statistically grounded, computationally efficient, and interpretable framework for clinical anomaly detection under limited supervision, with demonstrated practical utility in real-world clinical settings such as steroid profile analysis.

Abstract: Detecting anomalies in longitudinal clinical profiles is clinically important but difficult: abnormal evidence is often sparse, patient histories have unequal length, and expert explanations are costly. We propose INCLAIR, a framework that scores each observation against multiple historical contexts, aggregates evidence at the profile level, and generates grounded natural-language explanations under limited expert supervision. Under stated within-profile exchangeability assumptions, the complete mean subsequence score takes an order-$l$ U-statistic form, yielding a variance decomposition and an incomplete-subset approximation that controls combinatorial inference cost independently of profile length. The same analysis shows that mean aggregation attenuates localized anomalies by a factor set by the anomaly support and profile length, motivating validation-selected top-$k$ pooling. Across three clinical datasets, INCLAIR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. We further validate practical relevance through a case study on longitudinal steroid profiles, comparing INCLAIR's predictions and explanations against domain-expert assessments supported by DNA analysis. The results show that INCLAIR enables clinically actionable anomaly detection under limited expert supervision.

</details>


### [109] [MedLLM: An Open Medical Language Model at the Sub-Billion Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27490)
*Maxx Richard Rahman,Asim Ahmed,Mihan Mohagheghzadeh,Wolfgang Maass*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MedLLM is a 0.1B-parameter open medical LM trained via a three-phase pipeline. At sub-billion scale, medical competence splits by task type: context-grounded QA nearly matches 7B models, while knowledge-recall QA reveals a capacity bottleneck on tasks like MedQA. This dissociation is invisible at 7B scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open medical LMs have converged on 7B+ parameters, leaving the sub-billion regime entirely uncharacterized. The authors aim to probe how medical competence manifests under extreme parameter constraints and determine whether the failure modes at small scale reveal fundamental capacity bottlenecks masked at larger scales.

Method: MedLLM is trained through a fully open three-phase pipeline: (1) general pretraining with curriculum sequence-length scheduling, (2) domain fine-tuning on MedFineWeb — a reference-guided medical corpus curated from general web data via embedding similarity to medical QA data, and (3) preference-aligned fine-tuning combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with direct preference optimization (DPO).

Result: MedLLM reveals that medical competence does not degrade uniformly at sub-billion scale. On context-grounded QA, it comes within 2.9pp of a medically adapted 7B model and surpasses instruction-tuned general-purpose 7B baselines. On knowledge-recall QA, it stays near the task floor on MedQA yet significantly exceeds all 7B and sub-7B baselines on MedMCQA. This task-type dissociation is masked at 7B scale.

Conclusion: At sub-billion scale, medical language model performance bifurcates into two regimes: context-grounded reasoning is relatively preserved, while knowledge-intensive recall hits a hard capacity wall. This dissociation surfaces only when capacity is scarce, suggesting that scaling laws for medical competence are task-type-dependent and that sub-billion models can serve as diagnostic tools for identifying capability bottlenecks.

Abstract: Open medical language models have converged on a single scale: every widely used system runs at 7B parameters or more, leaving the sub-billion regime uncharacterized. We present MedLLM, an open 0.1B-parameter medical language model trained through a fully open three-phase pipeline: general pretraining with curriculum sequence-length scheduling, domain fine-tuning on MedFineWeb, a reference-guided medical corpus we release that is selected from general web data by embedding similarity to medical question-answering (QA) data, and preference-aligned fine-tuning combining SFT with direct preference optimization (DPO). Across medical benchmarks, MedLLM shows a pattern visible only at sub-billion scale: medical competence does not degrade uniformly under compression but splits by task type. On context-grounded QA it comes within $2.9$pp of a medically adapted 7B model and surpasses the instruction-tuned and general-purpose 7B baselines; on knowledge-recall QA it stays near the task floor on clinical-vignette MedQA yet significantly exceeds every 7B and sub-7B baseline on MedMCQA, indicating that where recall fails the constraint is model capacity rather than adaptation. This dissociation is masked at 7B, where both capabilities are present, and surfaces only when capacity is scarce.

</details>


### [110] [A dataset of rated conceptual arguments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27499)
*Emery Cooper,Caspar Oesterheld,Linh Chi Nguyen,Alexander Kastner,Ethan Perez*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques across 442 position texts on conceptual questions (AI safety, ethics, politics), rated by experts along dimensions of centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity. It proposes scoring functions and benchmarks LLMs, finding performance aligns with general capability rankings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs have progressed on tasks with verifiable answers (math, programming), but their ability to reason about "conceptual questions"—those lacking ground truth or accepted resolution methods (e.g., philosophy, AI safety, decision theory)—remains poorly understood. Since bottom-line conclusions are hard to evaluate, the authors argue that evaluating individual contextualized arguments offers a more reliable assessment pathway.

Method: The authors constructed a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques applied to 442 position texts covering AI safety, decision theory, ethics, and politics. Six expert raters provided 1,458 ratings along four dimensions: centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity. Two scoring functions were then proposed to aggregate these ratings, and a range of LLMs were benchmarked on the dataset.

Result: Model performance on the proposed argument evaluation benchmarks tracks general LLM capability rankings, suggesting that stronger general-purpose models also perform better at evaluating arguments on conceptual questions.

Conclusion: Evaluating arguments individually—rather than bottom-line conclusions—provides a tractable method for assessing LLM reasoning on open conceptual questions. The dataset and scoring framework offer a foundation for measuring progress in this under-explored area.

Abstract: Large language models have improved rapidly on tasks with verifiable answers, such as mathematics and programming. Much less is known about their ability to reason about what we call conceptual questions: questions for which no ground truth is realistically accessible and no widely accepted resolution methodology exists, but on which progress can still be made by debating arguments. Most philosophical questions are of this kind, as are central components of questions in AI safety, decision theory, and social choice. Our approach is based on the view that while bottom-line conclusions on such questions are hard to evaluate, individual contextualized arguments can be evaluated far more reliably. We therefore introduce a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques of 442 position texts, spanning topics from AI safety and decision theory to ethics and politics, with 1,458 ratings by six expert raters along dimensions including centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity. We propose two scoring functions and benchmark a range of models. Performance tracks general capability rankings.

</details>


### [111] [Automated Transcript Analysis for Detecting Flaws in Agentic Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27518)
*Jeff Mohl,Nelson Gardner-Challis,Magda Dubois,Harry Coppock,Benjamin Allan-Rahill,Kaelan Yim,Damian Sójka,James Mann,Justin Olive*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The authors developed AI-based scanners to automatically detect four types of validity issues in agentic benchmarks (ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, and answer format ambiguity). Tested on Inspect Evals benchmarks, the scanners identified verified quality issues across five widely used benchmarks, including cases that manual inspection would likely miss. Performance varied by benchmark, criterion, and model. The work serves as a proof of concept for automated benchmark quality auditing, while highlighting open challenges around standardization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual audits of agentic benchmarks (e.g., SWE-Bench-Verified) can uncover validity issues, but manual review does not scale. It is unclear whether automated methods can reliably detect flaws that compromise benchmark validity, creating a need for scalable, automated quality assurance tools.

Method: The authors developed AI scanners targeting four validity issue types: (1) ground truth access, (2) tool failure, (3) guessing vulnerability, and (4) answer format ambiguity. They created grading rubrics for each issue type to guide human labeling, then evaluated scanner performance against human labels on a held-out test set drawn from Inspect Evals benchmarks.

Result: The scanners identified verified quality issues in five widely used benchmarks, including cases unlikely to be caught by random manual inspection. However, not all issues were detected, and scanner performance varied substantially across benchmarks, validity criteria, and underlying models.

Conclusion: Automated transcript analysis is a promising proof of concept for auditing benchmark quality at scale. However, significant challenges remain—particularly broader standardization gaps in the evaluation field that degrade scanner performance—before scanners can support stronger quality assurance claims.

Abstract: Capabilities of frontier models are often assessed using agentic benchmarks. To trust these results, benchmarks must accurately measure what they claim to and be free from invalidating flaws. Previous manual audits of benchmarks such as SWE-Bench-Verified have uncovered several validity issues in transcripts. However, manual review is difficult to scale, and it is unclear whether automated methods can reliably surface flaws that compromise benchmark validity. In this paper, we developed AI scanners to detect four types of validity issues: ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, and answer format ambiguity. We produced grading rubrics for each to instruct human labeling, and evaluated the scanners against human labels on a held-out test set of Inspect Evals benchmarks. Our scanners identified several verified quality issues in five widely used benchmarks, including cases unlikely to be caught by random manual inspection. Not all cases were identified, and scanner performance varied substantially across benchmarks, criteria and models. We highlight several open challenges to be addressed to improve scanners for stronger quality assurance claims, including broader standardization gaps in the evaluation field that degrade scanner performance. Together, these results serve as a proof of concept for using automated transcript analysis to audit benchmark quality more broadly.

</details>


### [112] [AISPA: User-Centric System Prompt Auditing for Large Language Model Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28617)
*Xiangning Lin,Shenzhe Zhu,Shu Yang,Zhenyu Zhang,Haoqian Zhang,Yipeng Zhao,Chengxuan Qian,Tianwei Wang,Ziheng Zhang,Zhenlong Yuan,Dingcheng Wang,Juncheng Wu,Yuan Si,Jiaxin Liu,Baolong Bi,Robert Mahari,Tobin South,Dazza Greenwood,Zexue He,Rishi Bommasani,Sophia Kazinnik,Andreas Haupt,Samuele Marro,Erik Brynjolfsson,Alex Pentland,Jiaxin Pei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces AISPA, a user-centric framework for auditing system prompts in AI systems. Auditing 3,249 instructions across 88 commercial AI products reveals that while protective instructions are widespread (98.9% of products), they are shallow (only 24% cover all eight AISPA dimensions), and roughly 40% of products contain instructions working against user interests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: System prompts govern foundation model behaviors in commercial AI applications but are rarely disclosed, creating a serious trust and accountability gap. There is no systematic, user-centric framework for auditing what these prompts actually instruct models to do or not do.
