Method: The authors develop the AISPA framework, which examines system prompts along eight user-relevant dimensions. They apply this taxonomy to classify 3,249 instructions from system prompts in 88 commercial AI products, categorizing each as either protective (serving user interests) or problematic (working against them).

Result: Four core findings: (1) System prompt design varies dramatically across developers — some average 60+ protective instructions per product, others fewer than 5. (2) Protective instructions are nearly universal (98.9% of products) but shallow; only 24% cover all eight AISPA dimensions. (3) System prompts have grown longer and more protective over time. (4) Problematic instructions remain pervasive — ~40% of products contain at least one anti-user instruction, and protective/problematic instructions frequently coexist.

Conclusion: The findings underscore an urgent need for greater transparency, standardization, and independent oversight of system prompts in commercial AI products. The coexistence of protective and problematic instructions within the same prompts is particularly concerning.

Abstract: System prompts are instructions configured by developers to govern the behaviors of foundation models in AI applications. They are used throughout commercial AI products, but are rarely disclosed to the public or regulators, creating a serious trust and accountability gap in the wide deployment of AI systems. In this paper, we introduce Artificial Intelligence System Prompt Assurance (AISPA), a user-centric framework for systematically auditing system prompts in AI systems. AISPA examines specific parts of a system prompt and evaluates them along eight dimensions that matter to users. We then use this framework to review 3,249 instructions from system prompts in 88 commercial AI products, classifying each instruction as either protective (of users) or problematic. Our audit surfaces four core findings. First, system prompt design varies substantially across products and developers, with some organizations averaging over 60 protective instructions per product while others average fewer than 5. Second, protective instructions are widely adopted but shallow in scope: 98.9% of products contain at least one, yet only 24% cover all eight dimensions of the AISPA taxonomy. Third, system prompts have grown steadily longer and more protective of users, suggesting that user protection is becoming a more visible concern in commercial prompt design. Fourth, despite this progress, problematic instructions remain pervasive: roughly 40% of products contain at least one instruction that works against user interests, and protective and problematic instructions frequently coexist within the same prompt. Our findings highlight the need for greater transparency, standardization, and independent oversight for system prompts in commercial AI products.

</details>


### [113] [GLM-RAG: Graph Language Models for Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28397)
*Maya Arseven,Anette Frank,Beni Egressy,Johann Higl,Moritz Plenz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a graph language model (GLM)-based retriever for RAG over knowledge graphs and systematically compares it against GNN-based and vector-search-based retrievers. GLM retrievers achieve SOTA out-of-domain generalization on multi-hop benchmarks, GNN retrievers offer efficient high graph coverage, and vector search excels at single-hop tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RAG retrievers over knowledge graphs struggle to jointly capture graph structure and semantics. GNN-based retrievers model topology well for multi-hop reasoning, while GLMs are emerging but under-explored as retrievers. A systematic comparison across retriever paradigms—especially regarding transferability to unseen domains—is lacking.

Method: The authors propose a GLM-based retriever and conduct a comparative evaluation across three retriever paradigms: (1) GLM-based (finetuned graph language models), (2) GNN-based (graph neural networks), and (3) traditional vector-search-based retrievers. Evaluation spans single-hop and multi-hop RAG settings, with emphasis on in-domain performance and out-of-domain transferability.

Result: Finetuned GLM retrievers achieve state-of-the-art on two out-of-domain multi-hop benchmarks and remain comparable to prior work on in-domain multi-hop QA datasets, with performance scaling favorably as model parameters and subgraph coverage increase. GNN-based retrievers attain higher graph coverage with efficient training. The vector-search baseline performs best on single-hop datasets.

Conclusion: GLM-based retrievers offer superior out-of-domain generalization for multi-hop RAG over knowledge graphs, presenting a compelling direction for transferable retrieval. Each retriever paradigm has distinct strengths, suggesting that future systems may benefit from hybrid approaches tailored to the hop distance and domain characteristics of the target task.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over knowledge graphs requires retrievers that can effectively capture both graph structure and semantic information. Recent approaches have explored graph neural network (GNN)-based retrievers to model graph topology in multi-hop reasoning tasks. In parallel, graph language models (GLMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm that integrates graph reasoning and the semantic capabilities of language models. In this work, we introduce a GLM-based retriever and investigate the comparative strengths of GLM-based, GNN-based, and traditional vector-search-based retrievers in single- and multi-hop RAG settings, and with a particular focus on transferability to unseen domains. Our findings suggest that finetuned GLM retrievers generalize better out of domain, achieving SOTA on two multi-hop benchmarks. On in-domain multi-hop QA datasets they remain comparable to prior work, with promising scaling as parameters and subgraph coverage increase. GNN-based retrievers achieve higher graph coverage with an efficient training setup, whereas the vector-search baseline excels at single-hop datasets.

</details>


### [114] [AI Literacy: An Exercise in Power-Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27547)
*Brady D. Lund,Zoë Abbie Teel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper critiques current AI literacy frameworks as overly focused on technical skills and responsible use, arguing they reduce individuals to consumers. Drawing on Foucault, Freire, and digital literacy scholarship, it proposes a reconceptualized, critical AI literacy that fosters epistemic agency through contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI literacy frameworks emphasize technical competency and responsible use, which the authors argue enforce a passive "consumer" orientation. This fails to equip individuals with genuine epistemic agency — the capacity to critically evaluate, resist, and shape AI systems. The paper is motivated by the need to address how unequal AI access perpetuates epistemic injustices and to shift literacy toward empowerment and democratic participation in AI governance.

Method: The paper employs a conceptual/theoretical method, synthesizing Foucault's power-knowledge framework, Freire's critical pedagogy, and digital literacy scholarship to deconstruct current AI literacy paradigms and construct an alternative three-part framework.

Result: The paper proposes a tripartite framework for AI literacy: (1) contextual use — understanding how and when to deploy AI tools within specific sociotechnical contexts; (2) critical interrogation — evaluating AI systems' assumptions, biases, and power structures; and (3) participatory governance — engaging in the collective shaping and oversight of AI systems. This reframes AI literacy as cultivating epistemic "agents" rather than competent consumers.

Conclusion: AI literacy must be reconceived as a critical, empowerment-oriented practice that moves beyond technical proficiency. By fostering epistemic agency, such a framework can counter structural inequities in AI access and ensure broader democratic participation in the governance of AI as a knowledge-production system.

Abstract: As generative artificial intelligence becomes one of the most significant systems of knowledge production in our society today, questions relating to who can access and shape that production grow increasingly important in our discourse. This paper argues that the existing frameworks for AI literacy, which are dominated by technical competency and responsible-use principles, are insufficient because they enforce a "consumer" orientation toward AI rather than fostering genuine epistemic agency. Based upon Foucault's concept of power-knowledge, Freire's pedagogy of critical consciousness, and scholarship of digital literacy, this paper proposes a reconceptualization of AI literacy as a critical practice that equips individuals not just to use AI systems, but to critically evaluate them, resist their structuring assumptions, and participate in their governance. The paper further argues that unequal access to AI tools in society recapitulates longstanding epistemic injustices, and that a literacy framework oriented toward empowerment must account for these structural inequities. A three-part framework of AI literacy based on the notions of contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance frames this literacy as a cultivation of epistemic "agents" rather than the training of competent consumers of AI-generated information.

</details>


### [115] [Using Large Language Models for Idea Generation in Innovation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27553)
*Lennart Meincke,Karan Girotra,Gideon Nave,Christian Terwiesch,Karl T. Ulrich*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs (GPT-4) generate new product ideas that outperform human ideas in purchase intent (7x more likely to be top 10%), but are less novel and more similar to each other, especially with few-shot prompting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate whether large language models can effectively generate high-quality new product ideas, comparing AI creativity against human creativity in a controlled product development context.

Method: Three idea pools (human-generated by students, GPT-4 zero-shot, and GPT-4 few-shot) targeting college students with products ≤$50 were compared. Evaluation used: purchase intent probability (market research), text mining for pairwise similarity, and human raters for novelty assessment. Both average quality and top-percentile performance were analyzed.

Result: AI-generated ideas surpassed human ideas in average purchase intent (few-shot > zero-shot). However, AI ideas scored lower on novelty and showed higher pairwise similarity (few-shot worse). Crucially, AI ideas were 7x more likely to appear in the top 10% of all ideas by purchase intent.

Conclusion: LLMs offer a substantial, productivity-amplified advantage in generating high-quality product ideas despite reduced diversity and novelty. The 7-to-1 top-idea advantage is likely conservative given AI's greater output capacity.

Abstract: This research evaluates the efficacy of large language models (LLMs) in generating new product ideas. To do so, we compare three pools of ideas for new products targeted toward college students and priced at 50 dollars or less. The first pool of ideas was created by university students in a product design course before the availability of LLMs. The second and third pools of ideas were generated by GPT-4 from OpenAI using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, respectively. We evaluated idea quality using standard market research techniques to predict average purchase intent probability. We used text mining to assess idea similarity and human raters to evaluate idea novelty. We find that AI-generated ideas outperform human-generated ideas in terms of average purchase intent, with few-shot prompting yielding slightly higher intent than zero-shot prompting. However, AI-generated ideas are perceived as less novel and exhibit higher pairwise similarity, particularly with few-shot prompting, indicating a less diverse solution landscape. When focusing on the quality of the best ideas rather than the average ideas, we find that AI-generated ideas are seven times more likely to rank among the top 10 percent of ideas, demonstrating a significant advantage over human-generated ideas. We propose that this seven-to-one advantage is a conservative estimate because it does not account for the greater productivity of AI. Our findings suggest that despite some drawbacks, AI creativity presents a substantial benefit in generating high-quality ideas for new product development.

</details>


### [116] [DeepResearch Agent System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27562)
*Yong Huang,Yulu Huang,for the team Collaboration*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The DeepResearch Agent System is a 30B-parameter sparse-activation LLM (3B active per token) designed for deep retrieval, multi-step reasoning, and autonomous research. It features a dual-mode reasoning engine (ReAct + IterResearch), 128K context with hierarchical attention, multi-tool coordination, GRPO-based RL optimization, and achieves SOTA on agent search benchmarks including 87.3% on Humanity's Last Exam.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the limitations of existing LLMs in performing deep, multi-step, autonomous research tasks that require complex reasoning over long contexts, tool integration, and iterative refinement — while also improving inference efficiency over dense models.

Method: Sparse activation architecture (30B total, 3B active per token); hierarchical attention for 128K context; dual-mode reasoning (ReAct for basic multi-step and IterResearch for up to 20 iterative steps); multi-tool coordination (retrieval, computation, web search, file parsing); GRPO-based RL with token-level policy gradients; automated data synthesis via seed-based expansion.

Result: Sparse model is 3.2× faster than dense equivalents. Hierarchical attention yields +18.7% accuracy and +23.4% recall over standard long-context methods. Dual-mode reasoning gives +31.2% over single-pass baselines. Tool-use accuracy: 92.1%. GRPO improves training stability by 35% and convergence speed by 42%. Data pipeline achieves 92.5% usability. Benchmarks: 87.3% (Humanity's Last Exam), 85.3% (BrowserComp Chinese), 91.2% (WebWalkerQA).

Conclusion: The DeepResearch Agent System demonstrates that sparse activation, hierarchical attention, dual-mode iterative reasoning, and GRPO-based RL can collectively produce a SOTA open-source agent for complex research tasks, with strong efficiency and broad applicability across academic, business, R&D, and educational domains.

Abstract: The DeepResearch Agent System is a large language model system engineered for deep information retrieval, multi-step reasoning, and autonomous research tasks. Built upon a sparse activation architecture with 30 billion total parameters of which only 3 billion are activated per token, the system achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple agent search benchmarks while delivering 3.2 times faster inference compared to dense counterparts of equivalent scale. The system supports a 128K-token context window with hierarchical attention mechanisms that yield 18.7% accuracy and 23.4% recall improvements over standard long-context approaches. A dual-mode reasoning engine provides both a ReAct paradigm for basic multi-step problem solving and an IterResearch mode for high-performance iterative research with up to 20 reasoning steps, collectively delivering a 31.2% accuracy improvement over single-pass baselines. Multi-tool coordination integrates retrieval, computation, web search, and file parsing modules to achieve 92.1% tool-use accuracy. A reinforcement learning optimization framework based on the GRPO algorithm provides token-level policy gradients that improve training stability by 35% and accelerate convergence by 42%. An automated data synthesis pipeline with seed-based expansion achieves a 92.5% usability rate. Benchmark results include 87.3% on Humanity's Last Exam, 85.3% on BrowserComp Chinese, and 91.2% on WebWalkerQA. The system is fully open-sourced, including data synthesis, training, and inference code, and supports applications in academic research, business analysis, R&D support, and education.

</details>


### [117] [What makes prompts a graph: necessary and sufficient conditions for prompt graph engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27578)
*Sandeco Macedo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes "prompt graph engineering" as a formal definition for the now-common practice of structuring LLM workflows as explicit graphs. It reconstructs the concept's genealogy, offers a constitutive definition with four conditions (explicit structure, content-structure separation, executable semantics, first-class artifact), tests it against real systems, and outlines a research agenda.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industry has converged on graphs (in frameworks like LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow) as the de facto structure for multi-step LLM systems. However, the vocabulary remains imprecise—terms like "prompt engineering" still evoke single-string crafting. A shared, operational definition is missing, hindering rigorous research, systematic teaching, and tool interoperability.

Method: The authors conduct a conceptual analysis and genealogical reconstruction tracing the idea from dataflow graphs and build systems through prompt chaining and thought topologies to modern compiled graphs. They derive a constitutive definition via four necessary conditions, operationalize them as an inclusion/exclusion test, delimit boundaries against six neighboring concepts, and validate against six real systems (LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow, AutoGen, CrewAI, Claude Code subagents).

Result: The four-condition definition consistently includes all six systems that are genuine instances of prompt graph engineering while excluding borderline cases. The boundary analysis clarifies distinctions from prompt engineering, agent frameworks, workflow automation, and other adjacent concepts. A research agenda along four design tension axes is proposed.

Conclusion: The paper delivers an operational definition and shared vocabulary for a practice already widely exercised but imprecisely named. This formalization enables more rigorous research, better pedagogy, and clearer tool design in the emerging field of structured LLM system construction.

Abstract: Prompts stopped being isolated strings some time ago. In real systems, one model call feeds another, retrieval interleaves with generation, routers branch, and aggregators merge parallel results. Practice converged on a single structure to hold this together: the graph. Frameworks such as LangGraph, DSPy, and Prompt Flow expose it openly, and research systems already optimize it automatically. The vocabulary, however, lags behind. Graph names, variously, a reasoning topology inside one sampling strategy, a multi-agent conversation, or an orchestration artifact, while prompt engineering still evokes writing one good string. What is missing is a reference definition treating prompts as nodes of an explicit, executable, improvable graph. We build that definition through conceptual analysis over sources with persistent identifiers, complemented by primary grey literature. We reconstruct the genealogy of the idea, from dataflow graphs and build systems, through prompt chaining and the thought topologies (chain, tree, graph), to graphs compiled and optimized as artifacts. We then propose a constitutive definition of prompt graph engineering, state its four conditions (explicit structure, separation between structure and prompt content, executable semantics, and the graph as a first-class engineering artifact), and operationalize them as an inclusion and exclusion test. We draw the boundary against six neighboring concepts and apply the test to six real systems (LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow, AutoGen, CrewAI, and Claude Code subagents); it includes and excludes consistently. We close with a research agenda organized along four design tension axes. The contribution is an operational definition and a shared vocabulary for a practice that industry already exercises daily without naming precisely.

</details>


### [118] [From Minds to Models: The Intersection of Psychology and LLM Behaviours](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27579)
*Oliver Guidetti,Reza Ryan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study adapted the Implicit Association Test to probe racial sentiment bias in ChatGPT (GPT-3.5T, GPT-4, GPT-4T) using open-ended text prompts. A small significant main effect of race was found in initial ANOVA but disappeared under sensitivity analysis, with no pairwise differences surviving correction. Evidence for sentiment differences was deemed weak and analysis-dependent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs exhibit complex, non-linear, opaque decision-making reminiscent of human cognition, making them amenable to psychological methods. As LLMs are deployed in high-stakes domains like government and healthcare, there is a pressing need to adapt psychological tools — specifically the Implicit Association Test — to detect subtle, unobservable racial biases in model outputs.

Method: Fourteen base questions were crossed with eight racial categories and a race-agnostic control, generating 126 prompts. Each prompt was submitted once to GPT-3.5T, GPT-4, and GPT-4T (378 total responses). Sentiment scores were derived by retaining the source score for positive labels, negating it for negative labels, and coding neutral responses as zero. A two-way ANOVA tested effects of racial condition and model, supplemented by a rank-transformed sensitivity analysis and Tukey-corrected pairwise comparisons.

Result: The two-way ANOVA found a small but significant main effect of racial condition (p = .042, partial η² = .044), no effect of model (p = .933), and no interaction (p = .999). However, the effect vanished under rank-transformed sensitivity analysis (p = .145). Tukey-corrected pairwise comparisons revealed no significant differences. One uncorrected post hoc comparison (European vs. Indigenous Australian) was significant but reported only as hypothesis-generating.

Conclusion: Evidence for racial sentiment bias in ChatGPT was weak and dependent on analytical choices. The authors identify key limitations: sentiment scoring cannot disentangle evaluative bias from the valence of historical content, and design refinements are needed. They call for interdisciplinary collaboration to develop robust behavioural measures of model bias.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often compared with the human mind because their decision-making is complex, non-linear and difficult to interpret. Psychological methods developed to investigate unobservable mental processes may therefore help examine LLM behaviour, particularly in government and healthcare. Building on prompt-based adaptations of the Implicit Association Test, this study tested whether ChatGPT produced sentiment differences across racial conditions in open-ended text. Fourteen base questions were crossed with eight racial categories and a race-agnostic control, producing 126 prompts. Each was submitted once to GPT-3.5T, GPT-4 and GPT-4T, yielding 378 responses. Sentiment scores were derived from categorical labels and source scores: positive labels retained the source score, negative labels were assigned its negative, and neutral responses were coded zero. A two-way ANOVA found a small main effect of racial condition, F(8, 351) = 2.04, p = .042, partial-eta squared = .044, but no effect of model, F(2, 351) = 0.07, p = .933, and no interaction, F(16, 351) = 0.23, p = .999. However, the effect was not retained in a rank-transformed sensitivity analysis, F(8, 351) = 1.53, p = .145, and Tukey-corrected comparisons found no significant pairwise differences. An uncorrected European-Indigenous Australian comparison was significant, but was selected post hoc and is reported only as hypothesis-generating. Evidence for sentiment differences was therefore weak and analysis-dependent. Sentiment scoring also cannot distinguish evaluative bias from the valence of historical content elicited by a prompt. We outline design changes needed to address these limitations and argue for interdisciplinary development of behavioural measures of model bias.
  Keywords: Implicit Bias, Psychological Research Methods, Artificial Intelligence, ChatGPT, Large Language Models, Sentiment Analysis

</details>


### [119] [Wiring diagram extraction and gluing: a case study in classifying figure skating jumps using 3D dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27598)
*Jason Lo,Mohammadnima Jafari*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a gluing wiring diagram theory that enables iterative Hasse clustering to overcome the combinatorial complexity of single-shot clustering, validated on figure skating jump video classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hasse clustering becomes computationally infeasible as the number of expected clusters grows due to combinatorial explosion. The authors seek a way to decompose the clustering process into iterative steps without sacrificing the quality of the final result.

Method: The authors develop a theory of gluing wiring diagrams, which provides a formal framework for composing multiple smaller Hasse clustering operations iteratively. This modular decomposition allows the algorithm to scale by breaking a large clustering problem into manageable subproblems and then combining their graphical representations via the gluing mechanism.

Result: The iterative approach using gluing wiring diagrams achieves the same clustering outcome as a single, monolithic application of Hasse clustering. The method is empirically validated on the task of classifying figure skating jump videos, demonstrating practical effectiveness.

Conclusion: The gluing wiring diagram theory successfully enables scalable, iterative Hasse clustering, preserving correctness while circumventing combinatorial complexity. This opens the door to applying Hasse clustering to larger, more complex sequential datasets.

Abstract: Hasse clustering is an algorithm that extracts common patterns in sequential data and represents them in graphical forms. As the number of expected clusters grows, however, the algorithm can become infeasible to run due to combinatorial complexity. In this article, we describe a theory of gluing wiring diagrams, allowing iterative applications of Hasse clustering to achieve the same result as a single application. We test our theory in the context of classifying videos of figure skating jumps.

</details>


### [120] [World Action Planner: Generalizable Decision-Making with Action-Conditioned World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27599)
*Xiangcheng Zhang,Yilun Du*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: World Action Planner combines Vision-Language Models with a multi-task pose-image conditioned world model to enable robots to plan, simulate, and iteratively refine actions, achieving strong zero-shot generalization across novel tasks and environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Imitation learning-based policies excel in training environments but fail to generalize to novel scenes and compositional tasks. There is a need for agents that can reason and plan beyond their training distribution.

Method: The proposed World Action Planner integrates: (1) a Vision-Language Model for initial action plan proposal; (2) a multi-task pose-image conditioned world model for physically grounded rollout simulation; and (3) an iterative optimization and search procedure that refines plans by reasoning over imagined world model rollouts.

Result: The approach achieves superior performance on compositional tasks, new layouts, and zero-shot generalization scenarios, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art end-to-end policy models such as Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) and World Action Models (WAMs).

Conclusion: Decoupling high-level reasoning (via VLMs) from low-level physical grounding (via a world model) with iterative search yields a robust planning framework that generalizes far better than monolithic end-to-end policies.

Abstract: Building generalizable agents for diverse applications remains a fundamental challenge. While imitation learning-based policies succeed in specific training environments, they often fail to generalize to novel scenes and tasks. In this work, we propose World Action Planner, a robot planning system that leverages the reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and the physical grounding of a multi-task pose-image conditioned world model. Our system enables an agent to propose initial action plans and iteratively refine them via optimization and search, reasoning over imagined world model rollouts. We demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance across compositional tasks, new layouts, and zero-shot generalization scenarios, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art end-to-end policy models such as VLAs and WAMs. Project website at worldactionplanner.github.io

</details>


### [121] [CORE: In-Context Reconstruction for Unified Tabular Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27615)
*Yunfeng Zhao,Qingfeng Chen,Yue Tan,Shiyuan Li,Yili Wang,Yixin Liu,Shirui Pan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CORE proposes an in-context reconstruction framework for unified tabular anomaly detection, using decorrelated feature alignment and context-based reconstruction to detect anomalies across diverse datasets without labeled or synthetic anomalies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing unified TAD methods struggle with heterogeneous feature alignment (distance-based methods obscure semantics) and binary classification formulations that overlook diverse anomaly patterns and are misled by unrepresentative synthetic anomalies.

Method: CORE introduces two key components: (1) a decorrelated feature alignment module that directly maps heterogeneous features into a unified representation space while preserving semantic information, and (2) an in-context reconstruction module that reconstructs each sample using contextual normal samples to capture dataset-specific distributions, where reconstruction errors serve as anomaly scores.

Result: The paper claims CORE enables effective unified TAD on arbitrary unseen datasets without requiring labeled anomalies or synthesized negative samples.

Conclusion: Reformulating unified TAD as an in-context reconstruction problem, combined with semantics-preserving feature alignment, overcomes key limitations of prior classification-based and distance-based approaches.

Abstract: Tabular anomaly detection (TAD), which focuses on identifying abnormal samples that deviate from the majority in tabular data, has received growing attention. Recently, there has been an emerging trend towards unified TAD, which seeks to detect anomalies across different datasets using a single generalizable model. In unified TAD, aligning heterogeneous data remains challenging. While existing methods often rely on distance-based unified feature construction, they may obscure the semantics of the original features. Moreover, existing approaches typically formulate anomaly detection as a binary classification task, which may overlook diverse anomaly patterns from various datasets and be misled by unrepresentative synthetic anomalies. To address these challenges, we propose an in-COntext REconstruction approach for unified TAD (CORE for short). It introduces a decorrelated feature alignment module to directly align heterogeneous features into a unified representation space, which retains their semantic information. Meanwhile, CORE formulates unified TAD as an in-context reconstruction problem, eliminating the need for labeled or synthesized anomalies. Specifically, the in-context reconstruction module reconstructs each sample by leveraging contextual normal samples to capture dataset-specific distributions, such that reconstruction errors reflect its deviation from normality, facilitating unified TAD on arbitrary unseen datasets.

</details>


### [122] [Old Tricks, New Models: How Simple Image Transformations Break Modern AI-based Content Moderation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28187)
*Marco Alecci,Francesco Marchiori,Iyiola Emmanuel Olatunji,Tegawendé F. Bissyandé,Jacques Klein*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Evaluates the robustness of three commercial multimodal moderation APIs against simple image transformations. Finds all three can be bypassed using inexpensive, model-agnostic transformations (e.g., color inversion, grayscale), with varying vulnerability across harm categories. Concludes that foundation-model-based moderation APIs do not inherently provide reliable safety boundaries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Commercial multimodal moderation APIs built on large foundation models are increasingly replacing task-specific classifiers, promising broader policy coverage and better contextual understanding. However, their adversarial robustness relative to traditional classifiers remains unexamined. The paper investigates whether this architectural shift yields genuinely more robust image moderation.

Method: Large-scale black-box evaluation of three established commercial image-moderation services. Seven simple, model-agnostic image transformations (including color inversion, grayscale conversion, and others) are applied across multiple providers, datasets, harm categories, perceptual-similarity constraints, and transformation intensities. No gradients, surrogate models, or target system knowledge is required.

Result: All three commercial services can be bypassed using inexpensive image transformations. Fixed transformations like color inversion and grayscale conversion induce unsafe-to-safe decision changes while preserving human-recognizable content. Robustness varies substantially across datasets and harm categories, with multimodal content and self-harm showing pronounced vulnerabilities.

Conclusion: Replacing conventional moderation classifiers with foundation-model-based APIs does not, by itself, provide a reliable security boundary. Such systems must be evaluated under realistic transformations and deployed as one component of a layered moderation pipeline rather than as standalone safety filters.

Abstract: While automated content-moderation systems have become essential for screening harmful content at scale, conventional task-specific classifiers often provide limited policy cov- erage and contextual understanding. Recently, commercial multimodal moderation APIs built on large foundation models have been introduced with the promise of providing broader and more capable safety filters. In this work, we analyze whether this shift also yields more robust image moderation. We conduct a large-scale black-box evaluation on three established commercial image-moderation services and compare their robustness. By evaluating seven simple, model-agnostic image transformations across multiple providers, datasets, harm categories, perceptual-similarity constraints, and transformation intensities, we find that: (1) all three commercial services can be bypassed using inexpensive image transformations that require no gradients, surrogate models, or knowledge of the target system; (2) even fixed transformations such as color inversion and grayscale conversion induce unsafe-to-safe decision changes while preserving content that remains recognizable to humans; (3) their robustness varies substantially across datasets and harm categories, with multimodal content and self-harm exhibiting pronounced vulnerabilities. This yields the conclusion that replacing conventional moderation classifiers with foundation-model-based APIs does not, by itself, provide a reliable security boundary. Such systems must be evaluated under realistic transformations and deployed as one component of a layered moderation pipeline rather than as standalone safety filters.

</details>


### [123] [Hidden APIs in Language Models: Discovering Reusable Causal Interfaces from Forked Futures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27617)
*SiYuan Ma,Yiqin Luo,Zhangji,Canran Xiao,Albert Gao,Wei-Hsing Huang,Wei Wang,Qiwei Wu,Xinran Li,Jinfeng Wei,Qixin Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes "forked futures" — a causal framework that compares hidden states by sampling future operations after a prefix state forms and analyzing the resulting response distributions. It evaluates four interface types (Shared, Local, Mixture, Distributed) using prequential causal description length as a selection criterion. Shared interfaces achieve the lowest held-out description length across multiple LLMs and mediate substantially more target effects than null paths, supporting the existence of economical reusable causal interfaces in language models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current probing methods that examine hidden states based on identical model outputs fail to establish whether those states support a genuinely reusable internal interface for different downstream computations. The authors aim to move beyond correlation-based probing toward a causal, operation-grounded method for comparing and classifying how hidden states interface with future computations.

Method: The authors introduce "forked futures": after a prefix state forms, future operations are sampled and applied to that state, producing response distributions that serve as a causal signature. These signatures enable an empirical causal quotient over hidden states without researcher-specified labels. Four candidate interface architectures (Shared, Local, Mixture, Distributed) compete under prequential causal description length, constrained by future-signature fidelity and matched capacity. Evaluation includes model comparisons (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Llama-3-8B, plus a five-backbone sweep), figure-aligned transplantation analysis, and a blind four-class model-organism classification test across 16 architectures.

Result: Shared interfaces achieve the lowest held-out description length: 0.216 nats gain on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 0.294 nats on Llama-3-8B, with tightly clustered mean future-signature distortion. The five-backbone sweep preserves positive Sharedness Gain direction. In transplantation analysis, Shared interfaces show the strongest joint profile across target-correctness, locality, copy-preservation, and composite metrics. API-aligned paths mediate 0.749 of the target effect versus 0.150 for matched null paths. In blind classification, 14/16 architectures are correctly recovered, with one non-Shared→Shared error among 12 non-Shared organisms.

Conclusion: The results support the existence of an economical, reusable causal interface within the tested operation banks. However, the claim is explicitly conditional on the candidate architectures, interventions, and held-out futures used, acknowledging that the finding is bounded by the experimental framework rather than asserting universality.

Abstract: Identical language-model answers can arise from hidden states that support different future computations, so current-answer probes do not establish a reusable internal interface. We introduce forked futures: future operations are sampled only after a prefix state has formed, and states are compared through the response distributions induced by those operations. This yields an empirical causal quotient over hidden states without requiring researcher-specified latent labels. Shared, Local, Mixture, and Distributed interfaces then compete under prequential causal description length subject to future-signature fidelity and matched capacity constraints. In the two detailed model evaluations, Shared has the lowest held-out description length, with gains of 0.216 nats on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 0.294 nats on Llama-3-8B, while maintaining tightly clustered mean future-signature distortion; a five-backbone sweep preserves the positive direction of Sharedness Gain. The figure-aligned transplantation analysis gives Shared the strongest joint target-correctness, locality, copy-preservation, and composite profile, and API-aligned paths mediate 0.749 of the target effect versus 0.150 for matched null paths. In the blind four-class model-organism test, 14/16 architectures are recovered, with one observed non-Shared to Shared error among 12 non-Shared organisms. These results support an economical reusable causal interface within the tested operation banks, while keeping the claim explicitly conditional on the candidate architectures, interventions, and held-out futures.

</details>


### [124] [SCOPE: Synthetic Conditional Objectives for Policy Evolution in Black-Box Combinatorial Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27630)
*Nguyen Viet Tuan Kiet,Nguyen Huu Duc,Le Cong Bang,Tran Cong Dao,Huynh Thi Thanh Binh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SCOPE introduces a framework for black-box combinatorial optimization that learns synthetic objectives from search history to evolve diverse search policies, adaptively selecting objectives that best guide exploration, achieving consistent improvements under limited evaluation budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Black-box combinatorial optimization suffers from limited evaluation budgets with no gradient or structural information from the unknown objective function, making it difficult to decide where to explore next. Existing methods often rely on a single surrogate model or heuristic, which risks premature convergence or insufficient diversity.

Method: SCOPE operates in a bi-level loop: (1) the outer loop adaptively updates and selects synthetic objectives based on how effectively their induced policies discover promising regions in the true black-box landscape; (2) the inner loop evolves a portfolio of search policies using these diverse synthetic objectives, where each synthetic objective encodes a distinct preference over candidate solutions conditioned on accumulated search history. The framework reframes objective design as a mechanism for guiding policy exploration, maintaining structured diversity across discrete solution spaces.

Result: Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark problems demonstrate that SCOPE consistently improves black-box search performance under limited evaluation budgets and generalizes well across diverse combinatorial structures.

Conclusion: SCOPE effectively reframes objective design as a policy exploration mechanism, enabling structured diversity and adaptive guidance that outperforms single-surrogate approaches in black-box combinatorial optimization under constrained evaluation budgets.

Abstract: Black-box combinatorial optimization requires systematically identifying high-quality solutions under a limited evaluation budget, yet the unknown objective function provides little guidance for deciding where the search should explore next. We introduce SCOPE, a general framework for Synthetic Conditional Objectives for Policy Evolution in Black-Box Combinatorial Optimization. Rather than directly optimizing the inaccessible objective, SCOPE learns a set of synthetic objectives conditioned on the accumulated search history, where each objective is designed to expose a distinct and potentially useful preference over candidate solutions. These objectives are then used to evolve search policies that generate diverse candidates, whose true quality is subsequently assessed through black-box evaluations. The outer loop adaptively updates and selects synthetic objectives according to how effectively their induced policies discover promising regions. In contrast, the inner loop returns a portfolio of top-performing policies to reduce the risk of relying on a single surrogate preference. This formulation reframes objective design as a mechanism for guiding policy exploration, enabling the search process to exploit observed evidence while maintaining structured diversity across discrete solution spaces. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark problems demonstrate that SCOPE consistently improves black-box search performance under limited evaluation budgets and generalizes well across diverse combinatorial structures.

</details>


### [125] [ReDiPPO: Reference-Guided Value Calibration and Discrepancy-Aware Token Reweighting for Mathematical Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27631)
*Zhenrong Zhang,Fei Wu,Jun Du,Jianshu Zhang,Si Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReDiPPO proposes a reference-guided PPO framework that uses reference answers as privileged training signals to improve critic value estimation, and leverages the discrepancy between standard and reference-guided critics to reweight token-level advantages, boosting mathematical reasoning in LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In mathematical reasoning with long horizons and sparse rewards, standard PPO critics produce unreliable token-level credit assignment, leading to noisy advantage estimates and suboptimal policy updates. A more accurate value estimation method is needed.

Method: ReDiPPO employs dual critics: (1) a reference-guided critic that uses reference answers as privileged signals during training for accurate value estimation, and (2) a standard critic. The token-level discrepancy between the two value estimates quantifies reasoning difficulty and is used to reweight token-level advantages during PPO optimization.

Result: ReDiPPO improves value-estimation accuracy and consistently outperforms PPO, DAPO, and GSPO across diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks in final reasoning performance.

Conclusion: The reference-guided critic with discrepancy-aware reweighting effectively addresses the credit assignment challenge in mathematical reasoning RL, yielding superior policy optimization compared to existing methods.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning has emerged as an effective paradigm for enhancing the mathematical reasoning capabilities of large language models. Among existing policy optimization methods, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) remains particularly appealing because its learned critic can, in principle, provide token-level credit assignment. However, in mathematical reasoning tasks characterized by long reasoning horizons and sparse outcome rewards, reliable token-level credit assignment remains challenging. The standard critic often fails to accurately evaluate intermediate reasoning states, resulting in noisy advantage estimates and suboptimal policy updates. In this paper, we propose ReDiPPO, a Reference-guided and Discrepancy-aware PPO framework for mathematical reasoning. ReDiPPO introduces a reference-guided critic that uses reference answers as training-time privileged signals to provide more accurate value estimation. Meanwhile, it retains a standard critic and quantifies the token-level reference-standard discrepancy between the standard value estimate and the reference-guided value estimate. This discrepancy serves as an indicator of difficult reasoning states and is used to reweight the corresponding token-level advantages during PPO optimization. Extensive experiments on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ReDiPPO improves value-estimation accuracy and consistently outperforms strong policy optimization baselines, including PPO, DAPO, and GSPO, in final reasoning performance. Our code is available on https://github.com/cii030/ReDiPPO.

</details>


### [126] [HALO: Heterogeneous Admission through Localized Obligations for Safe Agentic Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27636)
*Taewoo Park,Kyeonghyun Yoo,Kiseok Kim,Seunghyun Yoo,Hwangnam Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HALO is a runtime protocol for heterogeneous AI agent responses that selectively preserves supported components whose prerequisites remain valid, rechecks actions before dispatch, and allows blocked actions to be replaced by fresh candidates, outperforming whole-response rejection in both structured tests and PX4/Gazebo simulations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic AI systems produce heterogeneous responses (notices, requests, handoffs, actions) whose components may become unsupported due to changing conditions before external use. Whole-response rejection discards useful components, but independent checking risks retaining dependent components whose prerequisites have been invalidated — a correctness gap HALO addresses.

Method: HALO is a runtime admission protocol with three mechanisms: (1) localized obligations that preserve any component whose declared prerequisites are still supported, (2) exact rechecking of each action just before dispatch, and (3) a blocking-and-replacement scheme where blocked actions are replaced exclusively by fresh, newly generated candidates rather than stale alternatives.

Result: HALO matched 96/96 admission expectations and passed 20/20 protocol tests. In structured-response replay, it retained 248/248 supported components (including 128/128 unaffected by unrelated changes) versus 0/248 for whole-response rejection. Across ten cold-start PX4/Gazebo sessions, HALO blocked every stale route, observed zero matching stale setpoints, and completed all fresh recoveries.

Conclusion: HALO demonstrates that fine-grained, obligation-aware admission control at runtime can salvage useful components from heterogeneous agent responses while maintaining safety, outperforming coarse-grained whole-response rejection and providing a practical solution for dynamic environments where response components age at different rates.

Abstract: Recent agentic AI systems may return a heterogeneous response containing notices, requests, handoffs, and actions. Conditions can change before external use, so components from the same response need not remain supported together. Rejecting the whole response discards useful components, whereas checking components independently can leave a dependent without its prerequisite. We present Heterogeneous Admission with Localized Obligations (HALO), a runtime protocol that preserves supported components whose declared prerequisites also remain supported, rechecks each exact action before dispatch, and allows blocked actions to be replaced only by fresh candidates. HALO matched all 96 admission expectations and passed all 20 protocol tests. In structured-response replay, it retained 248/248 supported components, including 128/128 unaffected by unrelated changes, while a whole-response policy retained 0/248. Across ten cold-start PX4/Gazebo sessions, HALO blocked every tested stale route, observed no matching stale setpoint, and completed all fresh recoveries.

</details>


### [127] [HealthCAT: An Interpretable Encoder-only Transformer Framework for Health Indicator Prediction and Temporal Interpretation of Wearable Sensor Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27635)
*Xiaotong Yu,Joshua Y. Kim,HaeJin Lee,Kalina Yacef*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HealthCAT is a Transformer-based framework for wearable sensor data that combines an Encoder-only Transformer with an Attentive Class Activation Token to achieve both high predictive accuracy and time-step-level interpretability, outperforming baselines by up to 17% in F1-score while providing validated, class-specific temporal explanations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deep learning methods for wearable sensor data prioritize predictive accuracy over interpretability, limiting their utility in health research where understanding when and how behavioural patterns occur is critical for monitoring, analysis, and intervention design.

Method: HealthCAT integrates an Encoder-only Transformer architecture with a novel Attentive Class Activation Token (AttentiveCAT) mechanism. This produces class-specific interpretations at each time step, which can be mapped onto domain-relevant behavioural cycles (e.g., time-of-day). The framework was evaluated on two real-world wearable sensor datasets (306 participants total) and validated through masking experiments that tested whether identified time steps carried significant predictive value.

Result: HealthCAT outperformed deep learning baselines by up to 17% in F1-score and 12% in accuracy on both datasets (p<0.05). Masking experiments confirmed that time steps identified by HealthCAT carried significantly more predictive value than random selection across all masking conditions (p<0.05).

Conclusion: HealthCAT bridges the gap between predictive performance and interpretability in wearable sensor analysis, enabling a shift from aggregated summary metrics to fine-grained temporal pattern analysis. This supports health monitoring, behavioural pattern analysis, and intervention design by revealing not just what activity patterns predict health outcomes, but when and how they occur.

Abstract: Wearable sensors continuously capture fine-grained multivariate time-series data, providing opportunities to model behavioural patterns associated with health outcomes. However, existing deep learning methods prioritise predictive accuracy over interpretability, limiting their application in health research. In this study, we present HealthCAT, a flexible framework that integrates an Encoder-only Transformer with an Attentive Class Activation Token (AttentiveCAT) to generate class-specific, time-step-level interpretations. These interpretations can be mapped back onto behavioural cycles that are relevant to the domain (e.g., time-of-day), supporting individual-level analysis of wearable sensor data. We evaluated HealthCAT using two real-world wearable sensor datasets (306 participants in total). HealthCAT outperformed deep learning baselines by up to 17\% in F1-score and 12\% in accuracy on both datasets ($p<0.05$). In masking experiments, the time steps identified by HealthCAT carried significantly more predictive value than random selection across all masking conditions ($p<0.05$), indicating that the identified time steps are predictively informative. By coupling predictive performance with validated time-step-level interpretability, HealthCAT moves wearable sensor analysis beyond aggregated metrics towards temporal patterns that support health monitoring, behavioural pattern analysis, and intervention design in health research. The significance of this work is that it enables accurate prediction of health indicators from wearable sensor data while providing insights into when and how physical activity patterns occur, rather than relying solely on aggregated summary measures.

</details>


### [128] [Evaluating and Pricing Advertisements in AI-Generated Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27686)
*John L. Turner-Smith,Zimeng Huang,Yuhan Fu,Yihang Zhang,Tonghan Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the lack of reliable click-through intent signals for advertising in LLM-driven answer engines by constructing supervision via a psychologically grounded agent simulation framework. The resulting parameter-efficient evaluator predicts click-through intent and ad quality dimensions as smooth, differentiable estimates, outperforms frontier zero-shot judges, and directly underpins a principled pricing mechanism with truthful bidding properties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As advertising becomes embedded within LLM-generated responses, evaluating ad quality requires click-through intent signals. However, behavioural logs are unavailable, human annotation is difficult to calibrate, and frontier LLM judges conflate intent with surface linguistic fluency. This creates a foundational gap: principled pricing presupposes a continuous intent signal, but generating such a signal presupposes unavailable supervision.

Method: The authors construct missing supervision using a psychologically grounded agent simulation framework, then distill it into a parameter-efficient evaluator that predicts click-through intent and three companion ad quality dimensions as smooth, differentiable estimates. Upon these estimates, they derive the unique payment rule for truthful bidding under best-of-k allocation and extend the mechanism to non-monotone allocations.

Result: The evaluator surpasses frontier zero-shot judges on relevance sensitivity (79% vs. 60-67%), tracks graded content degradation, generalises without error to 103 fictional products, and agrees with human preference in 86% of pairwise judgements across five annotators, with agreement rising alongside evaluator confidence. The derived pricing layer demonstrates truthful-bidding optimality.

Conclusion: By constructing supervision through agent simulation and distilling it into a differentiable evaluator, the paper closes the loop between ad quality evaluation and principled pricing for LLM-driven answer engines. The same differentiable signal can also serve as a training objective for ad generation.

Abstract: As search increasingly shifts toward LLM-driven answer engines, advertising is becoming embedded within the generated response itself and should therefore be evaluated for both user utility and commercial value. The key challenge is click-through intent: behavioural logs are unavailable, human annotation resists calibration, and frontier LLM judges conflate intent with linguistic fluency. These gaps compound, as principled pricing presupposes a continuous intent signal, while generating such a signal presupposes supervision that is currently unavailable. We construct the missing supervision through a psychologically grounded agent simulation framework, and distil it into a parameter-efficient evaluator that predicts click-through intent, together with the three companion dimensions of ad quality, as smooth, differentiable estimates. Validated through sign-certain behavioural perturbations, the evaluator surpasses frontier zero-shot judges on relevance sensitivity (79% versus 60-67%), tracks graded content degradation, generalises without error to 103 fictional products, and agrees with human preference in 86% of pairwise judgements across five annotators, with agreement rising in the evaluator's confidence. Upon its estimates we build the pricing layer directly, deriving the unique payment rule under which truthful bidding is optimal, demonstrating it on a best-of-k allocation, and extending the mechanism to non-monotone allocations. The same differentiable signal stands ready as a training objective for ad generation.

</details>


### [129] [Rehearse: Stepping Back from the Confidence Cliff in Self-Improving Autoresearch](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27687)
*Jiazhen Ji,Shouhong Ding*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Autoresearch agents suffer a "confidence cliff" where their ability to pre-judge code modifications degrades from ~83% to ~57% accuracy as successful changes accumulate. The Rehearse method addresses this by using focused outcome memory of past attempts, restoring late-loop accuracy to 83.5% and improving results across multiple domains under fixed training budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoresearch loops waste compute on failed training runs. While prior work focuses on idea generation, the authors identify that the agent's pre-execution judgment—deciding *before* training whether a change will help—is equally critical. The paper investigates how this judgment reliability degrades over the course of an autoresearch trajectory and seeks to mitigate this degradation.

Method: The authors first quantify the problem using two data sources: (1) public AutoSOTA logs showing helpful-modification rates dropping from 70% to 43%, and (2) a new benchmark of 366 same-baseline modification pairs from 39 paper-derived tasks, where an LLM judge (with candidate rationales but no history) is evaluated for pre-execution accuracy. They identify the "confidence cliff": selective accuracy (accuracy on strict-consensus verdicts) drops from 82.8% to 56.9% late in the loop. Rehearse is then proposed as a lightweight skill: propose multiple ideas, compare them pre-execution, run only the most promising, and judge using a focused memory of similar past attempts and their outcomes.

Result: On the 296-pair subset with strict-consensus verdicts, the LLM judge achieves 79.5% accuracy. However, on the full 366-pair benchmark, selective accuracy falls from 82.8% (early) to 56.9% (late). Rehearse's focused outcome memory raises late selective accuracy to 83.5%. Across 4,000 budgeted training runs over three loops (nanochat, image classification, time-series forecasting), Rehearse improves the endpoint metric under the same training-run budget.

Conclusion: Pre-execution judgment is a critical bottleneck in autoresearch loops, and its reliability erodes over time due to the confidence cliff. Incorporating focused memory of similar past attempts via Rehearse substantially restores judgment accuracy and yields practical gains across diverse ML tasks, improving the efficiency of automated machine-learning research.

Abstract: Autoresearch improves machine-learning code by proposing changes, running full training jobs, and keeping changes that improve the metric. The efficiency of this loop depends not only on generating ideas, but also on the agent's ability to decide, before spending a training run, whether a proposed modification is likely to work. We study how the reliability of this pre-execution judgment changes over the course of an autoresearch trajectory. In public AutoSOTA logs (Li et al., 2026; Tsinghua FIB Lab, 2026), the fraction of helpful modifications falls from 70% in the first two iterations to 43% by iteration 6+. On 296 same-baseline modification pairs from 39 paper-derived AutoSOTA tasks, each containing one modification that improved the metric and one that did not, with measured outcomes hidden, an LLM judge given candidate rationales but no prior-attempt history reaches 79.5% accuracy on the pairs where strict consensus returns a verdict. On the full 366-pair benchmark, however, this ability weakens substantially late in the loop. As successful changes accumulate, selective accuracy - accuracy conditioned on a strict-consensus verdict - falls from 82.8% to 56.9%, while the judge remains willing to decide. We call this operational pattern the confidence cliff. Rehearse implements the loop change as a lightweight skill for autoresearch loops: propose several ideas, compare them before execution, run the most promising, and judge with a focused memory of similar past attempts and outcomes. This focused outcome memory raises late selective accuracy to 83.5%. Across 4,000 budgeted training runs over three loops, Rehearse improves the endpoint under the same training-run budget on nanochat, image classification, and time-series forecasting.

</details>


### [130] [Guiding Large Language Models with Genetic Programming-Evolved Heuristic Knowledge for Dynamic Multi-Mode Project Scheduling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27698)
*Yuan Tian,Yi Mei,Mengjie Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper explores using GP-evolved scheduling rules to guide LLM-based decision-making in dynamic multi-mode project scheduling. Four knowledge injection mechanisms (Feature Selection, Feature Hint, Rule Reference, Rule Follow) are evaluated across scheduling performance, token consumption, stability, and rationale alignment. GP-derived guidance improves LLM decisions, with Feature Selection offering best token efficiency and Rule Follow achieving strongest performance at higher token cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can flexibly interpret scheduling information and explain decisions, but zero-shot LLM decisions suffer from lack of domain knowledge, high token consumption, and query variability. GP-evolved priority rules encode domain expertise but are rigid. Rather than using LLMs to support GP (the common hybrid direction), the authors propose the reverse: transferring knowledge from high-quality GP rules into LLM decision-making to combine the strengths of both approaches.

Method: The authors extract knowledge from high-quality GP-evolved priority rules and inject it into an online LLM decision maker via four mechanisms: (1) Feature Selection — simplifying the decision context by presenting only GP-identified important features; (2) Feature Hint — highlighting which features matter without removing others; (3) Rule Reference — providing GP rule logic as a reference; (4) Rule Follow — supplying explicit GP decision logic for the LLM to follow. These are evaluated on scheduling performance, token consumption, decision stability, and feature focus in generated rationales.

Result: GP-derived guidance generally improves the unguided LLM across all metrics. Feature Selection provides the best token efficiency. Rule Follow achieves the strongest scheduling performance but at greater token cost. Guidance also improves decision stability (reducing variance across repeated queries) and shifts the features emphasized in LLM-generated rationales. The representation of injected knowledge matters: simplifying context or providing explicit logic outperforms merely highlighting important features.

Conclusion: Transferring knowledge from GP-evolved rules to LLMs is a viable and effective direction. The choice of knowledge injection mechanism involves a trade-off between performance and token efficiency. Explicit decision logic (Rule Follow) yields the best results, but Feature Selection offers a more cost-effective alternative with competitive performance.

Abstract: In dynamic multi-mode project scheduling, activities have alternative execution modes and uncertain durations, while precedence relations and limited resources constrain their execution. Heuristic priority rules support fast online decisions, but their design requires substantial domain expertise. Genetic programming (GP) hyper-heuristics can automatically evolve such rules. Large language models (LLMs), meanwhile, provide a flexible interface for interpreting scheduling information and explaining decisions. However, zero-shot LLM decisions may lack domain knowledge, consume many tokens, and vary across repeated queries. GP-evolved rules therefore provide a potential source of scheduling knowledge for guiding LLM decisions. Unlike existing LLM--GP hybrids that use LLMs to support heuristic evolution, we transfer knowledge in the reverse direction, using knowledge extracted from high-quality GP rules to guide an online LLM decision maker. We extract knowledge from high-quality GP rules and inject it through Feature Selection, Feature Hint, Rule Reference, and Rule Follow. These mechanisms are evaluated in terms of scheduling performance, token consumption, decision stability, and the feature focus expressed in generated rationales. GP-derived guidance generally improves the unguided LLM, but its representation matters. Simplifying the decision context or supplying explicit decision logic is more effective than highlighting important features. Feature Selection offers the best token efficiency, whereas Rule Follow achieves strong performance at greater token cost. Guidance also improves decision stability and changes the features expressed in generated rationales.

</details>


### [131] [SpatialCLI: Learning to Reason With Spatial Tools, Then Without Them](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27703)
*Yang Zhou,Zixuan Huang,Sunzhu Li,Zhuo Yang,Chen Zhang,Shunian Chen,Caijun Yan,Jianyao Xu,Shunyu Liu,Weijie Fu,Peiliang Li,Xiaozhi Chen,Yuxiang Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SpatialCLI is a three-stage framework (Call, Learn, Internalize) that teaches vision-language models to use spatial specialist tools and progressively internalize their perceptual capabilities, achieving significant gains on spatial reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: General VLMs reason well at the task level but miss fine-grained visual details, while specialist vision models capture those details but lack task-level reasoning. Bridging this capability gap in embodied agents is the core motivation.

Method: A three-stage framework: (1) Call — exposes specialist vision models as spatial tools; (2) Learn — uses Cold-Start Supervised Fine-Tuning and agentic reinforcement learning to improve tool use; (3) Internalize — verbalizes successful tool-use trajectories to distill specialist capabilities into the VLM, enabling tool-free inference after training.

Result: On MindCube, SpatialCLI improves Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct from 29.3% to 84.6% with tools, surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol with tools (72.1%). After internalization, the model retains 73.8% without tools. A new benchmark, SpatialCLI-Bench, with 516 examples across localization, segmentation, depth, and pose is introduced.

Conclusion: SpatialCLI effectively bridges the gap between general VLMs and specialist perception models through a teach-use-internalize paradigm, yielding strong performance both with and without tools at inference time.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used in embodied agents to interpret visual inputs, reason about spatial relationships, and make task-level decisions based on that reasoning. However, a fundamental capability mismatch remains: general VLMs can reason about the overall task but often miss the visual details that determine success, while specialist vision models can capture those details but cannot translate them into task-level decisions. In this work, we propose SpatialCLI, a framework that teaches VLMs to reason with spatial tools and progressively internalize the specialist perceptual capabilities they provide. SpatialCLI proceeds in three stages: (1) Call exposes specialist vision models as spatial tools to augment the VLM's perception; (2) Learn uses Cold-Start SFT and agentic RL to improve tool use; and (3) Internalize verbalizes successful tool-use trajectories to internalize specialist perceptual capabilities. We further introduce SpatialCLI-Bench, a 516-example benchmark for compositional perception across localization, segmentation, depth, and pose. On MindCube, SpatialCLI raises Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct from 29.3% to 84.6% with tools, surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol with tools (72.1%), while retaining 73.8% without tools after internalization.

</details>


### [132] [Albilich: Steerable Proof-State Orchestration for LLM-Based Mathematical Research with CAS Integration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27705)
*Ting Gong,Michael Ruofan Zeng,Yong Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Albilich is an open-source agentic framework for AI-assisted mathematical research that integrates long-horizon reasoning, computer algebra systems, literature retrieval, and persistent context management. It achieves strong results on the RealMath benchmark and open group theory problems from the Kourovka Notebook.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs can contribute useful ideas to mathematical research, coordinating, evaluating, and reproducing long-horizon proof attempts remains challenging. There is a need for a structured, reproducible, and scalable environment that supports sustained mathematical reasoning with tool integration.

Method: Albilich is an open-source agentic harness combining: (1) long-horizon reasoning capabilities, (2) integration with computer algebra systems (CAS), (3) literature retrieval mechanisms, and (4) persistent SQLite-based context management for maintaining state across extended proof attempts. The system is evaluated on RealMath and on open problems in group theory from the Kourovka Notebook, with ablation studies isolating the contributions of CAS and an advisor agent.

Result: Albilich solved 10/10 problems on RealMath with CAS and 9/10 without CAS. On Kourovka Notebook problems, it produced a counterexample to Problem 21.142 and proved a strengthening of Problem 20.2. Ablation on Problem 17.91 showed a 32.0% token reduction when CAS is enabled. Ablation on Problem 21.142 showed higher verifier-rejection rates and failure to synthesize proof routes without the advisor agent.

Conclusion: Albilich demonstrates promise as a human-steerable, CAS-boosted environment for scalable AI-assisted mathematical research, with ablations confirming the value of both CAS integration and the advisor agent component.

Abstract: Large language models can contribute useful ideas to mathematical research, yet long-horizon proof attempts remain difficult to coordinate, evaluate, and reproduce. We present Albilich, an open-source agentic harness for autoresearch in mathematics that combines long-horizon reasoning, computer algebra systems (CAS), literature retrieval, and persistent SQLite-based context management.
  We evaluate Albilich on the RealMath benchmark (Zhang et al. 2025) and on open problems in group theory from the Kourovka Notebook (Khukhro and Mazurov 2026). It solved 10/10 problems on RealMath with CAS and 9/10 with no CAS. On the Kourovka problems, Albilich produced a counterexample to Problem 21.142 and a proof of a strengthening of Problem20.2. Anablation on Problem 17.91 demonstrates 32.0% token reduction when CAS is enabled. An ablation on Problem 21.142 demonstrates higher verifier-rejection rate and failure to synthesize proof routes in the absence of the advisor agent. These results support Albilich as a human-steerable, CAS-boosted environment for scalable AI-assisted mathematical research.

</details>


### [133] [MECA: A Mechanism-Centered Agent for Constructing Well-Specified and Valuable Mathematical Conjectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27709)
*Wentao Long,Yunfei Zhang,Chenyi Li,Zaiwen Wen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MECA is a multi-agent framework for automated mathematical conjecture generation that jointly develops candidate statements and their supporting "mechanisms" (reasoning principles connecting assumptions to conclusions). Explorer agents propose and test mechanisms, while critic agents assess validity and research value. Evaluated against baselines on reconstructing target conclusions and generating 100 semi-open problems, MECA produces well-specified, research-worthy conjectures that challenge current automated provers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI-assisted mathematical discovery struggles because open problems and conjectures are often too broad, underspecified, or lack clear pathways to proof or refutation. The authors identify a gap: automated systems need to produce conjectures that are not only interesting but also well-specified with identifiable mechanisms connecting assumptions to conclusions, enabling substantive mathematical support while preserving an unresolved core.

Method: MECA is a multi-agent framework with two agent types: (1) Explorer agents that propose mechanisms (inequalities, invariants, decompositions, reductions), test their applicability, and revise candidate conjectures accordingly; (2) Critic agents that assess mathematical validity and research value, guiding refinements to assumptions, scope, and conclusions. This mechanism-centered refinement process iteratively transforms broad research directions into precise, well-supported conjectures.

Result: Evaluation in two settings: (1) Reconstructing preselected target-paper conclusions from target-conditioned but article-blind source materials, where MECA outperformed a generate-and-revise baseline. (2) Generating 100 semi-open problems from literature-derived seeds and existing open problems, which were then tested through independent proof and refutation attempts by automated provers. The mechanism-centered refinement produced well-specified conjectures that remained challenging for current automated provers.

Conclusion: Mechanism-centered conjecture refinement via the MECA framework effectively produces well-specified, research-worthy mathematical conjectures. By jointly developing statements and their supporting mechanisms, the approach bridges the gap between broad research directions and precise, attackable problems, yielding conjectures that are both mathematically substantive and resistant to trivial resolution by existing automated provers.

Abstract: Automatically constructing well-specified and valuable mathematical conjectures remains a central challenge in AI-assisted mathematical discovery. Many existing open problems and conjectures are often too broad, underspecified, or difficult to connect to plausible proof or refutation strategies. We view a mathematical mechanism as a structure or reasoning principle that connects the assumptions of a candidate problem to its target conclusion, such as an inequality, invariant, decomposition, or reduction to an intermediate claim. We present MECA (MEchanism-centered Conjecture Agent), a multi-agent framework that constructs conjectures by jointly developing candidate statements and their supporting mechanisms. Explorer agents propose mechanisms, test how they apply, and revise the candidate conjecture accordingly, while critic agents assess their mathematical validity and research value. Their feedback guides changes to the assumptions, scope, and conclusion. Through this process, MECA transforms broad research directions into precise conjectures with substantive mathematical support while retaining a clearly identified unresolved core. We evaluate MECA in two complementary settings. First, we compare it with a generate-and-revise baseline on reconstructing preselected target-paper conclusions from target-conditioned but article-blind source materials. Second, we construct 100 semi-open problems from literature-derived seeds and existing open problems and evaluate them through independent proof and refutation attempts by automated provers. Our results indicate that mechanism-centered refinement produces well-specified and research-worthy conjectures that remain challenging for current automated provers.

</details>


### [134] [New Synchronous Computation Dynamics for Hopfield Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27720)
*Francisco Requena-Domínguez,Rafaela Benítez-Rochel,Ezequiel López-Rubio*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a new synchronous dynamics (SD-DDF) for Hopfield networks using a Discrete Differential Filter to update multiple neurons simultaneously, maximizing energy decrease per step while guaranteeing convergence and reducing total processing time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The original Hopfield network uses asynchronous (sequential) updates—one neuron at a time—which is slow. The authors aim to accelerate processing by enabling synchronous updates of multiple neurons simultaneously, while ensuring convergence and maximizing energy reduction at each step.

Method: The authors introduce the Discrete Differential Filter (DDF), a new tool that solves the combinatorial optimization problem of selecting which subset of neurons to update synchronously to achieve maximal energy decrease while guaranteeing convergence. Based on DDF, they develop SD-DDF (Synchronous Dynamics based upon Discrete Differential Filter). The paper provides theoretical justification and four computational experiments to empirically measure speedup.
