Result: Empirical results from four computational experiments demonstrate that SD-DDF achieves significant speedup in processing time compared to the original asynchronous Hopfield dynamics, while maintaining convergence guarantees.

Conclusion: The proposed DDF tool and SD-DDF synchronous dynamics successfully reduce processing time in Hopfield networks by enabling convergent, multi-neuron simultaneous updates that maximize per-step energy decrease.

Abstract: The dynamics of the original Hopfield network is asynchronous (sequential) (updates the state of only one neuron per time step). In this paper, we propose a new tool and a new dynamics to reduce the processing time by updating one or more neurons simultaneously per instant while ensuring process convergence and aiming for the maximum energy decrease at each step, thus guaranteeing the shortest total processing time. From the point of view of synchronous dynamics, calculating the next network state at which energy decreases the most from the current state while ensuring convergence is itself a combinatorial optimization problem. We develop and use a new tool to solve it. We call this new tool Discrete Differential Filter (DDF) and, based upon it, we develop a new synchronous dynamics which we call SD-DDF (Synchronous Dynamics based upon Discrete Differential Filter). In this paper, we review the original asynchronous dynamics for Hopfield networks and present a new tool and a new synchronous dynamics with its theoretical justification and four computational experiments to assess the speed up in processing time empirically.

</details>


### [135] [Baikal: Structured Search for Deep Research over Data Lakes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27726)
*Dhruv Agarwal,Rishitha Guttapalle Mohan,Aarti Kumari,Ashi Sinha,Athulya Anil,Kavitha Srinivas,Horst Samulowitz,Andrew McCallum*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Baikal frames deep research over data lakes as a budgeted search problem, clustering heterogeneous evidence into semantic regions and using adaptive search policies (e.g., UCB, ε-greedy) to balance exploration and exploitation, achieving 28–36% improvement over strong baselines on HybridQA and TAT-QA benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing iterative retrieval-and-generation methods for LLM-based research agents tend to overexploit locally promising evidence, failing to cover distinct semantic regions within a fixed subquestion budget. This leads to narrow, biased reports lacking diversity and groundedness.

Method: Baikal casts deep research as budgeted search: it first clusters heterogeneous evidence (tables and passages) into semantic regions, then generates region-grounded subquestions. Finding quality serves as reward to update region-level value estimates. Search proceeds under multiple policies — random, LLM-guided, Bayesian ε-greedy, and UCB — to balance exploration and exploitation across regions.

Result: Evaluated on 15 queries each over HybridQA (10,993 tables, 227K Wikipedia passages) and TAT-QA (2,757 tables, 13K financial passages), Baikal's best configuration improves report scores by 28% on HybridQA and 36% on TAT-QA over the strongest baselines (DeepSearcher, OpenCode research agent). Gains are attributed to improved groundedness, diversity, and utility under the same subquestion budget.

Conclusion: Structured semantic exploration via region clustering and adaptive search policies significantly improves systematic research and discovery over heterogeneous data lakes, demonstrating clear value over unguided iterative retrieval approaches.

Abstract: Deep research over data lakes requires an LLM agent to investigate evidence across thousands of heterogeneous tables and passages to synthesize a report. Existing methods perform iterative retrieval and generation, letting accumulated context determine what to investigate next, which can overexploit locally promising evidence and fail to cover distinct semantic regions under a fixed budget. To address this, we cast deep research over data lakes as a budgeted search problem and present Baikal - a framework that clusters heterogeneous evidence into semantic regions, then searches over them adaptively to balance exploration and exploitation. Within each selected region, Baikal generates and investigates region-grounded subquestions, using finding quality as rewards to update region-level value estimates and guide search under policies ranging from random and LLM-guided selection to Bayesian $ε$-greedy and UCB. We evaluate Baikal on 15 queries each over HybridQA and TAT-QA data lakes containing 10,993 and 2,757 tables, respectively, together with 227K Wikipedia passages and 13K financial report passages. We assess research quality with a new rubric covering groundedness, relevance, diversity, and utility, and use GPT-5-mini to score Baikal and strong baselines, including DeepSearcher and an OpenCode research agent with retrieval and clustering variants. Across both data lakes, Baikal performs strongly under several region-selection policies; its best configuration improves report scores over the strongest baselines by 28% on HybridQA and 36% on TAT-QA. Our analyses attribute these gains to organizing and exploring semantic evidence regions, which improves groundedness and diversity and yields more useful findings under the same subquestion budget. These results demonstrate the value of structured semantic exploration for systematic research and discovery over heterogeneous data lakes.

</details>


### [136] [VeriSkill: A Self-Evolution Framework for Program Verification Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27733)
*Changguo Jia,Tianqi Zhao,Zhiyou Xiao,Weiming Zhang,Minghui Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VeriSkill is a self-evolution framework for program verification that attributes failures to skill deficiencies, distills diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, and iteratively refines skills while preserving semantics, outperforming baselines across tools, agents, and LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Program verification with LLM agents requires generating specifications, annotations, lemmas, and tool invocations—all dependent on reusable skills. Existing skill self-evolution methods fail because they cannot reliably identify which specific skill caused a failure or extract actionable signals from opaque verifier feedback.

Method: VeriSkill introduces a three-part framework: (1) failure attribution that maps verification failures to specific skill deficiencies, (2) distillation of diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, and (3) iterative refinement of candidate skills with a strict acceptance criterion—only revisions that improve verification performance while preserving program semantics are admitted.

Result: VeriSkill consistently outperforms all baselines across multiple verification tools, agent frameworks, and LLM backends.

Conclusion: Targeted skill attribution combined with semantics-preserving refinement is key to effective self-evolution for program verification, and VeriSkill provides a robust framework that generalizes across diverse toolchains and model backends.

Abstract: Automating program verification with LLM agents requires generating specifications, annotations, auxiliary lemmas, and tool invocations, all of which depend on reusable skills. A natural remedy is skill self-evolution: distilling skills from trajectories and refining them through feedback. However, existing evolution methods struggle with program verification tasks because they cannot reliably identify skill-specific failures or extract actionable signals from opaque verifier feedback. In this paper, we propose VeriSkill, a self-evolution framework built for program verification. It attributes verification failures to skill deficiencies, distills diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, and iteratively refines candidate skills, admitting only revisions that improve verification performance while preserving program semantics. Experiments show that VeriSkill consistently outperforms all baselines across multiple verification tools, agent frameworks, and LLM backends.

</details>


### [137] [SpecCal: Ambiguity-Aware Candidate Calibration for Infrared Spectrum-Based Molecular Structure Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27788)
*Yixuan Chen,Bo Liu,Yusen Tan,Guokun Yang,Wenjie Du,Jun Xia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SpecCal is a training-free, plug-and-play framework that re-ranks and augments candidate molecules from existing IR-to-molecule models by enforcing spectral consistency, improving top-k reconstruction accuracy without requiring any parameter updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: IR spectra provide limited structural information because different molecules with similar functional groups can produce highly similar spectra. Existing models generate ranked candidate sets based on learned preferences rather than spectral constraints, failing to fully capture all structurally plausible molecules consistent with the observed spectrum.

Method: SpecCal takes candidate outputs from any base IR-to-molecule model, re-ranks them, and introduces additional structurally plausible alternatives guided by spectral consistency. It is training-free and model-agnostic, requiring no parameter updates.

Result: SpecCal consistently improves top-k reconstruction at both SMILES and scaffold levels across multiple benchmarks and diverse base models.

Conclusion: Calibrating candidate sets under spectral ambiguity via SpecCal offers a practical, generalizable approach to improving molecular reconstruction from IR spectra without retraining underlying models.

Abstract: Inferring molecular structures from infrared (IR) spectra is a fundamental yet challenging problem. A key difficulty is that an IR spectrum provides limited structural information: different molecules may share similar functional groups and local vibrational patterns, leading to highly similar spectral responses. Thus, even when an observed spectrum has a unique underlying structure, reconstructing it from the spectrum remains ambiguous. Existing IR-to-molecule models usually generate a ranked set of candidate molecules, but this set is largely determined by the model's learned generation preference and may not fully capture the structures that best satisfy the observed spectral constraints. To address this limitation, we propose SpecCal, a training-free candidate calibration framework for IR-to-molecule prediction. SpecCal operates on the candidate outputs of existing base models and improves the prediction set by re-ranking current candidates while introducing additional structurally plausible alternatives guided by spectral consistency. The framework is plug-and-play and model-agnostic, requiring no parameter updates for integration with diverse base models. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that SpecCal consistently improves top-k reconstruction at both SMILES and scaffold levels across different base models. Further analyses demonstrate that calibrating candidate sets under spectral ambiguity provides a practical way to improve molecular reconstruction from IR spectra. The code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SpecCal-B18A.

</details>


### [138] [Annotating Topical Legal Insights from Case Proceedings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27792)
*Subinay Adhikary,Dwaipayan Roy,Debasis Ganguly,Shouvik Kumar Guha,Kripabandhu Ghosh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LeDA is a web-based annotation system for legal documents that enables dynamic, on-the-fly creation of annotation tags without a predefined ontology, facilitating the discovery of concepts/topics from legal case proceedings for downstream tasks like case retrieval and judgment prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Structured representations of legal documents (as "bags of concepts") outperform flat bag-of-words representations for downstream legal NLP tasks. However, pre-defined ontologies for legal concepts are often unavailable, necessitating a system that allows annotators to discover and define concepts dynamically as they examine documents.

Method: The authors propose LeDA (Legal Data Annotation), a web-based annotation system whose key novelty is dynamic tag creation — annotators can create new annotation labels on-the-fly rather than being constrained to a fixed ontology. The system supports both annotation and adjudication of entities/concepts. It was deployed with 3 assessors to annotate legal concepts from Indian Supreme Court case proceedings.

Result: LeDA was successfully used by 3 assessors to annotate and adjudicate legal concept names from Indian Supreme Court proceedings, producing bags-of-concepts representations suitable for downstream tasks such as prior case retrieval and judgment prediction.

Conclusion: LeDA effectively addresses the gap in legal document annotation where pre-defined ontologies are lacking, enabling iterative concept discovery. The resulting structured semantic representations can enhance various legal NLP applications.

Abstract: In this paper, we mainly concentrate on finding concepts or topics from the legal case proceedings, since adopting a structured representation for legal documents, as opposed to a mere bag-of-words flat text representation, can significantly enhance processing capabilities. To achieve this objective, we put forward a set of diverse concepts for legal case proceedings. With this motivation, we propose LeDA, a system for Legal Data Annotation. The system offers the generic functionality of annotating and adjudicating entities or concepts within documents via a web-based interface. A novel feature of our system is that it allows to dynamic create new tags for annotation, which is a particularly useful provision for situations where there exists no pre-defined ontology for the entities (concepts) that need to be annotated - these being rather discovered by annotators as they continue examining more documents. The system that we demonstrate is currently in use to annotate a set of concepts from legal documents to construct semantic representations of documents as bags of concepts that can then be used for several downstream tasks, such as prior case retrieval, judgment prediction, and so on. Along with the system features in general, we also describe how LeDA was used by 3 assessors to annotate and adjudicate legal concept names from Indian Supreme Court case proceedings.

</details>


### [139] [MemeBench: What LVLMs Miss When Interpreting Culture-Dependent Memes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27798)
*Weihang Wang,Kainan Tu,Jielei Zhang,Run Yang,Boheng Sheng,Yuchen He,Yu Xie,Pengyu Chen,Peiyi Li,Huyang Sun,Longwen Gao,Zhouhui Lian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemeBench introduces a diagnostic benchmark of 1,253 Chinese and English memes using the VIKR schema (Visual, Identity, Knowledge, Reasoning) to pinpoint where LVLMs fail in meme interpretation. It reveals a persistent Visual-Knowledge gap (22.6% in the best model) and demonstrates that entity-guided retrieval (KAR) partially repairs Knowledge gaps at the cost of Visual coverage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LVLMs accurately describe visual content but fail at interpretation when meaning depends on cultural entities, background knowledge, and community conventions. Existing meme benchmarks reduce evaluation to holistic scores or labels, obscuring where and why explanations break down. The authors aim to diagnose specific failure modes along a structured decomposition of the interpretation process.

Method: The authors construct MemeBench (1,253 Chinese/English memes from ACG subcultures) with human-written reference explanations annotated under the VIKR schema: Visual clues, Identity links (named entities), Knowledge units (cultural facts), and Reasoning mechanisms. They evaluate 26 LVLMs by scoring each VIKR dimension independently to quantify coverage and gaps. They then introduce KAR, an entity-guided retrieval baseline using CultureBase, and test it against generic retrieval across four controlled models to assess whether targeted evidence can repair diagnosed gaps.

Result: All 26 LVLMs cover Visual clues more reliably than Knowledge units, with the strongest model showing a 22.6% Visual-Knowledge gap. The KAR retrieval baseline improves VIKR Success by 3.6–7.4% over baselines across four models. Both KAR and generic retrieval improve Identity and Knowledge scores but consistently reduce Visual coverage. KAR repairs more answers and breaks fewer than generic retrieval.

Conclusion: MemeBench provides fine-grained, diagnostic evaluation showing that LVLMs' core deficiency in meme interpretation is knowledge, not vision. Targeted entity-guided retrieval can partially close this gap, but trade-offs exist — retrieval improves knowledge dimensions at the expense of visual grounding. The VIKR framework enables precise diagnosis of interpretation failures and measurement of whether interventions address the right gaps.

Abstract: Large vision-language models have improved at describing visual content, but accurate descriptions do not ensure interpretation when meaning depends on knowledge beyond the pixels. Memes expose this gap because they rely on cultural entities, background knowledge, and community conventions. Most meme benchmarks reduce interpretation to labels or holistic scores, obscuring where an explanation breaks down. We introduce MemeBench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,253 Chinese and English memes with human-written references and quality-controlled VIKR annotations, centered on anime, comics, games, and adjacent online subcultures. Its VIKR schema decomposes explanations into Visual clues, Identity links, Knowledge units, and Reasoning mechanisms. Across 26 LVLMs, every model covers visible content more reliably than the knowledge needed to interpret it, and even the strongest retains a 22.6% Visual-Knowledge gap. To test whether this diagnosis can guide improvement, we introduce KAR, an entity-guided retrieval baseline built on CultureBase. Across four controlled models, KAR raises VIKR Success by 3.6-7.4% and, compared with generic retrieval, repairs more answers and breaks fewer. Yet both retrieval conditions improve Identity and Knowledge while reducing Visual coverage in every comparison. MemeBench reveals whether an interpretation succeeds, what is missing, and whether targeted evidence fills the diagnosed gap.

</details>


### [140] [STEREODISCO: Discovering Stereotypicality in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27824)
*Farane Jalali Farahani,Corina Dima,Mojtaba Nayyeri,Raphael H. Heiberger,Steffen Staab*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: STEREODISCO adapts the semantic differential method to systematically discover stereotypical axes in LLM internal representations by probing ~2,000 WordNet-derived antonym axes; applying it to LLAMA-3-8B and MISTRAL-7B reveals novel stereotypical dimensions and shows LLMs agree more with each other than with human social psychology findings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior computational stereotype research is limited to a small set of pre-defined semantic axes from social psychology and relies on static word embeddings, leaving two gaps: (1) which other semantic axes carry stereotypical associations in LLMs, and (2) how such axes are internally represented in modern LLM activation spaces.

Method: The STEREODISCO framework has three stages: (1) construct ~2,000 candidate semantic axes from WordNet antonym synsets; (2) recover each axis geometrically in the LLM's activation space using probing classifiers trained on antonym word pairs; (3) identify stereotypical axes by statistically testing whether social group concept projections along an axis deviate significantly from a null distribution, indicating systematic stereotyping.

Result: Applied to LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT and MISTRAL-7B-INSTRUCT: (a) the two LLMs agree more with each other on social group ratings than with human judgments from social psychology, suggesting LLM-encoded stereotypes diverge from human-documented ones; (b) novel stereotypical axes were discovered, including humble vs. proud, narrow-minded vs. broad-minded, and cowardly vs. brave, which were independently validated by human annotators.

Conclusion: STEREODISCO enables large-scale, systematic discovery of stereotypical axes in LLM representations, revealing that LLM stereotypes both overlap with and diverge from human social psychology findings. The framework opens the door to more comprehensive stereotype auditing beyond pre-defined axis sets.

Abstract: LLMs encode, convey, and perpetuate stereotypes. Prior computational research focuses on a small set of semantic axes investigated in social psychology, and operates on word embeddings produced by language models, leaving open which other semantic axes carry stereotypical associations in LLMs and how LLMs internally represent such axes. We introduce STEREODISCO, a framework that adapts the semantic differential method (Osgood et al., 1957) to the systematic study of stereotypes in LLM internal representations. STEREODISCO constructs approx. 2,000 candidate semantic axes from WordNet antonym synsets, recovers each as a geometric axis in the LLM's activation space via probing, and identifies stereotypical axes via a statistical test over concept projections. As a case study, we apply STEREODISCO to social group stereotypes with LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT and MISTRAL-7B-INSTRUCT. We find that the two LLMs agree with each other on social group ratings more than with humans, suggesting that LLM-encoded stereotype content diverges from that documented in social psychology. We also discover stereotypical axes not investigated in prior work -- including humble vs. proud, narrow-minded vs. broad-minded, and cowardly vs. brave, which human annotators independently confirm.

</details>


### [141] [Sign Language Question Answering: A New Task, Benchmark, and Baseline for Sign Language Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27826)
*Shiwei Gan,Lichen Wang,Xiao Liu,Yafeng Yin,Kuizhuang Liu,Sanglu Lu,Lei Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Sign Language Question Answering (SLQA), a new task for evaluating sign language understanding through natural language questions. The authors construct two benchmarks (SignQA) from PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily with five question categories, and propose a baseline model featuring Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling and in-domain knowledge transfer, outperforming existing vision-language models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing sign language understanding tasks (continuous SL recognition and SL translation) are limited by their predefined objectives, requiring fixed mappings from sign videos to glosses or sentences. This provides only a narrow assessment of semantic comprehension. The authors argue that answering arbitrary natural language questions about SL videos offers a more flexible and comprehensive evaluation of true SL understanding, encompassing multiple reasoning capabilities beyond mere recognition and translation.

Method: The authors propose three key contributions: (1) A new SLQA task formulation where models answer natural language questions about sign language videos. (2) Two SignQA benchmarks built from PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily by automatically generating QA pairs from gloss and sentence annotations using designed templates, yielding five categories: position reasoning, structural reasoning, visual search, gloss recognition, and translation understanding. (3) A baseline model with a Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling module and an in-domain knowledge transfer strategy that leverages existing SLU tasks to improve question-aware temporal feature modeling.

Result: The proposed baseline consistently outperforms representative vision-language models across all five question categories on both benchmarks, establishing a strong reference point for future SLQA research.

Conclusion: SLQA provides a more comprehensive and flexible framework for evaluating sign language understanding. The SignQA benchmarks and the proposed baseline model lay a solid foundation for advancing research in this new direction, with datasets publicly released to facilitate further work.

Abstract: Recent advances in sign language (SL) understanding (SLU) have led to remarkable progress in tasks such as continuous SL recognition and SL translation. However, these tasks are designed with predefined objectives, requiring models to learn a fixed mapping from sign videos to glosses or spoken-language sentences. As a result, they provide only a limited assessment of whether a model truly understands the semantic content of SL videos. To address this limitation, \textbf{we first propose a new task, Sign Language Question Answering (SLQA)}, which evaluates SL understanding by requiring models to answer arbitrary natural language questions about SL videos. Unlike previous SLU tasks, SLQA provides a more flexible and comprehensive evaluation framework that assesses multiple reasoning capabilities beyond recognition and translation. To facilitate this task, \textbf{we further construct two SignQA benchmarks} based on PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily by automatically generating question-answer pairs from existing gloss and sentence annotations using carefully designed templates. The resulting datasets cover five complementary question categories, including position reasoning, structural reasoning, visual search, gloss recognition, and translation understanding. \textbf{Finally, we propose a simple yet effective baseline model} equipped with a Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling module and an in-domain knowledge transfer strategy, enabling effective knowledge transfer from existing SLU tasks while enhancing question-aware temporal feature modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our baseline consistently outperforms representative vision-language models across all question categories, establishing a strong benchmark for future research on SLQA. Datasets are available at:{https://huggingface.co/datasets/hulala/SignQA-2026}.

</details>


### [142] [MemTxn: A Transaction Boundary for Source-Supported Updates and Complete-State Recovery in Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27834)
*Hanshuai Cui,Zhiqing Tang,Zhi Yao,Fanshuai Meng,Qianli Ma,Weijia Jia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemTxn is a governance layer for persistent LLM agent memory that provides transaction-like reliability: it validates memory writes against source evidence, resolves conflicting facts with a temporal resolver, and recovers state after faults using a durable snapshot journal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Persistent memory in LLM agents enables reuse across sessions, but erroneous writes can persist and corrupt future behavior. Existing systems focus on storage/retrieval without providing transaction boundaries for reliable updates and recovery.

Method: MemTxn operates as a governance layer outside the answer model with three core mechanisms: (1) Ordered PatchTest to validate whether writes are supported by their source, (2) a Temporal Resolver to select the visible version when facts conflict, and (3) a durable snapshot journal to recover application-visible state after faults.

Result: On an item-disjoint audit, MemTxn accepts all 60 supported originals and rejects all 179 hard negatives. Under persistent multi-key faults on LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo, it restores the complete declared active map without knowing the physical write set. On MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation, it achieves the highest average F1 across all 12 answer-model configurations, outperforming Dense by 17.06–24.07 points in five representative settings.

Conclusion: MemTxn demonstrates that adding a transactional governance layer outside the answer model effectively ensures memory reliability in persistent LLM agents, combining write validation, conflict resolution, and fault recovery into a unified framework.

Abstract: Persistent memory lets long-running large language model agents reuse information across sessions and tasks. Yet errors in writable memory can persist and corrupt future behavior. Existing systems improve storage and retrieval, but they do not provide a transaction boundary for reliable updates and recovery. We therefore propose MemTxn, a governance layer outside the answer model. MemTxn verifies whether an update is supported by its source. It also selects the visible version when facts conflict and restores the application-visible state after a fault. The system uses Ordered PatchTest to validate writes, a Temporal Resolver to select versions, and a durable snapshot journal to recover state. On an item-disjoint audit, MemTxn accepts all 60 supported originals and rejects all 179 hard negatives. Under persistent multi-key faults on LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo states, it restores the complete declared active map without knowing the actual physical write set. On MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation, MemTxn achieves the highest average F1 across all twelve answer-model configurations. It outperforms Dense by 17.06--24.07 points in five representative settings.

</details>


### [143] [Crossing the Margin Cliff: Toward Relearn-Robust LLM Unlearning via Margin Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27836)
*Xiangyu Yin,Jiaxu Liu,Zhen Chen,Chih-Hong Cheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM unlearning methods universally fail under relearn attacks (finetuning on 20 forget examples recovers held-out performance). The authors identify a "margin cliff"—a geometric regularity where forget and retain per-token margins collapse into a narrow band. They propose Margin Calibration (MC), a plug-in polish using a non-saturating margin hinge + KL probe that restores forget-side pressure, achieving state-of-the-art robustness across TOFU, MUSE-News, and Phi-3.5 benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior LLM unlearning methods appear effective in isolation but are consistently fragile under relearn attacks—fine-tuning on just 20 forget examples substantially recovers supposedly "unlearned" knowledge. This fragility is poorly understood, and no existing method provides principled defense. The authors aim to (1) diagnose the geometric cause of this fragility and (2) develop a robust solution.

Method: First, the authors conduct an empirical diagnosis of 14 post-hoc unlearning methods (gradient-based, preference-based, distillation-based) on TOFU, revealing the "margin cliff": per-token answer margins for forget and retain converge into a narrow band above the retain reference. They prove this cliff arises when the retain coupling holds diagnostic log-odds of forget content above a floor—a condition induced by token-saturating losses at stationarity. Second, they propose Margin Calibration (MC): a plug-in polish adding (a) a non-saturating margin hinge loss anchored at the reference model's per-token margin, and (b) a KL divergence probe on a disjoint instruction corpus. This restores gradient pressure on forget-side tokens where native losses saturate. Under a gradient-dominance condition (verified by instrumenting the polish's on-trajectory gradient signature), the stationary set lies on the cliff-crossing side, yielding an upper bound on relearn margin lift.

Result: Across TOFU (3 Llama-3 sizes, 3 forget tiers), MUSE-News on Llama-2-7B-hf, and a Phi-3.5 panel, a single frozen MC configuration wins all 14 head-to-head forget aggregates and all populated relearn cells. Panel-mean post-attack ROUGE-L drops from 0.41 (unpolished) to 0.18 (MC). MC also lowers membership inference AUC on 13/14 methods. The primary cost is reduced retain-side utility. A deployment variant achieves comparable gains without a retain-trained reference model.

Conclusion: LLM unlearning fragility under relearn attacks is a systematic geometric phenomenon (the margin cliff) caused by token-saturating losses. Margin Calibration provides a principled, plug-and-play solution that substantially hardens unlearning against relearn attacks while maintaining practical deployability.

Abstract: Large language model unlearning is consistently fragile under relearn attacks. On TOFU, fine-tuning on twenty forget examples substantially recovers held-out forget-set ROUGE for every method we evaluate, and we trace this fragility to optimization geometry. The per-token answer margin of fourteen post-hoc methods spanning gradient, preference, and distillation families converges into a narrow band above the retain reference in 41 of 42 method--size cells, a regularity we call the margin cliff. We prove that this cliff follows whenever the retain coupling holds the diagnostic log-odds of forget content above a floor, a condition that token-saturating losses induce at stationarity and that we verify directly on 34 of 42 cells. Margin Calibration (\textsc{MC}) is a plug-in polish adding a non-saturating margin hinge anchored at the reference's per-token margin plus a KL probe on a disjoint instruction corpus, restoring forget-side pressure where the native loss saturates. Under a stated gradient-dominance condition, whose on-trajectory gradient signature we measure by instrumenting the polish, its stationary set lies on the cliff-crossing side, yielding an attack-budget upper bound on the relearn margin lift. Across TOFU (three Llama-3 sizes, three forget tiers), MUSE-News on Llama-2-7B-hf, and a Phi-3.5 panel, a single frozen configuration wins all 14 head-to-head forget aggregates and all populated relearn cells (panel-mean post-attack ROUGE-L $0.41$ to $0.18$) and lowers raw membership AUC on 13/14, with reduced retain-side utility as the main cost. A deployment variant matches these gains without a retain-trained reference.

</details>


### [144] [Virtual Process Dossier: A Process-Aware Data Catalogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27840)
*Lukas Kubelka,Alexander Bott,Frank Döhner,Saksham Kiroriwal,Georg Zeeb,Julia Butte,Julius Pfrommer,Jürgen Beyerer,Tobias Käfer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The Virtual Process Dossier (VPD) is a Knowledge Graph-based data catalogue that captures workflow provenance for multi-stage manufacturing, enabling FAIR dataset access and AI-driven optimization by distinguishing data from individual workflow steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multi-stage manufacturing, downstream AI-based optimization tasks require the ability to distinguish between datasets generated during individual workflow steps. Existing data catalogues lack explicit capture of both prospective and retrospective workflow provenance, hindering FAIR data access and effective AI downstream use.

Method: The authors propose the Virtual Process Dossier (VPD), comprising three components: (1) the VPD ontology as the semantic core of the catalogue; (2) a provenance framework that integrates ontology instantiation directly into the production environment to capture both prospective and retrospective provenance; and (3) a human-centered user interface for interacting with the VPD Knowledge Graph.

Result: The paper delivers a complete system: a semantic ontology for modelling manufacturing workflows and their data products, a provenance framework for automated ontology instantiation within production environments, and a UI for human interaction. The ontology and code are publicly released on GitHub.

Conclusion: VPD successfully provides a FAIR, provenance-aware data catalogue tailored for multi-stage manufacturing, enabling AI-based optimization tasks to reliably distinguish and consume workflow-specific datasets. The open-source release facilitates adoption and further research.

Abstract: We propose the Virtual Process Dossier (VPD), a Knowledge Graph-based data catalogue that also captures workflow provenance. We developed VPD for multi-stage manufacturing use-cases where downstream AI-based optimization tasks require to distinct between datasets generated during individual workflow steps. VPD provides these datasets in a FAIR manner and makes both prospective and retrospective workflow provenance explicit. Our contributions are: (1) the VPD ontology that serves as the catalogue's semantic core; (2) the VPD provenance framework that integrates ontology instantiation into the production environment; and (3) the VPD user interface that provides human-centered interaction with the VPD Knowledge Graph. The ontology and code are available at https://github.com/kubeluk/VirtualProcessDossier .

</details>


### [145] [Simplifying Neural Networks During Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27854)
*Lorenzo Sciandra,Samuele Fonio,Roberto Esposito*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a Neural Collapse (NC)-inspired training framework that monitors representation dynamics via the Inverse Fisher Criterion to identify when and where a deep network can be simplified — replacing trailing layers with a lightweight classification head — achieving substantial parameter reduction while maintaining accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep overparameterized networks are costly to train and deploy. Two empirical phenomena — Neural Collapse (structured geometry of final-layer representations and classifiers) and the Tunnel Effect (only a subset of layers is essential for feature extraction) — suggest that significant parts of deep networks may be redundant. The authors aim to unify these perspectives into a principled, dynamics-aware method for network simplification during training.

Method: The authors propose an NC-inspired training framework that monitors layer-wise representation dynamics using the Inverse Fisher Criterion (IFC), a stable proxy for variability collapse. During training, IFC trajectories are tracked to determine (1) the split point between feature extraction layers and classification layers, and (2) the training stage at which simplification is viable. Once these are identified, the trailing layers are replaced with a lightweight classification head, and training continues on the reduced model.

Result: Experiments on image-classification benchmarks across MLP, VGG, and ResNet architectures demonstrate that the proposed method achieves substantial parameter reductions while maintaining accuracy comparable to the full model.

Conclusion: Monitoring Neural Collapse dynamics via the Inverse Fisher Criterion provides an effective, principled signal for simplifying deep networks during training, offering a practical approach to reducing model complexity without sacrificing performance.

Abstract: Understanding and exploiting the training dynamics of overparameterized deep neural networks remains a central challenge in modern machine learning. Recent evidence on Neural Collapse (NC) shows that class representations and classifiers exhibit highly structured geometry, while the Tunnel Effect suggests that only a subset of layers is essential for feature extraction. We combine these two perspectives and propose an NC-inspired training framework for simplifying deep networks during training. Our method monitors representation dynamics through the Inverse Fisher Criterion, a stable and efficient proxy for the variability collapse behavior, to identify both the split point between feature extraction and classification and the training stage at which simplification becomes viable. We then replace the trailing layers with a lightweight classification head and continue training the reduced model. Experiments on image-classification benchmarks across MLP, VGG, and ResNet architectures show that the proposed method achieves substantial parameter reductions while maintaining accuracy comparable to that of the full model. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at: https://github.com/LorenzoSciandra/NNS.

</details>


### [146] [Back to All-Entity Ranking: Sampler-Dependent Evaluation in Continuous-Time Dynamic Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27861)
*Minwoo Yu,Young-guk Ha*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Using sampled negatives in CTDG next-destination prediction benchmarks introduces dependencies on the negative distribution and candidate-set size, altering model rankings and ablation conclusions. The authors recommend all-entity ranking against a fixed catalog to eliminate this variability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard evaluation in CTDG next-destination prediction uses sampled negative destinations, making results conditional on both the sampling distribution and the number of negatives chosen. The paper systematically investigates how this conditioning distorts model comparisons and module-ablation conclusions.

Method: The authors conduct a factorial evaluation crossing repeated vs. new positives with seen vs. unseen negatives across six models on four datasets (LastFM, MOOC, Reddit, Wikipedia). They use a minimal scorer based solely on pair-history membership and controlled representation interventions to isolate how time-varying source-destination history and model operations transmit sampler influence to evaluation scores.

Result: On three of four datasets, at least one model pair changes relative order between the expected Uniform-20 metric and the full catalog. The measured effect of the same module changes in both magnitude and direction with candidate-set size and training objective.

Conclusion: Model-superiority and ablation conclusions from sampled-negative benchmarks are conditional on the candidate configuration. All-entity ranking against a fixed, enumerable destination catalog removes negative-selection freedom and sampling variation, and should serve as the primary evidence for architecture comparisons on CTDG benchmarks.

Abstract: Next-destination prediction in continuous-time dynamic graphs (CTDGs) commonly ranks an observed interaction against sampled negative destinations. The resulting score is conditional on both the negative distribution and the number of candidates chosen by the researcher. We show that a non-uniform negative distribution changes the Bayes-optimal ranking, while even a finite candidate set drawn uniformly can destabilize model rankings and measured module effects.
  Time-varying source-destination history membership and model operations that use this information directly transmit the sampler's influence to the evaluation score. We examine this mechanism using a factorial evaluation of repeated and new positives against seen and unseen negatives, a minimal scorer based solely on pair-history membership, and controlled representation interventions. Across six models on LastFM, MOOC, Reddit, and Wikipedia, at least one model pair changes relative order between the expected Uniform-20 metric and the full catalog on three of the four datasets. The measured effect of the same module also changes in magnitude and direction with the candidate-set size and training objective.
  These results establish that model-superiority and ablation conclusions from sampled-negative benchmarks are conditional on the stated candidate configuration. All-entity ranking evaluates every destination in a fixed catalog, eliminating negative-selection freedom and sampling variation while retaining the original CTDG scorer. We therefore recommend all-entity ranking as the primary evidence for architecture comparisons on CTDG benchmarks with an enumerable, fixed destination catalog.

</details>


### [147] [Orca: Neural Operators for Causal Reasoning in Continuous Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27867)
*Gerrit Großmann,David A. Selby,Sebastian J. Vollmer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Orca is a framework that combines structural causal models with neural operator learning to enable causal reasoning—including interventions and counterfactuals—over continuous-time systems with irregular observations and feedback loops.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional structural causal models (SCMs) assume static variables measured once and typically forbid cycles. However, real-world systems (patients, climates, economies) evolve continuously, are sampled at irregular intervals, and contain feedback loops. Existing causal frameworks lack the mathematical machinery to handle functions of time as nodes and mechanisms that map between function spaces.

Method: Orca models each node in a causal graph as a function of time, with each causal mechanism implemented as a learned neural operator—a map between function spaces. The architecture extends neural operators to: (1) take multiple parent functions as input, (2) respect the arrow of time (causality in time), and (3) treat latent exogenous noise as an inferred function that can be reused for counterfactual reasoning. The framework is formalized as a model class combining continuous-time dynamics with structural causal semantics.

Result: The paper demonstrates counterfactual reasoning on synthetic continuous-time examples, showing that Orca can successfully perform interventions and answer counterfactual queries in temporally evolving systems.

Conclusion: Neural operator learning provides a natural and principled foundation for extending causal reasoning to continuous-time settings. Orca opens the door to causal inference in dynamical systems observed at irregular intervals with feedback, with code publicly released.

Abstract: Structural causal models are the standard language for reasoning about interventions and counterfactuals, but they describe static variables, typically measured once, and usually forbid cyclic dependencies. Many systems we care about, such as patients, climates, and economies, instead evolve continuously in time, are observed at irregular time points, and contain feedback loops. We argue that neural operator learning provides a natural foundation for causal reasoning in this setting, and propose Orca, a framework in which each node of the causal graph is a function of time and each mechanism is a learned map between function spaces. We extend existing neural operator architectures to express causal mechanisms: a mechanism computes the function value of a node from its parent nodes by taking several parent functions as input, respects the arrow of time, and treats latent exogenous noise as a function that can be inferred and reused for counterfactuals. We formalize the model class and demonstrate counterfactual reasoning on synthetic continuous-time examples. Code is available at https://github.com/gerritgr/orca

</details>


### [148] [Search as Computation Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27871)
*Alexander Tuisov*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper formalizes costly computation as a terminal computation-allocation problem, derives Bellman equations for optimal allocation, relates value of computation (VOC) to information-theoretic quantities, and shows that maximizing approximate VOC recovers classical search algorithms like weighted A*.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many algorithms expend internal resources (e.g., simulations, node expansions, bandit pulls) before producing a final decision, yet are typically evaluated only on terminal output quality. The authors aim to unify these disparate procedures under a common decision-theoretic framework.

Method: The authors formalize terminal computation-allocation problems: costly computations generate observations that update beliefs about a latent environment, with utility determined solely by terminal decision loss. They derive Bellman equations characterizing optimal allocation policies under three regimes (fixed budget, priced computation, exact certification). They then analytically relate VOC to mutual information (myopic under log loss), knowledge-gradient quantities (under simple regret), and show information gain provides only a one-sided bound. The framework is illustrated across bandit pulls, tree simulations, and node expansions with different computation topologies. Finally, under a frontier-resolution and heuristic-error model, maximizing approximate VOC is shown to recover weighted A*, with A* and greedy best-first search as limiting cases.

Result: (1) Mutual information equals myopic VOC under log loss; (2) under simple regret, VOC corresponds to a knowledge-gradient quantity; (3) information gain can arbitrarily misrank computations but provides a one-sided upper bound on VOC; (4) maximizing approximate VOC recovers weighted A*, A*, and greedy best-first search under an explicit frontier-resolution model; (5) the framework unifies bandit, tree search, and node expansion settings without claiming universal optimality of any single acquisition rule.

Conclusion: The paper identifies a shared decision problem underlying diverse computation-allocation settings. Rather than asserting one universally optimal acquisition rule, it provides a coherent theory that situates existing algorithms as special cases of approximate VOC maximization, thereby clarifying their implicit assumptions and trade-offs.

Abstract: Many algorithms spend an internal resource before returning a decision and are evaluated only by the quality of that terminal output. We formalize such procedures as terminal computation-allocation problems: costly computations produce observations, update beliefs about a latent environment, and matter only through terminal decision loss. Bellman equations characterize optimal allocation under fixed budgets, priced computation, and exact certification. We then relate value of computation (VOC) to information. Mutual information equals myopic VOC under log loss, whereas under simple regret VOC is a knowledge-gradient quantity; moreover, information gain can rank computations arbitrarily poorly, although it gives a one-sided upper bound on VOC. Bandit pulls, tree simulations, and node expansions illustrate the same model under different computation topologies. Finally, under an explicit frontier-resolution and heuristic-error model, maximizing approximate VOC recovers weighted A*, with A* and greedy best-first search as limiting cases. The theory identifies a shared decision problem without asserting that one acquisition rule is universally optimal.

</details>


### [149] [An Empirical Study of Coordination Mode as the First-Class Citizen in From-Scratch Multi-Agent Coding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27877)
*Yanyu Ren,Yunfeng Bai,Xizheng Wang,Li Chen,Dan Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MSEval is a new benchmark for multi-agent coding that uses real-world full-stack projects, measures functional success alongside latency and token cost, and reveals that organizational topology rivals model capability in determining speed-cost-quality trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-agent coding benchmarks suffer from three critical flaws: they rely on synthetic environments, ignore practical time and monetary costs, conflate reasoning with communication, and reward superficial completion. There is a need for a rigorous, reproducible standard that evaluates how multi-agent teams actually build software under real-world constraints.

Method: MSEval is grounded in 10 authentic full-stack projects across 10 domains, scored via hierarchical requirements and deterministic rubrics. Its execution engine, LegoGent, tests 10 collaboration topologies where agents coordinate through periodic sync intervals and deploy via native CI/CD pipelines. The automated grader TAgent dynamically probes implementations to jointly measure functional success, latency, and prefix-cached token cost. 100 runs were conducted.

Result: Organizational topology rivals model capability in shaping the speed-cost-quality trade-off. For identical tasks and models, varying topology shifts scores by over 30 points and doubles wall-clock time. Structured pipelines converge fastest with highest quality, while heavy managerial oversight degrades performance.

Conclusion: MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for measuring how multi-agent teams actually build software, demonstrating that how agents are organized (topology) is as important as which model they use.

Abstract: Multi-agent vibe coding promises to accelerate software development, yet existing benchmarks rely on synthetic environments that ignore practical time and monetary costs, conflate reasoning with communication, and reward only superficial completion. We introduce multi-agent from-scratch evaluation benchmark, MSEval, evaluating multi-agent coding on real-world tasks. Grounded in 10 authentic, full-stack projects across 10 domains, MSEval scores performance using hierarchical requirements and deterministic rubrics.
  Its execution engine, LegoGent, tests 10 collaboration topologies where agents coordinate via periodic sync intervals and deploy through native CI/CD pipelines. Concurrently, the automated grader TAgent dynamically probes implementations to jointly measure functional success, latency, and prefix-cached token cost. Across 100 runs, MSEval reveals that organizational topology rivals model capability in shaping the speed--cost--quality trade-off. For identical tasks and models, varying the topology shifts scores by over 30 points and doubles wall-clock time. Structured pipelines converge fastest with the highest quality, whereas heavy managerial oversight degrades performance. Ultimately, MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for measuring how multi-agent teams actually build software. The benchmark is released at https://github.com/robinren03/MSEval.

</details>


### [150] [Not All Tokens Deserve Equal Credit: Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation for Long-CoT Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27888)
*Qiangqiang He,Zhongheng Wu,ZiJian Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper analyzes on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) for RLVR, finding that privileged teacher signals produce unreliable answer-aligned directions and primarily reflect counterfactual sensitivity rather than learning value. The authors propose Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation (CSCR), which downweights credit for highly sensitive tokens within GRPO, and demonstrate consistent improvements on long-CoT math reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Critic-free RLVR methods like GRPO uniformly broadcast response-level rewards across all tokens, ignoring that tokens contribute unequally to outcomes. OPSD attempts to address this via dense token-level supervision from a privileged self-teacher, but the authors question whether the induced likelihood shifts actually encode reliable, answer-aligned information. The goal is to diagnose this premise and develop a better credit assignment strategy.

Method: The authors first conduct a diagnostic experiment: they fix each sampled trajectory and re-score it under two opposing outcome conditions (correctness vs. incorrectness), then analyze token-level shift directions. They find that most tokens shift in the same direction regardless of outcome, with few sign reversals and substantial overlap. Large shifts concentrate on substitutable surface-form tokens, while reasoning-critical tokens are less sensitive. Based on this, they propose CSCR, an extension of GRPO that identifies tokens with high counterfactual sensitivity, reduces their credit, and renormalizes token-level advantages to preserve the original credit budget and verifier-determined direction.

Result: CSCR consistently outperforms the GRPO baseline on long-CoT mathematical reasoning benchmarks at matched policy updates. Ablations confirm that privilege-induced directions are unreliable, moderate downweighting of sensitive tokens is most effective, and stronger modulation destabilizes optimization.

Conclusion: Privileged self-distillation signals in OPSD do not provide reliable answer-aligned optimization directions; their magnitudes reflect counterfactual sensitivity rather than token-level learning value. CSCR offers a simple, effective correction by reallocating credit away from highly sensitive tokens within the GRPO framework.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is central to improving long-CoT reasoning in large language models. Critic-free methods such as GRPO convert response-level rewards into advantages and uniformly broadcast them across tokens, overlooking their unequal contributions to the final outcome. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) instead provides dense distributional supervision by minimizing the forward KL divergence between an unprivileged policy and a privileged self-teacher, implicitly assuming that the resulting likelihood shifts encode reliable answer-aligned information. We test this premise by fixing each sampled trajectory and re-scoring it under two opposing outcome conditions, one asserting correctness and the other incorrectness. Most affected tokens shift in the same direction under both conditions, with few sign reversals and substantial overlap in the induced optimization signals. Large shifts also concentrate on highly substitutable surface-form tokens, whereas tokens carrying problem-specific reasoning content are less sensitive. These findings show that privileged shifts fail to provide reliable answer-aligned directions, while their magnitudes primarily reflect counterfactual sensitivity rather than token-level learning value. Based on these observations, we propose Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation (CSCR), a simple extension of GRPO that reduces credit for highly sensitive tokens and renormalizes token-level advantages to preserve both the original credit budget and verifier-determined direction. On long-CoT mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CSCR consistently outperforms GRPO baseline with the same number of policy updates. Targeted ablations further corroborate our diagnosis: privilege-induced directions are unreliable, moderate downweighting is most effective, and stronger modulation destabilizes optimization.

</details>


### [151] [Dynamic Spectral Filtering for Temporal Graph Learning: Learning Evolving Propagation Operators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27891)
*Yan Kong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DSF proposes evolving graph propagation filters over time by treating Chebyshev polynomial coefficients as recurrent temporal states, achieving strong link-prediction performance with dramatically lower parameter counts, GPU memory, and training time compared to existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing temporal graph learning focuses on evolving node states or encoding interaction histories, but neglects whether the graph propagation mechanism itself should evolve. The authors identify an opportunity to explore operator-centric temporal dynamics with an emphasis on computational efficiency.

Method: DSF represents propagation at each snapshot using a Chebyshev polynomial filter with vector-valued, time-dependent coefficients. These compact multi-order coefficients are treated as recurrent temporal states, updated via a recurrent branch with multiplicative global and order-specific gating mechanisms. The temporal state size is independent of node count, yielding extreme parameter efficiency.

Result: On MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit temporal link prediction, DSF achieves AP scores of 0.7851, 0.9088, and 0.9860 with 93K–133K parameters, 68–182 MB peak GPU memory, and 1.6–2.1 s/epoch. Compared to DEFT, it uses 8.3–8.6× fewer parameters, 25–33× less GPU memory, and 5–19× less training time, with competitive or better performance. Against all baselines, GPU memory is 3.3–38.6× lower.

Conclusion: Direct spectral-response evolution serves as a strong temporal inductive bias when computational efficiency is a primary requirement, offering a compelling trade-off between predictive performance and resource consumption.

Abstract: Temporal graph learning is commonly organized around the evolution of node states or the encoding of interaction histories. We study an underexplored, operator-centric question: should the graph propagation mechanism itself evolve over time? We introduce Dynamic Spectral Filtering (DSF), which represents propagation at snapshot t by a Chebyshev polynomial filter with vector-valued, time-dependent coefficients. DSF explicitly treats these compact multi-order coefficients as recurrent temporal states. A recurrent branch proposes updates, while multiplicative global and order-specific gates regulate their magnitude. The temporal state is independent of the number of nodes. On MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit temporal link-prediction benchmarks, converged DSF runs attain AP scores of 0.7851, 0.9088, and 0.9860, respectively, with 93K to 133K trainable parameters, 68 to 182 MB peak GPU memory, and 1.6 to 2.1 seconds of training per epoch. Against the closely related DEFT baseline, DSF is better on MOOC, within 0.001 AP on Reddit, and modestly lower on Wikipedia, while using 8.3 to 8.6 times fewer parameters, 25 to 33 times less GPU memory, and 5 to 19 times less time per epoch. Relative to all measured alternatives, it uses 3.3 to 38.6 times less GPU memory. These results support direct spectral-response evolution as a useful temporal inductive bias when computational efficiency is a first-class requirement.

</details>


### [152] [MMHBench: A Multi-Perspective Benchmark for Mental Health Understanding in Long-Form Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27895)
*Jinpeng Hu,Erqiang Wang,Shan Wang,Zhuo Li,Peipei Song,Xun Yang,Meng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MMHBench is a multimodal benchmark for mental health understanding in long-form videos, featuring 268 videos and 2,184 questions across third-person assessment and first-person perspective-taking. A Multi-Agent Question Generation framework ensures question quality. Evaluation of 22 MLLMs reveals the task remains highly challenging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing mental health benchmarks reduce understanding to coarse-grained classification, failing to assess whether models truly comprehend psychological phenomena or merely exploit superficial correlations. There is a need for nuanced, multi-perspective evaluation grounded in complex behavioral and contextual reasoning.

Method: The authors introduce MMHBench with 268 long-form videos and 2,184 questions organized into two settings: (1) third-person assessment (605 questions) evaluating interpretation of observable behavior and multimodal evidence, and (2) first-person perspective-taking (1,579 questions) requiring perspective-conditioned reasoning about mental states. A Multi-Agent Question Generation (MAQG) framework simulates diverse social roles to synthesize multi-perspective questions, refined through multi-role feedback, iterative optimization, and expert-guided verification.

Result: Extensive evaluation of 22 MLLMs (open-source and closed-source) demonstrates that long-form video mental health understanding remains highly challenging, with significant performance gaps indicating the difficulty of the benchmark.

Conclusion: MMHBench exposes the limitations of current MLLMs in nuanced mental health reasoning from long-form video, highlighting the need for models that can integrate multimodal evidence and perform perspective-conditioned inference rather than relying on shallow cues.

Abstract: Mental health understanding in long-form videos requires nuanced reasoning over observable behavior, interpersonal context, and latent psychological states. Existing benchmarks largely reduce this task to coarse-grained classification, providing limited insight into whether models truly understand psychological phenomena or rely on superficial correlations. To address this limitation, we introduce MMHBench, a comprehensive multimodal benchmark for multi-perspective mental health understanding, comprising 268 long-form videos and 2,184 carefully curated questions. MMHBench organizes the evaluation into two complementary settings: (1) third-person assessment, consisting of 605 questions that focus on the interpretation of observable behaviors and multimodal evidence, and (2) first-person perspective-taking, comprising 1,579 questions that require perspective-conditioned reasoning to identify the interpretation of the mental state supported by the available multimodal evidence. We propose a Multi-Agent Question Generation (MAQG) framework that simulates diverse social roles to synthesize questions from multiple perspectives. The generated questions are refined through multi-role feedback and iterative optimization, followed by expert-guided verification to ensure quality and validity. Extensive evaluation of 22 representative multimodal large language models (MLLMs), spanning both open-source and leading closed-source models, demonstrates that long-form video mental health understanding remains highly challenging.

</details>


### [153] [A Cross-Architecture Audit of Direction-Based Inference-Time Defences in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27910)
*Xiangyu Yin,Tora Bodin,Rohan Menon,Chih-Hong Cheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper systematically compares five inference-time defence methods against vision-language model jailbreaks across 15 model/layer configurations from four architectural families, finding that no single defence dominates; the image conditioning shift preserves utility best, while effectiveness varies by architecture, and directions are largely non-transferable across model families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Jailbreaking of vision-language models (VLMs) is a significant safety concern, and inference-time defences that subtract a calibrated direction from the residual stream are a common mitigation strategy. However, a systematic comparison of candidate directions across model architectures under controlled protocols is lacking, motivating this comprehensive benchmarking study.

Method: Five defence candidates are compared under a magnitude-controlled protocol that normalizes intervention size per prompt and pairs each direction with a same-norm random control: (1) mean image conditioning shift, (2) a CMRM-style refusal direction, (3) a ShiftDC-style attack-specific residual, (4) a prompt instruction to ignore the image, and (5) a random control. Evaluation spans 15 model-and-layer cells from four architectural families (LLaVA 1.5, Pixtral 12B, Qwen2.5 VL, Qwen2 VL 2B), measuring refusal recovery and utility preservation. Cosine alignment between text-only and multimodal refusal geometry is also analyzed.

Result: No single candidate dominates on both refusal recovery and utility preservation. The image conditioning shift leads on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B and is the only candidate whose utility loss stays at the measurement noise floor across all families. The prompt instruction leads on Qwen2.5 VL; the attack-specific residual leads on Qwen2 VL 2B. The image conditioning direction is direction-specific in 13 of 15 cells but strongly architecture-specific and non-transferable between LLaVA 1.5 13B and Pixtral 12B. The CMRM direction shows positive cosine alignment with the image conditioning shift in all 15 cells (mean 0.35, range 0.17–0.65), 15–25× the random vector null, with a sign test p-value of ~3e-5, indicating partially overlapping geometry from the two recipes.

Conclusion: Direction-based inference-time defences recover partially overlapping refusal geometry and must be calibrated separately for each language decoder family, as no single direction works universally and transfer across architectures is limited.

Abstract: Inference time defences against vision language model jailbreaks often subtract a calibrated direction from the residual stream at a chosen decoder layer. We compare five defence candidates across 15 model and layer cells from four architectural families under a magnitude controlled protocol that matches the intervention size for each prompt and pairs every direction with a random control of the same norm. The candidates are the mean image conditioning shift, a CMRM style refusal direction, a ShiftDC style attack specific residual, a prompt instruction to ignore the image, and a random control. No single candidate dominates on both refusal recovery and utility preservation. The image conditioning shift leads on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B and is the only candidate whose utility loss remains at the measurement noise floor in every family. The prompt instruction leads on Qwen2.5 VL, while the attack specific residual leads on Qwen2 VL 2B. The image conditioning direction is direction specific in 13 of 15 cells, but strongly architecture specific and nontransferable across the only dimension compatible pair, LLaVA 1.5 13B and Pixtral 12B. We also connect text only and multimodal refusal geometry. The CMRM direction has positive cosine alignment with the image conditioning shift in all 15 cells, with mean 0.35, range 0.17 to 0.65, 15 to 25 times the random vector null, and a sign test p value of about 3e-5. These results show that the two recipes recover partially overlapping geometry and that direction based defences should be calibrated separately for each language decoder family.

</details>


### [154] [IFHierBench: Hierarchical Instruction Following for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27912)
*Yuetian Mao,Chunyang Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: IFHierBench introduces a hierarchical instruction-following benchmark revealing that even top LLMs barely exceed 50% accuracy, with performance degrading sharply as constraint nesting depth increases, highlighting a critical gap in current models' ability to follow layered, scoped constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern LLM deployments increasingly use a single prompt to generate structured outputs where overall artifacts, sections, and nested fields each have specific constraints. Existing instruction-following benchmarks treat all constraints as a flat, uniform list and cannot verify whether a constraint is satisfied within its intended scope (e.g., a specific section). This misalignment with real-world layered-output requirements motivates a hierarchical benchmark.

Method: The authors construct IFHierBench with 600 prompts stratified across four constraint-tree depths. It encompasses 35 distinct constraint types, each prompt paired with a deterministic, scope-aware checker that verifies constraint satisfaction at every level of the output hierarchy. Seven proprietary and open-weight LLMs are evaluated using prompt-level accuracy as the primary metric.

Result: Even the strongest model achieves only marginally above 50% prompt-level accuracy. Accuracy degrades sharply as constraint-tree depth increases, demonstrating that reliably following nested, scoped constraints is a substantial and unresolved challenge for current LLMs.

Conclusion: Current LLMs lack robust hierarchical instruction-following capability. Future work should develop training methods that enforce constraint adherence at finer granularity to close this gap and improve real-world deployability.

Abstract: Instruction-following ability is critical for deploying large language models in real-world applications, where downstream components depend on the output satisfying specific constraints. Modern deployments increasingly handle the full task in a single LLM call, with one prompt specifying a layered output whose overall artifact, structural sections, and nested fields must each satisfy concrete constraints. Existing instruction-following benchmarks treat the constraint set as a flat list applied uniformly to the response, so they cannot scope a check to a particular section of the output. We introduce IFHierBench, a hierarchical instruction-following benchmark of 600 prompts stratified across four constraint-tree depths and 35 distinct constraints, each prompt paired with a deterministic checker that verifies satisfaction at every scope. Evaluating seven leading proprietary and open-weight models, we find that even the strongest model only marginally exceeds 50% prompt-level accuracy and that accuracy degrades sharply as constraint depth grows. Reliably following nested constraints remains a substantial gap for current LLMs, motivating future training methods that consider constraint adherence at finer granularity to achieve better instruction-following ability.

</details>


### [155] [One Anchor for All: Unified Multilingual and Multimodal Safety Alignment for LVLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27917)
*Enyi Shi,Fei Shen,Chuancheng Shi,Linxia Zhu,Shuyi Miao,Jinhui Tang,Tat-Seng Chua*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a neuron-level safety alignment framework (MLS-Neurons) that identifies and fine-tunes a minimal subset of neurons shared across languages and modalities to defend large vision-language models against compound multilingual-multimodal attacks, achieving state-of-the-art safety with only ~0.03% parameter updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing safety methods for LVLMs treat language and modality defenses in isolation, fail to handle compound multilingual-visual attacks, and suffer from scarce safety data and high fine-tuning costs. A unified cross-dimensional defense mechanism is urgently needed.

Method: The authors first identify monolingual/unimodal safety neurons via activation strength and downstream impact comparison between harmful and benign samples. They then intersect unimodal neurons within each language to obtain modality-shared safety neurons (MS-Neurons), and further intersect MS-Neurons across languages using English as a semantic anchor to derive modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons). Finally, only the MLS-Neuron subset (~0.03% of parameters) is fine-tuned with English safety supervision, which transfers to multilingual and multimodal scenarios.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks while preserving general model utility.

Conclusion: The MLS-Neurons framework provides an efficient and effective cross-dimensional safety alignment solution for LVLMs by leveraging a tiny subset of shared safety-critical neurons, enabling English-only supervision to generalize across languages and modalities.

Abstract: As large vision-language models (LVLMs) are deployed globally, the combination of multilingual instructions and visual information makes malicious attacks more covert and sophisticated than ever before. However, existing methods isolate language and modality defenses, which, coupled with the scarcity of safety data and high fine-tuning costs, makes it difficult for models to defend against compound attacks. To address this severe challenge, we propose a neuron-level cross-dimensional safety alignment framework driven by modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons). First, we identify monolingual and unimodal safety neurons by comparing responses to harmful and benign samples, quantifying functional saliency through activation strength and downstream impact. Then, by intersecting these unimodal neurons within each language, we extract modality-shared safety neurons (MS-Neurons) responsive to both visual and textual risks, bridging the safety representation gap between modalities. Furthermore, using English as a semantic anchor, we intersect MS-Neurons across languages to identify modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons), serving as key defenses against compound attacks. Finally, we update only this minimal subset of shared neurons (~0.03% of parameters), transferring English-only safety supervision to multilingual and multimodal scenarios. Extensive experiments show that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks while preserving general utility.

</details>


### [156] [Meta-Task: Turning Terminal Task Synthesis into a Terminal Task for Scalable Agent Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27929)
*Zhihong Pan,Jiyuan He,Kai Zhang,Yupeng Han,Ze Liu,Yuze Zhao,Yongcong Ye,Zhaohua Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Meta-Task reframes terminal task synthesis as an agent-driven, container-based generation loop where tasks are iteratively created, executed, and verified in situ. Fine-tuning on just 3,221 synthesized trajectories yields state-of-the-art results on Terminal-Bench 2.0, outperforming concurrent methods with far less data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training terminal agents requires diverse, verifiable tasks and high-quality interaction trajectories, but existing synthesis methods suffer from (1) weak reliability due to disconnected task generation and real execution, and (2) limited diversity/scalability from over-reliance on existing repositories.

Method: Meta-Task treats terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format task itself. An agent operates inside a real container, iteratively generating, executing, and verifying tasks in a closed loop for internal consistency. It decouples target task requirements along multiple dimensions, employs a multi-phase mechanism to dynamically design novel task specifications before producing tasks, supports optional external materials for diversity/realism, and applies LLM-as-Judge filtering for final quality assurance.

Result: Fine-tuning on only 3,221 Meta-Task synthesized trajectories achieves 22.5% Avg Pass@1 for Qwen3-14B and 31.8% for Qwen3-32B on Terminal-Bench 2.0, surpassing concurrent approaches while using significantly less training data.

Conclusion: The Meta-Task framework demonstrates that closed-loop, execution-verified task synthesis within real container environments can produce high-quality training trajectories efficiently, enabling strong terminal agent performance with minimal data.

Abstract: Training terminal agents at scale requires diverse, verifiable terminal tasks and high-quality interaction trajectories, yet acquiring such data remains a significant challenge. Existing synthesis methods face two key limitations: (1) weak reliability caused by the disconnect between task generation and real execution, and (2) limited diversity and scalability due to dependence on existing repositories. We propose Meta-Task, a framework that redefines terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format task itself: an agent operates within a real container environment to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks, so that synthesized components are checked for internal consistency and executability within the generation loop itself. Building upon this, we decouple the target task requirements along multiple dimensions, introduce a multi-phase mechanism that dynamically designs novel task specifications before producing the actual tasks, and incorporate optional external material support to enhance diversity and realism. We additionally apply LLM-as-Judge filtering to ensure the quality of the final training data. Experiments on Terminal-Bench 2.0 show that fine-tuning on only 3,221 Meta-Task synthesized trajectories achieves 22.5% and 31.8% Avg Pass@1 for Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B respectively, outperforming concurrent approaches with significantly less training data.

</details>


### [157] [The Geometric Nature and a Free Proxy for Flow-Matching Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27933)
*Ziyang Rao,Yiren Zhao,Weiyu Guo,Ben Fei,Yandong Guo,Hui Xiong*

Main category: cs.AI
