TL;DR: Proposes denoising acceleration (accel), a cost-free, highly-generalizable uncertainty proxy for flow matching (FM) that detects failing actions in real-time control by measuring bending in the denoising trajectory from a single forward pass, without extra training or resampling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Flow matching is widely used in embodied models but produces unreliable actions under misinterpretation or OOD inputs without exposing uncertainty. Existing uncertainty estimation methods for real-time control suffer from extra training costs, high computational overhead, and poor generalization.

Method: Provides a geometric interpretation of FM uncertainty in the velocity field, showing uncertainty as deviation from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction. Introduces denoising acceleration (accel), a proxy computed from a single forward pass that quantifies trajectory bending. Theoretically and empirically validates accel as a faithful uncertainty measure and tests it for online failure detection.

Result: Accel identifies failing rollouts well before termination, matching or outperforming costly resampling- and training-based baselines across settings under realistic deployment budgets.

Conclusion: Denoising acceleration is a practical, cost-free, and generalizable uncertainty proxy for flow matching that enables reliable online failure detection in embodied models without additional computational burden.

Abstract: Flow matching (FM) has become a popular action head paradigm for modern embodied models. However, as a conditional generative model, it does not explicitly expose its inherent uncertainty, producing faulty action chunks even when it misinterprets the scene or encounters out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. Therefore, determining when an FM-generated action can be trusted is essential for safe deployment, yet existing uncertainty estimation methods on real-time control suffer from several issues: extra training budget, high computational overhead, and low generalization ability. In this work, we provide a geometric interpretation of FM uncertainty in the velocity field, showing that uncertainty manifests as deviation from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction field. Building on this observation, we introduce denoising acceleration ($\mathrm{accel}$), a highly-generalizable and cost-free uncertainty proxy that measures the bending of the denoising trajectory from a single forward pass, without additional model evaluations, training, or resampling. We theoretically and empirically demonstrate that $\mathrm{accel}$ is a faithful proxy for FM uncertainty and further test its utility in online failure detection. Results show that $\mathrm{accel}$ identifies failing rollouts well before termination, matching or even outperforming costly resampling- and training-based baselines across settings under realistic deployment budget. Code and demos available at: https://github.com/rrrrrrzy/fm-geometry.

</details>


### [158] [Shapes from Examples: Foundations of Shape Learning in Recursive SHACL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27934)
*Bente Gortworst,Cem Okulmus,Magdalena Ortiz,Anni-Yasmin Turhan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper studies the automatic learning of SHACL shapes from positive and negative example nodes, focusing on a core fragment corresponding to the description logic ELI. It investigates fitting existence and most specific fitting computation under well-founded, stable, and supported semantics for recursive shape catalogues, establishing tight exponential-time upper bounds and polynomial bounds for relevant special cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SHACL shapes are essential for validating knowledge graphs, but manually crafting shapes is labor-intensive and error-prone. Automatic shape learning from examples (the fitting approach) addresses this challenge. The authors aim to provide a rigorous computational foundation for this task, particularly for recursive shape catalogues under multiple semantics, where prior theoretical understanding was lacking.

Method: The paper formalizes the fitting problem: given sets P (positive) and N (negative) of example nodes, compute a shape expression C in a core fragment of SHACL (equivalent to the description logic ELI) that validates all nodes in P and none in N. Shape names may be defined recursively in a catalogue. The authors analyze the problem under three semantics — well-founded, stable, and supported — and study both fitting existence (does any such C exist?) and most specific fitting computation (finding the logically strongest such C). They establish complexity bounds via reductions and decision procedures.

Result: The authors establish tight exponential-time upper bounds for both fitting existence and most specific fitting computation under all three semantics. They also identify relevant special cases where the complexity drops to polynomial time, providing tractable fragments for practical use.

Conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive complexity-theoretic characterization of SHACL shape learning via the fitting approach. The exponential-time upper bounds are tight, and the polynomial special cases offer practical avenues for implementation. The results apply uniformly across well-founded, stable, and supported semantics for recursive catalogues.

Abstract: SHACL shapes enable data graph validation, making automatic shape learning essential for knowledge graph applications. We investigate the well-known fitting approach to this task: given sets P and N of positive and negative example nodes from an input graph, compute a shape expression C, possibly using shape names defined in a recursive shape catalogue, that validates at every node in P and none in N. We focus on the case where C is written in a core fragment of SHACL corresponding to the Description Logic ELI. For the catalogue, we consider the well-founded, stable, and supported semantics. We address fitting existence and most specific fitting computation, establish tight exponential-time upper bounds for both problems, and obtain polynomial bounds for relevant special cases.

</details>


### [159] [From Scoring to Acting: Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27937)
*Xu Xia,Jinghua Piao,Min Yang,Xiaochong Lan,Jiaju Chen,Yong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OVCSD improves LLM agent skill internalization by using outcome-verified teacher supervision and comparative learning over teacher-student trajectory pairs, outperforming skill-free RL and existing self-distillation baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing on-policy self-distillation methods for LLM agents rely on action-level scoring along student-generated trajectories, which suffers from two key weaknesses: (1) teacher preferences lack validation against actual environment outcomes, and (2) action-level scores underutilize the rich information available from student rollouts, teacher rollouts, and their behavioral divergences. The authors argue for outcome-verified teacher supervision combined with comparative trajectory-level learning.

Method: OVCSD works in three stages: (1) failed student rollouts are organized into a prefix tree; (2) a skill-conditioned teacher is adaptively invoked from student-reached states, retaining only outcome-verified successful continuations; (3) localized comparative learning is applied at the first state where student and teacher trajectories diverge, distilling the post-divergence teacher suffix to transfer correct completion behavior.

Result: On ALFWorld and WebShop across three model scales, OVCSD consistently outperforms skill-free RL and existing self-distillation baselines, achieving up to 29.7 and 5.4 absolute success-rate gains over the strongest baselines respectively, while requiring less than 3% privileged interaction during training.

Conclusion: Outcome-verified supervision and comparative learning at trajectory divergence points provide a more effective and sample-efficient approach to internalizing skills in LLM agents compared to action-level scoring methods.

Abstract: Recent work on LLM agents is shifting from external capability elicitation to capability internalization, enabling agents to retain useful skills without retrieval at inference time. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers a promising direction, but many existing methods typically supervise students by scoring actions along student-generated trajectories. Such supervision has two limitations: teacher preferences are not validated by environment outcomes, and action-level scores underuse information from student rollouts, teacher rollouts, and their behavioral relationship. We therefore advocate outcome-verified teacher supervision and comparative learning over teacher-student trajectories. Based on this view, we propose Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation (OVCSD). OVCSD organizes failed student rollouts into a prefix tree, adaptively invokes a skill-conditioned teacher from student-reached states, and retains only outcome-verified successful continuations. It then applies localized comparative learning at the first state-aligned divergence and distills the post-divergence teacher suffix to transfer completion behavior. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop across three model scales show that OVCSD consistently outperforms skill-free RL and existing self-distillation baselines, achieving up to 29.7 and 5.4 absolute success-rate gains over the strongest baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively, while adding less than 3% privileged interaction during training.

</details>


### [160] [MARS-RA: Rank Aggregation for Credit Assignment via Multimodal Comparisons in Embodied Multi-Agent Cooperation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27967)
*Dawei Wang,Di Zhao,Xinyuan Liu,Marci Chi Ma,Xiaoyang Liu,Chengming Zhou,Gary Ushaw,Richard Davison*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MARS-RA reformulates multi-agent credit assignment as a rank aggregation problem, using LLM-generated pairwise comparisons to produce contribution scores for potential-based reward shaping, with theoretical guarantees and empirical validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Credit assignment in cooperative MARL is challenging in embodied AI due to limited/delayed feedback and dynamic agent participation. Absolute credit estimation is brittle; a relative, comparison-based approach offers greater robustness.

Method: MARS-RA employs large multimodal models to generate contribution-based pairwise comparisons among agents, then applies rank aggregation to convert these comparisons into contribution scores. These scores drive potential-based reward shaping, which preserves policy optimality. Shapley values serve as an interpretive reference.

Result: Experimental results on diverse challenging tasks demonstrate that MARS-RA effectively guides agents toward cooperative behavior, outperforming baselines in settings with delayed feedback and dynamic agent populations.

Conclusion: Reformulating credit assignment as rank aggregation with LLM-generated comparisons is a viable and theoretically grounded approach, offering robustness to noise and dynamic team composition in embodied multi-agent settings.

Abstract: Credit assignment is a fundamental challenge in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly in embodied AI settings characterized by limited and delayed feedback as well as dynamically changing numbers of active agents. We propose MARS-RA, a framework that reformulates credit assignment as a rank aggregation problem using contribution-based pairwise comparisons among agents generated by large multimodal models. This shift from absolute to relative estimation ensures robustness against noise and dynamic agent participation, converting comparison results into contribution scores for potential-based reward shaping. We provide theoretical justification for the convergence and robustness of the proposed framework, and show that Shapley values can be used as an interpretive reference. Experimental results on challenging tasks of different types indicate that MARS-RA can guide agents toward effective cooperation.

</details>


### [161] [Share the Judge, Learn the Deferral: Where Specialization Helps LLM Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27984)
*Weining Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Specialization in evaluator systems is better placed in the deferral (routing) mechanism rather than in the judge's weights. Shared training of judgment with domain-specific adaptation at an audited release boundary outperforms splitting training data across specialized LoRA judges, while cascading small-to-large models via learned correctness heads achieves higher accuracy with lower compute.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic systems increasingly separate generation from evaluation, raising a practical architectural question: should domain specialization be embedded in an evaluator's model weights, or in the decision rule governing when to trust its judgment? The paper seeks to provide empirical guidance on this design choice.

Method: The authors study 99,952 public, rubric-conditioned examples across two experimental paradigms. First, they compare rubric-conditioned vs. rubric-agnostic evaluation, then train LoRA judges partitioned by criterion families versus a shared rank-64 adapter. Second, they test specialization-as-deferral using learned correctness heads to route examples through a 0.6B-4B-8B cascade on RewardBench 2, with 20 locked repartitions and exact one-sided 95% risk audits.

Result: Supplying the correct rubric improves accuracy by 2.11 points; an unrelated rubric costs 2.66 points. Splitting training data across eight criterion-family LoRA judges loses 10.05 points and cuts audited coverage from 24.44% to 5.43%. Initializing family adapters from a shared trained judge recovers accuracy to 76.85% (19.94 points above scratch). For deferral-based specialization, the 0.6B-4B-8B cascade achieves 89.40% accuracy vs. 84.75% for 8B alone at 0.415 normalized compute, passing risk audits, while margin-based rules stay near 84.8% accuracy at ≥0.94 compute.

Conclusion: A qualified design rule emerges: share the learning of judgment until sufficient data justifies a split, and place domain-specific adaptation in an audited release boundary (deferral mechanism) rather than fragmenting the judge's weights prematurely.

Abstract: Agentic systems have widened the gap between producing candidate outputs and reviewing them. This paper asks a practical architectural question: should domain specialization be built into an evaluator's weights, or into the rule that decides when its judgment can be trusted? We study 99,952 public, rubric-conditioned examples. Supplying the correct rubric improves locked-test accuracy by 2.11 points over a response-only control; replacing it with an unrelated rubric costs 2.66 points. Dividing the same training corpus among eight criterion-family LoRA judges, however, loses 10.05 points and cuts audited coverage at a 5% risk target from 24.44% to 5.43%. Matching the bank's stored capacity with one rank-64 adapter does not reproduce this loss. Nor is the result explained by learning rate or optimizer steps. Initializing the family adapters from a shared, trained judge recovers test accuracy to 76.85%, 19.94 points above scratch training at the same learning rate (95% interval 18.88-21.02). The result changes when specialization governs deferral rather than judgment. On RewardBench 2, learned correctness heads route examples through a 0.6B-4B-8B cascade without changing any reward score. Across 20 locked repartitions, the cascade attains 89.40% accuracy, compared with 84.75% for 8B alone, at 0.415 normalized parameter compute. Every run passes an exact one-sided 95% risk audit; margin-based rules remain near 84.8% accuracy while using at least 0.94 compute. These results suggest a qualified design rule: share the learning of judgment until there is enough data to justify a split, and place domain-specific adaptation in an audited release boundary.

</details>


### [162] [SKIMIX: Multi-Agent Harness-Time Scaling with Skill Mixture for Dynamic Harness Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27994)
*Jia Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SKIMIX is a multi-agent framework that uses embedding-based skill retrieval, submodular anti-dilution routing, and adaptive skill evolution to enable agents with distinct skill portfolios to collaborate iteratively. Experiments across six reasoning benchmarks show multi-agent collaboration improves open-ended mathematical reasoning but yields limited or negative gains on multiple-choice tasks, with non-monotonic agent scaling and most gains occurring in the first refinement round.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents increasingly depend on large, diverse skill libraries, three core challenges arise: selecting relevant skills from a large pool, combining skills across agents without redundancy, and maintaining/updating skills over time. Existing approaches lack principled mechanisms for all three simultaneously.

Method: SKIMIX employs a multi-agent framework with three key components: (1) embedding-based skill retrieval to match agents to relevant skills; (2) submodular anti-dilution routing that selects agent subsets while minimizing skill overlap and maximizing marginal contribution; and (3) adaptive skill evolution that allows agents to refine their skill portfolios based on collaboration outcomes. Agents collaborate through iterative refinement rounds.

Result: Multi-agent collaboration substantially improves open-ended mathematical reasoning performance but provides limited or negative gains on multiple-choice tasks. Agent-count scaling is non-monotonic — adding agents does not consistently improve results. Most performance improvements emerge during the first refinement round, with diminishing returns thereafter.

Conclusion: Task characteristics fundamentally determine whether skill-level ensembles provide benefits. The findings offer practical guidance for scalable agent design: multi-agent skill collaboration is most effective for open-ended generation tasks, agent count should be carefully tuned rather than maximized, and iterative refinement beyond the first round yields marginal returns.

Abstract: AI agents increasingly rely on large skill libraries, but selecting, combining, and maintaining skills remains difficult. We propose SKIMIX, a multi-agent framework in which agents with different skill portfolios collaborate through iterative refinement. SKIMIX combines embedding-based skill retrieval, submodular anti-dilution routing, and adaptive skill evolution. Across six reasoning benchmarks, multi-agent collaboration substantially improves open-ended mathematical reasoning but offers limited or negative gains on multiple-choice tasks. Agent-count scaling is non-monotonic, and most improvements arise during the first refinement round. These results show that task characteristics determine whether skill-level ensembles help and provide practical guidance for scalable agent design.

</details>


### [163] [MMLDSum-LLM: Multimodal Long-Document Summarization with Visual-Alignment and Keyword-Aware](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28006)
*Xianpeng Zhang,Jiahua Yang,Dongyu Chen,Lei zhang,Jian Ma,Xu guohuan,Haonan Lu,Tianhuang Su,Chuangchuang Wang,Kai Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces MMLDSum-Bench, a benchmark for multimodal long-document summarization, and MMLDSum-LLM, a two-stage training framework combining supervised fine-tuning with specialized losses and GRPO-based reinforcement learning to address attention drift and cross-modal misalignment in existing multimodal LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal long documents contain sparsely distributed critical evidence across paragraphs and modalities. Current multimodal LLMs suffer from attention drift in long-range dependency modeling and inter-modal alignment gaps, leading to key information omission and cross-modal hallucinations during summarization.

Method: (1) MMLDSum-Bench: a benchmark covering multiple domains, context-length scales, and visual-textual modality distributions. (2) MMLDSum-LLM: a two-stage training framework — Stage 1: supervised fine-tuning with visual-alignment weighted loss and keyword-aware weighted loss; Stage 2: GRPO with a multi-objective reward combining keyword coverage, image-text alignment, ROUGE, and length control. Evaluation uses LLM-as-a-judge scoring, atomic-claim precision/recall, image-text alignment (ITA), and ROUGE.

Result: Extensive experiments on MMLDSum-Bench, comparing against leading closed-source and open-source multimodal models under a unified evaluation protocol, demonstrate that MMLDSum-LLM significantly improves key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency.

Conclusion: The proposed benchmark and training framework effectively mitigate attention drift and cross-modal misalignment issues, yielding substantial gains in summarization quality for multimodal long documents across diverse domains and modality distributions.

Abstract: Multimodal long documents are core carriers of professional knowledge, where critical evidence is sparsely distributed across paragraphs and modalities. This easily causes key information omission and cross-modal hallucinations in summarization by multimodal LLMs. These issues stem from attention drift in long-range dependency modeling and gaps in inter-modal alignment. To address this, we introduce MMLDSum-Bench, a high-quality benchmark for multimodal long-document summarization, covering multiple domains, context-length scales, and visual-textual modality distributions. We further propose MMLDSum-LLM, a reproducible two-stage training framework that combines supervised fine-tuning with visual-alignment weighted loss and keyword-aware weighted loss, followed by GRPO with a multi-objective reward (keyword coverage, image-text alignment, ROUGE, and length control). Extensive experiments on MMLDSum-Bench, comparing against leading closed-source and open-source multimodal models under a unified evaluation protocol - including LLM-as-a-judge scoring, atomic-claim precision/recall, image-text alignment (ITA), and ROUGE - demonstrate that our approach significantly improves key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency.

</details>


### [164] [MUL-T: Decoding Spatial Cellular Architecture in Multiplexed Tissue Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28030)
*Farzaneh Seyedshahi,Kai Rakovic,Adalberto Claudio Quiros,John LeQuesne,Ke Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MUL-T is a lightweight transformer that frames tissue architecture analysis as a masked contextual prediction task over discrete cell tokens, learning [CLS] embeddings without task-specific supervision. It consistently outperforms classical baselines and matches a foundation ViT model across multiple clinical tasks with far fewer parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for modelling tissue organisation in multiplexed imaging rely on handcrafted features (marker intensity statistics, cell-type proportions) that fail to scale or generalise across cohorts with heterogeneous marker panels. There is a need for a representation learning approach that captures higher-order cellular interactions without manual feature engineering and can operate efficiently across diverse datasets.

Method: The authors propose MUL-T, a lightweight transformer that reframes tissue architecture modelling as a masked contextual prediction task over discrete cell tokens. The model learns contextualised [CLS] embeddings in a self-supervised manner, without task-specific supervision, enabling it to capture higher-order cellular interactions across heterogeneous marker panels.

Result: MUL-T consistently outperforms classical feature-based baselines across multiple clinically relevant downstream tasks: core-level tumour pattern classification, patient-level grading, PD-L1 positivity prediction, and cross-dataset treatment response prediction. It achieves performance comparable to a foundation ViT model despite substantially fewer parameters and lower training cost.

Conclusion: Self-supervised contextual learning over discrete cell tokens using a lightweight transformer offers a scalable, generalisable, and computationally efficient alternative to handcrafted features for tissue architecture analysis in multiplexed imaging, matching much larger models in performance.

Abstract: Understanding tissue organisation in multiplexed imaging requires modelling both cellular phenotypes and their spatial context. Existing approaches typically rely on handcrafted features, such as marker intensity statistics or cell-type proportions, which often fail to scale or generalise across cohorts with heterogeneous marker panels. We introduce MUL-T, a lightweight transformer framework that reframes tissue architecture as a masked contextual prediction task over discrete cell tokens. By learning contextualised [CLS] embeddings without task-specific supervision, the model captures higher-order cellular interactions while remaining computationally efficient. We evaluate MUL-T on several clinically relevant downstream tasks, including core-level tumour pattern classification, patient-level grading, PD-L1 positivity prediction, and cross-dataset treatment response prediction. Across tasks, MUL-T consistently outperforms classical feature-based baselines and achieves performance comparable to a foundation ViT model, despite substantially fewer parameters and lower training cost.

</details>


### [165] [DataClawEval: A Benchmark for Data Engineering Agents in Real Industrial Harness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28033)
*Debin Meng,Jiaming Yang,Zefang Zong,Tengyue Xu,Haining Xie,Yang Li,Peng Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DataClawEval is the first benchmark for evaluating autonomous agents on end-to-end data engineering tasks across five execution engines (PySpark, MySQL, HiveSQL, PrestoSQL/Trino, FlinkSQL), using 100 production-grade tasks with deterministic rule-based evaluation in isolated sandboxes. Evaluation of 16 frontier agents shows the best model achieves only 74.9 overall, with strong domain specialization and no single model dominating across engines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM benchmarks focus narrowly on Text-to-SQL translation or data analysis, ignoring the broader, complex domain of end-to-end data engineering. There is no comprehensive benchmark for evaluating autonomous agents on real-world data engineering workflows, leaving a critical gap in assessing LLM capabilities for production data engineering tasks.

Method: The authors introduce DataClawEval, a benchmark comprising 100 end-to-end data engineering tasks derived from production-grade code by enterprise data engineers. Tasks span five execution engines: PySpark, MySQL, HiveSQL, PrestoSQL/Trino, and FlinkSQL. Each task is executed in a case-specific, isolated sandbox and evaluated using deterministic, rule-based scripts (rather than LLM-as-a-judge). Sixteen frontier agents are evaluated against this benchmark.

Result: The strongest model achieves only 74.9 overall score. No single model dominates across all engines; instead, each model excels on a different execution engine, revealing strict domain specialization rather than general-purpose proficiency. Autonomous data engineering remains an unresolved challenge.

Conclusion: Autonomous data engineering is a formidable, unresolved challenge that current frontier agents cannot adequately handle. The field requires further advances beyond current LLM capabilities, and DataClawEval provides a robust, reproducible foundation for measuring progress. The dataset, containerized environments, and evaluation scripts are publicly released.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly being deployed to automate complex workflows, promising to revolutionize data management and processing. However, existing benchmarks predominantly focus on simplified Text-to-SQL translation or data analysis, leaving the critical and complex domain of end-to-end data engineering largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce DataClawEval, the first comprehensive benchmark designed specifically to evaluate the end-to-end task completion capabilities of autonomous agents in real-world data engineering scenarios. Built upon production-grade code authored by professional enterprise data engineers, it comprises 100 rigorous, end-to-end tasks spanning five execution engines: PySpark, MySQL, HiveSQL, PrestoSQL/Trino, and FlinkSQL. Rather than non-deterministic LLM-as-a-judge scoring, each task is executed within a case-specific, isolated sandbox and graded by deterministic, rule-based scripts. Evaluating 16 frontier agents exposes critical limitations: The strongest model attains only 74.9 overall, and no single model dominates, as each excels on a different engine, revealing strict domain specialization rather than omnipotent proficiency. Thus, autonomous data engineering remains a formidable, unresolved challenge. We release our dataset, containerized environments, and deterministic evaluation scripts at https://github.com/Dicemy/DataClawEval/tree/master

</details>


### [166] [SKILL-KD: Contrastive Skill Distillation for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28048)
*Qiming Shi,Yibo Dou,Jiawen Zhu,Yulong Tao,Linbo Jin,Zhaolu Kang,Yunfan Zhou,Di Weng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SKILL-KD is a contrastive skill distillation framework that extracts actionable skill patches from teacher-student trajectory discrepancies, iteratively refines them through re-evaluation, and consolidates them with drift-aware history to improve weaker LLM agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing skill acquisition methods treat skills as experience summaries or direct demonstration compressions, but weaker student agents often cannot infer missing behaviors from their own failures, and teacher trajectories are too implicit to serve as reusable guidance. This creates a representation gap that SKILL-KD addresses by making skills an explicit distillation medium.

Method: SKILL-KD operates in three stages: (1) contrastive skill distillation — given a student failure and a teacher success on the same task, it distills the actionable discrepancy into a textual skill patch; (2) iterative refinement — the patch is evaluated by re-running the student; if failure persists, the patch is refined; (3) Drift-Aware Skill Consolidation — maintains trace-linked edit histories and decides whether each patch should add, delete, modify, or skip rules to prevent skill drift from repeated local updates.

Result: Across five agent benchmarks and two student settings, SKILL-KD consistently improves frozen student agents over fixed-model adaptation baselines.

Conclusion: Skill patches distilled from teacher-student discrepancies provide an effective and reusable mechanism for transferring capabilities from stronger to weaker LLM agents, outperforming prior adaptation methods without requiring student model fine-tuning.

Abstract: Skill-based prompting has become a practical mechanism for improving large language model (LLM) agents, yet existing skill acquisition methods often treat skills as experience summaries, memory entries, or direct summaries of successful demonstrations. This creates a mismatch for weaker student agents: when a student fails because it lacks task knowledge or operational strategy, its failed trajectory may not contain enough evidence to infer the missing behavior, while the teacher trajectory may be too implicit to be internalized as reusable guidance. We propose SKILL-KD, a contrastive skill distillation framework that treats skills as an explicit distillation medium between agents of different capabilities. Given a student failure and the teacher trajectory on the same task, SKILL-KD distills their actionable discrepancy into a textual skill patch, evaluates the patch by re-running the student, and iteratively refines the patch when the student still fails. To prevent repeated local updates from causing skill drift, SKILL-KD further maintains trace-linked edit histories and performs Drift-Aware Skill Consolidation, deciding whether each patch should add a new rule, delete or modify an existing rule, or be skipped. Across five agent benchmarks and two student settings, SKILL-KD consistently improves frozen student agents over fixed-model adaptation baselines.

</details>


### [167] [IndustryForge-27B: A Domain-Enhanced Multimodal Foundation Model for Industrial CAD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28050)
*Nianchen Deng,Jiaxin Ai,Tao Hu,Shu Zou,Yurui Dong,Siqi Li,Xinyu Cai,Xuemeng Yang,Licheng Wen,Hongbin Zhou,Hairong Zhang,Pinlong Cai,Botian Shi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: IndustryForge-27B is a multimodal foundation model fine-tuned from Qwen3.5-VL-27B using a unified multi-task SFT recipe on ~52k industrial CAD samples across six sub-corpora. It achieves +33.65 pp average improvement over its base model on CAD benchmarks, surpasses GPT-5.4, and retains general capabilities with no catastrophic forgetting, serving as a unified substrate for full-stack industrial agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: General-purpose multimodal models fail on industrial CAD tasks (interpreting engineering drawings/3D screenshots, generating parametric CAD scripts and Windows COM API code across parts and assemblies), while single-task fine-tuning is too narrow for diverse agent needs. A unified model covering the full spectrum from design to software operation is required.

Method: Built on Qwen3.5-VL-27B. Curated and integrated six industrial CAD sub-corpora (~52k multimodal samples): CAD-VQA, text2cadquery, text2cadquery-assembly, com_2d, com_3d, and com_assembly (covering Inventor/SolidWorks). Trained with a unified multi-task supervised fine-tuning (SFT) recipe.

Result: IndustryForge-27B improved over the base model by +33.65 pp on average across four CAD benchmarks and outperformed GPT-5.4 on all four. On eleven general-capability benchmarks, it retained and slightly improved performance (+1.56 pp mean) with no catastrophic forgetting.

Conclusion: IndustryForge-27B provides a unified starting point for downstream industrial-agent projects, spanning CAD design to industrial-software operation, from parts to assemblies, and from single-shot generation to closed-loop self-improvement.

Abstract: Automating industrial CAD design and manufacturing places distinctive demands on multimodal foundation models: the model must see engineering drawings and 3D geometry screenshots, write correct parametric-modelling scripts and Windows COM API code, and cover the full range from single parts to assemblies. General-purpose multimodal models fall short on these tasks, while single-task fine-tuning is too narrow to support the diverse calls that upper-layer agents issue. We build IndustryForge-27B on top of Qwen3.5-VL-27B by curating and integrating six industrial-CAD sub-corpora totalling $\sim$52k multimodal samples---CAD Visual QA (CAD-VQA), parametric CAD code (text2cadquery), assembly-level CAD code (text2cadquery-assembly), and three COM sub-corpora for Inventor / SolidWorks (com_2d / com_3d / com_assembly)---and training with a unified multi-task SFT recipe. Across four CAD-domain benchmarks IndustryForge-27B lifts the base model by $+33.65$~pp on average and outperforms the strong closed-source model GPT-5.4 on all four; across eleven general-capability benchmarks it retains, and slightly improves upon, the base model ($+1.56$~pp mean, no catastrophic forgetting). IndustryForge-27B will serve as the common substrate for downstream industrial-agent projects, providing a unified starting point for a full-stack industrial agent that spans from CAD design to industrial-software operation, from parts to assemblies, and from single-shot generation to closed-loop self-improvement.

</details>


### [168] [SemPIC: Learning Semantic Position-Independent KV Caches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28069)
*Hui Xie,Peng Xiao,Yutong Deng\textsuperscript,Shuoran Dou,Jian Yang,Jinyang Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SemPIC trains a LoRA-based Writer to compile position-independent cached KV states for documents via behavioral distillation, improving reuse under changing contexts. A learned boundary-conditioned baseline reduces attention deviation; KV Gradient Checkpointing cuts training memory. Across models and tasks, SemPIC raises mean micro-F1 from 0.53 (KV Packet) to 0.60, nearing Full Recompute at 0.62.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-context retrieval and agentic workloads reuse documents under varying instructions, histories, and orders. Prefix caching fails to exploit this reuse, and position-independent caching (PIC) is unreliable because independently compiled KV states lack the future context in which they will be consumed.

Method: SemPIC trains a LoRA-enabled Writer to compile native per-layer document KV states through behavioral distillation, while the pretrained decoder remains an unchanged Reader. Adaptation is confined to offline cache construction, preserving the standard KV interface. A learned boundary-conditioned baseline diagnoses attention deviation near reusable-block boundaries. KV Gradient Checkpointing reduces peak training memory without severing gradients through cached KVs.

Result: Across three models and four tasks, SemPIC improves mean micro-F1 over KV Packet from 0.53 to 0.60, approaching Full Recompute at 0.62.

Conclusion: SemPIC effectively bridges the gap between efficient KV caching and full recomputation by adapting document representations offline, enabling reliable position-independent reuse with minimal performance degradation.

Abstract: Long-context retrieval and agentic workloads repeatedly reuse the same documents under changing instructions, histories, and document orders. Prefix caching cannot exploit this reuse, while position-independent caching (PIC) remains unreliable because independently compiled KV states lack the future context in which they will be consumed. Our diagnostics show that a learned boundary-conditioned baseline sharply reduces attention deviation near reusable-block boundaries but leaves interior and task-level residuals, motivating adaptation of the document representation itself. We present \emph{SemPIC}, which trains a LoRA-enabled Writer to compile native per-layer document KVs through behavioral distillation while retaining the pretrained decoder as an unchanged Reader. Adaptation is confined to offline cache construction, preserving the standard KV interface and cache-hit decoding path. We further introduce KV Gradient Checkpointing, which reduces peak training memory without severing gradients through cached KVs. Across three models and four tasks, SemPIC raises mean micro-F1 over KV Packet from 0.53 to 0.60, approaching Full Recompute at 0.62.

</details>


### [169] [Echoverse: Deep, Evolving Environments for Training Computer-Use Agents at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28074)
*Yash Pandya,Sahil Gupta,Sarthak Harne,Archana Yadav,Kavyansh Chourasia,Hussein Mozannar,Vibhav Vineet,Sara Abdali,Corby Rosset,Yash Lara,Ahmed Awadallah,Ece Kamar,Akshay Nambi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Echoverse is a system that generates stateful, login-gated synthetic environments for training computer-use agents, featuring a co-evolution loop that simultaneously repairs environments and trains models. A 9B model trained on 12 Echoverse environments reaches 67.1% accuracy (within 14 points of its frontier teacher), with deep environments, targeted failure interaction, and environment-model co-improvement identified as key drivers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training computer-use agents requires interactive applications, but real-world applications are login-gated and stateful, making them impractical for large-scale training. While recent pipelines can generate synthetic environments in bulk, the bottleneck has shifted from quantity to quality — specifically, what is inside each environment. The authors identify three critical properties that determine training returns: behavioral depth, targeting of actual failure interactions, and co-improvement with the model.

Method: Echoverse compiles specifications into stateful applications with tasks graded against each application's own database. It employs a co-evolution loop that processes every graded rollout twice: (1) as repair signals to improve the environment, its tasks, and its verifier; (2) as training signal for the model. The system supports both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, using a reward that combines a grounded verifier with a dense per-step judge.

Result: A 9B model trained on 12 Echoverse environments improves from 36.5% to 67.1% across 14 evaluation splits, within 14 points of the frontier teacher model. Deep environments raise live-site accuracy (80.0→85.0 and 48.0→65.0) while shallow ones hurt it (80.0→75.0). Drilling one interface control across renderings transfers to held-out widgets and the open web. Repairing a single environment lifts trained model accuracy from 16.2% to 38.5%. RL with the combined reward raises held-out scores from 58.8% to 68.0%.

Conclusion: Behavioral depth, targeted failure interaction, and co-evolution between environment and model are essential for effective computer-use agent training. The authors release four environments with applications, seed data, and grounded graders as a benchmark.

Abstract: Computer-use agents learn from what their actions change, so training one needs applications it can act on, break and reset. The applications that matter most are login-gated and stateful, so synthetic environments stand in for them. Recent pipelines generate such environments in bulk, which moves the bottleneck from how many exist to what is inside each one. The returns, we find, come from three properties: how much behavioural depth an environment carries, whether it targets the interaction an agent actually fails, and whether it improves alongside the model. We present Echoverse, which compiles specifications into stateful applications whose tasks are graded against the application's own database, and a co-evolution loop that reads every graded rollout twice: as repairs to the environment, its tasks and its verifier, and as training signal for the model. Trained on twelve such environments, a 9B model improves from $36.5\%$ to $67.1\%$ across fourteen evaluation splits, within fourteen points of the much larger frontier model that taught it. We examine each property in turn. On the same domains, shallow environments push live-site accuracy below the base model ($80.0 \to 75.0$) while deep ones raise it ($80.0 \to 85.0$ and $48.0 \to 65.0$); drilling one interface control across many renderings transfers to held-out widget families and to the open web; and repairing a single environment lifts the model trained on it from $16.2\%$ to $38.5\%$. The same worlds serve as reinforcement-learning environments, where a reward combining the grounded verifier with a dense per-step judge raises held-out score from $58.8\%$ to $68.0\%$. We release four environments as a benchmark, with their applications, seed data and grounded graders. Code: https://aka.ms/echoverse

</details>


### [170] [Group-Reflective Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28076)
*Binbin Zheng,Zijun Xie,Guanqun Zhao,Enlei Gong,Xing Ma,Xiaoliang Fu,Zeyu Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GRSD improves RLVR for LLM agents by deriving capability-aligned, outcome-discriminative guidance from on-policy trajectory groups, using contrastive reflection between successes and failures to refine turn-level credit assignment via a self-teacher.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Terminal rewards in RLVR provide only coarse trajectory-level supervision, entangling successful behaviors, recurring mistakes, and incidental choices. Existing self-distillation methods that use externally retrieved or single-trajectory extracted skills can mismatch the policy's current capability or remain path-specific. There is a need for guidance that is both aligned with the policy's capability and discriminative of outcomes.

Method: GRSD operates per prompt: (1) the policy reflects on each trajectory in an on-policy group of verified rollouts; (2) a stop-gradient snapshot contrasts reflections from successful vs. failed rollouts to construct group-level privileged guidance; (3) a self-teacher conditions on this guidance to refine turn-level credit assignment by modulating outcome-based advantages while preserving the verifier-determined learning direction.

Result: Experiments across multiple agentic environments and model scales show that GRSD consistently outperforms competitive baselines and generalizes more effectively to unseen tasks.

Conclusion: Capability-aligned, outcome-discriminative guidance derived from on-policy group reflection significantly improves RLVR for LLM agents, yielding both stronger performance and better generalization than existing approaches.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is effective for training large language model agents. However, terminal rewards provide only coarse trajectory-level supervision, leaving successful behaviors, recurring mistakes, and incidental choices entangled in the same outcome signal. Existing agentic self-distillation methods enrich sparse supervision with natural-language skills, but skills retrieved externally or extracted from a single trajectory by stronger models may mismatch current experience, exceed the policy's capability, or remain path-specific. We propose Group-Reflective Self-Distillation (GRSD), which derives capability-aligned and outcome-discriminative guidance from the policy's own verified rollouts. For each prompt, the policy reflects on each verified trajectory in an on-policy group, and a stop-gradient snapshot contrasts the resulting reflections from successful and failed rollouts to construct group-level privileged guidance. Conditioned on this guidance, a self-teacher refines turn-level credit assignment by modulating outcome-based advantages while preserving the verifier-determined learning direction. Experiments across multiple agentic environments and model scales demonstrate that GRSD consistently outperforms competitive baselines and generalizes more effectively to unseen tasks.

</details>


### [171] [Distilling Answer Set Programming Theories from Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28086)
*Nelson Higuera Ruiz,Markus Hofmarcher,Claudiu Leoveanu-Condrei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether large language models can autonomously generate complete and correct Answer Set Programming (ASP) theories from scratch within a 1-hour time limit, using a neurosymbolic approach with a solver in the loop. Tested on three VQA benchmarks (CLEVR, GQA, CLEVRER), three of four frontier models achieve near-perfect accuracy on CLEVR and GQA, and strong results on CLEVRER, while GPT-5 shows surprising brittleness, especially when provided with reference theories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manually writing ASP theories is difficult and time-consuming. The authors aim to explore whether modern LLMs, operating within a fixed agent harness and solver loop, can autonomously and efficiently distill complete, correct ASP theories from scratch — a task that requires both reasoning and program synthesis capabilities.

Method: A neurosymbolic protocol is employed: models receive a single prompt and an empty file, then iteratively refine ASP theories with a solver in the loop under a 1-hour constraint. Nine models spanning frontier (Claude Sonnet, Claude Opus, GPT-5, DeepSeek V4 Pro), mid-tier, and open-weights categories are evaluated on three VQA benchmarks (CLEVR, GQA, CLEVRER). An ablation adds handwritten reference theories from other datasets to test robustness.

Result: Three frontier models (Sonnet, Opus, DeepSeek V4 Pro) achieve 100% on CLEVR, 92.8%–98.8% on GQA, and 92.7%–95.3% on CLEVRER. GPT-5 reaches 98.7% on CLEVR but drops sharply to 41.8% on GQA and 86.7% on CLEVRER. When provided with reference theories from other datasets, the three robust frontier models show at most ±3.4 pp variation, while GPT-5 degrades by 3–19 pp.

Conclusion: Frontier LLMs can autonomously synthesize correct ASP theories for non-trivial VQA benchmarks, but performance is model-dependent and not strictly correlated with scale. GPT-5 exhibits notable brittleness, especially under distribution shift from reference theories. The released artifacts (code, prompts, theories) provide a benchmark for future neurosymbolic program synthesis research.

Abstract: Writing Answer Set Programming (ASP) theories from scratch is a difficult and time-consuming task. We take a neurosymbolic approach to study whether a model can distill complete and correct theories, given a fixed agent harness with the solver in the loop. The protocol is dataset-agnostic: with a single prompt and an empty file as the starting point the model is given a 1-hour time limit to derive a complete theory. We chose VQA as the application domain, three benchmarks (CLEVR, GQA, CLEVRER), as these are publicly available and non-trivial. In order to study the model scale required for solving this task we nine different models: four frontier (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5, DeepSeek V4 Pro), two mid-tier (DeepSeek V4 Flash, gpt-oss-120b), and three open-weights (qwen3.6-27b, gpt-oss-20b, qwen3.5-9b). Three of four frontier models reach 100% on CLEVR and 92.8%-98.8% on GQA; on CLEVRER, Sonnet, Opus, DeepSeek V4 Pro score 92.7%-95.3%. GPT-5 reaches 98.7% on CLEVR but drops to 41.8% on GQA and to 86.7% on CLEVRER. Adding handwritten reference theories from other datasets moves the other three frontier models by at most +/-3.4 pp but reduces GPT-5's accuracy by 3-19 pp. We release the code, prompts, and theories distilled.

</details>


### [172] [Diversifying Personalized Research Ideation against AI-Induced Homogenization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28087)
*Rui Xu,Yunke Wang,Linwei Tao,Wenjie Xuan,Yong Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DivAlign is a four-stage pipeline that generates personalized AI research directions for individual researchers while simultaneously reducing thematic redundancy across the broader research community, addressing the problem of homogenization in AI-assisted ideation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI research ideation systems suffer from two key blind spots: (1) coarse researcher representations produce generic, mainstream suggestions lacking individual grounding, and (2) independent recommendations lead to community-wide portfolio concentration around high-probability themes. Both issues contribute to homogenization of research agendas.

Method: DivAlign employs a four-stage pipeline: (1) extraction of fine-grained researcher profiles, (2) generation of profile-conditioned candidate research directions, (3) scoring along three alignment dimensions—Executability, Comprehensibility, and Growth Potential, and (4) selection of researcher-local directions while minimizing community-level redundancy. Evaluation uses a benchmark of 95 AI researchers across five subfields.

Result: DivAlign reduces community-level redundancy while preserving researcher-direction fit. Compared to coarse single-shot ideation, average pairwise similarity drops from 0.331 to 0.294 and nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.704 to 0.608. Against the independent top-choice variant, nearest-neighbor similarity falls from 0.663 to 0.608 while retaining 99.9% of the researcher-direction fit score.

Conclusion: DivAlign demonstrates that alignment-preserving de-homogenization is achievable: fine-grained researcher profiles combined with community-aware selection can diversify research portfolios without sacrificing individual fit, offering a path toward more varied and grounded AI-assisted scientific ideation.

Abstract: AI-assisted research ideation has emerged as a promising paradigm for accelerating scientific discovery, with systems now capable of generating research directions conditioned on papers, topics, or lightweight researcher contexts. Yet current systems largely optimize individual suggestions in isolation. This leaves two blind spots. First, coarse researcher representations may elicit mainstream directions that appear broadly feasible, but lack sufficient researcher-specific grounding. Second, independent recommendations can concentrate a community's portfolio around recurring high-probability themes. To address these blind spots, we propose DivAlign, a four-stage pipeline for alignment-preserving de-homogenization. DivAlign extracts fine-grained researcher profiles, generates profile-conditioned candidate directions, scores them along three alignment dimensions (Executability, Comprehensibility, and Growth Potential), and surfaces researcher-local directions while reducing redundancy across the community portfolio. On a benchmark we construct from 95 AI researchers across five subfields, DivAlign reduces community-level redundancy while preserving researcher-direction fit. Compared with coarse single-shot ideation, it lowers average pairwise similarity from 0.331 to 0.294 and nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.704 to 0.608. Compared with the independent top-choice variant, DivAlign reduces nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.663 to 0.608 while retaining 99.9% of the researcher-direction fit score. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Ruixxxx/DivAlign.

</details>


### [173] [PerturbMap: Cross-Context Transfer of Single-Cell Perturbation Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28090)
*Panpan Cui,Yiqi Liu,Wenhao Sun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PerturbMap predicts missing perturbation effects in a target cellular context by combining a local low-rank base model with transported source-context responses, weighted by route reliability validated on anchors, outperforming baselines on a melanoma Perturb-CITE-seq dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-cell perturbation atlases typically have incomplete coverage: a given perturbation may be measured in some cellular contexts but missing in others where its effect is needed. Existing approaches either discard the available source-context measurements (wasting experimental evidence) or naively copy/calibrate them across contexts (risking signal distortion). A principled method is needed to transport perturbation effects across contexts while preserving fidelity.

Method: PerturbMap models a missing recipient-context effect as the sum of (1) a recipient-local low-rank base prediction and (2) accepted transported proposals from source contexts where the same perturbation was measured. Source-to-recipient transport uses ridge regression experts fit on paired training perturbations. Proposal acceptance is gated by route reliability weights estimated on held-out validation anchors. This yields a structured transfer learning framework that selectively incorporates cross-context evidence.

Result: On the Perturb-CITE-seq melanoma cohort, PerturbMap achieves a 4.1% MSE improvement over the recipient-local low-rank base alone and outperforms FedAvg, zero-response, raw-copy, calibrated-copy, and identity-shuffled affine controls. It stays within 2.82×10⁻⁶ MSE of a stronger centralized token-matched pooled reference. Top-10 counterpart retrieval by cosine similarity improves from 74.5% (low-rank base) to 80.5% (PerturbMap) on a condition-mean specificity diagnostic.

Conclusion: PerturbMap effectively transfers perturbation effects across cellular contexts by adaptively weighting transported source responses, yielding meaningful gains in prediction accuracy and specificity over both local-only and naive transfer baselines, while approaching the performance of a centralized pooled model that uses a stronger training interface.

Abstract: Single-cell perturbation atlases rarely measure every intervention in every cellular context: a query perturbation is often observed in one or more source contexts but missing in the recipient context where its effect is needed. Ignoring those measured responses discards query-specific experimental evidence, whereas copying or weakly calibrating them across contexts risks transferring the wrong signal. We propose PerturbMap, which predicts a missing recipient-context effect by combining a recipient-local low-rank base with accepted proposals that transport the same perturbation's measured source responses through source-to-recipient ridge experts fit on paired training perturbations, with proposal weights determined by route reliability estimated on validation anchors. On the Perturb-CITE-seq melanoma cohort, PerturbMap improves full-effect MSE by 4.1\% over a recipient-local low-rank base and achieves lower MSE than FedAvg, zero-response, raw-copy, calibrated-copy, and identity-shuffled affine controls. It remains within $2.82\times10^{-6}$ MSE of our centralized token-matched pooled reference, which uses a stronger training interface. A condition-mean specificity diagnostic shows the same direction: same-recipient top-10 counterpart retrieval by cosine increases from 74.5\% for the low-rank base to 80.5\% for PerturbMap.

</details>


### [174] [An Instrument to Evaluate Governance Proposals: AI Policy Analysis at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28094)
*Paulo Carvao,Claudio Mayrink Verdun,Isabel Adler,Jeffrey Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a transparent, rubric-based framework for analyzing AI governance proposals across multiple policy attributes, using mixed methods (expert input + computational text analysis) to surface tradeoffs rather than prescribe outcomes, and benchmarks commercial LLMs against a domain-trained rubric-calibrated model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI policy debates tend to collapse into binary positions that hide underlying tradeoffs and normative assumptions. There is a need for a systematic, transparent framework that structures analysis around multiple attributes, making priorities and tensions explicit without dictating which policy is "better."

Method: A mixed-methods approach: (1) qualitative insights from subject matter experts inform the design of policy attribute rubrics; (2) computational text analysis quantifies the relative emphasis of different policy objectives; (3) comparative visualizations support interpretability and cross-policy comparison; (4) commercial LLMs are benchmarked against a domain-trained, rubric-calibrated model with explicitly defined analytical assumptions for rubric-based policy analysis.

Result: The framework produces multidimensional policy assessments that surface tradeoffs rather than resolve them. It demonstrates a transparent hybrid methodology combining SME feedback with computational validation. The rubric-calibrated model serves as a benchmark for evaluating how general-purpose LLMs perform on rubric-based policy analysis tasks.

Conclusion: The jurisdiction-agnostic framework enables policymakers, analysts, and researchers to evaluate whether a framework's embedded priorities align with their own normative commitments. By making attribute selection, rubric construction, and weighting schemes explicit, it supports relevance-and-alignment-focused analysis rather than assessing policy effectiveness or desirability.

Abstract: This paper introduces a policy analysis framework for systematic, transparent assessment of AI governance proposals in an evolving and contested regulatory landscape. AI policy debates often collapse into binary positions that obscure underlying tradeoffs and normative assumptions. The framework structures policy analysis around multiple policy attributes, allowing users to surface priorities and tensions without prescribing outcomes. We use a mixed-methods approach that integrates qualitative insights from subject matter experts with computational text analysis to inform the design of policy attribute rubrics. This quantifies the relative emphasis of different policy objectives and presents them through comparative visualizations that support interpretability and cross-policy comparison. The paper also examines the use of commercial LLMs for rubric-based policy analysis, benchmarking their outputs against a domain-trained rubric-calibrated model with explicitly defined analytical assumptions. Rather than assessing policy effectiveness or desirability, the framework focuses on relevance and alignment across attributes. By making analytical assumptions explicit, including attribute selection, rubric construction, and weighting schemes, the framework enables users to evaluate whether its embedded priorities align with the users' own normative commitments. The approach is jurisdiction-agnostic and intended to support policymakers, analysts, and researchers navigating complex AI governance environments.
  Contributions: (1) multidimensional policy assessment through empirically grounded rubrics that surface tradeoffs rather than resolving them; (2) a transparent hybrid methodology combining feedback from subject-matter experts with computational validation; and (3) use of domain-trained rubric-calibrated models as a benchmark for comparing different general-purpose large language models.

</details>


### [175] [SciDataSailor: Deep Scientific Data Exploring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28098)
*Jiyong Rao,Yicheng Qiu,Chi Zhang,Chunfeng Song,Runkai Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SciDataSailor introduces a paradigm called Deep Scientific Data Exploration, where LLM agents navigate hierarchical scientific repositories, interpret heterogeneous files, execute analyses, and synthesize cross-file evidence. The framework uses Monte Carlo Tree Search with four novel mechanisms to synthesize tool-interactive trajectories, producing training (SciDataSailor-SFT-2K) and benchmark (SciDataSailor-Bench) datasets across 27 scientific datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific datasets are organized as hierarchical repositories with heterogeneous, interdependent files, making inspection, integration, and analysis labor-intensive. While LLM agents excel at planning, reasoning, and tool use, existing research overlooks their ability to interact with real scientific data assets through executable environments. This gap motivates the need for agentic exploration of scientific data.

Method: The authors propose SciDataSailor, which frames trajectory synthesis as Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with four task-specific mechanisms: (1) difficulty-stratified exploration seeds to ensure diverse starting points, (2) dual-feedback first-play urgency to balance exploration and exploitation, (3) hierarchical strategy-to-tool action generation for structured decision-making, and (4) entropy-guided branching to prioritize informative paths. This framework synthesizes tool-interactive trajectories used to build SciDataSailor-SFT-2K (supervised fine-tuning) and SciDataSailor-Bench (evaluation).

Result: The framework produces SciDataSailor-Bench with 627 meta-information summarization tasks and 586 scientific question-answering tasks spanning 27 datasets across life, earth, and physical sciences. SciDataSailor-SFT-2K provides 2,000 trajectories for supervised fine-tuning of LLM agents.

Conclusion: SciDataSailor establishes a structured paradigm and framework for deep scientific data exploration, enabling LLM agents to autonomously navigate, interpret, and analyze complex scientific data repositories through MCTS-guided trajectory synthesis.

Abstract: Scientific datasets are commonly organized as hierarchical repositories containing heterogeneous and interdependent files, making their inspection, integration, and analysis labor-intensive and reliant on domain expertise. Although large language model (LLM) agents have advanced substantially in planning, reasoning, and tool use, existing research has largely overlooked their ability to interact with real scientific data assets through executable environments. We introduce Deep Scientific Data Exploration, an agentic task paradigm in which agents navigate repositories, interpret heterogeneous files and schemas, execute analyses, integrate cross-file evidence, and produce conclusions grounded in executed observations. To operationalize this paradigm, we present SciDataSailor, a framework for synthesizing tool-interactive trajectories by balancing broad exploration with targeted exploitation. SciDataSailor instantiates trajectory synthesis as Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with four task-specific mechanisms: difficulty-stratified exploration seeds, dual-feedback first-play urgency, hierarchical strategy-to-tool action generation, and entropy-guided branching. Using this framework, we construct SciDataSailor-SFT-2K for supervised fine-tuning and SciDataSailor-Bench for evaluation, with the latter comprising 627 meta-information summarization tasks and 586 scientific question-answering tasks across 27 datasets spanning the life, earth, and physical sciences.

</details>


### [176] [MIND: Lightweight and Effective Memory Injection Defense for LLM Agents via Intent-Aware Information Bottleneck](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28103)
*Dongyi Liu,Haixing He,Xiaobao Wu,Jia Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MIND is a lightweight defense against memory injection attacks on LLM agents. It uses an intent-aware Information Bottleneck to extract compact intent-behavior representations, filtering redundant information while preserving attack signals, enabling efficient malicious memory detection without repeated LLM auditing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Memory-augmented LLM agents are vulnerable to memory injection attacks where poisoned memories divert agent behavior. Existing defenses are either computationally expensive or suffer from information redundancy in multi-turn contexts.

Method: MIND employs an intent-aware Information Bottleneck (IB) that extracts compact representations capturing the relationship between initial user intent and turn-level behavior. The IB preserves intent-relevant cross-turn attack signals while filtering task-irrelevant and repetitive information. A lightweight detector then identifies malicious memories from these representations.

Result: On ReAct-StrategyQA, MIND reduces mean ASR-r and ASR-a by 55.4% and 55.3% respectively, while matching the undefended agent in average accuracy and latency.

Conclusion: MIND effectively defends against memory injection attacks by mitigating information redundancy without incurring the overhead of repeated LLM auditing, achieving strong attack mitigation while preserving task performance and inference efficiency.

Abstract: Memory-augmented LLM-based agents are vulnerable to memory injection attacks: Agents may retrieve poisoned memory from attackers, which diverts their behavior from initial user intent and finally causes task failure. However, existing defense mechanisms either incur high computational cost or suffer from information redundancy in multi-turn contexts. To address these challenges, we propose Memory Intent-Aware Neural Denoising(MIND), a lightweight defense framework for memory injection attack. Our preliminary analysis reveals that benign and poisoned trajectories exhibit distinguishable relationships between the initial user intent and subsequent behavior. Building on this observation, MIND employs an intent-aware Information Bottleneck(IB) to extract compact intent--behavior representations from the initial intent and turn-level behavior. The IB preserves intent-relevant cross-turn attack signals while filtering task-irrelevant and repetitive information, and a lightweight detector identifies malicious memories from the resulting representations. As such, MIND mitigates information redundancy in multi-turn contexts while avoiding the overhead of repeated LLM auditing. Extensive experiments show that MIND reduces attack success rates while preserving task accuracy and inference efficiency. Notably, on ReAct-StrategyQA, MIND reduces mean ASR-r and ASR-a by 55.4% and 55.3%, respectively, while matching the undefended agent in average accuracy and latency.

</details>


### [177] [Beyond Rephrasing: Book-Level Organization Improves Synthetic Textbook Data for Mid-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28109)
*Jiawen Tao,Miao Peng,Yaoming Li,Xiaokun Yuan,Mengzhou Wu,Wenhan Yu,Guoan Wang,Nuo Chen,Tong Yang,Maxm Pan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Synthetic textbooks improve language model pre-training not just through content quality, but through their book-level document organization. The authors build a pipeline that creates 686K coherent textbooks (32B tokens) and show via controlled experiments that packaging related content into structured books yields significant downstream gains (+1.02–1.17) over equivalent content in fragmented or rephrased formats.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on synthetic textbook data for LM pre-training has focused on content quality and local rewriting style, overlooking whether organizing related content into coherent, book-length documents matters. This paper investigates document-level organization as an independent factor in synthetic pre-training data design.

Method: The authors develop a scalable synthesis pipeline: (1) retrieve source material from a pre-training corpus, (2) cluster it into topical units, (3) plan hierarchical tables of contents, and (4) assemble source-grounded sections into complete textbooks. This yields 686K books (32B tokens) across 15,000+ disciplines (Full condition). Controlled comparisons include: a Split condition (same content but sections treated as independent documents), a RandomConcat control (sections from different books joined, matching length), and a Rephrase condition (individual documents rewritten under the same style scheme without clustering, TOC planning, or book assembly). Experiments use mid-training mixing with Llama models.

Result: Replacing natural books with the synthetic corpus improves downstream performance by +1.09 on average. Controlled comparisons isolate document packaging: Full outperforms Split by +1.02, Full outperforms RandomConcat (ruling out document length as the sole driver), and Full outperforms Rephrase by +1.17, demonstrating the value of structured synthesis. On Llama3-8B, Full also surpasses both RandomConcat and Natural Books.

Conclusion: Book-level document organization is a significant and independent axis for synthetic pre-training data design. Coherent structuring of related content into full textbooks provides gains beyond content quality, rewriting style, or document length alone.

Abstract: Synthetic textbook data has improved language model pre-training, but prior work largely treats the benefit as a property of generated content or local rewriting style. We study a different factor: whether related content is organized into coherent book-level documents. We contribute both a scalable synthesis pipeline and controlled evidence that this organization matters. The pipeline retrieves source material from a pre-training corpus, clusters it into topical units, plans hierarchical tables of contents, and assembles source-grounded sections into complete books (our Full setting), yielding 686K textbooks (32B tokens) across 15,000+ disciplines. Replacing natural books in a mid-training mix with this corpus improves downstream performance by +1.09 on average. Controlled comparisons then disentangle the relevant design factors. A content-matched Split condition holds generated text and tokens fixed but treats each section as an independent document; Full's +1.02 mean gain isolates document packaging. A length-matched RandomConcat control that joins sections from different books remains below Full, ruling out document length alone. A retrieval-pool-matched Rephrase condition independently rewrites individual retrieved documents under the same audience-by-style scheme, without clustering, TOC planning, or book assembly; Full's +1.17 gain demonstrates the value of structured synthesis. On Llama3-8B, Full likewise outperforms both RandomConcat and Natural Books, supporting book-level organization as a useful axis for synthetic pre-training data design.

</details>


### [178] [BlueprintRepair: Typed Local Edits for Failed Lean Proof Blueprints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28110)
*Ruslan Khrulev*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BlueprintRepair introduces a structured, schema-checked interface for repairing Lean proof blueprints via ten local graph operations. Tested on BlueprintTrace (142 controlled failures), typed edits match free-form patching/rewriting in solving localized failures but are significantly cheaper (1.30x vs patching, 2.06x vs rewriting) and converge within fewer completion tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based Lean proving systems often organize proofs as dependency graphs (blueprints), but existing repair approaches use free-form source patches or full rewrites that lack structural guarantees. The authors aim to provide a constrained repair interface that prevents unintended changes to target theorems, enforces dependency integrity via schema checking, and reduces token costs.

Method: BlueprintRepair defines ten local, schema-checked graph operations for modifying proof blueprints, where each operation names the node it edits to preserve the target theorem. Lean checks every applied change, and accepted repairs must declare all dependent blueprint lemmas. The authors construct BlueprintTrace, a benchmark of 142 controlled failures with complete accepted/rejected repair trajectories. Three interfaces — typed edits, exact source patches, and complete module rewrites — are compared under matched source, feedback, model, and budget using one episode per state. Two models are evaluated: DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3.6-Flash.

Result: With DeepSeek-V4-Flash, all three interfaces solve nearly identical numbers of localized failures. Typed repair is cheapest per solved state (patching costs 1.30x more, rewriting 2.06x more). Within 10,000 completion tokens per task, typed repair reaches nearly all its final coverage, while free-form interfaces lag behind. Qwen3.6-Flash solves fewer states overall but maintains typed repair as the cheapest interface, places it ahead on proof-authoring states, and reproduces the localized efficiency pattern.

Conclusion: Typed, schema-checked repair operations are competitive with free-form approaches on localized proof failures while offering substantial cost savings and faster convergence. The structured interface provides safety guarantees (target theorem preservation, dependency declaration enforcement) without sacrificing repair capability, making it a practical choice for LLM-based proof engineering.

Abstract: LLM-based Lean proving systems increasingly organize a proof as a blueprint: a dependency graph of formal statements. We introduce BlueprintRepair, a repair interface that lets a model change this graph through ten schema-checked local operations. An operation names the node it edits, so the target theorem cannot be changed. Lean checks every applied change, and an accepted repair must declare every blueprint lemma its proof uses. We also construct BlueprintTrace, a benchmark of 142 controlled failures with complete accepted and rejected repair trajectories. We compare typed edits, exact source patches, and complete module rewrites under matched source, feedback, model, and budget, one episode per state and interface. With DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the three interfaces solve almost the same number of the benchmark's localized failures. Typed repair is the cheapest per solved state (patching is 1.30x as expensive, rewriting 2.06x), and within 10,000 completion tokens per task it reaches almost all of its final coverage, while both free-form interfaces are well behind. A second model, Qwen3.6-Flash, solves fewer states but keeps typed repair cheapest, puts it ahead on the proof-authoring states, and repeats the localized pattern.

</details>


### [179] [ConMem: Contribution-Aware Memory for Long-Horizon Manufacturing Inspection Logs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28126)
*Bingchen Liu,Yuanyuan Fang,Lei Liu,Guangyuan Dong,Xing Fu,Yuanyuan Gao,Shuyue Wei,Xin Li,Xiangtian Meng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ConMem is a contribution-aware memory framework that prioritizes high-value inspection evidence using Shapley-style estimation, achieving 76% QA accuracy while reducing input tokens by 88.2% and response time by 86.6%, and successfully retaining weak early degradation signals across multiple inspection cycles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon steel equipment inspection requires reasoning over heterogeneous records from multiple inspection cycles. Existing RAG systems treat historical logs as static corpora without estimating diagnostic value, causing them to miss early risk signals. There is a need for a memory system that can identify and retain diagnostically valuable evidence under constrained budgets.

Method: ConMem operates in three stages: (1) functional-role-aware segmentation that splits inspection logs into functional evidence units, (2) Shapley-style contribution estimation to quantify each memory unit's diagnostic value for downstream tasks, and (3) selective retention of high-value evidence under a constrained memory budget to support a human-in-the-loop early-risk screening system.

Result: ConMem achieves 76.0% QA accuracy on a real-world dataset, outperforming the strongest directly comparable baseline. Compared to naive 8K-context LLM baselines, it reduces average input tokens by 88.2% and response time by 86.6%. Ablation studies confirm that both functional-role-aware segmentation and contribution-based valuation help prioritize weak degradation signals. Practical deployments show ConMem retains weak early signals across three inspection cycles, enabling early-stage seal-wear alerts for on-site inspectors.

Conclusion: ConMem provides an effective memory framework for LLM-assisted long-horizon equipment inspection by prioritizing diagnostically valuable evidence. It enables early-risk detection that conventional RAG systems miss, with demonstrated practical utility in real-world steel equipment inspection deployments.

Abstract: Long-horizon steel-equipment inspection requires reasoning over heterogeneous records accumulated across repeated inspection cycles. Existing retrieval-augmented generation systems treat historical logs as a static corpus and retain records without estimating their diagnostic value, failing to report early risk. To this end, we propose ConMem, a contribution-aware memory framework for LLM-assisted equipment inspection, supporting a human-in-the-loop early-risk screening system. Specifically, our ConMem first segments inspection logs into functional evidence units, then estimates each memory unit's contribution to downstream diagnosis through a Shapley-style estimation, and finally retains high-value evidence under a constrained memory budget.
