In experiments, we evaluate ConMem on real-world dataset and ConMem achieves 76.0% QA accuracy, exceeding the strongest directly comparable baseline. Relative to the naive 8K-context LLM baselines, it reduces the average number of input tokens by 88.2% and response time by 86.6%. Ablation studies also show that the functional-role-aware segmentation and contribution-based valuation are helping prioritize weak degradation signals for targeted field inspection. Practical deployments further confirm that ConMem retains the weak early signal across three inspection cycles, providing an early-stage seal-wear alert targeted for on-site inspectors.

</details>


### [180] [CDAE: Enhancing Perturbation Robustness in Pretrained Language Models with Contrastive Denoising](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28236)
*Sina Heydari,Amirreza Abbasi,Mohsen Hooshmand,Majid Ramezani*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CDAE refines BERT embeddings via contrastive learning and denoising autoencoding to achieve perturbation-invariant sentence representations, outperforming both raw BERT and SimCSE in embedding stability under semantic-preserving perturbations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pre-trained language model embeddings, while effective, are brittle to semantically neutral perturbations like synonym substitution, masking, and word dropout. There is a need for lightweight methods that can stabilize these representations without sacrificing semantic fidelity.

Method: A lightweight Contrastive Denoising Autoencoder (CDAE) that jointly optimizes a contrastive loss (pulling perturbed views of the same sentence together) and a reconstruction loss (recovering the original sentence from its perturbed version), applied as a post-hoc refinement on top of frozen BERT embeddings.

Result: CDAE consistently yields higher embedding similarity under perturbation compared to original BERT embeddings and SimCSE baselines, with gains increasing under stronger perturbation intensities, demonstrating enhanced representation stability while retaining semantic information.

Conclusion: The framework effectively improves sentence embedding stability through perturbation-invariant learning, positioning contrastive-denoising as a promising direction for robust sentence representation. Code is open-sourced.

Abstract: Pre-trained language models have significantly improved sentence representation learning, yet their embedding remain sensitive to semantic preserving textual perturbations such as synonym substitution, masking and word dropout. This work proposes a lightweight Contrastive Denoising Autoencoder (CDAE) that refines pre-trained BERT embedding by jointly optimizing contrastive and reconstruction objective to learn perturbation-invariant representation. We evaluate the proposed framework using multiple perturbation strategies with varying strengths and compare it against the original BERT embeddings and SimCSE. Experimental results show that CDAE consistently preserves higher embedding similarity under perturbations, with the improvements becoming more pronounced as framework effectively enhances representation stability while preserving semantic information, highlighting perturbation-invariant learning as a promising direction for improving sentence embeddings. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ComputationIASBS/CDAE

</details>


### [181] [AgenticASR: Refining Speech Recognition in Real-World Scenarios via an Agentic Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28175)
*Zixuan Jiang,Binghao Qiang,Jiaying Chi,Yanqiao Zhu,Kai Yu,Xie Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Agentic Speech Recognition (AgenticSR), a task that transcribes speech into clean, intent-preserving text by removing disfluencies and resolving self-corrections in real time. The proposed AgenticASR system uses an ASR-Refiner architecture that continuously revises output as new audio arrives, operates on unbounded streams, and achieves state-of-the-art results on a new bilingual benchmark (AASR-Bench) validated by human expert agreement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Verbatim ASR transcripts retain disfluencies (fillers, repetitions, false starts, self-corrections) that increase reading effort, obscure speaker intent, and degrade downstream task performance. Existing spoken-to-written methods operate on completed audio/transcripts and cannot revise earlier output when later speech recontextualizes it. This motivates a streaming, intent-preserving transcription paradigm.

Method: AgenticASR employs an ASR-Refiner architecture: an ASR front end produces initial transcripts, and a Refiner component iteratively transforms a bounded active context window, replacing corresponding output spans as new audio arrives. This enables continual emission and revision over arbitrary-duration streams. The system is evaluated on AASR-Bench, a newly introduced bilingual benchmark with fine-grained atomic rubrics, validated via a human-AI agreement study against independent expert judgments.

Result: AgenticASR achieves the highest AASR-Bench scores among all evaluated systems across multiple ASR front ends. The human-AI agreement study confirms rubric-based automatic evaluations align with expert assessments. Ablation studies characterize the effects of Refiner capacity, context length, and the quality-latency trade-off between online and offline inference modes.

Conclusion: AgenticASR provides a practical framework for streaming, intent-preserving clean transcription. The combination of the AgenticSR formulation, the ASR-Refiner architecture, and the AASR-Bench benchmark establishes a foundation for future work in real-time spoken-to-written conversion.

Abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) has achieved substantial gains in transcription accuracy, yet verbatim transcription does not necessarily produce readily usable text. It retains fillers, repetitions, false starts, and self-corrections that increase reading effort, obscure the speaker's final intent, and propagate unresolved or abandoned content to downstream tasks. Existing spoken-to-written methods process completed audio or transcripts but cannot revise emitted text when later speech changes how preceding content should be interpreted. We therefore formulate Agentic Speech Recognition (AgenticSR), an audio-to-clean-text task that removes disfluencies, resolves self-corrections, and normalizes written form while preserving the speaker's final intent. AgenticASR implements this task through an ASR--Refiner architecture that repeatedly transforms a bounded active context and replaces its corresponding output span as audio arrives. This enables continual emission and revision over streams of arbitrary duration. We also introduce AASR-Bench, a bilingual benchmark with fine-grained atomic rubrics. Across multiple ASR front ends, AgenticASR attains the highest AASR-Bench scores among evaluated systems. A human--AI agreement study shows that rubric-based judgments align with independent expert assessments. Ablations characterize Refiner capacity, context length, and the quality--latency trade-off between online and offline inference. Together, these results establish AgenticASR as a practical framework for intent-preserving clean transcription during ongoing speech. Code, AASR-Bench, and a demo will be released at https://github.com/AnXMuy/AgenticASR.

</details>


### [182] [WIDE: Boosting Adaptive LLM Inference via Token-level Dynamic Width Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28418)
*Haozhe Hu,Hao Wu,Peiran Yin,Chao Han,Yunpu Ma,Xiaoyu Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WIDE is an end-to-end differentiable token-level dynamic width pruning framework for LLMs that enables fine-grained, neuron-block-level sparsity, coupled with a pruning-kernel co-design for practical acceleration, achieving up to 1.98x (prefill) and 4.95x (decoding) kernel speedups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Static structured pruning is hardware-friendly but suffers accuracy degradation under aggressive sparsity due to input-agnostic computation. Dynamic sparsity methods improve quality but remain coarse-grained (layer-level) and struggle with practical real-world acceleration. WIDE bridges this gap by enabling fine-grained, token-level dynamic pruning that is both quality-preserving and practically fast.

Method: WIDE proposes: (1) a differentiable token-level pruning framework where each token dynamically selects attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups (neuron-block granularity); (2) a two-stage training pipeline to learn token-wise sparse execution patterns; and (3) a pruning-kernel co-design that decomposes dynamic sparsity acceleration into mask reordering, hardware-agnostic block-level skipping, and hardware-dependent intra-block skipping for efficient execution.

Result: At 50% sparsity, WIDE achieves a 55.1% performance boost over state-of-the-art dynamic depth pruning (calibration-only). Under inference workloads: kernel-level speedups of 1.98x (prefill) and 4.95x (decoding), with end-to-end acceleration of 1.68x and 1.55x respectively.

Conclusion: WIDE successfully combines fine-grained dynamic pruning granularity with practical kernel-level acceleration, outperforming both static structured pruning in quality retention and existing dynamic sparsity methods in real-world speedups across both prefill and decoding phases.

Abstract: Pruning is a promising approach for improving the efficiency of LLMs. Existing static structured pruning methods are hardware-friendly and can deliver practical throughput gains, but their input-agnostic computation allocation often causes substantial accuracy degradation under aggressive sparsity. Recent dynamic sparsity methods improve quality retention by adapting computation to individual inputs, yet they remain largely limited to coarse-grained structural decisions and their practical acceleration under real-world inference scenarios remains challenging. To address these challenges, we present WIDE, the first end-to-end differentiable token-level dynamic width pruning framework designed for both prefill and decode scenarios. WIDE enables fine-grained computation allocation by allowing each token to dynamically select attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups, extending dynamic pruning beyond layer-level decisions to neuron-block-level granularity. Through a two-stage training pipeline, WIDE learns effective token-wise sparse execution patterns and achieves substantially better quality retention than existing approaches. To make such fine-grained dynamic pruning practical, we further propose a pruning--kernel co-design framework that decomposes dynamic sparsity acceleration into mask reordering, hardware-agnostic block-level skipping, and hardware-dependent intra-block skipping, enabling efficient execution across different granularities. At 50% sparsity, WIDE provides 55.1% performance boost when compared to the state-of-the-art dynamic depth pruning under calibration-only settings. Under prefill and decoding inference workloads, WIDE achieves close-to-theoretical kernel-level speedups of up to 1.98x for prefill and 4.95x for decoding, as well as 1.68x and 1.55x end-to-end acceleration. Our code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/LLM-Pruning/tree/main/WIDE.

</details>


### [183] [Qwen-UI-Agent Technical Report: Toward Next-Generation Real-World Centric Foundation GUI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28227)
*Hanzhang Zhou,Panrong Tong,Xu Zhang,Quyu Kong,Chenglin Cai,Tianyu Xia,Gongjie Zhang,Jianan Zhang,Long Li,Long Chen,Lei Wang,Gaole Dai,Pengxiang Li,Liangyu Chen,Yue Wang,Steven Hoi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Qwen-UI-Agent is a foundation GUI agent that operates across mobile, computer, web, and DeepSearch environments. It combines GUI and CLI actions, uses a data flywheel for autonomous improvement, and employs online RL with 10,000+ concurrent environments. It achieves SOTA on mobile benchmarks (82.1% MobileWorld, 92.2% MobileWorld-Real, 97.5% AndroidDaily) and competitive results on computer/browser tasks against frontier models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GUI agents lack reliability on real devices, cross-platform workflow capabilities, combined GUI+CLI interaction, long-horizon task completion, proactive service initiation, and autonomous self-improvement. The authors aim to build a real-world centric agent that addresses all these limitations simultaneously.

Method: The system features: (1) diverse sandbox environments plus a large-scale real-device mobile runtime; (2) a unified action space interleaving GUI operations with CLI execution, generating batched actions per model turn; (3) an AutoResearch-style data flywheel where agents construct tasks/environments, diagnose failures, and plan iterations; (4) online RL training on 100+ turn trajectories with 10,000+ concurrent environments for accelerated rollout; and (5) a lightweight harness layer enabling proactive service initiation and stateful cross-platform workflows.

Result: Mobile-use: 82.1% on MobileWorld, 92.2% on MobileWorld-Real, 97.5% on AndroidDaily. Computer-use: 79.5% on OSWorld-Verified, 40.0% partial-progress on OSWorld-v2. Browser/GUI grounding: 73.6% on WebArena, 81.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro. These results are state-of-the-art on mobile and competitive with frontier models (Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.6 Sol) on computer and browser tasks.

Conclusion: Qwen-UI-Agent demonstrates that a unified, real-world centric foundation GUI agent can achieve leading performance across mobile, computer, and web environments. The combination of real-device runtime, unified action space, autonomous data flywheel, and large-scale online RL provides a viable path toward general-purpose GUI agents suitable for practical deployment.

Abstract: GUI agents have the potential to become a general purpose executor over existing digital devices. To advance them toward real-world use, we envision agents that operate reliably on real devices, execute workflows across platforms, combine GUI interaction with CLI execution, complete long-horizon tasks, proactively initiate useful services, and autonomously improve their capabilities with minimal human effort. Guided by this vision, we present Qwen-UI-Agent, a real-world centric foundation GUI agent spanning mobile, computer-use, web, and DeepSearch environments. Qwen-UI-Agent combines diverse sandbox environments with a large-scale real-device mobile runtime. Its unified action space interleaves GUI operations with CLI execution and generates batched actions in a single model turn. An AutoResearch-style data flywheel uses agents to construct tasks and environments, diagnose failures, and plan subsequent iterations. Online RL supports training on trajectories exceeding 100 turns, with over 10,000 concurrent environments accelerating rollout. A lightweight harness layer supports proactive service initiation and stateful workflows across mobile and computer.
  Across a broad suite of evaluations, Qwen-UI-Agent sets state-of-the-art performance on mobile-use benchmarks while delivering competitive performance on computer- and browser-use tasks against frontier models, including Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.6 Sol. On mobile use, it achieves 82.1% on MobileWorld, 92.2% on MobileWorld-Real, and 97.5% on AndroidDaily. On computer use, it achieves 79.5% on OSWorld-Verified and a 40.0% partial-progress score on OSWorld-v2. On browser use and GUI grounding, it achieves 73.6% on WebArena and 81.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro, respectively.

</details>


### [184] [Metaphor Tracer: A Theory-Informed Analysis of Hidden States](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28434)
*Marc Heimann,Roxana Assadi Moghaddam,Olga Brovkina,Mark Pettifor,Lutz Goetzmann*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates what a language model's hidden states reveal about the organization of a single text, proposing two per-token metrics — aggregator and differentiator — computed in a single forward pass without training. The aggregator identifies token positions that consolidate textual structure, and experiments across three models show it tracks a token's structural role independent of type-level features like surprisal or attention, validated against engineered registers and psychoanalytic annotations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how language models internally represent the organizational structure of a single text, moving beyond type-level (lexical) measures to capture token-level structural properties that are relational and text-specific — operationalizing a theoretical view of meaning as positional rather than essentialist.

Method: Two unsupervised scores are computed from hidden states in one forward pass: the *aggregator* (whether a token position consolidates the whole text into a stable configuration) and the *differentiator* (whether other tokens are transiently carried into its subspace). Constants were frozen on one discovery text; all other texts served as confirmatory. Validation uses: (1) an engineered register with known boundaries, (2) a psychoanalyst's blind annotations of clinical transcripts, and (3) a transfer test comparing models whose token structures do/don't travel with lexical type, including a matched base/instruct pair.

Result: The aggregator is distinct from classic information measures and salience: as a signifier repeats, surprisal and attention drain but aggregator holds — it marks structural place. The aggregator tracks register boundaries (6/6 cells) and matches the psychoanalyst's markings (34/36 cells) with graded increments above lexical controls, a pattern no type-level measure reproduces. In the transfer test, the model whose token structure travels with lexical type reads singular discourse worst; instruction tuning raises fidelity without moving type-transfer. This demonstrates structural value is a property of a token's place in *this* text, not its vector alone.

Conclusion: Hidden states encode a relational, positional organization of text that is irreducible to type-level features. The aggregator operationalizes a pre-existing theoretical stance — that meaning is constituted by a token's place within a specific discourse — and provides empirical evidence that language models capture this structural dimension, with implications for how we interpret model internals and textual coherence.

Abstract: What do a language model's hidden states say about the organization of a single text? From one forward pass, without training, we score every token position on two properties. The *aggregator* measures whether the position consolidates the whole text into a stable configuration. The *differentiator*, whether other tokens are transiently carried into its subspace as the model reads: metaphor in its root sense, transport. Constants were frozen on one discovery text; every other is confirmatory.
  The aggregator is not, in the classic sense, an information measure, nor a measure of salience. Across three unrelated models, as a signifier repeats, its surprisal and its attention drain while its aggregator score holds: the channel marks a token's place in the text. That this tracks a reading rests on independent ground truth: an engineered register the aggregator follows across its boundaries (6/6 cells), and a psychoanalyst's marking of clinical transcripts, fixed before the instrument existed, in 34/36 cells, with a graded increment above lexical controls and dissociations no type-level measure reproduces. A transfer test gives the result its shape: the model whose token structure travels with lexical type reads the singular discourse worst, and in a matched base/instruct pair tuning raises fidelity without moving type-transfer. Structural value is a property of a token's place in *this* text, not of its vector alone: a relational rather than essentialist reading of hidden states, operationalizing theory that predated the instrument.

</details>


### [185] [SVR: Self-Verifying Refinement via Joint Verdict-Confidence Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Test-Time Compute](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28457)
*Hongyu Chen,Liang Lin,Guangrun Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SVR is a multi-turn RL framework that trains a language model to use its own self-verification (correctness verdict + confidence score) as an adaptive stopping policy, achieving strong math reasoning accuracy with far fewer inference turns than fixed-budget methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Uniform test-time compute budgets waste computation on easy inputs, and verifier-guided refinement relies on external feedback. The goal is to learn an internal, oracle-free control signal that enables adaptive compute allocation and autonomous answer retention.

Method: SVR trains a model via GRPO on fixed-horizon trajectories. At each turn, the model outputs a solution, a discrete correctness verdict, and a confidence score. It retains the answer only when verdict=Correct and confidence exceeds a threshold; otherwise it refines. Rewards promote solution correctness, calibration-aware self-verification, and stop-ready correct states. Adaptive stopping is used only at inference; ground-truth correctness is never exposed in prompts or required at inference.

Result: On seven math reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3.5-2B, SVR achieves 0.563 macro-average accuracy with only 2.99 average inference turns. It exceeds standard GRPO, strong multi-turn baselines, and a fixed-budget oracle-guided reference, while requiring substantially fewer turns than fixed ten-turn inference.

Conclusion: Learned self-verification can serve as an effective internal control signal for adaptive test-time compute allocation, enabling efficient and accurate multi-turn reasoning without external feedback or oracle guidance.

Abstract: Scaling test-time computation can improve language-model reasoning, but uniform budgets waste computation on easy inputs, while verifier-guided refinement relies on external feedback. We introduce Self-Verifying Refinement (SVR), an oracle-free multi-turn reinforcement learning framework that learns to use self-verification as a compute-control policy. At each turn, the model produces a solution together with a discrete correctness verdict and a confidence score; it retains the current answer only when the verdict is Correct and confidence exceeds a threshold, and otherwise continues refinement using its own self-verification. Ground-truth correctness is used only to construct training rewards and is never exposed to the policy through refinement prompts or required at inference. SVR is trained with GRPO on fixed-horizon trajectories using rewards that promote solution correctness, calibration-aware self-verification, and stop-ready correct states; adaptive stopping is activated only at inference. On seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3.5-2B, SVR achieves a macro-average accuracy of 0.563 with only 2.99 inference turns on average. In the evaluated complete-system comparison, it exceeds standard GRPO, strong multi-turn baselines, and a fixed-budget oracle-guided score-feedback reference while requiring substantially fewer turns than fixed ten-turn inference. These results demonstrate that learned self-verification can serve as an effective internal control signal for answer retention and adaptive test-time compute allocation.

</details>


### [186] [AI and Authenticity in Islamic Research: A Critical Evaluation of Generative AI Reliability, Hallucination, and Source Fidelity in Quranic, Hadith, and Fiqh Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28237)
*Muhammad Sajjad Akbar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study empirically evaluates six generative AI systems on their ability to provide authentic Islamic knowledge across 50 open-ended questions, finding they are useful as assistive learning tools but not sufficiently reliable as authoritative religious sources without human scholarly verification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite growing Muslim adoption of generative AI for religious guidance, there is limited empirical evidence on the authenticity, verifiability, and trustworthiness of AI-generated Islamic knowledge in high-trust religious contexts.

Method: A mixed-method evaluation of six leading generative AI systems using 50 realistic open-ended Islamic questions spanning Qur'anic interpretation, Hadith, Fiqh, ethics, pastoral advice, and Madhhab-sensitive topics. Responses were collected from participants in Australia and the UK, then analyzed for domain accuracy, citation verification, hallucinations, jurisprudential consistency, uncertainty handling, source provenance, and geographical variation.

Result: Current generative AI systems are valuable as assistive tools for introductory Islamic learning but should not be treated as authoritative sources for religious rulings or Islamic research without verification against authenticated primary sources and qualified scholarly expertise.

Conclusion: The study provides one of the first comprehensive empirical evaluations of AI reliability in Islamic knowledge, offering practical guidance for researchers, educators, AI developers, and the Muslim community, while cautioning against uncritical reliance on AI for religious authority.

Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used by Muslims for religious guidance, Qur'anic interpretation, Hadith explanation, jurisprudential rulings, and Islamic education. Despite its growing adoption, there is limited empirical evidence on whether current AI systems provide authentic, verifiable, and trustworthy Islamic knowledge suitable for high-trust religious contexts. This study evaluates six leading generative AI systems using fifty realistic open-ended Islamic questions covering Qur'anic interpretation, Hadith, Fiqh, ethics, pastoral advice, and Madhhab-sensitive topics. Responses were collected under real-world conditions from participants in Australia and the United Kingdom and analysed using a mixed-method framework examining domain accuracy, citation verification, hallucinations, jurisprudential consistency, uncertainty handling, source provenance, and geographical variation.
  The study addresses four research questions: (1) How accurate and authentic are AI-generated responses across major Islamic knowledge domains? (2) To what extent do AI systems produce hallucinations, incomplete citations, or unverifiable religious references? (3) How consistently do models handle jurisprudential disagreement, Madhhab diversity, and uncertainty? (4) Are current AI systems sufficiently reliable for religious guidance, Islamic education, and scholarly research?
  Overall, current generative AI systems are valuable as assistive tools for introductory Islamic learning but should not be treated as authoritative sources for religious rulings or Islamic research without verification against authenticated primary sources and qualified scholarly expertise. This study provides one of the first comprehensive empirical evaluations of AI reliability within Islamic knowledge, offering practical guidance for researchers, educators, AI developers, and the wider Muslim community.

</details>


### [187] [Operationally Guided Placement-Aware Learning for Industrial Online 3D Bin Packing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28257)
*Dheeraj Poolavaram,Aanchal Rajesh Chugh,Sebastian Dorn*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OPAL is a learning-based framework for industrial online 3D bin packing that improves space utilization by 15.1% through operationally guided candidate generation and 6.3% through learned ranking, achieving 0.49 mean space utilization on the BED-BPP benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on online 3D-BPP has focused primarily on optimizing the policy for selecting among candidate placements, while candidate generation and representation remain largely geometry-driven. Industrial settings impose additional constraints beyond space efficiency—stability, compactness, and balance—that geometry-only approaches fail to adequately address.

Method: OPAL introduces three components: (1) OG-EMS (Operationally Guided Empty-Maximal-Space generator), which evaluates multiple anchors per free-space region and prioritizes low, well-supported, compact, and spatially diverse placements; (2) an xLSTM-based Placement Encoder that models dependencies among geometric and operational candidate attributes; and (3) a lightweight recurrent core that combines placement embeddings with item and pallet state to rank feasible actions, trained via proximal policy optimization (PPO).

Result: On the BED-BPP benchmark, OPAL achieves a mean space utilization of 0.49, representing a 15.1% improvement from operationally guided candidate generation and a 6.3% improvement from learned ranking, while maintaining robust inference-time performance.

Conclusion: Operationally guided candidate generation and learned placement-aware representation significantly outperform geometry-driven baselines for industrial online 3D-BPP, demonstrating that both candidate quality and learned ranking are essential for achieving high space utilization under real-world constraints.

Abstract: The online three-dimensional bin packing problem (3D-BPP) is a longstanding challenge in logistics and industrial palletizing. Recent learning-based methods use a learned policy to select among feasible candidate placements. Performance depends on the candidate generator and representation, especially in industrial settings where packings must be space-efficient, stable, compact, and balanced. However, prior work has mainly optimized the policy, while candidate generation and representation remain largely geometry-driven. We address this gap with OPAL, an operationally guided placement-aware learning framework for industrial online 3D-BPP which combines an Operationally Guided Empty-Maximal-Space generator (OG-EMS), an operational representation for each candidate placement, and a masked ranking policy trained with proximal policy optimization. OG-EMS evaluates multiple anchors within each free-space region and prioritizes low, well-supported, compact, and spatially diverse placements. An xLSTM-based Placement Encoder models dependencies among geometric and operational candidate attributes, while a lightweight recurrent core combines the resulting embeddings with the current item and pallet state to rank feasible actions. On the BED-BPP benchmark, OPAL achieves a mean space utilization of 0.49, with improvements of 15.1% from operationally guided candidate generation and 6.3% from learned ranking, while maintaining robust inference-time performance.

</details>


### [188] [LLM-Guided Evolutionary Search for Constraint Model Reformulation to Improve Solver Efficiency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28268)
*Kostis Michailidis,Dimos Tsouros,Nguyen Dang,Tias Guns*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper explores using LLMs within an evolutionary framework to automatically reformulate constraint models for better solver performance, introducing Profile-Diverse Retention (PDR) — a diversity-based context selection strategy using Maximal Marginal Relevance on runtime profiles — and demonstrating that diversity-aware retention with validation-based selection yields superior held-out speedups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Combinatorial optimization models are sensitive to formulation choices that significantly impact solver performance. While LLMs can generate correct constraint models from natural language, even correct models can be expensive to solve. Prior retention strategies for iterative LLM-based improvement prioritize recency or best performance but fail to diversify the context, potentially missing better reformulations.

Method: An evolutionary framework inspired by Automatic Heuristic Design (AHD), where an LLM proposes candidate reformulations that are verified and benchmarked against a user-defined baseline. The key contribution is Profile-Diverse Retention (PDR), which applies Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) to instance-level runtime vectors to select a behaviourally diverse set of prior attempts for the LLM prompt context. Strategies are systematically evaluated on eight CSPLib problems with validation-based final model selection.

Result: Iterative reformulation produces substantial held-out speedups. Strategies that retain a diverse context (via PDR) outperform those retaining only recent or fastest attempts. Validation-based model selection further improves held-out speedups across all strategies.

Conclusion: LLM-driven iterative reformulation is a viable method for performance-oriented model improvement, and explicitly diversifying the retained context via PDR — rather than relying solely on recency or performance — is key to achieving better results.

Abstract: Combinatorial problems appear in numerous industrial applications. A common approach is to formulate these problems as declarative constraint models that can subsequently be compiled to and solved by a range of back-end solvers. Recent work shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can produce correct models from natural language, but even a correct model can be expensive to solve because performance remains sensitive to modelling choices. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs can automate performance-oriented model reformulation. Inspired by Automatic Heuristic Design (AHD), we use an evolutionary framework in which an LLM proposes candidate reformulations that are verified and benchmarked against the user-defined baseline model. We compare AHD-adapted search strategies that control which prior attempts, instructions, and measured feedback enter each prompt. Existing retention strategies prioritize recency or performance, but do not explicitly diversify the context. To cover this gap, we introduce Profile-Diverse Retention (PDR), which applies Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) to instance-level runtime vectors to retain behaviourally diverse attempts. We systematically evaluate the strategies on eight CSPLib problems using validation-based final model selection. The results show that: (i) iterative reformulation can produce substantial held-out speedups; (ii) strategies that keep the retained context diverse outperform those that retain only recent or the fastest attempts; and (iii) validation-based selection improves the held-out speedup of every strategy.

</details>


### [189] [MemHarness: Memory Is Reconstructed, Not Replayed](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28272)
*Rong Wu,Daocheng Fu,Licheng Wen,Xuemeng Yang,Shu Zou,Jianbiao Mei,Yuxin Wang,Hairong Zhang,Yu Yang,Tao Hu,Cong Zhang,Botian Shi,Pinlong Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemHarness proposes a framework where LLM agents actively reconstruct retrieved past experiences conditioned on the current context, rather than replaying them verbatim. Trained end-to-end with GRPO, it outperforms static memory baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop, prevents negative transfer, and improves intrinsic reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory-augmented LLM agents treat retrieved experiences as static records replayed verbatim, ignoring the mismatch between abstract stored memories and the agent's concrete, evolving decision-time context. This "replay" paradigm frequently causes negative transfer. Humans, by contrast, adapt retrieved memories to fit the present—a capability current agents lack.

Method: MemHarness introduces a unified policy model that, at each decision step, critiques and reconstructs retrieved experiences conditioned on the current state, producing context-grounded guidance before acting. This reconstructive ability is acquired through end-to-end training using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).

Result: MemHarness substantially outperforms both pure RL and static memory-augmented baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks. It demonstrates strong robustness in out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. The reconstruction objective prevents negative transfer and serves as latent guidance that fundamentally improves the agent's intrinsic reasoning capabilities during training.

Conclusion: Actively reconstructing memories to fit the current context, rather than passively replaying them, is a more effective paradigm for memory-augmented LLM agents. The reconstructive approach not only mitigates negative transfer but also enhances core reasoning, suggesting a promising direction for building more adaptive and robust agent systems.

Abstract: Retrieving past experiences has become a common strategy to enhance large language model agents. However, most existing memory-augmented agents treat retrieved experiences as static records to be replayed verbatim, injecting them into the context regardless of whether they align with the agent's current situation. This ``replay'' paradigm ignores the gap between the abstract, general nature of stored experience and the concrete, ever-changing states encountered at decision time, frequently causing negative transfer. In contrast, humans rarely recall past experiences verbatim; instead, they reorganize and adapt retrieved memories to fit the present context. Inspired by this, we propose MemHarness, a framework that equips LLM agents to actively harness and reconstruct past experiences based on the present context. At each decision step, a unified policy model critiques and reconstructs the retrieved experience conditioned on the current state, producing context-grounded guidance before acting. This reconstructive ability emerges naturally through end-to-end training with GRPO. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show that MemHarness substantially outperforms pure RL and static memory-augmented baselines, demonstrating strong robustness in out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. Furthermore, our analyses reveal that this reconstruction objective not only prevents negative transfer but also serves as latent guidance during training, fundamentally improving the agent's intrinsic reasoning capabilities.

</details>


### [190] [OSReward: Instituting Standardized Evaluation for Cross-Platform Computer-Use Reward Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28609)
*Qiushi Sun,Kanzhi Cheng,Yian Wang,Bowen Yang,Hang Yan,Liheng Chen,Fangzhi Xu,Zichen Ding,Nuo Chen,Jialin Cao,Xingdong Gong,Zehao Li,Kaiming Jin,Xinfeng Yuan,Zhoumianze Liu,Jingyang Gong,Zhangyue Yin,Jiahui Gao,Zhiyong Wu,Tianbao Xie,Jianbing Zhang,Ben Kao,Lingpeng Kong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OSReward introduces a benchmark and open reward models for evaluating VLM judges of computer-using agent trajectories, revealing systematic reliability gaps in current judges and providing cost-effective alternatives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLM judges are increasingly used to verify whether CUA trajectories fulfill task instructions, but their reliability has never been systematically examined. Human verification doesn't scale, creating an urgent need to assess and improve automated CUA trajectory judgment.

Method: The authors introduce OSReward, a benchmark with CUA trajectories from diverse agents across platforms, labeled via multi-stage human annotation. They derive OSReward-Hard (challenging cases) and OSReward-Multi (fine-grained scoring). They then construct OS-Shepherd-100K, a reasoning-annotated training corpus, and train open reward models (OS-Shepherd 9B and 35B).

Result: Even SOTA VLMs exhibit systematic leniency bias, mislabeling failures as successes. Frontier models that are reliable enough are too expensive at scale; affordable open models perform poorly. OS-Shepherd models match commercial judge performance at 30-60% lower cost.

Conclusion: Current VLM judges for CUA trajectories are not sufficiently reliable, but open, purpose-trained reward models like OS-Shepherd can deliver trustworthy, scalable, and cost-effective automated evaluation for the CUA community.

Abstract: Computer-using agents (CUAs) are advancing rapidly across the digital world. A CUA trajectory records the agent's actions, states, and reasoning. Verifying whether it fulfilled the task instruction is central to CUA evaluation, data curation, and reinforcement learning. Neither human-written verifiers nor human annotators can provide such verification at scale, so the field increasingly turns to vision-language models (VLMs) as judges of CUA trajectories. But a fundamental question has long gone unexamined: are these VLM judges reliable enough? To study it systematically, we introduce OSReward, a realistic, high-quality benchmark that evaluates VLM judges on CUA trajectories. The trajectories come from diverse agent backbones executing human-verified instructions across platforms, then rigorously labeled with ground-truth verdicts through multi-stage human annotation. Building on it, we derive OSReward-Hard, a challenge set concentrating genuinely hard cases, and OSReward-Multi for fine-grained efficiency and alignment scoring. The most comprehensive evaluation of VLM judges to date finds even state-of-the-art models fall short of an ideal judge, sharing a systematic leniency bias that mislabels failed runs as successes. The few reliable enough to trust are too expensive to run at scale, while affordable open models trail far behind. To close this gap, we construct and release OS-Shepherd-100K, an open corpus of reasoning-annotated trajectory judgments for the CUA community. On it, we train OS-Shepherd (9B and 35B), open reward models that supply low-cost, stable, and reliable reward signals, matching commercial judges at 30-60% lower cost than the frontier. Extensive analyses further inform the design of reliable CUA reward at scale. Our code, benchmark, dataset, and model checkpoints are available at https://os-copilot.github.io/OSReward-Home/.

</details>


### [191] [Tycho: Active Abstraction with Programmatic World Models for ARC-AGI-3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28287)
*Jens Lehmann,Andrei Aioanei,Sahar Vahdati*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ARC-AGI-3 formalizes abstraction as interactive skill acquisition where an agent must infer game rules and goals while minimizing actions. Tycho, a coding-agent system, separates actionable observations from animation frames and builds game-specific models. Claude Opus 4.8 with actor-requested delegation achieves 88.49 mean RHAE; GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 reach 100.00 RHAE on all 183 levels. The paper introduces "active abstraction" — deciding when to construct, repair, use, or bypass a model during costly interaction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Abstraction in ARC-AGI-3 is reframed as an interactive problem: an agent must infer rules, hidden state, and goals of unfamiliar games while constrained by action efficiency. This shifts the challenge from static pattern recognition to active skill acquisition under a limited interaction budget, requiring agents that can model, test, and adapt hypotheses on the fly.

Method: The authors formalize ARC-AGI-3 environments as parameterized rendered deterministic Moore machines. Tycho, a coding-agent system, structures raw interaction history by separating actionable observations from intermediate animation, level-completion, and game-over frames. From this structured history, the agent constructs free-form executable hypotheses that can be modeled, tested, planned with, repaired, or bypassed. Four orchestration policies are compared under matched inference budgets across all 25 public games using Claude Opus 4.8, with evaluation on Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE) and game-balanced human-replay midranks.

Result: Actor-requested delegation to a model builder achieves the highest mean RHAE of 88.49 among four policies. With this policy, GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 both achieve 100.00 RHAE, completing all 183 levels with midranks of 98.5 and 100.0 respectively. Opus 5 uses 61% fewer scored actions than aggregate human baselines. Notably, automatic repair after verification failures improves transition-matching accuracy but yields only 83.07 RHAE, demonstrating that accurate transition reproduction does not equate to identifying the objective or improving action quality.

Conclusion: Strong play requires not only building accurate simulators but also deciding when to construct, repair, use, or bypass a model. The authors term this joint problem "active abstraction": generating a testable model from costly interaction and strategically determining when acquiring or using it is worth its cost. Transition match alone is insufficient; effective action selection demands metacognitive control over the modeling process.

Abstract: ARC-AGI-3 turns abstraction into an interactive problem of skill acquisition. A player must infer an unfamiliar game's rules, hidden state, and goal while maintaining action efficiency because every move counts. We formalize these environments as parameterized rendered deterministic Moore machines and introduce Tycho, a coding-agent system that constructs and uses game-specific models during interaction. Tycho separates actionable observations from intermediate animation, level-completion, and game-over frames. From this structured history, an agent can model, test, plan with, repair, or bypass a free-form executable hypothesis.
  In one matched public-set run per policy, we compare four orchestration policies on all 25 public games using Claude Opus 4.8 under matched inference budgets. Actor-requested delegation to a model builder obtains the highest observed mean Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE), 88.49. With this selected policy, GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 both reach 100.00 RHAE and complete all 183 levels. Their game-balanced first-run human-replay midranks are 98.5 and 100.0. Opus 5 uses 61% fewer scored actions than the aggregate official human baselines.
  Automatic repair after verification failures produces models that reproduce observed transitions much more accurately, yet reaches only 83.07 RHAE. Transition match indicates whether a simulator reproduces observed dynamics, not whether it has identified the objective or improves the next action. Strong play also requires deciding when to construct, repair, use, or bypass a model. We call this joint problem active abstraction: generating a testable model from costly interaction and deciding when acquiring or using it is worth its cost.

</details>


### [192] [One Human, $N$ Agents: Audit-Budget Allocation for LLM Agent Fleets under Miscalibrated, Correlated Confidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28317)
*Cesare Zavattari,Alessandro Tommasi,Giuseppe Prencipe*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Under a limited audit budget, confidence-ranked auditing of LLM agents becomes worse than random when miscalibration exceeds a threshold δ*. Counterintuitively, δ* rises as budget shrinks, and cross-family correlation is dominated by shared difficulty. Open-weight LLMs show near-constant (useless) confidence near or beyond δ*, while a proprietary model is informative and below it.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human oversight of multiple LLM agents is severely budget-constrained (B ≪ N audits per round). Agents may report miscalibrated confidence adversarially, and errors can be correlated across agents, raising the question: when does confidence-based auditing actually help versus hurt relative to random selection?

Method: The authors model the problem as budgeted noisy inspection under a two-level Gaussian copula, capturing both agent-level miscalibration and correlated errors across agents. They derive a theoretical miscalibration threshold δ* beyond which confidence-ranked auditing underperforms random auditing. They then empirically evaluate five open-weight LLMs and one proprietary model, measuring confidence calibration and replaying audit policies on recorded traces.

Result: Two findings reverse conventional expectations: (1) δ* increases as the audit budget shrinks, meaning tighter budgets tolerate more miscalibration before confidence-ranking fails; (2) cross-family correlation is not low — shared task difficulty dominates over model lineage. Open-weight LLMs exhibit near-constant, operationally useless confidence at or beyond δ*, while the proprietary model is informative and falls below the threshold. Policy replay confirms the theoretical ordering.

Conclusion: The paper provides a quantitative criterion for "vacuous oversight" — when confidence-based auditing is guaranteed worse than random. The practical implication is that most current open-weight LLMs fail this criterion, rendering confidence-guided human oversight ineffective, while at least one proprietary model passes.

Abstract: A single human must audit $N$ LLM agents under a budget of $B \ll N$ audits per round, guided by self-reported confidence that may be adversarially miscalibrated and by correlated errors. We model this as budgeted noisy inspection over a two-level Gaussian copula and locate the miscalibration threshold $δ^*$ past which confidence-ranked auditing is \emph{worse} than random. Two a-priori expectations reverse: $δ^*$ \emph{rises} as the budget shrinks, and cross-family correlation is not low---shared difficulty dominates lineage. Five open-weight LLMs show operationally useless (near-constant) confidence, point estimates at or beyond the flip though CIs straddle it; a proprietary model is informative and lands below it. We give a quantitative criterion for \emph{vacuous} oversight, and replaying policies on recorded traces confirms the ordering.

</details>


### [193] [PathView-Bench: Can Multimodal Large Language Models Achieve Fine-grained Multiscale Understanding of Pathology Images?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28318)
*Zongyi Chen,Yu Liang,Jie Lin,Liansheng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PathVU is a vision-anchored benchmark with 308K samples across 14 VQA tasks, designed to evaluate fine-grained, multiscale visual understanding of MLLMs in pathology. Testing 18 models reveals substantial limitations in region localization, spatial reasoning, and quantity estimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing pathology MLLM benchmarks focus on final diagnostic outputs (answers, captions, reports) and fail to assess whether models truly understand the multiscale visual content required for pathology reasoning. There is a need for fine-grained, programmatically scored evaluation of visual understanding capabilities.

Method: PathVU is built from 23 public pathology datasets with human-supervised labels and spatial annotations. It operates at two fields of view — Region FOV (high-resolution local regions) and Slide FOV (macro whole-slide views). Raw annotations are converted into deterministic task targets, enabling programmatic scoring across 14 VQA-style tasks: region localization, visual recognition, quantity estimation, spatial reasoning, and insufficient-context judgment. The benchmark spans 28 organs, 61,673 images, 308,070 samples, and 7,253,526 annotations.

Result: Evaluation of 18 MLLMs (general-purpose, medical-domain, and pathology-oriented) reveals substantial limitations across all model categories on fine-grained visual tasks, with even advanced models struggling on multiscale pathology images.

Conclusion: PathVU provides a reproducible foundation for developing and evaluating pathology MLLMs with explicit multiscale visual understanding, exposing critical gaps in current models' capabilities beyond surface-level diagnostic answer generation.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to analyze pathology images. However, dominant multimodal benchmarks in pathology mainly score final diagnostic answers, captions, or reports. These evaluations provide limited insight into whether a model understands the multiscale visual content needed for pathology reasoning and decision-making. We introduce PathVU, a vision-anchored benchmark for fine-grained and multiscale visual understanding in computational pathology. Built from 23 public pathology imaging datasets with human-supervised labels and spatial annotations, PathVU evaluates MLLM understanding in two fields of view: Region FOV for high-resolution local regions and Slide FOV for macro whole-slide views. By converting raw annotations into deterministic task targets, PathVU enables programmatic scoring of region localization, visual recognition, quantity estimation, spatial reasoning, and insufficient-context judgment. The benchmark contains 14 VQA-style tasks, 61,673 images, and 308,070 samples across 28 organs and 7,253,526 annotations. Evaluating 18 representative general-purpose, medical-domain, and pathology-oriented MLLMs, we observe substantial limitations even in advanced models on fine-grained visual tasks across multiscale pathology images. PathVU provides a reproducible basis for developing and evaluating pathology MLLMs with explicit multiscale visual understanding.

</details>


### [194] [Paying for Honesty Without Knowing the Truth: Reputation-Penalty Design for LLM Marketplace Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28330)
*Mingdai Yang,Shicheng Fan,Kejing Yu,Duohao Wang,Li Sun,Hao Peng,Philip S. Yu,Zhiwei Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM agents acting as merchants fabricate product attributes even when instructed to be honest. The authors propose CARP, a reputation-penalty mechanism that suppresses dishonest sellers without requiring ground truth, and SPARC, a reflection mechanism that makes the penalty behaviorally binding. Together they close most of the consumer-welfare gap relative to a perfect-information oracle.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based autonomous merchants increasingly fabricate product attributes under competitive pressure, even when instructed to be honest. Platforms lack ground truth and only observe noisy, biased complaint signals, making naive verification infeasible. The challenge is designing a mechanism that deters fabrication without access to the truth, while remaining robust to strategic gaming and complaint noise.

Method: CARP (Complaint-Adaptive Reputation Penalty): a reputation-penalty mechanism featuring (1) a deadband that forgives complaint noise, and (2) state-dependent severity that counters reputation-driven detection erosion. CARP requires no product-level ground truth and is robust to strategic manipulation. SPARC (Self-interested Penalty-gated Reflection): a byte-clean, code-gated reflection mechanism that makes the CARP penalty behaviorally binding by linking fabrication to lost sales, triggering penalty-gated self-correction reasoning in LLM merchants.

Result: CARP suppresses sales volume of low-rated liars while protecting honest sellers. Paired with SPARC, the system closes most of the consumer-welfare gap relative to a perfect-information oracle and achieves the best welfare among all compared policies. LLM merchants fabricate when lying is costless but restrain themselves when fabrication costs them sales — a self-interested response, not compliance. The effect is consistent across models with supporting confidence intervals.

Conclusion: LLM merchant fabrication is a real problem that can be effectively mitigated without ground-truth access. The combination of a noise-tolerant reputation mechanism (CARP) and a behaviorally binding reflection mechanism (SPARC) achieves near-optimal consumer welfare by making honesty economically self-interested rather than relying on instruction-following compliance.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly act as autonomous merchants that write their own product listings, and under competitive pressure, they fabricate attributes to win sales. Even under instructions to be honest, they fabricate attributes in a majority of listings across models. A platform's obvious remedy---verifying each claim against the truth---is unavailable, because it observes only a noisy, biased complaint signal, never the ground truth. We design CARP, a reputation-penalty mechanism with a deadband that forgives complaint noise and a state-dependent severity that counters reputation-driven detection erosion. CARP requires no product-level ground truth and is robust to strategic gaming. CARP protects consumers by suppressing the sales volume of low-rated liars while sparing honest sellers. Paired with SPARC, it closes most of the consumer-welfare gap relative to a perfect-information oracle, without ever accessing the truth. It also achieves the best welfare of the policies we compare. We further show that this felt penalty becomes behaviorally binding through SPARC, a byte-clean code-gated reflection mechanism: LLM merchants fabricate when lying is free but restrain themselves when fabrication costs them sales, a self-interested response rather than compliance. We trace this distinction to penalty-gated self-correction reasoning, and observe the binding across models, with supporting confidence intervals.

</details>


### [195] [Correcting What You Cannot See: Credit Assignment for Perception Distillation in Multimodal Reasoners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28336)
*Feng Xiong,Leyan Xue,Hongyu Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PCD (Perception-Correction Distillation) is a label-free method that identifies correctable perception failures in multimodal reasoning by using the product of downstream failure and teacher-student disagreement as a soft AND gate for distillation weighting. It improves over on-policy distillation (OPD) by separating perception and reasoning rollouts, yielding significant gains across multiple benchmarks (e.g., 8B→2B from 44.50 to 47.28; 32B→8B from 56.94 to 61.22).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy distillation (OPD) uses trajectory-level rewards that cannot distinguish whether an incorrect answer stems from a perception failure or a reasoning failure. The Perception Success Rate (PSR), which aggregates multiple reasoning attempts over a shared perception, remains ambiguous because low success could reflect either poor perception or inherently difficult reasoning. The authors aim to isolate and correct perception failures specifically, enabling more targeted and effective multimodal distillation.

Method: PCD identifies correctable perception failures using two complementary signals: (1) downstream answer failure and (2) teacher–student disagreement. Their product acts as a soft AND gate, activating distillation emphasis only when both witnesses concur. This multiplicative rule is theoretically motivated via Bayesian evidence combination and is shown to be the unique normalized bilinear gate that vanishes when either witness is absent. The approach uses separated perception–reasoning rollouts (decoupling the perceptual encoding from the reasoning chain) and mean-preserving weighting, leaving the core reasoning objective unchanged.

Result: Across eight benchmarks, PCD improves OPD's 8B→2B macro average from 44.50 to 47.28 (+2.78) and the 32B→8B result from 56.94 to 61.22 (+4.28). Ablation studies on matched 2B setups show that removing PCD and separated rollouts reduces held-out average by 2.22 and 0.88 points, respectively, confirming both components contribute meaningfully.

Conclusion: Effective multimodal distillation depends not only on what the teacher predicts, but also on identifying when perception is the appropriate target of correction. PCD's witness-based gating mechanism and separated rollout strategy provide a principled, label-free way to achieve this, yielding consistent and substantial improvements over standard on-policy distillation.

Abstract: On-policy distillation provides dense supervision for multimodal reasoners, but its trajectory-level reward cannot determine whether a failed answer arose from perception or subsequent reasoning. Perception Success Rate (PSR), estimated from multiple reasonings sharing one perception, remains ambiguous because low success conflates perceptual insufficiency with reasoning difficulty. We introduce \textbf{Perception-Correction Distillation (PCD)}, a label-free method that identifies correctable perception failures using downstream failure and teacher--student disagreement as complementary witnesses. Their product, , forms a soft AND gate that strengthens distillation only when both witnesses are present. We motivate this rule through Bayesian evidence combination and show that multiplication is the unique normalized bilinear gate that vanishes when either witness is absent. PCD uses separated perception--reasoning rollouts and mean-preserving weights, leaving the reasoning objective unchanged. Across eight benchmarks, PCD improves the 8B 2B macro average from 44.50 with OPD to 47.28 and the 32B 8B result from 56.94 to 61.22. In matched 2B ablations, removing PCD and separated rollout reduces held-out average by 2.22 and 0.88 points, respectively. Effective multimodal distillation therefore depends not only on what the teacher predicts, but also on identifying when perception is the appropriate target of correction.

</details>


### [196] [How Benchmarks Mis-Score Computer-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28367)
*Zihan Dong,Zhiyuan Ma,Zekun Wang,Yunqing Li,Zirou Liu,Ruixuan Deng,Qishi Zhan,Rui Qian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper audits failure-scored trajectories across five CUA benchmarks, finding 15.3% of FAIL verdicts are erroneous (evaluator false negatives + broken tasks). It proposes a reliability framework and a three-tier diagnostic taxonomy showing verification/feedback and planning failures dominate execution errors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current CUA benchmarks rely on brittle scripted oracles that produce unreliable scores due to stale tasks, missing visual evidence, rejected valid alternatives, and opaque aggregate reports. There is no systematic framework for assessing evaluation reliability, and failure modes remain poorly diagnosed.

Method: The authors (1) organize evaluation problems into a reliability framework covering task construction, trajectory observation, scoring, and reporting; (2) manually audit 150 public failure-scored trajectories from five benchmarks (web, enterprise-workflow, desktop-control); (3) introduce a three-tier diagnostic taxonomy (verification/feedback, planning, execution/grounding) to classify genuine failures.

Result: 15.3% of FAIL verdicts are incorrect: 10.7% are evaluator false negatives (valid alternatives rejected) and 4.7% are broken tasks. Among genuine failures, verification/feedback and planning failures dominate over execution/grounding errors. Single scalar success rates obscure these distinctions.

Conclusion: CUA evaluation needs stage-specific design rules rather than scalar metrics. The reliability framework and diagnostic taxonomy provide actionable guidance for constructing more robust benchmarks, particularly for long-horizon tasks.

Abstract: Computer-use agents (CUA) are being deployed to browse the web and operate desktop software, yet their benchmark scores are still commonly produced by brittle scripted oracles. A score is the output of a pipeline in which tasks can be stale, trajectories can omit decisive visual evidence, evaluators can reject valid alternatives, and aggregate reports can hide the cause of failure. We organize these problems into a reliability framework spanning task construction, trajectory observation, scoring, and reporting. We then audit 150 public failure-scored trajectories from five web, enterprise-workflow, and desktop-control benchmarks, find that 15.3\% of FAIL verdicts are wrong: 10.7\% are evaluator false negatives and 4.7\% are broken tasks. For genuine failures, a three-tier diagnostic taxonomy shows that verification/feedback and planning failures dominate execution/grounding errors, while a single scalar success rate can not explain. We connect these findings to newer long-horizon CUA benchmarks and derive stage-specific design rules for CUA evaluation.

</details>


### [197] [HyperClaim: Fine-Grained Cross-Modal Hypergraph Reasoning for Video Misinformation Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28375)
*Xiangbo Wang,Jiasheng Zhang,Xingtong Yu,Luoqiang Lei,Delvin Ce Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HyperClaim is a discriminative temporal hypergraph framework for video misinformation detection that models higher-order interactions among query phrases, contextual text, and short temporal frame spans, outperforming global fusion and reasoning-based baselines on three benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing video misinformation detection methods (global multimodal fusion and free-form reasoning) under-represent localized authenticity cues arising from coupled higher-order interactions among query phrases, contextual text, and short temporal frame spans. Pairwise graph formulations cannot capture these multi-way cross-modal dependencies.

Method: HyperClaim constructs a sparse heterogeneous hypergraph over query tokens, evidence tokens, and sampled frames. It applies (1) confidence-aware filtering and source budgeting to form compact text-frame and short-range temporal evidence units, (2) adaptive soft-incidence reasoning with residual text-video calibration, and (3) discrepancy-aware readout for aggregating textual, visual, and hyperedge states. No generated rationales or external tools are used.

Result: Under the FactGuard temporal protocol, HyperClaim achieves 83.7% accuracy on FakeSV, 82.0% on FakeTT, and 87.3% on FakeVV, outperforming strong discriminative and reasoning-centric baselines. Learned incidence and attention weights reveal interpretable token- and frame-level structure.

Conclusion: HyperClaim demonstrates that explicitly modeling higher-order, localized cross-modal interactions via temporal hypergraphs preserves fine-grained structure that global fusion flattens, leading to state-of-the-art video misinformation detection without relying on external reasoning tools or generated rationales.

Abstract: Video misinformation detection is often approached through global multimodal fusion or free-form multimodal reasoning. Both paradigms can under-represent localized authenticity cues that arise from coupled interactions among query phrases, contextual text, and short temporal spans of frames. Because such interactions are inherently higher-order, pairwise graph formulations are insufficient to capture multi-way cross-modal dependencies, whereas hypergraphs offer a suitable representation for these relations. We propose HyperClaim, a discriminative temporal hypergraph framework for sample-level authenticity classification. Using the title or benchmark-provided paired text as a claim-like query, HyperClaim constructs a sparse heterogeneous hypergraph over query tokens, evidence tokens, and sampled frames; applies confidence-aware filtering and source budgeting to form compact text-frame and short-range temporal evidence units; performs adaptive soft-incidence reasoning with residual text-video calibration; and aggregates textual, visual, and hyperedge states through a discrepancy-aware readout. Without relying on generated rationales or external tool calls, HyperClaim preserves fine-grained cross-modal and temporal structure that global fusion tends to flatten. Under the FactGuard temporal protocol, it achieves 83.7%, 82.0%, and 87.3% accuracy on FakeSV, FakeTT, and FakeVV, respectively, outperforming strong discriminative and reasoning-centric baselines. Learned incidence and attention weights further reveal token- and frame-level structure.

</details>


### [198] [When Specifications Conflict: A Symmetry-Based Framework for Measuring LLM Preferences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28384)
*Tairan Wang,Liang Zhou,Zikang Zhan,Pingchuan Yan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A controlled experimental framework for studying how LLMs resolve conflicts between competing specifications, revealing systematic preference patterns (Formal ≈ Naturalized Formal > Pure Natural Language > Input-Output Examples) across 550 conflict instances and multiple domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs increasingly need to integrate inconsistent or conflicting information from multiple sources, yet there is a lack of controllable, attributable methods for analyzing how models resolve such specification conflicts. The authors aim to fill this gap with a principled experimental framework.

Method: The authors propose a controlled experimental framework with explicit conflicts between competing specifications. A symmetry-based design reduces confounding factors, enabling systematic comparison across representation types. They evaluate on an executable mathematical benchmark (550 conflict instances, 11 function families) and extend to heterogeneous specification conflicts in Boolean algebra, code generation, and the clinical domain.

Result: LLMs exhibit systematic—not random—preference patterns across representation types, with a consistent ordering: Formal ≈ Naturalized Formal > Pure Natural Language > Input-Output Examples. Example effects are further modulated by model capability and function family. The framework generalizes across diverse tasks and specification forms.

Conclusion: The framework provides a unified, controllable, and attributable approach for measuring how LLMs resolve conflicts between competing information sources, with results demonstrating consistent, non-random preference hierarchies across representation types and domains.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly required to integrate multiple sources of information that may be inconsistent or conflicting. However, there is still a lack of controllable and attributable methods for analyzing how models resolve conflicts between competing specifications. We propose a controlled experimental framework for studying model preferences under conflicting specifications. By constructing specifications with explicit conflicts, the framework enables model choices between competing specifications to be directly observed and analyzed. A symmetry-based design further reduces confounding factors, allowing preferences across representation types to be compared systematically.
  We evaluate the framework on an executable mathematical benchmark with 550 conflict instances spanning 11 function families, comparing four representation types: pure natural language, formal language, naturalized formal language, and input--output examples. Results show systematic preference patterns rather than random behavior, with a consistent ordering: $ \text{Formal} \approx \text{Naturalized Formal} > \text{Pure Natural Language} > \text{Input--Output Examples} $. Example effects further depend on model capability and function family.
  We extend the framework to heterogeneous specification conflicts in Boolean algebra, code generation, and the clinical domain, demonstrating its applicability across diverse tasks and specification forms. The framework provides a unified approach for measuring how LLMs resolve conflicts between competing sources of information.

</details>


### [199] [QuantWAMs: Calibrating at the Right Granularity for World Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28405)
*Jiacheng Zhou,Jinfan Lv,Ruixuan Li,Longtai Zhang,Yan Wang,Wenqiang Zhang,Lizhe Qi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: QuantWAMs is a post-training quantization framework tailored for World Action Models that jointly predict future observations and actions. It introduces three strategies—shared-basis outlier calibration, co-training-objective saliency, and fixed-intervention rollout auditing—to align quantization with deployment context, achieving near-lossless W4A4 quantization, ~71% memory reduction, and 1.4–1.6× speedups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods fail on World Action Models (WAMs) because they assume open-loop objectives, homogeneous model architectures, and calibration distributions that diverge from actual closed-loop deployment conditions. WAMs' iterative denoising and closed-loop execution make efficient deployment costly, motivating a PTQ framework specifically designed for their unique structure and rollout dynamics.

Method: QuantWAMs employs three tailored strategies: (1) Shared-basis outlier calibration pools activation evidence only across coordinate-compatible modules to handle architectural heterogeneity. (2) Co-training-objective saliency computes empirical Fisher scores from the joint video-action gradient and assigns weight precision at calibration-stable layer granularity. (3) Fixed-intervention rollout auditing revises denoising-step protection schedules using reachable closed-loop states, all without altering the precision budget.

Result: Under W4A4-dominant quantization, simulation mean performance differs from FP16 by only 0.2–0.7 percentage points across Fast-WAM and LingBot-VA on RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real-robot benchmarks. Peak weight-and-activation memory drops to ~29% of FP16, with 1.4–1.6× block-level speedups. Real-robot trials on an AgiBot G2 confirm deployment feasibility on three manipulation tasks.

Conclusion: QuantWAMs demonstrates that deployment-aware, structure-sensitive PTQ can compress World Action Models to W4A4 precision with negligible accuracy loss, enabling practical real-robot deployment with significant memory savings and inference speedups.

Abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and actions, but their iterative denoising and closed-loop execution make efficient deployment costly. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods are poorly suited to WAMs because they rely on open-loop objectives, homogeneous model assumptions, and calibration distributions that do not reflect deployment. We present QuantWAMs, a PTQ framework that aligns quantization decisions with the calibration context defined by model structure, rollout distribution, and task objective. QuantWAMs introduces three strategies: shared-basis outlier calibration, which pools activation evidence only across coordinate-compatible modules; co-training-objective saliency, which computes empirical-Fisher scores from the joint video--action gradient and assigns weight precision at a calibration-stable layer granularity; and fixed-intervention rollout auditing, which revises denoising-step protection schedules using reachable closed-loop states without changing the precision budget. We evaluate QuantWAMs on Fast-WAM and LingBot-VA across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real-robot manipulation with an AgiBot G2. Under a W4A4-dominant setting, the reported simulation means differ from FP16 by 0.2--0.7 percentage points. Real-robot trials further establish deployment feasibility on three manipulation tasks. For the targeted video and action blocks, QuantWAMs reduces peak weight-and-activation memory to about 29\% of FP16 and provides 1.4--1.6$\times$ block-level speedups.

</details>


### [200] [When Derived Measurements Mislead: Quantifying and Mitigating LLM Over-Trust with Privileged-Modality Reliability Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28421)
*Zongheng Guo,Tao Chen,Tianli Li,Mingzhe Cui,Yang Jiao,Lei Xie,Yi Pan,Xiao Hu,Manuela Ferrario*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces "Derived-Feature Over-Trust" (DFOT), a failure mode where LLMs treat derived measurements as direct facts or apply them outside their valid scope. Using a physiological sensing case study with 50,000 paired PPG-ECG records, the authors propose five estimands to quantify this phenomenon and demonstrate a baseline mitigation via ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation, showing improvements of 1.82–6.69 percentage points on four repair and specificity endpoints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Derived measurements are increasingly fed into LLM pipelines as though they were direct, ground-truth facts, yet their validity is instance-dependent. No existing framework systematically captures or quantifies the downstream failure when LLMs over-trust such measurements. The authors aim to formalize and benchmark this problem to enable principled mitigation.

Method: The authors define DFOT and operationalize it through a physiological sensing case study with two diagnostic tasks (D1 and D2): D1 tests acceptance of a PPG-derived rhythm contradicted by offline ECG; D2 tests rejection of a reliable PPG rhythm under misleading history. Five estimands are proposed — COTR, CIR, CRR, ESRM, and UHR — to quantify conflict over-trust, context-induced error, correct repair, evidence-specific repair margin, and utility harm. ECG serves as training supervision and offline reference but is never shown to the LLM. The framework is demonstrated on 50,000 paired PPG-ECG records using ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation as a baseline and PPG-only inference on a protocol-locked 187-patient test set.

Result: The baseline method improves four repair and specificity endpoints by 1.82–6.69 percentage points, with all paired confidence intervals excluding zero. Utility harm rate (UHR) increases by only 0.67 percentage points (95% CI: -0.4 to +1.7), indicating minimal additional unnecessary verification cost.

Conclusion: DFOT provides a common evaluation target for developing stronger mitigation methods against over-reliance on derived measurements in LLM pipelines. The privileged distillation baseline demonstrates that the problem is tractable but far from solved.

Abstract: Derived measurements increasingly enter large language model (LLM) pipelines as direct facts despite their instance-dependent validity. We define derived-feature over-trust (DFOT) as the failure in which a downstream LLM assigns such a measurement the epistemic status of a direct fact or uses it outside its valid scope. Using physiological sensing as a case study, D1 tests acceptance of a PPG-derived rhythm contradicted by offline ECG, whereas D2 tests rejection of an offline-confirmed reliable PPG rhythm under misleading severe history. ECG supplies training supervision and offline reference construction but is never shown to the LLM. Five estimands quantify this chain: conflict over-trust rate (COTR) and context-induced error rate (CIR) characterize D1/D2; correct repair rate (CRR) measures frozen-error repair; evidence-specific repair margin (ESRM) contrasts matched and patient-disjoint shuffled evidence; and utility harm rate (UHR) measures unnecessary verification among HIGH-reliability cases used without verification at baseline. The framework does not depend on a particular reliability generator. We demonstrate it on 50,000 paired PPG-ECG records using ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation as an illustrative baseline and PPG-only inference. On a protocol-locked 187-patient test, the baseline improves four repair and specificity endpoints by 1.82-6.69 percentage points, with all paired confidence intervals excluding zero; UHR increases by 0.67 percentage points (95% CI: -0.4 to +1.7). DFOT provides a common evaluation target for stronger mitigation methods. The code is available at https://github.com/Zongheng-Guo/When-Derived-Measurements-Mislead.

</details>


### [201] [A foundation model of numerical intelligence with cross-disciplinary generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28432)
*Chenghan Wu,Zongmin Yu,Liu Yang*

Main category: cs.AI
