TL;DR: UNICON is a foundation model that exhibits "numerical intelligence" — the ability to infer predictive relations from graph-based numerical examples and apply them to new queries, matching or surpassing specialist models across diverse scientific and social systems, including unseen disciplines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current large language models demonstrate intelligence through text, but scientific and social systems require models that can acquire and apply knowledge from numerical context. The authors identify a gap: no foundation model exists for "numerical intelligence" — the capacity to generalize predictive relations across diverse numerical domains from in-context examples, analogous to how LLMs generalize from textual context.

Method: UNICON (UNified In-Context Operator Networks) uses a graph-based in-context learning paradigm. Given examples from a system represented as graphs (e.g., physical systems, social networks), the model infers the shared predictive relation and applies it to new queries from the same system. The architecture is trained on diverse numerical datasets spanning multiple scientific and social disciplines, and can be combined with language-model agents for enhanced performance.

Result: UNICON approaches specialist-level performance across trained disciplines and generalizes to unseen disciplines without retraining. When augmented with language-model agents, it surpasses state-of-the-art specialists in entirely unseen disciplines. Training-corpus diversity is shown to directly improve cross-discipline generalization.

Conclusion: UNICON establishes the concept of a foundation model for numerical intelligence, demonstrating that a single model can learn transferable predictive relations across heterogeneous numerical domains. This positions UNICON as a foundational building block for broader AI ecosystems that integrate both textual and numerical reasoning.

Abstract: Intelligence is commonly understood as the ability to acquire and apply knowledge, adapt to unfamiliar situations and solve new problems. Large language models exhibit this capacity by inferring task-relevant knowledge from textual context and applying it to new tasks. Yet intelligence need not be confined to language. For scientific and social systems, we need models that acquire and apply knowledge from numerical context-an ability we call numerical intelligence. Here we introduce UNified In-Context Operator Networks (UNICON), a foundation model that exhibits numerical intelligence across disciplines. Using graph-based examples from a system as context, UNICON infers the predictive relation shared across them and applies it to queries from the same system. Across scientific and social systems, including those from disciplines absent from training, the same model approaches specialist performance without retraining. Combining UNICON with language-model agents yields further gains, enabling it to surpass state-of-the-art specialists in a discipline unseen in training. We further show that training-corpus diversity improves generalization to unseen disciplines. Together, these results establish UNICON as a foundation model of numerical intelligence and position it as a building block for a broader ecosystem of artificial intelligence.

</details>


### [202] [LeanCSP: A Framework for Certifying Constraint Reformulation and Solving in Lean](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28459)
*Pablo Manrique,Stefan Szeider*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents a Lean-based verification framework for constraint programming that provides both formulation-level parametric proofs (equivalence, equisatisfiability, symmetry-breaking correctness) and instance-level solver certificate checking via backends (MiniZinc, SMT-LIB, OPB), enabling end-to-end trusted solving without relying on external solvers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Constraint programming results demand trust at two levels: (1) that preprocessing reformulations are semantics-preserving, and (2) that solvers produce correct answers. Existing approaches lack a unified, formally verified framework addressing both levels within a single theorem prover.

Method: The framework is built in the Lean theorem prover. It supports parametric proofs of formulation-level properties (equivalence, equisatisfiability, symmetry-breaking correctness) across entire problem families. For individual instances, it provides translation backends to MiniZinc, SMT-LIB, and OPB, enabling verification of solver-produced certificates. Combining both levels yields end-to-end correctness guarantees.

Result: Verified symmetry breaking yields up to a 2×10⁷ reduction in solver search effort via a single parametric proof reused across all instance sizes. End-to-end certification remains affordable, taking at most a few minutes for the largest instances tested.

Conclusion: The framework demonstrates that combining formulation-level parametric verification with instance-level certificate checking in Lean is both practically feasible and effective, delivering significant solver performance gains while providing formal end-to-end trust guarantees.

Abstract: Constraint programming is a core technology for solving complex combinatorial problems in scheduling, planning, configuration, and verification. Trusting its results therefore demands guarantees at two levels: that reformulations applied beforehand are semantics-preserving, and that solvers produce correct answers. In this work, we introduce a framework that addresses both verification levels in the Lean theorem prover: it can be used to prove formulation-level properties, such as equivalence, equisatisfiability, and the correctness of symmetry-breaking constraints, parametrically for entire problem families; and to check solver-produced certificates for individual instances via translation backends to external formats such as MiniZinc, SMT-LIB, and OPB. Combining both levels yields an end-to-end workflow that establishes the satisfiability or unsatisfiability of a constraint problem without trusting the external solver. Experimental results show that our framework's verified symmetry breaking also pays off in practice: a single parametric proof per problem family, reused across all instance sizes, reduces solver search effort by a factor of up to 2x10^7, while the entire in-Lean certification stays affordable, taking at most a few minutes for our largest instances.

</details>


### [203] [A report-grounded vision-language foundation model for colonoscopy from 280000 routine reports](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28466)
*Jia Yu,Yan Zhu,Yili He,Zilong Wang,Xinyang Jiang,Peiyao Fu,Ruijie Yang,Tianyi Chen,Siyuan Li,Zhihua Wang,Fei Wu,Quanlin Li,Xian Yang,Pinghong Zhou,Shuo Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EndoCLIP is a colonoscopy vision-language foundation model trained on 125,756 lesion-level image-text pairs recovered from routine reports. It outperforms existing VL encoders on retrieval, report generation, and clinical classification, with its linear probe approaching expert-level performance on benign-vs-malignant classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Routine colonoscopy reports contain rich expert descriptions but summarize entire procedures rather than captioning individual frames, leaving clinical findings weakly linked to images. This underutilization of vision-language data motivates recovering finding-to-frame correspondence for scalable supervision.

Method: The authors developed EndoCLIP by progressively recovering 125,756 lesion-level image-text pairs from 280,476 routine colonoscopy records. They then trained a vision-language foundation model on these pairs and evaluated it on image-text retrieval, structured report generation, and six multi-centre clinical classification tasks in both zero-shot and linear-probe settings.

Result: EndoCLIP outperformed general-purpose and biomedical vision-language encoders across all tasks. Notably, on benign-versus-malignant classification, its linear probe approached the performance of 12 expert endoscopists in a blinded study.

Conclusion: Recovering finding-to-frame correspondence from routine documentation can transform it into scalable supervision, enabling clinical targets to be specified in natural language rather than requiring separate annotations for each task.

Abstract: Vision-language models remain underused in colonoscopy despite the rich expert descriptions recorded in routine reports. These reports document lesion appearance, size and location but summarise entire procedures rather than caption individual frames, leaving clinical findings only weakly linked to the corresponding images. Here we develop EndoCLIP, a colonoscopy vision-language foundation model trained on 125,756 lesion-level image-text pairs progressively recovered from 280,476 routine colonoscopy records. Across lesion-level image-text retrieval, structured report generation and six multi-centre clinical classification tasks, EndoCLIP outperforms general-purpose and biomedical vision-language encoders in both zero-shot and linear-probe settings. On benign-versus-malignant classification, its linear probe approaches the performance of expert readers in a blinded study involving 12 endoscopists. These results suggest that recovering finding-to-frame correspondence can transform routine documentation into scalable supervision, enabling clinical targets to be specified in language rather than separately annotated for each task.

</details>


### [204] [Towards Autonomous Aircraft Surveillance from Nanosatellites through On-Board Inference and Generative Data Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28470)
*Antonio Delgado-Rosa,David Muñoz-Valero,Enrique Adrian Villarrubia-Martin,Juan Moreno-Garcia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A workflow combining on-board edge inference with diffusion-model-based generative data augmentation is proposed to overcome nanosatellite downlink limitations and class imbalance in airborne surveillance, achieving improved detection accuracy (mAP from 77.9% to 82.2%) and real-time on-orbit processing at 25-30 FPS.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Airborne surveillance from low Earth orbit nanosatellites faces two interconnected bottlenecks: (1) limited downlink budgets make transmitting terabytes of raw imagery impractical, and (2) open satellite datasets for aircraft detection are scarce and severely class-imbalanced, hindering robust learning for rare aircraft classes.

Method: A dual-pronged workflow: (1) on-board inference on a 6U CubeSat using a low-power edge tensor accelerator with a quantised detector, and (2) generative data augmentation via a diffusion model fine-tuned with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to produce synthetic minority-class imagery, which is automatically pseudo-labelled by an intermediate detector and merged with classically augmented samples.

Result: The balanced dataset raised global mAP from 77.9% to 82.2%, minority-class F1-score from 0.683 to 0.811, and the quantised detector fits on-chip memory while achieving 25-30 FPS on orbit.

Conclusion: The computational tests support the proposed workflow as a viable decision-support tool for real-time, autonomous airborne surveillance from nanosatellites, contrasting favourably with the conventional bent-pipe architecture where satellites act as passive data collectors.

Abstract: Airborne surveillance from low Earth orbit is hindered by two interconnected bottlenecks: nanosatellites have a limited downlink budget, yet the conventional approach still transmits terabytes of raw imagery to the ground for processing, and open satellite datasets for aircraft are scarce and severely class-imbalanced. These limitations either delay timely decision-making or prevent standard detectors from learning robust representations of rare aircraft classes. In this paper, a workflow that combines on-board inference with generative data augmentation is proposed to address both limitations jointly. Inference is executed on a 6U CubeSat equipped with a low-power edge tensor accelerator, while a diffusion model fine-tuned through low-rank adaptation generates synthetic minority-class imagery. This synthetic output is automatically annotated, pseudo-labelled, by an intermediate detector and merged with classically augmented samples. The results show that the balanced dataset increases global mean average precision from 77.9% to 82.2%, with the minority class rising from F1=0.683 to F1=0.811, and that the quantised detector fits the on-chip memory and projects 25-30 frames per second on orbit. This approach contrasts with the conventional bent-pipe architecture, in which the satellite acts as a passive data collector. Therefore, the computational tests support the proposed workflow as a decision-support tool for real-time, autonomous airborne surveillance from nanosatellites.

</details>


### [205] [A Fuzzy Rule-based Neuro-Symbolic Approach for Pipe Severity Prediction in Sewer Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28481)
*Ngoc Thai Le,Thanh Ma,Umberto Straccia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A modular neuro-symbolic framework decouples perception (Swin Transformer predicting pipe defect CODEs) from reasoning (fuzzy-logic J48 decision rules), achieving substantial gains over direct image classification for sewer pipe severity assessment, while providing traceable, interpretable inference paths.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard automated sewer pipe severity assessment uses direct image classification, which is a "black box" where the relationship between visual defects and final severity scores is implicit and untraceable. There is a need for an interpretable framework that explicitly links defect observations to severity decisions.

Method: A two-stage neuro-symbolic framework: (1) Perception module — a Swin Transformer predicts 14 multilabel inspection CODE degrees from images. (2) Reasoning module — Weka's J48 decision tree is trained on ground-truth CODEs and severity labels, with its paths converted into 19 fixed IF-THEN rules. Inference uses fuzzy logic: t-norm activations from CODE conditions are weighted by rule confidence and aggregated via s-norms to produce class evidence. Three operator pairs (Product, Łukasiewicz, Hamacher) were evaluated on 3,244 images across five imbalanced severity classes. Ground-truth labels were obtained via consensus from five LLMs analyzing original inspector notes.

Result: The neuro-symbolic framework outperformed direct image-only classification, with improvements of 17.9% in accuracy, 12.2% in balanced accuracy, 23.0% in Macro F1, and 17.3% in MCC. The approach also provides traceable reasoning from predicted CODE degrees through rule activations to final severity evidence.

Conclusion: The modular fuzzy rule-based neuro-symbolic framework successfully combines competitive class-balanced performance with full interpretability, bridging the gap between visual defect detection and severity scoring in sewer pipe assessment through explicit, auditable IF-THEN reasoning chains.

Abstract: Standard automated sewer pipe severity assessment relies on direct image classification, creating a "black box" where the link between visual defects and final severity scores remains implicit. This study introduces a modular, fuzzy rule-based neuro-symbolic framework that bridges this gap by decoupling neural perception from symbolic reasoning. The perception module utilizes a Swin Transformer to predict 14 multilabel inspection CODE degrees directly from images. For reasoning, a DT, specifically Weka's J48, algorithm is trained on ground-truth CODEs and severity labels, and its paths are converted into 19 fixed IF--THEN rules. Inference operates via fuzzy logic: t-norm activations from CODE conditions are weighted by rule confidence and combined with corresponding s-norms to produce interpretable class evidence. We assessed Product, Łukasiewicz, and Hamacher operator pairs using a dataset of 3,244 images spanning five highly imbalanced severity classes. Ground-truth labels were robustly generated via consensus from five independent large language models analyzing original inspector notes. Our results show an improvement of accuracy, balanced accuracy, Macro F1 and MCC by 17.9%, 12.2%, 23.0%, and 17.3%, respectively, over image-only based classification.
  Overall, the framework combines competitive class-balanced performance with traceable reasoning from predicted CODE degrees to rule supports and severity evidence.

</details>


### [206] [SCOPE: Supply-Chain Operations through Coupled Policies for End-to-End Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28488)
*Yunhao Liang,Xianqi Cao,Pujun Zhang,Yuan Qu,Yongzhi Qi,Ningxuan Kang,Max Z. J. Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SCOPE proposes a composite policy model that unifies supply-chain replenishment decisions—assortment, sourcing, frequency, and routing—through shared token-based representations and coupled policies, outperforming stage-wise optimization on real data from Dingdong and JD.com.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Supply-chain replenishment involves four coupled decisions (which products, which source, how often, which routes), yet these are typically optimized in isolation by separate departments and systems, leading to stockouts, excess inventory, and unnecessary transportation costs.

Method: SCOPE tokenizes supply-chain entities (products, facilities, vehicles), embeds them in a shared operational representation, and maps each token type to its corresponding decision interface. Decisions are made sequentially, each conditioned on prior decisions, with a shared system-level utility evaluating the complete plan. The framework is instantiated for urban fresh-retail replenishment.

Result: On operational data from Dingdong and JD.com—representing different replenishment echelons—SCOPE consistently outperforms both stage-wise optimization methods and practice-oriented baselines commonly used in real supply-chain operations.

Conclusion: Learning and coordinating cross-department operational couplings yields more effective end-to-end supply-chain decisions than optimizing each decision stage in isolation.

Abstract: Can supply-chain AI move beyond isolated decision modules toward unified operational planning? A complete replenishment plan specifies which products each location carries, which upstream facility supplies it, how often it is replenished, and how deliveries are routed. These decisions are operationally coupled: the selected assortment changes the demand and load passed to later stages; source assignment and replenishment frequency reshape the delivery requests; and route feasibility and cost, in turn, determine the system value of the earlier choices. Yet in modern supply chains, these decisions are often handled by separate departments and optimized through separate systems, which can lead to stockouts, inventory exposure, and avoidable transportation. We propose SCOPE: Supply-Chain Operations through Coupled Policies for End-to-End Coordination, a composite policy model that represents supply-chain entities as tokens, contextualizes them through a shared operational representation, and maps each token type to the corresponding decision interface. Each decision builds on the partial plan formed by earlier decisions while the completed plan is evaluated using a shared system-level utility. We instantiate this framework in urban fresh-retail replenishment, where service frequency, assortment, capacity pressure, and road-network routing interact strongly, and evaluate it on real operational data from Dingdong and JD.com, two large-scale supply chains operating at different replenishment echelons. Across both settings, SCOPE consistently outperforms methods that optimize each decision stage separately, as well as practice-oriented baselines commonly used in supply-chain operations. These results show that learning and coordinating cross-department operational couplings lead to more effective end-to-end supply-chain decisions.

</details>


### [207] [InfoOps Bench: A live information operations safety benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28503)
*Dorian Quelle,Lisa-Maria Neudert,Jonathan Bright,John Gallacher*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a dynamic, continuously updated AI benchmark evaluating 17 frontier language models' resistance to state-backed information operations from Russia, China, and Iran, finding integrity scores ranging from 8.8% to 94.5%, with Chinese-developed models showing sharp compliance drops on China-critical claims.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: State-backed information operations increasingly leverage AI models to generate and amplify propaganda. Existing static benchmarks risk saturation as models are patched. A live, continuously updated benchmark using real-world, active information operation claims is needed to robustly measure model integrity over time.

Method: The authors built a benchmark from over 2,100 information operations sourced from a live monitoring pipeline tracking Russian, Chinese, and Iranian state-backed media. They tested 17 models from 8 providers across four prompt framings. Integrity is measured as the refusal rate (percentage of requests declined). Additional metrics include fact-checking rates, fabrication rates, and harmfulness of generated output relative to source material. A companion website provides weekly updates.

Result: Integrity scores varied dramatically from 8.8% to 94.5% (85.7-point spread), unexplained by model size. Fact-checking rates ranged from 2.9% to 72.9%. Some models fabricated harmful details exceeding the source material; others defused claims even while complying. Chinese-developed models (except GLM 5.2) exhibited a 48–70 percentage-point compliance drop on factually grounded but China-critical claims relative to matched benign claims, indicating politically motivated refusal behavior.

Conclusion: Most frontier models can be readily co-opted for state-backed information operations. Integrity is partly tied to general refusal tendencies, creating a tension between usability and safety. Chinese-developed models display politically asymmetric refusal behavior, sharply cutting compliance on China-critical content. The dynamic benchmark approach offers a saturation-resistant method for ongoing integrity assessment.

Abstract: In this paper we present an active, constantly updated AI benchmark which measures the integrity of frontier language models against being co-opted for state-backed information operations. We draw on over 2,100 information operations from a live monitoring pipeline which tracks Russian, Chinese and Iranian state-backed information assets. Alongside this paper, we release a companion website that tracks the most prominent claims spread by state-backed media outlets, updated weekly, available from: pattrn.ai/research/infoopsbench. The dynamic nature of the benchmark makes it resistant to saturation.
  In the benchmark, we test 17 models from 8 providers across four prompt framings. We find that most models can be co-opted for information operations. Integrity scores, defined as the percentage of refused requests, range from 8.8% to 94.5%, an 85.7-percentage-point spread not explained by model size. Model choice also changes the character of the resulting operation. Some models fabricate details and produce output more harmful than the source material, others defuse claims even while complying, and fact-checking rates vary from 2.9% to 72.9%.
  Integrity against information operations is at least partly related to refusal to produce content even for benign claims, illustrating the challenge of balancing model usability with safety. With one exception (Z.ai's GLM 5.2), the Chinese-developed models sharply cut compliance on factually grounded but China-critical claims, dropping 48-70 percentage points relative to matched benign claims.

</details>


### [208] [Selective Credibility-Limited Belief Update](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28523)
*Theofanis Aravanis,Costas D. Koutras*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces selective credibility-limited belief update, a framework where epistemic inputs are transformed into weaker proxies on a per-source-world basis before applying credibility-restricted transitions, unifying and extending both standard KM update and credibility-limited update.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing credibility-limited belief update treats epistemic input as indivisible, failing to model scenarios where only part of a compound input can be realized. The authors aim to capture cases where, relative to each source world, only a weakened version of the input is credible or achievable.

Method: The authors propose selective credibility-limited update operators defined semantically via transformation functions that map each source world and epistemic input to a weaker proxy, followed by credibility-limited transition. They provide both semantic characterizations and axiomatic characterizations, identify two sub-classes (consistency-preserving and maximal consistency-preserving operators), and prove that credibility-limited update and KM update are recovered as special cases.

Result: The framework yields a unified account strictly more expressive than both KM update and credibility-limited update. Two well-behaved sub-classes are characterized: consistency-preserving operators (proxy must be credible whenever the original input is consistent) and maximal consistency-preserving operators (proxy must be maximally informative among credible consequences).

Conclusion: The proposed framework provides a unified, strictly more expressive account of belief update that encompasses established approaches while supporting source-dependent selective acceptance, demonstrating that selective weakening of epistemic inputs before credibility-restricted transition is both semantically and axiomatically well-behaved.

Abstract: Belief update concerns changes in an agent's beliefs induced by changes in the underlying world. Standard Katsuno-Mendelzon update assumes that an epistemic input can be incorporated from every initially possible world, whereas credibility-limited belief update restricts, for each source world, the successor worlds regarded as credible or reachable. Nevertheless, existing credibility-limited approaches treat the epistemic input as an indivisible whole, and therefore cannot represent cases in which only part of a compound epistemic input can be realized. We introduce selective credibility-limited belief update, in which the epistemic input is transformed, relative to each source world, into a weaker proxy before the credibility-limited transition is performed. We provide semantic and axiomatic characterizations of the resulting class of update operators. We then identify two well-behaved sub-classes; namely, consistency-preserving update operators, which require every transformed epistemic input to be credible from its source world whenever the original epistemic input is consistent, and maximal consistency-preserving update operators, which additionally require the selected proxy to be maximally informative among the credible consequences of the original epistemic input. Finally, we establish the generality of the proposed framework by showing that credibility-limited belief update is recovered as a special case, while Katsuno--Mendelzon belief update emerges when credibility restrictions are removed and the transformation functions are taken to be identities. These results demonstrate that the framework provides a unified and strictly more expressive account of belief update, encompassing established approaches while supporting source-dependent selective acceptance.

</details>


### [209] [MANTA: Multi-Agent Network Topology Adaptation for Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28527)
*Mao-xun Huang,Jerry Wang,Yi-Cheng Lai,Zhengxin Zhang,Claire Cardie,Hen-Hsen Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MANTA is a framework that enables multi-agent systems to dynamically adapt their communication topology at inference time, rather than using fixed or offline-optimized structures. It initializes a task-conditioned topology and applies bounded updates during execution based on collaboration traces, achieving state-of-the-art results across five benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-agent systems treat communication topology as a fixed design choice or offline optimization target, missing the opportunity to adapt collaboration structures dynamically at inference time when the current organization proves insufficient for the task at hand.

Method: MANTA initializes a task-conditioned topology from prior structural experience before execution. During deployment, it monitors collaboration traces and applies bounded structural updates — modifying agent roles, communication links, execution order, information visibility, and validation pathways — while preserving the task interface and agent budget.

Result: MANTA achieved an average score of 74.0 across five benchmarks (information seeking, tool use, planning, workflow execution, mathematical reasoning), outperforming the strongest baseline by 5.8 percentage points and obtaining the best result on PlanCraft.

Conclusion: Inference-time self-improvement can be extended to the architecture of collaboration itself, demonstrating that dynamic topology adaptation in multi-agent systems yields significant performance gains over static communication structures.

Abstract: Large language model-based multi-agent systems improve complex problem solving through task decomposition, agent specialization, information exchange, and intermediate validation. However, existing systems typically treat communication topology as a fixed design choice or an offline optimization target. We introduce MANTA, a framework for Multi-Agent Network Topology Adaptation that enables communication structures to self-evolve at inference time. Before execution, MANTA initializes a task-conditioned topology from prior structural experience. During deployment, it monitors collaboration traces and applies bounded structural updates when the current organization becomes insufficient. These updates can modify agent roles, communication links, execution order, information visibility, and validation pathways while preserving the task interface and agent budget. We evaluate MANTA against representative single-agent and multi-agent baselines on five benchmarks spanning information seeking, tool use, planning, workflow execution, and mathematical reasoning. MANTA achieves the highest average score of 74.0, outperforming the strongest baseline by 5.8 percentage points and obtaining the best result on PlanCraft. These results show that inference-time self-improvement can extend to the architecture of collaboration itself.

</details>


### [210] [Rethinking Inference-Time Scaling in Local Computer-Use Agents: Failure Modes and Compute Tradeoffs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28573)
*Woongkyu Lee,Jungwook Choi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper systematically studies inference-time scaling for local computer-use agents across four dimensions (contextual, temporal, structural, parallel), finding that additional computation often yields diminishing returns and shifts failure modes rather than resolving them, suggesting selective compute allocation and failure-aware control are needed for resource-constrained CUAs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying autonomous computer-use agents locally is increasingly important for privacy, cost efficiency, and usability, but improving their performance under strict hardware constraints is challenging. While inference-time scaling benefits frontier models, its effectiveness for resource-constrained local models remains poorly understood, motivating this systematic empirical investigation.

Method: The authors conduct a systematic empirical study evaluating inference-time scaling across four dimensions — contextual (historical grounding), temporal (longer execution horizons), structural (two-stage agent decomposition), and parallel (parallel execution branches) — using Qwen3-VL-8B/30B-A3B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B, and OpenCUA-7B on the OSWorld benchmark.

Result: Contextual scaling improves trajectory stability and task accuracy but saturates with token cost, with failures shifting from repetitive/stalled trajectories to premature false successes. Temporal scaling reduces max-step stalls but does not substantially improve task success, merely extending erroneous trajectories. Structural decomposition introduces planning/formatting overhead in local two-stage agents. Parallel scaling partially mitigates these failures but at substantial computational cost.

Conclusion: Efficient local CUAs require selective compute allocation, failure-aware control mechanisms, and agentic frameworks designed around the specific capabilities and limitations of local models, rather than indiscriminately applying inference-time scaling.

Abstract: Deploying autonomous computer-use agents (CUAs) locally is increasingly important for privacy, cost efficiency, and practical usability, yet improving their performance under strict hardware constraints remains challenging. While recent studies show that inference-time scaling can improve frontier computer-use agents through additional computation during execution, its effectiveness for resource-constrained local models remains poorly understood. We present a systematic empirical study of inference-time scaling in local CUAs across contextual, temporal, structural, and parallel dimensions. We evaluate Qwen3-VL-8B/30B-A3B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B, and OpenCUA-7B on the OSWorld benchmark. Our results show that additional computation often yields diminishing returns while changing failure modes. Contextual scaling provides historical grounding that improves trajectory stability and task accuracy, but its gains saturate as token cost increases and failures shift from repetitive or stalled trajectories toward premature false successes. Temporal scaling similarly reduces max-step stalls, yet does not substantially improve task success, indicating that longer horizons often extend erroneous trajectories rather than correct them. We further find that structural decomposition can introduce planning and formatting overhead in local two-stage agents, while parallel scaling partially mitigates these failures at a substantial computational cost. Overall, our findings suggest that efficient local CUAs require selective compute allocation, failure-aware control mechanisms, and agentic frameworks designed around the capabilities and limitations of local models.

</details>


### [211] [DualG-MRAG: Decoupling Macro-Reasoning and Micro-Matching for Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28580)
*Jiacheng Tao,Qingyun Sun,Haonan Yuan,Ziwei Zhang,Jianxin Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DualG-MRAG proposes a dual-tier graph framework for Multimodal RAG, decoupling global structural reasoning (Macro Graph) from fine-grained evidence matching (Micro Graph), and using a GNN Retriever with dynamic programming decoding to extract explicit reasoning paths, outperforming baselines in multi-hop multimodal QA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MM-RAG methods fail at complex multi-hop reasoning because instance-level matching cannot capture cross-modal and cross-document relationships. Graph-enhanced methods face a fundamental dilemma: fine-grained visual features cause explosive graph expansion and retrieval noise, while coarse-grained representations discard critical local evidence.

Method: DualG-MRAG introduces a decoupled dual-tier architecture: (1) a Macro Graph for global topological routing that suppresses retrieval noise by isolating structural reasoning, and (2) a Micro Graph for precise local verification with fine-grained evidence. Retrieval is formulated as query-driven message passing via a GNN Retriever. A dynamic programming decoding mechanism extracts explicit reasoning paths directly from the GNN's forward pass to provide coherent structural guidance to the generative model.

Result: Extensive experiments show DualG-MRAG outperforms baselines on both evidence recall and complex QA accuracy in multimodal multi-hop reasoning tasks.

Conclusion: Decoupling macro-level structural reasoning from micro-level evidence matching, combined with GNN-based message passing and explicit reasoning path extraction, effectively resolves the granularity dilemma in multimodal graph-enhanced RAG and significantly improves multi-hop reasoning performance.

Abstract: While Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (MM-RAG) has shown promising results, it still struggles with complex multi-hop reasoning tasks. Existing methods primarily focus on independent instance-level matching, which often fails to capture explicit relationships across modalities and documents. Although Graph-enhanced methods introduce structural modeling, they face a fundamental challenge in multimodal scenarios: incorporating fine-grained visual features leads to rapid graph expansion and retrieval noise, whereas coarse-grained representations cause the discarding of critical local evidence. To address this dilemma, we propose DualG-MRAG, a Dual-tier framework that introduces a decoupled architecture comprising Macro-reasoning and Micro-matching Graphs for Multimodal RAG. Specifically, to suppress retrieval noise by isolating global structural reasoning from fine-grained evidence matching, we construct a Macro Graph for global topological routing and a Micro Graph for precise local verification. Subsequently, to enable dynamic relevance propagation across heterogeneous evidence sources, we formulate retrieval as a query-driven message passing process via a GNN Retriever. Furthermore, to provide the generative model with coherent structural guidance, we introduce a dynamic programming decoding mechanism that extracts explicit reasoning paths directly from the GNN's forward pass, replacing the standard input of isolated document chunks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DualG-MRAG outperforms baselines in both evidence recall and complex QA accuracy.

</details>


<div id='cs.SE'></div>

### [212] [OwlPath: Lossless Knowledge Compression for LLM Bug Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27249)
*Bo Zhang,Ren Pan,Huan Chen,Xiang Song*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: OwlPath compresses source code into an OWL2 ontology, enabling LLM-based software agents to retrieve structurally relevant code via SPARQL property-path queries. It achieves 2.06× recall improvement, 28.8% token reduction, and 39.5% runtime savings over the CodeGraph baseline on SWE-bench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based software engineering agents face context window constraints (~100K tokens). Standard retrieval models treat code as plain text, forcing agents to resolve multi-hop structural dependencies (subclass chains, transitive callers, interface implementations) through costly trial-and-error. There is a need for lossless knowledge compression that can answer such structural queries with minimal relevant code fragments.

Method: OwlPath is an OWL2 reasoning layer built atop CodeGraph. It uses tree-sitter to parse multi-language source code (Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go) into a unified OWL2 ontology. Two complementary modules: (1) a transitive-closure engine that resolves multi-hop structural relations via single SPARQL property-path queries; (2) OWL Software Knowledge Map (OWL-SKM), a precomputed ~3KB summary containing module trees, core APIs, and issue-related symbols for directing first-query targeting.

Result: On 18 SWE-bench Pro instances: 68.4% strict-apply rate (vs. 66.7% baseline), 28.8% token reduction, 39.5% runtime reduction. On 67-instance offline retrieval: 2.06× recall improvement (0.464 vs. 0.226), 88.1% hit rate (vs. 59.7%). On a 37-question structural retrieval benchmark: recall rises from 4.4% to 28.8%, with 69–80% accuracy on transitive caller and interface tasks.

Conclusion: OwlPath demonstrates that encoding source code into OWL2 ontologies with property-path reasoning significantly outperforms text-based retrieval for structural code queries, enabling LLM agents to resolve multi-hop dependencies efficiently with lower token cost and faster runtime.

Abstract: LLM-based software engineering agents are constrained by limited context windows: roughly 100K tokens must store structurally relevant code  subsets to resolve bugs. Standard retrieval models treat code as plain text, forcing agents to resolve multi-hop dependencies including subclass  chains, transitive callers and interface implementations through slow trial and error. We tackle this limitation with lossless knowledge  compression, encoding source code into an OWL2 ontology to answer structural queries using minimal relevant code fragments.
  We present OwlPath, an OWL2 reasoning layer atop CodeGraph, a widely used code intelligence platform with 500K+ GitHub stars, offering a unified  CLI for structural code retrieval. Powered by tree-sitter parsing, OwlPath supports multi-language repositories (Python, JavaScript,  TypeScript, Go, etc.) and encodes language-specific semantics into a unified OWL2 ontology. It adopts two complementary modules. First, a  transitive-closure engine fetches all structurally linked symbols via single SPARQL property-path queries, capturing multi-hop relations missed  by string matching. Second, the OWL Software Knowledge Map (OWL-SKM) precomputes a compact 3KB summary with module trees, core APIs and  issue-related symbols, directing agents to target modules in the first query.
  Evaluated on 18 SWE-bench Pro instances, OwlPath obtains a 68.4% strict-apply rate versus 66.7% for the CodeGraph baseline, cutting token usage  by 28.8% and runtime by 39.5%. In offline retrieval tests over 67 instances, OwlPath improves recall 2.06 times (0.464 vs 0.226) and reaches  88.1% hit rate compared to CodeGraph's 59.7%. On a 37-question structural retrieval benchmark, recall rises from 4.4% to 28.8%, with 69-80%  accuracy on transitive caller and interface tasks.

</details>


### [213] [Do Context Files Help Coding Agents? A Two-Agent Ablation Study on Real Repositories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27250)
*Prakhar Khatri*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A controlled ablation study across two frontier AI coding agents (Claude Code and Codex) on 17 real-world tasks finds that persistent context files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) do not measurably improve task correctness. Failures stem from implementation skill deficits—feature design, pattern selection, exact wiring—rather than missing repository knowledge. Task difficulty is agent-specific, which may explain contradictory findings in prior single-agent studies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Persistent context files are widely adopted as standard practice for guiding AI coding agents, yet empirical evidence regarding their effectiveness is contradictory. The authors aim to resolve this contradiction through a rigorous, controlled ablation study.

Method: A controlled ablation of context-injection strategy was conducted across two frontier agents (Claude Code and Codex), encompassing 17 real tasks drawn from 3 repositories (15 shared + 2 Codex-only), totaling 288 evaluated runs with gold-test evaluation. The study employs equivalence testing (bounded to ≤10–15pp), failure-mode triage, and a manipulation probe to assess whether AGENTS.md converts near-misses to passes.

Result: Context strategy shows no measurable effect on correctness for either agent (bounded by equivalence testing). Failure-mode analysis reveals agents fail due to implementation skill (feature design, pattern selection, exact wiring), not lack of repository knowledge. A manipulation probe confirms the real AGENTS.md never converts a near-miss into a pass. Additionally, borderline task difficulty is agent-specific (Spearman ρ=0.75), offering an explanation for prior contradictory single-agent findings.

Conclusion: Persistent context files do not measurably improve coding agent performance; failures are rooted in implementation capability, not knowledge gaps. Agent-specific task difficulty bands may explain prior conflicting results, and the authors recommend multi-agent designs and release all artifacts for reproducibility.

Abstract: Persistent context files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) are standard practice for guiding AI coding agents, yet evidence for their effectiveness is contradictory. We present a controlled ablation of context-injection strategy across two frontier agents (Claude Code and Codex), 17 real tasks from 3 repositories (15 shared + 2 Codex-only), and 288 evaluated runs with gold-test evaluation. Context strategy does not measurably move correctness on either agent (bounded to <=10-15pp via equivalence testing). A failure-mode triage reveals why: agents fail on implementation skill---feature design, pattern selection, exact wiring---not missing repository knowledge that a context file could supply; a manipulation probe confirms the real AGENTS.md never converts a near-miss to a pass on either agent. We further show that borderline task difficulty is agent-specific (Spearman rho=0.75), offering a candidate explanation for prior contradictions: single-agent studies draw tasks from different agents' informative bands. We release all code, data, and analysis.

</details>


### [214] [AgentS4D: Benchmarking Runtime Risks across the Execution Lifecycle of LLM-Based Workspace Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27294)
*Jiajun Zhou,Zhaoxuan Ke,Jihang Ye,Xuanze Chen,Shanqing Yu,Qi Xuan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AgentS4D is a sandboxed benchmark for evaluating LLM-based workspace agent safety across the full runtime lifecycle. It uses a four-dimensional framework (risk-entry sources, induction strategies, target harms, lifecycle checkpoints) with 328 risk-injected cases. Evaluation of 20 harness-LLM combinations (6,560 runs) shows 68% triggered unsafe signals, with safety varying significantly by both harness-LLM pairing and risk introduction method. Critically, 66.22% of runs were unsafe yet completed successfully, demonstrating that task completion alone cannot establish runtime safety.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing safety benchmarks for LLM-based workspace agents either test executability or verify trajectories but rarely unify where risks enter, how unsafe behavior is induced, which harms are targeted, and where evidence appears during execution. This fragmentation prevents systematic understanding of agent safety failures across the full execution lifecycle.

Method: The authors propose a four-dimensional runtime-safety framework: (1) six risk-entry sources, (2) six induction strategies, (3) nine target harms for case construction, and (4) seven lifecycle checkpoints for organizing post-run evidence. AgentS4D implements this as a sandboxed benchmark with 328 risk-injected cases. They test all 20 combinations of four harnesses (Hermes, OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) and five LLM backends (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, MiniMax-M3, Qwen3.7-Plus), producing 6,560 total runs.

Result: 4,461 out of 6,560 runs (68.0%) triggered prespecified unsafe signals. Safety varied substantially across the 20 harness-LLM configurations and depended on how risk was introduced. The same induction strategy produced markedly different safety outcomes when delivered through different risk carriers, and the same target harm elicited different responses when realized through different carriers and strategies. Notably, 4,344 runs (66.22%) were unsafe yet completed successfully, indicating task completion is a misleading safety indicator.

Conclusion: Runtime safety evaluation must account for complete agent configurations (harness + LLM), diverse risk conditions (varying carriers, strategies, and harms), and lifecycle-wide evidence retention. Testing only one form of a risk can hide critical weaknesses, and task completion cannot serve as a proxy for safety.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based workspace agents execute stateful, multi-step workflows across heterogeneous resources, external tools, and persistent state. Their safety must therefore be assessed from actions, side effects, and state changes throughout execution. Although recent benchmarks have advanced executable safety testing and trajectory-aware verification, they rarely provide a unified account of where risks enter, how they elicit unsafe behavior, which harms they target, and where supporting evidence appears during execution. We introduce AgentS4D, a sandboxed benchmark for lifecycle-wide runtime safety evaluation. Its four-dimensional runtime-safety framework uses six risk-entry sources, six induction strategies, and nine target harms to guide case construction, while seven lifecycle checkpoints organize post-run evidence. AgentS4D contains 328 risk-injected cases. We evaluate all 20 combinations of four harnesses (Hermes, OpenClaw, Claude Code, and Codex) and five LLM backends (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, MiniMax-M3, and Qwen3.7-Plus) on these cases, yielding 6,560 runs. Overall, 4,461 runs (68.0%) trigger prespecified unsafe signals. Across the 20 configurations, the observed safety of an agent system varies with both its harness-LLM pairing and how risk is introduced. Agent systems exhibit markedly different safety behavior when the same induction strategy reaches them through different risk carriers. They also respond differently to the same target harm when it is realized through different carriers and strategies. Moreover, 4,344 runs (66.22% overall) are unsafe yet complete. Thus, task completion cannot establish runtime safety, and testing only one form of a risk can conceal important weaknesses. Evaluations should examine complete agent configurations across diverse risk conditions and retain evidence throughout execution.

</details>


### [215] [A Taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork Requirements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27302)
*Anastasia Mavridou,Hazel M. Taylor,Sandy Lozito,Louise A. Dennis,Michael Fisher,Marie Farrell*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents a two-level hierarchical taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork (HRT) requirements, derived from 361 requirements across 14 cross-domain sources, validated by 5 domain experts and demonstrated on a corpus of 448 requirements from 19 sources across six HRT domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Requirements for human-robot teamwork are fragmented across disparate sources with no unified framework to address the complexities of collaborative human-robot tasks, particularly in safety- and mission-critical domains.

Method: The authors extracted a construction corpus of 361 requirements from 14 cross-domain sources (academic literature, industry standards, and regulatory guidance). Through iterative classification and refinement, they developed a two-level hierarchical taxonomy. Validation was performed via expert evaluation with 5 domain specialists and a utility demonstration on an independent corpus of 448 requirements from 19 sources spanning six HRT domains.

Result: The resulting taxonomy comprises 6 high-level categories (information provision, relational control, decision support, safety mechanisms, performance monitoring, and foundational system capabilities) and 21 low-level subcategories. Expert evaluation and the independent utility demonstration confirmed the taxonomy's validity and applicability across multiple HRT domains.

Conclusion: The proposed taxonomy provides a unified, cross-domain framework for classifying and organizing HRT requirements, addressing a critical gap in the field and offering a structured foundation for designing, evaluating, and regulating collaborative human-robot systems in safety-critical applications.

Abstract: Autonomous systems are increasingly deployed in safety- and mission-critical domains where humans and robots must operate as a team to complete complex tasks. Existing requirements for Human-Robot teamwork remain fragmented across disparate sources, with no unified framework that addresses complexities of collaborative Human-Robot tasks. We address this gap by presenting a taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork (HRT) requirements derived from analysis of (academic and industrial) literature, standards and regulatory guidance. We extracted a construction corpus of 361 requirements from 14 cross-domain sources. Through iterative classification and refinement, we develop a two-level hierarchical taxonomy comprising 6 high-level categories and 21 low-level subcategories that distinguish information provision, relational control, decision support, safety mechanisms, performance monitoring, and foundational system capabilities. We validate the taxonomy through expert evaluation with 5 domain specialists and a utility demonstration on an independently assembled corpus of 448 requirements drawn from 19 sources spanning six HRT domains.

</details>


### [216] [SIGIL: Compiling Agent Skills into Typed Harnesses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27309)
*Jayanaka Dantanarayana,Savini Kashmira,Lingjia Tang,Jason Mars*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Prose-based AI agent skills suffer from low step compliance (56%) despite passing output checks. The authors introduce Skill Compilation via SIGIL, using AG-IR to compile prose skills into executable harnesses, achieving 86% step compliance, 2.3x completion rate, and 0.58x token usage, with model-independent guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents increasingly use prose procedure files ("skills") loaded into context and executed via tool-calling loops. However, because the procedure is described to the runtime but never structurally encoded, the model re-derives control flow on every invocation and may skip mandated steps (e.g., verification). Empirically, agents complete only 56% of mandated steps, yet still produce artifacts that pass superficial output checks — a silent reliability failure. Manually writing harnesses (where procedure is program structure) solves this but is tedious and abandons the accessible, authorable surface that made prose skills popular.

Method: The authors introduce Skill Compilation, embodied in a system called SIGIL. Its core innovation is AG-IR, a typed agentic intermediate representation that cleanly separates model-owned cognition (reasoning, generation) from code-owned mechanism (control flow, verification, structured sequencing). SIGIL compiles a prose skill specification into an executable harness: the harness enforces mandated steps as program structure while still invoking the model for cognitive subtasks. This preserves the prose authoring experience while delivering deterministic procedural compliance.

Result: Across 30 skills and two model generations: compiled harnesses perform 86% of mandated steps (vs. 56% for prose), complete the full procedure 2.3x more often, and require 0.58x the tokens. Critically, the 86% step compliance is model-independent — it holds steady across two model generations, while prose compliance swings from 56% to 68%.

Conclusion: Compiling prose skills into harnesses via SIGIL/AG-IR yields substantial and consistent improvements in procedural compliance, completion rate, and token efficiency. The separation of cognition from mechanism provides model-independent reliability guarantees, addressing a fundamental limitation in how AI agents consume and execute procedural knowledge.

Abstract: AI-Integrated agents increasingly acquire capability from skills: prose procedure files loaded into a model's context and run by a tool-calling loop. A skill is described to the runtime but never encoded in it, so the model re-derives its control flow on every run and may skip mandated verification. Across 30 skills and two model generations, a prose agent performs only 56% of the steps its own skill mandates, while producing artifacts that pass output checks. The remedy is known: write a harness, in which the procedure is program structure. However, hand-writing harnesses is tedious and discards the authoring surface that made skills succeed. To address this limitation, we introduce Skill Compilation, realized in SIGIL, which compiles a prose skill into an executable harness. At its center is AG-IR, a typed agentic intermediate representation separating model-owned cognition from code-owned mechanism. Compiled harnesses perform 86% of mandated steps, complete the full procedure 2.3x as often, and require 0.58x the tokens. Notably, the guarantee is model-independent: the harness holds at 86% across two model generations while prose swings from 56% to 68%.

</details>


### [217] [TrustChain-Review: A Risk-Adaptive Blockchain and Game-Theoretic Framework for Trustworthy AI-Assisted Code Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27310)
*Mohammad Naserameri*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: TrustChain-Review combines blockchain-based evidence, game-theoretic incentives, and risk-adaptive governance to improve code review trustworthiness, finding that full-evidence governance maximizes trust and detection while risk-adaptive governance offers better cost-efficiency for routine changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI-assisted software development accelerates coding and review but undermines accountability: developers may submit unverified code, reviewers may rubber-stamp changes, and centralized reputation systems are opaque and hard to audit. A trustworthy, verifiable, and incentive-compatible review mechanism is needed.

Method: The TrustChain-Review framework integrates three components: (1) a blockchain-based evidence layer for immutable, verifiable review records; (2) a three-player game-theoretic model capturing developers, reviewers, and the platform; and (3) a risk-sensitive governance rule that escalates controls only when expected benefits exceed costs. Evaluation uses controlled simulations calibrated with the Diff Quality Estimation dataset, comparing six governance configurations over 30 independent runs on metrics including reputation accuracy, trust convergence, malicious/superficial review detection, net platform utility, governance cost, and cost-efficiency.

Result: The full-evidence configuration achieves the strongest outcomes in reputation accuracy, trust convergence, and detection of both malicious and superficial reviews, but incurs the highest governance cost. The risk-adaptive configuration significantly reduces governance cost and improves cost-efficiency by applying stricter controls selectively, though its trust and detection metrics fall below the full-evidence baseline.

Conclusion: Full-evidence governance suits high-risk or audit-sensitive code changes, while risk-adaptive governance provides a more practical cost-trust trade-off for routine, lower-risk contributions.

Abstract: Context: AI-assisted software development can speed up coding and review, but it also makes accountability harder to establish. Developers may submit insufficiently verified code, reviewers may approve changes with limited inspection, and centralized reputation records may be difficult to audit. Objectives: This study introduces TrustChain-Review, a framework that combines verifiable evidence, strategic incentives, and risk-sensitive governance to support more trustworthy code review. Methods: The framework includes a blockchain-based evidence layer, a three-player game-theoretic model for developers, reviewers, and the platform, and a rule that applies stronger governance when the expected benefit justifies its cost. The evaluation uses a controlled simulation calibrated with the Diff Quality Estimation dataset. Six governance configurations are compared over 30 independent runs using reputation accuracy, trust convergence, malicious-review detection, superficial-review detection, net platform utility, governance cost, and cost-efficiency. Results: The full-evidence configuration produces the strongest reputation, trust, and detection results, but it also has the highest governance cost. The risk-adaptive configuration lowers this cost and improves cost-efficiency by applying stronger controls selectively, although its trust and detection results are lower than those of the full-evidence setting. Conclusion: Strong evidence-based governance is most appropriate for high-risk or audit-sensitive changes. For routine or lower-risk contributions, selective governance offers a more practical balance between trustworthiness and operational cost.

</details>


### [218] [PROGRESS: Property-Guided Regression Search for Semantic Falsification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27359)
*Davis Tocheuk Mo,Noshin Ulfat,Matthew B. Dwyer,Soneya Binta Hossain*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: PROGRESS combines property-based testing with coverage-guided evolutionary search to generate tests that reach deep program states and detect semantic bugs, outperforming both regression-test generation and standalone property-based testing on 25 Java systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Search-based regression test generation achieves high structural coverage but lacks independent oracles—existing faults become encoded as expected behavior. Property-based testing provides semantic oracles but struggles to reach deep states or satisfy selective preconditions. Neither approach alone is sufficient.

Method: PROGRESS integrates three components: (1) an LLM pipeline that extracts intent-bearing code context to generate executable jqwik properties while limiting implementation leakage; (2) an extension of EvoSuite's DynaMOSA with property-aware fitness functions that reward precondition satisfaction and prioritize falsifying executions; and (3) binding of property parameters using jqwik generators to connect quantified inputs to evolving test sequences.

Result: On 25 large-scale Java systems, PROGRESS detected 328/562 current-version bugs (58%) versus 0 for regression-test generation. It satisfied all preconditions for 70/150 hard-to-reach properties versus 18 for standalone jqwik. Ablation studies confirmed that documentation and caller/callee context are critical for generating valid executable properties.

Conclusion: PROGRESS successfully marries the structural exploration strength of search-based testing with the oracle independence of property-based testing, preserving coverage while exposing faults that regression-derived assertions miss.

Abstract: Search-based regression-test generation effectively explores complex program structures, yielding high structural coverage, but its oracles are derived from the system under test: faults already present are recorded as expected behavior rather than exposed. Property-based testing offers independent semantic oracles, but depends on high-quality properties and gives little guidance for reaching deep states or satisfying selective preconditions.
  We present PROGRESS (PROperty-Guided REgression Search for Semantic Falsification), integrating intent-driven properties into coverage-guided, search-based evolutionary test generation to reach deep program states and detect violations of intended behavior. PROGRESS (1) extracts intent-bearing code context and uses a language-model pipeline to generate executable jqwik properties while limiting implementation leakage; (2) extends EvoSuite's DynaMOSA with a search objective and property-aware fitness function per property, rewarding progress through preconditions and prioritizing falsifying executions; and (3) binds property parameters and uses jqwik-provided generators to connect quantified inputs to evolving test sequences, steering generation toward coverage and bug-detection goals.
  We evaluate PROGRESS on 25 large-scale Java systems against regression-test generation, standalone property-based testing, and context ablations. PROGRESS detects 328/562 current-version bugs (58%) versus none for regression-test generation, and satisfies all preconditions for 70/150 hard-to-reach properties versus 18 for standalone jqwik. Ablations show documentation and caller/callee context are key to generating valid executable properties. PROGRESS preserves structural exploration while exposing faults missed by regression-derived assertions; we release a comprehensive artifact package.

</details>


### [219] [From Backlog Items to Security Guidance: Towards Continuous Security Compliance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27374)
*Ignacio García Núñez,Florian Angermeir,Fabiola Moyón Constante*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: An NLP system that detects security-relevant backlog items and links them to applicable security requirements, evaluated with industrial data from regulated domains. Includes a labeled dataset, a recall-oriented classifier, and a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline grounded in security policy documents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In regulated domains, engineering teams struggle to make security requirements explicit in backlog items. Engineers must infer security relevance from brief, free-form descriptions and lack timely guidance on which security requirements apply, creating gaps in continuous security compliance throughout the development lifecycle.

Method: A two-part NLP pipeline: (1) a security-relevance classifier fine-tuned for high recall to detect which backlog items have security implications, and (2) a four-stage retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline that grounds retrieval in security requirements documents (company-internal policies and CIS Benchmarks) to link detected items to relevant clauses.

Result: The classifier achieved F2=0.774 in-distribution and mean zero-shot G-measure ≈0.65 across five established benchmarks, matching or outperforming published classical-ML and open-source GPT baselines. A labeled dataset of 288 backlog items with Fleiss' κ=0.787 (substantial inter-annotator agreement) was released. In preliminary RAG evaluation, 12 of 24 retrieved security clauses were rated ≥4/5 for relevance by two practitioners.

Conclusion: NLP-based backlog enrichment shows promise for supporting engineers in identifying security requirements early in development, offering first indicators that proactive, automated introduction of security requirements can facilitate continuous security compliance in regulated software engineering contexts.

Abstract: Continuous software engineering in regulated domains requires engineering teams to address security throughout the development lifecycle. Yet making security requirements explicit in backlog items is still problematic. Engineers must instead infer security relevance of backlog items from brief, free-form descriptions and often lack timely guidance on applicable requirements. We present an NLP-based backlog enrichment system that detects security-relevant backlog items and links them to relevant security requirements. The approach combines a security-relevance classifier with a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline over security requirements documents. The approach was developed and evaluated in the context of a large enterprise in highly regulated domains. We present three contributions. First, we release a dataset of 288 backlog items labeled for security relevance by nine security practitioners, with substantial agreement (Fleiss' $κ=0.787$). Second, a recall-oriented classifier achieving $F2=0.774$ in-distribution and mean zero-shot G-measure $\approx 0.65$ across five established benchmarks, matching or outperforming most published classical-ML and open-source GPT baselines. Third, we preliminarily evaluated a four-stage security requirements document-grounded RAG pipeline with two practitioners on industrial backlogs using company-internal security policies and CIS Benchmarks. Of the retrieved 24 clauses, 12 were rated at least 4/5 for relevance. Our findings provide first indicators that NLP-based product backlog enrichment can support engineers in identifying security requirements early in the development process. With this work we aim to facilitate continuous security compliance through proactive introduction of security requirements in continuous software engineering.

</details>


### [220] [SWE-NFI: Studying and Benchmarking Coding Agents for Non-Functional Improvements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27409)
*Pengyu Xue,He Yang Yuan,Xin Wang,Junkai Chen,Haonan Zhang,Boyuan Chen,Zishuo Ding,Zhenhao Li,Weiyi Shang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: SWE-NFI is a benchmark of 188 tasks from real Python pull requests, evaluating coding agents on non-functional improvements (NFIs) via 92 executable rules. While the best agent achieves 70% functional correctness, all agents significantly lag behind human developers on structural NFIs (0.0–1.3 vs. 1.5 human reference).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing coding agent benchmarks focus almost exclusively on functional correctness, ignoring behavior-preserving, non-functional improvements (e.g., refactoring, readability, maintainability) that are routine in real-world software development. This gap limits the practical assessment of agents for realistic development workflows.

Method: The authors construct SWE-NFI, a benchmark with 188 tasks sourced from merged pull requests in open-source Python projects. They operationalize developer-oriented NFIs into 92 executable rules and combine these with functional correctness testing in a unified evaluation suite, measuring both functional and non-functional performance against human reference implementations.

Result: The best-performing agent reaches 70.0% functional correctness. However, all evaluated agents (both commercial and open-source) fall short of human developers on overall NFI capability. The gap is starkest for structural code improvements, where agent NFI scores range from 0.0–1.3 versus the human reference score of 1.5.

Conclusion: SWE-NFI provides a reproducible foundation for evaluating and advancing coding agents beyond functional correctness, highlighting that current agents cannot yet match human-level non-functional improvement capability, especially for structural changes.

Abstract: Although coding agents have achieved impressive performance on correctness-oriented benchmarks, their ability to make behavior-preserving non-functional improvements (NFIs) remains underexplored. In real-world software development, developers continuously improve software quality without changing observable behavior, yet existing benchmarks primarily evaluate functional correctness and provide limited support for assessing these non-functional improvements.
  In this paper, we present SWE-NFI, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on NFIs beyond functional correctness. Our benchmark contains 188 tasks constructed from real merged pull requests in open-source Python projects. We operationalize developer-oriented NFIs into 92 executable rules and develop a comprehensive evaluation suite that combines functional correctness testing with rule-based NFI evaluation.
  We evaluate state-of-the-art commercial and open-source coding agents. Although the best-performing agent achieves a 70.0\% functional correctness rate, all evaluated agents generally fall short of human developers in overall NFI capability. The gap is particularly evident for structural code improvements, where agents' NFI scores range from 0.0 to 1.3, compared with 1.5 for the human reference. Our benchmark and findings provide a reproducible foundation for evaluating and advancing coding agents beyond functional correctness.

</details>


### [221] [LimICE: Integrating LLM into ICE Framework for Efficient Loop Invariant Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27606)
*Kai Fan,ShiWen Yu,GuangSheng Fan,HaoAng Chi,WanWei Liu,Ji Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes Incremental ICE, a framework that decomposes loop invariant synthesis into incremental lemma generation inspired by IC3. It instantiates LimICE using LLMs with ICE-DT fallback, achieving state-of-the-art performance: solving 349/367 linear and 47/50 nonlinear benchmarks, outperforming LLM baselines by 12–24% in solved instances and 36–63% in speed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing learning-based loop invariant synthesis methods are monolithic and struggle to simultaneously satisfy all necessary conditions for complex invariants, because they cannot strictly constrain the learning process. The key insight is that loop invariants are naturally structured as ordered sequences of lemmas rather than single formulas, yet no prior approach systematically exploits this incremental structure within a sound learning framework.

Method: The authors propose Incremental ICE, which integrates the incremental induction philosophy of IC3 into the ICE (Implication Counterexample) learning framework. It defines a lemma-specific learning objective and introduces a counterexample filtering mechanism to ensure sound incremental learning. The instantiated tool, LimICE, uses LLMs to generate ordered lemma sequences and employs ICE-DT (a decision-tree-based invariant learner) as a fallback to complement incomplete lemma sequences.

Result: On 367 linear benchmarks, LimICE solves 349 (95.1%) in avg. 15.2s; on 50 nonlinear benchmarks, it solves 47 (94%) in avg. 8.8s. Compared to the SOTA LLM-based baseline, it solves 12–24% more instances and runs 36–63% faster. Against strong non-LLM baselines, it solves at least 86 and 27 additional instances on linear and nonlinear benchmarks respectively.

Conclusion: Incremental decomposition of loop invariant synthesis into lemma sequences, combined with LLM generation and a sound counterexample-guided learning framework, significantly outperforms monolithic approaches. LimICE establishes a new state of the art for learning-based loop invariant synthesis across both linear and nonlinear benchmarks.

Abstract: Loop invariant synthesis is a fundamental problem in program verification, yet the inherent undecidability makes it highly challenging. Recent studies have increasingly employed various machine learning techniques to generate loop invariants. However, most of these methods adopt a monolithic approach. Due to the inability to strictly constrain the learning process, learning-based methods struggle to simultaneously consider all necessary conditions and generate complete invariants when tackling complex problems. In fact, a loop invariant is often an ordered sequence of lemmas, rather than a single invariant formula. This motivates us to propose Incremental ICE, a novel learning framework for incremental synthesis. Our framework integrates the incremental philosophy of IC3 into the general invariant learning framework ICE. By defining a lemma-specific learning objective and introducing a counterexample filtering mechanism, we can achieve sound incremental learning. Under this framework, we instantiate a loop invariant synthesis tool, LimICE, which leverages LLMs to generate the ordered sequence of lemmas and incorporates ICE-DT as a fallback mechanism to complement the lemma sequence. Experiments on 367 linear benchmarks and 50 nonlinear benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. LimICE solves 349 (out of 367) linear problems on an average of 15.2 seconds and 47 (out of 50) nonlinear problems on an average of 8.8 seconds. Compared to the state-of-the-art LLM-based baseline, our approach solves 12-24% more instances while running 36-63% faster across linear and nonlinear benchmarks. LimICE also consistently outperforms strong non-LLM baselines and solves at least 86 and 27 additional instances on the linear and nonlinear benchmarks, respectively.

</details>


### [222] [Agentic Metaverse Services: A New As-a-Service Paradigm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28242)
*Xiaofei Xu,Quan Z. Sheng,Zhongjie Wang,Boualem Benatallah,Xiao Wang,Ruipeng Han*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper introduces Agentic Metaverse Service (AMServ) and Meta-AaaS, a new service paradigm where GenAI-empowered agents operate within the metaverse as encapsulated services offering perception, decision-making, execution, collaboration, and content generation capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The shift from conversational chatbots to agentic AI represents a major GenAI breakthrough, but there is a gap in understanding how agentic services can be systematically integrated into the metaverse environment to form a new service computing paradigm.

Method: This is a position/overview paper that: (1) traces the evolution of agents and services under GenAI empowerment, (2) articulates the roles and principles of agentic services in the metaverse, (3) defines the forms, characteristics, and principles of AMServ and Meta-AaaS, and (4) discusses typical application examples and future research directions.

Result: The paper establishes AMServ as a new metaverse service form and Meta-AaaS as its implementation approach, providing a conceptual framework for agentic services in virtual ecosystems. It identifies application examples and outlines new tendencies and research directions for this emerging paradigm.

Conclusion: AMServ and Meta-AaaS represent a significant opportunity for human society and the service industry in the AI era, poised to drive rapid development of emerging service industries by combining GenAI-powered agent capabilities with immersive metaverse environments.

Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is reconstructing the digital virtual world, upgrading agents through enhancing their abilities in autonomous learning, multi-modal interaction, content generation, and collaborative decision-making. In particular, the shift from conversational chatbots to agentic AI, the most recent significant technical breakthrough of GenAI, has brought a new form of services, agentic services and Agent-as-a-Service (AaaS), in which the agent's abilities are encapsulated, such as perception, decision-making, execution, collaboration, and content generation, to provide the customized agent services to users. The metaverse is a virtual ecosystem for human life, work, creation, and entertainment, supported by the new generation of digital technologies. Through combining agentic services and the metaverse, an Agentic Metaverse Service, denoted as AMServ, is produced for metaverse business processing, as a new form of metaverse service. The AaaS in the metaverse environment, denoted as Meta-AaaS, as an approach to realize AMServ, has become a new paradigm of agentic services and service computing. This paper overviews the evolution and new features of agents and services empowered by GenAI, reveals the roles and principles of agentic services in the metaverse environment, presents the forms, characteristics, and principles of the AMServ and the Meta-AaaS, discusses the typical application examples of the AMServ and the Meta-AaaS, and finally points out the new tendencies and research directions of the AMServ and the Meta-AaaS. The AMServ and the Meta-AaaS will bring great opportunities to human society and services in the AI era, and promote the rapid development of emerging service industries in the future.

</details>
