### [223] [Not as Sweet by Another Name: An Empirical Study of Format Robustness in LLM Document Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27648)
*Xiaoyu Zhang,Xianyun Cheng,Tianlin Li,Yuwei Zheng,Yue Yang,Yang Liu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Document format changes severely degrade LLM workflow reliability—accuracy drops up to 53.63% and over 41% of decisions drift when the same content is delivered in different file formats. The authors propose a format-aware metamorphic testing framework, conduct a 48,000-execution empirical study, and propose lightweight mitigation strategies recovering up to 44.21% of format-induced drift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-driven software systems increasingly support document-centric workflows (e.g., CSV uploads), yet existing robustness testing focuses solely on single-prompt inputs. No prior work investigates whether these systems maintain consistent behavior when semantically identical content arrives in different document formats—a critical gap given real-world deployment in high-stakes scenarios.

Method: The authors propose a format-aware metamorphic testing framework with three metamorphic relations designed to capture format-induced behavioral inconsistencies. They apply this framework in a large-scale empirical study covering four representative LLM workflows, four real-world tasks, and four document formats, totaling 48,000 workflow executions. They also design lightweight, user-side mitigation strategies that do not require model retraining.

Result: Format variation is a systematic and serious threat: accuracy drops by up to 53.63%, and over 41% of instances exhibit decision drift upon format switching. The proposed lightweight mitigation strategies recover up to 44.21% of the format-induced decision drift without retraining.

Conclusion: Document format is not a neutral wrapper but a critical factor affecting LLM system reliability. The findings call for dedicated testing frameworks and safeguards when deploying document-centric LLM workflows in high-stakes real-world settings.

Abstract: LLM-driven software systems are rapidly evolving from plain-text conversations to document-centric end-to-end workflows, where the same semantic content can be delivered in diverse document formats (e.g., CSV) through file upload interfaces. Yet existing testing work focuses on the robustness and reliability of models and systems whose input is a single prompt string, leaving a critical question unanswered: Can these document workflows maintain robust behaviors when the same content arrives in a different document format? To fill the gap, in this paper, we propose a format-aware metamorphic testing framework with three metamorphic relations to comprehensively evaluate the format robustness of end-to-end LLM document workflows. Based on this framework, we conduct a large-scale empirical study spanning four representative LLM workflows, four real-world tasks, and four document formats, comprising a total of 48,000 workflow executions. Our findings reveal that format variation poses a systematic and serious threat. Merely switching formats can cause accuracy to drop by up to 53.63% and trigger decision drifts in over 41% of instances. We further design lightweight mitigation strategies from the users' perspective that recover up to 44.21% of format-induced decision drift without model retraining. Our study demonstrates that document format is not a neutral wrapper but a critical factor affecting the reliability of LLM software systems, calling for corresponding testing and safeguards in the deployment in real-world high-stakes scenarios.

</details>


### [224] [Can Large Language Models Resolve Real Java Merge Conflicts? An Evaluation with a Calibrated LLM-as-Judge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27674)
*Bowen Shen*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes an LLM-based merge conflict solver with a calibrated LLM-as-judge evaluation metric, showing LLMs resolve 55-59% of Java merge conflicts (vs. 36.7% for traditional tools), with the gain coming from universal coverage rather than raw accuracy, while emphasizing that structural validity checks must remain deterministic.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional structured and semi-structured merge tools frequently abstain from resolving conflicts when their heuristics fail, leaving developers with unresolved conflicts. LLMs can produce candidate resolutions for nearly any conflict, but evaluating their output quality at scale is challenging because obtaining human judgments for every resolution is infeasible. This paper addresses both problems jointly: building an LLM solver that never sees the developer's answer and creating a scalable, trustworthy evaluation framework.

Method: The authors build an LLM solver as a generate-validate-retry agent using only inference-time signals (conflict markers, a Java parser, and duplicate-declaration checks). For evaluation, they propose a two-metric suite: (1) a developer-match LLM-as-judge implemented as a G-Eval metric, calibrated against ConflictBench's human labels to achieve 100% precision at 64.6% recall, ensuring trustworthy acceptances; and (2) a deterministic structural-validity check using no LLM. The approach is tested on real Java merge conflicts from ConflictBench, with a meta-evaluation on 292 human-labeled cases.

Result: Under the validated judge, LLM solvers match the developer's resolution on approximately 55% of true conflicts (conservative lower bound). In a coverage-fair comparison, LLMs achieve 55-59% versus AutoMerge's 36.7%, an advantage of 18-22 percentage points. This edge derives almost entirely from coverage: traditional tools abstain on 20-90% of conflicts, while the LLM under forced resolution abstains on none. Additionally, the LLM judge accepted 4 of 5 resolutions that failed the deterministic structural check, demonstrating that structural correctness cannot be reliably delegated to an LLM judge.

Conclusion: LLM-based merge conflict resolution substantially outperforms traditional tools in practice due to universal coverage, though raw per-conflict accuracy is comparable. A calibrated LLM-as-judge can serve as a trustworthy, scalable evaluation proxy when tuned for high precision. Crucially, deterministic structural checks remain essential and must not be replaced by LLM-based evaluation, as LLM judges can approve structurally invalid code.

Abstract: Merge conflicts are a recurring cost of collaborative software development, and the traditional structured and semi-structured merge tools that address them frequently abstain: when their heuristics do not apply, they leave the conflict unresolved. Large language models (LLMs) can instead produce a candidate resolution for almost any conflict, but measuring whether those resolutions are actually good at scale is hard, because obtaining human desirability judgments for every model output does not scale. We study both problems together on real Java merge conflicts from ConflictBench. We first build an LLM solver as a generate-validate-retry agent that uses only inference-time signals (conflict markers, a Java parser, and duplicate-declaration checks) and never sees the developer's answer. We then evaluate its resolutions with a two-metric suite: (1) a developer-match LLM-as-judge implemented as a G-Eval metric and, crucially, calibrated against ConflictBench's human labels before use, and (2) a deterministic structural-validity check that uses no LLM. On a meta-evaluation of 292 human-labeled cases, the judge reaches 100% precision (zero false accepts) at 64.6% recall, so every acceptance is trustworthy and every downstream rate is a conservative lower bound. Under this validated judge, LLM solvers match the developer's own resolution on about 55% of true conflicts (conservative floor), and under a coverage-fair comparison the LLMs (55-59%) beat the strongest traditional tool (AutoMerge, 36.7%) by roughly 18-22 points; the edge comes almost entirely from coverage, not raw accuracy, since the tools abstain on 20-90% of conflicts while the LLM under forced resolution abstains on none. Finally, the LLM judge accepted 4 of the 5 resolutions that fail the deterministic structural check, evidence that structural correctness must not be delegated to an LLM.

</details>


### [225] [A comparative analysis of automated techniques for security bug report identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27893)
*Muhammad Laiq*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A comparative evaluation of ML and LLM-based techniques for automatically identifying security-related bug reports, finding that SetFit (few-shot learning) achieves best overall performance (F1=0.80), while GPT-5.2 performs poorly in both zero-shot and few-shot settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The literature on automated identification of security-related bug reports is fragmented: studies evaluate different techniques against inconsistent baselines under varying experimental setups, making cross-study comparison unreliable. Practitioners lack clear, evidence-based guidance on which technique to adopt.

Method: The authors conducted a comparative analysis using benchmark datasets, evaluating seven techniques: three traditional ML models (Logistic Regression, SVM, Random Forest), three transformer-based models (BERT-base, RoBERTa, SetFit — a few-shot learning framework), and OpenAI's GPT-5.2. Evaluation spanned multiple datasets and included cross-project transfer learning experiments.

Result: SetFit achieved the best overall F1-score of 0.80, outperforming other techniques on three of four datasets. RoBERTa performed competitively. Logistic Regression remained a strong baseline in certain contexts. GPT-5.2 performed poorly in both zero-shot and few-shot settings. Cross-project transfer learning improved performance for data-scarce projects but degraded results for projects with strong project-specific characteristics.

Conclusion: Few-shot learning with SetFit is the most effective approach for security bug report identification. Traditional ML (especially Logistic Regression) remains a viable, cost-effective baseline. Large language models like GPT-5.2 are not yet reliable for this task. Practitioners should consider project-specific characteristics when applying transfer learning.

Abstract: Timely identification of security-related bug reports is essential to minimize the window of vulnerabilities in software systems. Manually screening incoming bug reports to identify security-related issues is time-consuming, error-prone, and non-scalable for large-scale software systems. Thus, a variety of automatic techniques, including traditional machine learning (ML) techniques and large language models, have been proposed to facilitate this task. However, the literature remains fragmented. Most studies introduce or optimize a particular technique and evaluate it against a limited set of baselines, often under different experimental setups. As a result, it is difficult to compare their results and draw reliable conclusions about the effectiveness of existing approaches, leaving researchers and practitioners without clear guidance on which techniques are most suitable for the task.
  To address this gap, we conducted a comparative analysis of several promising automated techniques to identify security-related bug reports using benchmark datasets. We evaluated Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, OpenAI's GPT-5.2, BERT-base, RoBERTa, and SetFit (a state-of-the-art few-shot learning framework).
  Our results indicate that SetFit achieves the best overall performance, achieving an F1-score of 0.80 and outperforming other techniques on three of the four datasets. RoBERTa performs competitively and approaches SetFit in some projects, while traditional ML techniques, particularly Logistic Regression, remain a strong baseline in certain contexts. In contrast, GPT-5.2 performs poorly in both zero-shot and few-shot settings. In addition, cross-project experiments demonstrate that transfer learning can improve performance for projects with limited data, but may degrade results for projects with strong project-specific characteristics.

</details>


### [226] [The Case for Vibe Modeling: A Missing Step in AI-Based Trustworthy Software Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27923)
*Shalini Chakraborty,Michael Mittermaier,Judith Michael*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper argues that AI-assisted development overemphasizes direct code generation and proposes "vibe modeling" as a lightweight intermediate abstraction between natural language prompts and code. A student survey explores perceptions of LLM output understanding, validation, trust, and the perceived usefulness of vibe modeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI-based software development practices prioritize direct code generation from natural language, neglecting intermediate representations that preserve human intent and facilitate reasoning about system behavior. This creates problems with understanding, validation, traceability, and trust in LLM-generated software artifacts.

Method: The authors conducted a student survey study examining perceptions across multiple AI-assisted development scenarios, assessing: (1) understanding of LLM outputs, (2) validation effort, (3) trust, and (4) perceived usefulness of vibe modeling as an intermediate abstraction.

Result: Results are positioned as formative groundwork intended to inform future research on trustworthy and explainable AI-based software engineering through vibe modeling. Specific quantitative or qualitative findings are not detailed in this abstract.

Conclusion: Vibe modeling is proposed as a promising direction for bridging the gap between natural language intent and generated code, with the survey results serving as a foundation for future studies on explainable and trustworthy AI-assisted software engineering.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate software artifacts from natural language prompts. While this enables rapid prototyping and lowers the barrier to software creation, it also introduces challenges related to understanding, validation, traceability, and trust. In this paper, we argue that current AI-based development practices focus too heavily on the direct generation of code and insufficiently on intermediate representations that preserve human intent and support reasoning about system behavior. We argue for vibe modeling as a lightweight intermediate abstraction between natural language interaction and code generation. To explore its potential, we present a student survey study that examines perceptions of LLM output understanding, validation effort, trust and the perceived usefulness of vibe modeling across several AI-assisted development scenarios. Our results are intended to inform future studies for trustworthy and explainable AI-based software engineering via vibe modeling.

</details>


### [227] [Specification-Guided Synthesis of Deadlock-Free Communication Protocol Refinements with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27964)
*Yang Li,Ping Hou,Nobuko Yoshida*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Syntropy is a framework that combines multiparty session types (MPST) with large language models (LLMs) to automatically synthesize protocol refinements that are guaranteed to be behaviourally correct and deadlock-free, achieving 95.6%–99.5% validity in evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ensuring behavioural correctness in distributed communication protocols is challenging, as subtle errors can cause deadlocks. Protocol refinement—safe substitution of a protocol while preserving correctness and compatibility—is essential. LLMs excel at code generation but lack behavioural guarantees, while formal methods like MPST offer rigorous deadlock-freedom guarantees but provide limited support for automatically constructing protocol refinements. No existing approach combines the generative power of LLMs with the formal guarantees of MPST for protocol refinement synthesis.

Method: Syntropy is a framework that integrates MPST specifications with LLMs for protocol refinement synthesis. It incorporates refinement constraints directly into the generation process, using MPST-based typing and refinement rules to constrain LLM outputs so that generated protocol variants provably satisfy deadlock-freedom and compatibility guarantees. The approach guides multiple LLMs to produce diverse refinements while enforcing formal correctness criteria throughout synthesis.

Result: A comprehensive evaluation shows Syntropy achieves 95.6%–99.5% validity (i.e., generated refinements satisfy MPST guarantees), maintains high syntactic correctness, and produces diverse, non-trivial protocol refinements across multiple LLMs.

Conclusion: Syntropy successfully bridges the gap between LLM-based code generation and formal MPST guarantees, demonstrating that embedding refinement constraints into LLM-driven synthesis can yield highly valid, diverse, and non-trivial protocol refinements suitable for deadlock-free distributed systems.

Abstract: Ensuring behavioural correctness in communication protocols is a central challenge in distributed software systems, as subtle inconsistencies can lead to deadlocks. In such settings, protocol refinement - the safe substitution of a protocol that preserves correctness and compatibility with other components - is essential. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in code generation and program synthesis, yet lack mechanisms to reliably produce outputs with correct behaviour. Formal specification approaches, such as multiparty session types (MPST), offer rigorous guarantees, including deadlock freedom, but provide limited support for automatically constructing protocol refinements. In this paper, we present Syntropy, a framework for synthesising protocol refinements guided by MPST specifications and LLMs. It incorporates refinement constraints directly into the generation process, ensuring the generated variants satisfy these guarantees. Our comprehensive evaluation indicates that Syntropy achieves 95.6%-99.5% validity while maintaining high syntactic correctness, and produces diverse, non-trivial refinements across multiple LLMs.

</details>


### [228] [Advancing Awkward Arrays for High-Performance CPU and GPU Processing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28145)
*Ianna Osborne,Manasvi Goyal*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Awkward Array now includes a GPU backend with CUDA/CCCL implementations that accelerate nested, variable-length data processing while preserving the Python API, with significant throughput gains on irregular workloads.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: HL-LHC analyses increasingly rely on accelerator hardware, but nested and variable-length data structures are difficult to accelerate on GPUs due to indirect indexing, segmented operations, and irregular memory access patterns, unlike dense numerical arrays.

Method: The authors developed a GPU backend for Awkward Array featuring CUDA implementations built on NVIDIA CCCL, optimized memory management, and segmented reduction algorithms for ragged arrays, along with an automated validation framework.

Result: Benchmark results demonstrate substantially improved GPU throughput on irregular workloads compared to CPU and CuPy implementations, while maintaining the existing Python programming model.

Conclusion: The CUDA-based GPU backend successfully bridges the gap between the user-friendly Awkward Array Python API and efficient execution of irregular, nested data structures on accelerator hardware for HEP workloads.

Abstract: Awkward Array is a Python library for representing and processing nested, variable-length data that is widely used in high-energy physics. As HL-LHC analyses increasingly rely on accelerator hardware, efficient execution of irregular workloads has become essential. While dense numerical arrays map naturally to GPUs, nested and variable-length data structures remain significantly more difficult to accelerate because they require indirect indexing, segmented operations, and irregular memory access patterns. We present recent developments in the Awkward Array GPU backend, including CUDA implementations built on NVIDIA CUDA Core Compute Libraries (CCCL), optimized memory management, and segmented reduction algorithms for ragged arrays. These developments preserve the existing Python programming model while substantially improving GPU throughput on irregular workloads. We describe the backend architecture, automated validation framework, and benchmark results comparing CPU, CuPy, and CUDA implementations.

</details>


### [229] [Integrating AI into Requirements Quality Learning in Software Engineering Education: A TPACK-Guided Empirical Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28176)
*Hansika Ekanayake Mudiyanselage,Rohan Jai Dharmaraj,Malik Abdul Sami,Zheying Zhang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This mixed-methods study (N=100) examines how TPACK-guided scaffolding of a multi-agent AI tool in a master-level requirements engineering assignment shapes students' AI use, understanding of user story quality criteria, and perceptions of AI benefits/limitations. Students used AI selectively for analysis rather than automation, with greatest improvement in structurally concrete quality dimensions like value articulation and testability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid adoption of generative AI in software engineering practice creates an urgent need for pedagogically grounded approaches to AI integration in SE education, particularly for conceptually intensive subjects like requirements engineering. There is a gap in understanding how structured instructional design can shape productive AI use while maintaining learning integrity.

Method: The authors employed a mixed-methods design with 100 master-level students and 72 analyzed submissions. The intervention was a TPACK-guided (Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge) assignment integrating a multi-agent AI tool into a requirements quality analysis task. Both quantitative alignment improvements and qualitative perceptions were assessed.

Result: Students used AI selectively, primarily for analysis and evaluation support rather than full automation. Alignment improvements were strongest for structurally concrete quality dimensions (value articulation, testability) and mixed for negotiability. Students reported conditional trust, active refinement behaviors, increased awareness of quality criteria, and moderate usability challenges.

Conclusion: TPACK-guided scaffolding can successfully align AI affordances with pedagogical goals and RE content, providing actionable design guidance for responsible AI integration in requirements engineering education.

Abstract: The rapid adoption of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in software engineering (SE) practice creates a need for pedagogically grounded approaches to AI integration in SE education, especially in conceptually intensive subjects such as requirements engineering (RE). This study examines a TPACK-guided integration of a multi-agent AI tool into a master-level RE assignment on requirements quality analysis. Using a mixed-methods design (N=100; 72 submissions analysed), we examine how structured assignment design shaped students' AI use, affected their understanding of user story quality criteria, and influenced their perceptions of AI's benefits and limitations. Results show that students used the AI tool selectively, mainly as support for analysis and evaluation rather than automation. Alignment improvements were most evident for structurally concrete requirements quality dimensions, such as value articulation and testability, while negotiability showed mixed effects. Students reported conditional trust, active refinement, and increased awareness of quality criteria, alongside moderate usability challenges. The findings show that TPACK-guided scaffolding can align AI affordances with pedagogical goals and RE content, offering design guidance for responsible AI integration in RE education.

</details>


### [230] [Agentic Method for Deterministic Validation of Legacy Code Migration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28271)
*Andras Ferenczi,Jordan Docherty,Mariya Bessonov,Matthew Findlay,Krishna Lingamneni*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper presents "Locksmith Loop," an agentic test-synthesis method for validating COBOL-to-Java migrations. It uses an iterative loop of witness search and parity-preserving mutations, instrumenting both source and target environments with mocks. When routing boundaries block exploration, an analyzer identifies "Locked Paragraphs" to overcome them. Evaluated on three programs (430–4,114 LOC), the method achieved up to 91.90% branch coverage on a production-like program and near-complete coverage on open-source ones, with all accepted tests passing deterministic parity checks between COBOL and Java.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Migrating legacy COBOL programs to Java requires extensive testing to ensure functional correctness, but this effort is complicated by a lack of test data and the difficulty of validating all corner cases. Existing approaches struggle to achieve deep branch coverage and reliable validation of the translated code against the original.

Method: The "Locksmith Loop" is an agentic test-synthesis method that works as follows: (1) Both the COBOL source and generated Java target are instrumented with mocks and executed off-mainframe on commodity hardware. (2) An iterative agentic loop performs "Witness Search" over input mocks to penetrate program branches. (3) Parity-preserving mutations are applied to generate new test cases. (4) When routing boundaries are reached, an analyzer identifies a "Locked Paragraph" — a condition preventing deeper exploration — and addresses it. The generated Java is validated against the COBOL reference using deterministic parity checks as an oracle.

Result: Across three COBOL-Java case studies (two open-source, one internal production-like, ranging from 430 to 4,114 source lines), Locksmith consistently improved coverage beyond input-search plateaus. It achieved near-complete coverage on the two open-source programs and 91.90% branch coverage on the internal production-like COBOL program. All accepted test cases produced Java output matching the COBOL reference under deterministic parity checks.

Conclusion: The Locksmith Loop demonstrates a novel approach for validating agentic coding output using a deterministic oracle. The method effectively addresses the test-generation bottleneck in COBOL-to-Java migration, achieving high branch coverage and reliable parity validation, making it a promising solution for legacy modernization testing.

Abstract: Migration of legacy COBOL programs to Java requires extensive testing to ensure correct functionality. This effort is often complicated by the lack of test data and the difficulty of validating all corner cases. In this paper we propose a novel agentic test-synthesis method, the "Locksmith Loop," which is initiated by preparing two runtime environments: the COBOL source and the generated Java target are each instrumented with mocks and executed off-mainframe on commodity hardware, then an iterative agentic loop performs Witness Search over input mocks to penetrate program branches, followed by parity-preserving mutations. When routing boundaries are reached, an analyzer identifies a Locked Paragraph: a condition preventing deeper exploration. Across three COBOL-Java case studies, spanning two open-source programs and one internal production-like COBOL program and ranging from 430 to 4,114 source lines, Locksmith consistently improved coverage beyond input-search plateaus, reaching nearly complete coverage on the two open-source programs and 91.90% branch coverage on the internal production-like COBOL program. The generated Java matched the COBOL reference under deterministic parity checks in all accepted test cases. Through these findings we demonstrate, to the best of our knowledge, a novel approach for validating agentic coding output using a deterministic oracle.

</details>


### [231] [From Textual Requirements to Microservice Architectures - A Comprehensive Evaluation of LLM-Based Design Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28307)
*Danyllo Albuquerque,José Renan,Guillermo Rodríguez,Guillermo Rodríguez,Emanuel Dantas,Ademar França,Mirko Perkusich,Kyller Gorgônio,Angelo Perkusich*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This study evaluates whether OpenAI's o3 LLM can generate microservice architectures from natural-language requirements, comparing zero-shot and few-shot prompting across two systems. Few-shot prompting achieves near-perfect service identification (F1=0.97) and substantially better communication recovery (F1=0.82) versus zero-shot, with expert assessment confirming FS outputs as more modular and plausible.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing microservice decomposition approaches are code-centric, limiting their use in early design stages where only textual requirements exist. Despite LLM advances, there is limited empirical evidence on their ability to synthesize complete microservice architectures—including service definitions and inter-service interactions—from natural-language requirements alone.

Method: A mixed-method study using OpenAI o3 under zero-shot and few-shot prompting conditions, applied to two systems (Bookstore, PetClinic) with one execution per system/condition. Evaluation combines: (i) quantitative comparison with reference architectures using precision, recall, and F1-score for service identification and communication recovery, and (ii) blinded expert assessment of correctness, completeness, modularity, and plausibility with open feedback synthesis.

Result: Few-shot prompting dramatically outperforms zero-shot: service identification F1 improves from 0.79 (ZS) to 0.97 (FS); communication recovery F1 improves from 0.61 (ZS, high recall/low precision) to 0.82 (FS). Expert evaluation corroborates these findings, rating FS architectures as more modular, coherent, and plausible than ZS outputs.

Conclusion: OpenAI o3 shows strong potential for requirements-driven microservice synthesis when guided by exemplar (few-shot) prompting, but results are model- and context-specific, derived from only two small systems, and do not constitute model-independent proof.

Abstract: Microservice architectures have become dominant for modernizing monolithic systems, yet identifying appropriate services remains challenging and largely manual. Existing decomposition approaches are predominantly code-centric, limiting applicability in early design stages where only textual requirements are available. Despite advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), limited empirical evidence exists on their ability to synthesize complete microservice architectures from natural-language requirements, including service definitions and inter-service interactions. This study investigates whether an LLM can bridge requirements engineering and architectural design, generating architectures solely from textual requirements and evaluating structural agreement and perceived quality of results. We conduct a mixed-method study using OpenAI o3 under zero-shot (ZS) and few-shot (FS) prompting across two systems (Bookstore, PetClinic), one execution per system/condition. Architectures are evaluated through (i) comparison with reference architectures using precision, recall, and F1-score for service identification and communication recovery, and (ii) a blinded expert assessment of correctness, completeness, modularity, and plausibility, plus open feedback synthesis. OpenAI o3 identifies services with higher agreement under FS prompting (F1 = 0.79 for ZS versus = 0.97 for FS). Communication recovery is more challenging: ZS produces dense architectures with high recall but low precision (F1 = 0.61), while FS improves agreement, reaching F1 = 0.82 and reducing unsupported dependencies. Expert evaluation corroborates these results, with FS architectures perceived as more modular, coherent, and plausible than ZS outputs. OpenAI o3 shows potential for requirements-driven synthesis when guided by exemplar prompting. Results are model- and context-specific from two small systems, not model-independent proof.

</details>


### [232] [Structural Validation of LLM-Generated Microservice Decompositions Using Source-Code Dependencies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28331)
*Daniel Silva,Renan Alves,Emanuel Dantas Filho,Ademar Sousa Neto,Mirko Perkusich,Danyllo Wagner Albuquerque,Kyller Gorgônio,Angelo Perkusich*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how well LLM-generated microservice decompositions preserve source-code structural dependencies. Using an automated validation pipeline on two systems, it finds that after controlling for mapping coverage, zero-shot and few-shot prompting yield equivalent structural adherence, and warns that apparent differences can stem from methodological bias rather than true architectural quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs can produce plausible microservice decompositions from textual requirements, it is unclear whether these decompositions respect the structural dependencies actually implemented in source code. There is a need to rigorously evaluate structural adherence and to determine whether prompting strategies genuinely affect decomposition quality or merely reflect coverage artifacts.

Method: The authors propose an automated validation pipeline based on static dependency analysis. They compare zero-shot and few-shot prompting of OpenAI o3 on the PetClinic and Bookstore benchmark systems, using two metrics: True Positive Dependencies (TPD) for preserved dependencies and True Violated Dependencies (TVD) for violated ones. A robustness analysis normalizes for differences in class-to-service mapping coverage to isolate genuine architectural effects from methodological bias.

Result: After normalization for mapping coverage, both prompting strategies produce equivalent structural adherence: TPD values of 68.0% for PetClinic and 83.3% for Bookstore. Raw (un-normalized) comparisons showed apparent differences between strategies, but these were artifacts of unequal coverage rather than genuine quality differences.

Conclusion: Structural evaluations of LLM-generated microservice decompositions must explicitly control for mapping coverage. Failure to do so risks attributing differences to prompting strategy when they are actually due to methodological bias. Both zero-shot and few-shot prompting can achieve comparable structural adherence once coverage is normalized.

Abstract: Decomposing monolithic systems into microservices is a key activity in software modernization. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate semantically plausible decompositions from textual requirements, it remains unclear whether these proposals preserve the structural dependencies implemented in the source code. This paper evaluates the structural adherence of microservice decompositions generated by OpenAI o3 for the PetClinic and Bookstore systems. We propose an automated validation pipeline based on static dependency analysis and compare zero-shot and few-shot prompting using dependency preservation (TPD) and dependency violation (TVD) metrics. A robustness analysis was conducted to control for differences in class-to-service mapping coverage. After normalization, both prompting strategies produced equivalent structural adherence, achieving TPD values of 68.0% (PetClinic) and 83.3% (Bookstore). The findings demonstrate that structural evaluations of LLM-generated decompositions should explicitly control for mapping coverage, as apparent differences between prompting strategies may otherwise reflect methodological bias rather than genuine architectural quality.

</details>


### [233] [Demystifying Solana Bots: From GitHub Blueprints to On-Chain Fingerprints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28424)
*Xiaoye Zheng,Yujing Chen,Minghao Wu,David Lo,Difan Xie,Daoyuan Wu,Xiaohu Yang,Zhiyuan Wan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A large-scale empirical study categorizing Solana bots into 15 types across 5 domains, analyzing 586 GitHub repositories and 44M+ on-chain transactions to reveal implementation patterns, operational pipelines, and trading behaviors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Solana's high throughput and low fees attract bot activity exceeding $250M daily trading volume, yet no systematic understanding exists of how bots are implemented and what on-chain fingerprints they leave.

Method: Dual-view empirical analysis: (i) mining 586 bot repositories from GitHub for implementation analysis, and (ii) examining 200 bot addresses on Solana with over 44 million on-chain transactions for behavioral fingerprinting.

Result: Derived a taxonomy of 15 bot categories across 5 domains (Trading Operations, MEV, On-chain Analytics, etc.); identified a common five-stage operational pipeline in implementations; uncovered systematic variation in on-chain trading behaviors across platforms and assets.

Conclusion: The study provides the first systematic characterization of Solana bots, offers recommendations for bot development and operation, and outlines future research directions for the Solana ecosystem.

Abstract: Solana is an emerging blockchain platform designed for high throughput and low transaction fees, making it inexpensive to submit transactions at scale and, consequently, increasing exposure to bot spamming and related financial exploitation. Solana bots are typically off-chain software systems that operate in a competitive on-chain execution environment by constructing and submitting transactions, and the bot-related transactions on the decentralized exchanges exceed 250 million dollars in daily trading volume in January 2026. Prior studies on Solana have examined system performance, smart-contract security, and specific on-chain phenomena. However, we still lack a systematic understanding of what Solana bots implement in practice and how these implementations manifest as observable on-chain execution fingerprints. To address this gap, we performed a large-scale empirical study of Solana bots from two complementary views: (i) 586 bot repositories collected from GitHub, and (ii) 200 bot addresses on Solana, with over 44 million on-chain transactions. Our study derives an implementation-grounded taxonomy of Solana bots comprising 15 categories grouped into five domains (e.g., Trading Operations, MEV, and On-chain Analytics), identifies a largely shared five-stage operational pipeline manifested in bot implementations, and uncovers systematic variation in on-chain trading behaviors of Solana bots across diverse trading platforms and assets. Based on our findings, we highlight future research directions, and provide recommendations for building and operating bots on the Solana blockchain.

</details>


### [234] [Emerging Challenges in Threat Modeling for GenAI-Augmented Systems: A View from the Trenches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28431)
*Nicolás E. Díaz Ferreyra,Manish Mahesh Kumar,Nohemí Villarreal,Pankaj Pantel,Immo Brueggemann,Riccardo Scandariato*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper presents an exploratory assessment of three GenAI-aware threat modeling methods applied to an industrial case study in an SME setting. It reveals gaps in coverage for GenAI-specific risks—particularly supply chain and human-centered issues—and reports practitioner feedback on usability and adoption challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional threat modeling methods like STRIDE are inadequate for capturing emerging risks introduced by Generative AI components in software systems. As GenAI becomes pervasive, there is a pressing need to evaluate whether existing GenAI-aware threat modeling techniques are practical and comprehensive enough for real-world SME use.

Method: The authors conducted a rapid literature review to shortlist relevant GenAI-aware threat modeling techniques. Three selected methods were then systematically applied to an industrial case study of a GenAI-augmented system within an SME. Practitioner perceptions regarding usability, integration effort, and adoption barriers were also collected.

Result: The three methods identified differing sets of threats, with limited overlap. Notable gaps emerged for GenAI-specific risk categories, especially software supply chain threats and human-centered security issues. Practitioners reported concerns about the effort required and challenges integrating these methods into existing SME development workflows.

Conclusion: Existing GenAI-aware threat modeling methods show promise but remain incomplete in coverage and face practical adoption hurdles in SME contexts. The findings call for further refinement of these techniques to address blind spots and improve usability for industrial practice.

Abstract: Threat modeling remains a central task in secure software engineering, as it enables the identification of security issues from system architectures. As Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly pervasive across software systems, traditional threat modeling methods (e.g., STRIDE) are insufficient to assess emerging GenAI-specific risks. In this work, we present the first results from an exploratory assessment of GenAI-aware threat modeling methods in a Small and Medium Enterprise (SME) setting. For this, we conducted a rapid literature review to select relevant techniques and systematically applied three shortlisted methods to an industrial case study involving a GenAI-augmented system. The results highlight differences in the threats identified by each technique and reveal limited support for certain GenAI-specific risk categories, particularly those related to software supply chains and human-centered security issues. We further report practitioners' perceptions of the usability and integration of these methods in SME development workflows, including their perceived effort and adoption challenges.

</details>


### [235] [CoGate: Confidence-Gated Co-Decoding for Secure Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28529)
*Minghao Hu,Lannan Luo,Allen Roush,Phillip Howard*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CoGate introduces confidence-gated co-decoding for secure code generation, where a security expert model's influence is modulated by its confidence level, preventing misleading guidance from uncertain predictions and outperforming prior co-decoding methods across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing co-decoding approaches for secure code generation blindly follow the security expert model's guidance without considering its confidence. When the expert encounters unseen patterns or OOD contexts, its low-confidence guidance can be misleading, resulting in insecure code.

Method: CoGate, a confidence-gated co-decoding framework that dynamically controls the security expert model's influence on the target LLM's token generation based on the expert's confidence score. When confidence is low, the gate reduces the expert's influence, allowing the base model to dominate the decoding process.

Result: CoGate outperforms existing co-decoding methods (CoSec+) across multiple LLM backends (CodeGen, DeepSeek-Coder, Qwen-Coder, StarCoder) and benchmarks (HumanEval, security suite, CWEval), achieving up to a 12.6% improvement in Func-Sec@10 on CWEval.

Conclusion: Confidence-gating is an effective mechanism for improving the reliability of co-decoding for secure code generation. By accounting for expert uncertainty, CoGate mitigates the risk of misleading guidance and yields more secure code outputs.

Abstract: Large language models are widely used for code generation, but they can also produce insecure programs due to patterns learned from their pretraining data. Decoding-time steering has become an important solution to this problem: a small expert model is combined with the target model at each step to generate more secure code, which is referred to as co-decoding. However, the acceptance rule for existing co-decoding approaches does not consider the expert model's confidence. When the security expert is unconfident due to unseen patterns or out-of-distribution (OOD) contexts, its guidance can therefore be misleading. To address the challenge, we propose CoGate, a confidence-gated co-decoding approach that controls the expert's influence on the co-decoding process based on its confidence. We implement our approach and evaluate it across multiple LLM backends (CodeGen, DeepSeek-Coder, Qwen-Coder, StarCoder) on several code generation benchmarks (HumanEval, security suite, and CWEval). Our approach outperforms existing co-decoding methods (CoSec+) across multiple benchmarks, achieving up to a 12.6% gain of Func-Sec@10 on CWEval.

</details>


### [236] [PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28587)
*Manyi Wang,Junjielong Xu,Pinjia He*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: SWE-bench-like benchmarks suffer from PR-Issue misalignment (13.6% in SWE-bench Verified). The authors propose PAIChecker, a three-phase multi-agent system combining pattern identification, cross-agent label synthesis, and code-level validation to detect such misalignments, achieving up to 92.12% binary accuracy on SWE-Gym and SWE-bench Multilingual.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SWE-bench-like benchmarks pair PRs with linked issues to evaluate LLM issue-resolution capability, but the PR-Issue pairings are often misaligned in practice due to the complexity of large repositories. This misalignment undermines benchmark reliability, yet no systematic study or automated detection method existed for this problem.

Method: The authors first conduct a systematic empirical study on SWE-bench Verified, identifying 13.6% misalignment across five patterns and eleven fine-grained scenarios. They then propose PAIChecker, a multi-agent system with a three-phase design: (1) specific pattern identification to recognize known misalignment patterns, (2) cross-agent label synthesis where multiple LLM agents independently assess and then synthesize labels, and (3) code-level validation that progressively verifies detection through code-level evidence.

Result: PAIChecker achieves state-of-the-art performance across all four LLM backbones evaluated. On SWE-Gym, it reaches up to 92.12% binary accuracy; on SWE-bench Multilingual, up to 91.67%. The empirical analysis reveals that 13.6% of SWE-bench Verified instances exhibit misalignment spanning five patterns across eleven fine-grained scenarios.

Conclusion: PR-Issue misalignment is a non-trivial problem in SWE-bench-like benchmarks. PAIChecker provides a reliable, scalable, and generalizable solution for automatically detecting such misalignments, enabling more robust benchmark construction in the future.

Abstract: SWE-bench-like benchmarks are widely used for evaluating LLM's issue resolution capability. They typically follow a common construction pipeline: each PR (Pull Request) is paired with its linked issue by extracting issue references from the PR description; the issue description is used as the problem statement, and the PR patch serves as the test oracle. However, due to the inherent complexity of developing and maintaining large repositories, such PR-Issue pairings are often misaligned in practice. In this work, we systematically study SWE-bench Verified instances, finding that 13.6% exhibit misalignment across five patterns in eleven fine-grained scenarios. To enable reliable and scalable construction of those benchmarks in the future, we propose PAIChecker, a multi-agent system for checking PR-Issue misalignment in SWE-bench-like benchmarks. Specifically, PAIChecker adopts a three-phase design that combines specific pattern identification, cross-agent label synthesis, and code-level validation, thereby enabling more accurate, generalizable, and progressively verified detection. Experiments on SWE-Gym and SWE-bench Multilingual show that PAIchecker achieves the best performance across all four LLM backbones, reaching up to 92.12% and 91.67% binary accuracy, respectively.

</details>


### [237] [Change2Task: From Repository Changes to Executable Coding Agent Tasks and Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28591)
*Haomin Qi,Xingliang Wang,Xuanqi Gao,Baihui Sang,Xin Zhang,Minghua Ma,Pengfei Gao,Yu Kang,Qingwei Lin,Saravan Rajmohan,Dongmei Zhang,Qi Zhang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Change2Task converts merged pull requests into verified coding agent tasks by aligning historical changes with modern repository states, achieving 79.6% task construction success across five task families and recovering 29.2% more verified tasks than a PR-based baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scaling coding agents requires a continuous supply of executable, verified tasks grounded in realistic software states. Existing approaches suffer from limited data, high setup costs, and stale environments. Leveraging repository history—specifically merged PRs—offers a rich, developer-validated source, but historical code often diverges from modern revisions, making direct extraction unreliable.

Method: Change2Task uses three reconstruction strategies—Patch Reversal, Code Mapping, and Agent Reconstruction—to align historical PR evidence with healthy modern repository revisions. It validates the full lifecycle: establishing a healthy base state, constructing the task state (reproducing the pre-PR condition), and verifying that applying the change restores the post-PR state. Multiple task types (Bug Fix, Feature Addition, Test Generation, API Migration, Security Repair) are derived from a single source change.

Result: From 1,130 source changes, Change2Task achieved 79.6% verified task construction success. It recovered 29.2% more verified tasks than a PR-based baseline on a matched candidate set. Historical and reconstructed cases reached up to 98.0% matched outcome agreement under agent evaluation. Reuse of modern bases reduced measured pipeline expenditure by 10.8%.

Conclusion: Change2Task effectively transforms merged PRs into diverse, verified coding agent tasks on modern repository states, enabling scalable, cost-efficient data generation for training and evaluation while maintaining high fidelity to original developer intent.

Abstract: Scaling coding agents requires a continuing supply of executable data for training, benchmarking, and continuous evaluation. Each task must couple a realistic software state with a specification, development tools, and reliable verification. To expand this supply, we present Change2Task, a system grounded in repository history that converts merged pull requests into verified tasks on healthy modern revisions of the same repository. It aligns historical evidence with evolved code, reconstructs task states through Patch Reversal, Code Mapping, or Agent Reconstruction, and validates the lifecycle from a healthy base to a task state and a restored state. By deriving multiple tasks grounded in developer evidence from maintained environments, Change2Task provides executable data for coding agent training and evaluation while reducing repeated environment setup, storage, and task construction effort. We evaluate the system through five common and widely adopted coding agent task families: Bug Fix, Feature Addition, Test Generation, Application Programming Interface Migration, and Security Repair. Starting from 1,130 source changes eligible for construction, Change2Task achieves 79.6% verified task construction success across these task families. On a matched candidate set, it recovers 29.2% more verified tasks than a construction baseline based on pull requests. Historical and reconstructed cases achieve up to 98.0% matched outcome agreement under agent evaluation, while reuse of modern bases reduces measured expenditure across the complete pipeline by 10.8%.

</details>
