### [238] [Digital Harf: A Clinically Integrated Multimodal AI System for Pervasive Arabic Speech and Language Therapy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27212)
*Asif Azad,Mohammad Sadat Hossain,MD Sadik Hossain Shanto,Sabri Boughorbel,Abdulrhman Aljouie,Bdour Alwuqaysi,Yahya Bokhari,Ayah Othman Sindi,Ehsan Hoque*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Digital Harf is an AI-powered speech and language therapy platform for Arabic-speaking children with Autism Spectrum Disorder, featuring an Agentic Synthetic Data Engine that automatically generates culturally relevant therapy content, achieving 90.1% clinical acceptance from 13 licensed Speech-Language Pathologists without manual curation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Arabic-speaking children with ASD face severe barriers: a shortage of qualified speech-language specialists, limited access to services outside urban centers, and a near-complete absence of culturally grounded digital therapy materials. Existing solutions are predominantly designed for Western linguistic and cultural contexts, leaving Arabic-speaking populations underserved.

Method: The authors developed Digital Harf, a pervasive multimodal AI platform with three integrated therapeutic modules (language therapy, speech intelligibility, picture description) that adapt to individual child performance. The key innovation is the Agentic Synthetic Data Engine (ASDE), which automatically generates culturally relevant images, prompts, and language tasks using explicit therapeutic and cultural criteria. The system was evaluated through expert review by 13 licensed Speech-Language Pathologists.

Result: ASDE-generated content achieved a 90.1% clinical acceptance rate without any manual curation or filtering. Expert evaluators also assigned strong ratings for cultural and linguistic alignment across the entire platform.

Conclusion: AI-driven therapeutic systems can be purpose-built for underrepresented linguistic settings with cultural grounding treated as foundational infrastructure rather than a post-hoc adaptation, as demonstrated by Digital Harf's successful deployment for Arabic-speaking children with ASD.

Abstract: Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder in Arabic-speaking countries face compounded barriers to effective speech and language therapy: a shortage of qualified specialists, limited service reach beyond urban centers, and a near-total absence of culturally grounded digital therapy materials. We present Digital Harf, a pervasive, multimodal AI platform that extends clinician-led speech and language therapy into the home. The system integrates three therapeutic modules - language therapy, speech intelligibility, and picture description - within a unified workflow that adapts to each child's performance over time. To address the critical shortage of Arabic therapy content, we introduce an Agentic Synthetic Data Engine (ASDE) that automatically generates culturally relevant images, prompts, and language tasks guided by explicit therapeutic and cultural criteria. Expert evaluation with 13 licensed Speech-Language Pathologists yielded a 90.1% clinical acceptance rate for ASDE-generated content without any manual curation or selection, and strong ratings for cultural and linguistic alignment across the full platform. Digital Harf demonstrates that AI-driven therapeutic systems can be built from the ground up for underrepresented linguistic settings, treating cultural grounding as core infrastructure rather than an adaptation afterthought.

</details>


### [239] [Evaluating the Vergence-Accommodation Conflict in Gaze-Based 3D Target Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27369)
*Mohammad Raihanul Bashar,Mohammadreza Amini,Aunnoy K Mutasim,Mayra Donaji Barrera Machuca,Wolfgang Stuerzlinger,Anil Ufuk Batmaz*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper investigates how the vergence-accommodation conflict (VAC) in head-mounted displays affects gaze-based 3D target selection performance, finding that increased visual depth significantly degrades performance and that a Variation in Diopter Fitts' law model captures this effect better than a linear model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current HMDs suffer from the vergence-accommodation conflict (VAC), which is known to affect interaction performance. Since VAC directly influences eye-movement behavior, it likely impacts gaze-based selection — yet this relationship had not been empirically investigated. The authors aim to fill this gap by quantifying how VAC affects gaze-based 3D pointing across varying depth conditions.

Method: The authors conducted an empirical study evaluating gaze-based 3D target selection performance across multiple depth conditions in a head-mounted display. They compared two modeling approaches — a standard linear model and a Variation in Diopter Fitts' law model — to determine which better captures the relationship between depth and selection performance.

Result: User performance with gaze-based selection significantly decreased as visual depth increased. The Variation in Diopter Fitts' law model captured this performance degradation more accurately than a linear model, providing evidence that VAC negatively impacts gaze-based pointing.

Conclusion: Gaze-based pointing in 3D environments is negatively affected by the vergence-accommodation conflict. Designers of gaze-based interaction for HMDs must account for depth-dependent factors. The Variation in Diopter Fitts' law model offers a superior predictive framework for modeling this depth-dependent performance.

Abstract: State-of-the-art head-mounted displays (HMDs) enable gaze-based selection in virtual environments. Yet, these HMDs suffer from the vergence-accommodation conflict (VAC), which is known to affect interaction performance. The VAC might influence gaze-based selection performance because it directly affects eye-movement behavior. Thus, in this paper, we investigate how the VAC influences gaze-based 3D target selection across varying depth conditions. Our results show that as the (visual) depth increases, user performance significantly decreases with gaze-based selection. Moreover, a previously suggested Variation in Diopter Fitts' law model captured this performance change better relative to a linear model. These findings provide evidence that gaze-based pointing is negatively affected by the VAC and highlight the importance of accounting for depth-dependent factors when designing gaze-based interaction in 3D environments.

</details>


### [240] [DP-LENS: A Density-Aware Polyfocal Lens with Topology-Driven Auto-Routing for Occlusion Management in Immersive 3D Analytics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27697)
*Nieyu Cao,Xian Wang,Lik-Hang Lee*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: DP-LENS is a density-aware polyfocal fisheye lens with LLM-driven auto-routing for exploring heavily occluded 3D datasets in VR. Two user studies (N=34) show it significantly reduces cognitive load, improves task efficiency, and garners higher user preference compared to industry-standard baselines and manual-only approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Exploring complex 3D volumetric datasets in immersive environments is challenging due to heavy occlusion and high cognitive load. Existing methods like World-in-Miniature and volumetric slicing fail to adequately balance local detail inspection with global context preservation, and manual navigation exacerbates physical fatigue. There is a need for a system that reduces cognitive burden, supports hands-free interaction, and decouples exploration efficiency from data scale.

Method: DP-LENS combines three components: (1) a density-aware polyfocal fisheye lens that deforms geometry to magnify regions of interest while preserving peripheral context; (2) a topology-driven auto-routing algorithm that computes optimal camera paths through occluded volumes; and (3) a Large Language Model (LLM) integrated for voice-based target selection to enable hands-free macro-navigation. The system was evaluated through two controlled user studies: Study 1 (N=18) compared manual DP-LENS against World-in-Miniature and volumetric slicing baselines; Study 2 (N=16) compared the LLM+auto-routing system against fully manual DP-LENS operation.

Result: Study 1 showed DP-LENS significantly reduced cognitive load, decreased task completion time, and improved user preference over both baselines. Study 2 demonstrated that the topology-driven auto-routing with voice-initiated LLM target selection further improved task efficiency, reduced cognitive load, and was preferred by users. Additionally, auto-routing partially decoupled exploration efficiency from data physical dimensions and mitigated physical fatigue.

Conclusion: DP-LENS, combining density-aware polyfocal deformation with LLM-driven auto-routing, offers a scalable and low-fatigue approach for exploring occluded 3D data in VR. The authors propose design implications for future spatially scalable 3D visual analytics systems, emphasizing the value of integrating deformable lenses, intelligent path planning, and voice-based AI interaction.

Abstract: Immersive environments, e.g., virtual reality (VR), offer a unique approach to exploring complex 3D datasets, where data is often heavily occluded and exploration incurs a high cognitive load. We propose DP-LENS, a density-aware polyfocal fisheye lens equipped with topology-driven auto-routing. While preserving peripheral context through geometric deformation and 3D perspective techniques, it enables users to explore 3D data with a lower cognitive load. To facilitate hands-free macro-navigation, we integrate a Large Language Model (LLM) to serve as a supplementary voice-based target selection tool that initiates the auto-routing algorithm. Two user studies with 34 participants investigate the potential benefits of this system. Our first study (N=18) compared the manual DP-LENS against two industry-standard baselines (i.e., World-in-Miniature and volumetric slicing) in heavily occluded 3D datasets. The results show that DP-LENS significantly reduced cognitive load, decreased completion time, and improved user preference. The second study (N=16) compared the topology-driven auto-routing system (initiated via voice commands) with a fully manual DP-LENS. The results show that the auto-routing system improved task efficiency, further reduced cognitive load, and garnered higher user preference. Furthermore, the auto-routing partially decoupled exploration efficiency from the physical dimensions of the data and mitigated physical fatigue to some extent. Based on the findings, we proposed design implications to inform the development of more spatially scalable and low-fatigue interactions for future 3D visual analytics systems.

</details>


### [241] [Creative Task Cards for Reflection, Self-Efficiency and Self-Regulation in CS1 Introductory Programming: Initial Insights](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27863)
*Corey Ford,Yinmiao Li,Rosa Van Koningsbruggen*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper introduces creative task cards aimed at fostering reflection, self-efficacy, and self-regulation among introductory programming students facing emotional challenges. A study with 29 students revealed value in taking breaks, using drawing to address cognitive overload, and breaking tasks into smaller steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Introductory programming students face emotional challenges (low sustained interest, lack of self-belief), yet typical instruction focuses on disciplinary strategies (e.g., debugging) rather than metacognitive or self-regulation strategies that could address these emotional hurdles.

Method: The authors designed creative task cards to support reflection, self-efficacy, and self-regulation. Twenty-nine students used these cards to complete a mock coding assignment in-class, followed by surveys and focus groups for qualitative evaluation.

Result: Qualitative insights showed: (1) students valued taking breaks, especially leaving the classroom to reflect with peers; (2) drawing helped students reflect on cognitive overload; (3) breaking work into smaller steps enhanced students' sense of capability and progress.

Conclusion: Creative task cards show promise as a low-cost intervention for supporting metacognitive and self-regulation strategies in introductory programming courses, addressing the emotional dimension of learning to code that is often overlooked in traditional curricula.

Abstract: Computer Science students in introductory programming courses struggle with emotional challenges such as low levels of sustained interest and a lack of self-belief. However, students are typically introduced to disciplinary strategies (such as debugging strategies) and not the metacognitive nor self-regulation strategies that could help them overcome such emotional challenges. This paper addresses this issue by introducing creative task cards designed to support students' reflection, self-efficacy, and self-regulation in programming assignments. To evaluate the cards, twenty-nine students used them to complete a mock coding assignment in-class and participated in surveys and focus groups. Our initial qualitative insights suggest that students: found value in taking breaks, particularly when they could leave the classroom to reflect with peers; could use drawing to better reflect on feelings of cognitive overload; and felt more capable progressing with their work once breaking it into smaller steps.

</details>


### [242] [VizPilot: Automated Onboarding for SVG-based Composite Visualizations using Multimodal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27938)
*Nishaanthini Gnanavel,Yong Wang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: VizPilot is an automated system that reverse-engineers composite visualizations using MLLMs, generating interactive onboarding experiences (guided scrollytelling and free exploration) directly from raw visualization artifacts via a browser extension, significantly reducing authoring effort and cognitive load for novice users.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Composite visualizations impose high initial cognitive load on novice users due to their structural complexity. Existing onboarding approaches are platform-dependent, require substantial manual authoring, and fail to handle the intricate structure of composite visualizations, limiting their general applicability.

Method: VizPilot employs two modules: (1) a Composite Visualization Analyzer using MLLMs in a two-stage pipeline that decomposes visualizations into components, extracts structured explanations, and maps them to precise SVG elements; (2) an Onboarding Interface supporting guided narrative scrollytelling and free exploration. Implemented as a browser extension, it requires only a brief description and optional source code from the developer.

Result: Evaluation via comparative analysis of input modalities, a usage scenario demonstrating reduced authoring effort, and a user study on cognitive load shows that VizPilot effectively automates onboarding authoring while improving usability and accessibility of composite visualizations.

Conclusion: VizPilot demonstrates that MLLM-driven reverse engineering of visualization structure can automate onboarding for composite visualizations, lowering both authoring burden and user cognitive load, thereby enhancing accessibility and usability.

Abstract: Composite visualizations integrate multiple visualizations to represent complex datasets effectively, but their intrinsic composite designs often impose a high initial cognitive load on novice users. Existing visualization onboarding approaches are typically platform-dependent, require substantial manual authoring effort, and struggle with the structural complexity of composite visualizations, limiting their general applicability. We present VizPilot, an automated visualization onboarding approach that reverse-engineers composite visualization structure to generate interactive onboarding experiences directly from raw visualization artifacts. VizPilot consists of two modules: a Composite Visualization Analyzer and an Onboarding Interface. Leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), the Analyzer employs a two-stage pipeline that decomposes a visualization into visual components, extracts structured explanations, and maps them to precise SVG elements for reliable highlighting and interaction. Implemented as a browser extension, VizPilot requires only a brief visualization description and optional interaction source code from the visualization developer to automatically generate onboarding content. The Onboarding Interface supports both guided narrative scrollytelling and free exploration, enabling users to learn visualization components progressively or on demand. We evaluate VizPilot through a comparative analysis of different input modalities, a usage scenario demonstrating reduced authoring effort, and a user study assessing its impact on users' cognitive load. The results demonstrate that VizPilot effectively automates the authoring of onboarding experiences while improving the usability and accessibility of composite visualizations.

</details>


### [243] [Investigating Effective Uncertainty Visualizations for Ordinal Crowdsourced Data of Crowding Conditions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28072)
*Bea Alexis Arcega,Annika Dominique S. Campos,Kathleen Therese Cruz,Aaron Ace Toledo,Briane Paul V. Samson*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper investigates how to effectively visualize uncertainty in crowdsourced railway crowding data to support commuter decision-making. Through an online study comparing different uncertainty visualizations, the authors found that cluster visualization best reduces cognitive load and maximizes confidence/trust, while bubble treemaps yield the highest accuracy in determining crowd levels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Commuters face unpredictable crowding in railway systems, and while crowdsourcing offers a way to collect localized user data, the inherent uncertainty in such ordinal data creates challenges for decision-making. Little is known about how to effectively visualize this uncertainty to support informed commuting choices.

Method: The authors designed and compared different uncertainty visualization techniques for representing variability and reliability in crowdsourced ordinal crowding data. These visualizations were evaluated through an online user study measuring metrics such as cognitive load, user confidence, trust, and accuracy in determining crowd levels.

Result: Cluster visualization was found to be best suited for reducing cognitive load while maximizing user confidence and trust. Bubble treemaps led to higher accuracy when participants were determining crowd levels.

Conclusion: Different uncertainty visualization techniques offer distinct trade-offs: cluster visualizations optimize for user experience (low cognitive load, high trust/confidence), while bubble treemaps optimize for task accuracy. Designers of commuting information systems should select visualization types based on the primary goal—ease of interpretation versus precise decision-making.

Abstract: Commuters often encounter crowding in railway systems, particularly in queues where passenger density varies throughout the day. This introduces uncertainty in crowdedness, making it difficult for individuals to anticipate conditions and plan their trips effectively. Crowdsourcing has been a valuable method for collecting localized user data. But the unpredictability of crowds and the uncertainty of crowdsourced information pose new challenges for decision-making. However, we know little about how to effectively visualize uncertainty in crowdedness to support informed commuting decisions, particularly when using crowdsourced ordinal data. Here, we investigated different uncertainty visualizations and their effectiveness in representing the variability and reliability of crowdsourced crowding data. They were evaluated through an online study, and we found that cluster visualization is best suited to reduce cognitive load while maximizing user confidence and trust. On the other hand, participants showed higher accuracy in determining crowd levels when using bubble treemaps.

</details>


### [244] [A Mathematical Framework for Reading the Autopsias' Meta - Compositional System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28155)
*Patricio F. Calatayud,Pablo Padilla Longoria,Álvaro Martínez Ramírez*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper proposes using topological mathematical tools to address readability problems in dynamic/kinetic music notation (cynetic musicography), using the Autopsias meta-compositional system as a case study to begin constructing a mathematical framework for orthographic rules in dynamic scores.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: New computer-based dynamic music scores (using animation, algorithmic processing, etc.) suffer from inherent readability problems. The authors argue that mathematical tools—analogous to how pitch-class set theory aids music analysis—can systematically address these orthographic challenges and improve composer-performer communication.

Method: The authors bridge traditional printed scores to dynamic computational re-appropriations, then apply basic topological concepts to analyze both the writing and the performance of the Autopsias composition. This mathematical analysis serves as the foundation for constructing new orthographic tools for dynamic musicography.

Result: Performances of Autopsias demonstrate that mathematical frameworks (akin to pitch-class set theory) are useful for understanding both music information and its performance. The study reveals the necessity of expanding orthographic rules to improve composer-performer dialogue in the context of dynamic scores.

Conclusion: Mathematics, particularly topology, offers a viable foundation for developing readability standards and orthographic conventions in dynamic musicography, with Autopsias serving as a promising initial case study for this framework.

Abstract: Background. New forms of music writing using computers have arisen in the past 20 years. Most of them use the capacities of digital manipulation of data like animation, algorithmic processing, cinematic view, and much more. These scores use dynamic musicography, and all of them share a problem. They have readability problems. We will argue that this problem can be addressed by mathematical tools. Aims. Take the Autopsias [Autopsies] meta-compositional system as a study case for starting the construction of a mathematical framework that can overview the readability for cynetic musicography. The Autopsias system is the process of transforming a musical score dynamically. Methodology. We will start to build a mathematical framework by taking a group of basic topological concepts, and applying them after a bridge between a printed score and a dynamic computational re-appropriation of it has taken place. We will observe the writing and the performing of the several performances of the Autopsias composition, and analyze them from a mathematical perspective, in order to get the ability to start constructing a new set of orthographical tools for the performance of dynamic musicography. Main Contribution. The performances of Autopsias show that mathematics, as with pitch-class sets, can be helpful for understanding music information, as well as its performance. Also show the necessity of augmenting the set of orthographic rules, in order to improve the dialog between composers and performers.

</details>


### [245] [Student Perceptions and Preferences Regarding AI-Generated Instructional Videos in Computing Education](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28203)
*Esse Ciego,Shubbhi Taneja,Wilson Wong,Amanpreet Kapoor*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A survey of 170 computing students found AI-generated educational videos on Markdown were rated as high-quality and accurate, with nearly half unable to identify them as AI-generated. However, students expressed limited comfort with widespread classroom adoption, preferring AI videos only for simple, supplemental, and visual use cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the rapid emergence of AI video generation tools enabling cost-effective creation of personalized educational videos, there is a gap in understanding how students perceive AI-generated video content. CS education research has focused primarily on text-based AI tools, leaving the pedagogical implications of AI-generated video unexplored.

Method: A descriptive post-test survey study was conducted with 170 computing students at two U.S. institutions. Participants watched three 3-minute AI-generated videos on Markdown (created with Knowlify) and then completed a survey assessing their perceptions of the videos' quality, accuracy, and usability, as well as their broader attitudes toward AI-generated video adoption in education.

Result: Students rated the Markdown videos as high-quality, accurate, and usable. Nearly half could not determine whether the videos were AI-generated. However, students expressed limited comfort with widespread classroom adoption of AI videos. They preferred AI videos for simple, supplemental, and visual use cases, while voicing concerns about lower-quality or inaccurate content, reduced instructor interaction, and diminished educational value.

Conclusion: AI-generated educational videos are perceived positively in terms of quality but face student skepticism regarding broad pedagogical adoption. Instructors should deploy AI videos purposefully — for supplementary, simple, and visual content — while preserving meaningful instructor interaction to address student concerns about educational value.

Abstract: Students differ in how they prefer to engage with learning resources, with some favoring textual materials and others visual or video-based content. Recent advances in generative AI have led CS education research to focus on text-based AI tools for developing learning resources. However, advances in AI video models and the rapid proliferation of AI video generation tools have made it possible for instructors to create high-quality personalized educational videos efficiently and cost-effectively. Understanding students' perceptions of AI-generated videos is thus critical for helping CS instructors know when and how to use them purposefully. To address this gap, we conducted a descriptive post-test survey study in which 170 computing students at two U.S. institutions watched three 3-minute AI videos on the Markdown markup language created with Knowlify. Students then completed a survey about their perceptions of the Markdown videos and their broader views on the use of AI-generated videos in education. Students rated the Markdown videos as high-quality, accurate, and usable, with nearly half unable to determine whether the videos were AI-generated. At the same time, students expressed limited comfort with the widespread adoption of AI videos in the classroom. They preferred AI videos for simple, supplemental, and visual use cases, while expressing concerns about lower-quality or inaccurate content, reduced instructor interaction, and diminished educational value.

</details>


### [246] [Toward Annotation-Efficient Continuous Emotion Arousal Quantification via Group-Level EEG Dynamic Neural Synchrony](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28204)
*Guandong Pan,Yaqian Yang,Shi Chen,Yi Zheng,Yi Zhen,Hongwei Zheng,Shaoting Tang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper proposes group-level EEG dynamic neural synchrony (DNS) measured via Correlated Component Analysis (CorrCA) with sliding windows as a principled, annotation-efficient signal for continuous emotional arousal quantification. Across four datasets (142 subjects, 207+ hours), DNS shows valence-dependent differences, correlates more strongly with arousal's first derivative than raw arousal, and is optimized with moderate windows (10–30s), positive lags, and first-order difference features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Continuous emotional arousal quantification is currently bottlenecked by the costly, time-consuming, and labor-intensive need for per-subject manual annotation. The authors seek a group-level neural marker that can bypass individual-level labeling, making large-scale emotion monitoring more feasible.

Method: Correlated Component Analysis (CorrCA) combined with sliding-window computation is applied to EEG data from four datasets (142 subjects, >207 hours). DNS is computed as a group-level synchrony measure. The relationship between DNS and emotional arousal is systematically evaluated, including comparisons with raw arousal values versus first-order derivatives, and sensitivity analyses over window sizes, lag parameters, and EEG feature types. Validation employs subject-split replication and block permutation tests.

Result: Three key findings: (1) DNS shows significant valence-dependent differences (p<0.003), with positive emotions eliciting higher synchrony. (2) DNS correlates more strongly with the first-order derivative of arousal than with raw arousal values, indicating it captures rate of emotional change rather than static intensity. (3) Optimal DNS-arousal coupling occurs with moderate windows (10–30s), positive lags (0–10 steps), and First-order Difference features from the dominant CorrCA component. Subject-split replication and permutation tests confirm these are not statistical artifacts.

Conclusion: DNS is established as an empirically validated, group-level neural marker that enables annotation-efficient continuous emotional arousal quantification, offering a principled alternative to labor-intensive manual per-subject labeling.

Abstract: Continuous emotional arousal quantification remains bottlenecked by time-consuming and labor-intensive manual annotation. This work investigates group-level EEG dynamic neural synchrony (DNS) as a principled signal for continuous arousal quantification that bypasses per-subject manual labeling. Using Correlated Component Analysis (CorrCA) with sliding-window computation across four EEG datasets spanning 142 subjects and over 207 hours, we systematically evaluate DNS as a group-level marker for emotional arousal dynamics. Three key findings emerge. First, DNS exhibits significant emotion information from valence-dependent differences (all p<0.003), with positive emotions eliciting higher synchrony. Second, DNS correlates more strongly with the first-order derivative of arousal than with raw arousal values, revealing that neural synchrony captures the rate of emotional change rather than static intensity. Third, we provide the first systematic characterization of how DNS-arousal coupling depends on key methodological choices, finding that moderate windows (10-30 s), positive lags (0-10 steps), and First-order Difference feature of EEG from the dominant CorrCA component yield consistently strong coupling. Subject-split replication and block permutation tests confirm these associations are not statistical artifacts. Our findings establish DNS as an empirically validated group-level marker toward annotation-efficient continuous emotional arousal quantification.

</details>


### [247] [Identifying a Level-up Pathway for AI-assisted Counterspeech through Elaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28239)
*Han Li,Inhwan Bae,Natalie Bazarova,Drew Margolin*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This study evaluated three generative AI-assisted counterspeech writing systems (varying by assistance stage: co-writing vs. re-writing, and mode: guided vs. unguided) in a randomized controlled trial. AI assistance increased perceived counterspeech effectiveness while preserving authenticity, primarily by enabling more elaborate, informative, and lexically sophisticated writing. Perceived effectiveness was the strongest predictor of willingness to counterspeak publicly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vaccine-skeptical content on social media has profound societal impact, and community-driven counterspeech is a promising participatory response. However, ordinary users struggle to craft effective counterspeech, limiting their willingness and ability to engage constructively. The paper investigates whether generative AI can help bridge this gap.

Method: The authors designed and evaluated three generative AI-assisted counterspeech writing systems that vary along two dimensions: assistance stage (co-writing vs. re-writing) and assistance mode (guided vs. unguided). A randomized controlled trial was conducted with social media users, who wrote counterspeech responses to both statistical and narrative vaccine-skeptical content.

Result: AI-assisted writing increased perceived counterspeech effectiveness across both evidence types while largely preserving authentic self-expression. Perceived effectiveness was the strongest predictor of willingness to counterspeak publicly. AI's primary benefit was facilitating more elaborate writing—producing messages that were more informative, analytical, and lexically sophisticated.

Conclusion: The findings suggest a "level-up" pathway for AI-assisted, community-driven counterspeech: AI can help cultivate more effective and motivated counterspeakers, thereby contributing to higher-quality public discourse on pressing societal issues.

Abstract: Given the profound societal impact of vaccine-skeptical content on social media, community-driven counterspeech has emerged as a promising participatory response to contest and curb such objectionable content. Yet crafting effective counterspeech remains challenging for ordinary users, limiting their willingness and ability to engage constructively. We designed and evaluated three generative AI-assisted counterspeech writing systems that vary by assistance stage (co-writing vs. re-writing) and mode (guided vs. unguided) to support lay users' responses to vaccine-skeptical content. We ask whether AI can help users craft counterspeech perceived as both effective and authentic, which forms of AI support work best, and through what mechanisms. In a randomized controlled trial with social media users, participants wrote counterspeech responses to both statistical and narrative vaccine-skeptical content. Across evidence types, AI-assisted writing increased perceived counterspeech effectiveness while largely preserving authentic self-expression, and perceived effectiveness was the strongest predictor of willingness to counterspeak publicly. AI's primary benefit was facilitating more elaborate writing, producing messages that were more informative, analytical, and lexically sophisticated. These findings suggest a level-up pathway for AI-assisted, community-driven counterspeech, which helps cultivate more effective and motivated counterspeakers, contributing to higher-quality public discourse on pressing societal issues.

</details>


### [248] [Effects of Auditory Information for People With Visual Impairments in Highly Automated Vehicles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28544)
*Mark Colley,Tobias Aescht,Omid Rajabi,Max Rädler,Pascal Jansen,Enrico Rukzio*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A study comparing three levels of auditory information (low, medium, high) for visually impaired users in automated vehicles found that medium-level information optimally improved trust, user experience, and perceived safety, while high-level information reached saturation. The work provides design guidance for accessible AV communication.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated vehicles promise improved mobility accessibility for everyone, but current design and research on information visualization neglect users with visual impairments. There is a gap in understanding how to communicate relevant information to visually impaired passengers in fully automated vehicles.

Method: The authors designed a combined visual and auditory communication concept for visually impaired users inside fully automated vehicles. An online video-based study (N=35, including 12 participants with visual impairments) compared three levels of auditory information: low (safety-relevant only), medium (safety + vehicle control + route updates), and high (medium + sightseeing + destination information).

Result: Trust and user experience significantly improved with additional auditory information. Perceived safety also improved but with a less robust effect. However, information saturation was observed at the medium level, indicating that high-level information provided diminishing or no additional benefits.

Conclusion: Medium-level auditory information appears optimal for balancing informativeness with cognitive load. The findings guide designers toward adequate—not excessive—information communication to improve the accessibility of automated vehicles for users with visual impairments.

Abstract: Automated vehicles promise to improve accessibility and access to personal mobility for everyone. However, their design and current research trends in visualizing relevant information do not reflect this commitment to accessibility for users with visual impairments. Therefore, we designed and implemented a visual and auditory communication concept for people with visual impairments seated inside fully automated vehicles. Furthermore, in an online video-based study (N=35, 12 with visual impairments), we compared three levels of auditory information communication: low (safety-relevant information only), medium (additionally including vehicle control and route updates), and high (additionally including sightseeing and destination information). Results showed that trust and user experience significantly improved with additional information, with a corresponding, albeit less robust, effect on perceived safety. However, they also revealed that a potential information saturation was reached with medium information. Our work helps to improve the accessibility of automated vehicles by guiding designers towards adequate information communication.

</details>


### [249] [Multi-Session User Experience Assessments of Computationally Optimized Automated Vehicle Functionality Visualizations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28552)
*Mark Colley,Pascal Jansen,Svenja Krauss,Enrico Rukzio*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper applies multi-objective Bayesian optimization to efficiently design in-vehicle visualizations for automated vehicles, balancing passenger trust, perceived safety, and cognitive load. An online study (N=74) demonstrates the method's effectiveness but reveals limitations when optimizing for subjective measures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional empirical evaluation of AV passenger visualizations is time-consuming, costly, and limits the exploration of design parameters. The authors seek a more efficient, scalable method for optimizing visualization designs.

Method: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization was employed to iteratively optimize AV visualization design parameters across multiple sessions. The optimization targeted three objectives: maximizing passenger trust and perceived safety while minimizing cognitive load. The approach was evaluated through an online study with 74 participants.

Result: The Bayesian optimization method effectively identified visualization design parameters that improved trust, safety, and predictability. The approach proved more efficient and scalable than traditional methods. However, shortcomings emerged when optimizing for subjective measurements.

Conclusion: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization is a viable and efficient tool for AV visualization design, though its application to subjective metrics requires careful consideration of the identified limitations.

Abstract: Understanding automated vehicles (AVs) is crucial to improving their acceptance. Numerous approaches to visualizing relevant traffic information to passengers have been proposed and empirically evaluated. As this is time-consuming, costly, and reduces the possible design parameters, we employed multi-objective Bayesian optimization to optimize the design of visualizations in AVs. In particular, we evaluated multi-session aspects involving iterative optimization. We optimized the design for passenger trust and perceived safety while minimizing cognitive load. Results from an online study (N=74) show that this method effectively identifies visualization design parameter values that improve trust, safety, and predictability while making the design process more efficient and scalable. However, shortcomings of the computational approach when optimizing for subjective measurements are highlighted and discussed.

</details>


### [250] [CrossAtlas: Evaluating Projection Techniques for Spatial Referencing in Cross-Reality Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28583)
*Haoyang Yang,Chenyang Zhang,Elliott H. Faa,Weijian Liu,Lily Seika Chisholm,Benjamin Lee,David Saffo,Feiyu Lu,Blair MacIntyre,Yalong Yang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: CrossAtlas investigates how different bidirectional projection techniques between VR (3D) and desktop (2D) views affect spatial referencing in cross-reality collaboration. A study with 24 dyads shows spherical (equirectangular) projection often outperforms planar variants and remains robust across curved layouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-reality collaboration between immersive (VR) and desktop users is growing, but little is known about how bidirectional projection techniques — mapping between 3D immersive layouts and 2D desktop views — influence communication and spatial referencing. Different mappings preserve or distort geometric relationships (adjacency, orientation, coverage) in different ways, yet no prior work systematically compares their collaborative effects.

Method: The authors developed CrossAtlas, a synchronized PC-VR collaboration platform integrating multiple bidirectional projection techniques: three planar projection variants and one spherical variant (equirectangular). They conducted a controlled study with 24 dyads (48 participants) who completed spatial referencing tasks under different projection-layout conditions, collecting both performance metrics and subjective measures.

Result: Projection choice significantly shaped collaboration quality. The spherical (equirectangular) projection variant frequently outperformed planar projections and demonstrated greater robustness across different object layouts with varying curvature.

Conclusion: Bidirectional projection technique selection is a critical design factor in cross-reality collaborative systems. Spherical projections like equirectangular offer more reliable spatial referencing than planar alternatives, particularly when object layouts vary in curvature, suggesting they should be preferred for cross-reality collaboration tools.

Abstract: Cross-reality collaboration increasingly connects immersive and desktop users within synchronized workspaces, yet little is known about how bidirectional projection techniques between immersive 3D layouts and desktop 2D views influence communication. Spatial referencing depends on shared spatial understanding, but different mappings preserve and distort geometric relationships in different ways, altering perceived adjacency, orientation, and coverage across collaborators' views. We present CrossAtlas, a synchronized PC-VR collaboration platform that integrates multiple bidirectional projection techniques, including three planar projection variants and equirectangular, a spherical projection variant, across layouts of varying curvature. In a controlled study with 24 dyads, collaborators completed spatial referencing tasks under different projection-layout conditions while we collected performance and subjective measures. Our results show that projection choice strongly shaped collaboration, with the spherical variant often outperforming planar projections and remaining robust across object layouts.

</details>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [251] [Recursive transformers for semiconductor thermo-mechanical reliability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27251)
*Kart-leong Lim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper evaluates three recursive transformer architectures (Tiny Recursive, Depth Recursive, and Simple Recursive) for surrogate modeling in engineering design with small, low-dimensional datasets. Through hardware-aware analysis on thermo-mechanical package analysis and Laplace PDE solving, the authors demonstrate that recursive weight-sharing transformers offer an optimal balance of prediction accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational cost compared to over-parameterized conventional transformers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional transformer architectures are over-parameterized for the small, low-dimensional datasets common in engineering design, where generating large simulation data (e.g., FEA) is expensive. Excess parameters cause overfitting and wasteful memory/compute overhead. The authors argue for shifting focus from adding learnable parameters toward adding compute capacity instead.

Method: The authors conduct a hardware-aware evaluation comparing three recursive transformer paradigms: (1) Tiny Recursive Model, (2) a proposed Depth Recursive Transformer, and (3) a Simple Recursive Transformer. They systematically benchmark these against predictive performance metrics (Recall, Mean Reciprocal Rank), parameter count, and FLOPs. Validation is performed on two low-dimensional tasks: thermo-mechanical reliability analysis of advanced semiconductor packages (stress and warpage prediction under thermal cycling via FEA) and a Laplace PDE iterative numerical solver for capacitance fields.

Result: Recursive weight-sharing transformers provide an effective and generalizable trade-off between prediction accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational cost for small-data engineering surrogate modeling. The proposed Depth Recursive transformer architecture is highlighted as a practical design choice under resource-constrained scenarios.

Conclusion: For engineering surrogate modeling with small, low-dimensional datasets, recursive weight-sharing transformer architectures are superior to conventional over-parameterized transformers. They mitigate overfitting while maintaining accuracy and reducing memory/compute demands. The paper provides practical design guidelines for selecting recursive transformer architectures in resource-constrained engineering applications.

Abstract: Transformer-based surrogate models are increasingly used to replace expensive first-principles simulation in engineering design. But conventional transformer architectures are often over parameterized for the small, low-dimensional datasets typical of engineering design spaces, where large simulation data is expensive to generate. Under these conditions, excess parameter capacity leads to overfitting rather than improved accuracy, while also incurring unnecessary memory and compute overhead. This motivates a shift towards architectures that focus on additional compute rather than additional learnable parameters. This paper presents a hardware-aware evaluation of three recursive transformer paradigms for surrogate thermo-mechanical analysis of advanced packages: a)Tiny Recursive Model, b) our proposed Depth Recursive transformer, c) and a simple recursive transformer. We systematically compare their predictive performance (Recall, Mean Reciprocal Rank), parameter count, computational complexity (FLOPs), providing practical design guidelines for selecting recursive transformer architectures under resource-constrained scenarios. We validate this principle on two low-dimensional engineering prediction tasks: 1) thermo-mechanical reliability analysis of advanced semiconductor packages, where stress and warpage from thermal cycling must be evaluated repeatedly across a design-of-experiments sweep under costly finite element analysis (FEA). 2) Laplace PDE iterative numerical solver for capacitance field. Overall, recursive weight-sharing transformers provide an effective and generalizable trade-off between prediction accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational cost for small data engineering surrogate modeling.

</details>


### [252] [Regularizing modality contribution drift in multimodal continual learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27260)
*Zhen Zhang,Jielei Chu,Bin Liu,Tianrui Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper identifies Modality Contribution Drift (MCD), a decision-level shift in relative modality contributions during multimodal continual learning, quantifies it with a new metric, and proposes CMCDR — a regularization method with replay-based and replay-free variants to preserve modality contribution structures across incremental tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MMCL methods focus on cross-modal representation alignment or semantic similarity but neglect whether the relative contributions of individual modalities and their interactions remain stable across incremental tasks. This decision-level shift, termed Modality Contribution Drift (MCD), causes catastrophic forgetting that current methods fail to address.

Method: The authors first formalize and quantify MCD using a score that combines contribution-strength and relative-reliance changes under controlled interventions on modality subsets. They then propose Continual Modality Contribution Drift Regularization (CMCDR) with two variants: (1) a replay-based version that uses modality-subset interventions on stored old samples to compare contribution profiles between the current and a frozen previous model, constraining changes in modality-specific and interaction contributions; (2) a replay-free version that uses current-task samples as probes and distills the frozen model's old-task contribution responses, regularizing the profile without exemplars.

Result: Experiments on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual visual question answering demonstrate the generality and effectiveness of CMCDR in mitigating forgetting compared to existing MMCL methods.

Conclusion: Modality Contribution Drift is a critical yet overlooked source of forgetting in MMCL. CMCDR effectively preserves modality contribution structures across tasks, and its dual replay-based/replay-free design makes it broadly applicable across different MMCL settings.

Abstract: Multimodal continual learning (MMCL) aims to learn emerging knowledge from multimodal data while preserving knowledge. To mitigate forgetting, current MMCL methods usually focus on cross-modal representation alignment or semantic similarity, but they overlook whether the relative contributions of individual modalities and their interactions remain stable across incremental tasks. We term this decision-level shift Modality Contribution Drift (MCD) and quantify it with the MCD score, which combines contribution-strength and relative-reliance changes under controlled interventions on modality subsets. Theoretical and empirical analyses further explain why current MMCL methods cannot reliably mitigate this drift. To this end, we propose Continual Modality Contribution Drift Regularization (CMCDR), which preserves the modality contribution structure of previously learned tasks. Since MMCL settings differ in whether old exemplars are available, CMCDR includes both replay-based and replay-free versions. The replay-based version uses modality-subset interventions as diagnostic probes on stored old samples, compares their contribution profiles between the current model and a frozen previous model, and constrains changes in old-sample modality-specific and interaction contributions. The replay-free version uses current-task samples as probes and distills the frozen model's old-task contribution responses, thereby regularizing the observed contribution profile without exemplars. Experiments on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual visual question answering validate the generality and effectiveness of CMCDR.

</details>


### [253] [DoTime: A Synthetic Benchmark Generator for Interventional and Counterfactual Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27263)
*Dennis Thumm,Billy Tim Anthony,Ying Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DoTime is a generator of multivariate temporal structural causal models with interventions, providing scalable benchmarks for interventional and counterfactual time-series estimation. It supports continuous-time intervention windows, counterfactual sampling with positivity guards, regime-switching SCMs, and deterministic intervention profiles. The paper also demonstrates that an interventional prior-fitted network (PFN) consistently outperforms an observational model of identical capacity across all tested structures and seeds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for causal inference over time series are predominantly observational, small-scale, or domain-specific, leaving interventional and counterfactual estimation—critical for healthcare, policy evaluation, and climate science—severely under-evaluated. There is a need for scalable, open, and theoretically grounded synthetic benchmarks with ground-truth interventions and counterfactuals.

Method: The authors introduce DoTime, a generator of multivariate temporal structural causal models (TSCMs) with interventions. Key technical contributions include: (1) continuous-time intervention windows, (2) counterfactual sampling modes with a positivity guard, (3) regime-switching SCMs as a strict generalization of interrupted time series, (4) non-stationary dynamics via switching SCM parameters, and (5) deterministic ramp and sinusoidal intervention profiles placing structural breaks inside the evaluation window. The generator is released as the `dotime` PyPI package with four frozen evaluation suites (100,000 training trajectories, eight named identification structures). The method also evaluates a falsifiable claim: that interventional training yields measurable direction-accuracy gains over observational training, tested via a prior-fitted network (PFN) across three training seeds under structure-matched evaluation.

Result: Under structure-matched evaluation on held-out episodes, the interventional PFN achieves a positive direction-accuracy gap over the observational model in every structure, trajectory length, and seed tested—confirming the falsifiable claim across all experimental conditions.

Conclusion: DoTime fills a critical gap in causal time-series benchmarking by providing rich, intervention-aware synthetic data with exact ground truth. The consistent superiority of interventional training supports the argument that exposure to interventional distributions during training confers a measurable advantage for causal direction estimation in temporal settings. The generator also shows promise as a prior for causal foundation model development.

Abstract: Most benchmarks for causal inference over time series are observational, small, or domain-specific, leaving interventional and counterfactual estimation under-served exactly where it matters most, such as in healthcare, policy evaluation, and climate science. We introduce \textbf{DoTime}, an open, scalable, and theoretically grounded generator of multivariate temporal structural causal models (TSCMs) with interventions, released as the \code{dotime} PyPI package together with four frozen evaluation suites. Beyond existing work, it adds capabilities absent from prior generators: continuous-time intervention \emph{windows}, counterfactual sampling modes with a positivity guard, regime-switching SCMs as a strict generalization of interrupted time series, non-stationary dynamics by construction with switching SCM parameters, and deterministic ramp and sinusoidal intervention profiles that place trends and structural breaks \emph{inside} the evaluation window. Moreover, it demonstrates the suitability of the generator as a prior for a causal foundation model reference implementation. The released suites span a training-scale snapshot of $100{,}000$ trajectories and eight named identification structures, each with exact ground truth: paired interventional trajectories from the same SCM throughout, and shared-noise counterfactuals in the continuous-time suite. We ship reference baseline implementations with an evaluation harness, and pose a falsifiable claim: interventional training buys a measurable direction-accuracy advantage over an observational model of identical capacity. It is tested across three training seeds per arm. Under structure-matched evaluation on held-out episodes, the interventional prior-fitted network's (PFN) gap is positive in every structure, trajectory length, and seed tested.

</details>


### [254] [PlatformBid: An Auto-Bidding Benchmark from a Unified Advertising Platform's Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27265)
*Shengtian Yang,Yewen Li,Peng Jiang,Zhiyi Lyu,Bo An,Peng Jiang,Qingpeng Cai,Lei Feng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PlatformBid is the first auto-bidding benchmark from a unified ad platform perspective, evaluating methods across three competitive settings (homogeneous, heterogeneous, promotional). The authors also propose BidFlow, a novel flow-matching-based auto-bidding method that achieves +0.68% target cost improvement in online Kuaishou experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional auto-bidding research focuses only on the DSP side (maximizing advertiser conversions). However, modern integrated ad platforms (e.g., social media, e-commerce) combine SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange functions, creating a need to jointly optimize both advertiser conversions and total platform revenue. Existing benchmarks lack this unified platform-centric perspective.

Method: The authors introduce PlatformBid, a comprehensive benchmark with three evaluation settings: (1) homogeneous competition (identical algorithms), (2) heterogeneous competition (diverse strategies), and (3) promotional competition (budget surges during events). They systematically evaluate classical control methods, RL-based methods, and generative auto-bidding methods. Additionally, they propose BidFlow, a novel flow-matching-based auto-bidding approach that uses expressive policy representations to handle dynamic competitive environments.

Result: The benchmark provides systematic evaluation across multiple method families. BidFlow demonstrates strong performance in dynamic competitive settings. Online A/B experiments on Kuaishou show a +0.68% improvement in target cost, validating offline-online consistency of PlatformBid.

Conclusion: PlatformBid fills the gap in platform-centric auto-bidding evaluation and provides a standardized benchmark for future research. BidFlow's offline and online results confirm the benchmark's practical relevance and the effectiveness of flow-matching for auto-bidding under competition.

Abstract: Real-time bidding is central to computational advertising, comprising three elements: Supply Side Platform (SSP) selling ad impressions, Demand Side Platform (DSP) bidding for advertisers, and Ad Exchange conducting auctions between them. Traditional auto-bidding algorithms focus solely on the DSP side, maximizing advertiser conversions by adjusting bids against competitors. However, current big ad platforms, such as social media and e-commerce companies, now integrate SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange functions internally. From such ad platforms' perspective, the goal of the auto-bidding algorithms is not only to maximize the advertisers' conversions, but also the total revenue of the platform. Given the lack of platform-centric evaluation frameworks and the pressing need to advance auto-bidding research, we propose PlatformBid - the first comprehensive benchmark designed from a unified ad platform's perspective. To accurately reflect the real-world auto-bidding scenarios, we define three representative settings: (1) homogeneous competition with identical algorithms across advertisers, (2) heterogeneous competition with diverse algorithmic strategies, and (3) promotional competition where some advertisers surge budgets for boosting sales during promotional events like Black Friday. We systematically evaluate a broad spectrum of existing auto-bidding methods across these settings, encompassing classical control methods, RL-based methods, and recent generative methods. Besides these methods, we further propose a novel auto-bidding method based on flow-matching, termed BidFlow, which leverages the flow-matching method's expressive policy representation to effectively handle dynamic competitive environments. Online experiments on Kuaishou further show a +0.68\% improvement in target cost, providing deployment evidence for the offline-online consistency of PlatformBid.

</details>


### [255] [Beyond KV Reconstruction: Functional Reconstruction for MLA Draft Models in Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27269)
*Weiye Shi,Fanxu Meng,Muhan Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Converting MHA/GQA models to MLA for cache efficiency degrades draft-token acceptance in speculative decoding. The authors propose Functional Reconstruction, an end-to-end post-conversion optimization that reproduces original attention outputs, significantly improving acceptance rates across diverse configurations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MLA offers memory-efficient long-context inference via compact latent KV states, but most open-source checkpoints use MHA/GQA. Direct conversion introduces attention-function errors from low-rank factorization and RoPE handling that harm speculative decoding's draft-target agreement, undermining acceleration gains.

Method: The paper formulates MLA draft construction as functional reconstruction rather than cache compression. Their end-to-end (E2E) method optimizes each converted MLA attention module to reproduce the post-output-projection response of the original MHA/GQA counterpart on calibration hidden states, without requiring verifier logits or supervision. This converter-agnostic procedure preserves the converted cache and inference graph.

Result: Evaluated across 192 configurations (4 Llama/Qwen draft-target pairs, TransMLA and MHA2MLA converters, HF and vLLM backends, 4 tasks with 200 prompts each): Functional Reconstruction materially improved acceptance in 37 of 64 matched task cells, left 26 unchanged, and materially decreased only 1, using a 0.5-percentage-point reporting tolerance.

Conclusion: Functional Reconstruction effectively bridges the accuracy gap between direct MHA/GQA-to-MLA conversion and the needs of speculative decoding, enabling MLA's cache efficiency without sacrificing draft quality. The method is practical, converter-agnostic, and requires no retraining from scratch.

Abstract: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) is increasingly important for long-context LLM inference because compact latent states replace the growing key-value (KV) cache and reduce decoding memory traffic. Yet most capable open checkpoints use multi-head or grouped-query attention (MHA/GQA), so conversion is needed to obtain MLA's cache efficiency without retraining from scratch. Speculative decoding offers complementary acceleration, but its speedup depends on agreement between draft proposals and target verification. We find that direct MHA/GQA-to-MLA conversion can sharply reduce this agreement: low-rank factorization and RoPE handling introduce attention-function errors that may be tolerable for standalone generation but substantially lower draft-token acceptance. We therefore formulate MLA draft construction as functional reconstruction rather than cache compression. Our end-to-end (E2E) method optimizes each converted MLA attention module to reproduce the post-output-projection response of its original MHA/GQA counterpart on calibration hidden states. This converter-agnostic post-conversion procedure preserves the converted cache and inference graph and requires neither verifier logits nor verifier supervision. We evaluate 192 model-converter-backend-method-task configurations spanning four Llama/Qwen draft-target pairs, TransMLA and MHA2MLA, HF and vLLM, and four 200-prompt tasks. With a 0.5-percentage-point reporting tolerance, Functional Reconstruction materially improves acceptance in 37 of 64 matched task cells, leaves 26 practically unchanged, and materially decreases one. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://github.com/swyhahaha/FunctionalMLA.

</details>


### [256] [RLPF: Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback for Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27271)
*Huihao Jing,Haozhe Cui,Wenbin Hu,Shaojin Chen,Haochen Shi,Changxuan Fan,Yuxuan Liu,Hanyu Yang,Sirui Zhang,Ziyi Chen,Haoran Li,Yangqiu Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RLPF is a reinforcement learning method that trains code agents to optimize both correctness and runtime efficiency using staged rewards: progress-based ordering for failed programs and relative efficiency ranking for correct ones. Fine-tuning Qwen3-32B boosts correct-and-runnable solutions from 11.1% to 54.6% and relative efficiency from 8.1% to 38.6% on PerfCodeBench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing code models use execution feedback only for correctness, ignoring runtime efficiency. Two correct programs can differ greatly in speed. The gap is that runtime is a fragile reward: it only matters after correctness, varies across tasks, and provides no signal when most samples fail to compile/run. The authors aim to train agents that prefer faster correct implementations, not just treat efficiency as a post-hoc evaluation metric.

Method: RLPF (Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback) structures execution outcomes into a staged composite reward. For failed programs, it ranks them by execution progress (e.g., how many tests passed, whether compilation succeeded). For correct programs, it computes relative improvement: the runtime gap between a baseline and an expert reference, measuring how much closer the agent gets. This provides useful gradients both before and after correctness. The method is applied to fine-tune Qwen3-32B on PerfCodeBench.

Result: Fine-tuning with RLPF increased correct-and-runnable solutions from 11.1% to 54.6% and relative efficiency from 8.1% to 38.6% on PerfCodeBench. The model became competitive with stronger open-weight systems and showed modest transfer to EffiBench-X. Ablations showed model-generated references provide weaker but useful supervision, and the full composite reward outperforms correctness-only or runtime-only baselines in reliability.

Conclusion: Code agents can be trained not only to pass tests but to actively optimize their programs for runtime efficiency. RLPF demonstrates that staged, progress-aware rewards make runtime a viable training signal, enabling models to learn both correctness and performance jointly.

Abstract: Code models are increasingly trained with execution feedback, but most training signals still stop at correctness. This leaves an important gap for systems code: two programs can pass the same tests while differing greatly in runtime. We study how to train code agents to prefer faster correct implementations, rather than treating efficiency only as an evaluation metric. The key difficulty is that runtime is a fragile reward. It is meaningful only after a program is correct, varies across tasks, and gives little guidance when most sampled programs fail to compile or run. We propose \textbf{RLPF}, reinforcement learning from performance feedback, which turns execution outcomes into a staged reward. Failed programs are ordered by execution progress, while correct programs are ranked by their relative improvement from the baseline toward the expert reference. This gives useful feedback before correctness and performance-sensitive feedback after correctness. Fine-tuning Qwen3-32B with RLPF on PerfCodeBench raises correct-and-runnable solutions from $11.1\%$ to $54.6\%$ and improves relative efficiency from $8.1\%$ to $38.6\%$. The trained model becomes competitive with stronger open-weight systems, and its optimization behavior transfers modestly to EffiBench-X. Additional studies show that model-generated references provide useful but weaker supervision, and that the full composite reward is more reliable than correctness-only or runtime-only baselines. These results suggest that code agents can be trained not only to pass tests, but also to optimize the programs they write.

</details>


### [257] [SDO: Structure-Aware Data Organization for Efficient LLM Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27273)
*Jinliang Gao,Ning Yang,Hai Wang,Baili Xiao,Pin Lyu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SDO is a plug-and-play data organization framework that dynamically organizes mini-batches and controls sample exposure across training epochs using embedding-space structure, accelerating LLM post-training convergence without permanently excluding any samples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM post-training treats data organization as static preprocessing via embedding-based grouping, which cannot adapt to evolving sample exposure during optimization. This leads to redundant updates for some samples and under-optimization for others, as all samples receive similar exposure regardless of their differing optimization needs.

Method: SDO operates epoch-by-epoch on frozen external embeddings. Within each epoch, locality-aware batching constructs coherent mini-batches via KNN neighborhood traversal. Across epochs, an exposure-balanced scheduling mechanism tracks per-sample participation and reduces sampling probability for over-exposed samples. The framework requires no model warm-up training overhead.

Result: SDO accelerates convergence across SFT, DPO, and GRPO, with the largest gains in the early-to-mid training phase. It produces more coherent gradients and more balanced accuracy across question types without permanently excluding any training samples.

Conclusion: Dynamic, structure-aware data organization with exposure-driven feedback is an effective and general approach for improving LLM post-training efficiency across multiple training paradigms.

Abstract: Post-training of large language models is expensive, and existing efficiency improvements mainly focus on selecting informative samples or designing training schedules. However, data organization itself is usually treated as a static preprocessing step: embedding-based grouping methods construct fixed partitions before training and cannot adapt to the evolving sample exposure during optimization. As a result, all samples receive similar exposure despite their different optimization needs, leading to redundant updates for some samples while leaving others under-optimized. To address this problem, we propose SDO (Structure-Aware Data Organization), a plug-and-play data organization framework with an exposure-driven feedback mechanism that organizes mini-batch composition and sample exposure according to representation-space structure. SDO operates epoch by epoch on frozen external embeddings, avoiding model warm-up training overhead: within each epoch, locality-aware batching forms coherent mini-batches via KNN neighborhood traversal; across epochs, exposure-balanced scheduling records per-sample participation and reduces the sampling probability of over-exposed samples to preserve long-term coverage. Across SFT, DPO, and GRPO, SDO accelerates convergence, with the largest gains observed in the early-to-mid phase, producing more coherent gradients and more balanced accuracy across question types without permanently excluding training samples.

</details>


### [258] [Rethinking EEG-Based Disease Diagnosis: Decoupling Instance Representation Learning from Subject-Level Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27274)
*Zhiyuan Ma,Zeyuan Li,Zhiyi Lu,Jiacheng Hao,Youlang Du,Zhen Jiang,Xinche Zhang,Yuhao Sun,Sen Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BridgeMIL is a two-stage framework for EEG-based disease diagnosis that decouples instance representation learning from subject-level supervision. Stage 1 pretrains an encoder via temporal and sub-bag alignment with variance-covariance regularization, avoiding inherited instance labels. Stage 2 transfers the encoder to an attention-based MIL aggregator with feature retention. It outperforms baselines by 4.28 percentage points across three EEG datasets and five backbones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard EEG diagnostic pipelines assign inherited subject labels to every segmented instance, incorrectly assuming all instances are equally reliable. While MIL avoids this by treating subjects as bags, end-to-end MIL suffers from limited subject-level samples. The key insight is that supervision should align with the subject-level objective, but representation learning should exploit abundant unlabeled instances without assigning disease labels to individual windows.

Method: BridgeMIL decouples into two stages. Stage 1 pretrains the encoder via self-supervised learning: it aligns temporally nearby EEG windows and independently sampled within-subject sub-bags using contrastive-style alignment, while variance and covariance regularization prevent representational collapse and reduce redundancy without negative pairs. Stage 2 freezes or lightly tunes the pretrained encoder, appends an attention-based MIL aggregator, and applies supervision only at the subject (bag) level. Feature retention mechanisms limit representation drift during this transfer.

Result: BridgeMIL achieved the highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone combinations, with an overall mean accuracy of 76.57% — 4.28 pp above the strongest baseline. Analyses showed substantial variation in inherited-label reliability across instances, greater sensitivity to subject scarcity than instance scarcity, and a more structured representation space with distinct subject-wise clusters and better inter-class separation.

Conclusion: Aligning supervision with the subject-level prediction objective while leveraging abundant EEG instances for representation learning — without assigning disease labels to individual instances — is critical for robust EEG-based diagnosis. BridgeMIL demonstrates that decoupling representation learning from subject-level supervision yields substantial and consistent improvements.

Abstract: EEG-based disease diagnosis requires one prediction per subject, yet common pipelines segment recordings into short instances, inherit the subject label for every instance, and train instance-level classifiers. This assumes that all instances provide equally reliable diagnostic evidence. Multiple instance learning (MIL) avoids inherited labels by treating each subject as a bag. However, EEG datasets contain far fewer subjects than instances, which can limit the quality of the representations learned by end-to-end MIL. We propose BridgeMIL, a two-stage framework that decouples instance representation learning from subject-level supervision. Stage 1 pretrains the encoder without inherited instance labels by aligning temporally nearby windows and independently sampled within-subject sub-bags. Variance and covariance regularization prevent collapse and reduce redundancy without negative pairs. Stage 2 transfers the encoder to an attention-based MIL aggregator, applies supervision only to subject predictions, and limits representation drift through feature retention. Across three EEG disease datasets and five representative backbones, BridgeMIL attains the highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone settings and an overall mean accuracy of 76.57%, 4.28 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline. Further analyses reveal substantial variation in inherited-label reliability across instances, greater performance sensitivity to subject scarcity than to instance scarcity, and a more structured representation space with distinct subject-wise clusters and improved separation between diagnostic classes. Together, these findings underscore the importance of aligning supervision with the subject-level prediction objective while learning from abundant EEG instances without assigning disease labels to individual instances.

</details>


### [259] [Flat Score, Amplified Failures: How the Error Budget Masks Damage in Quantized LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27275)
*Jiwon Jang,Kisu Yang,Heuiseok Lim,Hyunwoo Park*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Post-training 4-bit quantization appears lossless on standard metrics but systematically amplifies existing failure modes (e.g., tool-name hallucinations) without creating new ones. Standard benchmarks mask this damage via generous error budgets; tighter budgets or per-channel error analysis reveal the hidden cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To rigorously test the widely-held claim that 4-bit post-training quantization is "nearly lossless," specifically in the context of multi-turn, tool-calling language agents where reliability is critical, and to determine whether standard aggregate metrics conceal meaningful degradation.

Method: The authors conduct a systematic evaluation on the τ²-bench using two open-weight model families (dense and MoE variants) across two domains, testing at 16-, 8-, and 4-bit precision (eight cells, 456 episodes each). They compare standard task success scores against process-level analysis (per-channel error rates, failure mode classification, rank correlation of failure sets). They introduce shrinking error budgets, equivalence testing, and a targeted error-repair prompt as diagnostics to expose masked damage.

Result: Standard metrics show no statistically significant score drop after multiple-comparison correction; equivalence testing bounds change within ±7.5 points. However, process analysis reveals quantization amplifies existing failures (tool-name hallucination in telecom) by up to 2.5× (+17.6 points per task) while introducing almost no novel failures (rank correlation ≥ 0.94, only 0.18% novel events). The score stays flat because the benchmark's ten-error budget absorbs extra failures. Shrinking the budget to two errors exposes a 17-point gap, and a targeted repair prompt removes the damage precisely where it lives.

Conclusion: The claim that 4-bit quantization is lossless is misleading: it preserves task success scores only because standard benchmarks have generous error tolerances that mask systematic amplification of pre-existing failure modes. The authors recommend reporting per-channel error rates and success under shrinking error budgets alongside aggregate task reward to better surface quantization-induced degradation.

Abstract: Post-training quantization to 4-bit weights is widely reported to be nearly lossless. We test this claim for multi-turn, tool-calling agents, where it now matters most. On $τ^2$-bench, across two open-weight model families in dense and MoE variants and two domains (eight cells, 456 episodes each, at 16-, 8-, and 4-bit weights), quantization indeed looks free on the standard metric. No cell shows a score change that survives multiple-comparison correction, and in the cell that carries the largest process damage, equivalence testing bounds the change within $\pm$7.5 points. The process tells a different story.
