Quantization amplifies the failure the model already exhibits at full precision (tool-name hallucination in telecom, with the same directional trend in retail entity errors) by up to 2.5$\times$ in volume (+17.6 points per task), while creating essentially no new failures. The failure set is the same at every precision (rank correlation $\geq$ 0.94, 0.18% novel events). The score stays flat because the benchmark's ten-error budget absorbs the extra failures. Shrinking the budget to two errors re-exposes a score gap of 17 points, and it does so only in the one cell where quantization added error volume, exactly as the masking account predicts. A targeted error-repair prompt, run for five telecom models at every precision, removes the damage exactly and only where it lives. Both diagnostics, the per-channel error rate and success under a shrinking budget, come from logs benchmarks already collect; we suggest reporting them alongside task reward.

</details>


### [260] [Policy Gradient Steering: Interventions from Behavioral Objectives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27574)
*Yoann Poupart,Aurélie Beynier,Nicolas Maudet*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Policy Gradient Steering (PGS) formulates behavioral steering of models as a reinforcement learning problem, accumulating gradients over rollouts to construct removable task vectors. The method outperforms existing steering approaches in gridworld, chess, and football environments, enabling temporary, composable, and transferable behavioral adaptations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing activation steering methods for large language models fail to steer even simple policies in a two-route gridworld, revealing a fundamental limitation. There is a need for a more principled, reinforcement learning-based approach to dynamically alter model behavior at inference time with properties of composability and reversibility.

Method: Policy Gradient Steering (PGS) treats steering as a reinforcement learning problem. It accumulates policy gradients of a temporary behavioral objective over a small set of rollouts or demonstrations, constructing a removable task vector that can be added to the model's activations at inference time to alter behavior.

Result: In a two-route gridworld, PGS demonstrates calibration and reversibility. In chess puzzles, independently fitted PGS vectors for compatible tactical objectives accumulate constructively when combined. In competitive football, PGS alters specific team behaviors, and these effects transfer across different opponents.

Conclusion: Policy gradients provide a natural and effective interface for constructing temporary, composable behavioral adaptations across diverse decision-making domains, overcoming the limitations of existing activation steering methods.

Abstract: Activation steering has emerged in large language models as a lightweight alternative for dynamically changing a model's behavior at inference time. However, we show that existing steering methods fail to steer even a simple policy in a two-route gridworld environment. To address this limitation, we propose Policy Gradient Steering (PGS), which formulates steering as a reinforcement learning problem. PGS accumulates gradients of a temporary behavioral objective over a small set of rollouts or demonstrations to construct a removable task vector. We first demonstrate the calibration and reversibility of PGS in a two-route gridworld environment. Using chess puzzles, we then evaluate independently fitted PGS vectors both in isolation and in combination, finding that compatible tactical objectives accumulate constructively. Finally, in competitive football, we show that PGS can alter specific team behaviors and that its effects transfer across opponents. Together, these results show that policy gradients provide a natural interface for constructing temporary and composable behavioral adaptations across diverse decision-making domains.

</details>


### [261] [The Kinetics of Training: A Driven-Nucleation Rate Law for Emergence, Plasticity Loss, and Circuit Control in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27281)
*Lei Dong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Language model capabilities emerge only when all parts of a circuit align simultaneously in a single stochastic attempt — partial credit is worthless. This "joint alignment" bottleneck governs capability formation. The authors derive a rate equation, validate it forward (predicting ignition timing) and backward (predicting loss of learnability), locate the damage in attention heads committing to base data, and cure it by re-initializing query-key slices. They demonstrate that SGD noise fails the fluctuation-dissipation test and propose an annealing-based fix.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand why capabilities in language models appear suddenly rather than gradually, and to characterize the mechanistic bottleneck — joint alignment of circuit components — that governs this phase transition. The goal is to predict, diagnose, and control capability emergence.

Method: The authors analyze transformer language models (Pythia, up to 1.4B parameters) through: (1) ablation experiments measuring partial credit by removing individual circuit heads and measuring residual capability; (2) a rate equation framework parameterized by sites, attempts, drive, and an exponential barrier term; (3) forward prediction of capability ignition timing from precursor signals; (4) backward experiments where withheld capabilities lose learnability past a critical deadline; (5) fine-grained intervention by re-initializing query-key vs. value slices of attention heads; and (6) a controlled gated-attention model proving the deadline mechanism, plus a fluctuation-dissipation test on SGD noise with annealing as remedy.

Result: Key empirical findings: (1) Ablating one circuit part leaves a median 17% capability (vs. 50-83% predicted by partial credit), while random non-part heads leave 100% — confirming no partial credit (p=2e-10). (2) Forward prediction: capabilities ignite once a concentration floor is crossed (10/10 above, 0/12 below); arrival time is datable to 5% median error. (3) Backward: withheld capabilities never ignite past a critical step, yet validation loss falls smoothly — standard monitors are blind. (4) Re-initializing query-key slices restores learnability (6/6); value slices do nothing (0/6). (5) SGD noise fails the fluctuation-dissipation test; installing annealing melts and pins circuits on schedule.

Conclusion: Capability emergence in transformers is governed by a joint-alignment bottleneck where all circuit parts must simultaneously succeed in one stochastic attempt. This yields a predictive rate equation and explains sudden phase transitions. The damage from deadline expiration is localized to query-key alignment in attention heads, and annealing can replace SGD noise to control the process. The framework applies to conjunction circuits in transformers up to 1.4B parameters.

Abstract: A capability appears in a language model when the last parts of its circuit align in one stochastic attempt, and getting all but one right is worth nothing. We show this no-partial-credit joint alignment is the rate-limiting step of capability formation. Two fingerprints: in a shortcut-free apparatus a five-part circuit missing three waits as long as a three-part circuit missing three (1.19-1.37), so the wait counts missing parts, not size; and on Pythia across seven capabilities and three scales, ablating one part leaves a median 17% of the capability in 32 of 32 discriminating cells, where partial credit predicts 50-83% (p = 2e-10), while a random non-part head leaves 100%.
  One rare event whose barrier grows with missing parts yields a rate equation -- sites x attempts x drive x exp(-beta*K), minus destruction -- read three ways, each preregistered with frozen constants. Forward: a capability flat at baseline ignites at a step of our choosing once the mix passes a concentration floor (10/10 above, 0/12 below), and while still flat its arrival is datable from its precursor to 5% median error on six held-out models. Backward: the delay to learn a withheld capability grows with waiting until, past a critical step, it never ignites -- yet validation loss falls smoothly throughout, so standard monitors are blind to it. We locate the damage (heads commit to the base data) and isolate the cure: re-initializing only the query-key slices restores learnability (6/6) while the value slices do nothing (0/6). We prove the mechanism in a controlled gated-attention model: occupation forces a deadline whose consequences need no mixing assumption. Completed: SGD's noise fails the fluctuation-dissipation test, so we install one and anneal, melt and pin circuits on schedule. Scope: conjunction circuits in transformers to 1.4B.

</details>


### [262] [Benchmarking the Residual: What Long-Horizon Evaluations Add Beyond Matched Short-Task Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27283)
*Chao Peng,Zhiheng Lyu,Peijie Dong,Hande Dong,Qiang Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This position paper argues that long-horizon agent failures require rigorous decomposition: benchmarks should compute a "horizon residual" — the log-ratio between predicted success (from short-stage baselines) and actual full-task success — to isolate whether failure stems from error compounding, harder individual decisions, or trajectory-induced degradation (including context rot), rather than simply noting that longer tasks cause more failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing long-horizon benchmarks observe that agent performance degrades with task length but fail to distinguish among competing explanations: ordinary error compounding across more stages, inherently harder individual decisions in longer tasks, or trajectory-induced degradation where early execution actively makes later stages harder (e.g., context rot from accumulating text). Without this decomposition, benchmark results cannot meaningfully guide research on long-horizon reasoning.

Method: The paper proposes a formal framework: define the horizon residual as the log-ratio between a baseline prediction of full-task success (built from observed success rates on short, individual stages) and the actual full-task success rate. This comparison must use identical agent configurations and pre-specify how stages, checkpoints, information access, and budgets are chosen. A residual significantly different from zero indicates the full rollout diverges from what short-stage performance would predict; targeted follow-up experiments are then required to attribute this gap to specific mechanisms (error compounding vs. degradation vs. stage difficulty).

Result: This is a position paper and does not present empirical results. The contribution is conceptual: a measurement framework and terminology for rigorously diagnosing the sources of long-horizon agent failures.

Conclusion: Claiming a "long-horizon failure" requires more than observing that success drops with task length. The horizon residual provides a principled baseline comparison; a non-zero residual warrants further attribution experiments. Only then can the field determine whether interventions should target error compounding, context rot, or other forms of trajectory-induced degradation.

Abstract: Long-horizon benchmarks often show that agents fail more as tasks become longer. This observation is useful for deployment, but it does not by itself explain why failure occurs. More stages create more opportunities for ordinary errors to compound; longer tasks may also contain harder individual decisions or become harder as conversation history, tool outputs, and environment changes accumulate. We use trajectory-induced degradation to mean this last possibility: earlier execution makes later work harder. When the harmful accumulation is specifically the text visible to the model, it is often called context rot. In this position paper, we argue that to claim a "long-horizon failure", benchmarks must compare actual full-task success against a baseline prediction built from short, individual stages. We call the log-ratio between this prediction and actual success the horizon residual. The comparison must use the same agent configuration and specify in advance how stages, checkpoints, information, and budgets will be chosen. The residual shows that the full rollout differs from the chosen baseline; targeted experiments are still needed to explain why.

</details>


### [263] [APO: Unsupervised Atomic Policy Optimization for 3D Structure Prediction of Atomic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28553)
*Shentong Mo,Yatao Bian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: APO (Atomic Policy Optimization) is a fully unsupervised alignment framework for 3D atomic structure prediction that replaces costly ground-truth supervised learning with a dual-reward mechanism: a structural self-consistency reward via eigen-decomposition and a thermodynamic stability reward. It outperforms supervised baselines on crystal and antibody prediction while improving inference efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Supervised preference learning methods like FlowDPO require ground-truth coordinate labels, which are prohibitively expensive or unavailable for novel crystal phases and de novo proteins. This creates a critical bottleneck in data-scarce regimes, motivating an unsupervised alternative that leverages intrinsic physical consistency.

Method: APO adapts group-relative policy optimization to 3D atomic environments with a dual-reward mechanism: (1) a self-consistency reward that reinforces dominant latent structural modes via eigen-decomposition of sample similarities within generated groups, and (2) a stability reward enforcing thermodynamic plausibility. The model self-corrects by identifying physically plausible configurations without ground-truth references.

Result: APO consistently outperforms fully supervised baselines on crystal and antibody structure prediction benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art match rates and structural fidelity. It also straightens probability paths, significantly improving inference efficiency.

Conclusion: Intrinsic physical consistency can serve as a superior alignment guide compared to noisy supervised coordinate matching. Unsupervised alignment via APO eliminates the data bottleneck in structural modeling, enabling robust prediction in data-scarce regimes.

Abstract: Predicting the 3D structures of atomic systems is fundamental to advancing material science and drug discovery. While flow-matching models (, FlowDPO) have recently shown promise in this domain, their performance relies heavily on alignment with ground-truth coordinates via supervised preference learning. However, obtaining experimental labels for novel crystal phases or de novo proteins is prohibitively expensive, creating a bottleneck for structural modeling in data-scarce regimes. In this work, we propose (Atomic Policy Optimization), a fully unsupervised alignment framework that eliminates the need for ground-truth reference structures. APO adapts group-relative policy optimization to 3D atomic environments, utilizing a novel dual-reward mechanism: (i) a that reinforces the policy's dominant latent structural modes through eigen-decomposition of sample similarities, and (ii) a that enforces thermodynamic stability. Our framework enables the model to ``self-correct'' by identifying physically plausible configurations within sampled groups. Extensive benchmarks on crystal and antibody structure prediction demonstrate that APO consistently outperforms fully supervised baselines, achieving a new state-of-the-art in match rates and structural fidelity. Furthermore, we show that APO effectively straightens probability paths, significantly improving inference efficiency. Our results suggest that intrinsic physical consistency can serve as a superior guide for alignment compared to noisy, supervised coordinate matching.

</details>


### [264] [TIER-MoE: Trust-Informed Expert Routing via Conditional Modality Risk for Multimodal Fusion in Biomedical Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27289)
*Yu Chang,Anzhe Cheng,Chenwei Wu,Zhuoran Wang,Jiahao Chen,Tamoghna Chattopadhyay,Sophia I. Thomopoulos,Paul M. Thompson,Liyue Shen,Paul Bogdan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TIER-MoE introduces risk-guided modality routing in a mixture-of-experts framework, estimating per-sample modality reliability via prediction loss and combining it with subspace compatibility for sparse expert assignment, outperforming state-of-the-art multimodal fusion models on biomedical datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal fusion models lack mechanisms to detect whether a modality is unreliable, redundant, or poorly matched to a specialized expert. Current sample-adaptive fusion methods assign influence weights but do not reveal the underlying reason for a modality's (un)reliability in a given sample.

Method: TIER-MoE uses out-of-fold unimodal prediction loss as a learned risk signal for each modality per sample. This risk is combined with expert-specific subspace compatibility scores to perform sparse modality-to-expert routing via a mixture-of-experts architecture. A shared, always-active pathway preserves cross-modal complementarity alongside the risk-guided routing.

Result: TIER-MoE achieves superior predictive performance and probability calibration compared to state-of-the-art methods across four biomedical multimodal datasets (Alzheimer's disease, skin-lesion malignancy, retinal classification), with consistent gains in Macro-F1 and Brier score, plus strong zero-shot generalization to an external cohort.

Conclusion: Risk-based modality routing provides a principled alternative to raw influence weighting in multimodal fusion, improving both accuracy and calibration while offering interpretable signals about per-sample modality reliability.

Abstract: The promise of multimodal fusion lies in combining complementary sources of evidence, yet more evidence does not always yield a better prediction. Recent multimodal models have advanced fusion through richer cross-modal interaction and sample-adaptive fusion. However, the influence assigned to a modality during fusion does not reveal whether that source is unreliable, redundant, or poorly matched to a specialized expert. To address this limitation, we introduce TIER-MoE, a risk-guided subspace mixture-of-experts model that defines sample-specific modality reliability as the prediction loss its unimodal predictor is expected to incur. This risk is learned from out-of-fold predictions generated by models that were not trained on the corresponding sample. TIER-MoE combines the estimated risk with expert-specific subspace compatibility for sparse modality-expert routing, while an always-active shared path preserves multimodal complementarity. We evaluate TIER-MoE on four public multimodal biomedical datasets spanning Alzheimer's disease status, skin-lesion malignancy, and retinal classification. Results demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art methods in predictive performance and probability calibration, with consistent improvements in Macro-F1 and Brier score and strong zero-shot generalization to an external cohort.

</details>


### [265] [EvoCause: LLM-Guided Evolution of Causal Graphs for Root Cause Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27290)
*Lei Zan,Keli Zhang,Shifeng Xie,Jiale Zheng,Zehao Xiao,Zhiwei Dong,Ke Zhang,Ruichu Cai,Malik Tiomoko,Lujia Pan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EvoCause leverages LLM-generated semantic edits and expert labels to iteratively refine a causal graph for alarm root cause analysis, then uses the fixed refined graph at test time for transparent RCA predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RCA methods learn a static causal graph from observational data but cannot incorporate expert diagnoses of historical incidents to improve the graph. Closing this feedback loop would allow the graph to benefit from labeled incident data.

Method: EvoCause uses expert labels to constrain which alarms must be source nodes. An LLM proposes semantically plausible edge edits (additions/deletions) to satisfy these constraints, while deterministic code enforces node identity and acyclicity. The best graph is selected based on performance on a labeled alignment set. At test time, the refined graph produces predictions directly without LLM invocation.

Result: On synthetic data, EvoCause initialized with PC algorithm outperforms PC alone: Node F1 (+11.59 pp), Case EM (+9.40 pp), Graph F1 (+4.59 pp), nSHD (−0.2379). On the newly released TeleRCA benchmark (485,681 alarm events, 194 alarm types, 5,621 resources), replacing human-readable alarm titles with anonymous identifiers reduces Node F1 by 6.12 pp and Case EM by 8.04 pp, confirming that alarm-name semantics aid graph refinement.

Conclusion: EvoCause successfully closes the loop between causal graph learning and expert feedback via LLM-driven semantic edits, yielding significant RCA performance gains. Semantic information in alarm names measurably contributes to graph refinement quality.

Abstract: Modern telecommunication, cloud, and microservice systems emit correlated alarm cascades when components fail. Root cause analysis (RCA) aims to identify the small set of alarms that initiate each cascade. A common approach learns a causal graph from observational logs and predicts all zero-in-degree alarms in each incident-induced subgraph. However, the learned graph remains fixed and cannot benefit from expert diagnoses of historical incidents. We close this loop with EvoCause. Expert labels constrain which alarms should be source nodes but do not specify the edge edits needed to satisfy those constraints. EvoCause uses a large language model (LLM) to propose semantically plausible graph edits, while deterministic code validates node identities and acyclicity and retains the best graph on a labeled alignment set. At test time, the refined graph alone produces transparent predictions without an LLM call. We also release TeleRCA, an expert-annotated benchmark from a production telecommunication network containing $485{,}681$ alarm events spanning $194$ alarm types over $5{,}621$ resources. On synthetic data, EvoCause initialized with the PC causal discovery algorithm outperforms the unrefined PC baseline, raising Node F1, Case EM, and Graph F1 by $11.59$, $9.40$, and $4.59$ percentage points, respectively, while reducing nSHD by $0.2379$. On TeleRCA, replacing human-readable alarm titles with anonymous identifiers lowers Node F1 and Case EM by $6.12$ and $8.04$ percentage points, respectively, indicating that alarm-name information contributes to graph refinement.

</details>


### [266] [FADEx: Feature Attribution and Distortion-based Explanation of Dimensionality Reduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27463)
*Lucas Greff Meneses,Evandro S. Ortigossa,Claudio Silva,Luis Gustavo Nonato*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FADEx is a novel local, per-instance feature attribution method for explaining non-linear dimensionality reduction (DR) transformations. It uses first-order Taylor expansion and Singular Value Decomposition with weighted least squares to provide DR-agnostic explanations, local feature attributions, and distortion analysis, outperforming existing methods in robustness and reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Non-linear DR techniques are opaque — it is difficult to understand how individual features influence instance positioning in the reduced space. Existing DR explanation methods suffer from limitations such as multiple attributions per feature and restricted applicability to specific DR methods, hindering their practical use.

Method: FADEx leverages local linear approximation via first-order Taylor expansion and Singular Value Decomposition. It computes local linear models using weighted least squares, eliminating the need for out-of-sample data mapping. This makes it agnostic to the specific DR method while simultaneously providing local feature attributions and distortion analysis.

Result: Through qualitative and quantitative evaluations, comparisons with existing methods, and case studies, FADEx demonstrates effectiveness and versatility. It yields robust and reliable explanations, outperforming existing approaches in several aspects.

Conclusion: FADEx addresses key limitations of prior DR explanation methods by being DR-agnostic and providing consistent, interpretable local feature attributions with distortion analysis, making it a versatile tool for understanding and analyzing DR behavior.

Abstract: Dimensionality Reduction (DR) is a fundamental tool for high-dimensional data exploration, reducing the complexity of latent spaces of machine learning models, and assisting in the explanation of complex opaque models. However, non-linear DR techniques often function as opaque transformations themselves, making it challenging to understand how individual features influence instance positioning in the reduced space. This lack of transparency complicates the analysis and interpretation of structural patterns, hindering the ability to reason about the organization of high-dimensional data based on the projected layout. In order to address this challenge, dimensionality reduction explanation methods have shown promise in improving the understanding of the observed groups and cluster structures. Unfortunately, existing DR explanation approaches tend to suffer from limitations such as multiple attributions per feature and restricted applicability to specific dimensionality reduction methods, which hinder their use. In this work, we propose FADEx, a novel local per-instance feature attribution method that leverages local linear approximation via first-order Taylor expansion and Singular Value Decomposition to provide explanations. FADEx computes the local linear models via weighted least squares, eliminating the need for out-of-sample data mapping, making it agnostic to the DR method, while simultaneously providing local feature attributions and distortion analysis. Through qualitative and quantitative evaluations, comparisons with existing methods, and case studies, we demonstrate FADEx's effectiveness and versatility in providing explanations and analytical resources for analyzing the behavior of DR methods. The results indicate FADEx yields robust and reliable explanations, outperforming existing approaches in several aspects.

</details>


### [267] [THGFM: Dual-Branch Temporal Heterogeneous Graph Fusion Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27303)
*Yixin Peng,Diego Collarana,Er Jin,Stefan Decker*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: THGFM is a web-scale temporal heterogeneous graph model that combines parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with relation-aware specialization via a dual-path architecture, and integrates relative time into attention scores via Rotary Temporal Attention, achieving consistent improvements over baselines on multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing temporal heterogeneous graph learning methods struggle to balance parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with relation-aware specialization, and they typically treat time as additive features outside the attention kernel rather than incorporating it directly into the attention mechanism.

Method: THGFM employs a dual-path architecture: (1) a Shared-Space Temporal Attention branch for cross-type transfer, (2) a Relational Type-Partitioned Temporal Attention branch for relation-aware specialization. These are fused via Type-Conditioned Non-Competitive Gated Sum Fusion, which applies independent feature-wise gates per type without zero-sum competition. Additionally, Rotary Temporal Attention incorporates relative time by rotating query and key embeddings by half-phases of relative time before computing attention scores.

Result: THGFM achieves a +3.25% mean gain across six tasks. Key gains include +12.37% on OAG-CS PV, +4.87% on PF-L2, +1.18% on PF-L1, and +4.24%, +3.73%, +4.61% on OGBN-MAG, HTAG-ArXiv, and HTAG-DBLP respectively.

Conclusion: The dual-path fusion design with non-competitive gating and Rotary Temporal Attention effectively addresses the core challenges of temporal heterogeneous graph learning, enabling strong performance across diverse academic graph benchmarks at web scale.

Abstract: Temporal heterogeneous graphs offer a natural abstraction for dynamic relational systems in which diverse node and relation types co-exist and evolve over time. Learning on such graphs requires jointly modeling cross-type structural heterogeneity and the temporal dynamics of interactions, yet existing methods still struggle to reconcile parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with relation-aware specialization, and typically inject time only as additive features outside the attention kernel. We propose \textbf{THGFM}, a web-scale temporal heterogeneous graph fusion model that addresses both limitations within a unified dual-path architecture. THGFM couples a \textit{Shared-Space Temporal Attention} branch for parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with a \textit{Relational Type-Partitioned Temporal Attention} branch for relation-aware specialization, and integrates them through \textit{Dual-Path Relational--Shared Fusion}, instantiated with \textit{Type-Conditioned Non-Competitive Gated Sum Fusion}: a adaptive mechanism that assigns independent, type-conditioned feature-wise gates to the shared and specialized branches, allowing both to be amplified or suppressed without zero-sum competition. To directly incorporate relative time into the attention score, THGFM further introduces \textit{Rotary Temporal Attention}, which rotates queries and keys by half-phases of relative time before matching. THGFM consistently outperforms baseline graph transformer models on academic graphs benchmarks, delivering a $+3.25\%$ six-task mean gain, with peak relative gains of $+12.37\%$ on OAG-CS PV, $+4.87\%$ on PF-$L_2$, and $+1.18\%$ on PF-$L_1$, and $+4.24\%$, $+3.73\%$, and $+4.61\%$ on OGBN-MAG, HTAG-ArXiv, and HTAG-DBLP, respectively.

</details>


### [268] [A Montage-Agnostic Encoder for Calibration-Light Cross-User Gesture Recognition from Surface Electromyography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27565)
*Jethro Odeyemi,W. J. Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A montage-agnostic encoder for sEMG pattern recognition uses shared-weight electrodes indexed by physical coordinates, enabling cross-user training. It outperforms per-user Hudgins+LDA baselines on two databases (DB1, DB2) but not on DB5. Performance gains are robust to training pool size above nine subjects; the baseline's signal fidelity, not subject count, drives cross-database comparison trends. Self-supervised pretraining offered no benefit over adequately supervised models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pattern-recognition myoelectric control remains confined to the lab because gesture recognizers fail to transfer across users, requiring costly per-user labelled calibration. The authors aim to enable cross-user generalization by eliminating montage-specific parameters.

Method: A montage-agnostic encoder reads each electrode with shared weights and identifies it by its physical (x,y) coordinate rather than its channel index. This allows one architecture to ingest arbitrary channel counts without montage-specific parameters. The encoder is trained across multiple users. Three key architectural components were isolated in a budget-matched ablation. A subject-count sweep (9–39 training subjects) measured scaling behavior. Self-supervised pretraining was also evaluated against supervised training.

Result: The encoder exceeds a per-user Hudgins+LDA baseline by +0.234 macro-F1 on DB1 (all held-out subjects) and +0.108 on DB2, but falls below on DB5. Each of the three key components accounts for over half of 3-shot macro-F1. The cross-user margin is nearly flat from 9 to 39 training subjects. Cross-database performance trends are driven by per-user baseline strength (signal fidelity), not subject count. Self-supervised pretraining yielded no benefit once supervised training was adequate.

Conclusion: Cross-user sEMG pattern recognition is viable with a coordinate-based, montage-agnostic encoder. Performance relative to an LDA baseline depends on the baseline's signal fidelity and training budget, not merely the number of training subjects. Self-supervised pretraining adds no value when supervised data suffice.

Abstract: Pattern-recognition control promises a myoelectric prosthesis that responds to many intended gestures rather than one or two, but the promise has stayed in the laboratory. A recogniser trained on one person rarely transfers to the next, and useful performance usually demands a fresh round of labelled calibration from the end user. A montage-agnostic encoder is introduced that reads each electrode with shared weights and locates it by its physical coordinate rather than its index, so one architecture ingests any channel count without montage-specific parameters. Trained across users, it exceeds a per-user Hudgins and linear-discriminant classifier by 0.234 macro-F1 on DB1 for every held-out subject and by 0.108 on DB2, and falls below it on the ten-subject DB5. Each of the encoder's three key components individually accounts for more than half of its 3-shot macro F1 in an otherwise budget-matched ablation study. A controlled subject-count sweep shows the margin is close to flat from nine training subjects to thirty-nine, so the training pool binds only as a stability floor below which cross-user training fails to converge; what tracks the direction of the comparison across the three databases is instead the strength of the per-user baseline, which signal fidelity sets. Comparing against an LDA baseline depends on budget spent training models and on how good that baseline is, and self-supervised pretraining had no benefits once a supervised model was adequately trained.

</details>


### [269] [Position, Not Provenance: Separating Reasoning Mediation from Sycophancy in Medical Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27304)
*Supratik Bhowal,Subhrajyoti Basu,Aritra Gir Mahanta,Anik Pal Chowdhury*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CoT-Mediate is a behavioral framework for testing whether medical VLMs causally rely on their own chain-of-thought reasoning. It uses controlled perturbation of clinical attributes in generated reasoning and finds that prefix-forced continuation yields higher mediation faithfulness than re-prompting, and that contextual position—not stated provenance—primarily determines reasoning use.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing medical VLMs generate CoT reasoning before answering clinical questions, but it is unclear whether this reasoning actually causally drives predictions or is merely epiphenomenal. Prior work lacks rigorous causal mediation analysis tailored to the clinical domain.

Method: The authors propose CoT-Mediate, which perturbs a single clinically meaningful attribute within a model's own generated reasoning and measures whether predictions follow the edit. It uses a dual-arm protocol: (1) re-prompted evidence vs. prefix-forced continuation, and (2) a provenance-controlled intervention that varies only the attributed source of identical reasoning to separate mediation from sycophancy. Evaluated on LLaVA-Med and MedGemma using 1,000 VQA-RAD samples each.

Result: Prefix-forced continuation consistently yields higher mediation faithfulness than re-prompting. Removing visual evidence increases reliance on injected reasoning. Laterality is the least faithfully tracked clinical attribute across both models. Provenance analysis reveals distinct model-specific deference behaviors, and contextual position is the primary determinant of reasoning use rather than stated provenance.

Conclusion: The mechanism for injecting reasoning substantially affects measured faithfulness. Medical VLMs rely on contextual position rather than stated provenance when using generated reasoning. The framework provides a principled method for auditing causal reasoning fidelity in clinical VLMs.

Abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) generate chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning before answering clinical questions, but whether this reasoning causally influences predictions remains unclear. We present CoT-Mediate, a behavioral framework that perturbs a single clinically meaningful attribute within a model's own generated reasoning and measures whether the resulting prediction follows the edited reasoning. Our framework combines a dual-arm protocol comparing re-prompted evidence with prefix-forced continuation, together with a provenance-controlled intervention that varies only the attributed source of identical reasoning to disentangle reasoning mediation from sycophancy. We evaluate LLaVA-Med and MedGemma on 1,000 VQA-RAD samples each. Prefix-forced continuation consistently yields higher mediation faithfulness than re-prompting, while the provenance analysis reveals distinct model-specific deference behaviors. Across both models, removing visual evidence increases reliance on injected reasoning, whereas laterality is the least faithfully tracked clinical attribute. These results show that the mechanism used to inject reasoning substantially affects measured faithfulness and that contextual position, rather than stated provenance, is the primary determinant of whether medical VLMs use their generated reasoning.

</details>


### [270] [Recognition and Label-Free Adaptation Across Recording Sessions in Surface-EMG Gesture Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27568)
*Jethro Odeyemi,W. J. Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A montage-agnostic encoder trained on data from one recording session is applied unchanged to a different session, outperforming per-user LDA and published source-only methods on NinaPro DB6, with feature-statistic alignment providing effective test-time adaptation while batch-normalisation re-estimation fails.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Day-to-day variability in electrode placement, skin condition, and limb position causes recognition accuracy to degrade across recording sessions in myoelectric control systems. Requiring 20-minute recalibration after every doff/don event is impractical for daily use. A solution that transfers across sessions without recalibration is needed.

Method: A montage-agnostic encoder is trained for cross-user, cross-montage transfer using data from one recording session (source) and applied unchanged to a different recording session (target) on 10 intact subjects from NinaPro DB6. Performance is compared against: (1) a per-user LDA classification pipeline, (2) two published source-only approaches. Five label-free test-time adaptation methods are evaluated, including feature-statistic alignment and batch-normalisation re-estimation.

Result: The encoder achieves 0.688 macro-F1 across sessions versus 0.540 for the per-user LDA pipeline. On the per-window metric, it surpasses both published source-only baselines. Of five adaptation methods, only feature-statistic alignment improves every subject; batch-normalisation re-estimation causes the architecture to collapse entirely. Aligning feature statistics to the new session recovers performance approximately equivalent to a single labelled calibration repetition.

Conclusion: A montage-agnostic encoder can effectively transfer across recording sessions without recalibration, significantly outperforming conventional pipelines. Feature-statistic alignment is a simple and effective test-time adaptation strategy, while standard domain-adaptation techniques like batch-norm re-estimation can be detrimental for this architecture.

Abstract: Recognition accuracy obtained during a recording session does not persist when a user puts on the electrodes again after the electrodes had previously been removed. The electrodes may have moved slightly, the skin may be drier or wetter, or the elbow may be positioned differently; these factors all contribute to day-to-day variability and therefore represent a major obstacle to implementing successful pattern-recognition based myoelectric control systems in daily practice. However, simply recalibrating a user's hand for 20 min at every doff/don event is a clearly unrealistic expectation. A montage-agnostic encoder built for cross-user, cross-montage transfer is trained here using data collected during a particular recording session, and then applied to data collected later in a different recording session without adjusting anything, on the ten intact subjects of NinaPro DB6. The performance of this approach is compared to that of a per-user LDA classification pipeline, and to that of two published approaches that only rely on source data collected from the same recording session. Carried unchanged across recording sessions, the encoder retains 0.688 macro-F1 against 0.540 for the per-user pipeline, and, on the per-window metric the published baselines use, sits above both published source-only results, a band of two points that locates the encoder rather than ranking it. Of five label-free test-time adaptations, only feature-statistic alignment improves every subject; batch-normalisation re-estimation, a standard method in the domain-adaptation literature, collapses this architecture entirely. Aligning the encoder's feature statistics to the new session recovers about what a single labelled calibration repetition would.

</details>


### [271] [ROCS: Request-Oriented Compute Sharing for Efficient Large-Scale Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27744)
*Yuxin Chen,Liang Luo,Buyun Zhang,Jian Jiao,Boda Li,Haoyu Wang,Tongyi Tang,Ao Cai,Zijian Shen,Zhengkai Zhang,Wenyi Xie,Ryan Dick,Han Liu,Neng Shi,Bin Yu,Jianbo Xiao,Shuyao Bi,Hongtao Yu,Yuanwei Fang,Zhuoran Zhao,Sijia Chen,Yang Chen,Shuqi Yang,Qianru Li,Zikun Liu,Wei Ling,Sihan Zeng,Longhao Jin,Jiaxin Lu,Yinbin Ma,Jiawei Li,Yichen Ruan,Yong Ler Lee,Birmingham Guan,Zijian Li,Jianbo Sun,Zhengyu Zhang,Zeliang Chen,Xiaohan Wei,Yuchen Hao,GP Musumeci,Venkatesh Ranganathan,Yantao Yao,Chunqiang Tang,Wenlin Chen,Santanu Kolay,Ellie Dingqiao Wen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ROCS proposes a recommendation inference paradigm that shares request-side computation across candidates, deferring request-candidate interactions to improve efficiency. It introduces GLM for feature-interaction architectures and DCA for sequence architectures, plus IKBO for GPU optimization, achieving up to 3x QPS gains without quality loss in production systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern recommendation models scale feature-interaction and sequence modules for better prediction quality, but production cost constraints limit scaling. The key insight: each user request evaluates many candidates, and request-side features are shared across those candidates — an inefficiency that traditional per-candidate evaluation fails to exploit.

Method: ROCS (Request-Oriented Compute Sharing) defers request-candidate interactions, isolates candidate-dependent representations, and evaluates shared portions once per request. It introduces two architectural components: (1) Generalized Layer Masking (GLM) to enforce candidate isolation in feature-interaction architectures, and (2) Deep Cross Attention (DCA) to extend request-oriented sharing to sequence architectures. For deployment, In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) co-designs GPU execution to accelerate ROCS models.

Result: On public benchmarks, ROCS consistently improves the quality-efficiency tradeoff across backbones. In production: up to 3x QPS improvement on retrieval models without quality degradation; 0.5% relative LogLoss improvement with 50% QPS gain on a short-form video ranking model. Deployed across large-scale systems spanning ads/organic surfaces, retrieval/ranking stages, and over two orders of magnitude in inference complexity.

Conclusion: ROCS demonstrates that restructuring recommendation inference to share request-side computation across candidates yields substantial efficiency gains without sacrificing — and sometimes improving — prediction quality. The approach is production-validated at scale across diverse recommendation workloads.

Abstract: Modern recommendation models gain prediction quality by scaling feature-interaction and sequence modules, but production cost constraints cap how far systems can scale.
  In this work, we propose Request-Oriented Compute Sharing (ROCS), a modeling and inference paradigm that exploits a unique property of recommendation inference: each user request is evaluated against many candidates, while request-side features are shared across candidates. ROCS defers request-candidate interactions as late as possible, isolates candidate-dependent representations, and evaluates substantial portions of the model once per request rather than once per candidate, significantly improving inference efficiency while maintaining or improving prediction quality. To realize this paradigm, we develop Generalized Layer Masking (GLM) to enforce candidate isolation in feature-interaction architectures, and Deep Cross Attention (DCA) to extend request-oriented sharing to sequence architectures. To support efficient GPU deployment, we co-design In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) that significantly accelerates ROCS model execution.
  Experiments on public benchmarks show that ROCS consistently improves the quality-efficiency tradeoff across recommendation backbones. On production-scale workloads, ROCS achieves up to a 3x QPS improvement on retrieval models without quality degradation and a 0.5% relative LogLoss improvement with a 50% QPS gain on a short-form video ranking model. ROCS has been deployed across large-scale recommendation systems spanning ads and organic surfaces, retrieval and ranking stages, and more than two orders of magnitude in inference complexity, delivering significant online gains at reduced infrastructure cost.

</details>


### [272] [ZUNA1.1: A more flexible EEG foundation model for Denoising and Super-resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27308)
*Christopher Warner,Jonas Mago,JR Huml,Beren Millidge*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ZUNA1.1 is a 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder that flexibly reconstructs variable-length EEG signals (up to 30s) with arbitrary channels and scalp locations, outperforming standard methods like spherical spline interpolation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing EEG reconstruction methods like spherical spline interpolation (as in MNE) are limited in flexibility. The authors sought to improve upon their prior ZUNA1 model by creating a more flexible architecture capable of handling variable-length sequences, arbitrary channel configurations, and partial temporal reconstruction.

Method: ZUNA1.1 employs a 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder architecture. It supports reconstruction of variable-length EEG sequences up to 30 seconds, with an arbitrary number of channels at arbitrary scalp locations, and can reconstruct arbitrary temporal intervals within channels as well as entire channels.

Result: ZUNA1.1 performs at least on par with the earlier ZUNA1 model while being significantly more flexible. It substantially outperforms standard EEG denoising and reconstruction methods, particularly spherical spline interpolation from the MNE package.

Conclusion: ZUNA1.1 advances EEG signal reconstruction by combining strong performance with unprecedented flexibility in handling variable channel counts, scalp locations, sequence lengths, and partial temporal reconstruction. The model is released open-source under Apache 2.0.

Abstract: We introduce ZUNA1.1, a 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder for flexible EEG signal reconstruction. ZUNA1.1 is capable of reconstructing variable length sequences of up to 30s, with an arbitrary number of EEG channels at arbitrary scalp locations, and can reconstruct arbitrary temporal intervals within channels in addition to reconstructing entire channels. We demonstrate that ZUNA1.1 performs at least on par with our earlier ZUNA1 model, while being far more flexible and capable of handling a wide range of reconstruction tasks. ZUNA1.1 continues to substantially outperform standard EEG denoising and reconstruction methods such as spherical spline interpolation, which is ubiquitously deployed in the MNE package. The ZUNA1.1 model is released open source under the permissive Apache 2.0 license.

</details>


### [273] [Modeling Decisions in Blockchain Analytics: A Leakage-Aware Evaluation of Tree-Based vs. Sequential Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27350)
*Michał Bartnicki,Jarosław A. Chudziak*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper examines Sybil bot detection on Ethereum, finding that when label leakage from high-signal smart contracts is eliminated via a Blind-Spot protocol, tree-based models (XGBoost) outperform Transformer/BiLSTM sequence models in accuracy, latency, and energy efficiency. The authors introduce a Transaction Grammar representation capturing rhythm, EVM execution structure, and intent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current Sybil detection methods increasingly rely on deep learning over blockchain transaction sequences, but two problems exist: (1) complex sequence models are computationally expensive for real-time monitoring, and (2) reported performance may be inflated by label leakage from high-signal smart contracts. The authors aim to rigorously test whether sequence models genuinely outperform simpler alternatives once leakage is controlled, and whether resulting models are practical for low-latency deployment.

Method: The authors propose a leakage-aware evaluation framework consisting of: (1) a Blind-Spot protocol that removes shortcuts tied to high-signal smart contracts to prevent label leakage, and (2) a Transaction Grammar representation that encodes wallet behavior across three dimensions — rhythm (temporal patterns), EVM execution structure (call traces), and intent (semantic purpose). They then compare Transformer and BiLSTM sequence models against XGBoost and SVM baselines for Ethereum actor classification under leakage-controlled conditions.

Result: Under leakage-aware evaluation, XGBoost outperforms Transformer-based sequence models in classification performance while simultaneously offering lower inference latency and reduced estimated energy consumption. This challenges the prevailing narrative that sequential deep learning is necessary for blockchain actor classification.

Conclusion: Structural complexity differences among organic users, Sybil bots, and MEV bots can be effectively captured by tree-based tabular models when leakage is mitigated, without requiring expensive sequence models. The Transaction Grammar representation and Blind-Spot protocol together enable practical, low-latency, and energy-efficient Sybil detection suitable for real-time deployment.

Abstract: Sybil bots are Ethereum actors that imitate legitimate users to extract airdrop rewards or influence governance. Recent Sybil detection methods increasingly use deep learning and treat blockchain activity as a quasi-linguistic sequence. However, complex sequence models are computationally expensive for real-time monitoring, and their reported performance may be inflated by label leakage from high-signal smart contracts. We ask whether and how organic users, Sybil bots, and MEV bots differ in the structural complexity of their transaction histories; whether sequential models outperform tree-based tabular models once leakage is reduced; whether transaction order or timing provides the stronger behavioral signal; and whether the resulting models are practical for low-latency deployment. Our approach to leakage-aware Sybil bot detection consists of a Blind-Spot protocol and a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior. The former eliminates shortcuts associated with high-signal contracts, whereas the latter models wallets using rhythm, EVM execution structure, and intent. We evaluate this approach on Ethereum actor classification by comparing Transformer and BiLSTM sequence models against XGBoost and SVM baselines. We contribute a framework for leakage-aware Ethereum actor classification and a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior. Our results demonstrate that, under leakage-aware evaluation, XGBoost outperforms Transformer-based sequence models while providing lower latency and estimated energy use.

</details>


### [274] [Compression-Based Behavioral Similarity for Open-World Sybil Discovery on Ethereum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27370)
*Michał Bartnicki,Jarosław A. Chudziak*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A training-free, compression-based behavioral graph framework for discovering Sybil actors on Ethereum, using symbolic transaction grammars and gzip-based Normalized Compression Distance to detect bots without requiring direct token transfer links.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Sybil detection methods rely on token transfer graphs (missing actors without direct financial links) or closed-set ML classifiers (vulnerable to adversarial evasion and temporal drift). The authors aim to determine whether compression-based similarity can differentiate Sybil bots, organic users, and arbitrage bot wallets without direct financial links, and how robust behavioral graphs are under temporal drift and adversarial perturbations.

Method: A symbolic Transaction Grammar is synthesized from EVM traces, capturing transaction rhythm, execution structure, and functional intent as three separate modalities. High-signal contracts are filtered using a novel Blind-Spot Protocol. Gzip-based Normalized Compression Distance (NCD) constructs a behavioral similarity graph for Sybil discovery. Validation is performed against supervised ML baselines, a temporal split, and synthetic camouflage stress tests.

Result: The NCD-based behavioral graph can expand suspicious seed wallets to discover Sybil candidates without explicit funding links. The method demonstrates robustness under temporal drift and adversarial camouflage stress tests, outperforming or matching supervised baselines in open-world settings while requiring no training.

Conclusion: The framework offers a leakage-aware, training-free local discovery primitive suitable for open-world blockchain audits. It is positioned as a practical tool for Sybil candidate discovery rather than a formal open-set recognition system, emphasizing deployability and robustness over closed-set classification accuracy.

Abstract: Sybil attackers are Blockchain actors that adopt the characteristics of regular users to exploit airdrops or influence governance. Current methods of Sybil actor detection include constructing graphs, which requires token transfers between examined wallets. Machine learning algorithms have been employed as well, but they treat the task as a closed-set classification problem, making them vulnerable to frequent changes in attack strategies or evasion tactics. We address the following questions: can compression-based similarity differentiate Sybil bots, organic users, and arbitrage bot wallets without direct financial links? What is the effect of high-signal contracts on the discovery of Sybils, and how robust are behavioral graphs under temporal drift and adversarial perturbations? Our approach synthesizes a symbolic Transaction Grammar from EVM (Ethereum Virtual Machine) traces, capturing separately transaction rhythm, execution structure, and functional intent. The high-signal contracts are filtered with our own protocol, called the Blind-Spot Protocol. Gzip-based NCD is used to construct a behavioral graph for Sybil discovery. We validate this framework against supervised machine learning baselines, a temporal split, and synthetic camouflage stress tests. Ultimately, we contribute a leakage-aware behavioral framework for Sybil candidate discovery. Its core NCD primitive requires no supervised training and can expand suspicious seed wallets without explicit funding links. We position the method as a training-free local discovery primitive for open-world blockchain audits, rather than as a formal open-set recognition system.

</details>


### [275] [Explorative Modeling: Unlocking a Third Pretraining Axis and End-to-End Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27372)
*Alexi Gladstone,Heng Ji,Yilun Du*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces Explorative Modeling (XM), a paradigm that factors the training loop by exploring multiple candidate matches between generated and real data, training on the best match. This exploration axis scales monotonically with model and data size, yields dramatic efficiency gains (up to 6.2x sample efficiency), achieves near-SOTA FID on ImageNet, and enables end-to-end reconstructive generative modeling competitive with diffusion at 16-256x fewer inference steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the success of end-to-end training in deep learning, generative modeling remains an exception — existing scalable approaches factor the generation procedure to handle multi-modal distributions, which prevents true end-to-end generation. The authors aim to overcome this limitation by shifting factorization from the generation procedure to the training loop.

Method: Explorative Modeling (XM) factors the training loop instead of the generation process: during training, the model explores K candidate matches between generated outputs and data samples, then trains only on the best match. This forces predictions to commit to specific modes rather than averaging across them. The approach applies across continuous (images, video) and discrete (language) domains, and can be used both as a pretraining axis atop existing generative models and as a standalone end-to-end generative paradigm.

Result: Scaling exploration yields monotonic performance improvements: gains increase from 7% to 36% as data scales, and 13% to 23% as models grow. FLOP efficiency improves by 4.1x, sample efficiency by 6.2x, and parameter efficiency by 47%. Achieves 1.43 FID on ImageNet without guidance (near-SOTA). In reconstructive generative modeling, matches diffusion performance with 16-256x fewer inference steps.

Conclusion: Explorative Models establish a new pretraining axis (beyond parameters and data) for generative models and simultaneously function as a standalone end-to-end generative modeling paradigm, unlocking scaling generalization and enabling more end-to-end training of generative systems.

Abstract: The deep learning revolution, kicked off by AlexNet, taught us that end-to-end training beats decomposing a problem into hand-designed stages. Generative modeling, however, has remained the exception-despite generative models being remarkably capable, they are still not trained end-to-end. This is because, at its core, generative modeling is about handling distributions with many modes, and existing scalable approaches handle this the same way, by factoring the generation procedure, which prevents end-to-end generation. In this work, we introduce Explorative Modeling, a new paradigm that instead factors the training loop, exploring K candidate matches between model generations and data, and training on the best, so predictions commit to modes rather than blurring them. We find Explorative Models (XMs) useful in two settings. First, increasing exploration adds a third pretraining axis beyond parameters and data for existing generative models-where scaling exploration monotonically improves performance across both continuous and discrete domains (images, video, and language). Notably, gains from exploration increase with scale, climbing from 7% to 36% as data scales and from 13% to 23% as models grow, with efficiency gains more than doubling at 3x the compute. Concretely, exploration improves FLOP efficiency by 4.1x, sample efficiency by 6.2x, parameter efficiency by 47%, lifts the strongest of image-generation recipes to a near-state-of-the-art 1.43 FID on ImageNet without guidance, enables scaling how end-to-end existing models are, and unlocks scaling generalization. Second, XMs enable end-to-end reconstructive generative modeling, matching diffusion on control tasks with 16-256x fewer inference steps. Together, these results establish XMs as both a new pretraining axis for existing generative models and a standalone end-to-end generative modeling paradigm.

</details>


### [276] [The Convergence Behavior of Adam under Heavy-Tailed Noise](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27383)
*Yijiang Pang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: First convergence guarantees for plain Adam under heavy-tailed noise (bounded p-th moment, p∈(1,2]), derived via a generalized online-to-nonconvex conversion framework with discounted regret analysis. Adam converges to (ρ,ε)-stationary points but with suboptimal iteration complexity; optimal rates are recovered when domain radius is known.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While Adam variants have been studied under bounded-variance noise, real-world deep learning often exhibits heavy-tailed stochastic gradients with only a bounded p-th central moment (p∈(1,2]). Convergence behavior of plain vector-form Adam in this regime remains uncharacterized, creating a theoretical gap that this paper aims to fill.

Method: The authors generalize the online-to-nonconvex conversion framework to handle heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise, then develop a discounted regret analysis for Adam without restrictive parameter coupling. They analyze convergence under both unknown and known domain radius settings.

Result: Adam provably converges to (ρ,ε)-stationary points under heavy-tailed noise. However, it exhibits suboptimal iteration complexity with p-dependent convergence, a suboptimality persisting even for p=2. When the domain radius is known (standard in related work), the rate improves to match optimal complexity.

Conclusion: The paper provides the first theoretical characterization of Adam's robustness and limitations under heavy-tailed noise, revealing that plain Adam is inherently suboptimal without additional structural knowledge like domain radius, while also showing that optimality can be restored under standard assumptions.

Abstract: We establish the first convergence guarantees for the plain vector-form \emph{Adam} optimizer under heavy-tailed stochastic noise. While several Adam variants are known to achieve optimal iteration complexity in bounded-variance nonconvex optimization, little is understood about their behavior when stochastic gradients admit only a bounded $p$-th central moment for some $p \in (1,2]$, a setting increasingly observed in modern deep learning. To address this gap, we generalize the recent online-to-nonconvex conversion framework to accommodate heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise. Building on this generalized framework, we develop a discounted regret analysis for Adam, without restrictive parameter coupling. Our results show that Adam converges to $(ρ,ε)$-stationary points under heavy-tailed noise. However, it exhibits a suboptimal iteration complexity and $p$-dependent convergence, a suboptimality that persists even in the bounded-variance case ($p=2$). When the domain radius is known and used to control the online-learner output, a standard setup in related literature, the convergence rate improves to match the optimal complexity. These findings provide new theoretical insight into the robustness and limitations of Adam in heavy-tailed regimes.

</details>


### [277] [FunL2O: LLM-Guided Feature Function Design for Learning to Optimize](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27389)
*Bingheng Li,Junyang Cai,Yupeng Zhang,Bistra Dilkina,Jayant Kalagnanam,Dzung T. Phan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FunL2O automates feature engineering for learning-to-optimize pipelines via LLM-driven program evolution in a FunSearch-style loop, consistently outperforming hand-crafted features across continuous and discrete optimization tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Feature design in L2O pipelines is currently manual, domain-specific, and largely overlooked as a bottleneck. Automating this process could unlock better performance and broader applicability.

Method: FunL2O employs a FunSearch-style evolutionary loop where an LLM proposes executable feature functions; each candidate is evaluated by retraining the target L2O model and measuring downstream optimization performance. The framework is evaluated on linear/quadratic programming (solution prediction, warm-starting) and mixed-integer optimization (GNN-guided backdoor branching, Predict-and-Search) using four different LLMs.

Result: Evolved features consistently outperform hand-crafted representations across all tasks, domains (continuous and discrete), and all four LLMs tested.

Conclusion: LLM-driven feature evolution is established as a general, effective approach to automating representation design in L2O, moving the field beyond manual feature engineering.

Abstract: Learning-to-optimize (L2O) methods accelerate repeated optimization by training models to predict solutions, warm starts, branching decisions, or other forms of solver guidance. A critical yet largely overlooked component of these pipelines is the feature function that maps problem instances to inputs for machine learning models. Existing L2O methods typically rely on hand-crafted features, making representation design manual and largely fixed across domains. We introduce FunL2O, the first unified framework for automating feature design through LLM-driven program evolution for L2O. In a FunSearch-style loop, an LLM proposes executable feature functions, while a fixed evaluation process retrains the original L2O model and measures downstream optimization performance. We evaluate FunL2O on linear and quadratic programming tasks involving solution prediction and warm-starting, as well as on mixed-integer optimization tasks using GNN-guided backdoor branching and Predict-and-Search. Across continuous and discrete optimization tasks and four LLMs, the evolved features consistently outperform hand-crafted representations. These results establish LLM-driven feature evolution as a general and effective approach to automating representation design in L2O.

</details>


### [278] [ECG-InterpBench: Benchmarking the Interpretability of ECG Foundation Models with Matched-Scale Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27404)
*Yixuan Duan,Wei Qiu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ECG-InterpBench is a benchmark that systematically evaluates the interpretability of ECG foundation-model representations using sparse autoencoders, comparing six models across reconstruction fidelity, clinical feature accessibility, and cross-seed reproducibility, revealing distinct interpretability profiles not captured by performance-centered benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ECG foundation-model benchmarks focus solely on downstream predictive performance, neglecting whether internal representations are decomposable, clinically interpretable, or reproducible. This gap limits understanding of model trustworthiness, robustness, and clinical alignment.

Method: The benchmark uses sparse autoencoders as standardized, capacity-matched measurement instruments applied to six frozen ECG foundation models. Evaluations span five encoder depths, five dictionary widths, and three random seeds, yielding a 450-cell interpretability atlas with 75 matched comparison blocks. Metrics cover sparse reconstruction fidelity, single-feature accessibility of 49 clinical ECG measurements, cross-seed feature reproducibility, patient-sampling uncertainty, and parameter sensitivity. A matched replication is conducted on MIMIC-IV-ECG.

Result: ECG foundation models exhibit distinct interpretability profiles. Reconstruction fidelity and clinical accessibility identify different leading models. Depth- and seed-dependent variation, patient-sampling uncertainty, and sensitivity to sparsity parameterization are all quantified. The MIMIC-IV-ECG replication confirms the divergence between reconstruction and clinical accessibility rankings.

Conclusion: ECG-InterpBench provides a capacity-controlled, reproducible framework that complements performance-centered ECG benchmarks, enabling rigorous comparison of ECG foundation models across distinct, clinically meaningful dimensions of representation interpretability.

Abstract: Existing benchmarks for electrocardiogram foundation models primarily evaluate downstream predictive performance, providing limited insight into whether their internal representations can be faithfully decomposed, clinically interpreted, or reproduced across independent analyses. We introduce ECG-InterpBench, a benchmark designed to systematically evaluate the interpretability of ECG foundation-model representations. ECG-InterpBench uses sparse autoencoders as standardized measurement instruments and matches their capacity across models to enable controlled comparisons. We evaluate six frozen ECG foundation models across five standardized encoder depths, five matched dictionary widths, and three random seeds, producing a 450-cell interpretability atlas comprising 75 exactly matched six-model comparison blocks. The benchmark evaluates complementary dimensions of representation interpretability, including sparse reconstruction fidelity, single-feature accessibility and coverage of 49 clinically meaningful ECG measurements, and cross-seed feature reproducibility. The evaluation further quantifies patient-sampling uncertainty, depth- and seed-dependent variation, and sensitivity to the sparsity parameterization. The benchmark reveals that ECG foundation models exhibit distinct interpretability profiles. A matched replication on MIMIC-IV-ECG confirms that reconstruction fidelity and clinical accessibility identify different leading models. The benchmark is accompanied by executable evaluation code, standardized manifests, cell-level metrics, and reproducibility audits. ECG-InterpBench complements performance-centered ECG benchmarks by providing a capacity-controlled and reproducible framework for comparing ECG foundation models across distinct dimensions of representation interpretability.

</details>


### [279] [Context-Informed Ship Trajectory Prediction via Conditional Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27418)
*Yuan Guan,Chandler Squires,Timothy Hu,Pradeep Ravikumar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes Conditional Informer, a Transformer-based model that frames ship trajectory prediction as conditional generation, using cross-attention to encode the physical dependence of vessel motion on environmental factors, and introduces Modality Masking to maintain robustness when sensor data is missing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Transformer-based trajectory prediction methods treat environmental factors as peer features rather than modeling the directional physical dependence—weather modulates vessel dynamics, not vice versa. Additionally, real-world sensor intermittency causes catastrophic degradation in multimodal models that learn spurious shortcuts.

Method: The authors propose Conditional Informer, an encoder-decoder architecture with a dedicated Conditional Attention mechanism where vessel state queries environmental contexts via cross-attention. They also introduce a Modality Masking training strategy that randomly drops modalities during training to prevent shortcut learning and ensure robustness during sensor fallback.

Result: On AIS and ERA5 datasets, Conditional Informer outperforms kinematic and concatenation-based baselines by 15.4% in prediction accuracy when context is available. Modality Masking reduces fallback error by nearly an order of magnitude compared to unconstrained models.

Conclusion: Encoding the directional physical dependence between environment and vessel dynamics through conditional attention, combined with modality masking for robustness, yields significant improvements in both accuracy and reliability for long-term ship trajectory prediction.

Abstract: Long-term ship trajectory prediction is a fundamental capability for maritime safety and autonomous navigation. While recent Transformer-based architectures have improved forecasting horizons, they predominantly rely on historical kinematic states, treating vessel motion as an isolated system. In reality, maritime navigation is profoundly modulated by extrinsic factors like weather and constrained by static vessel characteristics. Existing multimodal approaches fundamentally model the joint distribution over states and contexts, treating environmental variables as peer features rather than encoding the directional physical dependence of vessel dynamics on environmental conditions.
  In this work, we propose the Conditional Informer, a novel encoder-decoder architecture that formulates trajectory prediction as a conditional generation task. We employ a dedicated Conditional Attention mechanism where the vessel state explicitly queries environmental contexts through cross-attention, encoding the physical prior that weather modulates - but is not generated by - vessel dynamics. Furthermore, to address the intermittency of real-world data, we introduce a Modality Masking training strategy to prevent catastrophic degradation during sensor fallback. Extensive experiments on AIS and ERA5 data demonstrate that our approach outperforms kinematic and concatenation-based baselines by 15.4% in prediction accuracy when context is available. Crucially, Modality Masking prevents shortcut learning, reducing fallback error by nearly an order of magnitude compared to unconstrained models.

</details>


### [280] [Good Rankers, Bad Objectives: Bilinear Contrastive Critics under Expressive Policy Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27422)
*Ayushman Singh,Siddharth Aphale*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Contrastive critics, even with cosine bounding, fail as safe value proxies for action selection due to norm drift, miscalibration, and misranking; Bellman-trained TD-Q succeeds, and the paper attributes the failure to the contrastive training objective itself.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Contrastive critics are increasingly used not just for ranking but as value-like objectives for best-of-K selection, planning, and critic-guided generation. The paper investigates whether these critics are safe to maximize, identifying fundamental failure modes that persist across architectural fixes like cosine similarity bounding.

Method: The authors decompose contrastive critic regret using a controlled support analysis, evaluate cosine-bounded and hybrid critics on off-support action selection across four OGBench navigation tasks, assess score calibration and ranking fidelity, compare against Bellman-trained TD-Q in a parameter-matched function-class control, and conduct simulator rollouts to measure realized costs. A training/readout decomposition isolates the source of ordering loss.

Result: Cosine bounding does not prevent off-support action selection; most raw bilinear regret is attributed to norm drift. Contrastive scores are weakly calibrated or inverted in the top decile and fail to order fixed-query actions by value, while TD-Q succeeds. Realized costs manifest on PointMaze and an exact-Q* toy but not on AntMaze/HumanoidMaze due to controller self-correction. Raw-trained embeddings retain weak ordering after inference-time normalization, implicating the cosine training objective as the root cause of lost ordering.

Conclusion: Contrastive critics remain useful as compatibility rankers for navigation and manipulation, but action selection requires a value-calibrated scalar. Candidate maximization over contrastive scores is unsafe due to false positives from norm drift, score saturation, and in-support misranking.

Abstract: Good action rankings do not make a contrastive critic safe to maximize. These critics increasingly act as value-like objectives for best-of-$K$ selection, planning, and critic-guided generation. Unbounded bilinear scores can let large embedding norms inflate off-support values, but cosine bounding does not remove the failure. A controlled support decomposition attributes most raw bilinear regret to norm drift. Cosine and hybrid critics nevertheless select off-support actions from most pools and incur comparable regret. Contrastive scores are weakly calibrated or inverted in the top score decile across four OGBench navigation tasks, and they fail to order fixed-query actions by value. Bellman-trained TD-Q succeeds, including in a parameter-matched function-class control. Realized costs depend on the task: simulator rollouts reveal single-step selection costs on PointMaze and the exact-$Q^*$ toy but well-powered nulls on AntMaze and HumanoidMaze, where the controller can self-correct. A training/readout decomposition traces the lost ordering to the cosine training objective; raw-trained embeddings retain weak ordering after inference-time normalization. Candidate maximization can therefore exploit false positives caused by norm drift, score saturation, or in-support misranking. Contrastive critics remain useful compatibility rankers on navigation and manipulation tasks, but action selection requires a value-calibrated scalar.

</details>


### [281] [SE(3)-MeanFlow: Few-Step Protein Backbone Generation on Lie Groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27431)
*Yikun Bai,Binghang Lu,Yikai Liu,Elaheh Akbari,Soheil Kolouri,Linxuan Wang,Ping He,Shuchan Wang,Ruqi Zhang,Guang Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SE(3)-MeanFlow extends MeanFlow to SE(3) for protein backbone generation, enabling few-step sampling via closed-form Lie algebra targets and an alpha-Flow warm-up, matching or exceeding flow-matching baselines at significantly fewer network evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing diffusion and flow-matching models for protein backbone generation on SE(3)^N require hundreds of ODE integration steps, each with costly Lie group exponential maps, creating a bottleneck for high-throughput protein design. The goal is to drastically reduce the number of sampling steps while maintaining generation quality.

Method: (1) Extend MeanFlow from Euclidean space to SE(3) by deriving closed-form average-velocity identities in the Lie algebra so(3) and R^3, enabling simulation-free training. (2) Introduce an SE(3) alpha-Flow objective that eliminates the Jacobian-vector product from the rotation branch, used as a warm-up stage. (3) After warm-up, switch to a small-t stabilized MeanFlow loss for the remainder of pretraining and rectification-based post-training to refine few-step sampling.

Result: SE(3)-MeanFlow matches or exceeds flow-matching baselines using several times more sampling steps. Its advantage widens in the few-step regime, where rectification enables it to lead at every matched sampling budget, albeit with a modest reduction in diversity.

Conclusion: SE(3)-MeanFlow provides an efficient few-step generative framework for protein backbone design by operating natively in the Lie algebra, substantially cutting the inference cost while maintaining competitive or superior structural quality compared to multi-step flow-matching methods.
