Abstract: Generative modeling of protein backbones promises the de novo design of proteins with prescribed structural and functional properties. Existing diffusion and flow-matching models produce high-quality backbones on SE(3)^N, but inference requires numerically integrating an ODE over hundreds of network evaluations, each involving a Lie group exponential map - a bottleneck for high-throughput design campaigns. We introduce SE(3)-MeanFlow, a few-step generative framework that extends MeanFlow from Euclidean space to the Lie group geometry of protein frames. Working natively in the Lie algebra so(3) and in R^3, we derive closed-form average-velocity identities for rotations and translations, giving simulation-free training targets. We further introduce an SE(3) alpha-Flow objective that removes the Jacobian-vector product from the rotation branch and serves as a warm-up stage, after which training switches to a small-t stabilized MeanFlow loss that is used for the remainder of pretraining and for rectification-based post-training. In protein backbone generation, SE(3)-MeanFlow matches or exceeds flow-matching baselines that use several times more sampling steps, and its advantage widens in the few-step regime, where rectification lets it lead at every matched budget - at a modest cost in diversity.

</details>


### [282] [Neural Network-Assisted CLEAN for Channel Modeling in Low-SNR Regimes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27450)
*Chaofan Deng,Linyu Sun,Jaeho Lee,Arijit Raychowdhury*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NN-CLEAN is a hybrid multipath parameter estimation framework that integrates a multi-head residual neural network into the iterative CLEAN algorithm, replacing exhaustive grid search with efficient neural forward passes. It achieves >96% accuracy at 5 dB SNR, matches GS-CLEAN performance, and dramatically reduces computational complexity with near-flat runtime scaling across batch sizes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional Maximum Likelihood Estimation (e.g., CLEAN) offers high-resolution multipath parameter extraction but incurs prohibitive computational cost from exhaustive grid search. Data-driven deep learning methods lack physical grounding and fail to generalize across variable multipath densities and off-grid parameters. There is a need for an approach that combines the physical fidelity of model-based methods with the computational efficiency of neural networks.

Method: NN-CLEAN embeds a multi-head residual network directly into the iterative CLEAN extraction loop. The neural network performs rapid, parallelizable forward passes to estimate multipath parameters, replacing the exhaustive grid search. Residual subtraction is handled by exact mathematical models, ensuring that non-physical errors do not accumulate across iterations.

Result: Monte Carlo simulations show NN-CLEAN achieves estimation accuracy exceeding 96% at 5 dB SNR, matching the GS-CLEAN baseline. It substantially outperforms subspace methods and standalone one-shot neural networks. Execution runtime and memory consumption exhibit near-flat scaling as batch sizes increase, demonstrating highly efficient parallelization.

Conclusion: NN-CLEAN establishes itself as a robust, real-time channel estimation solution for MIMO systems, successfully bridging model-based physical fidelity with data-driven computational efficiency. Its parallelization-friendly architecture makes it particularly suitable for practical deployment in modern wireless communication systems.

Abstract: Accurate multipath parameter estimation is critical for modern wireless communication systems, particularly in challenging low-SNR environments. Traditional Maximum Likelihood Estimation algorithms, such as CLEAN, provide high-resolution parameter extraction but suffer from prohibitive computational complexity due to exhaustive grid search. Conversely, purely data-driven deep learning approaches lack physical grounding and struggle to generalize across variable multipath densities and off-grid parameters. To address these limitations, this paper proposes Neural Network-Assisted CLEAN (NN-CLEAN), a hybrid framework that embeds a multi-head residual network directly into the iterative CLEAN extraction loop. By replacing the exhaustive grid search with rapid, parallelizable forward passes while delegating residual subtraction to exact mathematical models, NN-CLEAN isolates physical multipath parameters without accumulating non- physical errors. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that NN-CLEAN achieves estimation accuracy exceeding 96% at 5 dB SNR, matching the traditional Grid-Search CLEAN (GS- CLEAN) baseline, while providing a massive reduction in computational complexity and substantially outperforming subspace methods and standalone one-shot neural networks. Crucially, NN-CLEAN exhibits a near-flat scaling in execution runtime and memory consumption as batch sizes increase. This highly efficient parallelization establishes NN-CLEAN as a robust, real- time solution for channel estimation in MIMO systems.

</details>


### [283] [Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27479)
*Aryan Mishra,Randy Martinez,Lizhen Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring (SCGR) uses group theory — specifically a Schreier-Coset graph built from a special linear group — to augment input graphs, creating low-resistance bypasses that mitigate over-squashing in GNNs while preserving original graph properties, achieving 5–40% reduction in effective resistance without massively inflating edge counts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GNNs suffer from over-squashing due to structural bottlenecks that restrict long-range information propagation. Existing graph-rewiring methods address this but introduce major drawbacks: prohibitive structural/computational bottlenecks, failure to preserve key properties of the original graph, and massive increases in edge counts. A method is needed that alleviates over-squashing without these costs.

Method: The authors propose Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring (SCGR), which augments the original input graph with a Schreier-Coset graph derived from a special linear group. This group-theoretic construction provides theoretical guarantees: the resulting graph exhibits a spectral gap and bounded effective resistance, effectively creating a low-resistance bypass for long-range communication.

Result: Empirical evaluations show SCGR reduces effective resistance by 5–40% across various learning tasks, effectively mitigating connectivity bottlenecks while maintaining competitive accuracy.

Conclusion: SCGR is an effective, theoretically grounded graph-rewiring method that mitigates over-squashing via group-theoretic augmentation, preserving original graph properties while avoiding the structural/computational overhead of prior approaches.

Abstract: The information flow in the graph neural networks (GNNs) is fundamentally constrained by over-squashing, where structural bottlenecks impede long range information propagation. Graph-rewiring methods, which modify graph topology, have been extensively used to alleviate this. However, existing approaches often introduce prohibitive structural and computational bottlenecks, fail to preserve the critical properties of original graphs, and increase the edge counts massively. We introduce a novel method Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring , a group-theoretic rewiring method that augments the input graph with a Schreier-Coset graph derived from a special linear group. Our method provides theoretical guarantees, a graph that exhibits spectral gap and a bounded effective resistance, creating a low-resistance bypass for long-range communication. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that SCGR reduces effective resistance by 5-40% across various learning tasks, effectively mitigating connectivity bottlenecks while maintaining competitive accuracy.

</details>


### [284] [Encryption-Compatible Clustered Federated Learning via Distributed Expectation-Maximization over Metadata](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28338)
*Michael Ben Ali,Imen Megdiche,André Péninou,Olivier Teste*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FLAMECHE reformulates metadata-based Clustered Federated Learning as a distributed Expectation-Maximization procedure with additive-only server updates, enabling compatibility with secure FL encryption schemes while resolving the CFL trilemma of privacy, communication, and computation trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Clustered Federated Learning methods face a trilemma: improving any two of privacy preservation, communication cost, or computational efficiency comes at the expense of the third. Metadata-based CFL approaches are communication- and computation-efficient but incompatible with standard FL privacy-preserving mechanisms. The work aims to bridge this gap.

Method: FLAMECHE reformulates metadata-based CFL as a distributed Expectation-Maximization (EM) procedure. The key design choice is restricting server-side updates to purely additive operations, which preserves the efficiency of metadata-based clustering while making the protocol compatible with practical secure FL schemes (e.g., homomorphic encryption).

Result: Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and heterogeneous scenarios demonstrate that FLAMECHE improves client model effectiveness and enables encryption-compatible metadata-based clustering, enhancing its positioning within the CFL trilemma.

Conclusion: FLAMECHE successfully demonstrates that metadata-based CFL can be made compatible with privacy-preserving mechanisms without sacrificing communication or computational efficiency, offering a better balance across the three dimensions of the CFL trilemma compared to prior methods.

Abstract: Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) addresses data heterogeneity in federated settings by grouping clients with similar data distributions to enable effective training. Existing methods face a trade-off between privacy preservation, communication cost, and computational efficiency. We formalize this as the CFL trilemma, according to which improving two of these dimensions comes at the expense of the third. A prominent paradigm relies on metadata (i.e., low-dimensional representations of client datasets shared with the server) to enable communication- and computation-efficient clustering. However, such approaches are not compatible with standard FL privacy-preserving mechanisms. To address this limitation, we propose FLAMECHE, which reformulates metadata-based CFL as a distributed Expectation-Maximization (EM) procedure, restricting server updates to additive operations while preserving efficiency. This design enables compatibility with practical secure FL schemes. We conducted extensive experiments on multiple datasets under various heterogeneous scenarios. Results show that FLAMECHE improves the effectiveness of client models. It enables encryption-compatible metadata-based clustering, enhancing its positioning within the CFL trilemma.

</details>


### [285] [Latent States in Neural Networks: Recovering the Temporal Structure of Drifting Data from Model Weights](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27482)
*Kevin Guan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Classifiers trained on temporally drifting data streams exhibit discrete latent regimes recoverable via HMMs fit to weight trajectories. These HMM-inferred states predict cross-window generalization better than temporal proximity or equal-size partitions, capturing structure beyond mere class distribution shifts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world data streams often undergo discrete regime shifts rather than continuous drift. The authors investigate whether these latent regimes can be recovered purely from the weights of sequentially trained models, without access to the underlying data, using HMMs on weight trajectories.

Method: Classifiers are trained on consecutive temporal windows from two datasets (Fakeddit for misinformation, Yelp for sentiment). Model weights are aligned across windows and chronologically ordered. An HMM is fit to this weight trajectory to infer a discrete latent state sequence. Generalization is tested by evaluating each window's classifier on data from windows sharing vs. not sharing its HMM-inferred state. Controls include temporal proximity, equal-size contiguous partitions, and residualization of class distribution divergence and lag.

Result: Within-state transfer outperforms cross-state transfer on both datasets. This advantage survives controls for temporal proximity and modestly exceeds equal-size partitions. HMM states correlate more strongly with class distribution shifts than with weight-space geometry. After residualizing out class divergence and temporal lag, the within-state advantage remains above permutation nulls on both tasks. Effects replicate across datasets but are attenuated on Yelp, attributed to its more stable label distribution.

Conclusion: Discrete temporal regimes can be recovered from model weight trajectories via HMMs. These regimes capture transfer-relevant structure beyond simple data distribution shifts, suggesting that model weights encode meaningful temporal segmentation information. The method's effectiveness depends on the degree of temporal variation in the underlying data distribution.

Abstract: A temporally drifting data stream may pass through discrete regimes rather than changing continuously. We ask whether such regimes are recoverable from the weights of models trained on the stream, using a hidden Markov model (HMM) fit to the chronologically ordered trajectory of those weights. We study this question in two domains known to drift over time: multimodal misinformation detection, using the Fakeddit dataset; and sentiment analysis, using the Yelp dataset. We train classifiers on consecutive temporal windows and fit an HMM to the trajectory of their aligned weights, recovering latent states that partition each timeline into coherent phases. On both datasets, classifiers generalize better to data from windows sharing the state of their training window than to windows across state boundaries. This within-state transfer advantage survives a control for temporal proximity and modestly exceeds the advantage recovered by a naive partition into contiguous states of equal size. Although the states are estimated solely from model weights, they correlate more strongly with shifts in the data's class distribution than with the weight-space geometry used to estimate them. After class divergence and lag are residualized out, the within-state advantage exceeds its permutation null on both tasks, indicating that the states recover structure relevant to transfer beyond the data distribution. Every effect replicates on both tasks but is attenuated on Yelp, whose label distribution is more temporally stable.

</details>


### [286] [A Lightweight Foundation Model for Collider Physics with Multi-Domain Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27501)
*Liangyu Wu,Qibin Liu,Alexander Yue,Julia Gonski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NEXUS is a lightweight (~3M parameter) autoencoder-based foundation model pre-trained on unsupervised collider physics data that transfers effectively to downstream tasks in both collider physics and out-of-domain scientific applications (gravitational waves, flood forecasting, neural activity), while being more computationally efficient than transformer-based alternatives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Foundation models show promise but are often computationally expensive (especially transformers) and underexplored for scientific datasets beyond NLP/vision. The authors aim to demonstrate that a lightweight, unsupervised pre-training approach on domain-specific scientific data can yield transferable representations benefiting multiple scientific domains, while enabling power-efficient inference suitable for real-time/edge deployment.

Method: A fully connected autoencoder with ~3M parameters is pre-trained in a fully unsupervised manner on large-scale charged particle track features from LHC collision data. Pre-trained weights are then fine-tuned on downstream tasks (kinematic regression, event classification) using small labeled datasets. Transfer is evaluated against equivalent architectures trained from scratch. Latent space interpretation and cross-domain application (gravitational waves, flood forecasting, neural activity) further probe the generality of learned representations.

Result: The pre-trained NEXUS model achieves improved accuracy on collider physics downstream tasks compared to scratch-trained equivalents, particularly in low-labeled-data regimes. The learned latent representations prove interpretable and transferable to three distinct scientific domains. NEXUS also demonstrates superior computational simplicity versus comparably scaled transformer models, supporting power-efficient inference.

Conclusion: Lightweight autoencoder-based foundation models pre-trained on scientific data can effectively generalize across diverse scientific domains while remaining computationally efficient. NEXUS opens the door to foundation model deployment in resource-constrained, real-time, and edge scientific experimental settings.

Abstract: We present a lightweight approach to foundation modeling (\textbf{NEXUS}) that leverages pre-trained learning from collider physics data towards out-of-domain tasks in other scientific datasets, using a fully connected autoencoder model with approximately 3 million parameters. The model pre-trains with no supervision over a large-scale collision dataset from the Large Hadron Collider modeled by charged particle track features. Downstream tasks for collider analyses, such as kinematic regression and event classification, are developed on pre-trained model weights and achieve improved accuracy with only small labeled datasets when compared to equivalent architectures trained from scratch. The benefits of pre-training are additionally investigated through latent space interpretation and application to other domains, including gravitational waves, flood forecasting, and neural activity. Furthermore, the relative computational simplicity of NEXUS is demonstrated compared to transformer approaches at comparable scale, opening the door to power-efficient inference and real-time or edge applications of foundation models in scientific experiments.

</details>


### [287] [Cybersecurity Detection Classification with Reasoning-enabled Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28460)
*Amol Khanna,Manu Nandan,Cristian Viorel Popa,Joan Pujol-Roig,Diana Bolocan,Laura Vasilie,Alexandru Apostu,Chase Helwig,Mihaela Gaman,Michael Brautbar,Edward Raff,Chase Midler,Sven Krasser*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses SOC alert fatigue by training a chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning classifier for endpoint detection triage. Using prompt optimization, self-training, and RL with verifiable rewards, the system achieves 82.6% accuracy. It introduces a separate calibrator to fix degraded label-token probabilities from CoT reasoning, improving benign recall by 43% and malicious recall by 18.3% over direct-label LLMs. A fine-tuned 30B model outperforms larger general-purpose models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Security Operations Centers suffer from alert fatigue because daily detection volumes exceed human triage capacity. Prior LLM-based approaches directly emit triage labels without explicit reasoning, limiting their reliability for automated triage. The authors aim to build a system that reasons about whether a detection is a genuine threat, improving both accuracy and confidence calibration for high-stakes automated decisions.

Method: The authors train a chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning-enabled triage classifier on real, human-labeled Windows endpoint detections. The training pipeline combines: (1) automated prompt optimization, (2) self-training (iterative pseudo-labeling), and (3) reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Because CoT reasoning degrades the label-token probabilities needed for reliable automated triage, a separate calibrator is trained to read the full reasoning trace and estimate the probability that the verdict is correct.

Result: The system achieves 82.6% test accuracy. At the high-confidence operating point for automated triage, it improves benign recall by 43.0% and malicious recall by 18.3% over a direct-label LLM classifier. The trained calibrator proves essential: an untrained confidence judge reduces high-confidence recall to zero. A fine-tuned 30B model significantly outperforms frontier general-purpose models, demonstrating that targeted training is more effective than simply scaling model size.

Conclusion: CoT reasoning enhances triage classification accuracy, but it introduces miscalibration in confidence scores that must be corrected with a dedicated calibrator. Targeted fine-tuning of moderate-sized models yields better results than relying on larger general-purpose LLMs, challenging the "bigger is better" assumption in security applications.

Abstract: A major issue in Security Operations Centers (SOCs) is alert fatigue, as the number of detections reported is more than staff can triage in a given day. Prior work prompts or fine-tunes large language models (LLMs) to emit a triage label directly, but does not train them to reason about whether a detection is a genuine threat. We train a chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning-enabled triage classifier on real, human-labeled Windows endpoint detections by combining automated prompt optimization, self-training, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. We find that CoT reasoning also degrades the label-token probabilities that automated triage relies on, so we separately train a calibrator that reads the full reasoning trace and estimates the probability that the verdict is correct. Our system reaches 82.6% test accuracy and, at the high-confidence operating point that governs automated triage, improves benign recall by 43.0% and malicious recall by 18.3% over a direct-label LLM classifier. We further show that the trained calibrator is necessary - an untrained confidence judge collapses high-confidence recall to zero - and that a finetuned 30B model significantly outperforms frontier general-purpose models, motivating targeted training over scale.

</details>


### [288] [Sparsity Induced Identifiability in Matrix Tri-Factorisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27507)
*Tingting Mu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: First rigorous theoretical analysis of sparsity-induced identifiability in general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation, using a novel decomposition strategy that splits the problem into two coupled auxiliary factorisation problems while preserving structural information needed for recovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While sparse two-factor matrix factorisation has been extensively studied theoretically, rigorous guarantees for sparse matrix tri-factorisation remain unexplored despite its greater modeling flexibility and practical importance in compression, denoising, and representation learning.

Method: A novel decomposition strategy that transforms the tri-factorisation problem into two coupled auxiliary factorisation problems, preserving the structural information necessary for recovering the original factor matrices from observations. This enables derivation of recovery guarantees and structural consistency results.

Result: Derived recovery guarantees and structural consistency results characterising how coefficient sparsity influences sufficient recovery conditions, convergence behaviour, spectral approximation error, high-probability bounds, and structure preservation. Monte Carlo experiments validate close agreement between theory and empirical observations.

Conclusion: The proposed theoretical framework provides the first rigorous characterisation of sparsity effects in real-valued matrix tri-factorisation, with the decomposition strategy serving as a key analytical bridge. Empirical results strongly support the theoretical findings.

Abstract: Matrix factorisation is a fundamental tool for exploiting low-dimensional structure in high-dimensional data, with applications such as data compression, denoising, structure discovery, interpretable representation learning, and dimensionality reduction. Compared to conventional two-factor models, matrix tri-factorisation provides greater modelling flexibility, while sparsity constraints often improve both interpretability and recovery performance. Although the role of sparsity has been extensively studied for two-factor matrix factorisation, rigorous theoretical guarantees for general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation remain largely unexplored. To address this gap, we establish, to the best of our knowledge, the first rigorous theoretical study for sparsity-induced identifiability in general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation. Our analysis is enabled by a novel decomposition strategy that transforms the original problem into two coupled auxiliary factorisation problems, while preserving the structural information necessary to the recovery of the original factor matrices from the observations. Building upon this decomposition, we derive recovery guarantees and structural consistency results that characterise how coefficient sparsity influences the sufficient recovery conditions, convergence behaviour, spectral approximation error, high-probability bounds, and structure preservation. Comprehensive Monte Carlo experiments validate the proposed theory and demonstrate close agreement between the theoretical results and empirical observations.

</details>


### [289] [Expanding Data-Agnostic Pivotal Instances Selection Models with Proximity Trees and Ensemble Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27522)
*Alessio Cascione,Mattia Setzu,Cristiano Landi,Paolo Maria Mancarella,Riccardo Guidotti*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a hierarchical, interpretable-by-design model that selects representative examples (pivots) for decision-making, inspired by decision trees. It supports single pivots, pivot pairs (proximity/oblique), and ensembles, is data modality-agnostic, and achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art interpretable models while using few pivots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing machine learning methods for complex decision-making often lack interpretability. Humans naturally reason by comparing new cases to a few representative examples. The authors aim to bridge this gap by designing a model that explicitly selects such representative "pivots" to construct an interpretable, case-based predictive framework.

Method: The authors propose a hierarchical pivot selection model inspired by decision trees, where predictions are based on similarity between input instances and selected pivots. The method extends to pivot pairs (akin to proximity and oblique trees) and supports ensembles for greater versatility. It is data modality-agnostic, using pre-trained networks for data transformation across tabular, text, image, and time series data.

Result: Experiments on diverse datasets (tabular, text, images, time series) show the approach outperforms alternative instance selection strategies and achieves competitive results against state-of-the-art interpretable models, all while maintaining a minimal number of pivots.

Conclusion: The proposed hierarchical pivot selection method offers an effective, interpretable-by-design predictive model that aligns with human case-based reasoning, generalizes across data modalities, and competes favorably with leading interpretable models using very few representative examples.

Abstract: As decision-making processes grow more complex, machine learning tools have become essential for tackling business and societal challenges. However, many existing methods rely on decision-making procedures that are difficult to interpret. Since humans naturally make decisions by comparing new cases with a few representative examples, we aim to design an approach that selects such pivots to construct an interpretable predictive model. Inspired by decision trees, we propose a hierarchical, interpretable-by-design pivot selection model based on the similarity between pivots and input instances. Our method functions both as a pivot selection technique and a standalone predictive model. Extending beyond single pivots, we incorporate pairs of pivots that are used by proximity and oblique trees, as well as ensembles, which enhance the versatility and effectiveness of our proposal. Additionally, our approach is data modality-agnostic, leveraging pre-trained networks for data transformation. Experiments across diverse datasets, including tabular data, text, images, and time series, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming alternative instance selection strategies and achieving competitive results against state-of-the-art interpretable models while maintaining a minimal number of pivots.

</details>


### [290] [Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps for Few-Step Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27529)
*Mansoor Ahmed,Yue-Tsz Fan,Hemanth Venkateswara,Murray Patterson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LKF introduces a latent-kernel discrete flow map that enables correlated multi-token updates in few-step discrete diffusion, outperforming distilled/rectified baselines on text generation by 2.1–3.3× in perplexity while maintaining diversity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing discrete diffusion and flow-matching models use factorized, per-token independent updates, which struggle with few-step generation when tokens are coupled (e.g., subject-verb agreement). Current solutions distill or rectify a slow teacher model, inheriting its quality ceiling. The authors ask whether correlated steps can be expressed natively from scratch.

Method: Propose Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps (LKF), a flow-map kernel that is a mixture of M factorized components sharing a single latent variable. Each component is cheap conditioned on the latent; the mixture sums over the latent in closed form for small M. One latent is drawn per sequence and reused across the entire trajectory, giving correlated completions at the same sampling time complexity as factorized models. MDLM is shown to be a special case at M=1.

Result: On LM1B and WikiText-103 unconditional text generation benchmarks, LKF learns strongly heterogeneous components and improves generative perplexity by 2.1× to 3.3× over likelihood baselines without diversity loss. Performance grows with M; at M=8, it surpasses distilled and rectified few-step samplers.

Conclusion: Native correlated-step modeling via latent mixtures in discrete flow maps enables high-quality few-step text generation from scratch, breaking the quality ceiling imposed by teacher-dependent distillation/rectification approaches.

Abstract: Discrete diffusion and flow-matching models denoise a sequence over many steps, but to keep each step cheap, they factorize the transition across positions and decide every token independently. This makes few-step generation challenging for text when the target couples two positions, such as a subject and a verb that must agree. An independent update commits to them separately, and many function evaluations are spent repairing the mismatch. Existing few-step methods buy back the lost correlation by distilling or rectifying a slow teacher, and so inherit the teacher's quality ceiling. We ask instead whether a model can express correlated steps natively, and answer with Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps (LKF), a from-scratch flow-map kernel that is a mixture of M factorized components tied by a single shared latent. Conditioned on the latent, each component is cheap, and the mixture is summed over the latent in closed form for small M. We show that a single step places mass on correlated completions with the same sampling time complexity as a factorized model, since one latent is drawn per sequence and reused across the entire denoising trajectory. We also show that the Masked Diffusion Language Model (MDLM) is a special case of our LKF model at M=1. The experiments for unconditional text generation on the One-Billion-Word (LM1B) and WikiText-103 benchmarks show that our LKF model learns strongly heterogeneous components and improves generative perplexity by 2.1x to 3.3x over the likelihood baselines without losing diversity. The gain grows with M, and at M=8, it surpasses distilled and rectified few-step samplers. The source code is available at: https://github.com/mansoor181/lkf.git

</details>


### [291] [When Does Explicit View Routing Work? A Controlled Study of Multi-View Graph-Text Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27530)
*Xiao Yue,Guangzhi Qu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether multi-headed graph-text retrieval models perform genuine semantic routing or merely architectural channelization. Using controlled experiments with verifiable text segments, external labels, and RDKit descriptors, the authors show that correct routing significantly improves retrieval metrics, but evidence is limited to explicit, externally grounded label and property routing, with topology specialization remaining inconsistent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph-text retrieval models map graph-description pairs to single embeddings, even when queries target specific semantic aspects (e.g., class labels, molecular properties). Multi-head architectures can separate these aspects, but changing the query head may alter retrieval regardless of semantic content—this is architectural channelization, not true semantic routing. The work examines when and whether this distinction can be empirically resolved.

Method: A controlled version of MV-GTA is constructed with: deterministic, verifiable text segments; isolated text encoders; view-specific graph heads; and relevance derived from external labels or RDKit molecular descriptors. Correct routing and per-sample derangements form a causal test. Experiments span BBBP and BACE datasets with matched three-seed comparisons between joint multi-head models and separately trained single specialists. Property paraphrase augmentation and hard-template consistency extensions are also evaluated.

Result: Correct routing improves label and property nDCG by 0.305–0.685 over deranged training. The expected graph head outperforms the best wrong head by 0.303–0.453. Topology specialization is inconsistent across datasets. In three-seed matched comparison: joint model achieves topology/label/property nDCG of 0.720/1.000/0.877 vs. single specialists at 0.633/0.976/0.859. Property paraphrase augmentation improves unseen-template nDCG by 0.140–0.147. Consistency and hard-template extensions reduce canonical retrieval in some settings.

Conclusion: Evidence supports explicit, externally grounded label and property routing with observed multi-interface consolidation. However, the work does not establish free-form routing, consistent three-view specialization, statistical equivalence to separately trained specialists, or superior downstream prediction performance.

Abstract: Graph-text retrieval typically maps a graph and its description to a single embedding, even when a query concerns only one semantic aspect, such as a class label or molecular property. Multiple heads can separate these aspects, but a change in the query head may alter retrieval even when the wrong text is sent to that head. Such behavior demonstrates architectural channelization, not necessarily semantic routing. We examine the conditions under which this distinction can be resolved. Our controlled version of MV-GTA uses deterministic, verifiable text segments; isolated text encoders; view-specific graph heads; and relevance derived from external labels or RDKit descriptors. Correct routing and per-sample derangements form a causal test of whether retrieval depends on content. On BBBP and BACE, correct routing improves label and property nDCG by 0.305 to 0.685 over deranged training. The expected graph head exceeds the best wrong head by 0.303 to 0.453. Topology does not specialize consistently across the two datasets. In a matched three-seed comparison, one joint model obtains mean topology, label, and property nDCG of 0.720/1.000/0.877; three separately trained Single specialists obtain 0.633/0.976/0.859. Property paraphrase augmentation also improves unseen-template nDCG by 0.140 and 0.147 over a matched-exposure canonical control. Consistency and hard-template extensions, however, reduce canonical retrieval in some settings. The evidence is therefore limited to explicit, externally grounded label and property routing and observed multi-interface consolidation. It does not establish free-form routing, consistent three-view specialization, statistical equivalence to specialists, or superior downstream prediction.

</details>


### [292] [Subtract or Replay? Exact Deletion from Language-Model Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27539)
*Vishwajith Ramesh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Exact deletion from language model memory depends on representation: addressable records support algebraic decrement, while entangled recurrent writes require rewinding and replaying. The paper validates this across two architectures (Gemma 3 with support-vector memory and Kimi Linear hybrid), demonstrating bit-identical recovery for subtractive approaches and exact amendment via replay.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper investigates the fundamental requirements for exact deletion (machine unlearning) in language models, arguing that the feasibility of exact deletion is not a matter of model scale or architecture per se, but of how memory represents individual records—specifically whether contributions remain addressable or become entangled through recurrent state updates.

Method: The authors test their distinction across two settings: (1) They replace Gemma 3's global-attention layers with support-vector memory at 1B, 4B, and 12B scales, applying low-rank recovery and comparing algebraic decrement with retained-key refit. They evaluate via KL divergence, perplexity, and unlearning audits including LiRA attacks. (2) They analyze a 48B Kimi Linear hybrid model, distinguishing additive writes (fixed decrement), diagonal decay (corrected decrement), and delta-rule contributions (suffix-dependent). They implement checkpointed rewind-and-replay to delete real clinical records at contexts up to 18,842 tokens, verifying bit-identical logits and recurrent states in a deterministic MLX implementation.

Result: For Gemma 3 at 1B with support-vector memory, decrement and retained-key refit agree to median KL divergence of 5.4×10⁻¹⁵ over 31 deletions, with +2.0% perplexity relative to matched fine-tuning. Masked-refit is indistinguishable from never-ingested baseline under elicitation, relearning, sampling, and LiRA. At 4B and 12B, the same certificate ordering holds but utility cost rises to 11.2% and 44.3%. In the Kimi Linear hybrid, additive writes permit fixed decrement and diagonal decay permits corrected decrement, while delta-rule contributions make 12–49% of a record's influence suffix-dependent. Rewind-and-replay achieves bit-identical logits and recurrent states to never-ingested baseline on real clinical records.

Conclusion: Exact deletion is a property of memory representation: subtract addressable records and replay entangled writes. The paper demonstrates that when contributions remain addressable (support-vector memory, additive writes), algebraic decrement suffices; when writes become entangled in recurrent state, checkpointed replay provides exact correction. This framework unifies deletion guarantees across model scales and architectures.

Abstract: Exact deletion from persistent language-model memory depends on how that memory represents a record. Addressable influence can be removed by algebraic decrement; influence transformed by later writes inside shared recurrent state requires rebuilding from before the write. We test this distinction in two pretrained models against explicit record-omitted references. First, we replace Gemma 3's global-attention layers with support-vector memory. After low-rank recovery at 1B, decrement and retained-key refit agree at the next-token output to median KL $5.4\times10^{-15}$ over 31 support-token deletions, with $+2.0\%$ perplexity relative to a matched fine-tune. A masked-refit proxy is indistinguishable from the never-ingested floor under elicitation, relearning, sampling, and LiRA attacks. At 4B and 12B, certificate ordering persists but utility cost rises to $11.2\%$ and $44.3\%$. Second, in a 48B Kimi Linear hybrid, additive writes admit a fixed decrement and diagonal decay a corrected one, whereas the delta rule makes $12$--$49\%$ of a record's contribution suffix-dependent. Checkpointed rewind-and-replay deletes real clinical records at contexts up to 18,842 tokens, matching never-ingested logits and all recurrent states bit for bit within a deterministic MLX implementation; replaying a correction provides exact amendment. Exact deletion is therefore a property of memory representation: subtract addressable records and replay entangled writes.

</details>


### [293] [Memory Efficient Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27546)
*Shuting Luo,Monika Mikhail Kanaan,Cameron Gordon,Anna Leontjeva,Simon Lucey*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates memory reduction for Tabular Foundation Models (specifically TabPFN) using model compression, achieving up to 7.6× memory reduction with similar performance, cutting deployment requirements by ~87%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While Tabular Foundation Models like TabPFN excel at in-context tabular ML tasks, their practical deployment considerations—particularly memory requirements—have been underexplored. The authors aim to fill this gap for practitioners.

Method: The authors apply model compression techniques (e.g., quantization, pruning, or knowledge distillation) to TabPFN and evaluate the trade-off between memory footprint and predictive performance.

Result: Model compression achieves memory reductions of up to 7.6× compared to uncompressed models, with minimal performance degradation, reducing overall deployment requirements by approximately 87%.

Conclusion: Model compression is an effective strategy for deploying Tabular Foundation Models in memory-constrained practical settings, offering substantial efficiency gains with negligible accuracy loss.

Abstract: Tabular Foundation Models, such as TabPFN, have received a large amount of recent attention due to their performance on in-context tabular machine learning tasks, which often exceeds classical baselines. However, practical deployment considerations of these models has received less attention. In this paper we investigate the memory requirements for these models. We demonstrate that employing model compression approaches can enable memory reductions of up to 7.6 with similar levels of performance, reducing deployment requirements by nearly 87%. Our work provides insight to practitioners seeking efficient deployment of these models in practical settings.

</details>


### [294] [Strategies for Milestone-driven Start-ups in Multi-activity Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27563)
*Zhengli Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper solves a stochastic control model for startup survival, where the entrepreneur chooses among multiple activities (controls) with different cost, drift, and volatility profiles to reach a success threshold before a failure threshold. The optimal policy is characterized by an "efficient frontier curve" that ranks controls by riskiness (drift-to-volatility ratio) and cost-effectiveness (drift-to-cost ratio), and the frontier can take different qualitative forms depending on parameters, leading to structurally distinct optimal strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Startup ventures must survive through multiple milestone stages, and entrepreneurs face complex choices among activities with varying risk-return-cost profiles. Continuous-time stochastic control models with three or more controls are notoriously difficult to solve, yet real-world entrepreneurial decision-making requires understanding how to optimally switch among multiple activities contingent on the firm's current state.

Method: The authors model the startup's state as a diffusion process with absorbing boundaries (success at an upper threshold, failure at a lower threshold). The entrepreneur selects among multiple controls, each with distinct drift, volatility, and cost parameters. The problem is solved using stochastic optimal control techniques, yielding an explicit characterization of the optimal policy through the construction of an "efficient frontier curve" that ranks controls by two key metrics: riskiness (drift-to-volatility ratio) and cost-effectiveness (drift-to-cost ratio).

Result: The optimal policy uses only controls from a set defined by the efficient frontier curve. Depending on model parameters, the efficient frontier can take different types, leading to qualitatively different optimal policy structures. This is the first stochastic control model to admit efficient frontier curves of multiple types, producing distinct strategic regimes.

Conclusion: The paper provides startups with intuitive measures—riskiness and cost-effectiveness—to evaluate activities, and offers insights into how optimal strategies change qualitatively depending on the specific scenario. The framework serves as a foundational block for studying entrepreneurial decision-making under milestone-oriented settings.

Abstract: New venture start-ups need to ``survive'' through multiple stages of reaching milestone targets. We investigate the strategies for start-ups in a milestone-oriented setting. We examine a model of an entrepreneurial start-up firm, where its state is captured by a diffusion process. The entrepreneur can choose between multiple activities (or controls), which incur different cost and determine the drift and the variance of the process. Depending on whether the process reaches a fixed upper boundary or a lower one, the start-up firm succeeds or fails. Continuous-time stochastic models with multiple ($\ge 3$) controls are typically very challenging to deal with. In this work, we are able to completely solve for the optimal policy and provide an explicit characterization of its structure. In particular, the optimal policy only uses controls from a set characterized by a so-called efficient frontier curve that orders the controls by two intuitive measures: riskiness (drift-to-volatility ratio) and cost-effectiveness (drift-to-cost ratio). A unique feature of our model is that depending on the model parameters, the efficient frontier curves can be of different types, resulting in qualitatively different structures of the optimal policy. As far as we know, this is the first study that analyzes a stochastic control model which admits efficient frontier curves of different types. Our work provides start-up firms with intuitive measures to evaluate their activities and offers valuable insights on how the optimal strategies in a milestone-oriented setting change qualitatively contingent upon the specific scenario. We believe the results provide a foundational block in the study of entrepreneurial decision-making.

</details>


### [295] [MUGEN: A Unified Framework for Efficient Motion Understanding and Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27581)
*Zhankai Ye,Yukai Jin,Bingyang Wei,Bofan Li,Yusen Wu,Fangyi Li,Shangqian Gao,Xin Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MUGEN is a unified motion-language framework that eliminates discrete codebooks and iterative decoding, using a single adaptive-length autoencoder to compress motion into a few continuous latent slots. A language model generates these slots in one draw for text-to-motion and reads them for motion understanding, achieving state-of-the-art results on generation, retrieval, and alignment metrics at minimal inference cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing unified motion-language systems rely on discrete motion codebooks that degrade generation quality. Stronger generators recover quality through expensive techniques: stacked residual codebooks, masked decoding, long autoregressive rollouts, multi-step denoising chains, and iterative diffusion heads. Critically, this complex decoding machinery only serves generation and does not benefit motion understanding. The authors seek a unified framework that achieves high quality without these costs.

Method: MUGEN employs three key components: (1) a single adaptive-length autoencoder that compresses motion of any length into a small number of continuous latent slots — the sole motion representation; (2) a language model that generates these latent slots for text-to-motion and reads them back for motion understanding; (3) depth-routed hidden states allowing each slot to access only the transformer depth it needs, plus a calibrated head that predicts a joint distribution over the full latent set, enabling a single draw to capture text-conditional cross-slot variation.

Result: On HumanML3D, MUGEN leads language-model baselines on FID while raising retrieval precision above the real-motion reference under the standard evaluator. It achieves the best CIDEr and BLEU@4 scores. On SnapMoGen, it surpasses the discrete-token state of the art on every retrieval and alignment metric. All results are obtained at a decoding cost of K LM steps, one draw, and one decoder pass.

Conclusion: MUGEN demonstrates that a continuous-latent, single-draw approach can unify motion generation and understanding without the quality-cost tradeoffs of discrete codebook methods, matching or exceeding specialized systems on both tasks while dramatically simplifying the inference pipeline.

Abstract: Grounding human motion in language, and language in motion, is a central step toward physical AI systems that can understand, generate, and communicate human behavior. Unified motion--language systems first coupled the two directions through a shared discrete motion codebook, but quantization limits generation quality. The strongest generators buy quality back at growing cost: stacked residual codebooks enlarge the representation; masked decoding stages, long autoregressive rollouts, and denoising chains of tens to hundreds of steps stretch inference; even the continuous-latent designs among them reach their latent only through an iterative diffusion head; and none of this decoding machinery serves understanding. We therefore propose MUGEN, a unified motion--language framework that pays neither cost: no codebook, one draw. A single adaptive-length autoencoder compresses any-length motion into a few continuous latent slots, the system's only motion representation: the language model generates them for text-to-motion and reads them back for motion understanding. Depth-routed hidden states let each slot read from the transformer depth it needs, and a calibrated head predicts a joint distribution over the full latent set, so a single draw carries the text-conditional, cross-slot variation a description permits. At a decoding cost of K language-model steps, one draw, and one decoder pass, MUGEN leads language-model baselines on FID on HumanML3D while raising retrieval precision above the real-motion reference under the standard evaluator, achieves the best CIDEr and BLEU@4 scores, and surpasses the discrete-token state of the art on every retrieval and alignment metric on SnapMoGen.

</details>


### [296] [Prox: Training-Free FFN Activation Sparsity via Approximate Intermediate-Channel Salience in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27591)
*Jinyi Liu,Wei Chen,Pengyu Chen,Xinyi Yuan,Minghe Bai,Guoquan Wu,Jun Wei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Prox is a two-stage, training-free framework that enables sparse execution of SwiGLU feed-forward networks in LLMs by constructing channel masks from magnitude rankings rather than exact intermediate state values, achieving up to 1.99× decoding speedup at 70% sparsity without significant quality loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: FFNs dominate memory traffic and computation in LLM inference. Existing training-free activation sparsification methods degrade model quality at high sparsity due to poor channel-selection strategies. The SwiGLU intermediate state offers an effective channel-selection signal but requires costly dense computation to obtain.

Method: Prox uses a two-stage approach: Stage 1 leverages input sparsity and quantized proxy weights to construct a shared channel mask by approximating the magnitude ranking of the intermediate state entries without computing exact values. Stage 2 computes only the selected channels exactly, enabling sparse execution of all three projections (gate, up, and down) in the SwiGLU FFN.

Result: Prox outperforms all training-free baselines across ten LLMs from six model families at all sparsity levels, achieves up to 1.99× end-to-end decoding speedup at 70% FFN sparsity, and is compatible with quantization and sparse attention techniques.

Conclusion: The key insight — that sparse execution only requires the channel mask from magnitude ranking, not exact intermediate values — enables a practical and effective training-free sparsification framework that substantially accelerates LLM inference without compromising model quality.

Abstract: Feed-forward networks (FFNs) dominate memory traffic and computation in large language model (LLM) inference, making them a primary target for activation sparsification. However, existing training-free methods suffer substantial model-quality degradation at high sparsity due to limitations in their channel-selection strategies. We observe that the SwiGLU intermediate state provides a highly effective channel-selection signal, but obtaining it requires costly dense computation. To address this, we present \emph{Prox}, a two-stage training-free framework for sparse SwiGLU FFNs. Prox hinges on the key insight: sparse execution requires only the channel mask induced by the intermediate state, which can be constructed from the magnitude ranking of its entries rather than their exact values. Specifically, Stage 1 uses input sparsity and quantized proxy weights to construct a shared mask; Stage 2 computes the selected channels exactly, enabling sparse execution of all three projections. Across ten LLMs from six model families, Prox outperforms training-free baselines at all sparsity levels, achieves up to a $1.99\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup at 70\% FFN sparsity, and is compatible with quantization and sparse attention.

</details>


### [297] [Compliance2LoRA: On-Demand Safety Alignment on Arbitrary Policy Subsets via Hypernetwork-Generated LoRA Adapters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27594)
*Pankayaraj Pathmanathan,Furong Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a hypernetwork-based framework that generates policy-compliant LoRA weights on demand, enabling a single large reasoning model to dynamically adapt to arbitrary subsets of safety policies without combinatorial retraining overhead or long-context inference costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing post-training alignment for LRMs requires training separate models for each safety policy subset, causing combinatorial overhead. In-context learning alternatives avoid retraining but incur heavy computational costs from long context generation. A method is needed that allows flexible, on-demand policy adaptation on a single model without these tradeoffs.

Method: The authors propose an adaptive hypernetwork that takes safety policy specifications as customizable inputs. This hypernetwork functions as a LoRA adapter generator: it learns to produce policy-compliant LoRA weights conditioned on the desired policy subset. These generated weights are then added to a downstream LRM, enabling policy-compliant response generation without modifying the base model.

Result: The framework enables on-demand policy adjustments on a single LRM without sacrificing task performance, validated across reasoning models of different sizes and multiple evaluation datasets.

Conclusion: Adaptive hypernetwork-based alignment is an effective and practical approach for multi-policy compliance in LRMs, eliminating combinatorial training overhead and long-context inference costs while preserving performance.

Abstract: Post-training alignment in large reasoning models (LRMs) has significantly improved their adaptability to diverse safety compliance settings. However, as LRMs personalization for downstream users takes center stage, the demand for varying levels of policy compliance grows as different user-specific LRMs must adhere to distinct subsets of safety policies. Training a separate LRM for each policy subset introduces severe combinatorial overhead. While in context learning methods overcome this combinatorial overhead, they introduce additional computational challenges associated with long context generation. To address this challenge, we propose \ours, a unified adaptive hypernetwork-based framework for multi-policy compliance. In our framework, safety policies serve as customizable inputs to a LoRA adapter generator, which learns to produce policy compliant LoRA weights for downstream LRM. When added to the LRM these weights enable the generation of responses compliant with the specified policy subsets. In this work, we demonstrate that training such a hypernetwork enables on-demand policy adjustments on a single LRM without sacrificing task performance across reasoning models of different sized and different evaluation datasets. This highlights the effectiveness and practicality of adaptive hypernetwork based alignment in LRMs.

</details>


### [298] [Back from the Future: Key-Value Cache Management by Counter-Causal Surprise](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27600)
*Stephen Gould,Anton van den Hengel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a KV cache eviction strategy that removes tokens predictable from future context, using a counter-causal attention pass to score redundancy, with a fast single-layer approximation for efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: KV caches in LLMs grow linearly with context length, consuming GPU memory and limiting long-context generation. Existing compression/eviction methods aim to reduce this footprint, but the authors seek a simple, training-free method that directly leverages the model's own representations to identify redundant cache entries.

Method: The proposed method scores KV cache entries by running a counter-causal attention pass — each token attends only to its future context (subsequent tokens) — reusing existing cached key/value representations. Tokens that are well-predicted by future tokens are deemed redundant and evicted. A single-layer variant restricts this pass to only the last transformer layer, trading minimal accuracy for significant speedup during refresh cycles.

Result: The method achieves competitive or improved performance compared to state-of-the-art KV eviction methods across various open-source LLMs and benchmark datasets.

Conclusion: Counter-causal attention provides an effective, training-free signal for KV cache eviction, and the single-layer approximation offers a practical speed-accuracy trade-off for deployment.

Abstract: Key-value (KV) cache management through compression and eviction strategies has emerged as an important research direction in recent years. Computational demands of large language models (LLMs) and their multi-modal variants during output generation can be partially alleviated by caching previous key and value calculations needed by subsequent scaled dot-product attention operations. However, this leads to another problem: the size of the resulting KV cache grows linearly with context length and quickly consumes all available GPU memory when either the prompt or the generated output are long. KV cache management periodically prunes entries from the cache thereby reducing its memory footprint while attempting to retain sufficient information for accurate generation. A by-product is faster inference speed. We propose a simple yet effective KV eviction scheme motivated by the insight that past tokens which can be well-predicted from more recent tokens are redundant and their associated keys and values can be removed from the cache. To score entries for eviction we run the model on the tokens in their original order, reusing the key and value representations already stored in the KV cache, and applying a counter-causal attention mask so that each position attends only to its future context. This is in-distribution, tied directly to the actual cache contents, and requires no additional training. To further reduce cost, we additionally propose a fast single-layer approximation that restricts the counter-causal pass to the last transformer layer, achieving a significant speedup per refresh cycle at marginal accuracy cost. We evaluate our strategy on various open-source LLMs and benchmark datasets showing competitive or improved performance over other state-of-the-art methods. Reference code is available at https://github.com/metacognitionai/counter_causal.

</details>


### [299] [Kalman Meets Curriculum: Efficient Dynamic Prompt Selection for Adaptive RL Finetuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27610)
*Haodong Zhu,Yangyang Ren,Yanjing Li,Sheng Xu,Haiguang Liu,Linlin Yang,Baochang Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KGPS reformulates RL prompt selection as a dynamic state estimation problem using a Kalman filter to track evolving prompt difficulty, eliminating the need for extra rollouts while adaptively handling non-stationary training dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL finetuning of LLMs requires prompts of appropriate difficulty, but difficulty evolves non-stationarily during training. Existing methods face an accuracy-efficiency trade-off: evaluation-based selection is accurate but expensive, while prediction-based selection assumes stationary difficulty and fails under policy drift.

Method: KGPS models each prompt's latent success rate in logit space via a linear-Gaussian state-space model, where process noise scales with policy update magnitude. A Kalman filter maintains a calibrated Gaussian posterior over prompt difficulty. Prompts are selected by maximizing posterior-expected training utility, favoring intermediate difficulty while naturally revisiting uncertain prompts. No additional rollouts beyond standard training are required.

Result: KGPS achieves state-of-the-art among online prompt selection methods across mathematics, planning, and geometry reasoning benchmarks with multiple RL algorithms. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, KGPS uses 83% fewer rollouts than DS while improving average performance by 0.12 points across six math reasoning benchmarks.

Conclusion: KGPS consistently improves both final accuracy and rollout efficiency over strong baselines, demonstrating that Kalman-filter-based dynamic state estimation effectively addresses the non-stationary prompt selection problem in RL finetuning of LLMs.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) finetuning significantly enhances the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet its effectiveness critically depends on selecting prompts of appropriate difficulty for the current policy. This is challenging because prompt difficulty evolves throughout training. Existing online methods therefore face a trade-off: evaluation-based approaches are accurate but expensive, while prediction-based approaches are efficient but typically assume stationary difficulty, making them ill-suited to RL's non-stationary training dynamics. To address these issues, we propose a Kalman-Guided Prompt Selection method (KGPS), which reformulates prompt selection as a dynamic state estimation problem rather than static difficulty prediction. KGPS models each prompt's latent success rate in logit space using a linear-Gaussian state-space model, with process noise coupled to the magnitude of policy updates so that uncertainty increases when the policy changes more substantially. A Kalman filter then maintains a calibrated Gaussian posterior over prompt difficulty, and prompts are selected by maximizing a posterior-expected training utility that favors intermediate-difficulty prompts while naturally revisiting uncertain ones. The resulting procedure is adaptive to policy drift and requires no additional rollouts beyond standard policy training. Extensive experiments across mathematics, planning, and geometry reasoning benchmarks, as well as multiple RL algorithms, show that KGPS consistently improves both final accuracy and rollout efficiency over strong baselines, establishing state-of-the-art performance among online prompt selection methods. For example, on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, KGPS uses 83% fewer rollouts than DS while even improving the average performance by 0.12 point across six math reasoning benchmarks.

</details>


### [300] [Real-Time Hard Peak Age-of-Information Safety with No-Regret Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27626)
*Wentao Zhang,Wentao Mo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces OCO-PAOI-Hard, a scheduling algorithm for safety-critical IoT systems that guarantees zero per-slot peak AoI deadline violations under adversarial conditions by recasting the fractional peak-AoI deadline as an affine half-space constraint, enabling hard real-time scheduling via time-varying online convex optimization with a polyhedral safe set.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety-critical IoT applications (industrial closed-loop control, V2X, remote teleoperation) require hard per-slot peak AoI deadlines, not just average bounds. Existing methods fail under adversarial settings: Whittle-index approaches assume stochastic channels, deep RL relies on simulator rollouts, and long-term constrained OCO allows sublinear cumulative violations—none guarantee zero per-slot violation.

Method: The authors reframe the fractional peak-AoI deadline as an affine half-space constraint on the resource-allocation vector, converting hard real-time scheduling into time-varying constrained online convex optimization over a polyhedral safe set. They propose a strictly causal proposal-shield-update loop: one Euclidean projection per slot enforces feasibility, the gradient step preserves no-regret behavior, and the virtual queue is demoted to an a-posteriori certificate. Closed-form static/dynamic regret bounds, a matching Ω(√T) minimax lower bound, a margin-safe variant for execution noise, and a deadline-induced competitive ratio are derived.

Result: On a four-sensor adversarial fluid-model trap channel, OCO-PAOI-Hard achieves zero modeled-state deadline violations across all ten seeds. Four representative baselines miss between 1.65% and 64.0% of slots. Empirical normalized regret remains below the theoretical envelope across two orders of magnitude in T.

Conclusion: OCO-PAOI-Hard provides the first scheduling framework that guarantees zero per-slot peak AoI deadline violations under adversarial conditions with O(√T) regret, validated both theoretically (matching minimax lower bound) and empirically.

Abstract: Safety-critical IoT systems such as industrial closed-loop control, V2X coordination, and remote teleoperation require every sensor's peak Age of Information (peak AoI, also abbreviated PAoI) to stay below a hard per-slot deadline, not merely an average bound. Existing approaches meet this requirement only under restrictive assumptions: stochastic channels for Whittle-index AoI, simulator rollouts for deep reinforcement learning, or sublinear cumulative violation for long-term constrained online convex optimization. Under adversarial coefficients, OCO-PAoI-Hard guarantees zero per-slot violation of the modeled AoI state under one-step viability and O(sqrt(T)) regret against any static safe comparator; packet-level safety requires stronger service assumptions. Our key observation is that the fractional peak-AoI deadline collapses exactly to an affine half-space constraint on the resource-allocation vector, turning hard real-time scheduling into time-varying constrained online convex optimization over a polyhedral safe set. A strictly causal proposal-shield-update loop enforces feasibility through one Euclidean projection per slot, the gradient step preserves no-regret behavior, and the classical virtual queue is reduced to an a-posteriori certificate. We establish closed-form static and dynamic regret bounds, a matching Omega(sqrt(T)) minimax lower bound, a margin-safe variant against execution noise, and a deadline-induced competitive ratio. On a four-sensor adversarial fluid-model trap channel, OCO-PAoI-Hard attains zero modeled-state deadline violations across all ten seeds, while four representative baselines miss between 1.65 percent and 64.0 percent of slots, and the empirical normalized regret stays below the theoretical envelope across two orders of magnitude in T.

</details>


### [301] [First-order Constrained Trilevel Optimization Over Distributed Networks for Robust Coreset Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27632)
*Yang Jiao,Kaixuan Jiao,Kai Yang,Nadjib Aitsaadi,Ilhem Fajjari,Renwei,Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper formalizes distributed robust coreset selection as a constrained trilevel optimization problem and proposes F²CTO, the first distributed first-order algorithm to solve it. The method combines hierarchical value-function reformulation with a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm, achieving an O(ε⁻³/²) convergence rate, with strong empirical results on reliable continual learning tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: IoT edge networks generate massive distributed data, making full-data training computationally prohibitive. Coreset selection is a natural solution, but local data is privacy-sensitive and real-world deployments demand model robustness. Existing work fails to unify these three aspects—coreset selection, robust optimization, and distributed learning—into a single principled framework, leaving a critical gap.

Method: The authors first characterize the hierarchical dependencies among the three components and formulate the problem as a trilevel optimization with level-wise constraints. They then propose F²CTO (Federated First-order Constrained Trilevel Optimization), which synergistically integrates: (1) a hierarchical composite value-function reformulation to handle the nested structure, and (2) a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm for decentralized execution. Convergence analysis establishes a non-asymptotic rate of O(ε⁻³/²) to an ε-stationary point.

Result: F²CTO is the first method for distributed robust coreset selection and the first distributed optimization approach for constrained trilevel problems. Theoretically, it achieves O(ε⁻³/²) convergence. Empirically, extensive evaluations on reliable continual learning benchmarks demonstrate both effectiveness and efficiency compared to baselines.

Conclusion: The work successfully bridges coreset selection, robust optimization, and federated/distributed learning within a unified trilevel optimization framework. F²CTO provides both theoretical guarantees and practical efficacy, opening a new direction for privacy-preserving, robust, and computation-efficient learning on distributed edge data.

Abstract: With the rapid advancement of the Internet of Things (IoT), massive amounts of data are generated across distributed edge networks. Training models on full data incurs significant computational overhead and storage bottlenecks, rendering coreset selection a critical paradigm. Furthermore, given the privacy-sensitive nature of local data and the escalating demand for model robustness in real-world deployments, developing an effective distributed optimization framework for robust coreset selection is vital, yet remains largely unexplored. To this end, this work first characterizes the hierarchical dependencies among coreset selection, robust optimization, and distributed learning, and formulates the distributed robust coreset selection as a trilevel optimization problem with level-wise constraints. Furthermore, to effectively solve the trilevel problem in a distributed manner, the \underline{F}ederated \underline{F}irst-order \underline{C}onstrained \underline{T}rilevel \underline{O}ptimization (F$^2$CTO) is proposed, which synergistically integrates a hierarchical composite value-function reformulation and a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, F$^2$CTO is the first method developed for distributed robust coreset selection, as well as the first distributed optimization approach for trilevel optimization problems with level-wise constraints. Additionally, we prove that the proposed method achieves a non-asymptotic convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-3/2})$ for finding an $ε$-stationary point. Extensive empirical evaluations on reliable continual learning demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed F$^2$CTO.

</details>


### [302] [Certifying when decision-time information justifies adaptive experimentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27651)
*Jia Bi,Samuel Pinilla,Chenyang Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OPAL is a framework that decides whether to enable adaptive experimentation at all, using precommitted contracts requiring non-trivial adaptation, controlled target risk, and positive executed value after cost. It establishes an impossibility boundary under unrestricted conditional outcome shift and demonstrates strict risk control on a large-scale Cell Painting dataset, uniquely combining non-zero activation with certified risk bounds among six compared methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most adaptive experimentation methods focus on how to adapt during experiments, but none systematically address whether adaptation should be permitted in the first place. Without such a gate, adaptive methods risk wasting resources on campaigns where adaptation cannot provably add value or meet safety guarantees.

Method: OPAL (Opportunity-aware Policy Authorization for Laboratories) uses a precommitted contract with three requirements: (1) non-trivial adaptation (adaptation must meaningfully change behavior), (2) controlled target risk (false-activation rate bounded below a prespecified limit), and (3) positive executed value after accounting for cost. The authors derive an impossibility result showing that source outcomes and unlabelled target covariates cannot uniformly support non-trivial authorization under unrestricted conditional outcome shift, and provide a target-calibrated recovery procedure. A frozen (pre-registered) gate is applied before any adaptation occurs.

Result: On an unseen 11,265-compound Cell Painting partition, the frozen gate selected 595 compounds, captured 384 positive opportunities, and achieved strictly positive executed value under least-favorable completion. The false-activation upper bound was 5.18%, below the 7.5% limit. Among six methods compared, only OPAL combined non-zero activation with this risk control. Additional locked pharmacogenomic and finite-campaign studies distinguish policy misalignment from non-certifiability.

Conclusion: Authorization constitutes a distinct and necessary layer for safe adaptive science, separate from adaptation policy design. OPAL demonstrates that precommitted, contract-based gating can provably control risk while enabling productive adaptive experimentation, establishing a foundation for certifiably safe adaptive laboratory workflows.

Abstract: Adaptive laboratories choose measurements during experiments, yet most methods begin after adaptation is permitted. We introduce Opportunity-aware Policy Authorization for Laboratories (\OPAL{}), a framework that decides whether adaptation should be enabled at all. \OPAL{} uses a precommitted contract to require non-trivial adaptation, controlled target risk and positive executed value after cost. We establish an impossibility boundary: source outcomes and unlabelled target covariates cannot uniformly support non-trivial authorization under unrestricted conditional outcome shift, and derive a target-calibrated recovery. Applied to an unseen 11,265-compound Cell Painting partition, the frozen gate selected 595 compounds, captured 384 positive opportunities and achieved strictly positive executed value under least-favourable completion; its 5.18\% false-activation upper bound remained below a 7.5\% limit. Among six methods, only \OPAL{} combined non-zero activation with this risk control. Locked pharmacogenomic and finite-campaign studies distinguish policy misalignment from non-certifiability, establishing authorization as a distinct layer for safe adaptive science.

</details>


### [303] [Evaluation Protocols and Cross-Subject Generalization in EEG Emotion Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27655)
*Hanting Suo,Yuwen Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper audits EEG emotion recognition evaluation practices, showing that reported accuracy depends critically on evaluation design. Using a DGCNN on SEED and SEED-IV, the authors demonstrate large gaps between subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, and cross-session protocols, and reveal that checkpoint selection via repeated test-set evaluation inflates performance. They argue these distinct protocols answer fundamentally different questions and should be reported separately.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reported EEG emotion recognition accuracy is confounded by the complete evaluation procedure — not just the classifier. The paper seeks to disentangle the target quantity, development procedure, and reporting rule to reveal how evaluation choices (subject-dependent vs. subject-disjoint, checkpoint selection, cross-session protocols) produce divergent performance estimates that are often conflated in the literature.

Method: The authors use one archived DGCNN pathway on the SEED and SEED-IV datasets. They decompose evaluation into three components (target quantity, development procedure, reporting rule) and systematically examine: (1) protocol-matched subject-dependent checks against public reference values; (2) subject-session trajectories across 30 matched runs with checkpoint selection via repeated test-set evaluation; (3) five-fold subject-disjoint evaluation comparing validation-selected checkpoints; and (4) held-out-subject generalization with BCa bootstrap confidence intervals. Supporting analyses include participant ranking stability across representations/time scales and a tail-risk ensemble evaluation.

Result: Protocol-matched subject-dependent SEED accuracy was within 1.47 points of the public reference; SEED-IV showed a 3.40-point unresolved gap. Repeated test-set checkpoint selection inflated mean window accuracy from 0.7855 to 0.8892. Subject-disjoint validation-selected checkpoints achieved near-perfect training-participant trial accuracy (0.9990 SEED, 0.9920 SEED-IV) but held-out participant accuracy dropped to 0.5348 (SEED) and 0.3954 (SEED-IV).
