The train-to-held-out gaps are inconsistent with simple underfitting. Participant rankings depended on representation and time scale. The tail-risk ensemble produced no positive gain in final evaluation.

Conclusion: Subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, and cross-session results answer different questions and must be reported separately rather than conflated. The evaluation procedure — not merely the classifier — determines reported accuracy, and common practices like repeated test-set checkpoint selection and protocol mismatches produce misleading performance estimates. Decomposing evaluation into target quantity, development procedure, and reporting rule provides a framework for more rigorous EEG emotion recognition research.

Abstract: Reported accuracy in electroencephalography (EEG) emotion recognition depends on the complete evaluation procedure, not only the classifier. We separate the target quantity, development procedure, and reporting rule, then use one archived dynamical graph convolutional neural network (DGCNN) pathway on SEED and SEED-IV as an illustrative case. In a protocol-matched subject-dependent check, the SEED result was within 1.47 percentage points of the public reference value; the 3.40-point SEED-IV difference remained unresolved. Across 30 matched SEED subject-session trajectories, checkpoint selection based on repeated test-set evaluation increased mean window accuracy from 0.7855 at epoch 80 to 0.8892. Under five-fold subject-disjoint evaluation, validation-selected checkpoints achieved training-participant trial accuracies of 0.9990 on SEED and 0.9920 on SEED-IV. Accuracy for entirely held-out participants was 0.5348 (95% conditional subject-level bias-corrected and accelerated [BCa] interval [0.4667, 0.5985]) on SEED. The SEED-IV estimate was 0.3954 ([0.3343, 0.4648]) and is reported only as secondary sensitivity evidence because its protocol-matched compatibility check remained unresolved. The observed train-to-held-out-subject gaps are inconsistent with simple optimization underfitting, but they do not isolate subject identity from implementation, preprocessing, representation, or distributional factors. Supporting analyses further showed that participant rankings depended on representation and time scale, while a development-selected tail-risk ensemble did not establish a positive gain in a separate final evaluation. Subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, and cross-session results should therefore be reported as answers to different questions.

</details>


### [304] [Looped Transformers with Source-Centered State Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27656)
*Bum Jun Kim,Kohei Hayashi,Shunsuke Kamiya,Masanori Koyama,Yusuke Iwasawa,Yutaka Matsuo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SCSE (Source-Centered State Evolution) is a method for looped Transformers that reconciles input conditioning with shared recurrent blocks by designating a learned anchor as a one-step fixed point, using a zero-deviation mask to guarantee exact anchor invariance while allowing nonzero deviations to drive recurrent computation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In looped Transformers with additive injection, the shared block must govern varying hidden states across depths, and input-conditioned signals reintroduced at each step can perturb the state even at a reference point. Existing approaches lack a principled way to preserve a reference while enabling input-dependent recurrence, creating a tension between input conditioning and reference-preserving shared recurrence.

Method: SCSE introduces three key components: (1) a learned anchor and initial deviation that retain input dependence; (2) a recurrence mechanism where nonzero deviations drive computation but zero deviation maps to zero; and (3) a zero-deviation mask that guarantees exact anchor invariance, making the anchor a one-step fixed point by construction. The zero-deviation forcing bias — the deviation produced when starting from the anchor — is explicitly set to zero, resolving a design degree of freedom in favor of anchor invariance.

Result: SCSE improves the controlled recurrent quality frontier across WikiText-2, WikiText-103, direct web-corpus pretraining, held-out web-text transfer, and LAMBADA completion. Ablation studies show the learned anchor and anchor-coordinate deviation recurrence are the primary contributors to performance gains. A case study grounds the anchor-response diagnostic in observed recurrent motion.

Conclusion: SCSE successfully reconciles input conditioning with reference-preserving shared recurrence in looped Transformers by guaranteeing exact anchor invariance. The zero-deviation forcing bias is identified as a design degree of freedom with variable task effects, and SCSE's choice to set it to zero proves beneficial across diverse language modeling benchmarks.

Abstract: Looped Transformers create a useful train- and test-time compute axis by reusing the same Transformer block over recurrent depth, increasing effective depth at a fixed parameter count. However, that shared block must then govern an entire trajectory of varying hidden states over trained and extrapolated depths. Furthermore, in additive-injection looped Transformers, an input-conditioned signal is reintroduced at every recurrent step, so applying the shared transition at an input-conditioned reference can still move the hidden state. In this paper, we propose Source-Centered State Evolution (SCSE), which is designed to reconcile input conditioning with reference-preserving shared recurrence. Specifically, SCSE retains input dependence through its learned anchor and initial deviation, allows nonzero deviations to drive recurrent computation while mapping zero deviation to zero, and guarantees exact anchor invariance through its zero-deviation mask. The designated anchor is thereby a one-step fixed point by construction. The zero-deviation forcing bias is the next deviation produced from the anchor itself and vanishes in SCSE, while nonzero deviations remain active and support state-dependent recurrent computation. Our theory shows that the zero-deviation forcing bias is a design degree of freedom whose task effect can be harmful, neutral, or beneficial; SCSE resolves this choice in favor of exact anchor invariance by setting the bias to zero. Across WikiText-2, WikiText-103, direct web-corpus pretraining, held-out web-text transfer, and LAMBADA completion, SCSE improves the controlled recurrent quality frontier. Ablation studies identify the learned anchor and the anchor-coordinate deviation recurrence as the primary contributors to the gain, and a trained-model case study grounds the anchor-response diagnostic in observed recurrent motion.

</details>


### [305] [Understanding Submodular Information Measure Based Objectives for Representation Learning: A Variance and Separation Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27660)
*Rishabh Iyer,Truong Pham,Anay Majee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper develops a unified theoretical framework linking Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) to classical representation learning concepts. It characterizes three key SIMs under Total Information (TI) and Mutual Information (MI) objectives: Graph Cut relates to variance and centroid separation, LogDet captures covariance-aware structure and Mahalanobis distance, and Facility Location induces imbalance-aware, mode-overlap-sensitive behavior. Controlled synthetic experiments validate these geometric and statistical interpretations, providing principled guidance for SIM-based objective selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite empirical success of SIM-based objectives (e.g., SCORE for contrastive learning), the geometric and statistical properties induced by different submodular information measures remain poorly understood, limiting principled objective selection.

Method: The authors develop a unified theoretical framework that mathematically connects SIM objectives (TI and MI variants of Graph Cut, LogDet, and Facility Location) to classical concepts: within-class and between-class variance, generalized variance/covariance volume, centroid separation, Mahalanobis distance, imbalance-aware separation, and nearest-mode representational overlap. These characterizations are validated through controlled synthetic experiments independently varying variance, covariance, class imbalance, class separation, and multimodal overlap.

Result: Graph Cut TI recovers within-class variance; LogDet TI recovers generalized variance and covariance volume; Facility Location TI induces imbalance-aware separation emphasizing rare/confusable classes. For MI: Graph Cut MI relates to centroid separation and Fisher discrimination; LogDet MI captures covariance-aware separation via Mahalanobis distance; Facility Location MI measures nearest-mode representational overlap. Empirical behavior in synthetic experiments closely matched theoretical predictions across all settings.

Conclusion: The paper provides the first unified geometric and statistical understanding of submodular information measures, offering principled guidance for selecting and designing SIM-based objectives in representation learning.

Abstract: Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for representation learning and multimodal learning. In particular, the SCORE framework~\cite{majee2024score} demonstrated that SIMs can serve as effective objectives for supervised contrastive learning. Despite their empirical success, however, the geometric and statistical properties induced by different submodular information measures remain poorly understood.
  In this work, we develop a unified theoretical framework connecting SIMs to classical concepts in representation learning and statistical pattern recognition. We show that Total Information (TI) objectives characterize intra-class structure: Graph Cut TI recovers within-class variance, LogDet TI recovers generalized variance and covariance volume, and Facility Location TI induces imbalance-aware separation that emphasizes rare and confusable classes. We further show that Mutual Information (MI) objectives capture complementary notions of inter-class structure: Graph Cut MI is closely related to centroid separation and Fisher-style discrimination, LogDet MI captures covariance-aware separation through Mahalanobis distance, and Facility Location MI measures nearest-mode representational overlap.
  We validate these theoretical characterizations using controlled synthetic experiments that independently vary variance, covariance, class imbalance, class separation, and multimodal overlap. Across all settings, the empirical behavior closely matches the proposed theory. Our results provide the first unified geometric and statistical understanding of submodular information measures and offer principled guidance for selecting and designing SIM-based objectives for representation learning.

</details>


### [306] [FedOGL: Combating Catastrophic Forgetting in Federated Open-World Multimodal Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27665)
*Zekai Chen,Haodong Lu,Shihao Li,Weiwei Ji,Xunkai Li,Xun Wu,Yinlin Zhu,Rong-Hua Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FedOGL is a federated graph learning framework that mitigates catastrophic forgetting in multimodal graph streams through client-side semantic-structural memory preservation and server-side category prototype sharing, achieving a 42.67% reduction in forgetting-induced performance degradation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated multimodal graph learning faces a unique catastrophic forgetting problem where old knowledge is erased not only at the classifier level but also through modality-semantic overwriting, topology-induced structural erosion, and federated memory fragmentation. Existing approaches fail to address this compound forgetting mechanism.

Method: FedOGL operates on two fronts: (1) Client-side — preserves historical decision behavior via replay and task-start distillation, and protects graph-propagation memory by projecting onto a globally shared structure basis. (2) Server-side — maintains and transfers compact category prototypes to enable cross-client knowledge sharing without exposing raw graph data.

Result: Compared to the best-performing baselines, FedOGL reduces catastrophic forgetting-induced performance degradation by 42.67%, while maintaining or improving performance on downstream tasks.

Conclusion: FedOGL effectively addresses the multi-faceted catastrophic forgetting problem in federated multimodal graph learning by combining local semantic-structural memory preservation with global prototype-based knowledge transfer.

Abstract: Federated graph learning enables collaborative training over decentralized graph data without sharing raw graph information. As such risks evolve, clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams, retain historical categories, and reject samples outside the known class space. In this setting, clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams while preserving historical categories and rejecting samples outside the current known class space. The core challenge is catastrophic forgetting, which in federated multimodal graphs is not merely a classifier-level failure: old knowledge can be erased through modality-semantic overwriting, topology-induced structural erosion, and federated memory fragmentation. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{FedOGL}, a semantic-structural memory preservation framework. On the client side, FedOGL preserves historical decision behavior through replay and task-start distillation, while protecting graph-propagation memory via projection onto a globally shared structure basis. On the server side, FedOGL maintains and transfers compact category prototypes to facilitate cross-client knowledge sharing without exposing raw graph data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, compared with the best-performing baselines, FedOGL reduces performance degradation caused by catastrophic forgetting by \textbf{42.67\%}, while maintaining or improving performance on downstream tasks.

</details>


### [307] [Tight Sample Complexity for Low-Rank Adaptation: Matching Bounds and Rank Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27680)
*Arunan J*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper provides tight statistical guarantees for Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), establishing matching upper and lower bounds of Θ̃(rd/n) on excess risk. It proves a rank-selection dichotomy: for constrained ERM, the optimal rank equals the intrinsic rank and over-ranking hurts; for nuclear-norm-then-truncate estimators, over-ranking is harmless. Experiments on synthetic and real NLP tasks confirm the predicted U-shaped validation loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LoRA generalization theory provides only upper bounds (Õ(√(rd/n)) or Õ(rd/n)) without matching lower bounds, and offers no formal guidance on choosing the LoRA rank r. This paper aims to close both gaps — establishing tight minimax rates and answering how rank selection affects performance.

Method: The paper uses a local Rademacher complexity argument to derive an upper bound of Õ(rd/n) on excess risk for the empirical risk minimizer over rank-r LoRA. A matching minimax lower bound of Ω(rd/n) is proved via a Fano-type packing construction over the rank-r subspace of R^{d×d}. The analysis assumes a well-specified locally quadratic regime where the target adaptation has rank at most r. For adaptive estimators, a nuclear-norm-then-truncate approach is analyzed. Empirical validation uses synthetic trace-regression and real LoRA fine-tuning on DistilBERT/RoBERTa with SST-2/MRPC.

Result: Three main results: (1) A tight upper bound of Õ(rd/n) via local Rademacher complexity. (2) A matching minimax lower bound of Ω(rd/n) via Fano packing, establishing Θ̃(rd/n) as the minimax rate. (3) A rank-selection dichotomy: constrained ERM suffers from over-ranking (optimal r = r*), while nuclear-norm-then-truncate estimators are robust to over-ranking with rate Θ̃(r*d/n). Experiments confirm U-shaped validation loss across all configurations; two of three configurations show statistically significant loss inflation at large ranks (p = 0.016).

Conclusion: The paper fully characterizes the statistical complexity of LoRA fine-tuning in the well-specified locally quadratic regime. The empirically observed over-parameterization penalty is identified as a property of unregularized ERM rather than the LoRA class itself. The rank-selection dichotomy provides formal guidance: practitioners using constrained ERM must tune rank carefully, whereas those using nuclear-norm-based adaptive methods can safely over-rank.

Abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard mechanism for fine-tuning large pretrained models, yet its statistical properties remain only partially understood. Existing generalization results provide upper bounds of the form O~(sqrt(rd/n)) or O~(rd/n), but a matching lower bound is missing, and the question of how to choose the LoRA rank r has no formal answer. Both gaps are closed here. A local Rademacher argument establishes an upper bound of O~(rd/n) on the excess risk of the empirical risk minimizer over rank-r LoRA, whenever the target adaptation has rank at most r. A matching minimax lower bound of Omega(rd/n) is then proved via a Fano-type packing of the rank-r subspace of R^{d x d}; the bound applies to any estimator whose output lies in the rank-r LoRA class. Combining the two yields a rank-selection dichotomy. For the constrained empirical risk minimizer, the optimal rank equals the intrinsic rank r*, and over-ranking strictly hurts. For adaptive estimators of the nuclear-norm-then-truncate type, over-ranking is harmless and the rate saturates at Theta~(r* d / n) regardless of r. Taken together, the three results characterize the statistical complexity of LoRA fine-tuning within the well-specified locally quadratic regime, and identify the empirically observed over-parameterization penalty as a property of unregularized empirical risk minimization rather than of the LoRA class itself. Predictions of the theory are verified on a synthetic trace-regression benchmark and on real LoRA fine-tuning across three (model, task) configurations covering DistilBERT and RoBERTa on SST-2 and MRPC. All configurations exhibit the predicted U-shape in validation loss, with two showing statistically significant loss inflation at large ranks (paired permutation p = 0.016).

</details>


### [308] [Event-Structured Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Differentiable Critical Clearing Boundaries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27681)
*Baoli Hao,Chenxi Hu,Ming Zhong,Ren Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ES-PINN is a physics-informed neural network that models power system transient stability across pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing phases with exact state chaining, enabling accurate CCT boundary estimation, sensitivity analysis, and direct CCT prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliable critical clearing time (CCT) estimation is challenging due to complicated fault-clearing dynamics requiring repeated simulations over many fault severities and clearing times. Existing methods lack a unified framework that enforces physical consistency across event boundaries.

Method: The authors propose ES-PINN, an event-structured physics-informed neural network that aligns its representation with pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing swing dynamics, enforces exact state chaining across event interfaces, defines a smooth trajectory-induced stability margin as a differentiable CCT boundary approximation, and provides a distilled readout for direct CCT prediction. A local residual-to-trajectory-to-CCT error estimate is also proved.

Result: Experiments on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems show ES-PINN consistently improves held-out trajectory and stability-boundary accuracy over matched neural-surrogate baselines across mechanical and electrical contingencies with multiple clearing configurations. Full-network DAE validation, multi-fault experiments, and runtime analyses further demonstrate effectiveness and computational efficiency.

Conclusion: ES-PINN provides a physically consistent, computationally efficient framework for transient stability assessment that outperforms existing neural surrogates in trajectory and CCT boundary accuracy across multiple test systems and contingency types.

Abstract: Transient-stability assessment determines whether a power system can recover after a disturbance and is therefore essential to preventing generator trips and cascading outages. A key metric is the critical clearing time (CCT), which specifies the maximum time available to clear a fault before synchronism is lost. Reliable CCT estimation is challenging because complicated fault-clearing dynamics require repeated simulations over many fault severities and clearing times. We propose an event-structured physics-informed neural network (ES-PINN) that aligns its representation with the pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing swing dynamics and enforces exact state chaining across event interfaces. A smooth trajectory-induced stability margin defines a differentiable approximation of the CCT boundary, enabling accurate boundary extraction, local sensitivity analysis, and optional direct CCT prediction through a distilled readout. We further prove a local residual-to-trajectory-to-CCT error estimate, in which exact event chaining eliminates separate state-interface defect terms. Experiments on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems show that ES-PINN consistently improves held-out trajectory and stability-boundary accuracy over matched neural-surrogate baselines across mechanical and electrical contingencies with multiple clearing configurations. Additional full-network DAE validation, multi-fault experiments, and runtime analyses further demonstrate the effectiveness and computational efficiency of the proposed framework.

</details>


### [309] [NMINE: Normalized Mutual Information Neural Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27710)
*Petra Eerikinharju,Marko Tuononen,Ville Hautamäki*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a fully neural estimator for normalized mutual information (NMI) combining a MINE-based mutual information estimator with neural marginal entropy estimators. Experiments on 1–8 dimensional Gaussian data show improved accuracy over KSG-based baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mutual information is unbounded and not comparable across datasets or dimensions. Normalized mutual information addresses this, but existing estimators suffer from sensitivity to dimensionality and numerical instability. A neural alternative is needed.

Method: Combines MINE (Donsker-Varadhan representation) for mutual information estimation with MI-NEE-inspired neural marginal entropy estimators that learn divergences from uniform reference distributions to recover entropies. This yields a fully neural NMI estimator as an alternative to k-NN-based approaches.

Result: On Gaussian data spanning 1 to 8 dimensions, the proposed neural NMI estimator outperforms a KSG-based normalized mutual information baseline in accuracy.

Conclusion: Neural estimation is a promising direction for normalized dependency measurement in continuous multidimensional settings.

Abstract: Mutual information is a general measure of statistical dependence that captures both linear and nonlinear relationships between random variables. For continuous and multidimensional variables For continuous multidimensional variables, mutual information must be estimated from samples. Because mutual information is unbounded, its values are not directly comparable across datasets, dimensions, or applications. Normalized mutual information addresses this limitation by converting mutual information into a normalized dependency score. Recent work has demonstrated the practical value of normalized mutual information in applications such as molecular dynamics {arXiv:2405.04980} and interpretable machine learning {arXiv:2409.16768}, but existing estimators remain sensitive to dimensionality and numerical stability {arXiv:2410.07642}.
  In this paper, we propose a fully neural normalized mutual information estimator for continuous variables. The proposed approach combines a MINE-based neural mutual information estimator {arXiv:1801.04062} with MI-NEE-inspired neural marginal entropy estimators {arXiv:1905.12957}. Mutual information is estimated using the Donsker--Varadhan representation, while marginal entropies are estimated by learning the divergence between each marginal distribution and a uniform reference distribution, from which entropy is recovered. The resulting estimator provides a neural alternative to k-nearest-neighbor-based normalized mutual information estimation {arXiv:2405.04980}.
  Experiments on Gaussian data from one to eight dimensions show that the proposed estimator improves accuracy over a KSG-based normalized mutual information baseline. These results indicate that neural estimation is a promising direction for normalized dependency measurement in continuous multidimensional settings.

</details>


### [310] [VESTIGE: A Knowledge-Guided Masking Strategy for Corruption-Aware Fine-Tuning of Genomic Transformers, Validated on Ancient DNA Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27712)
*Angshuman Chakravertty,Rahul Maheshwari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VESTIGE replaces the uniform masking distribution in standard masked language model fine-tuning with an empirically measured, position-specific corruption profile. Applied to ancient DNA reconstruction (where cytosine deamination creates predictable C→T/G→A gradients), it outperforms standard MLM at all tested widths while reducing cross-entropy by 13%, and produces high-fidelity ESMFold protein reconstructions (TM-score > 0.95) even under 10–30× amplified damage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard MLM assumes uniform reconstruction difficulty across token positions, but in degradation processes concentrated at predictable positions (e.g., aDNA termini), this assumption fails: the model can underperform a frequency-matched random predictor at peak damage sites. A masking strategy aligned with the true corruption profile is needed.

Method: VESTIGE is a parameter-free, drop-in replacement for the standard MLM collator. It rescales the empirically measured per-position corruption profile (from mapDamage2 for aDNA) so the mean C/G masking rate equals 15%, identical to standard MLM, isolating spatial redistribution as the sole variable. Tested on DNABERT-2 with a mammoth CDS corpus (two specimens, seven genes) across six terminal-zone widths and 626 paired windows, with model, data, seed, and hyperparameters held fixed. Protein reconstructions via ESMFold; biosecurity classification via 1D CNN.

Result: VESTIGE outperforms standard MLM at all six terminal-zone widths (Δ = +4.18 to +10.35 percentage points, all p < 10⁻⁸), reduces validation cross-entropy by 13% (3.274 vs. 3.757), and yields ESMFold TM-scores > 0.95 across all six reconstructions even under 10–30× amplified damage. Biosecurity AUC = 0.935 with 98.2% of windows cleared; the 1.76% remainder attributed to reference-genome features, not reconstruction artefacts.

Conclusion: VESTIGE demonstrates that aligning the MLM masking distribution with the true corruption profile yields significant performance gains. The principle is domain-agnostic, applicable to any measurable position- or context-specific degradation (FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, nanopore), establishing a knowledge-guided training paradigm for intelligent systems operating on degraded sequence inputs.

Abstract: Standard masked-language-model fine-tuning applies a uniform masking probability across every token position, assuming reconstruction difficulty is position-agnostic. When the degradation process is characterised and concentrated at predictable positions, this assumption fails: at peak damage sites the model can underperform a frequency-matched random predictor. We introduce VESTIGE, a parameter-free, drop-in replacement for the standard MLM collator that aligns the masking distribution with an empirically measured per-position corruption profile. We apply it to ancient DNA (aDNA) reconstruction, where cytosine deamination produces a position-dependent C-to-T / G-to-A gradient quantified per-position by mapDamage2. Rescaling so the mean C/G masking rate equals 15% - identical to standard MLM - isolates spatial redistribution as the sole variable, with model, data, seed, and hyperparameters held fixed across both DNABERT-2 runs on a mammoth CDS corpus (two specimens, seven genes). Across six terminal-zone widths and 626 paired windows, VESTIGE leads standard MLM at every width (Delta = +4.18 to +10.35 pp, all p < 10^-8), cuts validation cross-entropy by 13% (3.274 vs. 3.757), and yields ESMFold reconstructions with TM-score > 0.95 across all six reconstructions (three genes) even under damage amplified 10-30x beyond authentic PMD rates. A 1D CNN biosecurity classifier returns AUC = 0.935 and clears 98.2% of reconstructed windows, the 1.76% remainder attributable to reference-genome features, not reconstruction artefacts. The principle is domain-agnostic: any measurable position- or context-specific corruption profile - FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, or nanopore - substitutes directly for the PMD array, making VESTIGE a knowledge-guided training routine for intelligent systems operating on degraded or noisy sequence inputs.

</details>


### [311] [Towards joint scaling laws with optimal batch size schedules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27731)
*Jiaxiang Li,Zhiqi Bu,Shiyun Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper studies the interplay between learning rate and batch size schedules during training, derives a joint loss characterization from convex optimization, and proposes a closed-form optimal batch size schedule that yields joint scaling laws outperforming static batch size baselines in large language model training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern deep learning practices typically fix the batch size throughout training, ignoring how learning rate and batch size jointly influence training dynamics. The authors aim to address this gap by formally characterizing this joint effect.

Method: The authors analyze deep learning training dynamics through convex optimization theory, deriving a joint characterization of the loss function in terms of both learning rate and batch size schedules. This framework yields a closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any given learning rate schedule, and further produces joint scaling laws.

Result: The proposed dynamic batch size schedule, guided by the derived joint scaling laws, consistently outperforms static batch size baselines in large language model training experiments, demonstrating the practical significance of dynamic scheduling.

Conclusion: Dynamic batch size scheduling is a significant and previously overlooked factor in training dynamics. The joint characterization and scaling laws provide a principled approach to tuning both schedules simultaneously, with clear empirical benefits for large-scale model training.

Abstract: Modern deep learning typically keeps the batch size static throughout training, thus overlooking the joint effect of learning rate and batch size on the training dynamics. In this paper, we study the deep learning dynamics through the lens of convex optimization and derive a joint characterization of loss in terms of both schedules, applicable to general optimizers and model architectures. This characterization yields a closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any prescribed learning rate schedule, and further leads to joint scaling laws that consistently outperform static batch size baselines, highlighting the significance of dynamic batch size schedule in large language model training.

</details>


### [312] [Improving the Robustness/Accuracy Tradeoff Against Adversarial Attacks Using Information Bottleneck Distillation Through Dual Teachers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27737)
*Vincent Ryusuke Takahashi,Yoshinari Takeishi,Jun'ichi Takeuchi,Kave Salamatian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper extends the Information Bottleneck Distillation (IBD) framework by introducing a dual-teacher distillation approach: a clean teacher (trained on clean inputs only) and a robust teacher (trained via adversarial training). A cross-layer attention matrix transfers features from both teachers to the student, improving clean accuracy over IBD while preserving adversarial robustness. Results on CIFAR-10/100 are competitive with state-of-the-art methods like B-MTARD, especially on the harmonic mean metric.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing adversarial defense methods like IBD improve robustness but at the cost of degraded accuracy on clean inputs. The authors aim to mitigate this trade-off by enriching the distillation process with both clean and robust knowledge sources.

Method: The proposed method adds a clean teacher model (trained solely on clean inputs) alongside the standard robust teacher from IBD. Both teachers' features are transferred to the student via a cross-layer attention matrix mechanism during distillation. The student thus learns from both clean and adversarially robust representations simultaneously.

Result: On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, the method achieves higher clean accuracy than the original IBD while maintaining comparable adversarial accuracy. It is competitive with state-of-the-art dual-teacher methods (specifically B-MTARD), particularly measured by the harmonic mean between clean and robust accuracy. Additional analysis explores how different training settings affect the attention module.

Conclusion: Incorporating a clean teacher into the IBD distillation framework effectively mitigates the clean-vs-robust accuracy trade-off. The cross-layer attention-based dual-teacher approach yields a better balanced model, demonstrating that clean and robust knowledge can be complementary in adversarial defense.

Abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in classical machine learning problems. However, they are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Countermeasures proposed in the literature, notably Information Bottleneck Distillation (IBD) introduced by Kuang et al., degrade the classification accuracy on clean inputs while improving the robustness to adversarial inputs. In this work, we extend the IBD framework by introducing an extra teacher model (clean teacher) trained with only clean inputs, into the distillation process from a robust teacher model trained by adversarial training. The features of both clean and robust teachers are transferred to the student through a cross-layer attention matrix. Experimental results on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets show that the proposed method improves classification accuracy on clean samples compared to the original IBD, while maintaining similar accuracy on adversarial samples. Furthermore, our methods are competitive with state-of-the-art approaches, including the recent dual-teacher distillation framework B-MTARD, particularly in terms of the harmonic mean between clean and robust accuracy. We also analyze the impact of different training settings that have different influences on the attention module.

</details>


### [313] [DAS-PMVC: A Framework for Partial Multi-View Clustering via Dual Alignment and Structure Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27761)
*Shubin Ma,Liang Zhao,Chuanye He,Zhenjiao Liu,Liang Zou,Lin Yuanbo Wu,Yu Shao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DAS-PMVC proposes a partial multi-view clustering framework that addresses view misalignment through anchor graph structure alignment, structure-enhanced feature learning, and a dual alignment strategy combining contrastive learning with the Hungarian algorithm, achieving state-of-the-art clustering performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-view clustering suffers from the partial view alignment problem (PVAP), where data across different views are misaligned due to limitations in data collection devices. Existing methods struggle with view asymmetry and irrelevant samples, necessitating a framework that leverages view structure consistency and semantic relevance to mitigate these issues.

Method: DAS-PMVC comprises three components: (1) anchor graph structure alignment, which derives joint embedding representations with consistent latent space from anchor point relationships for initial view alignment; (2) structure-enhanced feature learning, which pretrains on view structure information and employs multi-view graph convolutional networks to extract deep latent features from the aligned graph, enhancing representation discriminability; (3) a dual alignment strategy, performing initial alignment via the anchor graph during pretraining, then refining alignment of latent features through contrastive learning loss and the Hungarian algorithm during training.

Result: Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that the DAS-PMVC framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in clustering performance.

Conclusion: The DAS-PMVC framework effectively addresses the partial view alignment problem in multi-view clustering by combining anchor graph alignment, structure-enhanced feature learning, and dual alignment optimization, showcasing superior effectiveness and superiority over current methods.

Abstract: In recent years, multi-view clustering has attracted widespread research interest. However, due to limitations in data collection devices, data across different views often suffer from misalignment, leading to the partial view alignment problem (PVAP). To mitigate the impact of view asymmetry and irrelevant samples, this paper proposes a framework for partial multi-view clustering via dual alignment and structure enhancement (DAS-PMVC), which leverages view structure consistency and semantic relevance. Specifically, DAS-PMVC includes three parts: \textbf{anchor graph structure alignment}, where sample joint embedding representations with consistent latent space are derived from anchor point relationships for initial view alignment; \textbf{structure-enhanced feature learning}, where the model learns view structure information through pretraining and combines multi-view graph convolutional networks to further extract deep latent features from the aligned graph structure to improve the discriminative power of representations; and \textbf{a dual alignment strategy}, where initial alignment is performed through the anchor graph in the pretraining phase, and contrastive learning loss and the Hungarian algorithm are introduced in the training phase to further optimize the alignment of latent features. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that the DAS-PMVC framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in clustering performance, showcasing its effectiveness and superiority.

</details>


### [314] [Train Small, Deploy Large: Zero-Shot GNN Transfer Through Geometric Renormalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27767)
*Robert Jankowski,Pedro Almagro-Blanco,Marián Boguñá,Melanie Weber,M. Ángeles Serrano*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GNNs trained on geometrically renormalized (coarse-grained) replicas of large graphs can be directly transferred to the full-resolution graph with minimal performance loss, suggesting structural similarity matters more than graph size for transferability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training GNNs on massive graphs (millions of nodes) is infrastructure-sensitive and costly. The authors ask whether a model trained on a smaller, scaled-down replica can be deployed zero-shot on the full graph, obviating the need for expensive large-scale retraining.

Method: The authors propose a zero-shot transfer protocol: a GNN is trained on a coarse-grained version of the target graph produced via geometric renormalization (GR). The learned weights are then directly transferred to the original, full-resolution graph without any fine-tuning or retraining. Experiments span synthetic and real-world networks.

Result: Training on GR-scaled replicas preserves much of the original-scale predictive performance while dramatically reducing training cost. Learned representations and predictive trajectories remain aligned across scales, and structural similarity rather than network size emerges as the key factor governing transferability.

Conclusion: The findings indicate that scale-equivariant graph architectures are feasible and that structural similarity is more critical than sheer size for GNN transferability, opening a path toward more efficient large-scale graph learning.

Abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) can operate on large graphs but become infrastructure-sensitive at the scale of millions of nodes and typically require scalable training techniques for even larger graphs. This raises a central question: when can a model trained on a smaller, scaled-down replica of a graph be deployed on the full-resolution graph without retraining? We introduce a zero-shot transfer protocol in which a GNN is trained on a graph coarse-grained by geometric renormalization (GR), and the resulting weights are transferred directly to the original network. Across synthetic and real-world networks, training on GR scaled-down replicas preserves much of the original-scale predictive performance while significantly reducing training cost. We further find that learned representations and predictive trajectories remain aligned across scales. These findings suggest that structural similarity may be more important than network size in determining GNN transferability, opening a path toward scale-equivariant graph architectures.

</details>


### [315] [Beyond the Best Teacher: Expanding and Compressing the Reasoning Solution Manifold](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27770)
*Songshuo Lu,Zhi Chen,Yaohua Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RL-trained models often amplify only a subset of valid solution modes. The paper proposes an expand-then-compress framework: first training a complementary set of teachers via RGRPO, then distilling them into a single student via reliability-gated on-policy distillation with consensus-residual decomposition. The resulting student outperforms the strongest individual teacher across math, code, and instruction-following tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement learning amplifies only a subset of valid reasoning modes, so individual RL-trained policies should be viewed as local probes of a multi-basin solution manifold rather than globally reliable supervisors. A single teacher's incompleteness limits student performance.

Method: An expand-then-compress framework: (1) Expansion stage uses Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization (RGRPO) to train a sequence of teachers from a common initialization, with each round redirected toward examples uncovered by the accumulated teacher union. (2) Compression stage uses reliability-gated Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation (TU-OPD), where the student learns from its own response prefixes, with only reliable teachers contributing per example. (3) Consensus-Residual Decomposition preserves a winner teacher's excess token preferences over reliable peers to prevent specialist suppression during aggregation.

Result: On Qwen3-1.7B, the distilled student outperforms the strongest individual teacher across mathematical reasoning (+2.0%), code generation (+8.3%), and instruction following (+6.9%), while maintaining single-model inference.

Conclusion: Stronger students emerge not from selecting a single better teacher, but from deliberately constructing and compressing a complementary teacher union. The framework is domain-agnostic and establishes a simple yet powerful principle for multi-teacher distillation.

Abstract: A single reinforcement-learning run can produce a strong reasoner yet an incomplete teacher: it often amplifies only a subset of the valid solution modes. We argue that reinforcement learning (RL)-trained policies should therefore be viewed as local probes of a multi-basin reasoning solution manifold, rather than as globally reliable supervisors. Based on this view, we propose an expand-then-compress framework that couples teacher construction with multi-teacher policy distillation. In the expansion stage, Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization (RGRPO) trains a sequence of teachers from a common initialization and redirects each later round toward examples not yet covered by the accumulated teacher union. In the compression stage, reliability-gated Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation (TU-OPD) lets the student learn from its own response prefixes. For each example, only reliable teachers contribute, and their sampled-token OPD losses are weighted by their per-example quality. We further introduce Consensus-Residual Decomposition, which preserves a winner teacher's excess token preferences over its reliable peers, preventing specialist behavior from being suppressed during teacher aggregation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following show that the resulting Qwen3-1.7B student consistently outperforms the strongest individual teacher across all three domains, yielding relative improvements of 2.0%, 8.3%, and 6.9%, respectively, while retaining single-model inference. These results establish a simple but powerful principle: stronger students can be obtained not by selecting a single better teacher, but by deliberately constructing and compressing a complementary teacher union.

</details>


### [316] [RIPPLE: Generating Multi-Channel Phase, Not Recovering It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27775)
*Jaehyuk Lee,Yeajin Lee,Dayeon Shin,Donghun Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RIPPLE proposes generating, not recovering, multi-channel phase by using Griffin–Lim as a phase prior refined via rectified flow with an inter-channel phase loss, dramatically improving physical coherence metrics in spatial audio and seismograms where channel-independent recovery fails.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multi-channel waveforms (spatial audio, three-component seismograms), the physical content resides in inter-channel phase relationships. Standard pipelines generate magnitude spectra and recover phase per-channel (via Griffin–Lim, vocoders, or latent decoders), which cannot capture cross-channel phase structure. Magnitude-based metrics fail to detect this collapse, so pipelines score well while discarding physically critical information.

Method: RIPPLE reinterprets Griffin–Lim as a phase **prior** rather than a final estimator. Starting from the source phase (carrying inter-channel structure), a rectified flow model refines this prior toward the target phase. An explicit inter-channel phase coherence loss is applied during training. The method is generator-agnostic and tested across two domains: first-order ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation.

Result: RIPPLE outperforms recovery-based pipelines on coherence metrics used in downstream analyses. In the seismic case, per-channel recovery leaves S-wave polarization error near the random-expectation baseline of 57.3°, while learned phase reduces it to 33.8°—a decisive improvement consistent across architecturally distinct generators.

Conclusion: Phase should be generated rather than recovered in multi-channel settings. RIPPLE demonstrates that treating Griffin–Lim as a learnable prior, combined with rectified flow and inter-channel phase losses, restores the physical coherence that channel-independent recovery destroys, with results generalizing across unrelated physical domains.

Abstract: Generative models synthesize magnitude spectra with high fidelity, while phase is delegated to a recovery module---Griffin--Lim, a vocoder, or a latent decoder---applied independently to each channel. For multi-channel waveforms this delegation is costly: the physical content of spatial audio and three-component seismograms lives in the phase relationships between channels, precisely what channel-independent recovery cannot produce. The cost is also invisible, since the magnitude-based metrics common to both fields barely move when inter-channel phase coherence collapses---so a pipeline can discard the physical information in its output while still scoring well. We argue that phase should be generated, not recovered, and present RIPPLE (Rectified Inter-channel Phase with Prior-based LEarning), which reinterprets Griffin--Lim as a phase **prior** rather than a final estimator: initialized from the source phase, this prior carries the inter-channel structure to be preserved, and a rectified flow refines it toward the target under an explicit inter-channel phase loss. Tested on first-order ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation---two physically unrelated domains---RIPPLE outperforms recovery-based pipelines on the coherence metrics that downstream analyses consume. The seismic case is decisive: across architecturally distinct generators, per-channel recovery leaves S-wave polarization error near the $57.3^\circ$ random expectation, whereas learned phase reduces it to $33.8^\circ$.

</details>


### [317] [LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO): A Sampling-Time Low-Rank Scaffold for Recovering Reinforcement-Learning Gradient on Zero-Reward Cliff Prompts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27787)
*Ken Ding*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GRPO suffers from zero-gradient on "cliff" prompts where all rollouts fail. LSPO addresses this by fitting a temporary LoRA adapter on cliff prompts via supervised learning, re-rolling with the adapter, splicing successful completions back into the RL batch with importance-sampling correction, then discarding the adapter. LSPO outperforms DAPO across all 16 benchmark cells on DeepMath-103K.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In RLVR with GRPO, when all sampled rollouts for a prompt fail (termed "cliff" prompts), the group-normalized advantage is identically zero, yielding no gradient. This is a structural blind spot precisely at the frontier of the model's capability, where learning signal is most needed.

Method: LSPO operates per RL step: (1) detect cliff prompts (all rollouts incorrect), (2) fit a low-rank LoRA adapter via a brief supervised step on ground-truth solutions of cliff prompts, (3) re-roll cliff prompts using base+adapter, (4) splice successful completions into the RL batch with importance-sampling correction, (5) take a GRPO step on the base model only (adapter receives only supervised gradient), (6) discard adapter at checkpoint, yielding a base-only model.

Result: On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, across n=5 paired seeds at 1000 steps, LSPO matches or beats DAPO on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells: 15 strict wins, 1 tie. Gains include +10.7 pts on AIME24/pass@4, +6.7 on AIME24 & AIME26/pass@16, +2.4 on MATH500/pass@1. Mean improvement across all 16 cells: +3.8 points.

Conclusion: LSPO effectively recovers gradient signal from cliff prompts via a lightweight, disposable LoRA scaffolding mechanism, yielding consistent and substantial gains over DAPO across diverse math reasoning benchmarks without altering the final base model architecture.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) for mathematical reasoning suffers from a structural blind spot: on "cliff" prompts-those on which every sampled rollout in a group fails-the group-normalized advantage is identically zero, so GRPO produces no gradient on precisely the prompts at the frontier of the model's capability. We introduce LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO), a sampling-time mechanism that recovers this lost gradient. Each RL step, LSPO detects cliff prompts, fits a small low-rank (LoRA) adapter by a brief supervised step on their ground-truth solutions, re-rolls the cliffs with the base-plus-adapter model, splices the now-successful completions back into the RL batch with an importance-sampling correction, and takes a GRPO step on the base alone; the adapter receives only the supervised gradient and is discarded at checkpoint, yielding a base-only model. On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, evaluated over n=5 paired seeds per arm at a matched 1000-step reporting horizon, LSPO's 5-seed mean matches or beats a DAPO baseline on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells (15 strict wins and one exact tie), with gains of up to +10.7 points on AIME24/pass@4, +6.7 points on AIME24 and AIME26 at pass@16, and +2.4 points on MATH500/pass@1; averaged over the 16 cells the improvement is +3.8 points.

</details>


### [318] [Revisiting Predictive Process Monitoring in the Age of Foundation Models: A Comparative Study of Sequence, Tabular, and LLM Approaches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27797)
*Lennart Fertig,Lukas Kirchdorfer,Tobias Sesterhenn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A benchmark study comparing three modeling paradigms—classical deep sequence models (LSTMs), large language models (LLMs), and tabular foundation models with in-context learning—for predictive process monitoring across multiple datasets and tasks. Sequence models excel at next-activity prediction; tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal tasks; LLMs underperform despite higher cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The PPM field has been dominated by deep sequence models trained from scratch, but foundation models (LLMs and tabular foundation models) are emerging as alternatives. No systematic benchmark exists comparing these three paradigms, leaving unclear whether classical sequence models remain competitive.

Method: Controlled empirical benchmark comparing LSTM-based sequence models, LLM-based approaches, and tabular foundation models with in-context learning across multiple real-world event log datasets and standard PPM prediction tasks (next activity prediction, remaining time, time to next event). Both conceptual and empirical comparisons are provided.

Result: Sequence models (LSTMs) consistently perform best for next activity prediction. Tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal prediction tasks (remaining time, time to next event). LLMs generally lag behind all other approaches while incurring substantially higher computational cost.

Conclusion: Classical sequence models remain the strongest choice for next activity prediction in PPM. Tabular foundation models present a viable alternative for temporal tasks. LLMs, despite their popularity, are not yet competitive for PPM tasks given their inferior performance and higher cost.

Abstract: Predictive process monitoring (PPM) leverages event logs to forecast the future of running process instances, for instance, predicting the next activity, the remaining time until case completion, or the time to the next event. While PPM research in recent years has been dominated by deep sequence models trained from scratch, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models, foundation-model approaches---particularly large language models (LLMs)---are increasingly explored for PPM. At the same time, tabular foundation models with in-context learning capabilities offer a promising alternative but have not yet been systematically benchmarked for PPM. Thus, it remains unclear whether classical sequence-based models remain competitive in this evolving landscape. This paper compares the three modeling paradigms both conceptually and empirically through a controlled benchmark across multiple datasets and prediction tasks. The results show that sequence models consistently perform best for next activity prediction, whereas tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal tasks, with LLMs usually lagging behind despite higher cost.

</details>


### [319] [Learning-Augmented and Randomized Algorithms for Line Aggregation with Delays](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27807)
*Tianhang Lu,Runtian Ren,Shengcai Liu,Ke Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper designs learning-augmented and randomized algorithms for online aggregation with delays on a line metric. It proposes deterministic and randomized algorithms with formal robustness-consistency trade-offs, improves the randomized competitive ratio from the deterministic lower bound of 4 to e+1, and establishes a new lower bound of e for randomized algorithms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Online aggregation with delays is a fundamental problem where requests must be served with a latency-cost trade-off. Prior deterministic algorithms (e.g., Balance) achieve a 5-competitive ratio, bounded below by 4. The authors aim to improve upon this using randomization (which can bypass deterministic lower bounds) and to incorporate machine-learned advice (suggested service lengths) to achieve better practical performance while maintaining worst-case guarantees.

Method: The authors propose: (1) A deterministic learning-augmented Balance algorithm achieving (4/λ+1/λ²)-robustness and (4+λ)-consistency for λ∈(0,1]. (2) A randomized algorithm in the classical adversarial model with (e+1)-competitiveness against an oblivious adversary. (3) A randomized learning-augmented algorithm combining both ideas, achieving (e/λ+1/λ²)-robustness and (e+λ)-consistency. They also prove a lower bound of e for randomized algorithms. Numerical experiments validate the theoretical findings.

Result: The deterministic learning-augmented algorithm achieves (4/λ+1/λ²)-robustness and (4+λ)-consistency. The randomized algorithm achieves (e+1)-competitive ratio, improving over the deterministic 5-competitive benchmark and beating the deterministic lower bound of 4. The lower bound for randomized algorithms is tightened from e/(e-1) to e. The combined randomized learning-augmented algorithm achieves (e/λ+1/λ²)-robustness and (e+λ)-consistency.

Conclusion: Randomization and learning augmentation both provide significant improvements for online aggregation with delays. The randomized (e+1)-competitive ratio surpasses deterministic limits, and the e lower bound nearly matches this. Learning-augmented variants offer smooth robustness-consistency trade-offs, making them practically adaptable based on advice quality.

Abstract: This paper studies learning-augmented and randomized online aggregation with delays on a line metric. We consider advice given as online suggested service lengths, and evaluate the algorithms in terms of robustness and consistency. For each $λ\in (0,1]$, we first propose a deterministic learning-augmented \textsc{Balance} algorithm that is $(4/λ+1/λ^2)$-robust and $(4+λ)$-consistent. We also propose a randomized algorithm for the problem in the classical adversarial model, which is $(e+1)$-competitive against an oblivious adversary, improving over the deterministic $5$-competitive \textsc{Balance} benchmark~\cite{bienkowski2013chain}. Notably, this competitive ratio is even lower than the lower bound of $4$ for deterministic online algorithms. Moreover, we establish a lower bound of $e$ on the competitive ratio of randomized online algorithms, improving the previous lower bound of $e/(e-1)$. Besides, we combine the two ideas and obtain a randomized learning-augmented algorithm that is $(e/λ+1/λ^2)$-robust and $(e+λ)$-consistent. Finally, we conduct numerical experiments to complement our theoretical analysis and evaluate the empirical performance of our algorithms.

</details>


### [320] [Contrastive Concept Importance: Explaining Pairwise Class Decisions Through Automatically Extracted Concept Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27904)
*Roel Visser,Isaac Roberts,Barbara Hammer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Contrastive Concept Importance (CCI) attributes the logit margin between a target class and a foil class to semantic concepts, producing signed scores that reveal whether concepts support the target or the foil, enabling analysis of class-pair-specific model behavior beyond standard single-class concept attribution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard concept-based explanations answer only "why P?" by attributing contributions to a single output class. In practical scenarios—misclassification, class confusion, low-margin predictions—the more relevant question is "why P rather than Q?" Existing methods lack a principled way to provide contrastive concept attributions that decompose the logit margin between two classes.

Method: CCI computes concept importance scores by attributing the logit difference between a target class and a foil class to concepts in an automatically extracted visual concept basis (CRAFT-style). The resulting scores are signed (positive = supports target over foil; negative = supports foil over target) and can be decomposed into target-logit and foil-logit effects. This decomposition distinguishes globally important concepts from those specifically influencing a class-pair distinction, categorized as shared, one-sided, or directly contrastive.

Result: Evaluated on ImageNet class pairs, CCI reveals class-pair-specific model behavior not captured by ordinary (non-contrastive) concept importance. Highly contrastive concepts align with semantic superclass structure, indicating they affect fine-grained distinctions rather than broad category evidence. Insertion/deletion curves and logit-wise decomposition analysis validate the method's effectiveness.

Conclusion: CCI provides a principled framework for contrastive concept-based explanations, answering "why P rather than Q?" by attributing logit margins to semantic concepts. The signed, decomposable scores enable finer-grained analysis of model decision boundaries and class confusion, complementing existing single-class concept attribution methods.

Abstract: Concept-based explanations are a prevalent way to explain the decisions of complex black-box methods through semantically meaningful, human-interpretable concepts. To attribute the contribution of such concepts to a model's decisions, feature attribution methods are used to quantify how strongly each concept contributes to a model output. These attributions are typically computed for a single output class and therefore answer a non-contrastive "why P?" question. In many situations, however, such as cases of misclassification, class confusion, and low-margin predictions, the more natural question to ask is "why P rather than Q?".
  We introduce contrastive concept importance (CCI), which attributes the logit margin between a target class and a contrast, or foil, class to concepts in an automatically extracted visual concept basis. The resulting scores are signed, indicating whether a concept supports the target over the foil or the foil over the target, and can be decomposed into target-logit and foil-logit effects. This makes it possible to distinguish globally important concepts from concepts that specifically influence a class-pair distinction, including whether their effect is shared, one-sided, or directly contrastive.
  We evaluate the method on ImageNet class pairs using CRAFT-style concept bases, insertion and deletion curves, logit-wise decomposition analysis, and semantic class hierarchy. The results show that contrastive concept importance reveals class-pair-specific model behavior that is not captured by ordinary concept importance alone, and that highly contrastive concepts can be evaluated against semantic superclass structure to assess whether they affect fine-grained distinctions rather than broad category evidence.

</details>


### [321] [Class-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Counterfactual Explanation Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27905)
*Muhammad Adil Saleem,Syed Ali Raza,Mary-Anne Williams*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Adding predicted class information to the RL state representation significantly improves counterfactual explanation generation, yielding faster convergence, higher validity, and more effective exploration across diverse datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work using RL for counterfactual explanation generation formulates states exclusively from predictor features, ignoring the instance's predicted class. The authors hypothesize that incorporating class-awareness into the RL state representation can enhance exploration efficiency and policy optimality.

Method: The authors propose a class-aware RL method that includes the instance's predicted class alongside predictor-derived features in the state representation. This is compared against a class-blind RL baseline (identical except for excluding class information). Experiments span seven datasets from diverse domains and varying sizes. Feature importance is assessed post hoc using SHAP and LIME to evaluate the contribution of class-based features in action selection.

Result: Class-aware RL consistently outperforms class-blind RL in convergence speed, reward optimization, and episode length reduction during training. It generates significantly more valid counterfactual explanations. SHAP and LIME analyses reveal that the instance's class-based feature consistently ranks among the most influential predictors in the RL agent's action selection.

Conclusion: Class-awareness in RL state representation yields heightened clarity, faster learning, improved validity, and more effective counterfactual generation. Incorporating predicted class information is a simple yet impactful enhancement for RL-based CFE generation methods.

Abstract: Counterfactual explanations (CFEs) enhance the interpretability of black-box models by generating alternative instances with adjusted feature values that achieve a contrastive outcome. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising approach for CFE generation, enabling efficient exploration of counterfactual instances while ensuring control over key metrics like validity, sparsity, and proximity. Previous studies have formulated RL states exclusively using features derived from the predictors in the supervised dataset. This study explores the impact of including an instance's predicted class, alongside features derived from the predictors, in the RL state representation for generating CFEs. The hypothesis is that class-awareness enhances exploration efficiency and improves policy optimality. We compare the proposed class-aware RL method with the class-blind RL method, which is similar but excludes the instance's class information from the state representation. The comparison was conducted using seven datasets from diverse domains, varying in size. The results show that during training, class-aware RL offers benefits in terms of convergence speed, reward optimization, and episode length reduction. Moreover, it generates significantly more valid CFEs compared to class-blind RL. Finally, the instance's class-based feature consistently ranks among the most influential predictors in RL's action-selection, as shown by the SHAP and LIME values, underscoring the significance of class-awareness in RL for CFE generation. The impact is heightened clarity, faster learning, improved validity, and more effective counterfactual generation across diverse datasets.

</details>


### [322] [S-CEReBrO: Breaking the Memory Barrier in Continuous EEG Monitoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27913)
*Glenn Anta Bucagu,Thorir Mar Ingolfsson,Yawei Li,Luca Benini*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: S-CEReBrO introduces Windowed Alternating Attention to overcome Transformer memory bottlenecks in continuous EEG monitoring, achieving constant KV-cache memory, processing signals 100X longer than full self-attention, and reaching SOTA on 7 of 11 downstream tasks with up to 60% fewer parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformer-based EEG foundation models suffer from global attention mechanisms that tie attention memory state to signal duration, causing memory overflow during continuous monitoring. This makes them impractical for real-world, long-duration EEG applications.

Method: The authors propose S-CEReBrO, which uses a novel Windowed Alternating Attention mechanism that factorizes attention into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows. This ensures constant KV-cache memory by keeping only the active window's attention maps resident. The model is pre-trained on over 25,000 hours of EEG from 12,000+ subjects.

Result: Windowed alternating attention processes signals 100X longer than full self-attention and 3X longer than low-rank linear attention. It uses 55% of the memory and achieves 2.1X inference throughput compared to low-rank linear attention on long contexts. S-CEReBrO achieves SOTA on 7 of 11 downstream tasks with up to 60% fewer parameters.

Conclusion: S-CEReBrO represents a significant advance toward efficient, generalizable, and continuous EEG monitoring, addressing the core memory bottleneck that limited prior Transformer-based approaches in this domain.

Abstract: Foundation models offer a promising paradigm for Electroencephalography (EEG) analysis, leveraging generalizable representations from vast unlabeled datasets. Yet, Transformer-based architectures face a critical bottleneck: global attention mechanisms couple the attention memory state to the signal duration, causing memory overflow during continuous monitoring. To address this, we introduce S-CEReBrO (Streaming CEReBrO), an evolution of the CEReBrO architecture designed for continuous monitoring. Our novel Windowed Alternating Attention mechanism factorizes attention computation into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows, guaranteeing constant KV cache memory as only the active window requires resident attention maps. Empirical scaling analysis confirms that windowed alternating attention can process signals 100X longer than full self-attention and 3X longer than low-rank linear attention. Compared to low-rank linear attention on long contexts, windowed alternating attention requires 55% of the memory while increasing inference throughput by 2.1X. Pre-trained on >25,000 hours of recordings from >12,000 subjects, S-CEReBrO achieves state-of-the-art performance on 7 of 11 downstream tasks, with up to 60% fewer parameters. This work represents a significant step toward the realization of efficient, generalizable, and continuous EEG monitoring. An accompanying code repository is available.

</details>


### [323] [Exact Action Values Are Not Enough: Rollout-Verified Reinforcement Fine-Tuning of a Reasoning Model for Multi-Zone VAV Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27914)
*Takumi Shioda,Kohei Terashima,Tatsuo Nagai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A reasoning LLM (GPT-5) achieved competitive VAV control without building-specific training, but attempts to transfer this knowledge to a smaller open-weight model via TD3-guided reinforcement fine-tuning failed — the learned critic had unreliable within-state ranking despite near-perfect correlation, and RFT produced no sustained improvement, motivating transition-focused SFT before value-based RFT.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model predictive control and reinforcement learning for multi-zone VAV systems require building-specific modeling or training, limiting scalability. The authors investigate whether frontier reasoning LLMs can perform zero-shot VAV control from text, and whether that knowledge can be transferred to locally deployable open-weight models via reinforcement fine-tuning.

Method: Five controllers are evaluated in a physics-based four-zone emulator over three summer days: a Guideline 36 baseline, TD3, GPT-5 (zero-shot text prompting), and an open-weight model before/after TD3-guided RFT (200 steps with deterministic rollouts that restore state, apply one candidate action, and score via TD3). A critic audit compares across-time correlation vs. within-state action ranking. Transition prediction quality is also assessed.

Result: TD3 reduced HVAC electricity 4.5% vs. baseline with better temperature/CO2 compliance. GPT-5 achieved the largest reduction (6.2%) but with reduced ventilation margin. The learned critic showed near-perfect across-time correlation (r=0.9998) yet correctly identified the rollout-best action in only 5/10 states. RFT produced no sustained improvement; the open-weight model used more electricity than baseline and had 5-min predictions worse than persistence. GPT-5 predicted transitions far better.

Conclusion: Exact rollout scores rank actions but reveal neither next-state effects nor improvement direction. The unchanged transition errors after RFT suggest that transition-focused supervised fine-tuning should precede value-based RFT when distilling control knowledge from reasoning LLMs to smaller models.

Abstract: Multi-zone variable-air-volume control must balance thermal comfort, indoor air quality, and electricity use across several continuous actuators. Model predictive control and reinforcement learning are widely studied, but deployment typically requires building-specific modeling or training, limiting scalability. We first test whether a frontier reasoning model (an LLM trained to use additional inference-time computation) can achieve competitive VAV control from text without building-specific training. With that capability established, we then test whether TD3-guided reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) can transfer control knowledge into a locally deployable open-weight model. Five controllers are evaluated over three summer days in a physics-based four-zone emulator. Relative to a Guideline 36-based baseline, TD3 reduced HVAC electricity by 4.5% while improving temperature and CO$_2$ compliance. Without building-specific training, GPT-5 achieved the largest reduction (6.2%) but reduced the ventilation margin. For RFT, deterministic rollouts restore a saved state, apply one candidate, and follow TD3 to score each action. Auditing a learned critic against these rollouts exposed a failure hidden by its near-perfect across-time correlation ($r=0.9998$): within-state ranking was unreliable; the critic selected the rollout-best candidate in only 5 of 10 states. Even with the rollout verifier, 200 RFT steps produced no sustained improvement in sampled-action return; the open-weight controller used more electricity than the baseline before and after training, and its five-minute predictions remained worse than persistence. GPT-5 predicted transitions far better. Exact rollout scores rank sampled actions but reveal neither next-state effects nor an improvement direction. The unchanged transition errors motivate transition-focused supervised fine-tuning before value-based RFT.

</details>


### [324] [ODEWorld: A Continuous Predictive Architecture via Physical-Time Flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27924)
*Dongxiu Liu,Haoyi Niu,Peng Cheng,Yuan Gao,Xirui Kang,Sangli Teng,Koushil Sreenath,Xianyuan Zhan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ODEWorld introduces PT-Flow, a continuous-time latent world model that uses ODEs to parameterize dynamics, enabling efficient, arbitrary-resolution prediction (forward/backward) while resolving representation collapse and supporting both video generation and robotic control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physical time is continuous, yet existing world models operate in discrete time, leading to inefficiency in capturing real-world dynamics. The authors aim to bridge this gap with a continuous-time formulation.

Method: PT-Flow learns a continuous latent velocity field governed by an ODE in a structured representation space. Future prediction becomes temporal integration via an ODE solver. ODEWorld extracts time-variant features and enforces ODE properties on both the representation space and the velocity field to prevent representation collapse, enabling long-horizon reconstruction, arbitrary temporal resolution, and backward prediction.

Result: ODEWorld demonstrated strong performance in both video generation and robotic control tasks, successfully reconciling planning-oriented dynamics abstraction with visual realism.

Conclusion: ODEWorld offers a versatile, efficient continuous-time latent world model that outperforms discrete-time counterparts, particularly in long-horizon prediction, temporal flexibility, and downstream policy learning for control.

Abstract: In the physical world we inhabit, space and time are fundamentally continuous. However, existing machine learning paradigms for world modeling are largely confined to discrete-time prediction, thereby exhibiting significant inefficiency in capturing the dynamics of physical world. We introduce Physical-Time Flow (\textbf{PT-Flow}), a novel approach that learns a continuous latent velocity field operating in physical time. Crucially, the underlying dynamics of sequential data are parameterized by an ordinary differential equation (ODE) embedded in a well-structured representation space. Under this paradigm, the prediction of future can be recast as temporal integration via an ODE solver in the compressed latent space. Building upon PT-Flow, we construct \textbf{ODEWorld}, a continuous-time latent world model that is both efficient and versatile. By extracting time-variant features and enforcing ODE properties on both the dynamical representation space and the latent velocity field, ODEWorld effectively addresses the long-standing representation collapse issue in latent world model literature. This also enables high-quality image reconstruction even after long-horizon prediction. Moreover, its continuous nature allows for arbitrary temporal resolution and even backward prediction, which is impossible for most discrete-time models. Lastly, ODEWorld can provide rich planning-oriented information to facilitate downstream policy learning. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that ODEWorld successfully reconciles planning-conducive dynamics abstraction with visual realism, excelling in both video generation and robotic control. \href{https://dstate.github.io/odeworld_website/}{Project Website}.

</details>


### [325] [Harnessing the Potential of Optimizing Data Mixtures via Bayesian Domain Reweighting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27928)
*Xiang Yuan,Kaiqing Lei,Zhenyu Jin,Jun Shu,Deyu Meng,Zongben Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a Bayesian domain weighting method that infers optimal pre-training data mixture weights from a Dirichlet distribution with Gamma priors, achieving stable, efficient, and data-frugal optimization compared to search-based function-fitting approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing domain weighting methods for LLM pre-training either rely on strong structural assumptions (e.g., rank invariance, scaling laws) that introduce estimation bias, or use direct optimization which suffers from instability and prohibitive computational cost. A more principled, stable, and efficient approach is needed.

Method: The authors frame domain weighting as Bayesian inference, modeling domain weights via a Dirichlet distribution and incorporating Gamma prior information learned from observed data (validation losses). This probabilistic formulation enables stable gradient-based optimization of the weighting scheme without restrictive structural assumptions.
