The noise injection ensures stationary node representations retain diversity, with the limiting Dirichlet energy scaling predictably with noise variance and graph structure. This opens a new direction for designing deep GNNs that avoid representation collapse.

Abstract: Oversmoothing is a fundamental limitation of deep graph neural networks (GNNs), where repeated message passing causes node representations to become increasingly similar, eventually collapsing toward a low-dimensional subspace. This phenomenon limits the effective depth of message-passing architectures and motivates the search for mechanisms that preserve representation diversity. In this paper, we study a recurrent graph neural network in which independent Gaussian noise is injected after every propagation step and analyze the resulting architecture as a stochastic dynamical system. Under a standard global contraction assumption on the deterministic update, we prove that the hidden representations form a geometrically ergodic Markov chain admitting a unique invariant probability measure. Our main theoretical result establishes an explicit positive lower bound on the expected stationary Dirichlet energy, proportional to both the noise variance and the spectral gap of the underlying graph. Consequently, the stationary representations cannot collapse onto the constant manifold, providing a rigorous guarantee that asymptotic oversmoothing is prevented in the sense of non-vanishing Dirichlet energy. Our analysis reveals persistent stochastic perturbations as a fundamentally different mechanism for combating oversmoothing, complementing existing deterministic approaches based on residual connections, normalization, and graph rewiring. Finally, numerical experiments on both linear and nonlinear recurrent graph neural networks closely match the theoretical predictions, illustrating the emergence of a stationary distribution and the predicted dependence of the limiting Dirichlet energy on the noise intensity.

</details>


### [348] [TopoFormer: Topology Meets Attention for Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28259)
*Md Joshem Uddin,Astrit Tola,Cuneyt Gurcan Akcora,Baris Coskunuzer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Topoformer introduces Topo-Scan, a module that converts graph topology into ordered token sequences via node/edge filtrations, enabling Transformers to learn multi-scale structural representations without expensive persistent homology computations, achieving SOTA on graph classification and molecular prediction tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional persistent homology methods for capturing graph topology are computationally expensive (requiring costly diagram computations) and poorly integrated with deep learning. The authors aim to bridge topological data analysis with Transformer architectures in a scalable, parallelizable manner that preserves multi-scale structural information.

Method: Topoformer uses Topo-Scan, which decomposes a graph into a short, ordered sequence of topological tokens by slicing over node or edge filtrations. These tokens encode structural patterns from local motifs to global organization. The sequence is fed into a Transformer to produce graph-level embeddings, avoiding traditional persistent diagram computations entirely.

Result: Topoformer matches or exceeds strong GNN and topology-based baselines on graph classification and molecular property prediction benchmarks, while providing theoretical stability guarantees for the topological encodings and offering predictable, efficient compute.

Conclusion: The work establishes a new paradigm for integrating topological inductive biases into attention-based frameworks, demonstrating that parallelizable topological tokenization can unify and advance graph representation learning.

Abstract: We introduce Topoformer, a lightweight and scalable framework for graph representation learning that encodes topological structure into attention-friendly sequences. At the core of our method is Topo-Scan, a novel module that decomposes a graph into a short, ordered sequence of topological tokens by slicing over node or edge filtrations. These sequences capture multi-scale structural patterns, from local motifs to global organization, and are processed by a Transformer to produce expressive graph-level embeddings. Unlike traditional persistent homology pipelines, Topo-Scan is parallelizable, avoids costly diagram computations, and integrates seamlessly with standard deep learning architectures. We provide theoretical guarantees on the stability of our topological encodings and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across graph classification and molecular property prediction benchmarks. Our results show that Topoformer matches or exceeds strong GNN and topology-based baselines while offering predictable and efficient compute. This work opens a new path for parallelizable and unifying approaches to graph representation learning that integrate topological inductive biases into attention frameworks.

</details>


### [349] [HARGO: Heterogeneity-Aware Reward-Guided Optimization for RL Post-Training of LLMs on HPC Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28301)
*Tiangang Li,Xiangbo Tian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HARGO is a heterogeneity-aware RL post-training method that uses confidence-modulated advantage weighting to handle extreme task diversity in HPC domains, outperforming uniform-weight methods like GRPO across classification, QA, and generation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SFT alone gives LLMs HPC domain knowledge but fails to produce task-appropriate behavior (verbose QA answers despite good classification). RL post-training can fix this, but HPC tasks are extremely heterogeneous — 58x variation in answer length, three distinct reward distributions, and widely varying SFT accuracy — making uniform-weight RL methods like GRPO suboptimal. A method is needed that adapts to this heterogeneity without requiring task-type labels.

Method: HARGO (Heterogeneity-Aware Reward-Guided Optimization) introduces per-response importance weighting via confidence-modulated advantage. It computes two signals: (1) a discrimination signal from group-level reward contrast, and (2) a confidence signal from reference model log-probabilities. These are combined to modulate the advantage before computing per-response weights, all without requiring explicit task-type labels.

Result: Across 4 HPC tasks and 9 methods, HARGO achieves best performance on all three primary metrics: WinRate 54.62%, Data Race F1 91.30%, and PLP Similarity 0.8558. Ablation confirms both the discrimination and confidence signals contribute complementarily.

Conclusion: HARGO establishes the best overall alignment quality among compared methods for heterogeneous HPC tasks, demonstrating that heterogeneity-aware weighting is critical for effective RL post-training in multi-task HPC settings.

Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can equip large language models (LLMs) with domain knowledge for high-performance computing (HPC) tasks such as data race detection and benchmark question answering. However, knowledge alone does not guarantee task-appropriate behavior: the same SFT model that correctly classifies 88.65\% of C/C++ data race samples produces verbose, imprecise answers to factual queries, with 65.9\% of MLPerf responses exceeding 40 characters. Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training addresses this gap by optimizing for task-specific rewards rather than token-level imitation. Yet HPC tasks exhibit extreme heterogeneity, with binary classification, factual QA, and semantic generation differing by 58x in answer length, spanning three distinct reward distributions, and showing widely varying SFT accuracy. This makes uniform-weight RL methods such as GRPO suboptimal. We propose HARGO, Heterogeneity-Aware Reward-Guided Optimization, which introduces per-response importance weighting via confidence-modulated advantage: computing a discrimination signal from group-level reward contrast and a confidence signal from reference model log-probabilities, then modulating the advantage before computing per-response weights, without requiring task-type labels. Across four HPC tasks and nine methods, HARGO achieves the best performance on all three primary metrics: WinRate 54.62\%, Data Race F1 91.30\%, and PLP Similarity 0.8558. Ablation confirms complementary contributions from both signals. HARGO establishes the best overall alignment quality among compared methods for heterogeneous HPC tasks.

</details>


### [350] [Semi-Supervised Learning for Molecular Graphs via Ensemble Consensus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28304)
*Rasmus Tirsgaard,Laurits Fredsgaard,Marisa Wodrich,Mikkel Jordahn,Mikkel N. Schmidt*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper demonstrates that ensemble consensus-based semi-supervised learning improves molecular property prediction across diverse datasets and architectures, with individual models outperforming traditionally trained full ensembles while also reducing calibration error.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Labeled molecular data is scarce and expensive to obtain, while unlabeled data is abundant. Standard semi-supervised methods relying on label-preserving augmentations are difficult to apply in the molecular domain because small structural changes can drastically alter molecular properties, making augmentation design challenging.

Method: An ensemble consensus semi-supervised learning framework is employed, where multiple graph neural network models are trained simultaneously with an objective that enforces agreement among ensemble members' predictions on unlabeled data. This consensus-based training acts as a form of knowledge distillation, transferring collective knowledge across the ensemble.

Result: Ensemble consensus training increases model robustness. A single member of the consensus-trained ensemble outperforms a fully supervised ensemble in nearly all tested scenarios. Additionally, the method reduces model calibration error, yielding more reliable uncertainty estimates.

Conclusion: Ensemble consensus-based semi-supervised learning is a broadly effective strategy for molecular machine learning, overcoming the limitations of augmentation-dependent methods and delivering superior predictive performance and calibration without requiring domain-specific data transformations.

Abstract: Machine learning is transforming molecular sciences by accelerating property prediction, simulation, and the discovery of new molecules and materials. Acquiring labeled data in these domains is often costly and time-consuming, whereas large collections of unlabeled molecular data are readily available. Standard semi-supervised learning methods often rely on label-preserving augmentations, which are challenging to design in the molecular domain, where minor changes can drastically alter properties. In this work, we show that semi-supervised methods that rely on an ensemble consensus can boost predictive accuracy across a diverse range of molecular datasets, task types, and graph neural network architectures. We find that training with an ensemble consensus objective increases robustness in models and exhibits an effect similar to knowledge distillation; an individual member of an ensemble trained this way outperforms a full ensemble trained in a traditional supervised fashion in almost all cases. In addition, this type of semi-supervised training reduces calibration error.

</details>


### [351] [Beyond Geometric Complementarity: Coherent Overlap in Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28308)
*Huiyuan Tian,Bonan Xu,Shijian Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Expert Subspace Separation Index (ESSI) and controlled experimental designs to disentangle route coherence, candidate quality, and context interaction in sparse MoE language models. It finds that expert subspaces overlap substantially ("coherent overlap"), yet multi-expert routing still improves prediction — geometric similarity does not imply functional redundancy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on sparse MoE models conflates three distinct quantities: route coherence (how consistently experts are co-selected), candidate quality (individual expert capacity), and candidate-by-context interaction. The authors argue that existing geometric analyses fail to distinguish whether co-selected experts contribute distinct representation directions or merely provide redundant coverage, leaving the functional value of multi-expert routing poorly understood.

Method: The authors employ three methodological innovations: (1) the Expert Subspace Separation Index (ESSI) to measure subspace overlap among experts; (2) matched-route residuals and a prefix-controlled 2×2 factorial design (with factors: expert candidate and prefix context) applied across 39 cells in OLMoE, Mixtral, and DeepSeek; and (3) frozen-route interventions and a controlled Top-k training study to assess functional value. Three paired contrasts structure the empirical analysis.

Result: Three key findings: (1) Across six MoE architectures, expert subspaces overlap substantially, yet actual routes explain token representations better than matched alternatives. (2) In all 39 factorial cells, the selected candidate outperforms the strongest unselected rival, but the actual prefix narrows this advantage — all interaction effects are negative with 95% CIs below zero. (3) Geometric narrowing does not imply redundancy: frozen-route interventions show adding later experts improves next-token prediction in 24/39 comparisons; a controlled Top-2 vs. Top-1 training study favors Top-2 across all three seeds.

Conclusion: The authors characterize a "coherent overlap" regime: routing selects token-relevant experts from a shared geometric neighborhood, yet useful multi-expert computation persists without requiring disjoint linear coverage. This demonstrates that geometric similarity alone cannot determine redundancy or pruning value, providing a more nuanced framework for analyzing and designing sparse MoE architectures.

Abstract: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models route each token to multiple experts, suggesting a geometric account of their benefit: co-selected experts should contribute distinct representation directions. Existing evidence often conflates route coherence, candidate quality, and candidate-by-context interaction. We distinguish these quantities using an Expert Subspace Separation Index (ESSI), matched-route residuals, and a prefix-controlled $2\times2$ factorial; frozen-route interventions and a controlled Top-$k$ study assess functional value. Three paired contrasts organize the findings. First, across six MoE architectures, expert subspaces overlap substantially, yet actual routes explain token representations better than matched alternatives. Second, across the 39 factorial cells in OLMoE, Mixtral, and DeepSeek, the selected candidate explains more of the residual representation than the strongest unselected rival in every cell, yet the actual prefix narrows this advantage throughout: all interactions are negative, and every 95% confidence interval lies below zero. Third, this geometric narrowing does not imply functional redundancy: adding later experts improves next-token prediction in 24 of 39 frozen-route comparisons, while the other 15 estimates are inconclusive; a controlled training study also favors Top-2 over Top-1 in all three seeds. We call this joint pattern coherent overlap: routing selects token-relevant experts from a shared geometric neighborhood, while useful multi-expert computation persists without disjoint linear coverage. Separating these quantities clarifies why geometric similarity alone cannot determine redundancy or pruning value.

</details>


### [352] [Measuring Distortion in the Empty Regions of Dimensionality Reduction Scatterplots with the Gap Index](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28324)
*Jaume Ros,Alessio Arleo,Fernando Paulovich*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Gap Index (GI), a new quality metric for 2D dimensionality reduction projections that quantifies spatial distortion in empty areas (gaps) rather than focusing solely on point-wise relationships. GI decomposes the 2D layout into empty triangles, compares them to high-dimensional counterparts, and produces both a scalar aggregate and a spatial distortion map. It is shown to be sensitive to visually salient structural deformations that traditional metrics miss, while remaining computationally efficient and interpretable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing projection quality metrics (e.g., trustworthiness, continuity, stress) focus overwhelmingly on direct point relationships—distances, neighborhoods, or pairwise similarities—while ignoring distortions in the empty spaces of a 2D layout. Yet these empty regions often constitute visually meaningful features (clusters, gaps, shapes) that influence user interpretation. There is a need for a metric that captures distortion in these visually salient empty areas to give a more complete picture of projection fidelity.

Method: The Gap Index (GI) operates by triangulating the 2D projection (e.g., via Delaunay triangulation) to partition the space into empty triangles—triangles whose circumcircles contain no projected points. For each empty triangle, a corresponding high-dimensional simplex is formed from the same points, and the deformation (e.g., in terms of shape, area, or angles) between the 2D triangle and its high-dimensional counterpart is measured. These per-triangle deformations can be aggregated (e.g., averaged) into a single scalar GI value, or visualized as a heatmap overlaid on the projection to reveal regional distortion patterns.

Result: The Gap Index is demonstrably sensitive to small structural deformations that have high visual impact—deformations that popular metrics like trustworthiness, continuity, or stress fail to detect. The metric is fast to compute and produces interpretable outputs, both as a global scalar summary and as a spatial map of local distortion.

Conclusion: The Gap Index fills a critical gap in projection quality assessment by quantifying distortion in the empty spaces of 2D layouts. It complements existing point-centric metrics and provides users with a more comprehensive, visually meaningful evaluation of projection reliability. Its speed and interpretability make it practical for integration into visual analysis workflows.

Abstract: Quality metrics play a crucial role in the proper use of dimensionality reduction projections for visual analysis of high-dimensional data. They quantify the degree of distortion of a projection compared to the high-dimensional data and provide a reliable indication of how confident users can be in the structures they see in the resulting layouts. However, most popular metrics focus on capturing direct relationships between points (e.g., distances or neighborhoods) while neglecting distortions in empty areas of the layout, even though these often compose visually relevant features of a 2D layout. In this paper, we introduce the Gap Index (GI), a quality metric for 2D projections that captures visual distortion by measuring spatial distortion in empty areas of a projection. It does so by decomposing the space into empty triangles, which are then compared to their high-dimensional counterparts to compute the deformation. This per-triangle deformation can be aggregated into a single scalar value or overlaid on a projection to visualize regional distortion patterns. Results show that, contrary to popular quality metrics, the GI is sensitive to small structural deformations that have high visual impact. It is also fast to compute and interpretable.

</details>


### [353] [LEDGERMIND: Provenance-Constrained Multimodal Agentic Reasoning with a Structured Evidence Ledger](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28374)
*Enjun Du,Hange Zhou,Chenxu Du,Siyi Liu,Zirong Chen,Ziyu Zheng,Yongqi Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LedgerMind introduces a provenance-constrained state machine framework for multimodal agents, using a Structured Evidence Ledger with formal grounding verification and repair mechanisms to improve both answer accuracy and trajectory faithfulness beyond final-answer evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation of multimodal agents for VQA relies on final-answer accuracy, which obscures critical failure patterns: unsupported reasoning, phantom grounding (citation-backed hallucinations), over-reasoning on simple queries, and repair-time amplification. There is no mechanism to verify whether correct answers stem from grounded evidence or spurious shortcuts.

Method: The authors propose treating agent trajectories as provenance-constrained state machines. Tool outputs are normalized into a Structured Evidence Ledger (the state). Reasoning claims may only cite active ledger entries. Grounding is verified at entity and numeric levels. Repair occurs via typed state transitions that cannot introduce content without tool-produced provenance. The system, LedgerMind, incorporates: (1) a Three-Layer Grounding Protocol, (2) an Adaptive Dual-Path Dispatcher matching reasoning depth to question complexity, and (3) an Event-Triggered Verification-and-Repair engine with a formal provenance non-amplification guarantee.

Result: Experiments across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks and backbone MLLMs demonstrate that LedgerMind improves both answer accuracy and trajectory-level faithfulness compared to baselines.

Conclusion: Provenance-constrained agent design with structured evidence ledgers and formal repair guarantees offers a principled path toward more trustworthy multimodal reasoning, addressing failure modes that aggregate accuracy metrics fail to capture.

Abstract: Multimodal agents for visual question answering increasingly operate as multi-step trajectories that interleave perception, retrieval, and reasoning, yet evaluation still largely reduces to final-answer accuracy. This aggregate signal cannot tell whether a correct answer was reached through grounded evidence, language priors, or accidental error cancellation. We propose to treat a multimodal agent trajectory as a provenance-constrained state machine: tool outputs are normalized into a Structured Evidence Ledger that serves as the trajectory state, downstream reasoning and decision claims may cite only active ledger entries, grounding is checked at the entity and numeric level, and repair is realized as typed state transitions that cannot introduce content without tool-produced provenance. We instantiate this design as LedgerMind (Provenance-Constrained Multimodal Agentic Reasoning with a Structured Evidence Ledger), augmented by a Three-Layer Grounding Protocol, an Adaptive Dual-Path Dispatcher that matches reasoning depth to question complexity, and an Event-Triggered Verification-and-Repair engine with a formal provenance non-amplification guarantee. We use LedgerMind to target four recurring failure patterns that final-answer accuracy tends to obscure: unsupported intermediate reasoning, citation-backed entity hallucination (Phantom Grounding), over-reasoning on simple queries, and repair-time amplification. Experiments across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks and backbone MLLMs show that LedgerMind improves both answer accuracy and trajectory-level faithfulness.

</details>


### [354] [Hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo for Order-Optimal Neural Actor-Critic in Average-Reward CMDPs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28390)
*Ankur Naskar,Vaneet Aggarwal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper resolves the open problem of achieving order-optimal convergence in average-reward CMDPs with neural critics by introducing a hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) neural critic that overcomes the bias-cost trade-off, enabling a primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm with $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$ optimality gap and constraint violation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing primal-dual actor-critic methods for CMDPs with linear critics have order-optimal guarantees, but extending these to neural critics in the average-reward setting faces a fundamental bias-cost trade-off: under NTK analysis, reducing critic bias requires exponentially more optimization cost, blocking order-optimal convergence. The paper aims to break this bottleneck.

Method: The authors propose a hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) neural critic that simultaneously debiases across trajectory sampling levels and critic optimization iterations. The MLMC estimator achieves the bias of a long optimization run with only logarithmic expected sample cost by coupling coarse and fine-level estimates. This critic is then integrated into a primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with general policy parameterization.

Result: The proposed algorithm achieves both an optimality gap and a constraint violation of order $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$, establishing the first order-optimal convergence guarantees for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with neural critics and general policy parameterization, without requiring knowledge of the mixing time.

Conclusion: The hierarchical MLMC neural critic successfully resolves the bias-cost trade-off, enabling order-optimal primal-dual methods for neural CMDPs. The results are novel even in the unconstrained (standard MDP) setting, and eliminate the need for mixing time knowledge.

Abstract: Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs) provide a natural framework for reinforcement learning in safety-critical applications, where agents maximize long-term reward while satisfying long-term constraints. Although primal-dual actor-critic methods with linear critics are well understood, extending order-optimal convergence guarantees to neural critics in average-reward CMDPs has remained open. The main challenge is a fundamental bias-cost trade-off in neural critic estimation: under Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) analysis, reducing critic bias substantially increases critic optimization cost, preventing order-optimal convergence in the primal-dual framework. We resolve this bottleneck by introducing a hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) neural critic that performs debiasing simultaneously across trajectory sampling and critic optimization. The resulting estimator attains the bias of a long critic optimization run with only logarithmic expected sample cost. Building on this estimator, we develop a primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm that achieves both an optimality gap and a constraint violation of order $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$. This establishes the first order-optimal convergence guarantees for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with general policy parameterization and neural critics, while eliminating the need to know the underlying mixing time. Our results are novel even in the unconstrained setting.

</details>


### [355] [Why Are GUI Agents Correct but Late? Decode on the Decision-Time Critical Path, Tested with Pre-Compiled Policy Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28399)
*Zihan Dong,Rui Qian,Qishi Zhan,Dongshen Peng,Kaixin Li,Yu Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AAPT pre-computes a decision tree during idle screen time to eliminate autoregressive decoding latency on the critical path, improving success rate on transient GUI events from 0.50 to 0.79 without model modification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Computer-use agents fail on transient GUI events because autoregressive decoding occurs on the decision-time critical path; by the time the model generates the correct action, the relevant window has already disappeared. The authors aim to eliminate this latency without modifying the underlying model.

Method: AAPT uses idle screen periods to let a frozen multimodal model construct a bounded conditional policy tree containing observable guards, pre-authorized actions, and branch-specific deadlines sized to cover the model's decoding latency. When an event occurs, a lightweight observer matches change-gated frames to a prepared branch and immediately executes the action — no text generation needed at decision time.

Result: AAPT improved success rate from 0.50 to 0.79 in paired trials (p=1.8×10⁻³) with zero incorrect actions. Open-loop and predict-and-replan baselines scored zero. The effect was reproduced on an independent model over 126 pairs (p=4.9×10⁻¹³). An external benchmark showed complementary strengths: AAPT excels when candidate actions are pre-enumerable, while reactive execution wins otherwise.

Conclusion: AAPT demonstrates that anticipatory pre-computation can overcome decoding latency bottlenecks for time-sensitive GUI interactions, with branch routing identified as the primary causal bottleneck. The method is best suited to scenarios where candidate actions can be enumerated in advance.

Abstract: Computer-use agents often fail on transient GUI events because they produce the correct action only after the relevant window has already closed. We identify the main cause as expensive autoregressive decoding on the decision-time critical path. We propose Adaptive Anticipatory Policy Trees (AAPT), which eliminates this delay without modifying the underlying model. During idle screen periods, the same frozen multimodal model constructs a bounded conditional policy tree with observable guards, pre-authorized actions, and branch-specific deadlines. The tree is sized to cover the model's own decoding latency. When an event occurs, a lightweight observer matches change-gated frames to a prepared branch and immediately executes the corresponding action without generating new text. In paired trials with pre-registered endpoints and exact McNemar tests, AAPT improves the success rate from 0.50 to 0.79 within a contested decision window ($p=1.8\times10^{-3}$), while producing no incorrect actions. Both open-loop and predict-and-replan baselines achieve zero success because they still decode during execution. A preparation-time sweep shows that the gain emerges where the latency-based tree-sizing rule predicts, and ablations reveal three key requirements: fast observer decoding, valid tree planning, and accurate branch routing. A pre-registered oracle probe rejects our initial hypothesis and instead points to branch routing as the causal bottleneck. We further reproduce the effect on an independent general-purpose multimodal model over 126 paired trials ($p=4.9\times10^{-13}$). On an external benchmark, AAPT matches the overall performance of a reactive baseline, although the two methods exhibit complementary strengths. Together, these results suggest that AAPT performs best when candidate actions can be enumerated in advance, whereas reactive execution remains stronger when they cannot.

</details>


### [356] [On-Policy and Off-Policy Learning for Large Action Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28408)
*Imad Aouali*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This thesis develops structured Bayesian methods for on-policy contextual bandits and optimization-aware off-policy learning techniques to address the challenges of large action spaces, including regret bounds, bias-variance trade-offs, and efficient optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In large action spaces, both on-policy and off-policy contextual bandit learning suffer from inefficient exploration, sparse data coverage, high-variance importance sampling, extrapolation bias, and difficult optimization landscapes. Existing methods do not adequately address these compounding challenges.

Method: For on-policy learning: (1) meTS — a mixed-effect Thompson sampling extension that shares information across actions via hierarchical Bayesian modeling; (2) dTS — uses diffusion-inspired priors to model inter-action dependencies, yielding regret guarantees parameterized by an effective number of actions. For off-policy learning: (1) sDM — a structured direct method using latent variables; (2) concave, efficiently optimizable policy-weighted log-likelihood objectives to mitigate optimization error; (3) differentiable pessimistic methods combining exponential smoothing and PAC-Bayesian bounds to control the bias-variance trade-off of regularized importance-sampling estimators.

Result: The proposed on-policy methods (meTS, dTS) achieve regret bounds that scale with an effective number of actions rather than the full action space cardinality. The off-policy contributions demonstrate that optimization error can dominate estimation error in large action spaces and provide concave objectives that are efficiently optimizable, along with pessimistic methods that provably control the bias-variance trade-off.

Conclusion: Structured Bayesian priors and latent-variable models can effectively reduce the effective dimensionality of large action spaces in both on-policy and off-policy settings. Explicitly addressing optimization error and using differentiable pessimistic regularization are critical for reliable off-policy learning at scale.

Abstract: This thesis studies policy learning in interactive systems where an agent observes a context, selects an action from a very large set, and receives partial feedback. The main framework is contextual bandits, with two paradigms: on-policy learning, where the agent interacts sequentially with the environment and minimizes regret, and off-policy learning, where it learns from logged data collected by a logging policy. In large action spaces, both settings face major challenges: inefficient exploration, sparse data coverage, high-variance importance weights, extrapolation bias, and difficult optimization landscapes. The first part develops structured Bayesian methods for on-policy learning. We introduce meTS, a mixed-effect extension of Thompson sampling, and dTS, which leverages diffusion-inspired priors to model dependencies between actions. These methods share information across actions and yield regret guarantees depending on an effective number of actions. The second part addresses off-policy learning. We propose sDM, a structured direct method based on latent variables, show that optimization error can dominate estimation error in large action spaces, and introduce concave, efficiently optimizable policy-weighted log-likelihood objectives. Finally, we develop differentiable pessimistic methods based on exponential smoothing and PAC-Bayesian bounds to control the bias-variance trade-off of regularized importance-sampling estimators.

</details>


### [357] [QQWorld: Quantile-Quantile Matching for World Model Regularization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28415)
*Zhoushun Yu,Xiaoyu Hu,Xiangyu Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: QQWorld replaces LeWM's Epps-Pulley latent regularization with quantile-quantile matching (plus cross-batch ranking) to better control heavy-tailed deviations, improving planning success across four control environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LeWM regularizes latents toward an isotropic Gaussian using the Epps-Pulley (EP) objective, but EP's corrective gradients vanish for isolated tail samples, leaving heavy-tailed deviations insufficiently controlled. This degrades latent distribution quality and downstream planning.

Method: QQWorld replaces EP with a quantile-quantile (QQ) matching objective that directly aligns projected latent samples with rank-matched Gaussian quantiles, preserving effective corrective gradients in the tails. It also introduces cross-batch QQ, which expands the ranking pool using detached samples from prior batches, and analyzes the resulting bias-variance trade-off.

Result: Across four control environments, QQWorld improves LeWM's average planning success rate while consistently yielding better Gaussian alignment and thinner latent tails.

Conclusion: QQ matching with cross-batch ranking is a more effective latent regularization strategy than EP for world models, as it better controls tail behavior and improves planning performance.

Abstract: Latent world models enable efficient planning by predicting future states in a compact representation space, but their performance depends critically on the quality of the learned latent distribution. LeWorldModel (LeWM) regularizes its latents toward an isotropic Gaussian using the Epps-Pulley (EP) objective. We show that the corrective gradients of EP rapidly vanish for isolated tail samples, leaving heavy-tailed deviations insufficiently controlled. To address this limitation, we propose QQWorld, which replaces EP with a quantile-quantile matching objective that directly aligns projected latent samples with rank-matched Gaussian quantiles, thereby maintaining effective corrective gradients in the tails. We further develop cross-batch QQ, which enlarges the effective ranking pool using detached samples from previous batches, and characterize its bias-variance trade-off. Across four control environments, QQWorld effectively improves the average planning success rate of LeWM, while consistently yielding better Gaussian alignment and thinner latent tails.

</details>


### [358] [QAdapt: A Noise-Adaptive Neural Pre-Decoding Framework for Quantum Error Correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28422)
*Ran Miao,Rui Luo,Xiaohan Shan,Xiaoming Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: QAdapt is a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoder for surface-code QEC that adapts to evolving, heterogeneous hardware noise online, mitigates catastrophic forgetting, and reduces logical error rates and decoding latency across synthetic and real (Google Willow) benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: FTQC performance is bottlenecked by classical decoder latency and degraded by strong, heterogeneous, nonstationary hardware noise. Fixed neural decoders suffer from simulation-to-hardware distribution shift, motivating an adaptive pre-decoding approach that can adjust to evolving noise conditions in real time.

Method: QAdapt is a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoding framework for rotated surface codes. It captures local spatiotemporal correlations in syndrome data, sequentially adapts to evolving noise conditions (using techniques to mitigate catastrophic forgetting), and forwards the residual syndrome to a conventional global decoder, maintaining decoder compatibility.

Result: Across 110 synthetic out-of-distribution noise configurations, QAdapt consistently reduces logical error rate vs. the neural pre-decoding baseline. On Google Willow benchmark data without target-domain fine-tuning, it achieves up to 5.79% reduction in logical error rate and 9.32% reduction in backend decoding latency on the residual syndrome.

Conclusion: QAdapt offers a practical, decoder-compatible method for improving robustness and backend decoding efficiency in QEC under evolving hardware noise, bridging the gap between static neural decoders and real-world noise dynamics.

Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) relies on quantum error correction to suppress physical errors and preserve logical information at scale. In practice, however, performance is constrained not only by physical noise but also by the latency of classical decoders processing rapidly generated syndrome data. This challenge is exacerbated by hardware noise that is strong, heterogeneous, and nonstationary, as well as by the simulation-to-hardware distribution shift that can substantially degrade fixed neural decoders. We present QAdapt, a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoding framework for surface-code quantum error correction. QAdapt captures local spatiotemporal correlations in syndrome data, sequentially adapts to evolving noise conditions while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and forwards the residual syndrome to a conventional global decoder. Across 110 synthetic out-of-distribution noise configurations for rotated surface-code memory circuits, QAdapt consistently reduces the logical error rate relative to the neural pre-decoding baseline. On Google's Willow benchmark data, without target-domain fine-tuning, it achieves reductions of up to 5.79 percent in logical error rate and 9.32 percent in backend decoding latency on the residual syndrome. These results demonstrate that QAdapt provides a practical and decoder-compatible approach to improving the robustness and backend decoding efficiency of quantum error correction under evolving hardware noise.

</details>


### [359] [Kohn-Sham Spectral Embedding on Sparse Graphs at the Nishimori Temperature for Image Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28428)
*V. S. Usatyuk,D. A. Sapozhnikov,S. I. Egorov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KSSE replaces dense CNN classifiers with a sparse-graph spectral embedding evaluated at the Nishimori temperature of a Random-Bond Ising Model. Using quasi-cyclic LDPC graphs, circulant-block FFT spectral solvers, and star-domain surgery for topology optimization, it achieves 88.93% Top-1 on ImageNet-1000 with ~21M parameters — matching or surpassing models 10–30× larger.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense CNN classifiers are parameter-inefficient, scaling poorly with feature dimensionality. The authors seek a physics-inspired alternative that preserves representational capacity while drastically reducing parameter count, drawing on connections between belief propagation, Ising models, and spectral graph theory.

Method: Pre-trained features are mapped onto quasi-cyclic LDPC graphs. A regularized Laplacian (Kohn–Sham Hamiltonian) is constructed, and D independent channel spectral problems are solved via FFT on circulant blocks (leveraging Pontryagin self-duality of Z/pZ) plus low-order Rayleigh refinement (k_mode=5). Graph topology is optimized via star-domain surgery — edge shifts creating local convexity around codewords while bounding residual frustration. Multi-scale fractal analysis (D₂ spectrum) certifies a landscape transition enabling refinement. Six theoretical results are proved, including an Ihara–Bass identity linking BP to the Laplacian, trapping-set eigenvalue correspondence, additive channel separability, a surgery theorem, a quasi-stationarity perturbation bound, and a fixed-point convergence theorem.

Result: KSSE achieves 88.93% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1000 using frozen EfficientNet-B4 features (D=1792) with ~21.24M parameters. This outperforms Swin-L (197M, 86.4–87.3%) and matches ViT-H/14 (632M, 88.0–89.5%), while reducing model footprint by ~10× and ~30× respectively.

Conclusion: Sparse-graph spectral embedding at the Nishimori temperature, combined with star-domain surgery and FFT-based spectral solvers, enables compact classifiers that rival or exceed massive dense models. The approach opens a new connection between density functional theory, error-correcting codes, and deep learning classification.

Abstract: We introduce Kohn--Sham Spectral Embedding (KSSE), a physics-inspired energy-based model replacing dense CNN classifiers with a sparse-graph spectral embedding evaluated at the Nishimori temperature of an associated Random-Bond Ising Model. By mapping pre-trained features onto quasi-cyclic low-density parity-check graphs and constructing a regularized Laplacian acting as a Kohn--Sham Hamiltonian, we solve $D$ independent channel spectral problems in $\mathcal{O}(N\log N + k^2_{\text{mode}} N)$ time via FFT on circulant blocks (leveraging Pontryagin self-duality of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$) and low-order Rayleigh refinement. Graph topology is optimized using \emph{star-domain surgery}: rather than destroying information-carrying codewords by removing frustrated cycles, we construct edge shifts creating local convexity around codewords while bounding residual frustration to $ρ(B_γ)\leq 1+δ$. Multi-scale fractal analysis ($D_2$ spectrum) and fractal learning-rate landscape certifies a landscape transition from rough regimes ($D_2>3$) to star-domain basins ($D_2<1$), enabling Rayleigh refinement with $k_{\text{mode}}=5$ modes. We prove six theoretical results: a generalized Ihara--Bass identity linking belief propagation to the Laplacian; trapping-set eigenvalue correspondence; additive channel separability with an explicit exchange-correlation bound; a surgery theorem bounding frustration with attractor width $Ω(1/\sqrt{d_{\min}})$; a quasi-stationarity perturbation bound; and a fixed-point convergence theorem. In a transductive protocol on ImageNet-1000 with frozen EfficientNet-B4 features ($D=1792$), KSSE achieves \textbf{88.93\%} Top-1 accuracy using $\approx 21.24$M parameters, outperforming Swin-L (197M, 86.4--87.3\%) and matching ViT-H/14 (632M, 88.0--89.5\%) under standard inductive setups, while reducing model footprint by $10\times$ and $30\times$, respectively.

</details>


### [360] [Oracle-Budgeted Molecular Optimization with Short-Term Graph Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28437)
*Jiannan Yang,Veronika Thost,Xiang Ling,Tengfei Ma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A plug-in module called short-term graph memory uses an online graph neural surrogate to pre-screen candidate molecules, enabling more selective use of a limited oracle budget. It consistently improves optimization scores across multiple generators at no extra cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Molecular optimization under limited oracle budgets requires not only generating good candidates but also deciding which ones to evaluate. Existing generators lack a mechanism to learn from previously evaluated molecules to prioritize future oracle queries, leading to inefficient use of the fixed budget.

Method: The authors propose short-term graph memory, a plug-in module that maintains an online graph neural network surrogate. This surrogate is trained on previously evaluated molecules and used to pre-screen each round's candidate pool, ranking molecules by predicted utility so the fixed oracle budget is allocated to the most promising candidates. The module preserves the underlying generator's architecture and native update rule.

Result: Applied to a fragment-based generator on a standard benchmark, the module improves mean top-10 scores without additional oracle cost and never underperforms the baseline at any budget. Gains extend to all four tested generators at a tight budget of 1,000 oracle calls. Analysis reveals that benefit at larger budgets depends on two generator properties: breadth of search and effectiveness of native exploitation of oracle feedback.

Conclusion: Short-term graph memory offers a simple, architecture-preserving method to spend a fixed oracle budget more selectively, with evidence identifying which types of generators benefit most from surrogate-guided selection.

Abstract: Molecular optimization is commonly performed under a limited oracle budget, which makes deciding what to evaluate as important as deciding what to generate. We introduce short-term graph memory, a plug-in module that preserves the generator architecture and native update rule while learning from previously evaluated molecules to prioritize subsequent oracle queries. The module maintains an online graph neural surrogate that pre-screens each round's candidate pool, so the fixed oracle budget is spent on molecules with higher predicted utility. Applied to a fragment-based generator on a standard molecular optimization benchmark, it improves the mean top-10 score at no extra oracle cost and never falls behind the base on any oracle; the gain extends to all four generators we tested at a tight budget of one thousand calls. We then analyze how surrogate-guided selection interacts with the exploration and exploitation behavior of different generators. Its benefit at larger budgets is consistent with two properties of the backbone: how broadly it searches, and how effectively its native search already exploits oracle feedback. We provide a simple way to spend a fixed oracle budget more selectively, and evidence on which generators benefit from it.

</details>


### [361] [The Role of Causality in Algorithmic Recourse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28497)
*Srikanth Avasarala,Varun Gupta,Shahin Jabbari,Saber Salehkaleybar,Juba Ziani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Algorithmic recourse actions can cause individuals to game classifiers rather than genuinely improve, leading to model degradation. The authors propose a causal performative framework that models how recourse propagates through a structural causal model, characterize conditions for performatively stable solutions, and show causal recourse reduces gaming incentives and outperforms standard ERM.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing recourse methods focus on flipping predictions without considering whether recommended changes reflect true qualification improvement or strategic gaming. When deployed, these policies induce behavioral responses that degrade accuracy and become ineffective after retraining — a failure mode not adequately addressed by prior work.

Method: The authors formalize the problem through a causal performative framework: recourse actions are modeled as propagating through a structural causal model (SCM) that captures feature interactions and effects on the true label. This yields a non-convex optimization problem. They characterize conditions for existence of performatively stable solutions and propose iterative dynamics for efficient computation. The framework distinguishes between causal recourse (changes that improve true qualifications) and gaming.

Result: Recourse policies ignoring causal structure induce large, misaligned behavioral responses. In contrast, causal recourse leads to stable equilibria that reduce gaming incentives. Experiments on semi-synthetic and real credit datasets show the approach consistently outperforms standard empirical risk minimization and reduces the need for repeated model retraining under distribution shifts from strategic behavior.

Conclusion: Incorporating causal structure into recourse policy design yields performatively stable solutions that align individual behavior with genuine qualification improvement rather than strategic manipulation, improving both predictive accuracy and long-term policy effectiveness without frequent retraining.

Abstract: Algorithmic recourse aims to provide individuals with actionable changes to improve their predicted outcomes in high-stakes classification settings, such as loan and mortgage applications. However, most existing approaches focus only on flipping a model's prediction, without accounting for whether the recommended changes lead to genuine improvement in an individual's true qualifications or merely enable strategic gaming of the classifier. Consequently, deployed recourse policies can induce behavioral responses that degrade predictive accuracy and become ineffective after model retraining.
  In this work, we formalize this failure mode through a causal performative framework for recourse. We model how recourse actions propagate through a structural causal model, capturing interactions among features as well as their effect on the true label. These causal responses induce a non-convex optimization problem, even under standard convex losses. We characterize conditions under which performatively stable solutions exist and can be efficiently computed via simple iterative dynamics. Our analysis reveals that recourse policies that ignore causal structure can induce large, misaligned behavioral responses, whereas causal recourse leads to stable equilibria that reduce incentives for gaming. Experiments on both semi-synthetic and real credit datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms standard empirical risk minimization while reducing the need for repeated model retraining to accommodate distribution shifts caused by strategic agent behavior.

</details>


### [362] [Same Graph Cross-Task Transfer in GNNs: Protocols and Predictors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28525)
*Neelam Akula,Surbhi Kumar,Murat Kantarcioglu,Baris Coskunuzer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper formalizes transfer learning between node classification (NC) and link prediction (LP) on the same graph, proposes a leakage-free evaluation protocol, and finds that NC→LP transfer is reliably beneficial on homophilic graphs while LP→NC transfer is fragile and only positive in a structure-dominant regime. A new metric, the CoTask Score (CTS), is introduced to summarize joint task utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of cross-task transfer between NC and LP on the same graph use incompatible splits, unrealistic observed-graph assumptions, and inconsistent negative sampling, making prior conclusions unreliable. The authors aim to rigorously characterize when and why transfer between these two tasks succeeds or fails under a unified, leakage-free framework.

Method: The authors formalize same-graph NC-LP transfer and design a leakage-free protocol: (1) fixed node and edge splits, (2) a shared message-passing graph that excludes evaluated edges to prevent data leakage, and (3) fixed negative samples for LP. They evaluate across three GNN backbones (GCN, GraphSAGE, GPS) on both homophilic and heterophilic graphs. They further propose the CoTask Score (CTS) to quantify joint performance when a shared encoder serves both tasks simultaneously, and analyze dataset statistics (especially homophily) as predictors of transfer success.

Result: NC→LP transfer is consistently beneficial on homophilic graphs. LP→NC transfer is fragile: naive representation reuse can degrade NC accuracy. LP→NC becomes reliably positive only in a structure-dominant regime where LP is easy but NC is unsaturated, suggesting LP functions as structural pretraining. Simple dataset statistics, particularly homophily, effectively guide mechanism choice and help avoid negative transfer.

Conclusion: Same-graph NC-LP transfer is strongly directional and predictable. The proposed leakage-free protocol and CoTask Score provide reliable tools for evaluating and optimizing multi-task graph learning. Homophily serves as a practical indicator for whether transfer will be beneficial, and LP acts best as structural pretraining in specific regimes.

Abstract: Many real-world graphs support multiple predictive tasks over the same underlying structure, creating an opportunity to reuse supervision across node classification (NC) and link prediction (LP). However, existing evaluations often rely on incompatible splits, observed-graph assumptions, and negative sampling rules, making conclusions about same-graph cross-task transfer unreliable. We formalize same-graph NC-LP transfer and propose a leakage-free protocol that fixes node and edge splits, uses a shared message-passing graph that excludes evaluated edges, and employs fixed negatives for LP. Across three backbones (GCN, GraphSAGE, GPS), we find that transfer is strongly directional and predictable: NC $\to$ LP is consistently beneficial on homophilic graphs, while LP $\to$ NC is fragile and can even degrade accuracy under naive representation reuse. LP $\to$ NC becomes reliably positive mainly in a structure-dominant regime where LP is easy but NC is unsaturated, suggesting that LP acts as structural pretraining. Finally, we introduce the CoTask Score (CTS) to summarize joint NC+LP utility when a shared encoder must serve both tasks, and show that simple dataset statistics, especially homophily, can guide mechanism choice and help avoid negative transfer.

</details>


### [363] [$β$-OPSD: Deriving with Policy Optimization, Training with Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28582)
*Jiawei Xu,Minghui Liu,Juzheng Zhang,Tom Goldstein,Furong Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Vanilla on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is brittle because it corresponds to a fixed KL penalty weight of β=1 in a broader policy optimization family. The authors generalize this to β-OPSD, where β interpolates between a reference policy and a privileged teacher, and implement it efficiently via token-level logit mixing rather than costly RL. This improves stability and reasoning performance on math benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) improves reasoning language models but is brittle in practice, requiring substantial engineering to work reliably. The authors aim to identify and resolve the structural source of this instability, providing a principled and efficient solution.

Method: The authors (1) reveal that vanilla OPSD is the β=1 case of a broader policy optimization family where β weights the KL penalty anchoring the student to a reference policy; (2) propose β-OPSD, deriving its optimal policy as a geometric interpolation between the reference policy and the privileged teacher; (3) avoid costly RL by converting the closed-form solution into a distillation target, implemented efficiently by mixing token-level logits; (4) incorporate return-to-go credit assignment to align token updates with sequence-level objectives.

Result: β-OPSD consistently outperforms vanilla OPSD on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with improved optimization stability and downstream reasoning performance.

Conclusion: β-OPSD provides a principled route from self-distillation to policy optimization and back, preserving the efficiency of OPSD while adding controllable regularization. Tuning β offers a practical mechanism to trade off proximity to a reference policy against teacher guidance, resolving the brittleness of the original method.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a promising approach to improve reasoning language models, but it remains brittle in practice: making it work reliably often requires substantial engineering effort. We identify a structural source of this difficulty: vanilla OPSD is precisely the $β=1$ member of a broader policy-optimization family, where $β$ weights the KL penalty anchoring the student to a reference policy. This equivalence turns $β$ from an implicit value fixed at one into a controllable regularization parameter, yielding a more general formulation that trades off proximity to a reference policy against privileged teacher guidance. We introduce $β$-OPSD and derive its optimal policy as a geometric interpolation between the reference policy and the privileged teacher. Directly optimizing this objective with reinforcement learning, however, would be costly and high-variance. Rather than optimize the RL objective directly, we turn its closed-form solution into a distillation target. Each value of $β$ selects a target along the reference-to-teacher path, which we implement efficiently by mixing their token-level logits. In this way, inexpensive distillation approximates the solution of expensive policy optimization. Return-to-go credit assignment further aligns token updates with the sequence-level objective while retaining the simplicity of OPSD. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that $β$-OPSD consistently outperforms vanilla OPSD, improving optimization stability and downstream reasoning performance. Our results provide a principled route from self-distillation to policy optimization and back without sacrificing the efficiency that makes OPSD practical.

</details>


### [364] [KAISEN: Reproducible Subgroup Fairness Auditing for Clinical Risk Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28608)
*Sparsh Roy,Samuel Girmachew,Nishita Chavan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KAISEN is a five-phase audit pipeline for clinical risk models that stress-tests each component — subgroup stratification, disparity measurement, mechanism diagnostics, post-hoc mitigation, and drift monitoring — on a synthetic benchmark of 16 disease tasks and 15 social-determinant axes, revealing that significance thresholds, Platt scaling, proxy-based diagnostics, and CUSUM monitoring all exhibit critical failure modes that undermine audit trustworthiness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical risk models exhibit systematic subgroup disparities, and audit pipelines meant to detect and mitigate these disparities are rarely stress-tested to the point of failure. It is unclear which audit components can be trusted and under what conditions, creating a risk that flawed audits provide false confidence.

Method: The authors present KAISEN, a five-phase audit pipeline: (1) subgroup stratification, (2) disparity measurement via equalized-odds difference (EOD), (3) mechanism diagnostics to classify whether disparities arise from model-driven vs. proxy-label sources, (4) post-hoc mitigation using per-group threshold optimization and Platt scaling, and (5) drift monitoring via CUSUM. Each phase is stress-tested on a synthetic benchmark spanning 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes from Healthy People 2030, and three prespecified intersections, with known ground truth throughout.

Result: Four key findings: (i) Statistical significance tracks EOD only after standardizing by each axis's minimum detectable effect (rho 0.56 → 0.78). (ii) Per-group threshold optimization consistently reduces EOD (48/48 runs), but Platt scaling performs no better than chance (19/48 improved), suggesting variance reporting is essential. (iii) The mechanism diagnostic perfectly classifies 144 controlled cases but fails on all 48 model-driven cases under proxy misspecification, with no failure signal. (iv) CUSUM false alarms and missed shifts are driven by cohort realization rather than disease, making threshold transfer across cohorts unreliable.

Conclusion: Each audit component exhibits specific, reproducible failure modes that undermine trust. Significance must account for detectable effect floors, Platt scaling's variance matters more than its mean, proxy-based diagnostics can fail silently, and CUSUM thresholds do not transfer across cohorts. All results are synthetic and do not establish clinical validity; code and artifacts are released.

Abstract: Clinical risk models routinely achieve strong aggregate performance while producing materially different error rates across patient subgroups. Audit pipelines have been proposed to catch this, but their components are rarely stress-tested, so it is unclear which parts of an audit can be trusted and under what conditions. We present KAISEN, a five-phase audit pipeline covering subgroup stratification, disparity measurement, mechanism diagnostics, post-hoc mitigation, and drift monitoring, evaluated to the point of failure on a synthetic benchmark of 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes from Healthy People 2030, and three prespecified intersections. Four findings follow. (i) Significance tracks each axis's gap against its own minimum detectable effect: rank correlation between significance count and raw equalized-odds difference (EOD) across the 15 axes is rho = 0.56, rising to rho = 0.78 once EOD is standardized by that floor. (ii) Per-group threshold optimization reduces EOD in 48 of 48 held-out runs (paired delta = -0.285, 95% CI [-0.313, -0.252]), while group-wise Platt scaling -- the better calibrator -- behaves as a coin flip on EOD (19 of 48 runs improved, 95% CI [0.26, 0.55]) with mean effect near zero, so what an audit should report is the variance, not the average. (iii) The mechanism diagnostic classifies 144 of 144 controlled cases correctly but recovers none of 48 model-driven cases under proxy misspecification, with no signal that it failed. (iv) CUSUM failures and false alarms track cohort realization far more than disease: at the reference threshold, all 27 false alarms and 7 of 8 missed shifts come from different seeds (chi-squared p = 0.002), so a threshold tuned on one cohort fails to transfer. All results are synthetic with known ground truth and do not establish clinical validity. Code, artifacts, and scripts reproducing every number are released.

</details>


<div id='cs.IR'></div>

# cs.IR [[Back]](#toc)

### [365] [OneShot: Index-in-Ranking with Neural Scoring for Large-Scale Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27475)
*Ziwei Li,Shuyao Li,Xufeng Cai,Xue Zou,Yiming Ma,Huiting Lu,Wujie Yan,Zhichen Zhao,Yang Lu,Zhe Wang,Rui Luo,Zhengyu Su,Dan Zhang,Ji Liu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: OneShot proposes an end-to-end retrieval framework that jointly learns index structure and ranking objectives, resolving the traditional misalignment between ranking accuracy and indexing efficiency. Deployed in Instagram's recommendation system, it achieves 20% recall gains and 10x efficiency improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In large-scale retrieval, ranking accuracy (alignment between predictions and user behavior) and indexing efficiency (structural grouping for fast search) are fundamentally misaligned objectives. Existing systems separate these concerns, limiting expressiveness—particularly the pervasive dot-product bottleneck that constrains interaction modeling at retrieval scale.

Method: OneShot is an end-to-end, in-model index learning framework that jointly optimizes index construction and ranking objectives within a single holistic architecture. It moves beyond the dot-product bottleneck by scaling neural scoring with richer interaction modeling, natively aligning the learned index structure with the ranking loss.

Result: Fully deployed in Instagram's short-video recommendation system, OneShot drove significant improvements in daily user sessions, engagement, and time-spent. It achieved a 20% recall gain at operational ranking volume and a 10x efficiency improvement at equivalent recall levels.

Conclusion: OneShot demonstrates that jointly learning the retrieval index and ranking objectives resolves a fundamental structural tension in modern recommendation systems, enabling both higher recall and faster search at billion-scale industrial deployment.

Abstract: In modern recommendation systems, retrieval serves as a primary stage responsible for filtering billions of candidate items down to thousands prior to refined ranking. To make this massive search effective and efficient, the system relies on ranking accuracy and indexing efficiency. However, these two objectives are traditionally misaligned: while the former optimizes for the alignment between ranking predictions and user behavior, the latter optimizes for a structural grouping of item representations which enables fast search among billions of candidates. Thus, despite extensive efforts to scale up interaction modeling for retrieval, they remain fundamentally limited by the structural misalignment between the ranking objectives and the proximity-learned index. In this work, we address this long-standing dichotomy by proposing a new holistic retrieval framework, OneShot. It is an end-to-end, in-model index learning framework that natively aligns index learning with ranking objectives. Using this joint learning as a structural foundation, OneShot pushes the boundaries of retrieval expressiveness by scaling interaction modeling with neural scoring beyond the persistent dot-product bottleneck. OneShot is fully deployed in Instagram's industrial short-video recommendation system, driving significant wins in user daily sessions, engagement, and time-spent. Additionally, OneShot achieves a $20\%$ recall gain at the operational ranking volume and a 10x efficiency improvement at an equivalent recall level.

</details>


### [366] [Hierarchical Reranking for Scalable Financial RAG System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27523)
*Joohyun Lee,Sungwoo Hong*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper proposes Hierarchical Reranker, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework optimized for financial document analysis. It introduces pre-retrieval optimization, a two-stage ranking architecture, and long-context management to handle hybrid text-table structures at scale. The system achieved NDCG@20 of 0.7918 across FinQA, FinanceBench, and ConvFinQA benchmarks and placed second in the ACM-ICAIF '24 FinanceRAG Challenge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RAG systems struggle with the unique demands of financial documents — specifically hybrid text-table structures (e.g., 10-K filings, tabular disclosures) and the massive scale of these datasets. Manual analysis requires expert reasoning and extensive time, motivating an automated, domain-optimized RAG pipeline that can reliably process such data.

Method: The Hierarchical Reranker framework comprises three integrated components: (1) Pre-Retrieval Optimization — query normalization, keyword expansion, and table transformation to enhance query clarity and search efficiency; (2) Hierarchical Reranker Architecture — a two-stage ranking mechanism improving retrieval precision; (3) Long-Context Management — adaptive input partitioning and fusion to preserve reasoning accuracy under extensive document contexts.

Result: The system achieved an NDCG@20 score of 0.7918 and demonstrated superior factual consistency across FinQA, FinanceBench, and ConvFinQA benchmarks. It secured second place in the ACM-ICAIF '24 FinanceRAG Challenge, validating robustness.

Conclusion: The work delivers a deployable, domain-optimized RAG pipeline that enhances accuracy and scalability in financial reasoning, with potential applications in automated audit reporting and quantitative investment analysis. Source code will be open-sourced upon acceptance.

Abstract: Analyzing financial documents such as 10-K filings, tabular disclosures, and macroeconomic reports demands expert reasoning and extensive time. However, existing Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems often struggle to process hybrid text-table structures or the massive scale of financial documents. To address these challenges, we propose Hierarchical Reranker, a RAG framework designed to improve retrieval performance and generative reliability across large-scale financial datasets. The system integrates three key innovations: Pre-Retrieval Optimization, enhancing query clarity and search efficiency through normalization, keyword expansion, and table transformation; Hierarchical Reranker Architecture, improving retrieval precision through a two-stage ranking mechanism; and Long-Context Management, preserving reasoning accuracy through adaptive input partitioning and fusion under extensive contexts. Across multiple benchmarks, including FinQA, FinanceBench, and ConvFinQA, the proposed system achieved an NDCG@20 score of 0.7918 and demonstrated superior factual consistency. Its robustness was further validated by achieving second place in the ACM-ICAIF '24 FinanceRAG Challenge. This work presents a deployable, domain-optimized RAG pipeline that enhances both the accuracy and scalability of financial reasoning, paving the way for automated audit reporting and quantitative investment analysis. The source code will be made publicly available on GitHub upon acceptance.

</details>


### [367] [Heterogeneous Ranking in Industrial-Scale Recommender Systems: A Case Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27577)
*Di Bai,Jintao Liu,Zhenwei Tang,Peifan Wu,Nada Al-Thawr,Luoshu Wang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: HA-MoE introduces a heterogeneity-adaptive multi-gate mixture-of-experts architecture for unified ranking in heterogeneous content feeds (Google Discover), paired with LENS, a lightweight observability framework for diagnosing expert specialization, and evaluated using a novel Dual-Level AUC metric. Offline and online A/B tests confirm consistent gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unified recommendation feeds like Google Discover mix diverse content types (web articles, short/long videos, UGC) from the open web, each with distinct feature densities and user interaction patterns. Standard unified ranking models suffer from negative transfer and majority bias, making it difficult to sustain high performance across all content segments simultaneously.

Method: HA-MoE (Heterogeneity-Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts) integrates explicit heterogeneity context (content type signals) into both gating networks and expert representations, enabling specialized expert routing without heavy operational cost. LENS (Lightweight Observability Framework) tracks expert specialization and functional heterogeneity across retraining. Evaluation uses DL-AUC (Dual-Level AUC), combining global ranking performance with cross-segment ranking correctness.

Result: Offline evaluation on large-scale industrial data shows consistent improvement over baselines. Online A/B testing demonstrates significant gains in feed activity and exploration metrics, validating the method for industrial-scale heterogeneous feed ranking.

Conclusion: HA-MoE effectively addresses heterogeneity in unified recommendation feeds through content-type-aware expert specialization. Combined with LENS observability and DL-AUC evaluation, the framework provides a practical, deployable solution for industrial multi-task ranking under content diversity.

Abstract: Heterogeneous recommendation feeds present complex challenges that extend beyond those found in highly homogeneous environments (e.g., music-only or video-only closed-ecosystem platforms). In Google Discover, a unified feed integrates diverse content sourced from the decentralized open web, including web articles, long-form and short-form videos, user-generated content (UGC), and beyond. Different content types exhibit distinct feature densities and user interaction patterns. Building a unified ranking model that sustains high performance across such heterogeneity, while avoiding negative transfer or majority bias, remains a significant industrial challenge.
  This paper presents an end-to-end case study on the industrial-scale multi-task ranking of heterogeneous feeds, grounded in real-world deployment. We introduce HA-MoE, a heterogeneity-adaptive multi-gated mixture-of-experts architecture that incorporates explicit heterogeneity context into both gating networks and expert representations. This approach enables effective specialization without significantly increasing operational overhead. To support reliable deployment, we introduce LENS, a lightweight observability framework that provides interpretable diagnostics of expert specialization and tracks this functional heterogeneity across continuous retraining. We evaluate our method using Dual-Level AUC (DL-AUC), a heterogeneity-aware evaluation metric that combines global ranking performance with cross-segment ranking correctness. Offline evaluations on a large-scale industrial dataset demonstrate consistent improvements over baseline models. Furthermore, online A/B testing confirms gains in feed activity and exploration metrics. Together, offline and online results validate the effectiveness of our approach for managing heterogeneity in industrial-scale recommender systems.

</details>


### [368] [An Exploration Graph with Continuous Refinement for Efficient Multimedia Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27623)
*Nico Hezel,Kai Uwe Barthel,Konstantin Schall,Klaus Jung*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper introduces crEG (continuous refining Exploration Graph), a novel graph-based ANNS method that enables rapid construction of compact exploration graphs with competitive search performance, plus an optional edge optimization algorithm. It uniquely guarantees undirected graphs with even degrees and continuous connectivity, and highlights the under-explored problem of "exploratory search" where queries are part of the database, showing that high ANNS efficiency does not guarantee good exploratory search performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph-based ANNS methods suffer from slow construction speeds or high memory requirements. Furthermore, the problem of "exploratory search" — where the query itself belongs to the database (crucial for recommendation and exploration systems) — has been largely overlooked, and there is no guarantee that ANNS-optimized methods perform well in this setting.

Method: The authors propose crEG, a continuous refining exploration graph construction algorithm that produces undirected graphs with even degrees and guarantees connectivity at all times. An optional edge optimization algorithm further improves effectiveness. The method is specifically designed for both standard ANNS and exploratory search scenarios.

Result: Experiments show that crEG achieves state-of-the-art search performance with rapid construction. Critically, the results reveal that high efficiency in standard ANNS does not necessarily translate to good performance in exploratory search, validating the need for specialized approaches like crEG.

Conclusion: crEG offers a fast, memory-efficient graph construction method with guaranteed connectivity, making it well-suited for both traditional ANNS and the practically important but under-studied exploratory search paradigm. The work underscores that exploratory search merits distinct consideration beyond standard ANNS benchmarks.

Abstract: As datasets and the dimensionality of feature vectors continue to grow, Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) in large multimedia databases becomes increasingly relevant. Graph-based approaches have demonstrated to offer the best trade-off between retrieval precision and search time. Despite their ability to deliver search times several orders of magnitude faster than exact search techniques, existing methods suffer from slow constructions speeds or high memory requirements. This paper presents a "continuous refining Exploration Graph" (crEG), a novel approach for rapidly constructing a compact exploration graph with state-of-the-art search performance. Additionally, it provides the ability to enhance its effectiveness even further through an optional edge optimization algorithm. Both algorithms are specifically designed to produce and operate on undirected graphs with even degrees and guarantee graph connectivity at any time, a property particularly valuable for "exploratory search", where the query is part of the database elements. Although such queries provide an advantageous starting point for graph search algorithms, they have been rarely considered in the context of ANNS, yet are crucial for recommendation and exploration systems. Our experiments demonstrate high efficiency in ANNS does not necessarily translate to a good performance in "exploratory search".

</details>


### [369] [Dynamic Exploration Graph: A Novel Approach for Efficient Nearest Neighbor Search in Evolving Multimedia Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27640)
*Nico Hezel,Kai Uwe Barthel,Bruno Schilling,Konstantin Schall,Klaus Jung*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper introduces Dynamic Exploration Graph (DEG), a graph-based ANNS algorithm that extends the Exploration Graph to support dynamic datasets via a connectivity-guaranteeing vertex deletion algorithm and a distribution-agnostic graph expansion method, achieving state-of-the-art performance in both streaming and static scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Graph-based ANNS algorithms excel on static datasets but struggle with dynamic datasets where points are continuously added or removed. Existing solutions lack robust mechanisms for maintaining graph connectivity and balanced structure under continuous data alterations.

Method: DEG extends the continuous refining Exploration Graph with two core innovations: (1) a novel vertex deletion algorithm that guarantees graph connectivity upon node removal, and (2) a data distribution-agnostic method for graph expansion that maintains structural balance.
